The game's engine is impressive because the game can fill so many enemies on the screen, it feels as if you're fighting hundreds of foes at once. It's gonna get messy, so bring alot of ammo!

I'll admit that I bounced off this game pretty hard on my first try. I kind of had a fundamental misunderstanding going in and treated it just as a typical rougelike. I died a lot then gave up. After a break I went and read a beginners guide and fared much better on my next foray.
While the game definitely has rogue like elements, it's scope is a lot broader than that. Though combat happens in real time the game is essentially turn based, with each turn being deliniated by the opening of a new door. Squad management and placement is essential, as is resource management.
The goal is to take the generator, a diamond shaped device, from the beginning point to the exit. You begin with two squad members, though you can recruit up to four as the game progresses. I  recommend picking someone fast and someone tough as your starting line up. Leave the tough to protect the generator and use the speedy character to explore. Each level is procedurely generated the level map is hidden, apart from the starting room. Every time you open a door, the area beyond will reveal and there is a good chance monsters will spawn in some unlit rooms. Once monsters spawn you are going to play the next section in real time. The monsters will go straight for the generator and attack it, so this is why you need your tough there to defend it. If the generator is destroyed it is game over. The best bet is to use speedy as a mobile force to take out monsters nearby, but if the creatures reach the generator, fall back and help the tough defend. Once you have fought off the wave of monsters you are free to micro manage until you open the next door and the next wave begins.
The game has several resources you will need to survive. Firstly,  Dust, which you use to power rooms. Dust is finite and there is a chance you will get more every time you open a door. It's important to remember that monsters can't spawn in lit rooms, so what rooms you keep lit and which remain dark is an important strategy. You will never have enough dust to keep all the rooms lit. Also lit rooms have to be connected back to the starting point by a line of lit rooms, you can't have a hole in the line. In each room there can be several slots in the floor, small ones for turrets and support devices, and large ones for resources. So long as a room is lit, any devices you build in these slots will be powered and functional. Which brings us to the next resource, industry. Industry is used to build devices in rooms. You start with a small amount but can build production devices in the large floor slots. Every time a door is opened, production devices will produce new resources. The next resource is food, you use this to heal your heroes and to level them up. As with industry, you can build food production devices in large floor slots. The final resource is research, you use this to research new devices at the research crystals that can be found on each level. There are a tonne of research options avaliable from making better turrets to making better resource production devices. To add a further kink, some characters have a skill that allow them to increase the output of resource production devices if they are left in the room with them. As the game goes on and you rectuit your squad up to four, leaving squad members to bump up resources is important to keep up with production demands.
Each character is unique, with their own skill set and personality. You level them up using food and each level adds to their stats and often gives new abilities. Deciding who to level up and when is an important consideration, what new skills are they going to bring to the table, and what new skills are going to be a priority? Keep in mind, some characters aren't going to get along. I won't say too much so as not to spoil things, but on the lift between levels, pay attention to the chatter. Each character also has three inventory slots that you can put items in. What can be equipped depends on the character and each character has a specific type of weapon they can use as well as two other slots than can be equipped with armour and utility items. Items will drop randomly in combat at times or they can be found in rooms or purchased from the occasional merchant. There is a kind of group inventory as well where non equipped stuff is stored. The space in this is limited and at times you are going to lose stuff when you go from one level to the next so keep an eye on it and make sure you are keeping the most valuable loot.
Once you have found the exit, it's time to go. If you haven't fully explored the level you might want to finish the rest of the rooms first, but this is very much a risk and reward thing, especially as you get deeper into the dungeon. Sure, you might find some loot, but you will also have to fight waves of monsters each time you open a door. It's a fine balancing act. Once you are ready, get your fastest character and pick up the generator. You are going to have to carry it to the exit and carrying it slows your movement. You didn't think this was going to be easy, right? As soon as you pick up the generator there is a mass monster spawn in unlit rooms. You are going to be relentlessly attacked as you trudge the generator to the exit. What rooms you have lit here, where your squad is placed, what devices you have built in the lit sections leading to the exit, all of this is going to be key to survivng the gauntlet. Once you hit the exit you can push the lift button, breathe a sigh of relief and head for the next level. Some interesting lift chatter will occur. Pay attention.
And then we are on the next level. Things will be tougher, new monsters will spawn and the risk reward scale will tilt that little bit more to the risk side.
Dungeon of the Endless is a fantastic game and I can't recommend it enough. It mixes roguelike elements with squad tactics and resource management in a way I haven't really seen before. I think that is probably why I failed so bad on my first run. Once you wrap your head around what the game requires though, its an amazingly rewarding experience.
9 out of 10. Highly recommended!

In a world where dota and league of legends have firmly planted their flag in the moba genre, you would either have to be a revolutionary game designer or a complete idiot to try to compete with them.
In this case, Guardians of Middle-earth and their respective no-name developer team falls flat on its face in the latter category. The only way I could rationalize the developer's strategy for releasing this game is that this game was designed for five year olds. Gold mechanic too hard? Ok we removed it. Dota's 25 level cap too hard? LoL's 18? Ok we made it 14. Mana management too difficult? We got rid of that too.
In this dumbed down world, you max out your level in about ten minutes, but with no gold, you will never get an edge on your opponent. In an hour, you will be sitting there, everyone maxed at 14, praying something happens. In this joke of a world where some random hobbit can 1v1 the lord of Mordor himself, the biggest enemy to both teams is boredom.
I highly suspect that there's a payment scheme of somewhat that I would balk at, but honestly, if you can't retain a player for ten minutes, then whatever crafty method you devised for generating is the least of your problems.
The single redeeming factor of the game was the portraits of the characters in character selection. They were very artful, and I could only pray the graphic designers weren't tortured with seeing what mangled sprites their art was attached to.
Do not buy this game, do not recommend this game, do not talk about this game. It was free, and I still feel cheated for the time I spent playing it. I hope that whoever thought of this game still has an in with the production team of lord of the rings, because he is not going to make it as a video game developer.

The game is a roguelike tower defense/strategy game where opening doors to rooms is a "turn" where you collect resources and spawn monsters, and the progression of the game includes finding and using new characters to unlock them, trying out different structures to find what works best for you, and unlocking new "pods" which have varying effects on the game.
There are two difficulties: Easy and Too Easy. Dont let it fool you... [at least for me] Easy is actually Hard and Too Easy is more like Normal. The game is very challenging.
Despite the Difficulty, the game is a lot of fun and has a lot of replayability. I highly recommend it especially on sale or if you like roguelikes.
Continue reading for helpful info to get started with the game.
CHARACTER TYPE RUNDOWN:
Parties start with 2 characters and can have up to 4 (which you can find in the dungeon).
There are essentially 3 types of characters:
-Combat characters: High Health and/or Damage stats and are built for killing monsters whether it be defending your structures or weaker characters.
-Runner characters: High Speed stat and usually low Health. these guys are good for opening doors and running back to the safety of your structures. Some have high Damage as well but can easily die so you have to be careful.
-Operator characters: High Wit and usually low Health and/or low Damage. These guys are meant for their utility and sitting in safe areas operating your resource structures for extra resources. These guys also need the most protection.
OTHER TIPS:
-Early levels explore every room to collect as many resources and items as you can when the monsters are easy. Late levels find the exit ASAP... monsters in late levels get very strong.
-For resources structures: Early levels Industry>food>science. Later game food>industry>science.
-Level up "Operator characters" to the level that they get Operate(usually level 3 or 4) ASAP. It gets you a huge boost in resources by having them Operate your resource structures.
-Once you get an operator character leveled up to operate, try to level up one of your combat characters to max.
-Avoid having more than 3-4 unpowered rooms in one spot. This can cause monsters waves to all spawn together in a massive swarm that can overwhelm and kill your characters.
-For the easiest runs start with 1 Combat and 1 Operator.
-Best Party compositions: 2 Combat and 2 Operators or 1 Combat, 1 Runner, 2 Operators.

This is my second review of this game. This time is positive as I deleted my negative review.
So first off, the game looks incredible. The graphics are not as realistic as in some of the modern AAA titles, but are well made it their own way and are a pleasure to look at.
I have only played the story mode.
The pros:
- great story. The story is rich and your choices do matter. Normally I skip all the conversational cutscenes, but this ones made me watch and listen to every sinlge one,
- game is well made. I haven't encountered many bugs, and the ones I did, were minor and didn't have an effect on the game,
- variability. You can play the game however you feel like and do the quest in your own time,
- it isn't short. The game (story mode) will provide tens of hours of fun,
- and MOST importatnt: the devs listen. I gave this game a negative review because of the saving system in story mode, which allowed only 2 saves. One after sleeping and one was a checkpoint save. If you were trapped in 2 bad saves, you had to restart the whole chapter. So the devs listened, fixed the save system in a month and now it works perfectly. You have 25 save slots (synced with steam cloud) and you can save whenever you fell like it. This makes story mode awesome now.
The so-so:
- shooting. Its a bit annoying as the sway feels weird and the shots are sometimes more luck then anything else. I recommend you save game, before taking any shots,
- the chores, one of the missions is clolecting berries, fishing, repairing clothes and hunting. It feels more like a chore than a real quest.
The con: (POTENTIAL SPOILERS!)
- the only ''major'' bug was with the Jeremiah's last quest. The locations of the 'thing' you were looking for weren't marked on the map. Nonetheless it was pretty easy to find it.
Overall a great gaming experience that I would recommend to everyone. In few words, the game is like a smaller Skyrim or Fallout type of game, with the emphasis on survival aspect and not the killing aspect.
It's as haunting and difficult and irritating as it is beautiful, mysterious and loveable. A truly remarkable and original masterpiece!

404 is a fun, albeit short game with a big problem in the engine department.
First off, the bad: The game apparently uses unreal engine 4, which according to a developer in the forums means this will not work great on laptops, for whatever reason. That is why I have given this a negative rating. If in a future update they fix this, then it will be a great game, but until then, it is pretty much unplayable except at the lowest graphics settings. If you have a desktop, then there may be fewer problems for you.
That aside, the gameplay in this game is pretty fun. It has the minimalitic stylings of a game with mirrors edge, and the mechanics similar to spraying orange gel everywhere from portal 2. Only you have the added challenge of a power (bandwidth) meter that you need to keep filled in order to continue.
Given that this game is free to play, I can't gripe about the short playtime, and the level design in this game is pretty good, but not very difficult to master. The electronic music might not be to everyone's tastes, but I liked it. The story is pretty non-existent except for the cutscenes at the beginning and end, but the entire game is meant as a metaphor for internet neutrality. I'm not sure if it would convey that too well to someone who wasn't already in the know about such things, but it was fairly well executed nonetheless.
If you've got a desktop and an hour or so to spare, then definitely give this game a try, it is a fairly fun "runner" game.

This game is silly fun, yet way deeper than it might appear at first blush. Not only can your character be upgraded via implants and equipment, but weapons can be upgraded too. Single player story and stand-alone missions that can also be done via co-op are also joyful. Seriously, this is a delightful little game.

To preface: This is not a complete game. It was wrapped up to technically be finished, but it isn't even close to complete due to not having an ending and Class B bugs that cripple the bulk of PC users while their Android version is performing well. (quick score: 7/10 Game engine makes it almost unplayable in how frustrating it is to deal with, but a good game if fixed)
Pros:
- The RPG elements of purchasing upgrades for guns and melee weapons were well done. They are roughly the same for each weapon (Damage, Accuracy, Sockets, Clip Size for guns, and reload speed for guns) with negatives for melee weapons. The socket upgrades for gear as well as weapons helped some of the lackluster items have a use.
- It was nice seeing more scenarios for generic missions that don't relate to repeating the story missions for items or money.
- The different mini-games  were enjoyable and streamlined compared to the first game
- The story was passable. I wasn't annoyed by the progression, nor with the voice acting. The plot twists were the only questionable pieces of the game, which I'll cover in the Con section as spoiler free as possible.
- I liked the variety in upgrades for character abilities, though most  aren't useful in the game since only two can be equipped, leaving Bullet Time and whatever else you like to be in constant use during fights.
Cons:
- The game isn't 20+ hours of gameplay. It is 7 hours with up to 8 hours of grinding generic missions for XP and gear to help complete story missions.
- The ending doesn't even setup for a cliff-hanger. It idles out of gas half way up the cliff by fighting a bad guy's sidekick and stopping the game's story right there. (and even then, it is quite clear in the story, they both aren't bad guys at all)
- The melee weapons get two upgrades when they could have supplemented melee with improved attack speed as an upgrade option amongst other melee focused upgrades. Was a missed opportunity.
- Only two mission varieties: kill stuff, and rotate valve to stop gas from killing you. Some other options like King Of The Hill or Capture The Flag would have worked well and gave some other options for the side missions.
- Almost all of the NPCs stop progressing in their story after about mission 6. When talking to a few of them, they gave bits and pieces of what they did on the ship as well as their current motivations and almost suddenly, stops for the rest of the game. Clearly was rushed.
- The graphic engine is beyond broken. The system specs on the store page are not accurate and still are absurd considering this is an Android game built in Unity and ported to PC. My computer is above the minimum specs and gets 100-115 frames in the Hub and during every encounter drops to 45 to spurt back up to 100, regardless of my video settings. I have it at 800x600 and lowest video settings with shaders off and it still does that, but it is a little more consistent. When I played with the default settings, I was getting 4 frames a second during fights with more than 8 zombies. It makes the game unplayable if you want to not be frustrated during most of the game.
- The frame stuttering caused by the game engine makes using melee weapons scary in their own right.
- There is no way to circumvent fighting the invisible foes. Most one can do is engage Bullet Time when they appear or hopefully hit them as they rush you. It is the most annoying part of the game and I hate it every time they show up. They aren't challenging.
-----------------------
Overall Verdict: 7/10 would not recommend to buy due to game engine making it almost unplayable. The rest of the game itself is a decent experience I would recommend for about $10.

I was looking for coop game in FPS genre. This one looked promising.
I finished the game (so it is playable) but in general, I find it very unpolished, maiming the good general ideas with pitiful realization. I score this game as 4/10 only. See below why.
Strenghts:
1. stable coop, good coop game modes
2. good base environment (onboard a spaceship), good basic game idea (rpg elements, loot system)
Weaknesses:
1. graphic engine is extremely bad (i have a good medium rig, e.g. playing fallout 4 on ultra) yet it lagged extremely even on the lowest setting (even on dx9 mode), having FPS like 2-5 on bigger battles...really why not using an existing licensable engine (e.g. unreal) if you do not know how to make a good one...? On the top of it, it does not look that good at all...
2. skill tree is boring and badly realized, some skills are completely unusable, others are godlike. Passives have way too little effect. You can unlock 15-20 skills but can slot only 2... what is the purpose?
3. character selection has no meaning hence every character can use any weapon and skills do not matter that much (e.g. around lvl10 a peacemaker shot does 5-6k damage on LARGE range, a better aoe skill around 500 in close proximity...)
4. campaign story is boring, meaningless and lacks imagination.
5. weapon characteristics sometimes seem absurd. e.g. a lvl 10 purple weapon damaging x, on lvl 12 I find another purple damaging 6x ?
6. some weapons are completely unusable (e.g. plasma or laser) other just destroy everything (crossbow or peacemeaker or vulcan minigun). At the end we tried weapons to fight boredom (do we survive with these?) not because they are fun or better.
7. enemies are dumb and are not challenging at all, not even bosses. Their danger in their huge numbers, but not because they cannot be blown up with a single shot from e.g. a crossbow but because the game LAGS down to FPS 1 so your screen freezes and you cannot shoot... Main Boss at end of campaign was defeated using the following "tactics": Equinox (Jane character) skill popped up (invulnerability), 25k damage melee MJOLNR equipped, 6-8 hits on the head (skill expired), run away, wait until dumb boss finds the route to my character, pop shield egain, rinse and repeat 2 more times...wow what a hero I am.
Really sorry for this guys, I know I will not be popular, but I also beleive that you learn from mistakes not from admiration.

It's a great looking game, and it works best with an Xbox compatible controller (I used an FC30 Pro) but it also worked with touchscreen controls, though it was a lot easier to use the controller.

Once I started picking up the strategies of how to manage exploring and expanding while still protecting my core I really started to get into it and found it quite addictive. However, after playing for about 24 hours and still not being able to beat the game on the most difficult setting offered when you start a new game (that's
) I was starting to get pretty tired of going over the same ground and not having much to show for it; and I wasn't about to take the difficulty down to

Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power is a third part to a so-far trilogy of a breathtaking puzzle/role-playing game where you take three different roles from a nimble archer, a big husky warrior, and an intelligent wizard. This game takes you many places in a fictional and fantastical world, having the player solve mysteries and puzzles alike, while also running into enemies and other creatures getting in your way, or possibly going for the same goal! I like the robust and ease of changing characters in gameplay in order to combat or adapt to certain situations like using the warrior to break a bridge down, having the wizard use his awesome telekinetic powers to destroy walls, or using the flexible and feline-like archer to swing across vast gaps and through the environments in order to complete their tasks! I recommend this game whole-heartedly!
- 8 / 10

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game.
Trine 3 is still in early access, so the content will be limited. This is the first thing I want people to understand.
The game takes what the Trine series have already established, creative puzzles and level design, gorgeous graphics, and entertaining co-op gameplay, and then add in a new dimension, more specifically, the third dimension. Unlike it's predecessors, in Trine 3 you can move in and out of the background on all X, Y, and Z axis.
The additional dimension will evoke new  puzzle elements and a new way to think about puzzling and platforming. It's really hard to say if this is to the serie's benefit or detriment at this point simply because there's not enough of the game to really judge that quite yet. As mentioned before, Trine 3 is in early access, and as of this impression (v0.04 Build 2882) there's only the first 2 chapters, 2 challenge levels, and a sandbox map. There's only about 1.5 hours of gameplay, and because of the lack of content at the moment, it's very difficult to judge if the new dimension adds, or detract from the classic formula.
What I can say from the brief amount of gameplay I've experienced, is that the presentation and aesthetics is top shelf quality, the controls feel responsive, the puzzles (so far) are satisfying with out being too frustrating, and it was a joy to play. I'd just like to see a lot more of it.
For fans of the Trine series, Trine 3 seem to be shaping up to be of a great quality, but once again, be aware there is VERY limited amount of content so far. The game also suffers from some optimization issues as well, but overall it's on the right path.
$20 might be asking for a little much for what's currently available, but I would suggest at the very least, adding this to your watch list, and check it out again when it's in it's final release. It definitely is showing a lot of promise.
Pros:
- Gorgeous aesthetics
- Easy to learn
- Creative puzzles and level design
Cons:
- Not enough content currently (v0.04 Build 2882)
- Needs optimization

I loved the first two titles in the series, and I love the visuals of the third game, but gameplay-wise...it feels like an almost all-around downgrade to me right now. You can't grapple entire surfaces anymore, only specific spots on surfaces, can't move whole platforms with the wizard (not sure yet if blessing or curse), nor draw crates or beams, they are created when you press a button, etc. Right now the click-detection is seriously buggy, physics range from acceptable to horrendous, game-mechanics are communicated poorly (which is a big problem considering many of them are counter-intuitive) and the game is seriously unfinished. On top of all of that, the game suffers the typical shortfalls of a 3D platformer, such as impossible-to-gauge distances and random deaths from leaps of faith.
Could it be really good once finished? Absolutely, and I hope it will be. Would I recommend you buy it now? Absolutely not.
I will update my review in a while when the progress is a bit further along.
EDIT/UPDATE:
I just replayed the first levels (and the new levels they added), and they fixed many of the issues I had previously, and added cool new mechanics (new to Trine as a series) to the recently-added levels. I feel like now that there's over an hour of fun gameplay here, I can change my recommendation to "yes", they're hard at work and it shows.
EDIT/UPDATE 2:
I can't believe they just released....the game is super-short and still suffers from many of the complaints I previously brought up. Can not recommend at full price.

Assassin's Creed Syndicate, the game everyone was afraid to buy because of the god-awful game known as AC Unity... and after it came out 2 years ago... people still didn't like it, in fact people started to say the AC franchise was dead after it came out (thankfully Origins saved that) but lets see why exactly people hated it so much.
The story is about Jacob and Evie Frye, two assassins who go to London to stop Crawford Starrick from oppressing the people of London with gangs and child labour. They meet an Indian Assassin called Henry Green, who takes Evie to the Kenway mansion where they find out that Edward had found an artifact during his days as an Assassin called 'The Shroud of Eden' which Crawford Starrick is also looking for. That makes me wonder... why didn't we just get another game about Edward finding it... making it useful to the series? instead of a pointless game like Unity or Rogue? this plot happens all because of Edward and there's no real lead up to it so... okay then. Using the key and map that Edward left, Evie finds the shroud, but loses it to a Templar called Lucy Thorne. Some random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ happens, you kill people, start a gang, meet a dog called Desmond (haha funny) and then at some point Ubisoft decide to stop the story and tell you to liberate certain areas of London before proceeding with the story. What a♥♥♥♥♥♥way to increase game time. In AC Brotherhood did you have to take town all the Borgia towers before proceeding with the story? no. In AC4 were you stopped to be told to take down all the forts and legendary ships before going into the Observatory? no. So why do it here? these should be optional. You don't have to take them all down but its bloody annoying anyway. It slows down the game and its just boring. After doing this you'll finally face off Starrick, kill him and then the game ends. There's a lot of issues with this story, while I do like how its not trying to be too serious like Unity and just have a simple story, its too simple. Who are Evie and Jacob? whats their backstory? who's Starrick? in the intro Henry Green describes him as "ruthless as Reginald Birch" the guy who killed Edward Kenway and honestly, I don't see that. In fact during the entire game you barely see him, he's in a couple of cutscenes sitting behind a desk. Whoop-de-doo. Honestly they try to make him out as this huge evil villain but he's just not, he's not interesting, the Frye twins aren't interesting, nothing is. The story is just forgettable, nothing that pisses me off like Unity did, but just forgettable.
The gameplay, I have a serious issue with and I know so many others did too. Why the actual ♥♥♥♥ do you have a GRAPPLING GUN like this isn't Batman Arkham City, we don't need to go around doing that. Remember the good old days of climbing up huge towers as Altair, Ezio, Connor, Edward and all those guys? yeah those days are gone. Welcome to 'Batman Arkham City: Victorian London edition'. There's seriously no need to parkour anymore in this game. Its not like its optional either, the city is built for you to grapple across. That's another thing, the city is boring and dull, I mean maybe thats because I live in England so I don't find it interesting but even then, its just not fun at all. Its more lively than AC Unity's cities. Thats for sure, but its nowhere near as good as Firenze or Rome or the West Indies. Also the combat is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ its not unfair like in AC Unity but they decided to try out a hack 'n slash type of combat. This isn't Samurai Warriors, this is Assassin's Creed. I want to just counter and kill, not mash the X button to kill someone. Thankfully almost every problem in AC Syndicate is fixed in Origins.
The PC port... well I have a 1080ti, i7 6700 and 32gb ram and it runs at like 90fps... which isn't really the best considering that AC Origins runs with like 30-40 higher frames than that. This was back when Ubisoft wanted you to have the best♥♥♥♥♥♥possible to run it well.
Also the music is forgettable in this game too. A lot of violins, which does fit the Victorian era but its nothing catchy and every track sounds the same, also they re-used Ezio's theme again... obviously...
With forgettable characters, a mediocre and forgettable story, music that isn't really good, this AC game just sucks, its not fun, its not bad either. Its just sort of there, if there's a game like AC Syndicate that I could recommend, its the Batman Arkham games... or actually y'know what? just get a different Assassin's Creed game. AC1, 2, Brotherhood, Revelations, 3, Black Flag and Origins handle stuff in this game far better. Don't bother with this game, Unity or Rogue.

With so many MOBA's out there setting standards and defining the genre, you'd think it would actually be harder to fail than to succeed.  Somehow, this game managed to fail.
Gameplay:
- The lack of an auto-attack and the less-than-fluid feel of control is disappointing.
- The ability to upgrade and customize defensive towers was an interesting gameplay twist which I'd love to see implemented into other (better) MOBA's.
DLC Flood:
- I thought this may be similar to Hero Academy or other games where all of the fun of team or hero selection is limited by how much you spend to unlock.  Given the prevalence of free-to-play MOBA games, I was *shocked* to see that this game, at $19.99 or higher, had the gall to offer fairly expensive DLC packs for hero unlocks.  I ended up getting this game through one of the Humble Bundles, so I don't regret it.  However, I would not pay full price for this game or for any DLC packs.
- To clarify, however, the heroes can be unlocked in-game through play, and the DLC packs seem focused on unlocking them earlier or on alternate character skins.
Overall:
- I was very disappointed with this use of the LoTR license.  I'm certain I've played better Starcraft or Warcraft custom, community-made maps.  I was hoping they'd do something fun and unique, even if not totally compelling, on par with the Battle for Middle Earth games.  Unfortunately this game feels like it was rushed out the door, monetized, but incomplete (perhaps to coincide with movie releases.)  Get your Legolas fix elsewhere.

Well i have played this game for aprox 10 hours and i can say that at its current stage its not worth to buy it. The reason is that the game doesnt have enough features implemented to it and a lot of bugs.
The good:
+nice graphics
+the gameplay is verry fun
+the combat is ok (the enemary archers kitting you is verry annoying since you might end up chasing them to the enemy base)
+the crafting&gathering system are verry well done
The bad:
-a lot of bugs
-horrible UI for building stuff like walls and bugs out often. Editing a building is verry difficult since it doesnt always take your commands and its unintuitive.
-at the moment building any kind of buildings its pointless. Your people can sleep verry well outside even on a bed for example. So its mostly decorative and to increase your value as a town. I really dont see the reason to build anything because they dont provide any bonuses and they are far to little buildings at the moment.
-Mining or digging is verry poorly implemenred as well. For example if you want to mine in a mountain for example and then decide to go up you need to manually build ladders for them to go up or down for that matter otherwise the order to mine will not be done. Why cant this be done automatically by them? Digging also requires ladders to be built manually for every layer you go down because otherwise they cant haul what they have mined and they cant get out to eat and they will soon die. So you need to be carefull.
-Poor ui and inuititive. For example it took me a few hours to finally learn how to edit a building and when, i had to google on how you can build roads or walls etc. These are just a few examples but its an overall feeling.
-Verry ppor AI pathing. For example a lot of time i see my workers doing a hauling of an ore just to put it down and go pick up another ore imediatlly next to it and haul that one instead. Also they tend to take the longest paths when building anything or just leave their work completly do something else and then come back.
-Another bad thing is that devs are pushing updates at a verry low rate. This game is from june 2015. so for over one and a half year the game is still in alpha. Also the last update was October 2016. That means that the game development will go verry slowly and you wont be able to enjoy it at its full features.
My recommendation is not to buy this gama at its current state since it doesnt offer a lot of depth to it. Its fun to watch your people them build stuff, gather and fight but it seems shallow as you get depper into the game and the fact that a lot all of the buildings are useless and just cosmetic doesnt provide any depth to mid to late game.
I would wait untill this game goes into beta before buying it unless you really want to try it or support the devs.

Don't buy this if you aren't really good at FPS games in general. There are a few reasons why I say this:
1. Despite its lovely facade, the game is HARD. Small mistakes are punished instantly, resulting in the player restarting the level.
2. To add to the difficulty even more, the crosshair is nonexistant. You're only able to shoot "from the hip". Further, the gun doesn't shoot instant projectiles like many shooters. The gun shoots slow moving cubes, so you must accurately predict moving targets' paths.
3. Often, especially later in the game, there are several mission-critical targets flying around at once, and you need the presence of mind to accurately and rapidly shoot each one.
Long story short, the game is hard. Don't bother with it if you're not already reasonably good at the FPS genre.
For people who are generally competent at FPS games, this game has a lot to offer. Each level gives three stars based on your performance. The first star is just a gimme for completing the level. The second is a time star, meaning you can't just take the time to slowly aim all your shots if you want to perfect the level. The final star is for accuracy and is only awarded when you don't miss a single shot during the level. Perfecting a particularly hard level is a very rewarding experience.
If you love FPS and love a good rewarding challenge, this game is for you.

If you're looking for a way to describe this game, I'd define it as a mashup between System Shock, Killing Floor and Borderlands. You can tell that the guys who made this title really love games in general and wanted to take a chance to implement all those things they like. Still, the final product could be -a lot- better.
The visuals are surprisingly good for something that feels like an indiegame, the gameplay however gets stale very quick once you figured out your perfect setup. Especially melee-weapons are extremely effective and make guns pretty much obsolete since you don't need to reload which is one of the most annoying things to do in this game.
Reloading feels like it takes forever and only disturbs the rhythm of the game, even interrupting an animation one frame too early will undo the reloading process itself. Pretty much the only time you'll need a ranged weapon is for dealing with those pesky drones since they seem to be immune against melee-damage.
Enemies like the zombies which you'll encounter most of the time are either bullet sponges or die immediately, depending on the type of zombie you're dealing with. There's no real middle-ground, you either waste your time on killing enemies with extremely high lifemeters (especially bosses are a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥in that regard) or you're simply curbstomping whatever gets into your way. Enemies don't feel like they have any meaningful weaknesses, every shot you take feels the same.
The worst thing that could happen to you is ending up at the center of a zombie sandwich, once you're stuck in an obstacle you're as good as dead since there's no way to free yourself without turning yourself into a suicide-bomber. Speaking of explosives, they hardly seem to break up zombie-hoards which only makes you question the use of grenades at all. Even massive melee-weapons like the sword only seem to hit single enemies and never more than one target which makes it extremely hard to free yourself once you're surrounded.
When it comes to the special abilities in this game, all you'll need is bullet-time and that one ability which grants you temporary immunity to damage. Both of those abilities can be acquired very early and make the rest of the skill-roster feel very much obsolete, they're just THAT good. And they're pretty much the only thing that can you get out of those nasty situations which I've described earlier.
Collecting gear CAN be a fun experience but it gets old very fast, and I mean that in a literal sense. Pretty much any piece of gear you acquire is immediately obsolete after you're done with your latest mission. Even the so called epic and mythical items lack the "oomph" you'd expect from them, they're even weaker than regular gear most of the time to make up for their seemingly redundant ability bonuses.
Now in regard of the singleplayer experience (I never tried the multiplayer itself, I prefer to play horrorgames on my own), the ending of Dead Effect 2 feels extremely abrupt and only leaves you longing for a conclusion which will probably follow in a third installation of the series. At this point I'm left wondering how they're even going to expand on the locations if we already saw most of the ship in the first two games so far.
If you're looking for something to kill your time with, and you happen to see this game on sale, you might aswell give this zombie-sci-fi game a shot. On average you'll get one hour of playtime for each buck you spend (and that's just for the singleplayer experience) - if that's okay with you, you know what to get. Personally, I hope they'll try to fleshen out their gameplay a bit more since that's pretty much the bread and butter of this genre.

A Sci-fi Dungeon Crawler With A Few Innovative Twists
Overall Score: 8.5/10
Dungeon of the Endless is a dungeon crawler at its core: players explore dungeons, kill mobs, level up, gear up, and try to make it out alive. The premise is simple: you and a companion have crash-landed into a planet and must fight your way back to the surface across 12 levels. But the game is also a resource management simulator where you must adeptly balance production among four types of resources: food (to heal and level up), industry (to build modules), dust (to power rooms), and science (to research module improvements).
Modules come in two flavors: major and minor. Major modules let you produce resources whereas minor modules are designed to help you slaughter your foes and protect your crystal (more on this later). The minor module are typically defensive, such as turrets, poisonous gas, or futuristic devices that slow down mobs.  Modules can only be placed in rooms that players have powered on by allocating dust, a resources gained by slaying mobs and exploring the dungeon. You start each level of the dungeon with little dust and gradually gain more; managing which rooms you power on and off offers another layer of resource management.
You can lose in two ways: your party can be wiped out (duh!) or your crystal can be destroyed. What is the crystal, you ask? It's a crystalline structure that your party must haul from the bottom of the dungeon all the way to the surface. Perhaps it's worth a king's ransom or it contains the protrait of one of the party member's mothers -- I don't rightly know. At any rate, you must ensure that mobs do not whack at your crystal for too long as it causes you to lose dust (therefore reducing the number of rooms you can power) or, when the dust runs out, the crystal is destroyed and you lose the game. Not only must you protect the crystal as you explore the dungeon from waves of mobs, but you must also pick it up and bring it to the exit of each level of the dungeon. The crystal must weigh a ton because it slows down whatever characters picks it up to a crawl.
The game is primarily designed as a single player experience, but it's possible to cooperate with friends in online multiplayer (i.e., each person controls one or more characters). I haven't tried multiplayer yet, but my impression is that multiplayer will make this challenging game even harder, as success depends largely on reacting quickly to waves of mobs and collapsing defenses. I would probably reserve multiplayer mode for seasoned players who know what they're doing unless you're a self-professed masochist.
Overall, this is an excellent dungeon crawler for good for several playthroughs on different difficulties. The areas where the game falls short are that its inherent repetitiveness (clear a room, build modules, repair modules), though there are different characters to choose from and each level is randomly generated. I beat the game on the deceptively 'very easy' mode (an inside joke from the developers -- it's really 'normal' mode) on my second attempt, clocking in about eight hours of gameplay. I will probably try 'easy' (read: 'hard') mode in the future. I'd definitely recommend giving this game a shot if you enjoy the genre and want to support the developers.

The Trine series has always captivated me. They have delivered exactly what I like in this kind of game - bright colours, satisfying combat, some fun dialogue, and not puzzles that are not too difficult because I usually play games like this to wind down and not brain too hard!
Trine 3 is definitely more of the same, with the added bonus of having a new dimension to work with!
There are some issues for me. Particularly the controls now do not feel quite so responsive and it is very easy to hit the wrong key when moving, climbing up ledges just seems a bit jerky, and it is easy to go in the wrong direction.
Amadeus' control of objects gave me some pause too. Unless I have missed something the only way to move an object towards or away from the camera is to walk it in the appropriate direction, while you can move it left and right while standing still. Is there a control for this? (Hmm, maybe the scroll wheel like Zoya uses for controling rope length).
My final criticism is some of the delivery, particularly a few lines from Victoria Kruger just sounded phoned in. I hope for better enthusiasm in the delivery later in the game.
However, despite these points, I definitely recommend Trine 3. There are new abilities, like Zoya being able to tie objects and pull them and fasten them to other objects. Amadeus' box creation has been simplified by having a single hotkey rather than trying to create boxes while being attacked. But the best (so far) was when I first saw Pontius grab an enemy in mid jump and slam them down on their head! The Boss battle (I have played to just past the first boss) was fun and having the extra dimension did made the fight feel much more dynamic.
Cons:
Movement controls somewhat odd (at least for me)
Camera in some areas
Ledge grabbing could be better
Some line delivery
Pros:
Gameplay
Story (what I have seen so far interests me so I want to find out more)
Colours (so damn pretty!)
Dialogue
Movement and combat feel fluid (despite also being in the cons list I do believe the movement can only be improved and it is by no means at all broken, just in need of tweaking).
Final thoughts - this is how an Early Access game should be delivered. Something with real gameplay, nearly completely functional and with few rough edges to iron out. Frozenbyte have done well here and I am really looking forward to the finished product!

Undoubtedly one of the best puzzle games I have ever played. Don't let the name fool you- this game has essentially nothing to do with actual chemistry. It will, however, test your programming and 2D spatial reasoning skills. As a Reactor Engineer, you design programs based on simple commands to construct a desired molecule from given inputs. The pacing of the difficulty curve is exquisitely well-balanced; just as soon as you think you've seen all the game has to offer, it throws in an interesting new twist. Rather than merely tightening the handcuffs, new challenges nearly always offer a new mechanic that gets you to solve puzzles in a way you hadn't previously imagined.
My only real criticism of this game is that the puzzles must always been solved in essentially a linear fashion. Sometimes when you discover a critical bug in your solution, the thought of starting over right away can be drag. It would be nice to have the option to switch to another puzzle for awhile.
Still, if you've ever enjoyed puzzles, this game is not to be missed. 10/10

It's a procedurally generated dungeon exploration/tower defense strategy game.
You beat the game by escaping the dungeon and reaching the surface of Auriga.
On most game modes, there are 12 floors in the dungeon, and the primary objective of each floor is to have your heros take the crystal to the elevator room.
In order to do this, you must direct heros to open doors to undiscovered rooms. With each door opening, there is a chance of discovering beneficial tools or resources from the room, but also activates a potential wave of monsters from each discovered room without power or a hero.
The door mechanism is particularly fun in that each door is a decision of the layout of your tower defense map. You must plan your routes so that you can adequately defend your crystal and keep your heroes alive.
As you progress farther towards the dungeon exit, not only will monsters be stronger, but the monster dynamics will also change. Some monsters may only attack your modules, while other monsters will buff other monsters.
Simultaneously, you will level your heroes and modules and gain access to new abilities.You will probably have to tweak or change strategies to utilize your abilities and address the monster and map dynamics of each floor.
TL;DR
-dynamic map
-resource management
-intense amd dynamic monster waves
-smooth and pretty pixel art
-immersive audio
-unlockable upgradeable heros with abilities
-unlockable stories and pictures
-amusing items and heros

This game at the start doesn't look that great, but it surprises you through some really good gameplay. I really enjoyed having to pick my heros and actually pay attention to their stats as they are really important in this game. When you start a game you land with two heros and you are forced to manage three resources science, food, and industry. Science allows you to research more buildings and defenses allowing you to build new things, food levels up your heros and allows you to instantly heal them if their health gets too low, and industry is the currency for making buildings. When you first start off your heros are locked in a room with a crystal that provides power that they have to defend. They progress through the game by opening doors and managing power. In rooms that are not powered you cannont build defense modules or resource modules to for supplies. In the beginning defense modules are not worth much, but later managing your power becomes extremely important as you come to depend on those modules. When you clear a floor one of your heros must pick up the crystal and carry it to the elevator that you are searching for the entire level. This is a rogue like game so if one of your heros dies they are dead for good. The good news is that on your way up you can hire new heros to fill your ranks up to four heros, but if all of them die your screwed. If your hero dies while carrying the crystal your also screwed. There is one annoying bug in the game when you die the whole screen will become black and won't go back to the menu unless you hit the lower right hand corner, but it doesnt effect your gameplay at all. All in all I would rate this game a 8.5/10. The reason that this is not higher is because there are not other types of game modes besides the one I spoke of and they do have a good multiplayer, but it is essentially the same thing except everyone gets control of their own resources and hero and they get resources much slower.

What can I say about this game besides that it's ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic and I truly enjoyed it. At first, I figured it'd be your typical FPV type of game, but it's more than that. This game feels like a stealthy Bioshock. Besides having a sword and pistol at your disposal, you also have many abilities that allow you to be creative in how you get through the levels in this game. You can freeze time, possess animals to scout the levels, or you can store up and eventually unleash brutal attacks. That's one of the things I enjoy about this game, it's like a blank canvas waiting to be painted by you.
Though there are only 9 levels, each is designed in such a way that you want to explore just about every nook and cranny for sidequests, For the most part, the sidequests are unique and it adds a lot of time to the main storyline's gameplay. I'm not gonna lie, with some levels I spent up to two hours simplying navigating the map quite stealthily or exploring what's offered to me.
Besides the gameplay, the setting is something else that really stood out to me. It feels like a steampunk version of Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥and as previously stated, it greatly reminded me of Bioshock Infinite. Besides getting a glimpse of what this world has to offer through its gameplay, there are various journal and book entries that really flesh out the in-game universe of Dishonored. I honestly feel that more can be done within this setting, besides a sequel.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed this game and I give it a 4/5.

Cuphead is such a beautiful and addicting experience. Each fight feels naturally difficult without any sort of health-gating or gimmicks, leaving you always wanting more when you die. This is my very first review that I will be writing for Steam. I have nominated Cuphead for the 2017 Steam Awards as a Write-In nomination for "Sexiest Depiction of an Anthropomorphic Dice in Video Games" I considered nominating Cuphead for "Most Unexpected new Source of Waifus" Award but I mean come on have you Seen King Dice GOT DAMN!!!
Anyway now it's time to stop gushing over Daddy Dice King and get on with the review.
So Cuphead is a game apparently and a damn good one at that. I play so many different video games in my life and I really can't pinpoint any particular game that matches what Cuphead brings to the table perfectly but what you will be doing in the game is facing off against a bunch of different bosses across 4 different locations in the game world along with a few platforming levels tossed in aswell.
Each location is like a hub area where you can talk to a few NPCs, find secrets, go to a shop, and ofcourse access the bosses and platforming levels. You must defeat all bosses in an area before you can move onto the next.
There are also 2 platforming levels on each of the first three hub areas that are a bit different from the boss fights.
One thing you absolutely should know before you buy Cuphead is that it is very, very difficult and if you are someone who gets easily frustrated or enraged at even the slightest hint of a challenge this game may not be for you.  If you are a person that prefers to play games that you are certain that you can complete or easier casual games you may want to watch some gameplay and read more reviews before buying Cuphead.
For all my fellow lovers of Difficult and challenging games out there you should feel right at home. Cuphead can be a very difficult game but most of the time I think it feels very fair. When you die or fail at something in the game it almost always feels like it's your fault. You will know what you did wrong and through trial and error and lots of patience slowly the challenges of Cuphead can be overcome and you will feel an immense sense of accomplishment, relief, pride, joy or various other emotion thingies.
You will collect coins from NPCs and platforming levels. there are 5 coins to be found in each platforming level with secret coins hidden in each hub area of the game aswell. You will use these coins to buy your weapons and charms at Pork Rind's Emporium the in-game shop. Each weapon provides a unique way of playing the game with 6 different weapons to choose from.
Short fire range for big power or maybe maximum homing in on the target range with low damage, maybe you just want to charge up your shots for maximum damage.
Each weapon also comes with it's own EX-Move which is basically a special or more powerful ability that can be used when you have enough of your super meter charged up.
You will have four equipment slots the slots are as follows 2 weapon slots, 1 super art and 1 charm. You can switch between the 2 weapons you have equipped during combat by pressing the switch weapon button. The super arts are very special attacks or abilities that can be used when your super meter is fully charged up. The super meter is charged simply by dealing damage or parrying and will fill up automatically if you have the coffee charm equipped.
You will not start out with any super attacks but you can gain a new super attack at the mausoleums found in each hub area of the game. A mausoleum is basically a short challenge in parrying away all of the ghosts coming towards the vase in the center of the room.
Finally for equipable items in Cuphead there are charms which each give you a unique bonus. The heart charms will give you more health in exchange for a small reduction of damage done. The coffee charm will automatically refill your super meter and the smoke bomb will make you invincible when you dash.
Now if it's a good story you are looking for you may be dissapointed Cuphead has a very simple story that is read like pages in a childrens storybook at the beginning of the game and when you enter a new hub area for the first time.
Basically Cuphead and his best friend Mugbro are disobedint little degenerates that go behind The Elder Kettle's back *Their Gaurdian* and gamble at the Devil's Casino.
They were on a winning streak when suddenly Satan himself showed up and offers the boys the big bucks if they win just one more roll of the dice, but if they fail he will have their souls. Now Mugbro was smart enough to know that you kind of need your soul and that sometime you just need to know when to stop. But Cuphead head being the gambling addict that he was took the Devil up on his deal without even getting Mugbros consent first because he's a jerk.
In my own honest opinion Cuphead is just an absolutely phenomenal game that has given me so many hours of entetainment and frustration. This game does so many things so well that it's hard to find faults in it really.
Excellent catchy soundtrack just non-stop barrage of awesome head-rocking bangers! Smooth crisp visuals that perfectly capture that old old-school style of animation from the 30s that you just don't see much nowadays.
You can tell all of this stuff was pain-stakingly created with techniques and procedures to make everything as true to the era in which Cuphead is based off of as possible. Even the music sounds like something right out of an old cartoon.
Anyway yeah Cuphead is just plain awesome. I wasn't going to write this review just yet as this game hasn't been officially released and is currently only available on early access for a short time which also includes a bonus 10% off the price. Having grown up in the 80's where platform games were the norm and the birth of the first person shooter was a blocky pipe dream akin to the Windows 95 3D screen saver, anyway I'm still extremely fond of platformers and they hold a somewhat sentimental value to me, now I've been a fan of the previous 2 games in the Trine series and played them to death. I viewed a small youtube clip of Trine 3 a few months ago of a very much work in progress beta showing the opening level and my jaw just dropped, I was excited it was a continuation of the prequels and nothing seemed out of place.. but then something changed! a third dimension seemed to appear and the player was being moved into the distance, my mind then wanders and I start thinking "well that's the end of that then, if it ain't broke, why?? it's a platformer that was what made it so appealing, why change the format", should I have been worried.. Lets see.
Firstly it is still Trine the same 3 main characters our heroes, Amadeus the Wizard, Pontius the Knight and Zoya the Thief, each character possesses their own special skills which you will need to make your way through each level.
Amadeus: His skills include the ability to summon objects including boxes and platforms he can also manipulate contraptions and certain level objects, but he's pretty much useless in a fight.
Pontius: The knight outfitted with sword and shield, probably the main character you will use for hacking and slashing your way through bad guys.
Zoya: She has uber dexterity armed with a bow and grapple hook.
The level design is still that beautiful eye candy we're used to seeing in the previous games, but now with a more immersive and fantastic depth which is made ever more impressive when you start moving around into the now 3D environment.. see for yourself.
So far so good, I've been hitting this game hard as I learned to with the first 2, collect as many collectables as possible along the way to upgrade the characters abilities reach the end and then start all over again and search each level taking the graphics and atmosphere.
This game I have no doubt is going to be amazing when it is finally released, as it stands at the moment it is still fantastic I have discovered one or two glitches but nothing major.
The Trine series really are fantastic chill out titles and should be in every ones Steam library, so should you purchase this game... definitely! Whether you wait for the final release or grab it early access is entirely up to you.

I was very positively surprised by Dead Effect 1 and I bought Dead Effect 2 shortly after release. As it stands now, the game has too many flaws and I cannot recommend it.
Cons:
- The biggest flaw is the wrong hit detection. Whatever goes on under the hood, many shots and swings feel like they should hit but they miss. This is unfortunately applicable for both shooting and melee combat, but amplified for shooting because of the strange ballistics model. All shots are very slow, kind of like darts, so you have to lead the shot even when shooting for a short distance (10m). Hit detection is the one thing that a FPS should get right, and DE2 unfortunately doesn't.
- There are technical problems. The game stutters from time to time and sometimes there is a lag between your shot landing and the zombie body reacting - eg. you shoot the zombie in the head and half a second later the head explodes. These problems are intermittent and hard to reproduce but when they appear, they're very annoying.
- HUD and the whole UI is clearly created for mobile/touch devices and not changed for the PC release. In-game menus are a mess of horizontal scrolling and unclear buttons. Sometimes the button "Back" will return you to a previous menu, sometimes it boots you out of the menu altogether.
- The art design is horrible and completely relies on huge contrast, oversaturation and heavy postprocessing. The amount of bloom and lens flare makes it seem like you look through the cheapest and worse camera ever made. The postprocessing can be luckily toned down, the oversaturation and contrast cannot.
- The leveling and loot aspects are badly thought out. The level cap is 20 and the level of a gun is its most important number. The levels come very fast, which means that you shouldn't invest in any gear until you're level 20, because you outlevel all lower lvl weapons and armor during the next mission. Once you hit level 20, it's just a game of chance until you get the highest rarity gear - "Mythical". The rarities however are a complete joke, because mythical gear drops as often as regular one, which means in two or three matches you have everything you need. To summarize: The loot is quickly obsolete until you reach the maximum level and after you reach it it takes you about 60 minutes to get max rarity+max lvl gear.
- The story might be interesting, but most of it is hidden in datapads, small black, almost invisible tablets. The rest is told through the most atrocious voice acting I have heard in a game.
Pros:
- Many weapons have a good feel. The melee swings feel heavy, machine guns and shotguns have meaty sound effects and proper impact, sniper rifles tear everything apart.
- There is a good game hidden in there somewhere, but right now it's too deep.
I recommend Dead Effect 1 instead.

The world is quite nice looking and designed nicely in lots of places, but the issue is that the architecture is incredibly repetitive and becomes ubiquitous. Whilst one street or courtyard looks nice it also looks the same as the next.
As a Londoner I feel simultaneously at home with the streets but also irritated by the myriad of inaccuracies and ridiculous stereotypes. As well as the fact my native borough apparently has about 30 houses in it. In fact the size generally annoys me.
It's also fairly buggy with respect to getting caught on stuff or difficulty targeting enemies during fights, and personally I sometimes find the climbing controls annoying.
So onto the less negative stuff:
The lighting and weather effects can combine really well, the sight of a foggy gaslit street at night is lovely.
I really liked the detective DLC, felt better than all the investigating stuff in arkham / witcher games.
Jumping between boats, trains and carriages is quite fun.
The grappling hook is a massive time saver and adds to the general silliness of everything.
Story missions are actually not that bad and I liked both the twins acting and their interactions.
Has a pantomime villain with a fantastic moustache.
Verdict:
I don't think this is a good game, its uninspired buggy and repetitive. Despite all this I still enjoy making a big cuppa tea, listening to something more interesting and jumping about the rooftops of victorian London with a grappling hook and revolver in the rain. Get it on a sale if it goes under a tenner as long as you know that what you're getting isn't amazing.

Dishonored is a fantasy, steampunk-style world that has some open-world and RPG elements.  The graphics are nice looking and the game has run smoothly for me with no crashes or glitches in around twenty hours of play.  The magic elements are  also pretty cool, and I think pretty novel.  At least I haven't played another game with similar powers.  The ability to "transport" to ledges or up on roofs is pretty cool.  Also you can jump and climb pretty far, and also improve the climbing ability by upgrading your agility.
The main style of gameplay is stealth.  Some other games let you choose your style-- you can sneak or go in blasting.  Not so with Dishonored.  You lack the ammo for anything but the occasional, accidental encounter, so have to choose your battles and do stealth-type takedowns, or avoid encounters altogether to survive for long.
I think I've decided that I prefer the option to mix up the play style, and use either stealth or frontal assault, as the stealth-only is starting to seem a bit tedious to me. Thus, I probably won't be playing Dishonored a second time.
Still even with the stealth-only style, it is  interesting enough and fun enough to definitely be worth a play-through, especially if you can get it on sale.
If you really like stealth-style play, you will probably love Dishonored even at full price.

Pros:
-Quite a good choice of weapon and gear.
-fast paced.
-multiple difficulty level that can get very challenging depending of the mission type.
-bullet time (gotta love this thing).
-alright graphics.
-Incredibly satisfying zombie slaughter.
Cons:
-online latency often gets huge for no apparent reason,
-hit detection with some weapons is a bit off.
-will reset your settings at every update for no reason,
Subjective points:
-Cheesy story with a cheesy as hell voice acting.
-screw the bombers and the ninjas, especially at higher difficulties.
-the accuracy of the soldier is incredibly high, even when they move.
-controls are a bit clunky
If you want to spend a big time killing zombies to unwind after a rough day and you like futuristic designs, got for it. The story is, as many people said, B-series worthy. That said, who play zombie games like this one for the story ?
The accuracy system is a bit strange but you can overcome it quickly with the implants of your characters. The weapons selection is pretty wide. Want to use a shotgun ? Want to use a sniper rifle ? Want to use brass knuckles ? Want to use a laser rifle ? Want to use the goddamn Mjollnir ? Damn right you can. Upgrading the weapons costs quite a lot at the end but considering how much money you'll earn in the mission at the end, you'll be able to afford it. And like in all games, each weapon has a situation in which it is more useful.
I saw some people saying that you can't access the weapons, gears, implants and abilities menus without talking to a NPC. That is false. You'll be able to access weapons, gear and implants through two consoles in the hub after a while or in the multiplayer lobby directly. In single player, you'll have to speak with a NPC to access your abilities unfortunately but you'll be able to access it directly in the multiplayer lobby.
The regular zombies aren't anything amazing but the special zombies can be incredibly frustrating (I'm looking at you, TNT dealer). Bosses aren't incredibly hard but they deal quite a load of damage even with the best gear possible.
Amongst the soldiers you'll find ninjas after a while and they strike hard but you can usually kill them in one shot.
What pains me the most is how crap is the online stability, suddenly dropping your fps from 70-80 to 5-10 and simulteanously increasing your latency from 15ms to 700ms for no reason.
Overrall:
Long story short, 7.5/10. Defo not GOTY but not as bad as most of the negative reviews claim it is. It's an enjoyable game, alone or with friends. Story is full of cheese though.

As of this writing, Trine 3 is still "Early Access", meaning it is still a work in progress.  The game therefore is not yet complete. It has a few missing features and menu options that are not yet written.
Anyone familiar with the trine series of games and has enjoyed them will not be disappointed with Trine 3, the artifacts of power.   The 3dish side-scroller idea takes some getting used to, but within minutes you'll get the hang of it and start enjoying the new play style.
The side scrolling you're familair with from Trine 2 is still pretty much the same, except that now, when you press the up or down keys you will go deeper or closer into the enviroment.  Even so, there are times where the entire environment rotates to display a whole new landscape.  This was a pleasant surprise as this makes clear that the 2d landscape is actually 3d and not necessarily limited to just left, right, up and down movements.
Several of the mechanics of each character has been improved or changed slightly.  In Trine 2, The Wizard was not able to stand on a created box and hover it, but if he put something between himself and that box, he could hover the box and therefore himself.
In Trine 3, this loop hole has been closed.  Not only can the wizard no longer take advantage of this loop hole to carry himself anywhere; He also can't do it to toher characters.  It seems that objects that are being manipulated by one character are no longer affected by the abilities of another.
This is not aas bad as it might at first sound.  It forces the player to learn to use the characters abilities as they were intended, rather than using loopholes to get through some levels.   The player ultimately learns to better control the character, but loses the option of "Cheating" past an obstacle, leaving only the rage-quit option available on some tough levels.
Even so, it is still fun and enjoyable and a great addition to the under-valued series.
Having said that, there aren't very many levels yet, and the "Challenge" levels are short and limited to playing the thief.  The challenge levels end abruptly at the amusement park, which I assume the develops left there to test the mechanics of the game, and allow early access players something to play with while waiting for the new levels and features.
A glitch on the final screen of the chanllenges allowed me to walk through the mouth of the snake  and into the walls of the level, where my character was forever lost and unable to escape without restarting the level.  I'm sure this will be found and corrected before the next patch.
If you would prefer to wait for the whole experience and leave the testing for some one else, waiting might be a better option.
Paying for early access right now may not be worthwhile for some, but if you have enjoyed the Trine series or you feel it is under valued and you'd like to help the developers; by all means go ahead and get in now.
Personally, I can't wait for the next levels to be released.  Thumbs up.

As a fan of the original Trine games (especially #2), I was intruiged by the additional dimension being added to the traditionally 2d game. I have to admit I was expecting something more along the lines of Viewtiful Joe, where the 3d aspect of the game was more of a stylistic thing than actually being a 3d game.  Needless to say, I feel the third dimension has made this game less fun to play.
Fighting with Pontius has become frustrating as hell. Blocking seems to be basically useless now. I can't tell where I would be blocking so it seems like the best practice is just to mash the left mouse button until the enemies are dead. Trying to use any sort of strategies like blocking attacks just seems to get me killed at this point. I liked playing Zoya because she felt nimble and quick, but she feels clumsy now. Still, I feel fighting is easier with her since at least you can keep your distance from enemies while using the arrows which auto-aim.
I also lost count how many times I've died in the short time I've played simply because the camera angles are set in such a way that it's nearly impossible for me to tell whether or not it's a jump I should actually be able to make. Probably more often is when I hit space for jump and up the same time (since it still feels more like a 2d platformer than a 3d platformer) and end up jumping behind the platform I'm attempting to get onto.
I suppose in the end it's the controls that are really hurting this game for me right now. The way the chracters feel very imprecise and sloppy, and the lack of camera control in a 3d game only exacerbate these control issues. There's also a feeling of vagueness while actually in the game that's offputting. I'm (obviously) not the best at puzzle action games, but games like Ori and the Blind Forest is an example of a puzzleish game done well. I feel like most of the challenge in Trine  3 has more to do with my confusion about the presentation of the game moreso than the actual challenge of the game's puzzles.
I realize this game is still in development, but I feel like it's the design I'm fighting with at this point rather than bugs.
This game will no doubt improve as time goes on, but my issues with the game are so foundational I don't see how incremental improvements will address them.

Let's start off by saying if you haven't played previous entries in the Trine series, you should really just drop what you are doing and play through Trine 2 and the DLC. It's inexpensive, available on all kinds of platforms and one of the best and most beautiful games you will ever play. The art, music and gameplay are all tightened to the 9s and it's charm hasn't worn off one bit in the years it's been available.
Trine 3 is taking the old 2-d platform model and adding a 2.5/3-D component to the lovingly crafted setpieces. ultimately the levels still move forward in the same way, and the camera is fixed, always providing you with the best storybook-quality view that made previous Trine games such a feast for the eyes.
Overall, the 3-D experiment is a resounding success:
- Pontius is surprisingly agile, can wall-jump and glide with his shield. He's also fast as heck. I expect we'll need to see some slight nerfing for him, because he can jump higher and longer than Zoya now, especially using his no-cooldown dash move as a starter. He is pretty much  invincible in the Goblin combat sequences in this Early Access. He's got some clipping issues with his arm and placement of the shield, but these are all things i am sure will be fixed. While he's missing the hammer from previous entries so far, he obviously has had a lot of loving care put into his move set. His new ground-pound stomp (jump + duck) is really fun. He even uses his shield
to propel his heavy self through water!
- Zoya's archery skills are coming through pretty well in 3-d, although she can't aim upward unless she needs to for a puzzle reason - there were a bit of doing the dance of the secret square to get a proper angle based on where she was standing. In general, her controls didn't feel quite as responsive as one might hope. Unlike previous Trine entries, Zoya can't swing from nearly any cieling or ledge, only from defined points, usually marked with a metal ring. She also uses the ropes to solve puzzles by establishing a length of rope by spooling and unspooling it, then yanking things into place and tying them off. This got a little confusing in parts when i had about six useless loose ropes on the screen, but again, i think this kind of clean-up is what we can expect by the time the game is ready. Zoya is also lovingly animated with gorgeous transitions and watching her move is a real joy. the flowing robe is, in my opinion, a bit too much. i would seriously consider putting zoya in some tight pants and reducing the length of the skirt a tad, because it literally went up over her hood a few times in my playthrough. Hilarious, but hardly heroic. it will also solve any awkward upskirts that occur when she is sneaking. Zoya's wall jumping and climbing and some of the new rope puzzles are great, but it was frustrating that in the end she was a less successful jumper than Pontius, especially since she can't grapple to nearly anywhere, zoya feels more ground-bound than she ever has.
- Amadeus feels the least complete of the three so far. gone are the charming "draw a box or a line" mechanics of previous Trine entries, Amadeus has just gone full-on telekentic master now. The demo didn't give quite as much of an impression as to how he'll be used long term in the game, but. He can still summon a box and place it to help him platform. His animations look awesomely goofy but he's also come into his own in terms of confidence, and his new robes are slick as hell. It is entirely possible that the heroes will gain new moves and upgrades as with Trine 2, so who knows what kind of magical surprises are in Amadeus' future?
- Once you unite the three heroes, you'll get some switch-on-the-fly gameplay leading up to a boss fight. This will, of course, be what the meat and potatoes of the game will be, and I can't wait. The level design and art teams for Trine 3 have already delivered incredible transitions and surprises waiting beind doorways of all sorts of angles, and secrets to be discovered. The new save points are beyond gorgeous, and I'm excited to learn more about the game's villain!
- The game's boss fight was a wonderful display of how depth will be used in fighting the huge monsters introduced in Trine 2 and its DLC. No spoilers, but it was a beautiful monster, and a really fun fight.
- Multiplayer is, as promised, very buggy, and chock full of client rep issues. This is pretty normal for a game in this stage of development, so do not let it get you down, players! We did a full multiplayer run and both of us had a great time with the mechanics. For games that use the "unlimited" mode, and just in general, a small colored cursor or color pallette shift to differentiate cliens would be great. In close quarters, it was hard to tell whose Pontius was whose.
- There's a free-for-all level and even a few mod levels available in the workshops if you want to enjoy ballsing around as Pointus for an extra hour or three.
I am going to put this away and await the finished project!
