Whenever I hear the term "video game" I immediately think of the Serious Sam games. Pure 100% action packed mother♥♥♥♥ing balls to the ♥♥♥♥ing wall holy♥♥♥♥♥♥goddamn I'm getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked fun.
What is Serious Sam The First Encounter? It's an old-school First Person Shooter, you shoot things, pretty simple stuff, right? Well, the thing about Serious Sam is that it does it so well, all you really need in a game like this is shooting. None of that modern military shooter garbage where it pretends to be "realistic" or "tactical" and it takes itself too seriously. Ironically, Serious Sam doesn't take itself seriously at all, it's fairly ridiculous actually. Non of that two weapon limit crap and health regeneration that seems to be the norm nowadays, this game is seriously bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane cranked up to eleven.
So why is the game so good? It's fun, for one thing. It's you against a horde of enemies, you shoot everything that moves and it's extremely satisfying to do so. You have a wide arsenal of weapons to help you take on the extreme amounts of enemies flying at you constantly. Each weapon is so finely crafted and balanced to suit each situation in the game and you'll learn over time to know what weapon to use when and on what enemies. You can't just stick with the same weapon because you also have to worry about ammo conservation and it might not work as well as other weapons depending on what situation you're in. You'll slowly but surely adapt to the idea of switching weapons constantly and you better, or you'll get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked.
The insane variety of weapons you get is ludicrous, and you can carry them all at once. You got your shotguns, minigun, rocket and grenade launchers, laser gun, ♥♥♥♥ING CANNON and more. The game also gives you these weapons at a nice pace as you progress through the game. You'll need every single weapon because this game isn't easy, you will always be attacked by tons of enemies and you'll need to use whatever you have. As for the enemies, there's a very large variety of them as well, and some of the enemy designs are fairly amusing; like headless screaming suicide bombers called "Kamikazes", scorpions with chainguns, reptilian creatures that throw homing balls at you and many more.
The level design is nothing more than serviceable, which isn't a bad thing, it does its job, the enemy placement is occasionally very well and the game has nice pacing. You can also look for secrets which are fairly well placed actually, secrets help you out by rewarding your exploration with health and ammo. But what I like about the level design the most is that it isn't the maze-like level design of some other old-school and classic FPSs, THANK GOD (yeah, I'm talking to you, Doom 2!). All I want in a game like this is to shoot the ever living ♥♥♥♥ out of everything that moves and I don't want to spend time figuring out where I'm supposed to go. Occasionally mid-way or at the end of a level you'll be fighting a boss, and these aren't just bosses, they're the size of a building, they're massive and very fun to fight, some of which you will later encounter as regular enemies once you've defeated them.
The game also has a storyline, rather forgettable and it's nothing more than a setting for the game but the intro to the game sums it up very nicely. Humankind uncovers some advanced technology from another race, eventually they are attacked by aliens and at the point of being entirely doomed, they send Sam "Serious" Stone, a hero wounded countless times but never defeated, through an artifact called "The Time Lock"; which has the power to send a single person back in time, so Sam is sent thousands of years back in time when humankind had a fighting chance to defeat Mental, the evil bad guy who is responsible for all this mess; and thus Sam fights his way through Mental's horde and whatnot. The Protagonist is likeable and quite awesome though.
The game also has multiplayer. STAY FAR AWAY, besides the fact that the multiplayer is dead, deathmatch is so incredibly unbalanced and pointless. There's also co-op, and it's up to 16 players which is kind of awesome but in my opinion, this game shines the most in singleplayer.
It's also not a bad looker, while the graphical fidelity isn't incredible, it still has some nice textures and shadow effects, modeling is good but the animations are a bit meh. The game is also very colorful, even though it takes place in Egypt which is always great. Also, the soundtrack is fantastic, it fits the game very well. I also have to mention the excellent sound design in this game. If you listen closely, you can hear the enemies that you are about to encounter and each enemy has its own sound, so you know what to prepare for when you're about to enter a new area or a room. And when you are surrounded by enemies, you'll know which direction they are coming from because you can hear them very well no matter which direction (if you're using headphones, of course).
In conclusion, if you're into the golden age of FPS, then you've probably already played this game, if you haven't though; definitely be sure to give it a try. I'd go as far as to say that this is probably the best game to start with for people new to the FPS genre. And as a remake, this is just as good if not better than the original version.

Stonehearth is much like a city builder, but with some RPG/Adventure elements in it. The goal is to keep your Heartlings, or citizens alive by finding resources, building houses and defences and fighting off invaders.
When I first got into this game I had a hard time getting used to it. There were many game breaking bugs that got your Heartlings stuck or buildings that could not get finished. Most of the bugs have been fixed and you won't run into any for the most part. The ones that do are often easily shrugged off.
The game is quite easy to get into. The UI is quite easy to handle and you can easily access any information you might need. Important events like raids, level-ups or traders will pop up and notify you of their arrival. You can "slice" the ground  so you can see your mines underground and the same can be done for the buildings (although this might need some improvement for buildings with multiple floors).
Buildings can be made in any way you want as these can be build much like Minecraft block by block. After you're finished editing your building you can let your Heartlings build it for you. The game also offers some blueprint for you when you don't feel like building houses yourself and these too can be edited to your liking.
When building starts your heartlings will get everything they need to build the structure bit by bit. They even build scaffolding to make the building making it cool to see your buildings being build from the ground up.
Your heartlings will be able to be given specific roles. Like a carpenter, a farmer or a footman. This will allow them to level up in this respective tree which in turn will allow you more to make and progress your town further. Each role has their benefits and are overall very well balanced out. You will mostly want to have all of them every time.
While supplying your town with supplies is not hard all on its own, it does get a bit more exciting when enemies start appearing. Having to call back your citizens to the safety of your building while your footmen, knights, archers and clerics move in to take care of the threat. Combat is really fun, even when it's this simple it still gets you to hold your breath sometimes when its a close call for one of your soldiers.
The game does not have much story going on yet. But it is easy to see the potential the game has and the devs are working on the story as we speak. Which brings me to the next part.
Now, many people have been complaining about how slow the game has developed over the last months. And I can't blame them. But one thing you must keep in mind is that the development team is a small one. Personally I still back the dev team as they seem to actually care about the game.
I like this game. Quite a bit. It is a bit like minecraft but more strategy based. Which I like. The game's theme is great. Very cute and playful making even the biggest fights look cute and huggable. The game still lacks some contend but even now I would pay my 30 bucks for it and think it money well spent. I love the system of the game and the way it works. The UI is simple and much to my liking. My only real downside is that I too would wish for more content being thrown out more rapidly. I give this game a 8/10. Some might say this is way too high. But you just cant deny this game is a lot of fun and still has a whole lot of potential. I hope the game gets some big updates in 2017 and I feel like the devs will deliver on this. My advice? Buy this game! Support these developers. It's small companies like these that make the greatest games. If given the chance.

A significant improvement over AC: Unity but not without its flaws. Syndicate stars twins Jacob and Evie Frye set in Victorian London. As always with AC games, the world is beautiful and feels alive. The Frye twins are interesting protagonists and the game play aspect of being able to switch between characters for a slightly different play style is a nice change.
Unfortunately Syndicate also shares some similar problems as previous AC installments, namely repetition. The world map is filled with side missions and collectibles, alas most of them are pretty much the same and once you've collected a few vintage beer bottles or pressed flowers there's not much fun in finding more, unless you want to try different color schemes for your outfits in the crafting menu.
Speaking of crafting, the crafting system has been expanded this time around and you'll be able to craft new and more powerful weapons and armor which is a nice addition to the game. Skills and perks have been improved as well but at only 10 levels max it won't take you that long to reach the highest level.
Some side missions will have you encounter famous people from the Victorian era but game play wise these missions don't do anything new. The main missions do provide alternate ways of completing objectives, which is nice but in the end I found that it just didn't provide enough entertainment to revisit.
As with most AC games, don't expect great optimization or a steady frame rate and be prepared to struggle with numerous bugs and graphical glitches, though it's certainly not as bad as AC: Unity.
If you're a fan of the AC series then Syndicate is worth picking up. If not then this game will not change your mind as it's really more of them same except in a different setting.

Assassin's Creed syndicate screams of a francaise that has ran out of ideas. Its no wonder they went for the reboot option following this title. How to drop the ball 101.
This is a bog standard Assassins Creed game with all the usual guff, smoke bombs, darts, ranged weapon, melee combat weapon. For some reason you also manage to loot Batman's personal stash and get hold of the Bat Grapnel as well.
The game plods along with a meh plot set in London. It seems like the creators wanted something of Gangs of New York meets Marry Poppins. The ideas are correct but London itself is uninspiring and one dimensional. I couldnt have really told you the poor parts from the rich parts even being a Historian and a resident of the United Kingdom. In short it all melded together. The gang fight missions were nice but you had to troil through the usual assassins creed missions first. In this case its assassination, kidnap and rescue. *Yawn* In most cases I did a mission if I strayed towards it but ignored it and did my usual fast travel method of Assasins Creed map movement.
Combat was pretty dismal as well, there are 3 weapons to choose from and the "dynamic" combat really boiled down to bash attack, dodge or quick shot when need to and stun the guy when he blocks. Gone are the timed counters from previous games. The was little timing or skill involved and I quickly found myself able to take out multiple opponents above my level with the sneaky character much less the combat wombat. Combat felt very forced and more of a button bash that it did in previous titles. The weapons available were also very un-inspiring a Knife, Knuckle dusters and a Sword Caine. I stuck with a Knife the entire game because the graphics of the others simply seemed a bit lame. There were the usual multiple kill options in combat but I think the game rolls a dice to decide if you execute this ability, sometimes it happened others it didnt.
Free running has always been a staple of Assassins Creed, in this title you now hold A to go up and X to go down. Sure if I wanted to skill jump parkour Id play Mirrors Edge, but this still feels like it takes all the flow and control away from you. To make matters worse the pre mentioned Bat Grapnel means you can fly about like Batman, instead of climbing a building one aimed shot can take you right to the top. Sure you move quicker but it just takes away the whole point and feel of Assassins Creed.
The game only uses four types of bad guy which sucked big time. Gang members, Guards, Templars and Police.  Gone are the patrols of guards led by a captain or the guy with the big weapon etc. Again you button bash your way past these guys like you were... hmmm yes Batman.
The targets are also badly thought out, I will conceed the final bad guy Crawford Starrick has bags of bad guy charisma even if the final confrontation with him is more like a poorly thought out mini game than an actual finale.To top this off you even have a very predictable Bill the Butcher style guy leading the red enemy gang and he was voiced by Captain Jack Sparrow. *sigh*
I wanted to like Evie and Jacob Frye but both were quite one dimensional characters one violent the other sneaky *predictable*.
I really wanted to love this title but found the story pretty non existant. My usual too many weapons gripe was met with a not enough weapons complaint and I honestly couldnt wait for this to be over. The future / modern parts of the story were also lost to me and just served in wasting time, it doesnt fit what so ever and lets not even visit the World War I time line missions. Its as if a dev said "oh oh London lets cram everything we can in" That said Jack the Ripper DLC ( didnt bother) should have been part and parcel of the game although it was nice to see Spring Heeled Jack, although the game made no attempt to really explain this. So much potential in a historic and fine city lost.
If your a AC fan then go ahead and play this title but I wouldnt suggest getting it outside of a sale, if you havent played AC before avoid this one and play an earlier title you will find it much more satisfying!
Additional, having finished this title I decided to go back and play Assassins Creed 3 again. Can confirm there is more storyline and RP aspect in the first hour of gameplay than Syndicate's entire title. Disapointing.

Dishonored is a fantasy, steampunk-style world that has some open-world and RPG elements.  The graphics are nice looking and the game has run smoothly for me with no crashes or glitches in around twenty hours of play.  The magic elements are  also pretty cool, and I think pretty novel.  At least I haven't played another game with similar powers.  The ability to "transport" to ledges or up on roofs is pretty cool.  Also you can jump and climb pretty far, and also improve the climbing ability by upgrading your agility.
The main style of gameplay is stealth.  Some other games let you choose your style-- you can sneak or go in blasting.  Not so with Dishonored.  You lack the ammo for anything but the occasional, accidental encounter, so have to choose your battles and do stealth-type takedowns, or avoid encounters altogether to survive for long.
I think I've decided that I prefer the option to mix up the play style, and use either stealth or frontal assault, as the stealth-only is starting to seem a bit tedious to me. Thus, I probably won't be playing Dishonored a second time.
Still even with the stealth-only style, it is  interesting enough and fun enough to definitely be worth a play-through, especially if you can get it on sale.
If you really like stealth-style play, you will probably love Dishonored even at full price.

X-Com:UFO Defense, also known as UFO: Enemy Unknown, is one of the best games I have ever played in my life. No list of the best games of all time is complete without it. (I have put many, many hours into it, just not through Steam).
The 2012 remake is a very good game, but still doesn't quite do it justice.
OpenXCom is a free rebuild of the game that utilizes original game assets (so you still need to actually own this game). It fixes a bunch of bugs, and improves various interface inadequacies. It's still the same game, just polished more.
It also adds easy moddability, with some mods already added to the base installation but completely optional. So you can play completely vanilla, with an experience indistinguishable from the original game except for the absence of bugs - or you can play with a number of common sense improvements - or you can download mods that change and expand the game.
</Public Service Announcement>
It's got an enjoyable X-files-like atmosphere of investigating aliens.
It's got difficult but rewarding tactical combat.
It's one of the few games I know where "emergent gameplay" is not a meaningless phrase  - the way you can chain your low level actions into fantastic strategies. For some very simple examples, you can have one guy carry missiles and pass them on to another who carries the missile launcher, or have have one guy set the timer on a grenade, throw it to another, who throws it to another on the front line, who then throws it at an enemy... the 2012 game doesn't let you do that.
It lets you name your characters and watch them grow in abilities, which causes you to become attached to them and invested in their survival and success. And yet the game can be very unforgiving, and anyone may die with a single bad decision or some bad luck, no matter how skilled and well armored.
The research, base management, etc. are fairly simple but fun.
And then defending your base against alien retaliations, and seeing the same layout but on the tactical combat screen, is quite satisfying. You've built your base too open and without enough choke points around the entrances to defend against a swarm of enemies? You're going to have a hard time...
One of the best things about the game is how you're essentially fighting against a "master race", the Ethereals, who dominate all the other races they send against you with sheer mentalistic power. Their psionics sow terror and confusion among your troops, and are powerful enough to augment their atrophied bodies and let them be as fast, strong, and dangerous with weapons as their client races specifically bred for muscles or whatever. And then you can build a squad of soldiers who can beat the Ethereals at their own psionic game. Humanity, ♥♥♥♥ yeah!
There are many other reasons, big and small, but I'd be here all night.

Very little any more, at least if you patch it. But historically:
Bugs. The most notorious was the difficulty bug, which meant no matter what difficulty you chose, you were playing on the easiest. I'm not sure if Steam uses the patched version, but play with openxcom, and it won't be a problem.
Interface woes. Again, use openxcom and most of it goes away, even though the game looks almost exactly the same.
Balance woes:
- Psionics are overwhelmingly powerful, which means that as soon as enemies start using them against you, you're in trouble, and as soon as you develop your own psionics, the game becomes easy even on the hardest difficulty level.
You can send a few psionic soldiers to the supposedly super difficult final mission, and have them beat the final level on Turn 0 by chaining a certain ability... This is satisfying, in the "nothing is allowed to be THIS AWESOME in modern games any more" way. It does lower replayability, though, and I'd say the remake does psionics better - at least if you compare both games in their vanilla state.
- money can be too easy on higher difficulties, because of all the enemy equipment you'll be selling.
These issues can of course be fixed by playing the game via openxcom. For example there's an in-built "line of sight psionics" mod, which makes psionics a lot less abusable. There's also an option that makes enemy weapons explode when the enemy dies, like in the 2012 remake, which cuts down on profits from selling enemy gear.
Still remaining weaknesses include dated graphics (for those misguided souls who care about that), and some interface clunkiness. The gaming industry did learn a thing or two since 1994, there's no way around that. Nevertheless, we're looking at a timeless classic that I still come back to from time to time and never fail to have fun.
If you enjoy this kind of a tactical game, look up Chaos Gate. It's largely X-Com in W40k universe.
Still one of the best turn-based strategy games ever made!

Get Off My Lawn! is an arcade tower defense shooter that pits you against a very orderly alien invasion.  The controls are very simple, and can be played with one hand (two might be necessary for younger players).  For every alien destroyed, you earn orbs as currency that can be used for power ups and progressively strong weapons.  The content is age appropriate for most players (you do use firearms, but no violent deaths).
As with most 'free' games, you can spend real money to buy currency to accelerate your progress in advancement.  There is one achievement you can 'earn' by spending real money, so you can see who spent money on this game, and who didn't.  If you are an achievement hunter, don't fret, there is only one achievement that you have to buy, and many more that you can get without spending a single penny.

Dead Effect 2 is an interesting mashup of a few sci-fi shooter tropes that seems to work quite well.  I chuckled at the name of the game, Dead Effect because in fact it does remind me a little bit of two other sci fi shooters, Dead Space and Mass Effect.  Dead Effect 2 does in fact show some of it’s inspiration from these games with a touch of Borderlands and Doom thrown into the mix as well.  While the game that you get as a result isn’t exactly wholly unique, it is none the less quite fun and engaging.  With a play style that feels polished, focusing on tight combat zones, cramped hallways, and life or death firefights, it adds to the somewhat oppressive claustrophobic air that the game seems to be shooting for.  Only between missions when you have a chance to shop, upgrade, and talk to NPCs do the cramped quarters take a break and you’re given a somewhat gorgeous hub to breathe in.
The music is very enjoyable, and that’s something I appreciate because I found even two hours in still having it running.  I normally cut music within 10 minutes of playing a game, but the pseudo organ music helps to end the right vibe to the game.
A huge amount of gear is available, but unfortunately you’re only going to have the money to buy a small fraction of it, so make your choices wisely.  Do you go for the more long ranged rifle?  How about the automatic lead sprayer?  Maybe you’d be better off with a reliable melee weapon?  Then again it’s hard to skip the shotgun.  The game starts you with three classes, and I haven’t had a chance to try out the other two, but the main character I chose, “Gunnar” has a gruff ‘space marine’ esque vibe to him that hearkens back to the doom games all the way back in the 90s.  However you’re not limited to his playstyle when you choose him, you can gear and spec your character to be more ninja-like.  That is a freedom of gameplay that I appreciate.
The game does have it’s flaws.  Most notably the graphics are on the whole quite amazing.  Some of the effects are gorgeous and some of the character models of the enemies are great.  But that does set the counterpoint when you see a graphic that isn’t.  The first NPC you meet up with for example just looks…. Off.  It’s hard to describe why exactly, maybe her body proportions aren’t right, or her unit’s polygon count is too low, or then again maybe it’s just the distracting nipple bumps on her outfit, much like Rachel from Friends, circa the mid 90s.
Likewise the voice acting is decent, but not great.  The main character is terse, and when he does speak it’s somewhat cliched.  Then again so is the mysterious female npc, the mentally deficient engineer, and the horribly voice acted russian doctor.  This is probably the game’s biggest flaw in my book, you really want everyone to shut up so you can enjoy the games, the gunshots, the dog growls, and the zombie groans.  But unfortunately the mentally deficient engineer has to blubber his own name over and over in hodor like fashion even when you’re on a mission.
The one thing that I find very interesting and haven’t had a chance to test out is the co-op play.  I like that the ability for friends to drop into a mission as they like is integrated right into the gameplay.  More multiplayer only helps this type of game in my opinion.
As the final word on this review, I’d say that this game isn’t perfect, but if you want an action FPS in a semi horror / space genre, Dead Effect 2 delivers.  It doesn’t revolutionize the wheel, but it’s absolutely worth the entry price.
NOTE - I was given a free copy of this game in exchange for an honest and unbiased review.

SpaceChem is a really excellent puzzle game—if “puzzle game” is even the right way to describe it (more on this in a moment). It casts the player as an engineer working for an outer-space industrial operation—your job is to program and arange the reactors that recombine chemical elements for various industrial purposes.
Right up front it’s worth noting that SpaceChem isn’t actually a chemistry game. Ignorance of actual chemistry isn’t a hindrance. The actual game play consists of setting up tracks which carry chemical components around within a reactor, and inserting commands to make sure that what you want ends up where you want it. In some stages there is a further level of complexity where you must set up and connect multiple reactors to be used together.
All this has a lot more to do with computer programming than it does which chemistry. In fact, it seems fair to say that SpaceChem is like the fun part of programming separated from all the arcane knowledge and headache that go along with it. You are, in essence, issuing simple commands to a machine to enable it to complete complex tasks. (People who have coded may also feel some déjà vu as they set about finding the bugs in the operation of reactors they’ve already set up—it feels just like debugging code.)
Here is where SpaceChem is so different from most other puzzle games. Instead of being faced with a problem to which you must FIND a solution, here you are faced with an objective and you must DESIGN a solution. These stages are less puzzles than engineering tasks. And possible approaches to the SpaceChem stages are innumerable and call on your creativity as much as your deduction. This is emphasized by the feedback you get once you’ve completed a stage which compares your solution to all the others on record along several dimensions. For me, this added an incentive not just to beat a level, but to keep returning to my solution: surely I could find a way to do it faster, or with fewer instructions than the others who’d solved it. Thus the replayability of even a single stage is vast.
That is the real strength and focus of the game, the core structure of the problem solving. Some other elements are less strong. The visuals are very simple, though, for the most part, I think this brings an abstract elegance. The story, such as it is, is darkly comedic but tacked on and not really worth your attention. And the boss battles, essentially normal stages with some sort of twist in how you apply your chemistry, are awkward and un-compelling as if an afterthought to the game’s design.
But these complaints are peripheral to the core excellence of the game as an opportunity for creative, structured problem solving. (And don’t take the creative bit to mean it isn’t challenging. The difficulty of the game has been widely noted. Things start off easily enough, but don’t feel bad if you find the later stages very challenging—you have a lot of company.) So if you like puzzle games, coding, or a good challenge, SpaceChem is for you.
(In addition to my Steam copy, I’ve put in many hours on a DRM free copy, and a number on a copy for my tablet. The game's that good--I've acquired it more than once.)
I feel like I learned something, but I have no idea what.

This game is hard.  It's an unforgiving, rogue-like, turn-based and real-time, tower defense, dungeon crawler.  That's a lot of game types to mash into one game, but surprisingly, it works pretty well.  Just be prepared to lose your first few plays.
The game starts with your space ship crash landing and getting buried deep underground.  Your job is to find a way back to the surface, which happens to be 12 floors above your head.  You'll need to find the elevator to the next floor, killing the monsters that attack you in the process, and carry your Crystal (the power supply from your space ship) to the elevator in order to power it and reach the next floor.
Early levels give you a false sense of security by providing plenty of Dust (power) so you can keep most of the dungeon lit, thereby preventing monster spawns.  It also allows you to build up plenty of modules to create a stockpile of Industry, Science, and Food, which are the resources needed to build, upgrade, and level characters, respectively.  Your goal is to find the exit on each floor by exploring one room at a time.  You collect resources and monsters have an opportunity to spawn each time you open a door, thus each time you open a door begins a new "turn."  Monsters will only spawn in unpowered rooms without one of your heroes present, so you need to plan your defenses accordingly.  Later levels don't give you nearly enough Dust to power the dungeon, so you are both unable to collect resources and unable to build defenses.  Plus, many more monsters spawn and the monsters are more difficult to kill.  The game forces you to stockpile resources in the early levels, spending as little as possible in the first 7 floors so that you'll have enough resources remaining to survive the remaining 5 floors to escape the dungeon.
The complete lack of feedback as you progress through the early and mid levels of the dungeon are what make the endgame so brutally difficult.  The game simply doesn't provide any feedback as to how well you're doing overall.  A few small mistakes early on may not seem like a big deal, but they can cost you the game five levels later.  Losing the game after spending several hours working your way to the final few levels is a severe disappointment, particularly because it will seem like you’re doing a fantastic job right up to the point where you lose.  Simply knowing that you shouldn't be spending your resources early on is a huge help to surviving the final few floors of the dungeon, so keep that in mind in your first few playthroughs!
The mechanic to unlock characters is interesting, but I don't really like it.  Characters are randomly encountered as you play and you have the option to recruit them into your party, for a cost.  Characters are permanently unlocked if you keep them alive through three levels of your game.  I think this is a cool idea!  Unfortunately, your party is limited to four heroes, so you have to dismiss someone if you're at the limit.  This means you’re forced to choose between keeping your high-level heroes (which you’ve likely already dumped a ton of resources into upgrading) or risk losing the game to potentially unlock a new hero.  Obviously you want to unlock heroes so you can start the game with them later, but that's a pretty high cost considering your first few plays will likely take around 5 hours to complete as you get a feel for the game.  The replayability isn't all that spectacular, so wasting much of the game's prime enjoyment time unlocking characters is not ideal.
One mechanic that I absolutely can't stand is that the items don't actually tell you what they do.  "Such-and-such item unlocks _____ skill."  But what does that skill do!? You won't know until you equip the item, but that means you have to pay the merchant first, and if it turns out to be garbage you've wasted your precious resources.  I think a lot of this was intentional as the developers clearly tried to troll the players in many regards. (The fact that Hard difficulty is called "Easy" should be a clear giveaway of that fact.)
Multiplayer is not so great.  It's basically a harder version of the game with a handicap for the monsters.  Players are no longer allowed to pause, don't share resources, and independently control their own characters.  This makes coordination difficult, which is a problem considering you need quite a bit of coordination between hero placement, powered rooms, and the position of defenses if you're even going to have a chance of surviving.  Dungeon of the Endless is definitely meant to be a solo game.
Once you get past the flaws and develop your strategy to survive the dungeon, the game is actually pretty fun.  There are many different modules you can use to always have different defenses in your playthroughs, and there are quite a few characters to choose from, each with their own unique special abilities.  You can also start the game inside a number of different space ships, each of which alters the rules of the game in a different way.  The first time you beat the game will feel great!  Unfortunately, once you’ve played with each different starting space ship, you’ll likely get the feeling that you’ve seen everything the game has to offer (which is true) and the appeal to keep playing will wear off.  After all, even though the dungeon is randomly generated, you pretty much do the exact same thing on each play, the only differences being the heroes you use and the rule modification put in place by your space ship.
Overall a good game, but not great.  It won't keep you coming back again and again and again, but you should be able to get a few plays out of it before you get fed up with the repetition.

Looking back at my Steam library and my playing history, I must say I've played quite a lot of games over the past 9 months. (And suffering in school work as a result, but that's another story.) There are a lot of great games that I've played that were released just this year. It's hard to pick exactly one.
But if there was a sub-category for "Best FPS I've played that was released in 2014", it would be this one, hands-down. Why? Well...
Lovely Planet. It's as its namesake suggests. An incredibly cutesy, Japanese world with Japanese-styled characters. Everything pretty much looks like it came from some weird utopian anime with lovely planets and lovely worlds. But beneath that cute and cheery appearance lies a game that has far more depth than you would have thought it had.
For starters, despite its Japanese themes and Japanese-styled soundtrack, it was actually coded by a guy based in India. Vidhvat Madan - remember the name. I certainly would be. In terms of
, Lovely Planet is the most polished one that he's come up with yet. And the soundtrack...not by a Japanese, but by UK-based Calum Bowen. Incredibly catchy, and still miles better than the turd that passes for radio pop nowadays.
You're armed with a gun that shoots purple cubes of
love, and you use it to
love all the red
friends that you see around the map. They need your love. But don't shoot the gray ones, they already have enough, and any more than that will cause them to die from too much love. There are also a few types of fiendish traps strewn across the levels - for starters, apple bombs that trigger once you reach a certain point, you have to shoot them before they touch the ground, or else you go BOOM*! Other traps include a proximity trap which, when set off, renders a certain area unsafe after a few seconds - going into that area, uh, vapourises* you.
The first few levels start off easy, but after a while, you're involved in increasingly trickier scenarios. Take this one level for instance. I walk past an apple bomb, jump off onto a jump pad, and before I land on the jump pad the apple bomb I just walked past triggers and is launched into the air, along with ANOTHER apple bomb further along the way. You somehow have to turn around, shoot that bomb that you passed, then quickly turn back around and shoot the next bomb. All while you're probably in the air or trying to land on that jump pad. That was possibly the first level I really struggled with.
Lovely Planet's an incredibly punishing game. You have no crosshair (it feels really weird, mind you) and you have to judge your shots right. Most of the level solutions are learnt by rote - fail, fail and fail again, all while discovering how to pass some parts of the stage each time, and then perfecting the method for that one exhilaratingly perfect run. Good challenges, too - there's a speed challenge for beating a certain time, and an accuracy challenge where none of your shots go to waste.
The game also takes cues from games like Super Meat Boy - respawns are near-instantaneous so you don't have to wait too long to try again. Because you'll be trying again and again a lot of times.
I've been notoriously bad at FPS games, so I don't forsee myself being able to complete this one, unfortunately. But even if I didn't, I'd be damned if I claimed I didn't have fun with it.
Oh, and before I end off: I like reading PC Gamer Reviews because their writers have a masterful command of English. For the most part, I agree with them. However, I'm going to go out on a limb here and say I disagree with
. The presentation, contrary to what they say, is NOT MEDIOCRE. In fact, it's perfectly appropriate for this game. Not every FPS must look like CoD or Crysis.
I will concede though that they at least gave one of the better scores. Other critics don't appear to like it as much, and that's a real shame, because this is such a...wait for it...
gem. Okay, okay, I'm sorry, I'll stop now.
If you're into FPS games, you'll probably enjoy this, it might be worth full price to you then. If you're into FPS games with a large modicum of seriousness...put that all aside and get this. Don't be serious for a change.
If you're not either of the two, it's been bundled at least once so try trading for a key.
This feels mechanically different than the first game, but is still quite fun.
*
There is such a rewarding experience whilst playing this game, Lonely Planet does what other titles on Steam do not, all for a very low price.

Even though the game is still in early access long past its promised date, I think that is helping the game. Its like chicken: If you undercook it, you're going to get salmonella. In this case, if it's underdeveloped it wouldn't be very fun, engaging, and will break very, very often (not that it doesn't already, but that can be fixed in the future).
If you can work around the bugs and just wait for them to be fixed, the experience is quite enjoyable... that is until the game runs its life out at between 20 and 50 in-game days (if it lasts longer than that without your save completely dying, I applaud it). Again, that can and most likely will be fixed.
The developers keep adding in new and useful patches every so often, and even drop amusing update posts letting us know they're still there. The amount of people playing and supporting the game is also great. Just enough to keep it growing, but little enough that the "cooks don't spoil the broth", as they say.
All in all, I can't wait for the game to be fully completed, and see how it compares to it when the Sjindie Games video first came out when the game was first put into public early access. Right now it already is phenominal compared to then, and in the future I can only see growth.

Story driven through gameplay. Kind of Steampunky as it's set in a victorian kind of time.
The story in it self is classic, safe and revenge. The twist is that you can take revenge in many ways and the little choices as well as the major choices make the gameplay change later into the game. You can actually get three different ones if you care to play through it again. Levels change with your choices. It might sound cheezy but that doesn't happen to often.
You can go full stealth or full tilt - the powers you pick, or not, will help you decide. The game can be quite challenging at higher difficulties and you can opt out of powers as well, bar one.
The levels are large, have several ways of being completed with some in level extra goals if you like. Or just happenings. Your choice to help, hurt or ignore.
The AI is somewhat clever, lost patrols will be filled in, they'll call for help and so on. As far as AI's in games are smart this one is at least trying, not always very well, but it does put up a some resistance. The actual combat is pretty realistic, not to many bullets or swings with the sword is needed for you or the guards to make a mess of things. Mostly, a gunshot to the head is the end of it.
So not often you get a RPG FPS with a decent story to make it tick along with actually fleshed out opponents.
This game is amazing simple as that.

Disclaimer: I played the game hardly at all, but I highly doubt my impression would have improved over time.
I'm not sure if this game was TRYING to go for a B-film feeling or not, but if it did, it failed horribly. It would be one thing to satirize or parody a B-film, but this game has so many problems that I doubt this was the case.
The voice acting is grating. The voice acting was actually a big reason why I didn't play as long as I probably should have before writing this review. Yes. It's THAT bad. (Made even worse if you choose to play as the female character).
The shooting feels clunky. In early sections, I found myself taking shots at zombies' heads, with my aim PERFECTLY aligned in the middle of the head, only to have every shot miss. I was finally able to hit their heads after my moving my sights downwards more, towards their jaws/necks.
I found some kind of electric gun thing that could shoot a couple of shots and then stopped. I would click again, and just get a 'beep' signalling I couldn't fire.
Apparently, there actually is an indicator, albeit a subtle one. The reticle fades to gray.
Movement is PAINFULLY slow, even when sprinting.
Menus can only be accessed via NPCs.
The first NPC has her nipples showing through her shirt. Don't get me wrong, I love boobs as much as the next guy, but they should have a reason for appearing - Boobs and nips showing up in hentai games? Makes sense. Showing up at the strip club in GTA5? Makes sense. Shows up randomly in a game about shooting zombies? No sense.
Game feels like it wants to be a mix of Doom 3 and Borderlands, but lacks the polish and features to come even close.
On a more positive note, the graphics and environments looked very good, from what I could tell.
Edit: Changed the review so that it seems less like a personal attack on the devs, while still maintaining my criticism. On the internet, it can sometimes be easy to forget that the person on the other end is a living, breathing person with feelings - not just text on a screen.

So far, seven hours in, DE2 has been extremely stable. No crashes, no glitches. I have not even been able to find a bug. This plays like Unreal Tournament III, with zombies. Having a lot of fun with all the armor and weapon customization options, the addition of a Borderlands-style loot system really makes the game shine and keeps things from getting repetitive.
Couple suggestions, if any of the devs are reading reviews...
(1) Add models for the different armor sets in 3rd person. Some of the sets are fairly rare, and take a decent amount of work to get. It'd be nice to display them in coop.
(2) Add a functional jump mechanic so you can leap over crawling zombies, and also hop barriers to get to lower walkways.
(3) Add a 'lean out of cover' mechanic/animation for both the player AND for the Delta 13 soldiers. Nothing fancy, just something functional. Bind it to Q and E default. Secondly, add use of that mechanic as a separate AI package that the Delta 13 troops switch to when they are fighting the player, but not when they are fighting zombies. Their current package of smoothly advancing/crossing/firing between cover points makes perfect sense for fighting zombies, it's the most efficient and is the same thing that I do. However, that would never happen when fighting an opponent who also has firearms IRL, and these guys are supposed to be very highly trained, no? Have them fight from cover when engaging the player, and not move from it unless they've been flushed or flanked.
(Update at 11 hours). Revolvers and sniper rifles are useless in current form. Could be cut from the game entirely, especially the revolvers. Firing rate is abysmal, heavy recoil. For coop, sure, you might want a sniper, but most of the rooms are too small for it.
Melee is ok, but could use an overhaul. Too easy to get overwhelmed. This game plays best right now with the most powerful assault rifle you can afford and as many implants for recoil/accuracy as you can load. Headshot party.
Other than that, so far this is great fun. Currenty playing with Gunnar, going to try a run with Jane to see if the mechanics feel different.

The so called simulators occupy a really huge portion of the actual games, but as in every circumstance there is a big difference between a “real” simulator and a “point-and-click” one.
So if you are searching for something like “happy farm” this is definitely not the game for you:
We cannot take any excuses or shortcuts:
and, sometimes, within the given time period.
So for example you can’t pretend to treat a cultivation just by running on it a couple of time with your tractor but you must be meticulous just as you are supposed to be if you were on a real heavy duty machine doing the exact same work.
we have the classic base scheme where user is required to move around and follow a strict logic with certain actions in order to complete tasks
but then we are at total liberty to decide where to concentrate our efforts in order to maximize gain, for example.
, and so the same happens here: we have to earn in order to develop our farm but also to be able to paid for fuel and supplements needed by machinery, animals, and treatments to guarantee the weel0-being of our farm.
: in just a few minutes I managed to rapidly change perspectives and cameras in order to complete each job!
In this particular scenario keep in mind that
: there are a lot of keyboard combinations that are really useful during gameplay and we can learn all about them while completing the tutorial.
lights and shadows create a nice realistic touch on objects and animals, while landscapes (generated from real-world photos) really seem to animate while playing.
Also the music is quite a surprise: usually we have to deal with some “boring” soundtracks in this kind of games but here we have a really nice enthusiastic soundtrack which also plays as a nice distractor from some tedious assignments.
specially in opposition to those “semi-simulators” that we have seen at least one time on a friends smartphone or tablet.

This game has gotten a lot of criticism, mainly directed towards the pricing of the initial product and the (almost day-one) planned DLC. This criticism was (past tense) warranted and I for one would not have recommended this product at the cost of entry at day one.
However, this is about to change. Evolve is going free-to-play with (what seems to be) a rather fair F2P-model. Given that the main criticism against this game was it's high price tag coupled  with the rather lackluster amount of content it's fair to say Evolve now deserves a second chance. Or first most likely, seeing as only a few people ever bought in to Evolve.
The game itself isn't stellar and has it flaws, some of which are getting "balanced out" in the upcoming F2P "re-release". What the game has going for it is the fact that few games offer what Evolve offers with this level of polish: Asymmetrical multiplayer. 4v1. Evolve is unique for lack of better words. On top of that the core gameplay (gunplay, player movement, playing as the monster etc) is all really good.
Give Evolve a chance. If the game gets a good number of players it's going to be a blast and I'm certain that if given enough time and resources Turtlerock can make a good game great. After all these guys came up with Left 4 Dead, a game I have many fond memories from.

I was late to the video game party. Never really getting into the idea of playing games to beat them until 2007 or so. And I never got into old school shooters. That is, until the year the HD version of Serious Sam: TFE came out. I happened to stumble across a youtube video and thought it looked interesting. Played the demo, thought it seemed cool. Payed the $15-$20 it cost and then came magic. This is in my top 5 FPS games of all time and one of my personal favourite video games. This game introduced me to the old school FPS genre and it easily made me more interested in First Person Shooters in general. The classic version is pretty much just as good, but a lot of effort was done in the remake and the HD version gets rid of that one little texture annoyance from the classics, where looking around really fast made everything distorted from 0.2 milliseconds. Not as good as Doom or Quake, but I am just as nostalgic for it as those games, if not even more so. Just buy it, right now. Don't think about it, just do. If you're worried about the difficulty, very easy is hard to die on and playing in classic co-op, you have infinite spawns. So theres nothing to be worried about. This is also a very good game to introduce you to the old school genre. I hadn't done much with old school FPS (aside from beating 1-2 levels in Doom) and I learned a lot of techniques from this game. I never strafed much in games before and after the first 3 levels of this game I was dodging stuff left and right. It isn't for everyone, but even if you just want a fun game to play through with a friend for a little distraction, it offers that. Although, I might reccomend SSHD:TSE over this one, if you just want a quick game you can marathon with a buddy and then forget about. I however, think it is a downright classic.

So let's start this off with a question: Do you like Tower Defense? Do you like Exploration?
I personally hated tower defense games due to the scaling difficulty level and the constant annoyances.
Dungeon of the Endless isn't a lot like your typical tower defense game.
The map is randomly generated each level, BUT you get to choose the way you explore it, and you can choose where you put your defenses.
Monsters each have unique behaviors that don't change. Once you learn them you can use it to your advantage in any fight.
Heroes are customizable and have their own strengths, weaknesses, and then their own progression. The customization comes through items, and you can find them, buy them, sell them, and in a couple cases start with them.
There's a bit of micromangement, experimentation with strategies, but generally the game is less of a headache and involves less screaming than other roguelikes and tower defense games.
The devs are paying attention to game balance and still put out updates to fix bugs and keep the game fun, even after the actual development cycle is over.
Did I mention that the game has little social links between the characters?
Because it does and it gives even further depth to the characters you love.

Roulette, Apparently it has been around since the 18th century and despite being a seemingly original game it's claimed to be a blending of no-less than 7 different games from around Europe. Given how so many games of this kind exist its roots probably go back to mankind's earliest civilisations. But anyway, its a fusion and one that created something which was interesting enough to persist and spread across the world for over 300 years. Although I don't expect DotE to be around in 300 years time it can very much be compared to Roulette in many ways.
But first lets set expecations correctly. Is it tower defense? No. Not at all. There is a detailed meta-game in tower defense games which players have to learn and due to how restricted players are with tower placement in DotE it wouldn't be fair to really compare them. It has towers, they do specialize but that is about it. Next; Is it an RPG? Well, if you mean do you have stats, levels and loot then yes. It has an RPG character system but not really any more than a MOBA does. Is it a rouge-like? Absolutely. This game will have you on the edge of your seat even when you think things are going well because you just know that the RNG exists to throw a spanner into the works. So there you are, while it has none of the depth you would expect from any of the genres it borrows from they do exist in the most simple ways.
All of this means, DotE is Roulette in every way. It's a mash-up of other game elements and no matter how you edge your bets, no matter how well you play, no matter how many contigency plans you make you can be sure of one absolute fact - you will lose. Maybe not the game as a whole, but you won't ever feel like you can't possibly lose. The game is about planning for the inevitable disaster behind every door and the odds get more and more stacked against you as you progress.
If you like games where you want to feel like you're the underdog then this is it. DotE puts the player on the defensive in a way normally only seen in survival horror games but doesn't keep its hands around your throat continually so that you feel you can't breath. You open a door, you clench your buttocks and for a moment you hold your breath awaiting your teams fate - be that good, bad or just plain horrifying. Once that has passed, the pressure is off and you can take your time planning your next move. Furthermore, it has enough variety in squad configuration, character loadout and environments that you don't feel like you've seen it all after several hours of gameplay.
Here's hoping that SEGA asks the devs to make a sequel.

The twist is that you can take revenge in many ways and the little choices as well as the major choices make the gameplay change later into the game. You can go full stealth or full tilt - the powers you pick, or not, will help you decide. The game can be quite challenging at higher difficulties and you can opt out of powers as well, bar one.
The levels are large, have several ways of being completed with some in level extra goals if you like. Or just happenings. Your choice to help, hurt or ignore.
The AI is somewhat clever, lost patrols will be filled in, they'll call for help and so on. As far as AI's in games are smart this one is at least trying, not always very well, but it does put up a some resistance. The actual combat is pretty realistic, not to many bullets or swings with the sword is needed for you or the guards to make a mess of things. Mostly, a gunshot to the head is the end of it.

This game is amazing simple as that.

I love that I can assign them to their own beds! I love that the cook helps my farmer harvest the fields :D As you can see, I enjoy a lot of the little features in Stonehearth which is why I felt compelled to make this review and share my experience with others.
If you enjoy survival/strategy city-builders with cute pets and citizens + job/class advancements, then I highly suggest this game to you. Imo, this is one of those games that's worth the price tag. I love what the developers have done with the game so far and I'm happy to support this early access title.

This game is growing slowly because their team isn't all that big, and this gave is very complex in its coding to get it all right. One thing about this game that can't cease to amaze me is its creative aspects. Yes, a few more decorative items would be nice, and the ability to customise color and and decor on things like vases and doors, the limits to this game are still quite small. There is no one way to build, plot, or destroy anything. Which leads to my next thought - conrolling. For the first time in a while, a game where you make and change cities at will, without being the avatar is a big step. The most popular example of this are the Sims games, but this adds a survival aspect that Sims doesn't have. Each person has a role, and each with personality. I know, Sims is very similar in that way. But you can't go mining or build whatever, wherever in Sims games, with more than just money as a resourse. I quite enjoy this game, but I do have a gripe - rate of progression. No one wants to play a game where hours are spent on nothing, or the outcome of hard work is a small building for making medicine in. It become long winded when you can only do one task at a time. But overall, if I could rate this game, I would say a good B-. It's not bad, but it could be better. You've got me hooked, Stonehearth, but you have gotta improve a little. There are more pros and cons in this game, like the military aspect, and the random events, but I don't want to go on forever.

One player.  One map.  One mode.  Two guns and a handful of power-ups. Versus an endless horde.  Basically the premise of the game(loosely used within this review) is that you are trapped in an in-escapeable underground car park during a zombie apocalypse.  Your only aim is to kill zombies till you die... from the zombies or from boredom.  At least you get to choose.  Pick-up more ammo, a couple of power-up boosters but mainly just avoid being clawed by the undead crew about to make your day repetitive.  Very repetitive!
+ Numerous power-ups to collect.  Two types of ammo, infinite ammo, invulnerability shield, health, armor and kill all zeds.
+ A few hours of fun for achievement hunters to buff their game completed totals on their profile.
+ Its cheap.  Very cheap on sale.  Should only be considered on sale imo.
- Only two guns to kill the zeds with.  No melee makes this especially bad.
- Only one level.  Only one mode.  Zombies spawn and attack in one endless wave.  Until you die or give up.  Usually the latter.
- Terribly balanced.  Everything is easy at the start but once your score gets to 700k you will experience lulls in what you can do as ammo dries up. As a result power-up stop becoming available and you have to grind away until you rebuild your ammo supplies.
- No coop.  Would have made a big difference to the longevity and replayability of this game.  As it was I uninstalled after getting the last achievement.
* Pre-made graphics are nice to look at but there are only two zombie models.  Still at least they crawl, get up when shot to the floor and can have their heads & arms shot off.
* Okay gameplay.  Its basic and somewhat fun.  Move around.  Avoid zombies. Kill zombies. Pick-up powerups, reload/switch weapons.  Rinse and repeat.
Zombie Parking is superb.  Amazing!  Spectacular!! And then its developer woke up.  Okay so Im joking.  Is it complete pants!?  Well no.  But its no Dying Light!  Therefore if you will imagine Yet Another Zombie Defense but..... without the defense or any other gameplay elements other than shoot to kill!  This is what happens when you make game development accessible to everyone with half-a-brain.  Its a tech. demo at best.  One that should have been built upon, instead of wrapped up, packaged and sold as a going concern.  That - it isnt!
Gameplay is monotonous and not challenging in the least.  Essentially it could be called Zombie 'kiting' simulator for those of you that know what that is.  It does have a certain charm to it and yes there is a solid base for what could have been a decent zombie survival game but it needs more of everything.  More maps, more guns, more power-ups, more zombies, more levels.  Even the explosive fuel cans that can be used to blow-up zombie hordes are limited ffs!!
I know what you're thinking did I pay 80cents or only 5.... or something like that!?!  Yes I did get this on a decent discount but I expect thats what the developer was hoping for.  A quick cash-in on a good start but no follow-through.  Is it worth it!?  Maybe to some people.  I enjoyed my few hours (two games) playing it.
However I cant recommend this game unless you are an achievement hunter looking for a quick +1 completed game on your steam profile or one that loves killing zombies in any shape or form.  If you are, dont blame me - I tried to put you off.  Otherwise all serious gamers should just save their money and put it towards a coffee, some toffee, a beer or some gear.  Or whatever else takes your fancy.

pros: - random map

- diversity in battlegrounds and the lenght of the fields is a nice touch
- decent waittime for AI turn
cons: - no sanctuary and inferno, I know there was a vote by the fans and those 2 were excluded, but Inferno shouldn't have even been on a poll and Sanctuary actually was pretty diverse and nice faction to play with complex mechanics
- some random not often occuring crashes, but for now just 1 save got corrupted after trying to reload
- the battle gauge, tears/blood reputation and specializations from h6 are missing, which were nice
- random map no seas. I've created by now about 10-11 random maps with mixed terrain and there wasn't water in any of them. Dunno if it's some crazy luck or just water is missing from the generator.
---------------------------------
Summed up a solid hybrid between h3 and h5 with some nice game and battle mechanics. Would recommend it, if you wanna just chill and play casually the game.

Dead Effect 2 is like Dead Effect 1, only better. A complex story, better animations, weapons, everything you could ask for.
I'm a very big fan of the first game and I must say that the developers have outdone themselves with the second part, this time around they really have pushed the Unity engine to it's limits. The game uses Unity 5 but it looks like it was made with Cry Engine. And trust me, the game doesn't look like the phone version of it at all.
Originally, an mobile title which released in October 2015, it was later ported to Steam with microtransactions removed (which is AWESOME!!!). Dead Effect 2 is a direct sequel to the excellent 2013's Dead Effect where the story continues right after you kill Dr. Wagner.
Unlike the first game, Dead Effect 2 starts off with you given the option to choose among 3 playable characters with different class specialty and play style. Gunnar Davis is the heavy weapons specialist, Jane Frey takes point as the assault specialist and Kay Rayner whom is the close combat specialist, for those who prefer melee weapons. Each of these characters have their own "unique abilities" which you can improve on later in the game.
There are different game modes (which you can access after progressing with the storyline), in which you can play by yourself or go co-op with others.
As the title suggests, you'll be fighting TONS of zombies, with a variety of mutations, shapes and sizes! And if that bores you, don't worry because the game also has cyber dogs, extremely dangerous soldiers, security drones and insane boss fights to keep you occupied. Although not nearly as good as the other big titles out there, Dead Effect 2 feels extremely solid!
- The new addition to the PC version (which the phone version doesn't have) is the awesome co-op multiplayer mode!
- It has so much content and rare loots that could let you play for hundreds of hours and never get bored.
- A very big variety of weapons.
- Dead Effect 2 is EXTREMELY fun and highly addictive!
- Co-op mode works great and it's the perfect setting for the gamer couples out there.
- For a mobile title, the game has very good graphics.
- No microtransactions in sight. They were remove entirely at the launch of the game on PC and everything in the game can be bought by the in-game currency.
- Enemy A.I. is applaudable as they can react to the player and move accordingly. This provide an additional layer of difficulty to the game.
- It has a LOT of achievements.
- The game uses a variety of minigames during the mission (hacking, turning valves, opening lockers, etc).
- The frame rates drops drastically at some moments, so the game still needs some improvements.
- The animation feels sluggish most of the time. Enemies are slow at one point and suddenly they become unnaturally fast when attacking.
- Nobody plays the multiplayer, Steam Spy recorded only 64 max players as the peak record. Unless you have friends which owns the game, you can forget about playing multiplayer since finding an open lobby is pretty much a rare occurrence.
- The game doesn't have any jump animation which feels weird. Being a super soldier and all but you can't even jump over a small ledge.
- The game design is to be grindy as story missions progress. They become harder and the equipment needs stronger stats at each level, so you have to buy new weapons or upgrade your existing ones.
- The voice acting is okay.
- The mouse acceleration needs some improvements.
- You can't skip the cutscenes.
Even though Dead Effect 2 has quite some flaws currently, they really managed to come up with a very wonderful game which has a perfect combination for the genres (RPG + Shooter style) and with the right amount of work and dedication into the game, I'm confident that this game will hit the tables!
While multiplayer doesn't have many players yet, the singleplayer worths every penny and the co-op is a really fun place to spend you're time in. This game receives from me an 4.5/5, with hope in mind that most of the cons will get fixed.

Having played this game many years ago, not long after it first came out, I can't deny that nostalgia might be a heavy influence on my perception of this game.
That said, Septerra Core is enjoyable. The story, while not a unique experience, does it's job to motivate the characters and the world around you to action. Big bad scary guy who thinks he is the savior of the world, actually seeks to destroy it and rebuild it in his own divine image, yadda, yadda. Point is, if you've played a few RPGs, you've ran through this story before.
What is unique, perhaps for better or for worse depending on your tastes, is the gameplay. It's a derivative of the ATB system found in a lot of earlier JRPGs. The pacing is admittedly very slow. Don't expect most battles, regardless of your level or equipment to take any less than a minute to complete. While the game wants to appear to appear and play like a JRPG (mind you this is an entirely American CRPG) its Western side shines through in it's difficulty. The game is punishing, and never really relents. You can grind, and grind, and grind. But at the end of the day, your wits will have to be about you. Sure, you can cheese a lot of encounters with FATE cards (think games magic system) but you are limited in how many times you can use them before restoring your Core (think a shared MP pool between party members).
Presentation is what you would come to expect from a lot of Western RPGs of the late 90s. Developers really seemed to love their FMVs, which I should note as of the most recent patch, should play without any need for you to mess with the dreaded Quicktime. The music is definitely one of the weakpoints. I wouldn't say it's terrible, or will make your ears bleed. However, there isn't a single song, tune or sound effect that will be memerable, and perhaps more than a few that might actually annoy you (particularly with some commonly reused sound effects).
The real highlight for the game, at least in my eyes, is the attention the developers game to making this Western RPG feel  and play similarly to a JRPG. Remember that in the late 90s JRPGs still weren't really "clicking" overseas. Sure, the Final Fantasy games had started to become a bit of a household name at this time thanks to FFVII, but there were still a lot of WRPG players that weren't willing to adapt to the more thematic style of their Japanese counterparts. This game, while certianly not the only title, went a lot way to helping to bridge that gap. While Septerra Core might end up as more of a historical footnote in that regard, it is an overall fun and challenging RPG whose deficits are outweighed by it's uniqueness.

As a big fan of Trine 1 & 2, getting Trine 3 was a foregone conclusion for me - the trailers and gameplay videos had been whetting my appetite for quite some time already. I must admit though, the jump to 3D was a minor cause for concern. On the one hand it is the perfect direction to go for the series to prevent getting stale, and it offers many new possibilities for puzzles and level-design. On the other hand, the Trine games always were 2D puzzle-platformers at heart, and I wondered how some of the three heroes' abilities would translate to a 3D world.
So, was the wait for Trine 3 worth it? In short: yes, very much so - with the little caveat that only 2 story levels and 1 challenge level have been released so far and the game is still a bit buggy due to Early Access. The developers have promised to add updates and new levels regularly, with the full release coming later this year. Given Frozenbyte's track record I have no reason to doubt them, and judging by the quality of the currently released levels we are certainly in for a treat with the full Trine 3.
The levels are rather long, intricate and inventive, the music is awesome and the graphics are as spectacular as ever - with the added bonus that you can explore the levels a lot more thoroughly because they are fully 3D now. If you ever played the previous games in the series, especially the Goblin Menace levels, you know that the various scenes practically invited you to step into the background, and now finally you have the possibility to do just so. Still, I have to admit actually playing the game in 3D was quite a shock at first, as it means that even veterans from the first two games must relearn some of the character's moves. Especially Amadeus' and Zoya's abilities were distinctly changed and tuned to better fit the 3D world. So I would suggest you take your time in the tutorial level to fully train the new controls, otherwise even level 2 could proof somewhat frustrating. But give it a chance and you'll soon see that the new controls work perfectly well and offer a whole new world of opportunities.
However, not everthing is perfect. I should note that the combination of 3D levels and forced camera positions can make judging some jumps and distances rather difficult. I mostly noticed that when going out of the way to reach some hard to obtain experience shards. For me that is not such a big deal and is easily outweighed by the beauty and enhanced freedom of the game. But others might dislike that kind of trial and error. Still, seeing as death has not much of a penalty and checkpoints are abundant, most people should be able to live with it.
As for the other negative point, the game is currently in Early Access, and it shows. Don't get me wrong, it's perfectly playable, and a lot of fun too once you get used to the new controls. But at the current time a number of more or less annoying bugs still exist, from crashes when resuming a saved game to the music suddenly stopping on random during the gameplay. Also a lot of polish is still missing, so you might notice some missing dialog lines or performance issues due to bad optimization. All of these problems will surely be addressed by the developers until the release of the full game, but people considering to buy the Early Access version shoud adjust their expectations accordingly or else wait a little longer.

Zombie Parking is small zombie killing game. Worth playing for a bit of shooting fun.
You are in a car park with a whole lot of zombies, who are constantly coming out of the vents and from under the walls.
At your spawn area is a row of four items - armour, health, shotgun shells, and rifle bullets - which keep on respawning (although, after you have collected them, you have to wait a while for them to respawn).
The entire game is played in a one-level car park, so there's not a lot of scenery to explore.
The defence weaponry consists of a shotgun and a rifle. You start with some limited ammunition, but you can get more from the spawn area and zombie drops.
Killing zombies will cause a number of them to drop ammunition, armour, and health - as well as some rarer drops, such as double damage and infinity ammunition (the latter is poorly named, as it doesn't last forever).
When you do a few headshots, a red bar appears, and - while it is up - this is your chance to score a lot of points with zombie kills.
I thought that the hardest achievement for Zombie Parking would be to get 1,000,000 kills in one game - but it turned out that getting the armour and health achievements took longer, as - if you are playing the game properly - you hardly ever get hit by the zombies at all; not if you are careful, anyway; so, to get those two particular achievements, you basically have to allow yourself to be hit so that you can fill up again on armour and health.
At one point, when going for the 1,000,000 kill achievement, I was fighting zombies near a wall and somehow the game glitched, and I found myself outside of the car park building and was unable to get back in again - I was not happy. But it only happened once (mind you, I tried to keep away from the walls after that).
It took 3 hours and 10 minutes to get 100% of the achievements for this game - but you should be able to do it a lot quicker if 1) you don't walk through a wall by accident, and 2) you allow yourself to be hit a lot, so that you can keep filling up on armour and health.
Zombie Parking is fun little zombie killing game. It's a cheap buy, so you can expect to get what you pay for; but it's fine for what it is. Play it for a short while and then shelve it - you should get your money's worth out of it.
I only have three small criticisms of the game:
1) The setup implies that you can change the key bindings, but - as far as I could see - the bindings can't be changed (it would be preferable if they could be altered by players to suit themselves).
2) It would have been better if it had a melee weapon, in addition to the two firearms.
3) You can't save your game. It is quite easy to get massive scores in this game, but it's limited by how much time you want to spend playing it at any one time - so, it would be good if you could save your game and then continue it another day (as the game doesn't have levels, game saves are not highly needed, but it would be useful.
On balance, I would recommend this game.
Sure, it's based upon a small map (the car park) and it's repetitive (you just run around a lot and shoot), but for $1 you shouldn't be expecting a massive and amazing game.
The graphics, ambience, and gameplay look fine.
Play it for a bit of shooting fun - that's what it's all about.

This game has gotten a lot of criticism, mainly directed towards the pricing of the initial product and the (almost day-one) planned DLC. This criticism was (past tense) warranted and I for one would not have recommended this product at the cost of entry at day one.
However, this is about to change. Evolve is going free-to-play with (what seems to be) a rather fair F2P-model. Given that the main criticism against this game was it's high price tag coupled  with the rather lackluster amount of content it's fair to say Evolve now deserves a second chance. Or first most likely, seeing as only a few people ever bought in to Evolve.
The game itself isn't stellar and has it flaws, some of which are getting "balanced out" in the upcoming F2P "re-release". What the game has going for it is the fact that few games offer what Evolve offers with this level of polish: Asymmetrical multiplayer. 4v1. Evolve is unique for lack of better words. On top of that the core gameplay (gunplay, player movement, playing as the monster etc) is all really good.
Give Evolve a chance. If the game gets a good number of players it's going to be a blast and I'm certain that if given enough time and resources Turtlerock can make a good game great. After all these guys came up with Left 4 Dead, a game I have many fond memories from.

I recommend this game.  In certain respects, it is even harder than Serious Sam 3: BFE.  It entails blasting enemies level after level getting from point A to point B.  If you are a 'nit picky' guy or a mainstream FPS player, then you would be disappointed by the nostalgia.  The plot is esentially primarily written and, yes, it involves the Egyptians and aliens and, yes, the ideas are cliche/ farfetched.  Given that those same 'aliens and Egyptians' kind of mentality actually gives this game its own identity.  Most people complain about the game because they may not be reading the plot before completeing the level.  Here's why this game is harder than Serious Sam 3:  no sprinting, the enemies can block movement, the enemies block each other (a positive and a negative), the enemies will literally bounce off of structures (i.e. trees, corners, statues, etc.; this is especially prevalent with sirian werebulls, marsh hoppers, and kleers), the kamikazes appear to be faster in this game, as opposed to SS3:BFE but that may be due to the lack of sprinting, enemy ambushes will tend to surround you out of nowhere, you can't always go back for extra ammo, health and armor for most maps (if not all), and the Tommy gun uses the same ammo as the minigun.  Unfortunately, all of the Serious Sam games have an extremely small online community.  If you want to play multiplayer, then you better bring your friends because they may be the only ones who you will find to play with.
