I've bought this game during a sale. Payed $15.99, and I am still disappointed. I gave it the good old college try but got about 4 hours in before getting sick to my stomach from enduring it.
There are four factors that can sum up my experience with this game.
1)
: Absolutely horrendous and lazy. "Too many cooks spoils the broth" as they say, as the writing makes this game seem more like a fan-fiction, than a triple-A title. The thoughts and plot devices connecting each of the missions are incredibly, weak and paper thin. It makes it obvious most of the budget went into the facial animation for major historical figures, and fixing all of the technical errors in their new engine. The first two hours of gameplay thankfully didn't have a "play as a child and experience the death of your parent" section. It did however consist of ham-fisted characterisations of Jacob and Evie Frye.
Half of the dialogue is purely to set up Jacob's delivery of corny one-liner after one-liner like a bad 80s action movie, while his sister Evie shoots him jokingly condescending looks. After all, who can say no to a complaining man-child, who is always asking "why am I not stabbing a person wearing a nazi-like Templar armband right now?" (Because they actually do that in this one). The Crime Syndicate aspect in the game is clumsily rushed into the fore-ground by Jacob, with his bloodthirsty child-like glee, apparently because he's "always wanted to run a gang". Meanwhile Evie wants to do Assassin things and track down a piece of Eden (as always).
While the marketing team tries to paint the two as completely different play-styles, there really is no difference in gameplay between the two until you get to the final levels of progression, where they each are able to acquire 3 buffs that the other can't. Evie's being Stealth Boost, ACTUAL INVISIBILITY, and Throwing Knife Buffs, Jacob's being HP, Firearm, and Damage Buffs. The other 49 skills they can both acquire.
2)
: Assassinations have gotten boring, playing the same few animations of stabbing in the small of your target's back when you're in sneak mode. When the animation DOES differ (when your character is NOT sneaking), it often ignores the context of the environment and plays a random animation. The combat pacing (and choreography) is terrible. There is also now a combo meter, and combat is based around four different mechanics. Attacking, Guard-Breaking, Countering, and Dodging. For each press of the [Attack] button, your Assassin will strike at least twice. In a one on one battle you can mash the button and a normal enemy is helpless. If they're a "brute" enemy, (that is to say the bald-headed strong-man who is the ONLY character model for this archetype in the game) they might try to attack through your combo, which you can counter and ignore. The Syndicate fighting isn't even as well thought-out as the Arkham fighting system, as it doesn't reward you for timing your attacks. So feel free to button mash, and if you split attacks between more than one enemy they get REALLY confused. You never really feel threatened or in danger. If an enemy tries to shoot you from afar, there's no need to worry. You have several seconds to prepare and execute a Nicholas Cage-like bullet dodge with the dodge button. So you can dodge every bullet. Welcome to the Animatrix.
When you reduce an enemy's health to 0, they don't fall or die. They stay in a Punch-Out-esque slouched position, half heartedly attacking you until you perform a horrendously animated "finishing move" on them with the camera zooming in for dramatic effect. Mind you, it's not very dramatic when this happens with literally every single enemy in the game. The sound design is very lacking here as well, as many finishers use borderline stock sound effects for your fists and weapons impacting. Many of these are poorly synced to the animations as well.
3)
:  Everyone complains about the grappling hook/zip line. It is actually a very smart choice in design, and highlights a flaw in the setting. The broad streets of London, and tall flat faced buildings, do not allow AC's free-running/climbing mechanics to shine. One of the quintessential Assassin's Creed features does not translate well to a modernizing city. Who would've thought. I am glad the grapple mechanic was introduced, as it helps gloss over the fact that:
a) The setting was a poor choice for the style of game they were making, which is why they're going back to Ancient Egypt, avoiding Ultra-Wide city streets.
and
b) They absolutely botched the free-run nav-meshing and made it feel unsatisfying and clumsy to run across rooftops and parkour through the city.
The camera is also unbearably close to your character with a very minimal FOV. Very bad for those of you who experience simulation sickness easily, expecially seeing as it jumps around desperately trying not to clip through walls. There is no known way to change this. Not through in-game settings, or ini edits, so have fun on your collect-athon kids.
The clothing physics were also locked at 30 fps for my game, and so i was left wearing a card-board cape for the first hour of my experience. (I use a 60 hz monitor on a medium range rig). There is a fix for this at least, and it's relatively easy to find if you google it yourself.
4)
: Seems everyone in Industrial London is both deaf and legally blind. Citizen NPCs have absolutely NO impact on the environment. Everyone is there solely to react to you. None of their reactions trigger anything. They just stand there in wonder, or scream and beg you not to kill them. Meanwhile the guard standing 15 feet behind them has no idea of what's transpired because he's facing the opposite direction and apparently needs some hearing aids. Enemies have a visual range of maybe 20 feet or 6 meters, and no peripheral vision whatsoever. There is one such example early on in the game which i'd like to point out.
[There is a civilian talking with a guard who is also his friend. I killed the guard in front of him because he wouldn't move on, and I needed to pass him without being detected. The civilian man stood 	there screaming, hands at his side in a nuetral position. Meanwhile the guard behind him was completely unaware of what happened because he was facing 90 degrees to the left. The civilian didn't sound any alarms.]
The AI is bare-bones and is there for decoration.

Dishonored is my favorite game, ever. So you stop playing. A few months goes by, and you're found staring at your game library. Not sure what to play, you're just waiting for a game to present itself. And then, as you scroll by it for the twentieth time, you see it. Dishonored. The game so epic it permanently imprinted itself in your brain. You're PC can't run the newest games, and the games you have look ♥♥♥♥♥♥ compared to the new ones. But not Dishonored. It is so unique you find yourself coming back to it. Never before has stabbing Lady Boyle in the back felt so ♥♥♥♥ing good before. You're back in the amazing, spectacular, brutal world of Dishonored. You have returned to Dunwall to exact justice upon those who have betrayed, framed, and dishonored you. The epic journey is here again. The glorious game is found. Lady Emily awaits your arrival. Be a vengeful Assasin out to redeem your failures, or a Saint above any and all bloodshed, or someone in between.
The world is yours to mold, and every mission can be completed in such multitudinous ways that it makes my head spin.
The World is absolutey unique and a huge pleasure to be in. It feels real and down to earth, but at that same time is so fantastical and out there that it hits this fun limbo that it rolls around in.
The Characters all have something to offer, from the humble boatman Samuel, to the Lords and Ladies of Dunwall such as the Pendleton Brothers and the Ladies Boyle. Even characters with little screentime can leave a lasting impression.
The gameplay is an absolute treat, and even the seemingly mundane task of scaling walls with your blink power can feel free and liberating. Leaping from rooftop to rooftop and then plummeting into the streets below to hide from onlookers feels fresh, smooth and absolutely fun. There is a bit of a paradox though. The game puts a huge emphasis on the "Chaos" system. A sort of Karmic Balance where the more people you kill or destruction you wrought, the darker and bloodier the world gets. And trust me, the effects of chaos are really widespread. So one would assume "Hey! No biggy! I like playing the good guy anyway. No problem." Except for one thing:
Killing people is really really fun. Combat is exhilirating, and instead of many games like this where combat can boyle (hah) down to button prompts or mashing, the setting of Gristol and the City of Dunwall puts a dueling sword and a sub-item or ability in your hand. Maybe you like assasinating targets from the shadows, or setting up elaborate traps, or just blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up, you can do all those, and on top of that, you can engage in intense, fun, and surprisingly challenging and rewarding sword duels. I'm not going to list all the ways you can dispatch your foes.
But if you don't want to kill folks and stick to low chaos, you can do that. And it may just be my infatuation with this game talking, but I didn't mind the lack of fighting. Choking folks to sleep or Sleep-darting a target was still a blast to do. Even if it did expand the length of the game by at least 2 hours.
And heres another fun facet to this game: You don't need to stealth. If you want to be loud as hell and duel with every person you meet? You can totally do that. It's a totally viable way to play the game. (See the youtube series "Corvo Attano: Loudest man in Dunwall" to see an example.) However, that style of play can result in you sprinting through the game, that without the stealth can result in you finishing the story very fast.
But that isn't necessarily a bad thing. This game has absolutely huge replay value. (In fact, at the end of every mission, the game offers you the chance to run through that mission a second time on the spot. On top of stats of statistics including collectables, power-ups, special actions, the body count, and each individual coin on the level.) I myself have ran through this game 3 times now. (The low hour count is due to me playing it on an alternate account, and a concole.) And now that I have it here I will probably keep running through it.
And none of this covers the DLC/Expansions. Which there are 2 extra campaigns focusing on a side character who's very identity is a spoiler for THIS games main story. And if that isn't your style, there is a Mission pack called "The Dunwall City Trials." Which comes with a brawling/horde mode, assasin missions with a twist, and tons of small but (REALLY) hard challenges for the Aspiring Hero, or the Grizzled Assasin. This game has something to offer everyone. And I do mean that. Which leaves me with just one question...Do you think I'll get my own squad after what happened last night?
TL:DR: Dishonored has something to offer every type of gamer, from the casual to the dangerously obsessed. A playstyle for all, and for all the good fight.

Let me start by saying; if you haven't  heard of this game, then you don't get out enough. I've been replaying this game a bit more, and decided it was high time to write a review when looking at buying the DLC (which I also reccommend)
Dishonored, at it's core is a fisrt-person action-adventure stealth based game, with a great story that everyone can enjoy. I believe this was really one of the first games that said, "Here you go, you've got your world, your powers, you play this game your way!" And it really pays off.
The setting is an old Victorian Dystopia with some technologies that we today do not have. You are the Empress's Royal Bodyguard, and you're returning from an escapade in which you inquired other cities for aid during an ongoing plague caused by rats. That plague takes it's tole on the city, with most of it's citizens becoming infected, and survivors roaming the streets is rare. I'll save what happens next for you due to spoilers. But I don't even know why I'm not spoiling, it's like the first 10 minutes.
The story of Dishonored really touched me, and when I played each of the differrent endings, I genuinely felt extreme emotion towards characters that are quite brilliantly built.
The gameplay in this game is AMAZING for both seasoned stealth veterans and those new to the stealth genre. Different difficulty settings really do affect how enemies react to different situations. Harder difficulty means you're easier to detect, and the enemies are harder to fight. The first person perspective is different from most stealth based games which are generally 3rd person, but it really just makes the game all the more engaging. With a wide variety of different gadgets, mixed with your own powers and passive abilities, you really can play the game however you want to play it, and it is AWESOME.
Honestly, Dishonored is my favorite game of all time, and the best port of it is on the PC. It is a MUST buy for everyone. And I will recommend it to EVERYONE.

This game...This game used to be a reason for me to rush home from school. While the bigger Final Fantasy games were tearing up the console world (7 and 8 were on PC as well) this forgotten gem appeared in my life through luck. I was browsing the local Hastings for an interesting PC game to play. I had around $30 to spend from my allowance, and I found Redneck Rampage for around $15. So I immediately grabbed it because it looked hilarious. Well, not wanting to leave with just one game, I kept browsing. It was then I seen a "Jewel" Pack. It contained within it two of the most influential games I would ever play, Shogo Mobile Armor Division, and Septerra Core, for $10. Feeling pretty satisfied, I got back home, and immediately put in Shogo, because who doesn't want to run around shooting things in a mech suit? After a few days of playing it, I booted up Redneck Rampage, and, as I expected, the game was hilarious and consumed me for another week or so. Finally, I installed Septerra Core. The case had no information, no screenshots, or any detail what-so-ever. I had no idea what I was getting into. But then, before my eyes, a gorgeous intro cutscene played, and then I was on the menu. Excited now, I hit New Game as fast as possible. The amazing voice acting, the wonderful rendered 2.5D graphics, the menu options, the character equipment, the stats, the magic system...Everything just hit me like a tidal wave. It was different, but that was a good thing. The story was just wonderful. The lack of a soundtrack made it better to me, because it made it more immersive. There are no soundtracks in real life, so why would a role-playing game need a continuous one? I can't recommend this title enough. To alot of modern gamers, this may seem like trash, but this is by far a superior to many of it's current companions. Enjoy your time in Septerra Core, I know I have.

Ah, X-COM. There's a reason many of my family members say they've "lost a spouse to X-COM," or refer to themselves as "X-COM widows."
This is the very first PC game my father ever bought for me, way back in 1994. I had an old IBM PS/2. I was pumped about a real strategy game... and then my uncle took over the computer and played the game for nearly 16 hours a day. He has continued to do so for over 20 years. Thank goodness he moved out before I turned 18, because I rarely got to play until then. I sat for hours on end as a kid, just watching him blast away at aliens, build bases, swear because he'd lost his colonel and do it all over again with the next month. My father insisted that my computer stay with us, even though I had a much newer computer running XP, simply so I could play the game that I'd wanted to play for years.
Okay, enough about my childhood. The turn-based strategy game never had a better realization in the 90s; this was the god among games. I spent years trying to find a way to play this until I learned about Steam; I actually signed up for my Steam account for the sole purpose of buying this game. The price point of $4.99 is actually worth it, and I got lucky by picking up the entire series for a couple of bucks less.
Planning bases, managing research or manufacturing and hunting aliens defines the X-COM experience, and it's done in such a way that I forget that this game has been around since I started kindergarten. This game is a classic for a reason.
This game was among the biggest reasons of buying my very first PC, ages ago. With its timeless game concept, is still fun to date.

Spacechem is absolutely beautiful. It manages to capture the magic of computer programming and make its joys accessible to a wider audience.
Let me talk about actual programming for a minute. Programming is 90% problem-solving, 9% frustration, and 1% elation over the feeling of dominance. You start with a goal in mind; creating a program for a specific function. Via problem-solving, you figure out how to tell the computer to do what you want it to do. Once your program is finished, you run it, and find out it doesn't work. That's where the frustration comes in. You tweak your code, you run, it fails again. Lather, rinse, repeat about once per ten lines of code, then...VOILA! IT WORKS! It's a great feeling that I can't possibly describe sufficiently.
Spacechem's gameplay follows the exact same process. You start with a goal in mind; taking given input molecules and turning them into given output molecules. Via problem-solving, you figure out how to tell the game what you want it to do. Once your program is finished, you run it and find out something went horribly wrong. You tweak the commands, run it again, fail again, repeat again, until eventually...SUCCESS! YOU ARE WINRAR! You feel like a total bada**.
Amazing, I have no words.

I highly recommend this game. I thoroughly enjoyed playing it multiple times, and I'm the type of person who usually plays a game once, beats it, and moves on (though I do try to do everything in one sitting). Rogue-likes are relatively new to me, and I'm a bit frustrated I didn't discover the genre sooner (glad to see it's having a boom in recent years). There's a feeling of consequence to every action; patience, planning and flexibility are rewarded. Perseverence cannot be understated.
Some folks review the game negatively because of having to restart so often. While I experienced this, I also felt it was part of learning; like in Dark Souls, you screw up, you know what not to do next time. Sometimes that means going back to the bonfire to try the run again or abandoning the current game to start fresh (although random encounters and opportunities will always keep you on your toes).
However, one game when I was on around Floor 9, with my (up to that point) perfect party, tragedy struck: I lost everyone but Nanor, the slow, fat prison cook. I was about to abandon the game and restart, but I instead decided to go for it. The next floor found the Warden and another character, whom I used to hold a wing of the floor until I could recruit him (though he died before I could). Made it to the next floor, found another two heroes to help me, recruited one, the other died before I could. With almost no resources I was able to make it to the last floor. The Warden died in a wave that cost me almost all of my dust, and with no dust, no power. It was a labyrinth of rooms to the elevator on the other side of the level. I took my new companion, Nurse Ratchet, grabbed the crystal, and booked it. Half health with 3 rooms to go, Nanor sacrificed himself (after surviving all the way from the beginning) to allow her to make it to the elevator with only 1-2 seconds of health left (the whole level was red with enemies).
Had no idea it was the last level, and suddenly, victory. That will stay with me because of the permanent decisions I had to make on the fly to see the end. Great fun. Some other factors:
-Interesting characters
-Great humor
-Clever mechanics
-Fun art style

This JRPG style game isn't bad but it's held back by several flaws.
THE GOOD : the voice acting for the main characters, especially Maya is outstanding. The spell cards are fun to combine and the graphics for the time are pretty good. The character models aren't the best but I did like the backgrounds and lighting effects. What music is there is good although there's mainly over world and battle themes. Dungeons are generally silent. Sound effects are pretty good as well and satisfying to hear. The story isn't bad either. Sometimes you have to bring a certain character to an NPC to get them to say something specific or get a key item. Think about which character might be useful with a certain NPC or on what shell.  Your battle attack/spells have 3 levels of power leading to some strategy involved. Enemies can potentially be bypassed as in games like Earthbound and Chrono Trigger and there are no random battles, enemies are on screen almost always.
THE BAD: The dungeons get monotonous really fast, mainly because it's mostly about flipping switches to open doors that often lead to more switches. You're either opening doors or making new pathways and at the end you find a key item or fight a boss. Then you have to usually backtrack out of the dungeon manually which can get annoying if you just want to get out of there and don't care about exp and gold. An option to teleport out would have been helpful. There's also a lot of backtracking,  and clues to what needs to be done next can sometimes be confusing to figure out. Again, bringing the right character along on the right shell can be a big help in this aspect.
Another major glaring problem for me was the slow animations during battle and the sound effects  often took even longer, still playing even when the animations were done. This is especially a problem with the zombie enemies.  I found myself using machine gun characters when I could, just because their attacks are faster.
Characters take one turn at a time or combine turns during spells. You can't input commands usually until the character is done with their attack or spell/item usage unlike say a Final Fantasy game. This stuff is a bigger problem during the first half of the game, once you get a spell card that lets you attack all enemies it helps cut down on this some, but it's still a problem. I found myself running away from battles towards the end, just to get to the end of the game.
Overall I enjoyed Septerra Core for the voice acting and story/setting. The battle system isn't BAD as an idea, and the card concept is neat, it's just feels slow as heck, at least for me. The switch flipping and backtracking got on my nerves fast. If the battle system was just faster, I might not have minded the rest, because that's mainly what made the dungeons more of a chore than anything else. If you're the patient type you might find the battles less grating than I did.
I got it on sale here for a buck so it was worth the price. I'd give Septerra Core a 7/10. I'm going to overall recommend the game. Just be aware of the issues above if you decide to play.

EDIT 4 Oct 2014: I've had some more time to play so I have some new insight. First off, you will NEED a walkthrough. The game does give you precisely zero direction on where your objectives actually are. Second, combat is a CHORE. I find myself dumping as many bonuses as I can into my speed stats just so I can get through it quicker. To be clear, an attack is carried out usually by a combatant jumping toward their attack target, performing their attack animation, then jumping back into their position. This whole time, the entire ATB system stops so you can watch. Combat is structured much like Final Fantasy 13's combat, except far less fluid. You get three action bars, but only one action a turn, and any action you take drains your entire ATB meter. I learned this the hard way. The one thing it does have going for it is that its story is keeping me interested (I do enjoy a good story well told), but combat is going to have to start getting much quicker.

So i wrote a review on this game back in Alpha 8 telling people to avoid until it gets more content.
It is now at Alpha 19 and it has improved A HELL OF A LOT.
It's a great game with about 10-20 hours of play time in one zone (on normal difficulty). Its got a good balance of challenging and chill out time. You have plenty of time to build your stuff when you're not getting attacked.
The only issues i have with this game is:
Cannot stop harthlings from going to a certain point if they need to pick something up. I once had a hearthing run off in the middle of nowhere, get attacked by a golin camp and then hearthlings individually went and tried to pick up the stuff they dropped which ended up killing a heathling a day.
I still think the price is a bit too steep for the current state of it. I'd say its about £9-£12.

Building is still pretty clunky and awkward, don't expect to be able to "quickly build a house" becauase it takes time. And i'm not talking about the hearthlings taking time to build, i'm on about trying to design your own one.
I feel like there should be a feature where it shows you how monsters could get into your base. As i was playing a map once, building something on the side. And i came back and 3 wolves were in by base, killing a few workers because there was an single rock that allowed them to get up onto the platform all the way at the back of a mountain.
Overall: I think this game is worth a buy but only when its on sale. I wouldn't recommend spending the £18.99 on it just yet (sorry dev's, i know you need the income but if you put it down a bit, it might feel a bit more justifiable)

Wut.
But I digress.  On first glance this paints a grim picture on the state of the game but I'll get to why I was enthralled soon enough.
The basic premise of the game is you arrive to investigate the aftermath of the Dyatlov Pass incident.  This is a real-life incident that I encourage you to read about in advance to get some context, to help make the above warblings slightly less bonkers.  In a nutshell, what happened was there a number of explorers in Russia who went missing in the snow and all turned up dead, with various unexplained injuries in equally peculiar circumstances.  And obviously, hidden behind the iron curtain, not much information was made available to the wider world, hence making for the perfect breeding ground for conspiracy theories galore.  This game takes these anecdotes and strange phenomenon reports and integrates them effortlessly into an incredibly well crafted medium-sized world.  After a brief prelude which sees you progress from the train station to becoming lost in a blizzard, you arrive at one of the explorers' abandoned tents.  You are thereby introduced to your map and compass, things you will get to know intimately over the next while, and unleashed into the game world proper.  The map has a whole series of coordinates scribbled on the side, and it's down to you to track each of these locations down, using currently established waypoints and reading the environment.  As you come across more tents, the noted locations, as well as additional flavour notes scattered throughout, the map autoupdates with their locations to help make your job easier.  But there are other things to hinder you, like collapsed bridges or landslides which have obliterated tracks that are marked on your map.  The game world isn't overly huge and it funnels you well so you're never too lost and are free to persue whichever landmark you wish, and figuring out the correct routes becomes a joy and not a source of endless frustration.  But it's not so easy that the game won't turn you around every now and then and then you realise you've taken the wrong cave tunnel or split from your forest path too soon, which all helped with the immersion and sense of adventure.
So all this is the groundwork for some orienteering through a fantastic world, with the game doing a phenomenal job of environmental storytelling.  Uncovering each of the noted locations is a treat, and the destination is every bit as rewarding as the journey.  I won't say too much more to avoid spoilers but the setpieces at these locations are excellent.  As stated, the writing on the notes you discover is a bit average, and I think it suffers a fair bit due to translation.  That and the game could have done with a editor of greater experience for sure to cut down on the excess guff.
The game is just shy of 3 hours gameplay in it from start to finish, unless you're a completist and try to find all the additional journals/articles/notes scattered throughout.  In which case good luck, as you'll have to trawl every inch of the gameworld listening for the telltale sound of a piece of paper fluttering in the wind.  Seriously, play with headphones on in a dark room, this game does audio right.  There are of course additional coordinates scrawled on rock faces throughout the world to help you pinpoint these journal entries, with the scrawlings being in slightly more obvious locations on main routes, but there's no way to note the coordinates down on the map in the case you haven't found them yet, so there usefulness is slightly dubious (you could always use pen and paper but it's a missed beat on behalf of the game).
The game falls short of greatness due to the stilted text, but take an evening and lose yourself in the snow.  You won't regret it.

This game was interesting for the first half an hour or so, but when I realized the vastness of the map and how little I had to go on (both with the plot and about where I was, how fast I was moving, which areas were accessible...), it quickly became tedious to play. A long time ago in a galaxy... not really that far away, I used to play Rogue Squadron on my dad's old Windows 98. And I remember how much fun I used to have blowing up all of Mos Eisley in the same level over and over again. I was a demented kid, but I turned out alright. Didn't I?
Rogue Squadron 3D is a... sequel to the original trilogy? I think? It's not very clear what events are happening when. The story jumps all over the place. Because in one mission your getting Crix Madine (who is one of the generals in Return of the Jedi), but the final battle at the end states that what's happening is right after the Battle of Endor. So I think the majority of the story happens between A New Hope and Empire and/or between Empire and Return. But, honestly, that's not very important.
The story is very thin in this game and its presentation isn't the best. The most you get of any new developments in it come from the small pixelated heads inside ships, as you hear their comms back and forth. Basically, you play as Luke, leader of Rogue Squadron. You go on a ton of missions, and along the way you meet an Imperial who defects to your team and then meet a really mad Moff out of nowhere in the third act, and you beat him, and then there's a random battle at the end. And that's pretty much it.
While the story is pretty messy with tons of decisions that make no sense (One of which being- how do you know you can trust Kasan Moor? Wedge even asks Luke why they have here in the squad, and his only reply is, "Not now, Wedge." Um, I think this is a pretty big thing to be considering!), the gameplay is what takes the center stage for Rogue Squadron, and before I go any further into talking about the gameplay, let me give you this small suggestion:
BUY A CONTROLLER FOR THIS GAME
This game is nearly impossible to play without one. You can get by for the first few levels. It's awkward as hell, but you can get used to it. However, once you're in a snowspeeder and you have to rope up an AT-AT, you will fail. It is literally impossible to pull off with a mouse and keyboard. Do yourself a favor and plug in your old Xbox controller and you will go from getting no medals in levels to getting at least a bronze medal every time you play. At least, that's what happened with me. The control scheme is much better suited for a controller, and the ships are much easier to maneuver with a joystick.
You travel to various planets flying different types of Rebellion ships and perform various tasks against the Empire- whether it's protecting a convoy, blowing up gas containers, or freeing your friend from a prison train. All the ships handle well and have their own advantages and drawbacks. For example, the X-Wing is fast and has good range, but it's very weak on shields and firepower whereas the Y-Wing is slow and has poorer range but it can take a lot of damage and put out a lot as well. It's also fun to play with the secret unlockable starfighters. It's not like Starfighter, where you're constantly trying to move around a clunky ship through tight corridors. The controls are nice and smooth and you're always out in open areas with clear objectives to follow.
However, the biggest problem with the levels is that they are unnecessarily hard. They are hard on their own simply with how well the Empire's AI is programmed to fulfill their tasks- chiefest of which, is serving your head on a silver platter. But the biggest problem with the game's difficulty spikes rested in the stupid dumba** 3-life system Rogue Squadron has. I hate life systems because it breaks the pace of an otherwise fast-paced game. If you die or fail the mission three times you're sent right back to the main screen and have to sit through all the loading screens until you get back into the action again.
Along with that, several missions involve you defending and escort and OH MY GOD are those levels the f***ing worst! Especially the level on Kile II which is- let's all admit- just Hoth again. You have to protect these AT-PT walkers which can be killed off if a snowtrooper so much as sneezes on them, and they move at an agonizingly slow pace so they can't evade fire that easy, and you have to destroy all potential hazards towards them as fast and efficiently as possible or you will fail over and over and over and over again until you throw your controller at a while and have to buy a new one.
That all being said, the game looks pretty good for being so old. I doesn't look perfect (the draw distance is a a big hindrance at that) and the music sounds very tinny, but the other in-game sound effects sound great!
I had a ton of fun flying across the galaxy and maneuvering through tight canyons to blow up TIE Fighters, turrets, and Imperial walkers. While the story is nothing worth nosing through, I'd say this game has enough fun content to keep you coming back for more- especially with all the extras and secrets sprinkled throughout the game! I'm giving Rogue Squadron 3D a 7/10.

I loved this game as a kid, I used to be able to play it with both a mouse and a joystick, and we're talking like "9-year-old kid was able to play it with a mouse" kid of control acceptability. Wasn't easy, mind you, but it was doable.
Now I can't come close to playing the game with a mouse, and without my joystick (can't find it anywhere), the game is literally unplayable for me in any tradiational fashion except for with a keyboard (and that's even assuming this port is better for the joystick than it is for the mouse).
I've seen plenty of ports that had proper mouse sensitivity. This game tries to treat the mouse as if it's an entire joystick, and it flies like a two-legged dog with the mouse, meaning functionally speaking you can only fly using arrow-key controls unless you have a joystick, which is, understandably, quite annoying for a flight-based game.
Please, a couple of hours in control adjustments would massively improve this port. And, if possible, modify the mouse so that the mouse angle is not treated as a direct interface into the joystick (it takes forever to "release" when you turn, meaning that even on low sensitivity it's like driving a car that only accepts input every 5 seconds). The original game handled this better, and the fact that the game is not only aging, but also has bad controls on ports, is obviously disappointing for somebody who played it as a kid.
I truly want to recommend this game, as the game itself is great, it's just the port controls that are bad. I could even live with bad ports if the game was free, but I got it on sale and it was still $4. $10 for an old game with a crappy port? No, not even close to worth it, and that's coming from somebody who loved the original game. I'm actually going to see if I can find my disc of this game in my basement, just to actually be able to enjoy the game.

Was this game even tested? Enemies can detect you though walls from two rooms over. By using the "lean" function you can phase through doors and open them from the other side, or skip entire levels by picking up items hidden behind bookcases. Sometimes game functions simply stop responding, like trying to holster your weapons. You can mash the button or hold it down as long as you want, Corvo just won't put his sword away. Better load a previous save and pray the game doesn't mess up this time. Swarms of rats will sometimes just become "invincible" whereas usually you can hack them apart in a tense situation if you have to, leading to you dying in a corner from a pack of rats because you don't want to alert guards. But why not alert guards? You can just camp around a corner and aim at head-height and wipe out every guard in a building if you make enough noise. You can essentially remove pretty much every threat from the early levels by setting off an alarm, picking a comfy corner and sniping enemies as they round it, even on the highest difficulty setting. The AI will happily form a conga line and only draw their pistols about a second after seeing you clearly, even as they scream tactical information to each other like "Get around behind him" or "Follow me in". That's just background noise. The AI doesn't actually do any of that. They bum rush you like any other dumb enemy in any other game, and will shoot each other as often as they shoot you.
I can't reccomend this game. Yeah it has a lot of cool elements, but throwing a bunch of cool ♥♥♥♥ into a pot doesn't make a good soup. It plays like three different teams had three different ideas in mind for the game with little to no communication, and had to spend months cramming together these half-baked concepts just to get a finished product, with the word """""finished""""" here in the biggest possible quotation marks.
Worst of all? It's boring. I can barely remember the story beyond the most basic elements. Nothing drew me in about it. The plague is zombies! What a shocker! Everything runs on "Whale Oil", oh but it's in these neat cylindrical tubes? So basically it's just a battery? Ok. You can as previously mentioned just corner-snipe entire buildings of guards to death. If you're feeling adventurous, just run up to them and mash the left mouse button until they fall over. They're pathetically easy to beat in melee combat, and I never once even bothered to try to "block".
Overall, a really shoddily put together game. Nice graphics, nice atmosphere, forgettable story, painful mechanics, laughably bad glitches/bugs.

The trend of hyper-long games has left me with a lot of half-finished games in my library -  but Dishonored was never going to be one of those. I was hooked before I ever played it (what part of "magic steampunk parkour assassin" DOESN'T sound like a dream come true?) and once I started I knew I'd be in for the whole ride. The story is relatively generic but the setting and characters make it plenty interesting and compelling.
The gameplay is great fun, and I appreciate that the "good" and "bad" endings (which are based on how much chaos your actions cause in the city as a whole) make sense for the play style that cause them. Climbing around on rooftops and plotting the demise of the guards was awesome, and when you get into the fray you get to make use of some of the other cool abilities.
The setting itself is where the game really shines. The steampunk-esque (fantasy industrial? Whale-oil-punk?) world is full of detail from the grimy streets where commoners scuttle around like plague-rats to the sumptuous abodes of the nasty, plotting upper class. There's a clear aesthetic at work everywhere you look and the attention to detail is clear.

This game is one of few I truly like; most games have a set story, but we all know Bethesta, they always give you more than one outcome, this game is no exception, the game play is basically up to you(in a sense); you can be a lethal, chaos causing maniac, a stealthy assassin, or someone who doesn't kill if they don't have to.
The story deserves a medal, seeing as it grips you almost immediately; physics in the game could use some work and the graphics isn't the best, but it's a gamers rule "bad graphics doesn't make a bad game".
All in all, I give this a 9/10.

Well, well, well where to begin with Dishonored. It is safe to say that when the game was first announced I was incredibly hyped, Dishonored appeared to combine everything I love in a game, great gameplay, unique artstyle and graphics, intriguing story and world. It had all I could ask for in a game. With each trailer my anticipation grew, until finally I got my hands on Dishonored. I waited outside my local game store for half and hour on a freezing cold winter day just to get this game first thing in the morning. And oh boy was it well worth it, Dishonored was everything I wanted and even more once I delved into its many secrets.
Dishonored's plot is a rather simple one. You play as Corvo Attano, personal body guard to the Empress of Dunwall Jessamine Kaldwin. The game starts with Corvo returning home from a assignment to another city, uponing your return the Empress is assassinated right before your eyes, Corvo is thus framed for her murder and falsely imprisoned by the Royal Spymaster and usurper, Hiram Burrows. On the eve of Corvo's execution he escapes death with the help of a group of loyalists, he claim they wish to reclaim Dunwall and place the Empress's daughter and rightful heir Emily on the throne. After you escape you are confronted in your dream by a man known simply as the Outsider, he grants you supernatural abilities to aid you on quest for redemption.
The gameplay of Dishonored right of the bat is just amazing, Dishonored is one of those games that is easy to pick up difficult to master. Most of this stems from its controls, while the abilities are not what I would classify as complicated, with Blink funcitioning as teleport, Dark Vision serving as enviromental scanning, Bend Time slowing down time and so on. All of Corvo's abilities are incredibly easy to use, however it is how the player combines them that will seperated the hitmen from the true assassins. With enough practise you will be zipping through levels and enemies (if ou so chose) without even so much as touching the ground in some cases.
If you get caught or if you simply like going the banging and crashing route Dishonored's combat will not disappointing. When I first played I simply tried hacking and slashing my way through fights, I soon learned that while it got the job done it was doing a great injustice to the core mechanics Arkane had in place. Dishonored combat in meant to be more a game of cat and mouse, baiting your oppenant into an attack only for you to block it and subsequently slit their throat. When you can really nail the combat of Dishonored it becomes one of the most satisfying experiences I have had in gaming, and that is all before you combine your powers during combat, thats when the real fun begins.
Aside froms its combat Dishonored seperates itself from the pack in a number of other ways. The first and most notable of which is its art style. Initially it makes the graphics a little underwhelming but once you adapt to the artstyle the world becomes rather beautiful. While not outstanding from a techology standpoint, there aren't any amazing fog or particle effects, the textures have a sort of painted appearence to them, making it seem as though you are looking at a water coloured painting. At times during the game it is rather striking how much Dishonored can looking like a pianting in motion. This gives the game a very strong sense of atmosphere, especially in darker enviroments, the lighting combine with the striking art creates a beautiful contrast of colors which is just gorgeous. If there is a negative to this choice artstyle it is that sometimes the world can look a little bit flat and textures can appear muddy, however it doesn't distract from the overall game experience.
The biggest and greatest feat of Dishonored however is choice. Oh the amount of choices throughout a given level is quite astounding really. Each level gives you two overarching choices, lethal or non-lethal ways to deal with your main target. Now how you go about achieving this is entirely up to you. If you wish to go in gun blazing and slitting every throat you see, then go for it, more power to you. However if you are more of the caustious mind then you can slowly move through the level taking out or ignoring each enemy as you see fit. It is all really up to how you proceed, what route, what weapon, where or whether to hide a body, all this is up to you on your road to revenge.
If there is one negative I can say about Dishonored is that is a fairly short, taking roughly 12 or so hours complete a decent playthrough. Which wouldn't be a major issue as most single player games are that length these days except around the 10 hour mark you really feel like you are hitting your stride as Corvo before the game ends somewhat suddenly. It is a slight let down it what is otherwise an amazing title.
Also the two main sets of DLC and fantastic as well.

An RPG classic, updated with lots of ease of use and convenience tweaks, customization options, and improved modding support. (Yeah, I'm not a fan of the new 2.0 character sheet, either, but now the interface is very easily moddable, so you can change it if you want!) Story-wise it's not as developed as BG2; there's a lot of just wandering around having random encounters in the wilderness, and there's not much interaction with your party members. However, I actually prefer low-level 2nd edition D&D combat to high-level "mage chess," and there's an active modding community with plenty of ways to add NPC interaction and other enhancements to your game.
The biggest downside is that Steam makes you install updates before playing, which will break any mods you have installed and wreak havoc with your savegames using those mods. You have to backup your old modded game and launch it outside of Steam in order to keep playing. I don't know if this will get fixed in the future, but it's an important consideration if you're thinking about whether to buy BGEE from Steam or GOG.

Ok, I remember playing this title back when I was much younger and I was gifted this by a very good friend from Amazon VGF. First off, if you get this game, get it from gog. The fix for many issues in the steam version is uninstall the Quicktime that Steam installs and to torrent the executable form a gog download. If you're going to need to get the file from gog in the first place, you might as well purchase it outright from there unless it's deeply discounted on Steam. If you do get from steam, be sure to uninstall the quicktime that was auto installed and install the version that is in the game folder as this will fix some of the issues.
First off, anyone needs to realize that this game was originally released in 1999 so don't expect a mind blowing graphical experience. Also, the manual link on Steam doesn't populate anything so you'll need to go to the following link if you don't want to kludge around to see what works.
Combat revolves around an ABT that has different sections that fill as time moves on during combat. Enemies appear to have the same ability but they usually seem to only utilize their weak/quick attack from what I've seen since starting the game. The voice acting is pretty decent when you consider the age of the title.
Alright, now that we have all of that out of the way, we get down to the nitty gritty details of whether this game is worth your money and your time and the answer is No. If you're like me and have fond memories of playing this at a younger age, this will rip the blinds from your eyes and make you realize that not all games are worth the time invested in. The story is ok at best, the controls take a while to adjust to and never actually feel 'right' and the game doesn't give the option to remap them to where they feel more comfortable. If you enjoy jrpg's and can get past the technical issues, I would still recommend looking elsewhere as there is a decent collection of titles to choose from.

My only other experience with this genre is RimWorld. I really enjoyed that game but there was something missing from it for me. I think I found it in this game and that's design. I won't try to compare the two games that much but its just going to happen.
+Pros+
+Personalized building designs that allow you to create your own buildings from scratch
+Job progression through experience working with certain tasks (ie. a Farmer can become a Cook once they reach level 2 and have the necessary tool)
+Progression in the fact that you will be approached once your village becomes big enough to establish yourself as a town. You even get rewards for it( Edit: Tier 2 building templates, Tier 2 Random vendors, TIER 2 BGM!! )

-Cons-
-With cons I have to get nitpicky and this is where my RimWorld comes into play. Trust me I know its still EARLY in developement.
Edit: A serious Con for me but I know its just a bug and bugs will go away but since it's happened more times than once is this: You build a building. You put items in that building, chests, beds, etc. You get down to the last piece you want to put in the building and you get a stacking error where the outline of the piece goes into the building but that's it. For the Cons section, I truly had to reach deep within my nitpickery to come up with personal negatives. I can get over those things rather quickly honestly.
All in all this game is amazing for where its at. I want this game to keep continuing in its production and I will support it any way I can until its fully developed.

I played the original Assassin's Creed back in 2007. That game wowed me. The ability to climb ANY building? And I could be this cool ninja-like hooded killer that could coordinate just HOW he wanted to assassinate a target? Wow!
I played Assassin's Creed 2 in 2009. That game wowed me. They improved every mechanic from the first Assassin's Creed. I loved where it was going. The story was AMAZING! I felt a sense of progression as if I was growing up with Ezio Auditore (the assasssin in that game). We were with him from the moment of his birth to the moment of his death.
I played Assassin's Creed 4 in 2013. That game wowed me. They removed the ability to kill a target any way you wanted but in its stead, they allowed you to explore the open seas of the Caribbean. In addition, the story was amazing. Just like Ezio's story, the story in Assassin's Creed IV had progression to it. The person you were and the state of the world in the beginning of the game changes durastically by the end. It also tied some loose ends from AC3 that lingered.
Now, I come to this game. I am not wowed. In fact, I am disgusted by this game. For one, Ubisoft charges you REAL WORLD CURRENCY to buy virtual money. Yeah, you remember the money you had to earn in AC2, 3, 4? You can now just pay a low fee of $30 for 100,000 in game money. The money doesn't even get you anything special. You buy things just like you could in AC2 (medicine, bullets, etc).
The story in this game is absolute trash as well. The Jacob Frye voice actor sounds like a random guy they picked off the streets. "Hey buddy, if we bought you a pint, would you like to do the voiceover in our game?" The guy overexaggerates EVERYTHING he says. On top of that, the story seems to be going nowhere. The plot established from the first game is long gone. There is no sense of mystery. However, that is not because questions were answered. If anything, questions were UNANSWERED from the ending of Assassin's Creed 3. It doesn't seem to progress anything. It's just another Assassin's vs Templar's story with no ultimate end in sight.
That doesn't mean everything in this game sucks. In fact, the environment is AMAZING. The size of London as well as the beautiful graphics really captivates my eye. Unfortunately, the animation for both running and combat is trash. It looks like a game for babies where you're controlling Mr. Wiggles (I don't know what character that is, it just sounds like a character that wiggles his arms everywhere until he hits someone). The running animations look like they were ripped from 2004's Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas multiplayer mode.
I really wanted to like this game. I wanted to find a semblance to AC1 or AC2 but they've lost the plot. Ubisoft has lost the plot, guys. They plan on releasing a new AC game in 2018 so let's hope to heck they get on with the plot.
I give this game a 6/10 - it's a great game on its own but it doesn't live up to the hype of the Assassin's Creed series. They should have made this a spin-off series called 'Creed of Assassins' or something. At least then I'd understand it's a story taking place in the Assassin's Creed universe and not an actual continuation of the story.

First played this game a looong time ago, and it is still awesome and hilarious!

Serious Sam, the character, is a time traveller sent back to ancient Egypt to fight aliens for reasons. Serious Sam, the game, feels more like it came from another dimension, a dimension where shooters never turns dust brown and clothed in ridiculous pretensions of militaristic realism. It is bright, colourful, imaginative and wilfully shallow and stupid.
To my mind the most pleasantly surprising thing about Serious Sam is how simultaneously thoughtful and mindless it is. The mindlessness is obvious, you shoot all the aliens with the big guns. The thoughtfulness springs from varied nature of the enemies and weapons combined with how refreshingly fair and open the designers were about their scripting.
The scripting is simple but brilliant. This is a game that will shamelessly spawn enemies directly in front of you if that is what the scripting calls for. This is game that doesn't give a damn about real world physical possibility so if it clashes with their level design then it can take a hike. On the other hand it also never appears to use infinite re-spawning of enemies. This allows for the player to play with the scripting, triggering a wave of enemies and then retreating slightly to deal with them before progressing. This might sound shoddy but it isn't, it really isn't, it is actually great because it allows the player to fully play the game rather than just experience it as a rollercoaster. This is a game that is made to be played rather than merely taken as some sort of an interactive cinematic experience. I won't spoil it but if you pay attention you'll notice the game even establishes an informal convention regarding some optional waves of enemies where the trigger can be identified and avoided by the play if they just want to continue.
Honestly, this isn't the sort of game I love. I was never a fan of old school shooters. I like to sneak about and take things slowly rather than charging in all guns blazing and all guns blazing is Serious Sam's thing. I can't deny that this sort of thing has its place though and this is perhaps the best game I've played of this type of shooter. If you've just had a stressful week and just need something loud and stupid to comfort you then Serious Sam might be just the thing.

This game is a love letter to the developers daughter as it seems because she voice acted the character and the main is a female child. More importantly though it's an homage to Zelda II: The Adventure of Link from the NES days of yore...
I think Zelda II is highly under rated and one of the most challenging and fun Zelda games in the franchise... I'd even go as far to say as I enjoy playing it more than Ocarina of Time just because of it's simplicity but for some reason Super Chibi Knight just misses the mark in a lot of ways.
The art style isn't my cup of tea, it's a bit sloppy and childish looking but I guess that's the theme, I just wanted to try it for the RPG / Action elements but the problem with that is, the game mechanics are really bad. Hit boxes are very sensitive in this game and your characters reach animation is abysmal. You literally have to be micro pixels away from enemies in order to damage them. The sensitive hit boxes is a huge issue right from the beginning, but with some over leveling you can persevere and get through the first chapter. This however becomes a huge issue later in the game, even after you're maxed out, the enemies can kill you in only 4 or 5 hits and their range is far superior to yours.
There are two paths through the game, Beastmaster and Sorcerer... but it's more like sword spell... The Beastmaster side of things reminds me more of Adventure Island II and is the easier path to take through the game. The Sorcerer side (Sword Spell) is much more reminiscent of Zelda II... which is funny because that path takes place on an Island... go figure.
A word of warning, there are many missable achievements in this game, a lot of which are convoluted and cryptic and there are two points of no return which you are warned about before you proceed. If you don't happen to get things done in a specific chapter, then you'll have to start a new game from the beginning and try again. From what I can remember, Zelda II allowed you to backtrack to every area in the game so if you happened to over look something, you could always go back... this game doesn't allow for this... it's just lazy and sloppy game design in my books.
I bought it for 2 bucks and some change, so I'd say, yeah go for it... but for an 11 dollar price tag, it's not really worth the price. There IS a lot of replay value here if you can stomach the grind, but to beat the game skipping certain spells / abilities and not losing a single life is a bit too much in my books... It will call for heavy levels of aspergers and OCD... as well as not having a life... as the achievement states.
I appreciate the effort to re-create the magic that was Zelda II but Zelda II, it's not... 5 / 10. Needs a lot of fine tuning for the battle mechanics if it's going to stand up to a game as legendary and tight as Zelda.

Well, well, well where to begin with Dishonored. It is safe to say that when the game was first announced I was incredibly hyped, Dishonored appeared to combine everything I love in a game, great gameplay, unique artstyle and graphics, intriguing story and world. It had all I could ask for in a game. With each trailer my anticipation grew, until finally I got my hands on Dishonored. I waited outside my local game store for half and hour on a freezing cold winter day just to get this game first thing in the morning. And oh boy was it well worth it, Dishonored was everything I wanted and even more once I delved into its many secrets.
Dishonored's plot is a rather simple one. You play as Corvo Attano, personal body guard to the Empress of Dunwall Jessamine Kaldwin. The game starts with Corvo returning home from a assignment to another city, uponing your return the Empress is assassinated right before your eyes, Corvo is thus framed for her murder and falsely imprisoned by the Royal Spymaster and usurper, Hiram Burrows. On the eve of Corvo's execution he escapes death with the help of a group of loyalists, he claim they wish to reclaim Dunwall and place the Empress's daughter and rightful heir Emily on the throne. After you escape you are confronted in your dream by a man known simply as the Outsider, he grants you supernatural abilities to aid you on quest for redemption.
The gameplay of Dishonored right of the bat is just amazing, Dishonored is one of those games that is easy to pick up difficult to master. Most of this stems from its controls, while the abilities are not what I would classify as complicated, with Blink funcitioning as teleport, Dark Vision serving as enviromental scanning, Bend Time slowing down time and so on. All of Corvo's abilities are incredibly easy to use, however it is how the player combines them that will seperated the hitmen from the true assassins. With enough practise you will be zipping through levels and enemies (if ou so chose) without even so much as touching the ground in some cases.
If you get caught or if you simply like going the banging and crashing route Dishonored's combat will not disappointing. When I first played I simply tried hacking and slashing my way through fights, I soon learned that while it got the job done it was doing a great injustice to the core mechanics Arkane had in place. Dishonored combat in meant to be more a game of cat and mouse, baiting your oppenant into an attack only for you to block it and subsequently slit their throat. When you can really nail the combat of Dishonored it becomes one of the most satisfying experiences I have had in gaming, and that is all before you combine your powers during combat, thats when the real fun begins.
Aside froms its combat Dishonored seperates itself from the pack in a number of other ways. The first and most notable of which is its art style. Initially it makes the graphics a little underwhelming but once you adapt to the artstyle the world becomes rather beautiful. While not outstanding from a techology standpoint, there aren't any amazing fog or particle effects, the textures have a sort of painted appearence to them, making it seem as though you are looking at a water coloured painting. At times during the game it is rather striking how much Dishonored can looking like a pianting in motion. This gives the game a very strong sense of atmosphere, especially in darker enviroments, the lighting combine with the striking art creates a beautiful contrast of colors which is just gorgeous. If there is a negative to this choice artstyle it is that sometimes the world can look a little bit flat and textures can appear muddy, however it doesn't distract from the overall game experience.
The biggest and greatest feat of Dishonored however is choice. Oh the amount of choices throughout a given level is quite astounding really. Each level gives you two overarching choices, lethal or non-lethal ways to deal with your main target. Now how you go about achieving this is entirely up to you. If you wish to go in gun blazing and slitting every throat you see, then go for it, more power to you. However if you are more of the caustious mind then you can slowly move through the level taking out or ignoring each enemy as you see fit. It is all really up to how you proceed, what route, what weapon, where or whether to hide a body, all this is up to you on your road to revenge.
If there is one negative I can say about Dishonored is that is a fairly short, taking roughly 12 or so hours complete a decent playthrough. Which wouldn't be a major issue as most single player games are that length these days except around the 10 hour mark you really feel like you are hitting your stride as Corvo before the game ends somewhat suddenly. It is a slight let down it what is otherwise an amazing title.
Also the two main sets of DLC and fantastic as well.

It gets a recommendation...barely, even the 2.0 patch won't change that.  I won't spend too much time looking at the original game.  It was a wonderful game which deserves your time.  Instead I'll spend time looking at what was changed and if it is worth your time and money.  However they did little to expand beyond the original game and what they accomplished could be done, and has been done in some cases, with mods.
For the good, it's Baldur's Gate as it was when it was created with some engine upgrades and a little expanded content.  Baldur's Gate needs no more recommendation than its name, if you enjoyed Black Isle, Obsidian, and Bioware's entries, you'll enjoy this one.
The first you see at the title screen is the addition of a second campaign - The Black Pits.  There is no story or questing - this is a encounter mode where you kit out a party and fight a series of encounters with monsters and parties until you, or they come out on top.  This mode has real value for multiplayer games.  Grab your friends, grab some gear, then run in with your characters and beat up all the bad guys.
The second you see is the addition of the Bauldur's Gate II class kits and classes to the game.  These don't push too hard on the difficulty as your companions will only use the default classes (with the exception of the new companions).  If you play a multiplayer game with pregenerated characters, this could be a problem if you care about encounter balance.
There are four new companions - Neera, Dorn, Rasheed, and the hidden one.  For all but the hidden one, they come with more questing, dialogue, and story which makes them very valued.  The only problem being Dorn and Neera's overpowered capabilities which make them almost push button choices for a min-maxed party.
Edit: Just turned it back on and played for a while after the 2.0 patch.
Hoo boy, this update is either a love it or hate it update.
Some nice things are there, like the ability to have off-hand weapons and 2 handed weapons in inventory slots for easy weapon swapping without having to play with the inventory.  The journal was also updated and I will sit in disagreement with everyone and say it's better - the old journal was nasty.  There are five quicksave slots.  There is also a new class - shaman - which functions as a druid with spontaneous casting like a sorcerer with a few extra abilitites.  Equipment selection highlights characters which can use it and characters/loot stands out in pausing/maps/and in the overworld.  Incidentally I like the changes better over the old UI and feel this is what they should have aimed for when they made an enhanced edition - a real enhanced edition and not a 2015 pc port of an old game.  This is all, of course, based on preferences.
That said, the new UI does have its share of problems, several problems.  First, the interface is too gimmicy, something simpler would have done better and made for a less jarring transition between the old game and new updates- the new map screen demonstrates this.  Once the expansion is installed, the UI changes to a black background, which I do not like.
The worst of the changes are the bugs and crashes which come with it.  There are more bugs and crashes since the 2.0 overhaul, not enough to cause me to do any more than annoy me.  It does bother me that stability has gone down and the old 5 USD version of the game can manage it with fewer crashes if you have the right mods installed.
One thing I will say in agreement with other reviewers is - the wrong time to introduce a major overhaul of UI and gameplay is not years after release, it is prior to and on release.  Pushing this much change on the game will create a jarring change where you open the game and it's not the game you remember.  This will chafe with your player base you will receive a lot of much deserved criticism from all sides for your decision.
While the remaster does, at this point, do things differently enough to stand out as its own game, many of the changes were not that much beyond the original and feel experimental and sometimes unwelcome.  The UI is a case of love it or hate it.  It's biggest competition is Bauldur's Gate via the old version on GoG with mods to update it to work on current systems.  While I like this version enough to recommend it, that old version works well enough to be serious competition for this game and may serve your preferences better.

Final Fantasy, toned down in terms of length, and turned into 3D (in comparison to like, FF 1,2, and sorts). Gameplay-wise, you know little of what to do unless some characters explicitly specify you where to go, but fortunately the areas aren't as extensive and misleading as FF's are, so catching up to where you left at will be relatively easy.
Combat goes as follows: you can have up to 3 characters at any one time following you, each with different stats, play-style, and skills. When you're in combat, there is a bar under each of your characters that fills up as time goes on, with 2 3-digits numbers that represent your HP. The bar is divided into 3 parts; simply put, if you let it fill in one part, you can only use the basic weapons/moves which deals less damage, but if you let it fill up entirely, you can use more damaging moves (and the same goes for using cards, this game's equivalent of magic). You click on a character's frame when at least one bar is filled up, select the move you want to use (or use items, or invoke card powers), and target the enemy. There is a big bar of blue on top of the combat interface; that's your core energy, or what you'd call Mana, MP, SP, or whatever. NOTHING in combat regenerates, even post-battle (unless you manually use items or rest to recover those combat stats), so keep in mind when you do anything mid battle. The game is generous enough to tell you that when you use a certain move or card, the energy bar shows how much energy that move/card is going to use up, so you can plan your moves carefully. Overall, the combat feels balanced; challenging if you rush through the game with zero grinding, and rewarding if you decide to grind in one area.
However, the game does not tell you what any of your character's stats do, so you pretty much have to experiment with each, or deduce yourself what each does. Also, despite the game telling you where to go next explicitly through well-voiced NPC dialogues, it does not tell you what to do when you're in said location.
The plot is quite linear, with little, but appreciable amount of side-missions. The lore is, personally, rather extensive for a game that has no sequel. You go from place A to place B, go to C, then back to A for some quick stuffs, and move on to D.
Laziness overtook me. I'll just say that if you're someone who enjoys FF or JRPG in general, puzzles, and exploring, this game is worth the price.
P.S. get the official patch for this game, otherwise it's unplayable for Windows 7 and above. I wouldn't recommend installing the unofficial patch because it made the game run on like, 2 or 3 fps.

So I got this game for about $3 with all the DLCs on a sale a few days ago and whoo boy is it a blast, short answer, if you like turn based strategic resource management, and real time tower defense with controllable units with all kinds of crazy abilities, get this game. Now on to the in depth.
Pros
-The soundtrack for this game is amazing
-There is a huge variety of hero combinations, usually starting with 2 heroes, and being able to have up to 4
-You can change the way the game plays by selecting different escape pods
-There are hidden storylines between characters for you to discover that unlock you lore about the game and some cool concept art
-Multiplayer is a wildly different experience from the standard game, with each player getting to control a single character and everyone splits resources
Cons
-Multiplayer has a bug where when everybody selects ready it will only load the host into the game, while everyone else gets stuck on character select, this can be kind of frustrating for getting a game started, but I've never had problems once properly getting into a game
-The only 2 difficulties are Easy... and Too Easy. This is false advertising, this game is brutally punishing even on Too Easy until you really get comfortable with it
-The tutorial is pretty lackluster, it gives you the controls and that's about it, you have to figure most of the things out by yourself
-Most of the story lines, while really cool and often hilarious due to the dialogue, often end in characters getting debuffs or even dying, potentially ruining a hard run right at the end by killing off one of your strong heroes

Spacechem... Oh, Spacechem.. Where to start!?
Tax your grey matter to it's limit!
Do you hear the words "Puzzle game" and get a general feeling of dis-interest? Do you think about chemistry and then immediately stop thinking about chemistry? Fear not! Spacechem is one of THE MOST unique puzzle experiences you will EVER have! Don't be afraid of it's chemistry topic, either - For while the compounds you'll be breaking down and assembling are real, with appropriate atomic bonds, you don't need to understand a lick of chemistry to play.
The puzzles involve you designing the interior of atomic reactors, using robotic manipulators called "Waldos" that move on paths you specify and obey commands you place on those paths to grab, rotate, bond & de-bond atoms and a host of other actions to transform raw input compounds - one molecule at a time - into the matter you need.
The game is free of bugs and has high production values. There are enough levels to keep you working for a LONG time, split into different chapters taking place on different planets with the beginning of each chapter introducing a new reactor [game] mechanic. The levels get devilishly difficult and due to it's nature, there are almost infinite ways to solve any puzzle. As long as you output the correct compunds to the waiting shipping barge, exactly the steps you take to create that compound are entirely up to you!
This game will tax your problem-solving, logic and lateral-thinking. Highly recommended for those with an above-average IQ and highly recommended for anyone who wants to sink their teeth into a real mental challenge.
If you like having your mind blown then this is the game for you. Make your way through these brain teasers as you learn more and more about SCIENCE!!

I am not quite sure what I expected when I started up SpaceChem the first time. Perhaps "High School Chemistry: Puzzle Game Edition." If that had been the case, I probably wouldn't have complained. What I got, though, was something rather different and much more impressive.
At its core, SpaceChem is a process engineering simulator. It has a very smooth learning curve, and gives players plenty of time to ease into the systems and mechanics. But the really interesting part isn't simply managing to "complete" one puzzle to the next, but
you can complete each puzzle. There are multiple factors which are measured at the end of each level, which means that optimization is almost never a one-way road. You're balancing your emphasis on the time it takes to finish, the number of reactors you're using, and how complex the instructions within each reactor are. Of course, you could always take the lazy way and just try to get through each puzzle as fast as you can to see what's next, leaving optimization as something to look at in the distant future.
Why the interest in progression, though? Because SpaceChem actually has a good story. It's told largely through pure text logs at the start of every several levels, but it does an outstanding job of linking the player to the protagonist. You're not sitting at your computer or laptop solving some random puzzles, you're a chemical engineer working on complex problems with often less than adequate equipment and dire situations in the way of getting the job done. The way this is extended further to using your knowledge of the engineering processes to solve
-manufacturing problems is absolutely brilliant, and a fantastic example of telling a story through game mechanics.
As fair warning, though, even without working toward optimization, the game becomes quite challenging in the later parts. People looking for more casual puzzle games may want to think twice before diving into this one if they're planning to work through to the end.
