There are games that are good. There are games that make you addicted. Then there is XCOM...
It's the end of the 20th century. In response to growing alien threat, few governments decide to fund and XCOM organisation, solely dedicated to neutralising forementioned threat. Player becomes Commander of the force.
Game consists of two levels. On the Geoscape, you manage bases, research (come on, all this sweet loot left by deceased gray cabbage. I know you want it.), manufacture and more. Starting with single base (preferably western europe, you have radar coverage over whole Europe, part of Russia and Northen Afrcia), few soldiers and fighters equipped with conventional terrestial weapons. It is sufficient for the first few weeks, but after recovering UFOs and aliens, both dead and in custody, you will get better equipment: Laser weapons with unlimited ammo, powerful plasma-based armament, durable armors, UFO-looking fighters or even possibility to make your soldiers use their Psionical abilities against aliens. But to get this, you need to get some UFOs down. Send an Interceptor, and use his persuasive rockets to make aliens crash. Then, Tactical level starts.
Before engaging remaining UFO personel, you have to equip them: only equipment on the Skyranger (XCOM troop transport) will be aviable. Then you investigate crash/landing site, eliminating survivors of the crash and savaging their technology (ones that havent been destroyed during firefights, that is). Honestly, these are emotions: when panicked rookie accidently kills enemy Muton (typical tank) that was hidden in the fog of war with a rocket launcher, ready to kill my whole squad. Taking your first Etheral alive (remembering these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s can mind control♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you). The moment you have to choose wheather to lose your best soldier and have few remaining ones get back to Skyranger to escape, or risk all of them to finish the mission. Taking out your first allien base. Oh, yes, different mission types.
Other than fighting with crashed/landed UFO crews there are few more battle types. In order to make XCOM look incompetent, aliens can launch a Terror mission on one of the cities. In these missions, your score is determined not only by your casualities compared to the aliens killed, but also civilians alive at the end of the mission. Not engaging in this type of mission makes it almost certain that nation will sign a secret pact with aliens and leave XCOM project. On the other hand, when you encounter 10 chyssalids on the terror mission (community hated, extremly dangerous terror unit), that country can go **** itself.
Having a base close to the battlefield makes everything a bit easier. Therefore, it sould be no suprise that aliens will try to build bases on the earth. For you it's a pretty nice target: tremendous amount of artifacts can be salvaged, as long as you manage to neutralise the crew. To make it all a bit more balanced, you might find that one of your bases (you should have few of them, to have world covered by radars) will have visitors from outer space. Just saying. Last mission type is obviously visit on the Red Globe, where you put end to alien invasion. IF you won't get destroyed by the time you are ready.
Research and Manufacturing are important parts of the game, though simple: Labs discover and invent things, and engineers make them. Amount of the research topics is also worth mentioning, since there are no fewer than 60 topics, most of them giving new items, few of them giving you UFOpaedia entries, and few ones required to go to Mars.
Overally, i find it quite sad, that this game is much more complex than many modern games. If you manage to get through ancient graphics and interface, a bit challenging controlls and few other tiny problems, you get very good and addictive strategy.

This game may not look as pretty as the newer versions but the game play is still as addictive as ever. There are also a number of features in this original that the newer games still haven't matched, like having multple bases and the longer game experience not to mention my favorite, fully destructable terrain. If you love the newer XCOM games do yourself a favor and play the original X-COM.

So this was my refund request that I decided to paste into this review, please do note that I may not be the best "gamer" but I do find myself to be likely above average. This was also posted without being able to get mounts, which likely would have assisted in the game, but the reason for this is explained further down.
As someone who has played the first Chibi Knight multiple times through, this game was a disappointment in quite a few aspects. The issue for the game is in its game play along with some other technical issues.
It frequently crashed along with a variety of glitches that would interfere with game play. I would constantly encounter a glitch in which holding the down arrow to block would also move the camera down a good bit, and it would never return to its original position unless I died, or relaunched the game. Enemies would also glitch into floors and other objects making them unreachable, locking me into the area forcing me to relaunch if I were unable to leave the room and come back, even then sometimes the enemy would still be stuck. I've spent at least an hour just messing around seeing if I could fix the game and relaunching.
Battle mechanics felt clunky the whole game. Controls were unresponsive in dire situations and enemy attacks were absolutely infuriating. A great example of this would be the "Panda Witch" fight. This fight would start off with the Panda in the battle roaring, blasting you a good distance. The Panda would then roll at the player, and with experimentation, considering the game provides almost no guidance what so ever, the player would find out that they were to hit the Panda, causing it to bounce around the room. The witch, flying near the roof of the room, would be hit by this Panda EVENTUALLY (spending 2 minutes dashing under a panda with broken hit boxes is not fun at all). After the panda would hit the Witch out of the air, the Witch would fall to the ground, becoming helpless for a certain amount of time, letting the player wail on the Witch for damage. The Witch would recover and fly back into the air after the player deals a certain amount damage. The Panda would repeat its action, but the Witch would start blasting green orbs that home into the player that dissipate when they hit you, or after a few seconds. These move at a decent speed that the player could dodge with enough focus and skill. However, the problem with this phase is that the Witch would shoot out multiple orbs in quick succession, after the first orb is fire, about a second or less later the second one would be fired, making it almost impossible to dodge them. It is extremely difficult to jump over the first without getting hit, or sliding under it. The "easiest" way to dodge them is to run to the other side of the room before, or while she fires the first orb. However, you would then half to likely deal with the panda bouncing around the room, the chance to dodge this is highly unlikely. This has the possibility to have the Panda not hitting the witch out of the air once more. If the Panda cannot hit the Witch within a few bounces, the bubbles are likely to hit you, or the Panda will. This fight also has a third phase just like the second. This fight can most likely go on as long as it wants. Oh yea, blocking is completely useless in this fight. Almost like every other boss fight.

Very fun to play, almost zen-like.  The hearthlings are entertaining to watch as they go about doing their jobs.  A large part of the game play revolves around constructing facilities for your hearthlings to use, whether it be fields of carrot farms, large apartment complexes, intricate tunnel mines, imposing castle walls or simple homes for a peaceful village.
There are numerous jobs your hearthlings can learn, a basic research-tree allows players to explore new promotions each time you play the game.  It's currently not possible, or at least not easy, to have every job unlocked the first time you play it, so you will inevitably be tempted to start new towns to get the other jobs and try out new urban planning ideas.  It's very easy to get incredibly absorbed into the minutia, and obsess over the aethetics of your town.  Part of the fun is looking at what other people have built and getting inspired to construct your own version of real-world cities and towns.  Anyone who has an interest in architecture and interior design will easily become transfixed as this game has nearly an infinite possibilities that's only limited by your imagination.
While your doing all this, the game does follow a very basic script of events that you'll need to prepare yourself for.  Mostly being attacked by goblin raiders and stray wolves that are mostly random, but builds up to a massive and inevitable showdown with Oggo's army of Orcs.
My largest complaint is that the Normal mode doesn't feel balanced because of this inevitable fight with Oggo's Army.The first time it happens, it can be quite a shock, as you've spent 10+ hours being completely consumed by the cute visuals and light-hearted game play, only to see your entire village basically swarmed by a massive army of Orcs who then ruthlessly slaughter all of your hearthlings (beating them to death with clubs).  The game does feature a "Peaceful" mode, ensuring a completely violence-free experience, but which also then negates the need to promote hearthings for combat-related jobs (Footman, Archer, Knight, Herbalist, Cleric).  However, it is a nice option to have.
I don't just "like" this game... I love it.  I find the whole thing very endearing to play and would recommend this to anyone in a heartbeat.
A game worth every penny!

The world is kind of a heavy place lately, and it's become hard to escape and find that moment of peace we all could really use. Everywhere we look for entertainment or relaxation reminds us of the discord and disorder seen more and more through images of violence and confrontation. Where do you turn when you want to get away from the realities of the world we're being reminded of every day?
Of course everyone enjoys the challenge and hyperactive action of first person shooters but as some of us grow older we tire of their melodramatic, heavy handed, and needlessly intense nature. Could it be possible to have that same action in a more refined, artistic, and abstract style?
is exactly the kind of shooter to bring us this sort of peace so needed in an entertainment industry fueled by glorified aggression.
Like a series of condensed blasts of
's frantic chaos rolled up into a
world of simple origami aesthetics and uplifting pop-folk melody, this is definitely a game for the open minded.
has a very esoteric and eastern feel to it with it's outgoing style and upbeat pop melodies composed by multi-talented musician Calum Bowen, giving me nuances of saturday mornings as a youth watching Japanese children's programming on old VHS my Grandparents would tape and mail. While this is obviously a very personal feeling of nostalgia, there's a different form of it each player will end up discovering in their own way and tied somehow to their own past. If that reminiscent feeling isn't there for the player initially, it will be a new memory engraved into their mind in the same way our favorite things as a child stick with us.
Despite the heavy Japanese overtones from the bits of stylized text and the simplicity of it's cute and attractive design, the game was actually created by Delhi based QUICKTEQUILA and the bridging between cultures by this up-and-coming developer gives the surreal nature of it's atmosphere a touch of authenticity.
Beginning your journey into this
is almost overwhelming, assaulted with bright and stupefyingly cheerful audiovisuals. You're presented to an abstract world of random and seemingly unrelated trinkets and collage of colorful shapes,  sitting somewhere between the mysterious indie charm of
and the otherworldly grandiose of
.
Although the attractive and charming visuals may ease you into a false sense of ease and comfort, the game is no pushover. It features a very progressive learning curve that keeps you on your toes and constantly alert. The stages require finesse as you dance around a well choreographed ballet of bullets.
The first world titled simply 'City' gets you into the motions with some short and mostly linear pathways sprinkled with some adorable visual design through bright colors, odd decorations, and an onslaught of peculiar words and phrases in Japanese strewn about. Beating this first handful of levels is a lightning quick affair where each attempt will be over before you even realize it, leaving you craving the next hit of fast paced shooting and jumping action.
This pace quickly changes as you enter the second world and on as the levels begin to twist and turn into more complex patterns. Different enemies and obstacles appear forcing you to think quicker before every jump or turn of a corner, and new increasingly peculiar tasks become prevalent from protecting your distressed looking blue companions to shooting down cartoonish apples before they plummet to the ground. The obstacle-course like stages just get harder and harder, you'll begin retrying more and more, and you'll slowly become consumed in the competitive spirit of the World Records shown at the end of each stage.
will cause you to wear out your restart key as you mash it mercilessly to conquer that one seemingly simple stage and in good time. You'll eventually beat these difficult and meticulously planned later levels and instantly get a feeling of satisfaction, which quickly turns into the crush of defeat as you're shown a world record only to realize you are still seconds from being the best.

In some parallel universe where FPS games arose out of cute pastel platformers with geometric shapes and dodgable projectiles (instead of shooting monsters and zombies with chain guns while collecting key cards), this would be that genre's Super Mario Brothers.  It would be the game we all adoringly remember as teaching us all the basic mechanics of the FPS.  Somehow a game I never played before is making me nostalgic for a past that never existed.  If you have kids who wants to learn to play shooter games with you or their older siblings, start this game up and pass them the controller.  It will teach them the same way that solitaire taught your grandmother to use a mouse.

Let me paint you a picture. I'm sitting in my living room playing “Lovely Planet” for review purposes and junk. It's pretty adorable; that's my first impression. I'm running around a world that could easily be confused with “Katamari Damacy,” shooting little red squares and pins, rushing to reach the pink and purple flagpole that signifies the end of each short burst of a level. With every victory I'm shown my time, accuracy, and the stars I've earned. I finish each level in a few seconds... at first.
As I progress this cute little game takes a sinister turn. Suddenly I have to deal with innocent geometric dudes I can't shoot, platforms that disappear should I linger a moment too long, and giant apples I have to shoot before they hit the ground - all while bouncing and dodging (and screaming curse words so vile and bizarre that they haven't been conjured up, not in this plane of existence, anyway. Only in “Lovely Planet”).
Remember that level in “Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare?” I think it was called “Mile High Club” or something punny. Yeah, this whole damn game is that level. There are no screw ups, no second chances. I've never clutched a controller so tightly, a fact made all the more disturbing because I'm playing a game with a color scheme straight out of the Teletubby-verse.
Those with weak constitutions should avoid this title as the catchy music and rainbow explosion background will literally drive you to slavering madness as it mocks you; taunts you. You'll replay any given level a dozen times, each death increasingly unfair to you. Your shouts of disbelief will slowly transform into maniacal, sobbing laughter as you come to realize you're the devil and sinner in this Kafkaesque Hell of your own making. And finally, with victory nearly in your desperate, grasping reach, your sweat-slicked hands will betray you and you'll fall to your death.
And then you'll click retry. "Lovely Planet" is endearing, unapologetic in its challenge, and fun to play. This game has heart and charm usually absent in your standard 'tough as nails' fare, and it is a refreshing change of pace. For twitch gameplay enthusiasts and fans of the wonderfully weird, I can't recommend "Lovely Planet" enough.

Having played the game up until the first level of the second world, here's what I have to say:
I have no idea what the story is,
I have no idea why I'm doing what I'm doing,
I have no idea what anything is,
but I like it.
Nothing seems apparent in the beginning, however, slowly but surely, you get a good feel for what's going on. The gameplay is solid - one part FPS, one part platforming. Both parts perform well, and while there are enemies hiding around every corner, somehow you feel like it's your fault if you die. Even though you may not see an enemy at first, you will see one of their bullets whizzing by your head, and that usually gives you enough time to react. My only gripe here is the cherry bomb - once it hits the ground, you have to restart the level, and it's a bit jarring at first because you have to experience it a couple of times to understand what happened and why.
As for level design, well... it all seems really repetetive. That's really all I have to say that's negatie, though. You play one short level after another, and there after you beat a level, it gives you your time and a 'record' time for you to beat. After enemies are introduced, it's your job to exterminate them. Miss one, and you have to start the level over. Concept is really simple. Difficulty curve is slow, if not spot on - new mechanics and enemies are gradually introduced to you so you have time to get used to what's happening.
Graphics-wise, everything is simple and polygonal, however, that just helps to boost the aesthetics. The environment is colorful and cheery, with bright pastel-like colors. The music is a nice touch as well - not fast, but still cheery and upbeat, fitting in quite nicely with the environment.
So should you get this game?
If you're into FPS games like CoD and Battlefield and such, no, this game is probably not for you - you will not be offered a high-octane competetive FPS, as that is not what this game is about.
However, if you want to relax and have some fun without the competition and fast paced gameplay, go for it. You'll have a lot of fun with this game - it's very easy to pick up and play.

Fantastic.
The new updates to Baldur's Gate:EE released near Dragonspear make the game much better.
It always saddens me that the rich world of Faerun is only well-represented today/remembered by a handful of games that have extremely limited scope, and I'd really like to see more companies tell their stories using this type engine.  That said, Dragonspear is excellent.  I really enjoyed every minute of it, and (as an adult) had to fight the urge to binge through in a few sessions.
I'm writing this review to hopefully encourage people who liked BG & BG2 to give it a chance, in the hopes that this might encourage Beamdog to develop additional DLC for BG or BG2.  Would be great if they were able to spend more time on the overall story, create some new tilesets, and maybe introduce new characters areas for exploration.
Pro's:
+ Gampelay.
+ Being able to clearly see the benefit of different weapons/armor without busting out a calculator.
+ New story is ~ 20 hours long to complete.  I somewhat rushed and finished in about 22 hours.
+ Lot's of new dialogue is relevant and well-written.
+ Added character development for existing characters.
+ Possibly bridges BG & BG2.
Con's:
- Want moar.  moar moar moar.
- Some parts of the story seem generic or rushed, although the overall arc is well-written.
- Needs new tilesets. If tilesets were completely new, then they were not distinct enough.  ..I understand it's all The Sword Coast, but a little more diversity would be nice.
There seems to be an online PC/SJW or anti-SJW crowd pushing hate for this expansion.  I emplore you to really consider that Beamdog can't appeal to you, but ask yourself- are they really trying to wrong you?
Maybe it's just an age thing, but I don't have time to worry about whether a transgender character or feminist character are well-represented, and Beamdog would have to come out and state that they're clearly anti-LBGT/anti-feminist for it to even matter.
Also due to age, I've gamed long enough to see many good things just die.  Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and (stand-alone) Neverwinter Nights titles made up the majority of these isometric adaptations of AD&D rulesets and lore, and I've always liked them.  But those companies were either bought up by much larger companies (looking at you, EA), and their products were watered-down, or changed altogether.  It's indescribably uplifting to see at least somebody taking charge again, and reviving this genre.  So please, if you feel slighted- it's ok to share.  But please be absolutely damned sure harm was intended before waving the battle-standard; good things like this don't happen often, and many times they die too early.

OK, I am a sucker for these type of horror walking simulator games. But more often than not, they turn out to be not very good. This one is not great but I enjoyed it enough to play it through to the end. The big draw for me with this game is that the story is based on the mysterious, real life Dyatlov Pass Incident.
First of all, here's what it did right:
This game has great atmosphere. As an investigator researching what happened to  a bunch of Russian young people who were on an expedition out in the Siberian wilderness, you really feel like you are alone (or are you?) out there in the freezing cold. The visuals and the sounds effects really convey the environment to you in a believable way. Your sight is at times limited by the snow and the sound of the howling wind rises and falls as the weather conditions change. Just crank up the A/C in your house when you play to complete the immersion. The creepy music and the voice acting are good enough to ramp up the eerie factor.
Now here are the problems with the game:
The story has some great source material to start with, but I'll admit that I really don't get what was going on. Kholat fell into the same, non-linear read pages you find and try to piece together what happened approach to narrative. In the end, I am only sure of a few story points. There were so many things going on it was like the movies Devil's Path and Event Horizon  mixed together. Was it aliens? Demons? Government experimentation? Insanity? Who knows? There were so many things left unexplained. I really didn't want to spend more time searching for every last note or journal entry, because I don't think it would help much. Well that and the navigation in the game was at times tedious.
So this is where the balance between realism and fun comes in to play. You have a map and a compass you use to get around. But I had to read the forums to find out that the red half of the needle is what points north. Also the design on the dial made it look to me like north on the dial might be to your left. Like your character was holding the compass 90 degrees rotated to the left. Once I figured out what was what, it got a little easier to find my way around. I still ended up getting lost a lot and having to backtrack.
The game itself had few scares and was mostly just creepy. You soon learned that when you were out on the trail for the most part, you were safe. Only when you got to designated areas were you at risk from the wandering monsters.
There was at least one part of the game where I got physically stuck with no recourse but to road. And there were two times where I fell through the ground and fell into eternity. Speaking of reloading, the game Auto saved when you got to a campsite, or you picked up a new note. At least the devs gave a fast travel feature, but only between campsites. I was also glad that they didn't do the whole, batteries in your flashlight run out cliche, but since there is a full moon out in the game, there was almost no need for a flashlight.
OK, I think I have exhausted all I want to say about this game so I will leave you with this:
It was way better than 35 MM.

Cities: Skylines is a city builder developed by Colossal Order, the guys who were responsible for making the Cities in Motion series, and published by Paradox Interactive, and I have to say this is hands down the best city builder we’ve ever had on Steam .
The size of the game is astonishing, by default the game features a 36km^2 map which is almost ten times the size of the map we’re given in SimCity 2013, and with the help of mods from the Steam Workshop, this can be expanded to a mind boggling 100km^2. Even though there are no interactions between cities that are on different maps, it is frankly not necessary, with the help of the powerful yet easy to use building tool, you can build multiple cities on a single map.
Despite its humongous size, the developers paid close attention to details, in fact, detail is the word I’ll use to describe this game. From the entire traffic network, down to individual citizens, every aspect in Cities: Skylines are properly simulated. You’ll find lorries, colour coded depending on what they are currently carrying, delivering their cargoes to their designated factories, citizen actually living in a permanent home, and ambulances rushing to accident scenes, then little paramedics will get out of their vehicle, and few seconds later return with a patient on a stretcher.
I also love how water works in this game as well as the fluid physics, it is completely unnecessary to have it in a city builder but in this case it has added so much more to the experience. Water has currents and flows, so you'll want to pump water on the upstream and set up sewage pipes on the opposite end, else you’ll start pumping polluted sewage water back into the system. You can even drain a lake dry completely, or accidentally flooding your city because you demolished a dam, playing with water has never been so fun.
This is a city builder perfected, and with the support of Steam Workshop, further enriched by the endless creativity of the community. Cities: Skylines is a must buy for anyone who has the slightest interest in city builders.

TL;DR - If you like sim/survival games à la Gnomoria, Craft the World, etc... This game VERY worth it.

There are bugs. But nothing extremely game breaking at the moment, the devs seem to be doing a good job of cleaning up their code.
As some people mentioned, VERY CPU intensive. I've noticed that it seems the game has a memory leak problem, it'll run smooth for a few hours, but after 3-4 hours straight in one settlement, it starts to frame lag. Closing the program, waiting, and restarting fixes this. So at least it's not something permanent even if you have 30+ settles and a lot of business on the screen.
I love the Tech tree idea, I hope it will come with a lots more jobs and advacements.
Building design is HARD! If you're new, don't bother with it, take the default buildings and run with that. After a few games you can start banging your head on the design thing. It's not intuitive, that's the biggest problem, but once you get the functions, it DOES get  quite easy.
Pros
- FUN! The game might not be feature complete, but it's a hell of a lof of fun
- Slick UI and non-confusing X,Y,Z in 3D environment nagivation (not easy to do imho)
-Crafting! Gosh I love crafting, and this has already quite a few recipes. Could have a lot more, hope it gets more, but already very satisfactory
- Sound and music: bravo
- The two different tribes and map types give interesting variation in gameplay.
- Some jobs are retro compatible, e.g. cook will keep faming. Which is a very cool feature
- There are small quests and bigger mission types to get your town marked with township and such, so keep on going even if it seems you are at the end of progression, some nifty things are coming your way
- Nice graphics
Cons
- Seems the mobs are very scripted, completely not random. Depending on your difficulty, you will always get the same waves at the same time. There are random mobs and spawns on the map, but by now I can already mark down when the first 5-10 invasions will happen in a Mid or Hard game. Takes away from the excitement.
- Some bugs. Most annoying at the moment for me is that after level 6 or so while digging, mining highlight do not sticky. The task seems to be set in, but the yellow marker doesn't show. Hard to keep track of where I clicked.
- Current soldier AI is not very good. I've had my soldiers die because they completely split up when attacking, specially when chasing Archer/Ranged type enemies, and they end up dying 1 by 1 even at high levels because they just don't work together. Lots of micromanagement needed on your troops which can be annoying.
- Some parts of the game are no obvious. Where do you get sheep, or Poyos? Still need to find it out...
Suggestions
- Give workers levels too. They work so hard, and get nothing for it, poor things. But seriously, it would make sense to have your base workers be able to gain levels and maybe advance in things like: harvesting, mining, hauling (inventory expansions, etc...)
- Priority system for the regular worker tasks (see Craft the World)
-Allow remapping of the keys! I can't tell you how many times I send my damn tribe in alert mode because I am trying to turn a furniture piece to the left before placement, whoever took R as the alarm instead of ROTATION never played these games before :P
- It doesn't seem to have any benefit to level up a class to the max before promoting your Hearthling to the next job. Would be cool if some bonuses would stick. Specially when it comes to the military, as a Knight level 1 might get trampled even if he was a Footman level 6 before.
- Would be nice to be able to set patrol areas for your soldiers, instead of having them just marching in the base camp all the time
- And on/off switch for soldiers would be great. If not walking/training, they could function as regular workers
- Training area for soldiers/archers etc...
- MORE MAGIC! Love the cleric, need more
- Babies! Marriage, love, interactions, old age?
- Fishing!
- Multiplayer would be a blast, but I guess quite hard to do with Co-Op mode?
- Dyes for clothes, more clothes with bonuses for the various jobs
- Bit more functionalities for pets, don't even notice I have any most of the time

Slam Bolt Scrappers is a hybrid of Tetris-style puzzles with aerial combat thrown in. You control a person on a jet pack who collects pieces and assembles them into blocks to make weapons to destroy the other side, but to get the pieces, you need to fight aerial monsters and you have to wrestle them away from the enemy player.
I really didn't find much enjoyable about this game, really. As an avid fan of puzzle games, this was really a let-down, because the aerial combat is so much more important. You're not really given any time at all to strategically plan your board to get awesome weapon combos... even if you knock out your enemy, he'll be back in seconds to hassle you again. The only thing that might be worth it is the multiplayer, just for the fun of beating the crap out of your friends.
The graphics are cel-shaded and look alright. The music and sound work but aren't memorable. I used keyboard controls, and they seemed to work just fine. The only thing this game is really missing is fun.
If you're a big fan of frantic fighting-type games, then maybe you'll get more out of this than I did. I was really hoping for more puzzle-based gameplay from the screenshots, and I was let down. I certainly wouldn't recommend it at full price. If this looks good to you, wait for a sale.

This is a review of BG:EE without the DLC.
First and foremost, the original Baldur's Gate is a monument of RPG that withstood the test of time because of brilliant storytelling and mostly accurate D&D ruleset (2nd edition, which in essence is the same as every D&D standard ruleset ever).
. A game that stood proud for nearly 20 years with nice graphics (because of the isometric 3D) is a no brainer.
Then Enhanced Edition added compatibility for linux, steam, easier access to modding and some content in the form of additionnal characters with their own sidequests (some very good, some just ok). There is also an arena-style additionnal short campaign, but it's mostly irrelevant (it's nice that it's there. Some fun dialogue options but nearly 0 story element). So, all is fine and dandy.
However, when the extension Siege of Dragonspear launched, the game was updated to 2.0 (and 2.1 shortly after). This update consisted in an engine/UI update. Now that thing are settled a bit, I will say that
-: health bars are modern and usefull, but damn they are ugly.
-: contextual info can be globalized, but damn it's ugly now.
-: inventory has
stats, but damn is it... no actually it is still nice. Still uglier than before though ;)
-: spellbooks are still buggy and terribly ugly.
-: character info sheet is definitely better than before.
-: cancel/confirm buttons are inconsistently placed, which is disorienting at first. But you get used to it after 5-10 hours.
Overall, all this is minor details though.
Sadly, there is a bit more. 2.0 / 2.1 made several mods incompatible with the game. For a game which is nearly 20 years old, this means that a fair share of old mods may never work again with the game which nullifies a major selling point of the enhanced edition.
Additionnally, multiplayer is having major gamebreaking issues.
I think most players would play solo anyway, but it's always a shame to see a neat functionnality broken in one day just like that.
To sum it up:
-:
-: The enhanced edition tag is worth some quests, compatibility and steam access. Minor UI changes (slightly negative overall, but details are details).
-:
for breaking multiplayer, breaking some mods, unfortunate art design choices (sadly for them, BG was an extremely polished game so the smallest mistake just jumps out at you and gnaw your eyes out faster than any hamster ever will) and questionable conduct toward community of players (just trust me on that. Don't open the can of mutated carrion crawlers).

Once I got the controls figured out, I was pleasantly surprised. Realms of the Haunting is an action-adventure game that feels a lot like the original System Shock, with less sci-fi and more occult. The player starts by exploring a creepy old mansion, and the game's world gradually opens up far beyond that as the story progresses. A fine balance is spun between exploration, puzzles, and combat.
The atmosphere is what really defines this game. The graphics are pretty for the time, despite the fact that the game is emulated through DOSBox. A simple lighting system was effective at keeping me on edge and confusing the hell out of me, even when I knew where enemies were in a dark room. The visuals combine a practical mix of 2 and 3 dimensional models to create gigantic, detailed locations that can often be examined down to the smallest intricacies, although it is somewhat apparent that more work went into the mansion than the other areas.
Even with all that, it's not just the graphics. The story is told through both the game itself and amusing full-motion video cutscenes that give the player opportunities to glean more information through optional dialogue. On top of that, the two main characters provide plenty more audible exposition when the player chooses to examine inventory items or surroundings, and unlike most video game dialogues, I actually found all of this quite fun to listen to and watch, even if it is done in that cheesy 1990's glory. Kudos to the actors.
Nonetheless, the game suffers its share of problems. Most of the puzzles are of fair difficulty, but there are the occasional few that are very frustrating for all of the wrong reasons; Either not enough clues are present, or the solution is hidden in some spot nobody would check in five sweeps of the area. The combat also suffers from the awkward tank controls standard to the era that seem counter-intuitive to dodging the waves of projectiles that the game can produce. Some of the enemies do nothing but stand still, even when they're enemies capable of movement in other situations, and all it really does is make me wonder why the game decided to ease up all of a sudden.
Other than those issues, it's excellent. I enjoyed almost every minute.

I picked this up in one of the Humble Bundles, and recently decided to give it a try despite the negative reviews, seeing that it still was listed as "mostly positive" here. Unfortunately, this is not really a good game and I would struggle to recommend it to anyone.
First off, I'll at least mention the few things I liked about the game. The graphics are great. There's a few genuinely interesting locations to find, and a few neat vistas to admire. Audio isn't bad, and the sound cues for hidden items in the environment are a nice touch. Navigating with just a map and compass with no magic "you are here" marker was an interesting challenge.
Unfortunately, the rest of the game has major issues. Movement is clunky and annoying. Your character moves slowly and can't jump, which is a real pain given how easy it is to get stuck on the environment. The save system is punishing for no good reason, with no manual save option and autosaves only occuring at a select few safe places and when a note is collected.
The one monster in the game quickly ceases to be scary and quickly becomes extremely annoying. It appears during scripted events and randomly around the world in certain locations, and can instant-kill you for a lot of cheap deaths. It's also very easy to fall to your death on several of the paths, and getting stuck on the environment means you have to reload your last save. Any of these can easily put you back 10 or 20 minutes with the poor save system and how slowly your character moves.
The game world is a surreal caricature of a Russian mountain environment. There's giant skulls embedded in the scenery and lots of demonic/pagan artifacts scattered around with no explanation as to how they actually relate to anything. Additionally, the environment is difficult to navigate with the very poor controls. The game world consists of a few small open areas connected by twisting corridor-like paths.
And then there's the story. After finishing this game, I'm still trying to figure out what the developers were on when they wrote the script. I understand that this game is supposed to be based on the Kholat Incident as given in the intro video at the beginning of the game, but what we got was something else entirely. It's almost like someone's nightmare after playing Skyrim and a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game and then hearing about this story. The abrupt ending makes absolutely no sense and provides no closure at all.
Overall, I'm still scratching my head at what the developers were thinking. They crafted a beautiful, bleak mountain environment that fits perfectly with the survival-horror-walking simulator theme, but then proceeded to ruin the game with very poor controls, a bad save system, and a nonsensical story. Stay away.

It looks to have a deep, enigmatic story, right? It's even narrated by Sean Bean! Except that the story is quite superficial indeed, and the storytelling mediocre. It is told by journals and articles you find, but not by your exploration. The point of the exploration is just to find the text.
The gameplay comprises frustrating navigation using a compass, “find the hidden object by its sound” scenes, and several
frustrating chase sequences, which if you fail will cause you to reload annoyingly far from where you were. That's not a summary of the gameplay: that's literally the whole of the game.
I often, after finishing a game, like to go back and collect all the items to get a full sense of completion, but with Kholat I was happy to finish and stop there. Navigating the monotonous world is not rewarding, and the missing texts are not compelling.

Space Chem isn't really about space.  It isn't really about chemistry.
It's actually about programming.
But, don't let that throw you! It's a great little puzzle game.  So many games in the genre are about stripped-down gameplay, minimalistic controls and "emergent complexity".  SpaceChem is different.  It'll throw down a complex problem, a big bag of tools, and then stare at you expectantly, like your father.
Also like your father, the only reward it gives you in exchange for success is comparing you to your more accomplished peers and then giving you another challenge.
Someday, SpaceChem will love me back.

In my 25+ years of playing computer games, I've never seen a puzzle game as compelling and satisfying as SpaceChem. It's easily better than the classics (something you don't say easily), and it's head and shoulders above the often excellent contemporaries.
You build molecule factories in an almost-sandbox environment, with gradually ramping up complexity - all the puzzles have many solutions, and there's great replay value in optimizing your designs. If you like a challenge, just jump into it and see for yourself :)

The Rogue Squadron series (Shadows of the Empire, Rogue Squadron 3D, and Battle for Naboo) remains unique on PC for providing the fast, non-rails 3D objective-based arcade flight shooter experience on PC. This is the definitive game on PC forflight fans that are NOT looking for a flight simulator. The license allowed the devs to focus on gameplay over realism, and it paid off in spades. Harpooning a tank and weaving between it's legs manages to feel right because 'it's star wars' while providing a unique challenge, for instance. Some of the mission variety would feel terribly out of place in a flight game based on the real world, but Rogue Squadron is much more enjoyable for it.
Each mission's first playthrough locks the player's ship selection, with subsequent plays opening up additional ships after each victory. Medals are awarded for stats such as percentages of friendly saves, accuracy ratings, time to complete the mission, and hidden item collection. Earning each tier on all levels unlocks hidden missions.
The digital version available here runs far more smoothly than my aging CD's copy, with no graphical hitches whatsoever and the CTD end-mission bugs completely fixed. It's nothing short of a miracle, really.
RS3D is best played with a keyboard. Joysticks work, though the mouse is a bit oversensitive. The sound on the PC version was a selling point at the time, and the audio is as crisp as ever. For a mid to late 90s 3D title, the graphics have held up surprisingly well - largely due to the pace of the action, relative distance and constant motion of the targets, and a series of clever polygon tricks that still deceive in real time. Screenshots reveal flat 2D elements in all of the 3D models, though you'd never notice in normal play.
I would encourage perspective players to download the demo, either for this game itself or for Shadows of the Empire (this game was based off the demo level for Shadows, which served as a tech demo for 3D flight combat).

The first claims to have over 300 "improvements" to the game such as: you now have to confirm you want to travel somewhere instead of just clicking the zone, you have to confirm you want to memorize a spell, rather than just clicking on the spell. There is a "journal updated" box that now appears when you do a quest objective. This can be especially annoying when you're turning in a lot of items in. A good example: I just killed the Tanar'ri up near Baldur's Gate itself, I went back down to Nashkell because I had around a dozen winter wolf pelts to turn in to the merchant there; the journal updated for every single turn in.
I came back to the game after a while because I had given up on the demon fight originally, but after some time I was ready for it again. Coming back to all this frivilous BS is rather angering. Baldurs Gate is a old classic, a old gem and filled with nostalgia for many.
The EE version polishes the old and adds some similar mechanics that mods used to add to the game. The game still to this day holds up pretty well and the EE version do add on more content. I myself do not hold it in the highest regard but the monk they added is probably the best written out of them all while the Black Pits is fun to test builds or parties in but nothing extremely "must be played" since it is only an arena campaign not tied to the storyline of the Bhaalspawn.
What you get it what you buy, an enchanced version of the original game with a bit more content and some mod fixes glued on to it.
The writing can be a bit "Ham" at times, cheesy and such but people praise it for being very "funny" and "realistic" since it is the kind of thing you would hear around a table in pen and paper. I would prefer a more dark and "real" tone myself but I can see why it is found funny by old wolves who enjoyed pen and paper campaigns in and around the Sword Coast. The main story is not bad either. Sarevok is a iconic villian much like Jon Irenicus in game two. The game also lack a lot of "CnC", choices and consequences and it do not really give much of options for you beside being a goody good guy, a "I don't care but I do it anyway" neutral person and an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ most of the part , where all three lead to the same D turnabout no matter if you pick option A, B or C before hand. But it do not effect much in the end, but I think atleast it could given us more options. Mostly you are portrayed to be the good side countering the evil side. Not to spoil anything but you are more or less bound to be the good person and playing evil will render you not getting all rewards or losing reputation like mad. Which is a pretty bad thing to lose.
But the big big big but now is Siege of Dragonspear. It is tucked in a bit like someones fan fiction mod inbetween the two Baldurs Gate games and the ending chapter expansio nof Throne of Bhaal. Pretty much out of nowhere and it do not really fit. Some hate it for the writing, some hate it for being a cash cow, others find it to filled with shoe horned social justice things and other political agends, which I partially agree with. On the other hand I did not find the writing in retrospect to be so bombastic and excellent as people said it been before and I think I seen one or two well hidden, but non the less social justicy comentaries in the main game but so sublte and small they are barely noticeable. But beside that cocky commentary from some writers, the forced and poorly written SJW I found it atleast some what appealing to play, it was intriguing enough to pull me through it in about a weeks time.
But what I did not like was the similar event of no consequences or even worse, not really any options and the forced ending was not that good. Beside that, it is really hard to consider this canon and then look at BG2 where no one even mentions the Shining Lady ever or her crusade. Caelar Argent as the villian, a GOOD villian or anti-hero antagonist was to me very interesting but could been developed much more. I won't spoil it but I hope to hear more about her. A villian not hell bent on destroying the world, conquering it for doing bad or simply put being a lunatic chaotic evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was refreshing.
So some things been hits in the  Dragonspear expansion and Baldurs Gate at the core is still a cheesy at times but good RPG game. But there also been some misses in Dragonspear and people complain of the bugs. I had NPCs disappear so I could not recruit them. I might have managed to kill them by mistake, by pulling trolls to the camp but I did not notice that either way until I was looking for them in camp and they where nowhere. A bit more freedom and options, perhaps if they had made Dragonspear into a spin off, another branch in the Saga, a what if Irenicus never happended, it would been nice. But such is life.
6.5-7 I think is a decent grade if we do not inflate it like most gaming medias do today, maybe even 7,5 considering that Baldurs Gate was a great game on release, and one of few good RPGs in its time beside Fallout as far as I know. I will just preface this with one caveat:  You cannot rebind your controls without adjusting the DOSBox key mapping.  That's usually an "auto-fail" for me.  And given that this game uses mouse and arrow keys, it's going to be VERY awkward for most people to try to play.
That said... yea.  This game really surprised me.  It's not great, by any stretch of the imagination.  The engine certainly has lots of problems, with geometry tearing and popping around, combat that's awkward and more wedged in as an afterthought it seemed, and some fairly pixelized video.  If you're looking at this game as a first person shooter, you will be disappointed.
But that's not really what the game is.  What the game is, at its core, is a point and click adventure game.  Along the lines of 7th Guest, or Myst.  And on those lines, it holds its own quite well.  The acting, while stiff at times, really isn't that bad.  There's good use of props, costumes, even some decent makeup effects.  The pixelization of the videos actually does help them blend in better with the CGI backgrounds.  The puzzles are fairly decent overall, if sometimes easy to overlook a key item.  The story, while certainly no masterpiece, does a decent enough job pulling you along the way.
The game does stretch on one chapter too long, with an unnecessary end, but that part's short.  This is a game I never gave a fair chance until recently, and now that I have played it, I'm glad I did.  And if you don't mind some awkward controls, and sometimes painful combat, and do like the 90's adventure games, then by all means give this one a shot.

Initially I was a bit skeptical to buying and playing this game due to the criticism the series have gotten all over the Internet the last years. I played the Assassins Creed 3 almost five years ago and I loved it, but my computer back then were barely able to handle it so I never continued the series and then it fell out of memory.
Then I saw the trailer for this, and the buildup seemed so nice and the fact that there would be a playable female protagonist in a major installment seemed really interesting. I got it on the summer sale for half price due to my skepticism.
Now I have played through the main game, and I cannot but say that I am in awe. This is in no way a bad or rushed game, which some people claim as a kind of leftover from earlier mistakes in the series. But then again, when I play games like these and just stop for a moment to observe the animated world, all the details, all the small details in npc, their AI, all the meshes, textures, music and whatnot.. it blows my mind that there are not more bugs than it is.
In terms of programming and artistic work, writing and character development, these things are really masterful creations. Just as any other game of the same size.
I have no doubt in my mind that a lot of gamers take a little too much for granted and neglect all the effort it takes in order to create games like these.
Anyhow..
I really enjoyed the story and the characters, especially Evie, her character had that mysterious depth to it which is to be expected from an assassin. Jacob was more of the blunt tool, but I really liked his naive gentleness, like for example how he treated the horses when driving a carriage. Despite being twins, he gave the sensation of being the younger of the two mentally.
The analogy of their storylines and how they intertwine gives life to the story, and I read somewhere that the story seemed shallow and rushed. I wonder if gamers these days are refereeing to their own intellect when making those remarks, as the amount of details, fluff and buildup in the storys were more than enough to satisfy even me. And I am not even a nerd who is that well read into the lore of the series.
I also loved the detail that their personalities were mirrored in the soundtrack, once I became aware of this detail, it became rather obvious, and made the music seem like a inside joke, or inside story. The Soundtrack were in and of itself awesome, and seemed to read my mind on when to launch certain songs, as their timing were amazing.
Sure, there are some details that made me really annoyed throughout my gameplay, and I mean annoyed. Like for example, if you knocked out a guard, hid him behind the boxes you covered, whistled for another guard and when he approached, instead of knocking him out the character insisted on starting carrying the body of the already knocked out guard, ruining the cover, mission and my experience. For future games they should consider leaving the option for separate keys for separate actions, as layering functions on the same key may have devastating effects on the gameplay.
And not only the undercover cop seemed to have a subtle longing for a sexchange, because I met several npc's with the wrong voice for their apparent gender. Although this was far more amusing than annoying. The funniest moment would be when a young man was robbed and started screaming with the voice of an old lady to stop the youngster who have robbed him. I helped him only to hear him thank me as an old lady. Priceless.
As for the lore, as I have done som casual studying, it is nothing short of amazing. I love the metaphors and subtle hints, the obvious and esoteric references, occult parallels and all the other jazz down that road.
I guess that any initiated or well read and (truly) open minded intellectual with a fancy for gaming would enjoy this game.
Even I did, and I am not a good gamer, quite the opposite (which made me almost furious over my lack of skills at some points in the game) but I enjoyed the intellectual content of the game so much that I was not able to make me quit, instead I got a good exercise in the practice of profanity.
I am glad that I doubted the criticism and gave this game a chance, because it was absolutely worth it.
And I look forward to the coming installment, as Egyptian mythology and their esoteric teachings are one of my favorite fields which I have passed in my studies of the occult. I am curious to see how it is rendered through a gaming experience which this series offers so brilliantly.
Yes, I do absolutely recommend this game.

I happened to be strolling by the Store page for this while looking for something, and then saw all the negative reviews. After reading thru a few, I can say with some certainty that many of the accusations of bugs are factually incorrect as of now with update 2.1, or even with back the big update 2.0. I can't comment on the multiplayer or the new expansion, but I can safely say the singleplayer can be played almost completely as it was before, and if anything it's been vastly improved by small yet important tweaks. You can read more in the "Recent updates" section directly under the purchasing options of this page, but I'll provide probably the most telltale example: "Metal weapons will no longer risk breaking once the iron crisis has been resolved (BG:EE) (19766)". That was an oversight that stayed in this game since its creation in *1999* and though it can be rendered somewhat moot by the magical weapons you might acquire beyond that stage, anybody who rushes the story and/or picks less popular weapons was SoL for the past 15 years. But hey, "don't fix what ain't broken," right?
That said, a lot of the aesthetic changes were eye-sores to me.....but guess what? ALL but one of those changes are optional and can be switched off in the menu. I was on a BG bender for the past month when the 2.0 update came in the middle of my playthrough, and after restarting the game to see the changes I immediately logged off. BUT, a few days later I got back on, stopped being lazy and checked the Gameplay options, and sure enough, the sprite highlights, the health bars, the Story Mode difficulty addition - all can be switched right off, I can personally confirm those options were available within a week of the update. Even better, there now are more customization options for your party's AI and a few new Sound and Graphics options that get rid of some my own personal pet peeves. Also, I found and followed simple instructions on reinstituing Console Commands to try it out, and it still works perfectly.
I 1st received BG as a gift when I was a kid, and I've been playing it on and off for over a decade. I even still have the original CD packet, but jumped on this version when it was on sale. I don't regret it at all - BG:EE is better than the original, nostalgia be damned straight to hell. Beamdog's art and writing can clash sometimes with Bioware's, especially the former, but overall EE is a massive improvement. The implementation of the sequel's better mechanics alone is worth shelling out the cash for this, and I honestly think Beamdog did a very good job of sticking to what made BG great. Neera, Dorn, Rasaad, and especially Baelor are all decently-written and well-voice acted characters that I look forward to seeing more of as I start my BGII:EE playthrough. Again, I can't speak for the expansion, and after reading more into the "controversy" and watching a video on gameplay I have a few opinions of both sides, but I'll hold my tongue on that and stick to what I've actually experienced. In sum, BG:EE is not only still playable, but better than the original BG.

is a first-person adventure game that's 85% 'walking simulator' and 15% 'survival horror game' the likes of
or
, where you need to avoid and run away from an unkillable creature.
To put it mildly,
doesn't get raving reviews but I'm a bit of a Sean Bean fan and my friend
from
had a spare key for the game, so I was glad to be able to give
a chance after all.
To summarize, while it does have its merits I can't generally recommend
because it certainly isn't a game for everyone. The overall atmosphere is tense and the mountain landscape you need to find your way around looks impressive. But navigation is made difficult, which often leads to frustration, and the story is vague and unsatisfying. The few lines spoken by Sean Bean can't save the game, as it's clear he too struggled to find some motivation behind
's story to fuel his narration.
I only recommend
to people who're not looking for a compelling story but who may like a navigational challenge in the form of getting from point A to point B by using a map and a compass just like in real life, meaning you don't see where your character is on the map.
The first impression after starting up the game: the menu screen looks polished and there are a lot of options for video, audio and controls.
The game claims to auto-detect the optimal graphics settings for your computer. For me, it set the texture quality to 'medium' and everything else to 'low' (shadows etc.) or to 'off' (V-sync, AA, etc.). I have an i7 2600 CPU @ 3.40GHz (8 CPUs), 16 MB RAM and a GeForce GTX 960 4GB. While the GTX 960 4GB isn't what you'd call a high-end graphics card, it should be able to run a game like this at above-medium settings. After all, the game's minimum requirements are i3 and GeForce GTX 470! So I set the texture quality to 'epic' (the highest setting) and everything else to 'high' or switched on, and the game ran perfectly with those settings, of course.

After increasing the suggested settings by a lot (see above), the graphics look very nice.
During Act 1, the music consists of a lady humming a melancholic tune. It doesn't sound half bad but it's quite loud, so I lowered the music volume before I went off adventuring into the world of
. I shouldn't have bothered, though, because a minute later Act 2 started and the music was replaced with nothing but a few ambient sounds: the wailing wind, a howling wolf and the creaking of wood.
As a fan of Sean Bean's work as an actor I'm biased here, but I thought his narration was compelling enough for a walking simulator's voice over, even though it's clear he's had better material to work with.
The true story that inspired the makers of
is told before the game starts. A group of nine young people didn't return from a ski hike on a Russian mountain slope. Rescue teams found them dead at various distances from their tents. It seems something scared them enough to slice open their tent from the inside and run out half-naked into pretty much certain death. There were plenty of theories about what happened to them (avalanche, animal attack, tribesmen attack, fight among themselves, …) but all of them were quickly debunked. The most likely explanation remains that a sound drove them crazy, either literally (see 'theory of infrasound') or the rumbling wind produced a sound that made them
an avalanche was coming. Either way, the sound made them run off like crazy in not much more than their undies, and they were not able to find their way back to the tents through the darkness, causing them to fall down a ledge and/or freeze to death.
offers its own fictitious theory on what happened by having the player read notes and journal extracts that tell several fragmented stories. There are fragments telling of people being taken into secret government facilities where torturous experiments are performed on them, experiments that revolve around raising the dead, no less. You hear ghostly voices and see unearthly things like glowing glyphs on rocks. Meanwhile, there's luminescent ghosts and a fiery demon roaming the mountain, the latter chasing and killing you if he spots you. Also, sometimes there's an orange mist that surrounds you and from which the demon pops out to kill you. There's talk of all these elements in the notes and journal fragments you'll read, but the dots never get connected. The ending, too, is remarkably vague and unsatisfying, creating even more questions about the story that the writer of
is trying to tell.
Put all that together and… I don't know. Really, I can't make sense of the whole of the story
is trying to tell. And I'm not the only one, it seems. There are several forum threads on Steam and elsewhere with people spouting theories on what the player is supposed to make of the story, and no two opinions are the same. Some people clearly like vague stories like that, where
are actually the one telling a story to yourself by finding connections between elements that the author doesn't connect. And that's fine; to each his own. I personally think it's a lazy form of storytelling and I don't like it.
I even think the story of
may be construed as an insult to the real-life victims who died on the mountain. I mean: though we may never find out what really happened to them, fabricating a story fit for a conspiracy nut, intertwined with a fantasy ghosts-and-demon story doesn't really honour the legacy of the departed, does it?
There are two things you need to do when playing
:
You'll come across tents that act as portals to fast travel between. Apart from that, there are no objects you can interact with.
Trying to navigate the game world using the map and the compass is a pain because the map doesn't show your current position. If you want to travel to a specific place, you need to look at the map and the compass constantly, and even then you're likely to end up somewhere else.
Often, I found myself wandering in circles. Over and over again. I'd
I was walking in circles but I kept trying to find that one path I missed in order to finally reach a different part of the game world. This became frustrating after a while. Also, you start to notice your character walks at fairly slow speed. You can make him run but only for less than 5 seconds, because otherwise he needs more than 5 seconds to catch his breath.
I wanted to like the game and after a while I succeeded partly in spite of the game mechanics. I wanted to immerse myself in this impressive-looking snowy mountain landscape, but most of the time I was just walking the same paths over and over again. And because of the ridiculousness of the story that's supposed to connect to serious, actual events, the times I found a note or a journal fragment meant nothing but a save point. There was little feeling of accomplishment or advancement.

This game starts out by giving you a backstory. A couple of hints what happened. Then it throws you right in, and get's you thinking, in a way that only few games do. In a way that Alan Wake did, or Dear Esther, or Spec Ops, or Deus Ex HR. It pulls you in with it's amazing, harsh and brutal atmosphere. It looks great. It sounds good. It's well narrated. And then the game just frustrates the hell out of you, because to all the good makeup, they couldn't do simplistic but enjoyable gameplay.
First, the elephant in the room, the fact that it is a walking simulator. You can sprint for a couple of seconds, but that's pretty much unusable to get forward faster. Obviously they couldn't let you move faster, because even though the game does look enormous, in reality it's just a tiny world that is left to you to explore.
The game teases you. See a ledge to jump on, or a hole in wall that you could fit through? Nope, no such luck. Can't jump, can't crawl. Just have to go all the way back and go in a different direction.
The game annoys you by just plain bad enemies. Not only that the enemies are completly scripted, they just do not strike any fear into you. They walk around mindlessly, and then, all of a sudden, no matter if you were just right next to them or around the next corner, they sprint towards you and kill you. And since checkpoints are way spaced apart, enjoy walking all the way again.
It's damn frustrating. It starts great, it makes you desire more of the narration, and then it punches your nose right in with it's flawed and plain boring gameplay. It's a shame. Either cut those damn, useless monsters, and make it a purely narrated story, or fix the horror-elements so that it actually could scare an adult. But the way this is set up, it's just a waste of money - both yours and that of the developers.

X-Com UFO Defense or also known as Enemy Unknown outside North America was the brain child of Julian Gallop and his team at Mythos Games.  It was produced by Microprose and came out in 1994.  It was one of a few games I fell in love with in the early 90’s.  It was suspenseful, nail biting, frustrating, visually stimulating, gut wrenching and awesome all rolled into one.  At its time it was well ahead of its competition.  It includes base building simulator, player management, research, manufacturing, and turn based combat based on action points.  Each player has stats that are randomized.  You had to manage what the soldier could carry based on strength.  Type of weapon was determined by their aim and throwing grenades was determined by throwing accuracy.   You have to research materials gained from completed missions to develop and manufacture better weapons, defenses, ships and armor.  While working on your base you can take as much time as you need to buy and sell equipment, plan, manage base, manage ship inventory, manage research, manufacturing, and soldiers.  The selected research, manufacturing, and scanning for aliens only take place when you select the Geoscape to initiate the scanning.  Its also a pre requisite for Open X-Com for modded game play. Overall I still love this game and still recommend giving it go.

Then we get to the problems with knives and weapons, and I understand the mechanic where your lack of spit-shining your knives so that they menacingly glimmer in the sunlight as they spiral towards your victims head for more damage than the layman's unpolished murder utensil, but I honestly feel that it has no purpose in a game that tries to be more "realistic" in its combat weight. These men are wearing a bowler hat at most on their head, and you're telling me that the sweat of their brow is so significantly dense that it utterly deflects my knife as they scoff at me? Not to mention that if you do manage to stealthily kill a man with a knife, or by dropping barrels on him by severing their rope with a knife, all of their friends see the corpse and instantly predict the wind, trajectory, and velocity of your knife to know where you're standing five seconds later five stories up on a brick shanty. I've failed stealth missions entirely based on that, killing a man from a rooftop with a thrown knife, walking down the cobbled street for a spot of tea, and then his friends all showing up on my radar simultaneously shaking their fists and telling me I have no business here from twelve blocks over.
For a series about stealth, the amount of times I've been detected by not being witnessed doing a stealth kill is astonishing. Not to mention the times I've been told to kill a leader undetected, lure their guard away with a whistle and kill them, then watch as another man spawns right before my eyes from a bowler hat brought in with the breeze and blows my cover as his first action in this mortal coil.
Without any opinion on the story, I can't recommend this game based on how utterly unwieldy it is to play. It doesn't feel good to control, the stealth is a dice roll at best, and parts of the game force you to upgrade items that shouldn't need upgrading because of their core purpose.
With all of that said though, I've passed the steam deadline on refunds so I'll probably slog through the game for completion's sake alone.
Edit : I've tried to play more of it and my opinion on it only gets worse. I'm not going to put any more time into this miserable game. I'm being instantly killed at full health by a random grunt two levels below me after I've maxed out the health upgrades possible this early on, you don't get any items back when you die which means if you've been killed by the Second Coming like I keep experiencing your odds of surviving get infinitely worse and I'm not even on a mission I'm just trapped in this temporal flux of hatred.

Koi-Koi!
- Each player starts with 8 cards in hand, and 8 (shared) cards on the board.
- Each turn you first play a card from your hand, and see if you are able to form a "Yaku" (card combination) by combining it with one of the cards on the board. If you are able to form a Yaku, you get a certain amount of points depending on which Yaku you formed. If you were not able to form a Yaku, the card you played stays on the board. Next you draw a card, and see if you are able to use it to form a Yaku. If you are able to form a Yaku you get the points, if not the card stays on the board.
- Whenever you form a Yaku you can either call Koi-Koi or end the round. If you call Koi-Koi the round goes on, giving you a chance to earn more points by forming more Yakus. However, if you are not able to form another Yaku that round, or if your opponent forms a Yaku before you, you might end up getting no points at all that round.
- Whenever a player gains points, the opponent loses that same amount of points. The games goes on for either a fixed amount of rounds, or until a player reaches zero points.
The rules are fairly simple, and the game gets pretty fun once you are able to memorize all the Yakus, however just like with most other card games this one is also pretty much an RNG-fest, and the luckiest person will usually end up winning.
Still, I
enjoy it for quite a while. The multiplayer is pretty much dead though (which means that the grindy multiplayer achievements are a real pain), but I still recommend the game to people who are just looking to kill some time.

Another great Amplitude game! A mix between a roguelike and tower defense, you and 2-4 heroes must travel through 12 floors of monsters, looking for the exit. On the way your characters will converse with each other, find new heroes and unlock new escape pods to crash into the planet again.
As you move around each floor, each door you open leads to more monsters hunting you from the darkness, or new tools to help your team survive and escape. Like the other Endless games, manage your food, industry, science and dust carefully, or you may cripple your team. Industry is used to build your resource generators and your minor modules, things like turrets, healing crystals, slow fields, and other tower defense items, to keep the monsters from attacking your crystal at the start of the level. Science is used to recharge your heroes special abilities and to research upgrades for existing and new modules. Food is spent to recruit new heroes, level them up and heal them. Dust represents the health of your crystal and is used to light/power rooms (which allows you to build modules in them) and you want all the rooms lit that you can, because monsters come out of the dark rooms (just like my childhood).
Main objective? Keep that crystal alive. Find the floors exit and haul that crystal and your heroes to it. Repeat 12 times to win. Cry when you die on too easy at the 2nd floor.

Super Chibi Knight is a Zelda-like game which focuses on adventure, puzzles, and fighting baddies.
The map isn't huge, but it's densely packed with enemies, levels, quest givers, bosses, and secret areas. The enemies are brightly colored, with a very distinct art style. Levels start out flat, but later levels add moving platforms, switches which need to be activated by spells, and even deadly spikes.
The leveling system is very unique. There are three separate levels: Amor, Special, and Sword. You spend experience on each of these independently. Experience requirements will only increase for the skill you're leveling. This discourages min-maxxing, and makes it easier to level all of your skills without spending massive amounts of XP.
Super Chibi Knight is not a tough-as-nails Super Meat Boy clone. It's easy enough for young players or players who are new to gaming to pick up the controller and jump right into the game. But it's also varied enough for older players to enjoy it as well.
Before I started, I thought that this was just going to be a remake of the original, but the introduction of The Beastmasters adds a whole new level to the game. It's fun to run around as a tiny knight in armor. It's even more fun to ride atop a giant purple beast which breathes fire, a large bison which charges at enemies, or a chicken which can glide.
At the time of writing, the game isn't done yet. It took me 3.5 hours to get to the end of the Alpha version, and I expect a lot more content to be added to the game over time. The developer is actively taking feedback and constantly adding things to the game. This is one of the few "Early Access" games which I actually expect to be finished.
If you're still on the fence about this game, check out the original Chibi Knight which was created by the same developer. Many of the game mechanics are the same, but Super Chibi Knight feels a lot more polished and varied than its predecessor, and we haven't even seen its final version.

I got this for free from a giveaway and figured i'd never play it. I was home sick from work one day and was looking through my Steam list and decided to give it a go. The game has plenty of value, there's many hrs of gameplay in this title and although the controls feel odd & the graphics are a little dated you can tweak the dosbox config files to give you a little bit better picture.
You move around using the arrow keys, with caps lock as toggle run, A as jump, E as use and I to open your inventory. To drink a potion you must press I to open inventroy then left click it so it's in your "hand" then press U on the keyboard to use it. Kind of crazy system but once you get used to it then it's alright.
The combat is interesting because it has melee weapons as well as ranged, it can be hard to judge the melee range at times so I find it best to just stand back and spam the attack button until a hit collides then backpedal and keep swinging again.
Similar to other games of the time there are a number of puzzles you must solve by finding items hidden throughout the area and then using them on a certain object to continue. Thankfully this version of the game has the update that enables "easy puzzle mode" which auto equips the correct item when attempting to use something so you don't have to madly try everything in your inventory on everything, this cuts down on much frustration and makes for an overall more enjoyable experience.
The story is told through strange live action FMVs with terrible green screening, they look really bad by todays standards but the storyline is suitably cheesy that it just seems to work, I feel if the subject was more serious then the low quality would detract from it but I still found the FMVs enjoyable with their retro charm.
I would definitely recommend this game although I must say I preface this by mentioning I got the game free from an indiegala giveaway so you may be able to find someone who doesn't want their code that you can get it free from. Worth a look at this title to see what the state of gaming was back then as it feels pretty well made.

I'm currently in college and have next to no time on my hands. I played Baldur's Gate during winter break in 2015 with a couple of friends and had a great time, though we never got close to beating the game. I hadn't played it since until today. I saw the huge controversy surrounding the new expansion as well as the overhaul that it brought, which was implemented into even the base game. Furthermore, I saw many of the negative reviews it was getting on Steam. I had to get back into the game. I had to check it out. Oh. My. God. What have they done? This isn't what I payed for with my Christmas money.

While I would love to give this game a thumbs up - The story is interesting and well-written(as far as I have been able to get, at least), it's fun to play, the dialogue by characters is entertaining(again, as far as I have gotten thus far), it has amazing roleplaying potential, and the character customization(skills, skill points -not aesthetically) is really deep-
But I play this game online with a friend and the online is beyond broken. The game will crash randomly, not once, or twice in a blue moon. No, it crashes INCESSANTLY back-to-back-to-back. At this point I can't even play with my friend, as everytime he joins and I try to save the game, it crashes. Not to mention that we are playing on a LAN connection. A LAN. And still the multiplayer is horrifyingly broken.
In fact, I can't even play my save game without him, as regardless of whether he is in the game or not, whenever I try to save - it crashes. It also tends to corrupt your saves, if you're trying to play multiplayer, without rhyme or reason. We also had to roll back multiple saves, losing hours of progress, because the game decided it no longer liked X number of saves.
We've started up 4 new games, after hours of play, simply because we could not continue on a save game we had invested time in, as it became corrupted or the game decided it was done allowing us to play that save game.
So if you're looking to play with someone, I cannot recommend this game.
