Combo system is interesting, as instead of a basic Attack, Special, Jump kind of deal like SoR, it's got a kick and punch button. They both have about the same use, but you can mix them up for different crowd control and such. No melee weapons so far as I can tell, (I've gotten to stage 4) but you DO have a handgun that you find ammo for in boxes among apples for health recovery. The handgun is really handy too for picking those guys you jump kicked off the screen... again. A very welcome tweak.
Graphics are nice. They're kind of gritty, and remind me of old school Mortal Kombat. Although those animations may need some cleaning up. They look pretty stilted. Some enemies don't even have walking animations!
There's only two characters, and they seem pretty much the same save the (I think?) special attacks. I've always played Blaze in SoR for her speed and I love chaining suplexes like the jerk I am. So I hope that they either make the current female character play more like her, or just make another character for that.
Game could use a lot more polish, but that's no surprise if you're picking it up at this stage. It's definitely (even as of now) a must-buy for my fellow niche beat'em up fans if you're burnt out on Streets of Rage Remake.

I have played several classic recently and even Streets of Rage 3 today right before testing out The Takeover. My judgement of giving this game in its current state a thumbs down is solely based on the gameplay- the heart of any arcade-like game.
Pros:
- beautiful visuals
- great audio
- simple but entertaining combo system
- varied and interesting movesets
- unique feel to the characters
Neutral:
- slow
- blatant ripoff
Negative:
- horrible key configuration
- custom key configuration utterly bugged making the game almost unplayable
- common issues with gamepad inputs
- sluggish controls/ gameflow
- slow menu navigation
- intro sequence way too long, boring and not skippable
(- lives would be a welcomed addition)
While the game appears to be impressive, actually playing it yourself is a less fun experience. It is vastly polished in all aspects except gameplay. And that is the problem. It plays poorly. That is also not an issue linked to it being in Early Access. It's about fundamentals that can be fixed in a day or two. More so, it should have been the main task to work on in the early stages. I find it irritating that the game gets new content continously, but lacks addressing several mayor issues.
I am a very forgiving player, but The Takeover just lost focus on the most basic and most important aspects.
Yes, this game is shamelessly plagiarized from Streets of Rage. Calling it inspired is a sugar coated understatement. But since it's done really good and because of my fondness of the source material, I don't mind.
While coming from Streets of Rage 3, gameplay felt horribly slow. But after some time, I got used to the slower speed. I do prefer more fast paced Beat 'em ups, so I am a tad harsh in that matter. In all honesty, the speed in The Takeover is just alright and reminds of several classics. Criticising the speed would be just arguing about taste.
Despite the obvious love for detail (that trash hopping around when smashing somebody into the ground <3), I had to stop playing because of the numerous gameplay issues. Inverted directional inputs on an XBOX 360 controller is indeed a mayor turn off, topped off by unpolished general gameplay.
I can't recommend The Takeover in its current state. To change my mind, the developer needs to fix the fundamentals. That is something that should have been the mayor focus in the beginning. It's evident that the goal was to make it all flashy instead.
Don't let this harsh criticism fool you- I am looking forward to future updates, since this is a nice start.
Finally! Streets of Rage 4    10/10

From the outset, this game gave me a nasty case of the heeby geebies. Even the comic book style opening cut scene has an air of the macabre about it immediately plunging you in to a pit of dread. The setting and atmosphere the developers have managed to create is spectacular, spawning feelings of terror through sheer isolation and the contant sense of forboding. The anticipation of an encounter is the truly terrifying aspect of this game, keeping the hairs on the back of your neck on end from start to finish. There are some really creepy locations (the pitch black forest and bunker being the most stomach churning for me) and some heart pounding jump scares to be had, especially on your first play through. Although the mechanics for finding objectives had me puzzled at first, once you get the hang of using your map and compass, navigating becomes a lot easier. Getting to nerve to actually explore said co-ordinates however is another story...
I'm not sure Kholat would have much replay value however, as once the map has been explored and all of the encounters experienced, the game would lose it's strongest asset - fear of the unknown. Although the developers managed to build a convincing narrative as the game progressed and added some additional lore through the various journal entries scattered around, the ending was a huge let down and felt like an anti-climax to all of the effort that had been invested in to creating depth within the story and characters.
Despite this, the game is 100% worth a play through. Even if you ignore the plot line, the undoubtedly terrifying map alone will leave you a nervous wreck for most of the adventure. Solid 8/10 for me.

I just have to review this because of all these idiots coming out of the woodwork after the April 1 updates. Esentially what they did on April 1 is release a brand new DLC (Which also has terrible reviews under it.) and update Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate 2 with a plethora of improvements and modernizations. The updates improved the game DRAMATICALLY, but of course to improve you also have to change, and as we all know, change is scary.
The reviews which are at the time of writing shown as the most "helpful" are rather brainless expressions of shock at multiple changes of the UI and graphics. Before said updates, the game was was similar to how it was on it's original release, and it aged TERRIBLY. The NPC and creature models looked terrible, blending into the background to the point where you couldn't click on them right, the pause screen was a terrible mess, spells and effects were barely visible, opening a journal or fidning any sort of information was difficult and painful, you could never tell how far away a creature is from dying so any form of strategy was nigh impossible without full understanding of the game mechanics and complicated UI setup. Esentially, it was an unplayable mess for any modern gamer. I myself, who thinks the more complicated the better, and who usually gets into old games with ease, also found it very difficult to get any enjoyment out of the game, to the point where I completely gave up on it.
Then, they updated it, and suddenly nearly all the issues were solved. The characters were given a black lining around the model, letting you actually see animations and giving you a contrast between the background, something that is supposed to look like an ogre can actually be humanly indentified as an ogre now! Whenever you complete or progress a quest the journal entry that your character writes pops up on the screen for a few seconds (Letting you pause the game via space bar and read it, if you so desire.) whereasin before you had to press Escape, click on your Journal, click on the right quest then click on the right part of the quest and then attempt to find the new entry just for a little comment given by your character.
Character profiles now display more information, health bars are now shown above creature heads letting you actually know when something is about to die, difficulty options were added for more replaybility, challange or to give a helping hand to starters, the background now goes gray when you pause the game letting you more easily spot enemies, the UI was just generally improved graphically, and so much more!
For the first time in many years, Baldur's Gate is playable. And I am both annoyned and baffled that some people are angry over these changes, a vocal minority I hope.

SpaceChem is a puzzle game that deals with atoms and molecules.
I don't really think the story makes that much sense, but where this game really excells is in the puzzles.
The game is made up of chapters and levels. Each chapter will introduce one or two new new gameplay features. The levels take you through an easy tutorial of how to use the new element, and gets progressively more challenging. This learning curve is very good.
As for how the levels themselves work, you are given various tools and a grid. The job is to move elements (like hydrogen/carbon etc.) around, and join them to form molecules which you then pipe out. It initially seems easy but once you add mulitple reactors piping out to each other it quicky adds more of a challenge.
My only issue is, if I find myself becoming fixated on ridiculously complicated solutions. You can't skip levels if you are finding them too complicted. This means if you are completely stuck and can't progress unless you can solve each level sequentially.
This game is controlled with a mouse, but has keyboard shortcust to make things easier to control. This works really well, in my opinion.
The graphics are very simple, which is good as it makes it easy to see what exactly you're doing.
The music and sounds in this game are very nice.
There are extra challenges included once you complete the game, and ones that can earn you extras in TF2, it seems. This coupled with the wide number of challenges means the game definitely has a very good play-through time.

Searching for a survival game with challenge? Try The long dark. A game in which you can discover the great Canadian heartlands, where summer doesnt exist, and you die. Graphics are cartoonish white smush but still cool. Walking in the woods towards your ultimate peril passing the same looking tree for the hundredth time in a blizzard is the new black. Go fishing or hunting to nurture yourself and melt snow to water and drink it or die. Unfortunately you cant drink your own pee in this game :( Fight against fatigue, cold weather, wildlife, cabin fever and much much more. So the main attraction of this game is of course the survival mode, in which you survive until you eventually die. The easiest difficulty features no threat from wildlife, but after that it only gets worse. Last difficulty, Interloper, usually wont allow players to survive a week. Game also has different challenges from hunting a bear to hopeless rescue. Lastly; developers have added two first campaign episodes, that actually have non-player-characters, quests and more.
Heres some pointers from the game ive taken notice:
- Players have to face a legion of wolves that seem to grow from the earth itself. (unless u are playing the easiest difficulty in survival)
- If wildlife attack tears up your clothing, its usually the most rare or hardest to repair ones.
- There are two ways to fight fatigue, either by sleeping or drinking coffee, and the latter is hard to come by. (seems like Canadians only drink herbal tee and forgiveness.)
- Player character suffers from sprained ankles and wrists just by moving around in the snow.
- Bear carcass can disappear totally in couple of days in freezing temperatures.
- If you accidentally take antibiotics to, for example sprained wrist, they wont cure your food poisoning O_O (maybe the character just sprinkles them pills to their arms?)
- Dont. Go. Climbing. On. The. Ropes. Unless you are positive there will be no snow storms, you have 100% stamina and you are not wearing anything on you.

I have been playing TLD for several years since the early days of early access, it is one of the few of those that I did not regret buying and actually turned out to be what the devs promised and more. I spent most of my game time within the sandbox survival mode, since the - also awesome - story mode was only added with the game's completion. TLD features the most realistic, atmospheric and immersive survival experience of any game that I know of. While I do not consider it to be the 'ultimate' survival game because unfortunately even here there are artificially added dangers in the form of unrealistically aggressive wolves (might be called the 'furry zombies' of TLD) it is a significant step forward. To me, TLD will probably only be outmatched when a survival game is developed that pits you only against mother nature alone, in all it's fully realistic glory.
On top of this, the developer team is also one of the best I know of, they always had an open ear for the community, constantly worked on and improved the game and are generally one of the friendliest. Thank you Hinterland for a great game and all the best for the future.

PROS: The most realistic survival game you'll ever play. Hardly any bugs, very well optimized. Proper crafting, i.e. you can't build a huge house, you have to survive as you would IRL. Very fun, unique game.

Still one of my favorite games of all time despite its flaws. Definitely recommend if you like games that are repetitive, but require thinking ahead and prioritizing. If I had to compare it to another game, I would say it's not like most over survival/crafting games. It honestly plays like a first-person shooter/RTS, as weird as that sounds.

FIRST OF ALL, this is an old MS-DOS game, using the DOSBOX emulator. Now that this is explained, on to the review:
AMAZING game.
I bought it when I was 13 years old. I was amazed by its graphics, the good acted FMV scenes and the VERY well written storyline. Good to see that the game wasn't forgotten, and brought to Steam. I bought it again, and gonna probably play it again a couple of times. ^^
For the ones that don't know, this is a first person shooter (in the veins of Doom and Duke Nukem 3D), but with a horror theme, light adventure elements (an inventory system, interactions with the environment, etc). And the game also has an AMAZING story, told by great (even if a bit corny) FMV scenes (with real actors).  The game aged quite a bit, but its still quite playable. The soundtrack is still very good (and very creepy), the sound effects are still very realistic, and the gameplay is still fun to play.
Oh, and the game is quite long for a FPS. Not only there are 2 or so hours of FMVs, you also have some nice puzzles to solve, LOTS of enemies to fight and quite a few maps to explore. Don't expect to beat this game in less than 10 hours on your first try, specially if you don't use walkthroughs.

This is *the* classic X-COM, which I spent countless hours playing in my youth(?) and getting my nether regions handed to me. The premise is simple: Hostile aliens are invading earth, and you have to bring down their UFOs, handle crash sites, stop them from terrorizing civilization, etc. You can customize your ships, crew, soldiers (down to renaming them), and your base.
I heard a rumor the Steam version is the bugfix-rewrite OpenXCOM, but the version I received is just DOSbox running the original. So, it is not bug free. However, it is just as immersive, atmospheric, and all of those adjectives I can throw into a glowing review, as I can remember. The tactical battles are a balance of exciting and harrowing turn-based fun. I would say this game has stood the test of time.
Advice for playing this game: Find the manual. Read it! Save early. Save often. Realise it's not a brand new game. Experiment. And of course, have lots of fun.

It's worth it, trust me.  This is a game from 1993/4 which easilly holds up today; I'm only 7-8 hours in to playing the game and I feel a lot more coming.
The music and sound effects give an eerie feel, which I'm unsure is a deliberate choice or a side-effect of the limitation of old DOS games in general.  It definitely feels like you're playing on a piece of history.
Give it a real chance, modern video game player, and you will reap the rewards.

I have long been fascinated with the famous Dyatlov Pass Incident, and so when I learned that there was a game based on said incident, I had to play it.
The events are mostly shuffled off to the side in favor of fiction. Bits of story are revealed here and there as you discover notes scattered across the world And speaking of the world, I have to say that it is far too large for this type of game, especially since the in-game map can only be properly utilized at certain safe points, making it difficult, if not damn near impossible, to determine where you are at any given moment.
There is only one enemy in the game, but he can appear pretty much wherever he wants to. Deaths are also instantaneous; combat is a no-go, for whatever reason. This means that you'll spend far too much time running away from encroaching danger than you should.
Thankfully, the positive points outweigh the negative.
The location is pitch perfect; the snowy pass and darkened sky provide a perfect, oppressive atmosphere that drips with tension and menace. Even with the map issues, exploration is almost always enjoyable. The graphics and level design are excellent, making every new area you come across a joy to behold. Little easter eggs are scattered here and there. These don't have any impact on the story, but they certainly encourage exploration.
However, Kholat is still difficult to describe accurately. It's a game that really needs to be experienced on your own.
Despite all its flaws, it's still quite an enjoyable experience. I definitely recommend it.

This is a sort of re-review, as my previous review for an earlier version of the game was a tad harsher (but still positive).
The game has, as of a couple months back, received a major 2.0 update. This review is based on v2.2.3.
That update, v2.0, fixed some of the game's flaws, such as bad animations, and also added a huge feature: online multiplayer. Now, I've had issues with the online myself but it's possible to find players and should be decently playable for most people.
There's also various AI levels, which I believe weren't there before, letting you choose up to 4 difficulties. It feels as though the entirety of the single-player content has been given a touch up, but it's been a while since I last played before the update.
Another nice feature that I believe wasn't around before 2.00 is the addition of in-game card and yaku lists. This should let you easily and quickly check up on scoring conditions and such, which should help any newbies get into the game.
The one issue I see is that there's still basically no rule customization, which is an odd omission but not a very huge one. Other than the number of rounds (6 or 12), you can't really change much.
Another little issue is that it seems that the "Enjoy pack" DLC was phased out with the 2.0 update. This isn't a big deal, however, considering it was a free DLC, but I'm sure someone misses out the Ayano guide and her... big assets. Thankfully, there's a lot of new backgrounds, BGMs and guides in the base game (and more through the cheap DLCs) which make up for this issue. I also believe the "Enjoy pack" content was, at least partially, just included into the game, except for Ayano. So, no big deal.
All said and done, with the confusing animations gone and online multiplayer added (among other things), this is probably the best koi-koi game you can get on PC and a much better game than it was before the 2.0 update. I'm glad to see the developer has supported this little game so well, and is still releasing updates adding new content and fixing old issues.
I recommend it. Specially if you see it at 90% off, which seems to happen frequently enough!

Having played through the base game, Spacechem is a great puzzle game at it's core.
Pros - The puzzles. They become increasing harder as you go along, but it is pretty steady. Each set of puzzles build on skills you have acquired from the previous. There are challenges associated with many of the puzzles. You do not have to complete them to beat the game, but they really make you think and work for the achievement. They can be tough, but I enjoyed solving them. Nothing in the game is forced on you with the challenges and achievements. It saves your progress so you can keep moving forward in the game and go back later to beat the challenges. I really felt a sense of accomplishment finishing this game. Many puzzle games become the a+b =c formula and thus, boring. Space Chem held to the end.
The controls and UI worked really well. Learning the hotkeys helps. There are many videos on You Tube. Really cool after you beat a puzzle, you can see how others did it. I did not see any of my solutions online and there are may ways to solve each one. The instruction on new tools were good. Told you what you needed to know and left you to figure out how to employ them. The periodic chart was a useful addition.
Cons – The story outside the puzzles was a cheese sandwich with the crust (Try eating one and you'll see what I mean, dry and chewy, just sayin'). Not the worst I have seen, but after while I didn't bother. I mention this only to point out it does not take away from the great puzzles. That is the heart of this great gem. If you don't like the story, skip it. The graphics do not interfere with the game at all. They were functional.
I highly recommend this game if you enjoy puzzles that challenge your critical thinking and problem solving abilities. This is an exceptional game. Skip the story, solve the puzzles. You'll feel smarter, I do.

Spacechem. a very simple puzzle/logic game that is so simple its surprisingly NOT a flash game... and despite its name it has very little to do with actual Chemistry OR Space. =p it just uses both for visual themes and to provide a backdrop for the storyline. however if you still hate science in all ways you may find that its usage of the atoms to be dislikable at best. nonetheless even if Steven Hawking or Einstein or even Michio Kaku played this game they would find their science expertise as not a factor to actually play the game. =p you dont need to know science to play. but if you do know it and you love science then its just an added plus as you smile to yourself.
its simplicity however is trumped by its sheer mindnumbingly difficult puzzles. although it starts out easy it only progresses to become more and more difficult to the point where your problem solving skills are put to the greatest test. overall score i give a 10/10.
this game although has 2d graphics it doesnt need anything beyond that as anything more would detract from the game. not enhance it.
gameplay starts with the simple stuff and has a nice progression showing you the basic rules at the start. by the time you reach the third area that tutorial for the most part ends, only showing up when something new comes into play. however every level is for the most part the same with just a new twist on the solution. the game makes it so that when you beat a level you feel smart. it then shows you the rankings and you know just how "smart" you really are.
the soundtrack admittedly is just 3 songs and although they dont stand out, that is for the most part a plus as your full attention should be on the puzzle at hand and not on some blaring soundtrack that has no ability to fit with the game like many flash games. overall very nice to listen to if you do choose to listen. at times upbeat at other times dark.
story: although there is fairly very little it is a nice addition to the game and just adds some depth that is lacking in a few games of this genre. although i havent beaten it the character is at least remotely connectable and not just some random silent protaginist that the creator just makes it seem as if its you in only the partial, this is even IF you dont see very much of him except once in a while. thankfully you can view all previous bits of story so it can be reread to refresh your memory.
overall id highly recommend this game to almost everyone. "almost" being the keyword. if you hate anything related to science this game is not for you as the games theme is very much related, in addition if you ABSOLUTELY HATE being put to the test with each level then again this game is not for you as each level after the tutorial just becomes difficult, even IF you know what your doing it still takes time to figure out the puzzle. Logic is a must for this game. otherwise youll NEVER be able to beat it. even then after logging 19 hours on it im only just now reaching the 15th level. in other words about 20% through the game.
pros: simple, completely logic based, nice progression.
cons: almost nothing except the difficulty may not be for some.

Realms of the Haunting, a first-person adventure/shooter game developed by Gremlin Interactive in 1997.
You start the story as Adam Randall who ventures to a haunted house in order to investigate the mysterious circumstances around his father's death. As Adam enters the haunted house, the doors locks behind him and he is forced to journey throughout the entire house while looking for answers as well as means of escaping it.
Adam soon discovers the house contains portals to several different universes, and that he is the Chosen One who must prevent the final apocalypic battle between the forces of good and evil. From time to time you meet several guidances that share knowledge with you and assist you in your quest.
Realms of the Haunting has an interesting way of gameplay and story. From time to time, cinematics are played to inform the player more about the current state of the story. These cinematics are nicely done because it blends real-life characters with the virtual game world. However the game has a very complex level design which is sometimes confusing and you have to find your way out. Luckily maps can be found and inside your inventory, hints about items are given.  Also the puzzles can be very challenging which makes this game not easy but that makes it challenging. The controls for movement and shooting are somewhat awkward and cannot be easily changed but that's something you must learn to get used to. Realms of the Haunting is a game that is far ahead for its time and a true gem to play.
If you are into shooter-, adventure-, puzzle, horror- or retrogames, then Realms of the Haunting is definitely the game for you! They don't make games like this anymore these days!

I will admit to being a little biased here, as this is the fourth time I've bought this game - I bought the original UK version, the US version, the GOG download, and now again here on Steam. Why? Because I really, really like it.
Graphically, the game hasn't aged well, unfortunately. It came along at this time when everybody was transitioning from sprite-based 3D games to polygon-based 3D games, and rather than develop a new engine, the creators chose to use the revamped engine from their own game "Normality". Possibly the game was already in development when Quake came out and it would have cost too much to start again. It's still fairly pretty though, except for the low-resolution textures.
Sonically, the game is amazing. On the whole the voice acting is very good (David Learner, yeah!) except for a couple of overly-hammy moments, but the sound effects are where the game shines. The rolling thunder in and around the house, the whispered voices in the Tower, the sloshing of water and crunching of rats as you pass over them all add tremendously to the effect.
Gameplay wise, the game was quite innovative for the time. The developers themselves say in the making-of video they didn't want to just do "Doom [with] some cruddy logic", and what you have here is more of a point-and-click adventure game done from a first-person perspective, with some gunplay. For some reason people say this game is hard and you don't get enough healing potions, but I never had that problem. Maybe I've just played it too much. The controls may also be a pain for you if you're used to WASD with mouse, but I'd just come from playing Duke Nukem 3D and so found them quite intuitive.
The story of the game is it's highlight, though. What seems like a straight forward "investigate a strange house" plot quickly expands into something that covers the Knights Templar, the Book of Revelations, and a madman's plot to incarnate Satan in physical form. This is a reality-based survival game is playable in two modes: story mode and survival mode. The artwork, sound design, and music are extremely well executed.
In story mode the game is pretty boring and still somewhat buggy. You must complete the tasks in proper sequence otherwise you'll not be able to finish the game. However, you get to play a guided walk-through, where you get used to the gameplay mechanics and the geography of the game. At the time of writing, only the first two episodes of the story mode have been released, and the mode lasts for about 20 hours.
After playing story mode, or instead of it, the game can be played in survival mode. In this mode, you're the only human alive, and all the resources of the region are yours for the taking. This mode can be played in four difficulty levels. To many people, including myself, this is the highlight of the game.
While I said the game was reality-based, I use the term cautiously. I'm sick of the recent trend of zombies in games and movies. Thankfully, this game does not have zombies or monsters. Instead, the principal threats in the game are the weather, wolves, and bears. You must hunt, gather, and manage resources, and you must craft items to help with this cycle. However, this is where the game starts to show its limitations too. It's as if the game studio spent all its energy on the story mode, and the survival mode is a byproduct. In fact, the survival mode used to be called "sandbox". Because of this the number of things we can craft is severely limited, and the materials and items are rather quirky. For example, furs are oddly specialized, so you can't use wolf fur to repair a bearskin coat. You can craft shoes, mittens, trousers, coat, but never hats. In contrast all metals are just "metal", except when they aren't. While in reality, nearly all food tin cans are made of steel, the game just vaporizes cans after you have used their contents. If we were ever stranded on a place like Great Bear Island, we would quickly improvise a spear by binding some sharp stone or metal on a straight-ish fallen branch. Not in this game.
In conclusion, this game is for you if you like survival games but are tired of mystical elements. People have clocked in hundreds of hours of gameplay, and watching their streams on Twitch is pretty enjoyable too. However until the game studio makes some serious effort, the game will have obvious rough edges that might frustrate you.

This second free to play mystery visual novel with thriller, horror and supernatural themes by Eternal Night Studios, Ziel Graywords and Stw Projects feature a different male protagonist Gary with one half of a necklace who suddenly receives a visit in his sleep by a mysterious woman Alice where she asks Gary about a promise he made to her earlier and shows him the other half of the necklace, both of which Gary has no recollection of. After waking up from what he thought was a dream, he was led towards a mysterious large mirror where he could run away from it or to enter it, leading him to an adventure filled with fantasy, thriller, horror and mystery as he encounters 2 boys Royer and Henry, a girl Mary and Alice herself in multiple different dimensions - a forest that is constantly dark, a sinking ship, a kingdom inhabited by masked puppet characters, an orphanage and eventually Alice's garden.
For a mystery visual novel, the game does very well in the plot and in connecting and explaining the mystery together and how an earlier past experience by the protagonist and the featured main characters help to explain and support the significance of each dimension and the horrors encountered in that dimension. On the minus side, the game has a number of errors in the English version and the limited number of CGs and character sprites could be improved. Recommended for those who like a short mystery visual novel with horror and supernatural themes and easy achievements as a free to play game.

I had high hopes for this game. When checking out the steam page it reminded me of Marble Blast. Unfortunately, this game is very slow. You move like a snail, especially up slopes. It's frustrating. There's unforgiving deaths. There's "shortcuts" and an "energy bar", both of which I have no clue what they are and I've played for almost an hour. I feel like that should be like level 2/3 stuff. Instead, I've gone through four or five levels of just rolling around.
The third level would send you back a couple minutes of this snail-like movement if you died (there's checkpoints, but they're not spreadout correctly). After about eight minutes into the level, there's this bug that'll toss you over the wall, right back to the beginning. Come on. It's level three.
The fifth level has a floating clear pyramid with a "?" in it. I had hoped it would be one of the powerups that I somehow hadn't encountered 40 minutes into this game yet. But no, it just dropped me in the middle of no where and fell to my death. What the heck? That's not fun. If it took me like 10 seconds to get back, maybe, but it's just stupid with how slow you move. Deaths are unforgiving in this game, albeit easily avoidable. I wouldn't mind as much as long as it wasn't in the first five levels.
I'm five levels into the game and I have no idea what the point of these gems are. I'm thinking "Why should I care about these?" I eventually realized after going to the home screen there's a shop where you can buy a "slow-mo" mode (because this game isn't slow enough) and some other locked features.
Also, there's no way to adjust the in-game music/effects. Why not?
I realize that this was developed by one person over 5 months, and I can commend the developer. I couldn't make this. It looks great. But, that doesn't take away from how frustrating this game is. It's slow, it's unforgiving, and I feel like more of the mechanics should be introduced earlier.

This game is like Civ 5 for Roguelikes, and like Civ it CAN be fun, but then you realise you have spent a few hours accomplishing jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ I will break my review down below:
GRAPHICS/ART:
It's a retro-style game, so the canvas is limited, but the game certainly looks pretty good. Objects are clearly and distinctly present, so there is little to no confusion.
GAMEPLAY:
It's meant to kill time; you get random items, map layout, ally spawns, upgrades, merchants and exit spawns. The only thing for certain is the levelup skills and the two characters you pick at the start. It takes a LONG time to play a full game, and the gameplay never really picks up. It's heavily focussed on micro-management of up to four characters with unique stats and skills which allow them to excel in certain roles. However, the control and style in which this is done is quite rudimentary and provides the player with little input other than moving units or building defences.
Later on the difficulty snowballs rapidly and makes it even more painful to keep track of all four characters and make sure none of them die or get underlevelled; the 12th floor for me was especially painful as there are few places to install resource generators, making the gameplay even more tiresome as I had to move around and heal constantly just to try and find the exit in the gargantuan map.
I am not a huge fan of RNG being the primary focus of difficulty, ESPECIALLY when nearly every aspect of the game is decided by a roll of the dice, and it can take over an hour to realise you rolled pretty poorly for the late game.
CO-OP:
The only redeeming factor is that the co-op is nigh perfect; the connection is brilliant and easy to set up. However, if a character dies that player has to sit around and wait, becoming even more passive than usual until their teammates find a new character for them to play as, often requiring different types of equipment that the group does not have, making the experience further decline.
PROGRESSION:
None to speak of; you unlock new characters when you recruit them and either survive 3 floors in a row with them on your team, or win the game with them on your team. In multiplayer, the chance of them being unlocked is reduced the more players there are. The main issue arising from this is that it will almost always require you to get rid of one of your fully equipped, levelled character for the sake of unlocking a new one to start the game with. This will often result in quick defeat or increased difficulty, as there is NO INFORMATION given about the stats, abilities or equipment slots the character has before recruiting them, forcing the player to take a gamble. This is common in roguelikes, and not a huge issue for me, but for this game when 3 floors can take 15 minutes it was painful and dreary to think I would have to roll the dice countless times to try and get some characters I really enjoyed, as the base ones are bland and utterly boring.
OVERALL:
This game is not awful, but it barely scrapes through on being OK. It suffers from heavy reliance on RNG to have any semblance of replayability or progression, and couples it with gameplay that is as tedious as it is dreadfully time consuming.
Not worth buying unless you have nothing to do these holidays and want to watch your life pass as quickly as possible.
I rate it 10 points.

This game has so much potential, but just misses the mark due to some poor difficulty tuning and some lack of polish.
The game starts with "Easy" and "Too Easy" difficulties.  "Easy" is properly "Normal," or perhaps "Hard."  The strategic elements are really intriguing, and I like having characters that can equip items & level up.  The tower-defense-lite elements, mixed in, are neat too.  The soundtrack is nice, if a bit bland.
But (regrettably, like many games lately) the RNG elements are poorly balanced.  In this case, the imbalance centers mostly around the "Dust" aspect.  "Dust" is some kind of energy source, and you use it to power-up the rooms that you explore.  You can voluntarily power and unpower rooms, to manage your "Dust," which is strategic.  However, you accumulate dust very randomly, mostly by opening doors to new rooms.  Sometimes, +10 dust.  Other times, nada.  Powering rooms via dust (or rather, leaving them unpowered) is a double-whammy: your defenses won't operate in unpowered rooms, and enemies randomly spawn in unpowered rooms, always seeking to attack  your "crystal."  You don't  need to power the crystal room, but yoiu can't place any "towers" in it, either.  Monsters attacking your crystal will then cause you to lose dust, usually rather quickly.
It really boils down to the fact that a couple less-than-fortunate dust-related events, and the run will quickly spiral out of control and becomes irrecoverable.  Unlike some of the better rogue-like games (e.g., Binding  of Isaac, or Rogue Legacy), death provides you with nothing to show for it. At the end of a long run, there's very little impetus to start over.

As I cannot really talk about performance (which will almost certainly vary), I will talk about the genreal theme.
Rogue Squadron is all about flying the vehicles of the Star Wars universe in order to complete various objectives within the mission. THese objectives can range from destroying AT-ATs, protecting a building or convoy, disabling another vehicle, or just straight blowing things up.
You will be piloting vehicles such as X-wings, Y-wings, A-wings, Airspeeders, Tie Interceptor, Millenium Falcons, Naboo Starfighters, Ford Lincons (Yes, you can fly a Ford Lincon), though most missions will restrict you to one or two the first time around.

At first, I was happy I could finish this game, after some 13 years of stopping at Nashkel Mines and never going through with it. The graphical update is well-made, and I appreciate Linux-compatibility, even though AI path-finding is still a mess. With all that said, I did not miss much since 1998, I'm afraid.
Mechanically, this game didn't age well. Might not have been that good at the time either, but such was the zeitgeist. Design had come a long way since then, and has improved upon much of the formulae of these rpgs.
The breaking steel weapons, while integral to the main story, are quite irritating early on, as they represent no challenge besides managing the inventory of several party members. All of whom are limited in carry-capacity by their strength. While it does make sense that your wizard would not be able to carry four sets of metal armour on their back, neither does it for Minsc, nor my Dwarven defender main character. Money is all around the place, and after some time, you only look potions and arrows. Magic items available in shops are not all that good, and I have only spent money on purchasing the party's first +1 weapons, which are magical and do not break. I was sitting on over 50 thousand gold by the end, not even bothering with selling things after some time.
Outside of these early purchases, the way of progression is generally looting and pillaging, which made me feel like we were a party of murder-hobos masquerading as heroes (renown maxed with good deeds and not killing town guards). The game world feels static, many models are standing around the town of Baldur's Gate, yet people are pushing their own unconnected agendas with you playing the henchmen or merry matchmaker. Boring. I did go into length to do as many side-quests as possible, but it made little difference. The world did not come more alive for all my troubles.
The story was bland if anything, and conversational choices mostly boiled down to 1, being nice, 2, wanting money for being nice and 3, acting rude, stabbing people and generally not being very nice. There was no opportunity in changing the flow of conversations or saving face once you lost it, which is not fun. Many of the characters feel out of place, thrown into the setting as “that dude in front of a house who gives you a quest that takes you to the next location”. Companion characters not connected strictly to the main story come at you seemingly random, many in the middle of the wilderness or a road, and you most probably already have a full party of capable individuals and cannot be bothered to dismiss someone just to check out what this new random bloke could bring to the party. I simply went with an early-game group of lawful neutral and good individuals, as boring that might sound. I did get Khalid killed early on though, as he was not bringing anything to the party, however, Jaheira, our druid would have left if the fighter got dismissed.
Game-play wise, AD&D is really bad, and I wish they had gone with a better system. Then again, such was the time. In this game it is perfectly justifiable to make a bard character who then sits out all fights, singing and thus bringing +2 attack value to the rest of the party, because bonuses could mean that much. Then again, I made a steel wall made out of dwarf, a true craftsmanship of his kind I must say, who walked up to people and hit them for damage beyond the baseline health of most spell-casters. Exploding corpses were a triviality during our adventures. That said, fights are challenging and can be frustrating at times due to the nature of saving throws in the d20 system.
Memorizing spells was a bother, and I never liked it in D&D and its variants. It's not good design, and I am glad video game creators put these kind of player-limiting stupidity behind us.
As for the content added by Beamdog, the creators of this Enhanced Edition, well, I wish they didn't force so much their impossibly irritating, edgy female character, Neera. The encounter triggers a fight whether you like it or not, and ends in an offer to recruit the mage, whether you like it or not. Well, I just slit her throat. Good riddance! Her voice-acting was worse than that of Imoen's, and that is compliment I never thought I would give that character. All in all, Beamdog failed to improve on the mediocre writing already present in the game.
As a closing thought, I think I would have enjoyed Baldur's Gate more if the system was based on GURPS.
Thank you Beamdog, for breathing new life into my favorite series. Loved it!

Right now, the game is basically a playable demo, as it is in Early Access.  But, if you love those old school beat 'em up games that were in all of the arcades in the '80s and '90s, you'll love this game.  It definitely has very much of a Streets of Rage feel to it, which cannot be a bad thing.  It's not a copy, though.
Right now, the game consists of one stage with three parts, the last part being a boss fight.  After that, the game goes back to the title page.  Also, there's a survival mode where you can basically fight endless enemies in a gladiator type arena.  I didn't do so hot in that mode.  ;)  But, what is there so far of the main game is fantastic.  It's that old school 2.5D side scrolling action game us '80s (and probably '90s too) kids love.  Like in most of those games, you fight a select group of enemies in a part of the map, then you continue on to the next until you reach the end.  If you "die" along the way, you can restart the part you're on, you don't have to go back to the beginning, and retries are unlimited.  Or, at least, that's how it is in story mode.  There will eventually be an Arcade mode, and I'm thinking that may have limited lives, to really complete the old school arcade feel.  You have the usual basic moves of this type of game; jump, punch and kick.  Though, your character can also shoot fireballs from his hands, damaging a number of enemies.  Take care when using that, though, as it drains health.  And, you also have a pistol, but you have to find bullets for that.  The game play is fun and intense, just like you expect from this type of game.  The combat is tough, but not unfair.  If you've played this type of game before, you'll likely remember some of the strategies.  If not, you'll pick it up as you go.
The visuals are fantastic.  The game is 2.5D, but the backgrounds are all wonderfully done 3D objects, as are the characters.  The art itself has something of a cartoon look to it, giving the game a comic book feel.  The music is nice and doesn't get in the way, but it adds atmosphere.  The rest of the sounds are your basic butt kicking sound effects and whatnot.
Anyway, I'm glad I voted for this game on Greenlight and I'm glad I bought it.  It still has a long way to go, I have no doubt the developers have much more in store for us.  What they have so far is definitely promising and worth the money for fans of this type of game.

It's a bit of a fallacy to tout this (as its creators do) as an "old school" or "retro" FPS. This really doesn't play like any FPS I ever played in the 1990s. "Serious Sam" is really more of a bizarre genre hybrid all its own--an unholy mix of FPS and SHMUP that ultimately plays more like a SHMUP than an FPS (despite being in the first person). Much of the game play is navigating various patterned waves of enemies with absurd firepower in huge arenas--which sounds like a SHMUP to me.
So is it fun? Yes. For the first half, anyway. However, by level 6 or so you have seen everything there is to see in this game, so the next 7 levels of mowing down the exact same enemies in increasingly similar looking arenas can get tedious and redundant fast. I guess it's a classic case of too much of a good thing. Had this game been half as long it would have been twice as awesome. As it is, though, I was bored to tears by the time I finally reached the (admittedly awesome) end boss.
It's storyline is a joke, but the way you'll desperately run, dodge and shoot the tons of enemies surrounding you will make a good FPS player of you. I recommend it just for the slaughter.
The First Encounter has a short campaign compared to the 2nd encounter, finished it in about 4 hours, the second encounter takes about 8.

Shoot, shoot, shoot and shoot some more. That's Serious Sam for you. When it first came out it was something out of the ordinary. With a surprising success. Wandering through levels with some nice looking old egyptian architecture, you fight armys of monsters. This time, the word "army" is to be taken seriously, as you literally kill thousands of monsters from start to finish. A few simply "collect item" and "push switch" puzzles in between give some variety, but the big picture is just you, your gun and what you can shoot with it: EVERYTHING!
Sam himself is more or less a cheap copy of Duke Nukem, with a similiar rough voice (though not as cool sounding) and one liners, as well as some comedic relief and a few references to pop-culture. The HD Version really enhances the graphics, in direct comparison to the standard version. Give it a try for some mindless action, even with co-op!

VERDICT:
I think if I were you and if had a fairly tight budget I'd wait for it to go on sale.

OK, I'm going to be honest here. I only bought this on Steam becase I wanted to write a review of it, I love it that much.
This game brings back amazing memories.   Realms of the Haunting (or ROTH) is a superb game.  It probably looks quite dated now, but in the same way as Ultima Underworld... It's dated, but you can still have a damn good time playing it.
It was the first game to really play with the whole 3d-as-an-immersive-experience thing... teleporting to other "dimensions", random turns which end you up where you started... All great fun.  most games before it were simplistic 3d (Doom, Heretic, Wolf3d, Rise of the Triad etc).. This
ROTH (or Rise of the Helmet) as we used to call it in homage to Rise of the Triad, starts you off in a mansion that you're sent to (for some plot-crucial reason).  There, you discover that something is amiss, and you're there to sort the place out.  Before long, you start to question whether the things that are going on in the mansion are actually part of something a bit bigger.... At this point, I won't go any further, but suffice to say the game gets a whole lot more interesting than a creepy mansion-crawl.  Not to detract from the mansion at all.  Considering the level engine, the mansion is actually huge, and great fun (albeit scary fun) to explore...
Right from the start, ROTH sets the scene with amazing textures, fun spooky things happening, and a creature-spawn system which is neither random, nor predictable.      As you're getting your feet at the beginning of the game, you can end up dying a lot... As you progress though, you start to amass an interesting and diverse arsenal.  The end is a little like Painkiller: You end up using a lot of what you have, because it all has it's own place and uses.
The game isn't very polished.. it has flaws here and there.  But as an immersive, fun, interesting, different experience, I have to say ROTH has everything you need.   If you enjoyed DooM-era games with a  theme/twist (I'm looking at you Duke Nukem, System-Shock and Dark Forces), and you like a bit of suspense (kinda looking at Doom3, but more looking at System Shock), then you'll probably enjoy ROTH.
There are one or two puzzles that it can help to have a guide handy for.  Not because they're hard, but because they use mechanics that aren't often employed, so you can be forgiven for not thinking of it.
WELL worth a few quid, and about 10 to 15 hours of your time.  Grab a slice of nostalgia and play a golden oldie.

This is one of those games that I really wanted when I was young but did not have a computer that could run it at the time. By the time I did have a good computer I was onto other games like Sin and Half-Life.
I picked it up for just over a dollar on the Christmas sale - and I am extremely happy I did. This game is like the best of everything I remember from my early years of gaming.
I am nearly finished now - and it has been a surprisingly solid experience considering it is nearly 20 years old. It is definitely dated - the corridor like mazes and underwhelming shooting come to mind. But the adventure elements are fun and I haven't found the need for a walkthrough yet (I am on chapter 14 currently).
The level design for the most part is really good considering the 2.5d engine - the mansion in particular feels like an actual place with lots of interactive scenery and secrets to find. The graphics are also well drawn and the 3d modeling that is present really help the atmosphere thoughout the game.
The voice acting is solid - though the FMV cutscenes are like watching a low budget knock off of an episode of Are You Afraid of the Dark. Luckily the story is interesting and the characters are likable.
I do recommend this game to anyone who grew up with games from this era and anyone who is interested in retro gaming - especially if it is on sale.

Dishonored is a first-person game that takes place in a steampunk setting, in the city of Dunwall, after being framed for the murder of an Empress, you must clear your name and make things right, and at the same time dealing with those that conspired against you...
The game is gorgeous visually, so many details you may not even notice, between level design and architecture and items, superb...
I love the gameplay, the weapons, the abilities (personally, I use Dark Vision and Blink the most), the choice between stealth or straight-up murder, justice or revenge, the mechanics of this game are incredible... I have played through the game both stealthily, not killing anyone, not being detected in a low-chaos  way, as well as a kill everyone and everything and be a major jerk in a high-chaos way, and both can be equally as fun...
The story, while somewhat predictable, is still quite compelling and enjoyable... and everything you do affects which way the story goes, if you choose to behave in a good-natured way, you will have a good ending... if you are of ill-intent, your story will become dark...
The characters are great, you play Corvo, Lord Protector of the Empress, along the way you come across some other very fascinating people, Emily, Samuel, Havelock, Pendleton, Martin, Piero, The Outsider, Granny Rags, and many others...
Overall, I absolutely adore this game, everything about it, I love to explore every area, every item I can find, and various paths to my goal, brilliant game! 10/10, highly recommended!

Dishonored is a great game, though it suffers from a few problems.
It's a Deus Ex-like (aka a stealth game + FPS with open-ended levels and objectives) with very light RPG elements. I won't say much about the combat, since playing a DX-like full-combat style is for idiots who can't stealth and murder properly, or for people going on a 2nd or 3rd playthrough, and I've plyed it only twice on Normal and then Very Hard. It allows for creative and extremely elaborate ways of murder due to the tools you get. (One even wonders if the game's creators aren't serial killers...) Besides tools and weaponry, you also have "black magic", which you can upgrade by runes, found by following a quest marker while holding a beating heart in your hand.
Let's get one problem I have with the game right away: goddamn objective markers. Sure, you can disable them and all. But was the game designed with that in mind? Like most games made today, no. Thief (1 and 2, not the♥♥♥♥♥♥remake) had a very crudely designed map, but it conveyed the necessary amount of information. Deus Ex often gave you a satellite image and you had a compass, same as Thief. There were also other ways of finding your objective (for example, Thief 1's Bonehoard, where you could faintly hear the Horn of Quintus - your objective - playing in the distance, and its volume increasing as you got closer.)
But yeah, the level design is great and combined with all the stuff you have at your disposal it's great fun exploring the beautiful aesthetics (The game's objective of doing a "painting in motion" aesthetic was succesfully completed, though textures look muddy) and using your tools to get through obstacles and kill people with extreme prejudice.
The problem with magic is that it's way overpowered, and makes the game too easy. Especially, the Blink power (a short-range teleportation spell). Movement feels good, especially traversing through the rooftops running, jumping and blinking, and also doing hard jumps to get to the next objective - some really good fun! - but the game wasn't designed with Blink in mind (the spell was introduced because the beta testers had too low an IQ to play through the game.) The DLCs' level design shows great improval in this area (Well, at least Knife of Dunwall - never felt like playing the other one because it released after I finished everything): Streets are tighter, keeping you from blinking far away from everyone, buildings are taller and open areas are more spread to make it harder to blink anywhere. (Just the beginning of the first DLC shows that you're going to have a hard time blinking everywhere.)
Finally, the story. Meh. That would be pretty much all I would have to say except that the ending is dependant on how many people you kill, and it goes from happy ending if you killed only a few each level, to chaotic if you passed that threshold. No middle-ground. The changes the Chaos system (Low if you don't kill a lot of people, High if you do) makes to the final level is pretty cool though: Low Chaos, and it will be a morning, sort of peaceful, your boatman wishing you good luck. High Chaos, well, it's night-time, a storm is coming, and your boatman alerts everyone to your presence and says he hates you.
As I said, it's a really great game, and definitely worth it, especially the DLCs.

Much of the work has gone into The Ascendancy(SP?). You start with 7 hearthlings in your group to found your new home. To gain more you must meet set amounts in food, morale, and net worth. Each of these can be done easily enough. You generaly meet morale unless you just don't do anythng for your hearthlings, like building beds to sleep in or chairs and tables for them to eat at or growing them at food. Food can be attained right away from berry bushes until you can make a farmer's hoe to promote a hearthling to farmer to grow food yourself. And net worth comes from building things like a shared sleeping quarters, dining hall, roads, or designing your own buildings. On day ten you'll be approached by a royal herald who will give you a quest to become a township. If you complete this quest you get tier 2 building materials.

Please get in on the ground floor and watch this game grow. This game will be huge, and it will be such an amazing release one of these days. Trust me.

I want to like this game but too many things turn me off.
+The graphics are beautiful and look stunning at times
+The atmosphere is creepy and unsettling (- if you aren't into that)
+The soundtrack is pretty decent
- Terrible optimization. I have a PC that can run games like Arkham City and Mad Max on ultra settings. I can barely get 60 Fps on medium/low settings on this game.
- Strange map system that is difficult to understand
- Very challenging to navigate and easy to get lost (+ if you like that as an immersive factor)
- Saving. This is my biggest gripe:
this game has far too few save points, or the save points are too far from one another. Meaning, if your game crashes or you die, you get sent quite far back. Now this wouldn't be a problem at all if you could manually save, but sadly, no option is present. I have lost my will to keep playing because I keep dying and having to reload to the exact same spot I was at 20 minutes ago. In fact, half of my playtime was spent doing something I already did before, but didn't get saved.
It is a real shame because I am intrigued with this game but can not ignore these flaws enough for it to be fun for me.

Contains a surprising amount of depth, and unashamedly hard in difficulty (in a good and fair way). Strategizing with a full party of 4 friends is also what makes this game so brilliant. So, im not a big name in reviews, i'd never claim to be, but i love solid video games. This game is exactly that; solid. It takes the slightly beaten to death rouge-like genre and infuses it with a somewhat complex resource manement challenge that sperates novice and expert plays apart. Then there is a impressive roaster of playable characters that all feel unique yet generally fill similair roles, such as haveing a big hulky monsterkiller that is also a healer vs another bulky monsterkiller that has enough mental stats and abilites to be practial in other ways.
It's multiplayer is the real shocker for me, i love 4x games and all manner of strategy, but with this games real time combat with its calculated planning period between opening doors just tickles all kinds of skill sets in me as a gamer. Like to play tower defence? then have the team feed you the currency to build stuctures.
While this is a love letter to this game i bought on a whim for the chirstmas sale that turned into one of my new favorate games to play, there is some bad notes. There is a handful of visual glitches that happen from time to time, the pyro character has a bug that makes it somewhat unplayable, and while these issues can be remedied by save and quitting and then loading back up, nothing sucks more then setting a character to a task and then watching them stare down a pack of mobs and not acting. So, these minor bugs that seem to be well documented aside, I wholeheartedly approve fo this game and would suggest it to anyone, even at it's full price.

I suggest to reinforce your path to the elevator with turrets of all sorts, as things will get really bad really fast once you remove the cristal from the previous spot. This game has a good price-replayability ratio and it's a wise purchase, if you are a fan of roguelike games or tower defense ones. Fun to play it in coop with your friends too.

While there are a lot of negative reviews around the story mode, I don't think it's as bad as some reviewers make out. I think the expectations from the community were unfortunately unrealistic and reality didn't live up to the hype. The story mode is not bad by any means, but I think the developers made their own lives more complicated than was necessary. A much more simple and more open-world approach to the story would have been better in my opinion - clues being left for you to find as you explore, suggesting new areas, maybe even a route to escape. The story mode as it is, is very linear and feels like a very long tutorial with items and skills being deliberately rationed out to facilitate the story. “Realms of the Haunting” is a strange synthesis of three major early 1990s gaming trends: adventure games, full motion video, and old school first person shooters.  But while RotH seamlessly combines all three elements into a single package, it also arguably sounded their death knell in the process.  Released in late 1996, it was in direct competition with “Quake,” “Tomb Raider,” and, several months later, “Dark Forces 2,” three milestone games which set the trend for gaming in the late 1990s and left RotH’s dated looking, Doom style, 2D engine in the dust.  Likewise, the adventure genre was also on the wane, with just “Grim Fandango,” “Gabriel Knight 3,” and "The Longest Journey" to look forward to before going mostly dormant for nearly a decade.  By the end of 1997, the short lived full motion video craze would be eclipsed by the advent of dedicated 3D graphics cards, and mammoth 8 disc, FMV epics like “Phantasmagoria,” “Gabriel Knight 2” and “Under a Killing Moon” would be relegated to historical oddities.
Given this, it’s no wonder that RotH flopped on release.  It was conceived as the hottest game of 1995, but as a testament to just how quickly technology and gaming trends were moving in the 1990s, by the time it was released just under 2 years later, time had already passed it by.
Which is a shame, as this very well could have been the best game of 1995 had it been release just a year earlier. Despite the limitations of its engine, in its design the game is arguably a missing link between “Doom” and “Thief.”  The game world is highly interactable, with lots of objects to click and use.  Levels are also sprawling, labyrinthine, and nearly open world.  They rarely close off once you finish them, so if you really wanted to you could walk from one end of the game world to the other.  Plus, barring a few tedious, late game, mazes and switch throwing, the puzzles are mostly pretty fun and reminiscent of some of “Thief’s” best.
The best part, however, is the plot, which is a completely silly hodge-podge of b-horror films, 90s comic book clichés (there are undertones of both Garth Ennis’ “Preacher” and Neil Gaiman’s “Sandman”), and even, in the game’s dimension hoping with a female sidekick, shades of “Dr Who.”  Of course, comparing RotH to any of these sources is giving it way too much credit.  Its FMV sequences are often leaden and stretch on way too long, suffering from the bad, soap opera, editing technique where the video cuts to super long reaction shots of characters looking pensive after every single thing anyone says.  Plus, things get nonsensical fast, and about half way through the game, the FMV sequences mostly just focus on people appearing to tell you what absurd, magical artifact you have to track down next, before disappearing.  But, honestly, bad acting, z-grade special effects, and nonsensical plots are the main reason for playing 90s FMV games….so I mean none of this as a criticism.
Unfortunately, the game does show its age in some less enjoyable ways. Combat sucks, enemies tend to have way too many hit points, and strafe is locked to the “.” and “,” keys, which makes it unnecessarily difficult at times.  Likewise, in the grand tradition of old-school adventure games, many puzzles come down to pixel hunts, a fact which is made all the more frustrating by the fact that you have to search pixels both above and below you, rather than just on a flat 2D plane.
That said, RotH is such a bizarre genre mash-up that could never have been made at any other point in gaming history, that I couldn’t help but find it charming, despite its flaws.   This is exactly the game I dreamt of making as a kid back in 1995, when “Doom” and Sierra adventure games were my main obsessions. And ultimately its a facinating look back at an entirely unique species in the evolution of FPSs, despite (or, perhaps, because of) the fact that many of its unique genetic mutations have since been selected out of the gaming population.

Realms of the Haunting is unlike so many other games. Someone will tell you it's a Doom clone, and that would be too reductive. Some other will tell you it's an adventure, but that would mean discounting away the combat focus. And it's also a bit of a platformer, a horror story (complete with 90s videogame "quality" live-action scenes), and why not, something of a survival. It's many things at once, and for a good part, it succeeds in mixing them.
Perhaps we could say System Shock is the closest match. Hybrid mouse-keyboard interface, shooting and adventure elements, sprawling map with lots of backtracking. However, ROTH can't quite reach the greatness of SS, if only because it falls down after the first half, whereas Looking Glass' masterpiece keeps a crescendo throughout almost the entire game.
Yes, because while the controls can take a while to get used to, the first half of the game has the player exploring amazingly well-made mansions and temples, solving interesting (if hard) puzzles, being kept on their toes by dangerous but fair enemies, and generally following a gripping story. And then, the second half is ruined by generic otherwordly locations, obtuse puzzles, annoying enemies, and a plot that just stops making any sense.
I still recommend playing it, if only for the first half. As I said before, few games are like it, and for the time its quality stays up, it's genuinely one of the most interesting adventure-horror-shooters... screw that, one of the most interesting games around, period. It received a sort of spiritual successor in Clive Barker's Undying, which shares some of the same strengths and faults, fixing a few problems and introducing some new ones. Both games are well worth checking out, as long as you can forgive some issues.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: Realms of the Haunting is one of those games that I was both quite interested by and somewhat leery about. I was interested in this game for a few reasons: one, it's a hybrid of point and click adventure games and first person shooters; second, the premise looked really cool; and third, it was Let's Played by one of my favorite Youtubers (Kikoskia, for those curious). I was also leery about it, because this is a game made by Gremlin Interactive, the same company that made Normality, a game that had puzzles designed by people from a far-off land in which PCP fills the air. Fortunately, this game doesn't have quite as insane puzzle design as Normality, but it does get kinda silly at times. Also, there's quite a few "key-for-a-key" moments throughout the game. Thankfully, the developers put in an "Easy Mode" in which, once activated, clicking on a puzzle object will automatically use the relevant item in your inventory. Honestly, I don't see why they bothered with this; the only thing "Easy Mode" removes is the impulsive rubbing of objects on walls/locks/enemies/whatever.
As for the game's shooting, it's... different. Also, the controls are... different. Essentially, what happens is that you move as one would in old-school FPSes by using the arrow keys (also, I'd recommend checking the Steam Forums to learn how to change the control scheme, since in-game this game doesn't have customizable controls) while independently moving the cursor around with the mouse. The game does a quite bad job at explaining the controls to you as well; a great example being the consumption of healing salves. You'd think that you could just equip it and hit the use button, right? Nope. What you've gotta do is go into the inventory, left-click on the salve, then right-click on the same icon to use it. Pretty terrible, and the game makes no effort to explain this to you. In fact, I don't even think it was in the manual (although I couldn't really be arsed to read it; the controls should've just been a lot more intuitive).
Anyways, as far as combat goes, rather than point your crosshairs at the enemies, you instead click on the enemy when they are in your viewport. This means that it's impossible to miss your shot (unless you're using weapons that spawn projectiles as opposed to hitscanning), which is a great thing; ammo is kinda scarce. Most enemies pose no threat to you, so long as you're not rubbing your head on their chests or something. There really aren't that many enemies that have projectiles, and they only show up midgame and beyond. There's quite a few weapons in the game, but a lot of the later weapons are functionally the same.
Now, you may notice that I've only spent about eight hours on this game. This game can take a while longer, if you're patient and decide not to run everywhere. If you do feel like running everywhere, I can easily see a few hours being taken off of this game. Even then, there will be a lot of time gained from backtracking and Item Rubbing Quests. Because of this, I kinda feel like this game has about 40% padding and 60% actual content. The 60% is pretty dang good, but the 40% brings ya down (especially the Brain Hunt in Chapter 16; that was absolute garbage). Because of this, I'll give this game a 7/10 for the gameplay.
Story: It's pretty dang good, actually. If you like the older Shin Megami Tensei games like Nocturne and the Famicom games, this one will be right up your alley, if admittedly not as theologically interesting. It is primarily a story in which the story pushes the characters along, opposed to character arcs driving the story. You play as Adam Randall, a man who is trying to investigate some really weird goings-on with his dad, who he hasn't had much of a relationship with. Adam's perceived goal is in an abandoned mansion, but this mansion is a bit different. A bit... eldritch in nature. Then Belial shows up and things get interesting. WIthout spoiling too much, just know that if you're looking for incredible character arcs, this ain't the game for you. If you're looking for some jolly fisticuffs between angels and demons, you've come to the right place. 8/10.
Graphics: One disappointing thing straight out of the gate: this game's maximum resolution is 640x480. There's really nothing I found that I was able to do about that. However, given that this game is an FMV game made for Windows 95, it's a damned miracle this game even runs on a modern OS (and yes, I know it uses DOSbox, so it's not really that much of a surprise, but trust me; I know about getting FMV games to run on modern OSes). Even though the world and the textures may not be the highest-fidelity things out there, there is one thing this game gets right: the art style. It's really, really good. Seriously, the sight after opening the Sarcophagus is absolutely impressive. They did a really excellent job on this front. Also, I belive Gremlin Interactive's engine is based off of BUILD, so expect some really weird texture warping as you turn and tilt the camera if you don't already going into the game. Despite some residual technical issues that this game has, it still manages to look really top notch for '96, even holding some very impressive sights to this day. 4/5.
Sound: The voice acting isn't bad, but it's nothing that will really blow you away. The OST and sound design on the other hand, are actually quite good. One of the big standouts of this game is its music, which does a fantastic job setting up the mood of the area, even if it sometimes forgets to turn off the intense music after the intense stuff is long gone. As for the sound design, it's also done quite well; the monsters, the guns, all kinds of other ambient effects... they're all really good. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 7/8/4/4; cumulative score of 7.7/10. It's one of those games that has aged somewhat, but given that there is a lot of quite high quality content in this game, this age can be fairly easily ignored, save for Chapter 16's Brain Hunt which is still the worst part of the entire game.

This is one of my favorite games from the N64 era.  Upon firing it up, I was looking forward to the same arcade style space flight sim action that I grew to love nearly 20 years ago - good controls, nice visuals (even if somewhat dated now) and a wonderful difficulty curve in achieving increasingly difficult mission objectives for advanced unlocks.
However, I cannot recommend this version of the game until the developers who created this fix a camera problem experienced by many:
WHEN ACCELERATING IN THIS VERSION OF THE GAME, YOUR SHIP WILL CONSTANTLY FLY BEYOND THE CAMERA'S VIEW.
