It's a little frustrating at first, but Baldur's Gate is a journey worth taking. The mechanics take a lot of getting used to, even if you play through the tutorial first (which I highly recommend doing if it's your first time), but it's really rewarding once you make sense of it.

Remember that song, by that dude that people always plays at weddings? You know, the one by Barry White?
For me, that's Baldur's gate.
When it initially dropped, waaay back in 98 I was only a kid, and coulden't get past the first area of the game.
But I stuck with it, and the game rewarded me in oh so many ways. It was the first game I fell in love with, the one who opened my eyes to CRPG's and tabletop RPG.
Now, almost 20 years later, it's still my favorite game and i still play it. Often.
Now, this game is probably not for everyone. Some may find it slow, some may find it boring or tedious, while others may be overwhelmed by the walls of ingame text.
But if you're a fan of RPG's you shoulden't let this one (or it's sequel) slip past you.
In my opinion, the storyline of Baldur's Gate is the best one ever put in a computer game. (Though Morrowind comes in at a close second)
I have never played another game, where the story felt like such an unfolding mystery, and made such great sense, when you at last had the final piece of the puzzel, and were able to see the bigger picture.
The writing is great, the characters are fleshed out, the voice acting is (mostly) superb, and though the graphics are dated as hell, I would still say that they themselves are fantastic.
But for me, theese things are almost (almost!) secondary. The reason I say this, is because the engine, the gameplay itself, is what truly makes this game stand out for me.
There is an almost limitless number of posibilities, on to how you engage your enemies be it with blade or spell.
It takes some getting used to, and might seem clunky at first, but when you understand how the system works, you are rewarded with one of the deepest combat systems I have encountered to date. It's tactical and intricate, but at the same time as blunt and gritty as a meat cleaver.
And it runs on almost everything nowadays. (even Ipads)
The EE edition, also makes this a very customizable game.
You can tweak most anything to your liking, be it the graphics, the difficulty, or how much feedback you want the game to give you on various things going on behind the scene.
That being said, it IS an old game, and an old engine, wich means that if you really want, you can exploit it to such a degree that it breaks the game.
Baldur's Gate however, is so much more, than the sum of it's parts
What Baldur's gate manages really well compared to so many other games, is to really make you feel that you are on an adventure. To put you into the game world to such a degree, that you become oblivious to the real world around you.
In my opinion, Baldur's Gate is a timeless , classic masterpiece that everyone should allow themselves to experience.

"Dungeon of the Endless" is probably the most unique and original game currently available on Steam.  I cannot praise this game enough--from the art style, to the audio, to the challenge, to the fun factor, to the originality, etc.  It is an all around, well-made game.  No matter how many times the game is played, it still offers something new and unexpected because of all the randomized elements, such as dungeon layout and different events that may occur.
I really enjoyed the game because there are so many different gaming elements combined together.  At the core the game is a dungeon crawler.  Battles primarily take place with tower defense elements, since you buy weapons to place in rooms--you don't want your hereoes to do the bulk of the fighting since they are limited in their attacks and with their health points.  Naturally, in order to buy these defenses you have to use resource points--but you also need these resource points to build stronger resource generators and sometimes you'll need to spend those same resource points in shops to buy various weapons, armor, or items.  So resource management is another element to the game.  Another part of the game is also squad/team management; it is wise to place your characters in different rooms to maximize efficiency, such as having an appropriate character explore, 1 to defend/block a room from having monsters spawn, 1 to operate a generator to gain bonus resources, etc.
The game can be played online with each player taking control of 1 (or more) of the heroes on the team, and that's where things get really fun.  The game has been known to occasionally glitch while playing online, but that doesn't happen too often.  There are so many different strategies that can be utilized with each playthrough based on the ship being used as well as which heroes are used, and that's what makes the game feel fresh and new.
Be aware that since this game is a roguelike, if you die you lose all your progress.  So it can be very frustrating spending 5 hours over a couple days and you die when you are very close to finishing the game just because of continuous bad luck with opening doors.  That has not stopped me from playing--or enjoying--the game.  It always finds a way to challenge my mind, so I still cannot truly anticipate which strategy is best for countering the next move that the game may throw at me.  It is 1 of my favorite games currently because of how original and intense it can get, and I will keep playing for many years.  VERY highly recommended!

It's still vexing to me that there aren't more explicitly heavy metal-themed video games. The number is abysmally low: there's the Castlevania-esque platformer Slain, that Geomatrix game for the Dreamcast, the genre-bending gold standard Brutal Legend... and honestly that's about it. A handful of games like Guilty Gear or Splatterhouse feature metal soundtracks, but not many of them are actually crafted around any of the heavy sub-genres of music.
Last year I ran a four-part series covering the sparse options available at MetalUnderground, and now finally a new title gets added to that list – Metal Tales: Fury Of The Gods!  Moreso even than Brutal Legend, this game is all about championing the underground, featuring original music from a slew of unknown bands I've been covering at MU for years, like Despite, Striker, and A Breach Of Silence. Any metal fan won't be disappointed with the soundtrack, that's for sure. I was particularly delighted to see a section in the main menu showcasing each band that contributed music, along with a bio and links of where to find music from those groups.
So, music aside, what's going on with Metal Tales? The backstory is provided via a comic book presentation, when the intense passion of metal heads is converted into despair by an evil god who takes the stage at a live show and works some serious magic. All those metal fans are now walking zombies who need to be returned to their original forms through the power of heavy metal! On the gameplay front, Metal Tales is a top-down roguelike (remember that Smash TV NES game or the top-down Contra levels?) with some bullet hell aspects that gets more difficult the further into the map you go. The levels are also procedurally generated, so you'll get a different experience each time you die and start over, which will be fairly frequent.
At the start there are two characters to choose from, with more to be unlocked the further into the maze-like levels you venture. Likewise, there's permanent upgrades to buy that remain with your character across playthroughs like a power slide attack, as well as consumables like exploding amps and extra guitar pick health. While the game can be played successfully single player (and I've been having a blast doing so), its clearly meant to be a co-op experience with your fellow metal heads, since you can revive fallen team mates and more easily tackle bosses.
Speaking of enemies, there's a decent variety present between normal baddies, damaging terrain obstacles, trap rooms, and huge bosses with varying tactics. Honestly I was a little worried about the formula getting stale after a few areas, especially coming from an indie developer I'd never heard of before, but that's not the case here at all.  Each enemy type behaves different - some charge you, some hang back and fire ranged, some will break through obstacles and others can be herded, and so on. It's all very fast paced, so the end result is a pulse-pounding experience, of course aided by the soundtrack. Whether solo or co-op you're going to die quite a bit in the beginning, having to unlock skills over time and buy upgrades at the various shops, until eventually you'll be armed well enough to hit the later levels.
Considering its a first-effort from Nuberu Games, Metal Tales is a surprisingly polished game that scratches that retro itch. There's tons of little flourishes added in that complete the experience, like how when you go to the menu screen the music gets muffled as though you walked into the bathroom at a live show.
Alright, I've sung its praises, now for the negatives - what's the catch? Although polished, Metal Tales isn't perfect, and in particular it could use some more in-game prompts. I had literally no idea I could use screen clearing amp bombs until manually checking the controls in the menu screen, which is super helpful. There are some areas that also clearly require a different type of attack to break through and get at hidden objects, but no indication of what is needed or how to access them. Some of the items can also be counterproductive - for instance I once accidentally teleported to the store when I was about to beat a boss. After trekking back to the boss room, the fight started over with him at full health, and I promptly lost.
Those couple of learning curve issues aside that could easily be remedied with a patch, Metal Tales is a fast-paced good time for fans of old school roguelikes or heavy metal in general.

DISCLOSURE - I got a review copy for free. This review, written by me, was originally published on the
website (which I own, run and therefore give myself permission to republish!)
I think this is a first for this site - a computer game review. When the news story came in the other day, I just had to try it out so I begged a bit and the lovely folk at Nuberu sent us a test license to take it for a spin.
Metal Tales: Fury of the Guitar Gods is a game with a simple basis - shoot all the bad guys. It's a title you can pick up and start playing very quickly and enjoy for a the kind of blast you can have between meals without ruining your appetite. Only sometimes that five minute "quickie" turns into a half-hour three-course meal and you're late picking the kids up from school. Erm. Oops.
Evil heavy metal demons have taken over your favourite nightclub and you alone can save all your possessed fellow metalheads. Armed only with your trusty (upgradeable) guitar and the WASD keys (or a game controller) you have to wander from room to room, emptying them of evil spirits and gathering the booty before taking on the end of level nasty.
Imagine, if you will, Gauntlet meets Guitar Hero. The graphics and audio owe more than a bit to the plastic instrument wielding console favourite, and they're of a staggering quality. I love the little background animations and the menu effects. Oh, and the music... Included in the soundtrack are some cracking numbers from Despite, Striker and a bunch of others. Sometimes it's background, sometimes it's a featured track for the boss battles. It's all good.
I found the controls a little fiddly, but that's due to the fact that I generally suck at games. I think with a gamepad I'd have found things a little less challenging, but I did manage to finish the first level after a couple of goes. And then got roundly tonked shortly into the Festival stage.
There's a lot of replayability as the levels are randomly generated and you don't have to clear the whole stage to get to the end boss. However, spending the extra time can give you a chance to tool up and give yourself a better chance. Those bosses are randomly selected as well, so you don't have to progress through the levels to encounter them all. Idea for crap gamers like me who'd otherwise not get the chance to see those deeper into the game. They do take a lot of beating, though, as they seem to have a huge amount of health.
There are plenty of power-ups to grab, and there's a shop where you can spend game currency on more permanent features. This definitely makes a difference when you get to the bosses! Dual player fun is available as well, so you can battle on-screen with a friend.
The only real "bug" I noticed was that the introductory animation was voiced over in Spanish, despite my language options being set to English. However, the writing was in a language I can read and the voiceover artist had a lovely gruff style, so it was like listening to a gritty South American drama.
Metal Tales is a fun game. Very, very simple to pick up and one I've popped back to a few times over the last couple of days.

"If aliens invaded the earth, how would we respond?"
I think X-Com: UFO Defense answers that question perfectly.
Launching its attack against players in 1994, X-COM: UFO Defense (UFO: Enemy Unknown to Europeans) has the player building bases across the globe, researching alien technology, and keeping the aliens from taking over/destroying the earth and making humans their slaves.
Touted by many strategy fans as the best game ever, the game has a rather high difficulty, but the learning curve isn't that steep, thankfully. The aliens start sending more and more of their better troops the better you do, though.
I'm not sure if they were going for a Nightmare Fuelish atmosphere or not, but they sure managed to get one, especially on the game's battlescape, with the only music being just a low, pulsing drone. It's especially creepy during the nighttime missions.
If you're looking for a challenge, this game can certainly give you one, and yes, it IS fun. I feel confident you'll like the game, so I can recommend it in good conscience.

This is honestly the best survival experience you could ever ask for out of a game. The audio is a bone-chilling work of perfection, the graphics are a fantastic combination of artsy and realism, while the atmosphere of the game brings a surreal chill down your spine as you attempt to grapple with the cold reality of solitude in a quiet apocalypse.
The story mode is a great tutorial for new players, though the sandbox mode is where the game truly shines. Play the game on any of its 4 difficulty settings and you will have a rewarding experience, regardless of how long you manage to survive. Run free in the 7 different large maps (as well as 3 transition maps) on pilgrim, try your luck on voyageur, face countless hungry wolves on stalker, or attempt to survive the impossible on the game's hardest difficulty; interloper.
If you enjoy a thoughtful, open world game where you alone decide your fate, then this is the game for you. The capacity for immersiveness in the sandbox mode is unrivaled in any other game that has ever come before. 10/10. My favourite game to date.

This is the first time I've ever been killed in a video game by WIND.
Stark. Brutal. Beautiful.
You've never felt such a rush just getting through the night without freezing.
The mood, between the quiet crunch of your boots in the snow and the plaintive cello music occasionally playing, is perfect.  The poetry of survival.
I've been playing video games since the late 70's, consistently the whole way through.  You'd think I'd be pretty jaded by now, and I am.  It's a rare thing when I actually finish one.
But The Long Dark has completely captivated me. So much primal emotion conveyed, so much primal emotion discovered, with the simplest ingredients.  Upon describing this game to my wife, she said "it sounds like 'The Covenant': The Game" and I suppose she's not far off, at least the battling-of-the-elements and desperate bear-wrestling parts of the movie anyway.  I really love escaping into the mood of this game.  It is the epitome of the meaning behind the adage Less Is More.
The music doesn't get enough credit. It really is superlative. Cuts through my soul like butter.
The art is effective by being non-photo-realistic, both from a technical perspective (low-poly=smoother fps) and an artistic one (more expressive)
Other than the Grey Woman, I think all the actors so far are as good as they come. Especially considering Hinterland isn't a big studio and probably can't go for A-list talent.
The mechanics: this is why this game has staying power and should be a classic some day.  The mechanics of survival, presented in this fashion, are both a kick in the butt and extremely rewarding as you master them.  The UI could be more ergonomic for my tastes, but that's not really a complaint, as that really is a subjective thing.  It's not like I'm having to perform as many unneccessary clicks as I do on some Japanese console ports I've played recently or anything (I'm looking at you Bandai Namco and Konami).  And I really do love the paper-doll clothing system they use, it's fun to see how your look changes as you salvage or craft new clothing.
When I died on Day 3 of Story Mode because of WIND CHILL, I became infuriated, so much so that I almost rage-quit and never looked at this low-priced bought-on-a-whim game again.  Nevertheless, I persisted.
On my second go, I got much better at efficiently gathering wood, making tinder, breaking down branches, etc, and felt confident I was going to get through Day 3 this time.  Except at the last minute, drowsy and disoriented from the extreme cold (which is all simulated in the gameplay), I stumbled INTO my campfire and ended up dying again, this time because I could not figure out how to make bandages in time for the burns and the cold to overcome me.
Finally, on my third go, I got through Day 3 and pretty much have been hooked and having dreams about this game ever since.
I see the complaints about Story Mode being a bunch of fetch quests.  I can sympathize with these complaints because the narrative does move really slowly and the missions are indeed mostly fetch quests, but I don't know if a narrative with more momentum or action is even possible with this open world, sandbox gameplay.
Although I can sympathize with these negative opinions, frankly I'm glad the initial story missions play out the way they do.  Because they're basically tutorials that introduce the array of punishing gameplay components in a very orderly, piecemeal fashion and old farts like me who don't pick up new things all that fast will appreciate the gentler learning curve of these tutorials disguised as story missions.
So far, the cutscenes (which are a high point of story mode), happen twice near the beginning of Episode One and once again at the end of Episode 2.  There's plenty of story conveyed in between, but it's all via dialogue text. So the "payoff" emotion you get from cutscenes is indeed limited in Story Mode, which is a bit of a disappointment since you get two high-quality ones right near the beginning and it raises your expectations that this pace of story advancement will continue. It doesn't.  But nothing happens fast when you've got to gather your own wood and tinder to make a fire and then melt snow and then boil water just so you can have a sip of water that doesn't give you dysentery.
As I read through the negative reviews, I get the sense that they pretty much break down into those who want more action in their survival/crafting game (ARK, SubNautica), those who've been with the game since EA and don't like how Story Mode starts off so slow, both in plot development and available skills/equip (you don't get a gun until Episode 2 and bows are still locked by the end of Episode 2), and those who think the mechanics aren't realistic enough.  Well we're not worried about the people who want more thrills because this is obviously not their game and they apparently stumbled into the wrong room. The veterans of the game who don't like how the Story Mode limits them can be forgiven because Yes, story mode does tie your hands at the beginning. But if you've read this far, you know that in my case that was a good thing.  And those who think the mechanics aren't realistic enough, holy cow man, let's not forget this is a game, not a physiology simulator!  LOL
I also wonder if these complainers of the story have finished Episode 2, because we just got two plot twists and two new characters I did not see coming, and suddenly I'm really intrigued again.
While I wait for Story Mode to be completed, I find myself happily spending time in Survival Mode instead. Which is important to note, because I usually put open world games aside after I've completed the story.  Now that I have a handle on the mechanics, I'm simply enjoying playing with them, which is the hallmark of a great sandbox game.  If not for Story Mode as a tutorial however, I would have rage-quit Survival Mode for sure and considered this game wasted money, never to be played again.
SO yeah:  great sandbox game with intriguing story and expressive emotions, great production values considering the size of the studio, music art acting mechanics all especially good.  You just better hope you like the crafting/survival genre, because this game WILL test your mettle.

I've played a lot of hanafuda games in the "real" world, and this is a good start.
Koi-Koi Japan [Hanafuda playing cards] has a lot of the basics with some clever AI and a quick way to access rules, cards, and how the points are calculated. That's perfect. This game isn't a household game in the west. And these three aspects are INCREDIBLY important because Koi-Koi is the type of game that will play differently from home to home.
This version of Koi-Koi is nice for playing against AI. It's quick, and you feel a sense of accomplishment when you've bested the opposition. If you want to get some competitive Koi-Koi going, this should scratch that itch well enough.
However, there are no variations (to my knowledge) in the rules and point-counting. This may be a minor issue since there is possibly a "traditional" version that this game adheres to, but altering the rules for your style is what makes a game like this so appealing. It's why poker has so many variants, or why you can grab a deck of "Standard" playing cards and create a multitude of games.
I'm also not a fan of the impossibly-titted hostess of the game. Hanafuda, guys, not hentai.
Otherwise, if you've always been interested in this game and have never had someone to play with, you can't get much better in a virtual environment.

This is easily one of my favorite games of the past few years, and one of the best suprises I've come across on steam sales.  It's certainly not a title for everyone, but I'll run through the general gameplay and plusses/minuses for those who might be interested.
The game, as others have said, is a unique mix of party based dungeon exploration and tower defense.  As you open doors linking rooms in each level, there's a chance a nasty variety of monsters will spawn in any dark room (more about that in a moment) - making a run for your starting location which houses your precious power crystal.  If they destroy said crystal, or kill your last party member, it's game over.  To survive, you can either kill the monsters directly with your characters (which can be equipped or leveled up to gain new abilities) or through building offensive/defensive/support towers in the rooms you cleared.
The trick, and resource management aspect of the game, is that all rooms start of as 'dark' and have no power, meaning they can a) spawn monsters, and b) can't have any towers placed in them.  To alleviate these two problems, you can power the room with your precious 'dust' resource, which comes in nerve-wrackingly scarce amounts as the game goes on. So - as you run out of dust  and continue exploring, more rooms stay unpowered, which means you face potentially greater onslaughts of creatures with each door you open.
The goal is to locate the exit to each floor, and ferry your power crystal from the starting location to the exit.  Unfortunately, picking up the power crystal also opens any remaining doors on the floor and starts a never ending flood of creatures hell-bent on annihilating you, so each floor is a tense breath-holding sprint to safety.
For me, the interesting part of the game comes from the risk management (or 'push your luck') that comes into play on the higher difficulty. Enemies becoming crushingly difficult on the last few floors if you're resource starved, meaning you should be stocking up as much as possible on floors 1-6 (in addition to dust you earn science, food, and industry, which each have their own uses in building/leveling). However, these are also the floors where you likely won't have many heroes (you'll find more along the way in the standard game mode), and won't have access to useful skills.
So, when I find the exit do I leave immediately, or do I head off in the opposite direction to open more doors and stockpile resources (which could end in disaster if someone dies or a set of rooms gets depowered due to random events)? Similarly, if paths fork and I don’t have enough dust/heroes to keep enemies from spawning where do I put my priorities? Should I leave an area unguarded and hope for the best, or divide my forces and increase the risk of a lone party member perishing.
I find those sorts of decisions fun and always love playing when my back is to the wall. However, for others I can see how the gambling aspect of a resource management or tower defense game might not be a compelling reason to play.  But for the price and quality, I highly suggest you give it a go - it's one of those games that doesn't translate well on let's plays, it's a much better experience in your hands.

I have been having a blast with this game, but it isn't without its faults.
The Good:
The game is fun, it really is. It's a great experience that i've been enjoying ever since I got it. There's a ton of character customization options, almost too many, and the situations i've gotten into have been both hilarious as well as frustratingly difficult. Controlling 6 characters takes a bit of getting used to and a LOT of pausing, but the result is combat that feels tactical and rewarding when you get it just right. Characters have a limited AI that lets them handle themselves for basic actions, but always lets you give them specific orders so you don't have to babysit their every move. The world itself is charming and there are subtle (And not so subtle) pop culture references that made me chuckle when discovered.
The Meh:
The UI can be confusing at times, especially since the game's ruleset is from the earlier days of D&D. I tried explaining what THAC0 was to a friend, it took him a while to understand it. And durations of spells (Round? Turn? Hours?) are not explained well in game...or at all? I couldn't find it, I had to look it up. You can tough it out and learn by experience, but I feel the game could have been more user friendly if it tried.
The Bad:
Bugs. Oh god the game is buggy as heck. Is it playable? Yes, but it takes alot of jumping through hoops to get multiplayer working. Eventually it resorted to Hamachi virtual networking and port forwarding, but even then the game crashed and some pausing issues happened causing us to frequently restart the game entirely and load up a save. This happened with SOME friends, but not others!? LIke, what? Single player seemed decent, I haven't had any issues there, but multiplayer needs some serious work. It's functional, but barely.
Overall:
The game is good, and I would recommend it. Just expect to find yourself with a bit of a learning curve to handle, and some technical issues may arise, but the game is fun and engaging, and DIFFICULT.

This is a classic. Baldur's Gate set the standard for western RPGs and introduced a lot of people to the world of Forgotten Realms and Dungeons and Dragons. I didn't have the pleasure of playing the game when it was first released but I saw a couple of friends play it and become sort of obsessed with it. They would praise the game, it's characters, it's story, it's dialogue, get sort of frustrated with its mechanics, not because they were inherently bad but because they were angry at a party wipe or character death which would force them to reload a save.
They were frustrated but they wanted to play more. They wanted to finish that hard fight, they want to get the best possible outcome, they wanted to do everything.
Several years later I decided to get this game for myself. Wanted to try it and see what it really was. Truth be told it hasn't aged well but the new patch 2.0 did slightly improved it (more on the patch later). It's still feels old and outdated, you'll find almost no QoL gameplay mechanics, it will feel very slow paced for someone used to a subgenre of RPG games, but the game has qualities which make it a classic.
The story is pretty good (albeit I think BG:II is a lot better but this one is still nice), the characters are rich and interact with the world, you and between themselves, the dialogue is superb, serious when it needs to be, funny when it needs to be and even when it shouldn't. An important part when judging the storyline of the game is not only the story itself but how is represented to the player and how the player chooses to progress through it and BG:EE does that pretty well (again BG:EE II has dramatically improved on said aspect).
The combat might feel slow and sluggish at times, since it is technically a turn based RPG without actually waiting for the NPCs to finish their turn. This pseudo-turnbased combat works well at times and feels awkward at others but I believe it's not something to take away from the fun of the experience.

Nonetheless in order to accomodate for the release of the patch, they released a patch 2.0 for the game and the sequel.
The patch did a lot of thing which I will not mention here but it significantly altered the game. There was an outcry but many people who considered this a pointless and detrimental patch for the "old-school" players.

As a fan of survival games i've been having my eye on The Long Dark for a long time, untill i finally purchased it on it's last sale in EA status. Having now played through the single player campaign, i decided to write a short review.
TLD is as beautiful and unforgiving as mother nature herself can be. The artstyle and sights are very nicely done and create a very distinct and memorable athmosphere. The gameplay is simple, yet complex; especially the survival mechanics, where you have to ballance several factors at once and constantly in order to survive (food, drink, warmth, energy, smell, light source etc.).
While some might say that the storyline of Wintermute might be a bit slow and boring through the first two parts, i found it kind of with David Lynch's Twin Peaks, where the story slowly progresses through random normal daily occurances in order to get all the pieces of a huge and terrible underlying secret.
I didn't expirience any bugs or slowdowns, probably becouse by the time i played it, they have been patched out.
Long story short: i reccommend The Long Dark to any survival game players who appreciate a thought-provoking story in an athmospheric enviroment with a distinct but beautiful artstyle.
P. S.: The in-game intro also introduced me to the duo First Aid Kit and their wonderful music, which was another awesome thing that came from buying the game :)

An outstanding game. One of the best AC games, alongside AC 2 and Black Flag.
Conquering the boroughs was a bit repetitive, but switching between Jacob and Evie gives a range of options to eliminate your targets. This variety spices up the conquest activities, something that wasn't there in earlier AC games.
The main quest is extremely interesting, and more than that is the interaction of the Assassins with historical figures, like Alexander Graham Bell, Karl Marx, Charles Darwin and Charles Dickens. It gives a live insight into the character and charisma of these people.
The Darwin and Dickens DLC seemed unnecessary, and was a piece of forced comedy, irrelevant to the Assassins, Templars, Charles Darwin or Charles Dickens.
The Last Maharaja DLC is quite action packed, but 10 long missions are topped with a very faint and unemotional finale.
Jack the Ripper -- now there's a piece of work. This one is more of an Expansion Pack than just a DLC. The atmosphere of Jack the Ripper is so much more tense than the Main game, it gives a real sense of what Londoners must've been going through in August 1888. The uncertainty, mysteriousness and fear in the game is not as in horror games, but just enough for the standard AC player to feel a slight chill up his spine. The main campaign being as good as it is, this Expansion still beats it hands down.
Piece of advice -- If you can, play the World War 1 missions in the main game after finishing Jack the Ripper. Some lore in WW1 missions is a spoiler for the DLC campaign.

The short: A fun, cute, and refreshing civilization builder in the essence of its age-old predecessor: Dwarf Fortress.
The long: As a avid fan of civilization sims and a old school fan of Dwarf Fortress 2, I bought Stonehearth on a hunch that it might be a aptly port to the 3D plane. In return, I was award with a different experience all together. Normally, I am a hard skeptic when it comes to Early Access titles and new wave Indie games. I am proud to say that this is a, currently, diamond in the rough.
One of the first things I found with this game is the adorable graphics and artwork, which really appeal to its style. Everything looks nice and has a charming nature, even in the enemy designs. Gameplay-wise, Stonehearth serves really well as a civilization sim. Everything seems to mesh well together and controls are extremely easy to use. While earlier I ran into problems with the building controls, the recent alpha stage has fixed most of these problems and makes building and designing an awesome experience. Progression is very straightforward and aptly spaced parallel to your own speed. Combat, while simplistic, is easy to follow and pushes you to focus your troops into more diverse roles as your settlement grows. All in all, a very entertaining experience that makes me hopeful for a quality game the more it develops.
While the current stage has not as much content as some would hope for, the team working on this has been effective at maintaining an open discussion with its playerbase. They have also been very well timed in releasing updates on development as well as new alpha builds, which is something I hope to see with any Early Access game. As with games of this nature, the time old expression of "What do I do?" comes to mind for those who aren't well versed with games such as Dwarf Fortress or Gnomoria. However, the game is very easy to follow and figuring out your way is not as hard as such games mentioned.
Basically, if you enjoy games in the nature of Dwarf Fortress, but aren't ready for the complexity of such a title, Stonehearth is the game to play. Adorable, addictive, and a fresh take on civilization sim.

It is (mostly) efficient in what it does, we are immersed in the game, graphics are neat. But it is Early Access, and like in the vast majority of Early Access games, there are bugs. What is disturbing though, is when bugs do not get fixed for more than a year (and still aren't).
I just
the "new game" mechanism, it is original, fun, and efficient. Kudos to the dev team on this one!

I really liked the class system. It contains subclasses, related to the parent class. And a good point for the devs for allowing to switch classes without losing the (hardly) accumulated experience in a class!

Unless there is some mechanism that I did not find/understand, I was not able to put more than 1 fence at a time, and when you have to put 40 fences in place, it is long and painful to go back and forth between the storage area and the place where you wish to put the fence (plus, you can't manage anything else in the same time).
I'm sad that archers (or turrets) can't shoot over fences. It would allow for a more varied military stategy (which would come in handy in certain situations).
One other thing I did not understand, is how you use items stored in a chest/container. Maybe I am dumb, but I tried everything I could think of, and nothing works. My items are just lost (at least the ones I have to manually put somewhere, like fences, beds, ... , as for the rest, hearthlings will get them on their own).
It's been a long time (more than a year) that people complain about the healer not healing wounded earthlings. And it has not yet been fixed. What could possibly be that complicated to explain the delay for fixing this serious bug? This needs to be fixed asap, otherwise it literally kills the chances of surviving.
Warriors seem to be frenzy. Sometimes, they plan on their own to go assault an enemy encampment. Well, they are brave... Or actually stupid. I think it's that: they are stupid. I have no other possibility than forcing them to guard the city, in order to prevent them from committing suicide. This needs to be fixed.
Buildings still bug. I made the grave mistake to pause a building construction. And then it was stuck in the middle of the construction, and no matter than I deactivate and reactivate the construction, nothing happened. The half-built building was just sitting there, taking up space and being of no use. I couldn't even demolish it. Please fix this EASILY by allowing to demolish a building currenlty under construction. The button already exists but is disabled for some reason. Enable it. 5 seconds fix.
Other bugs: workers stuck under the earth, stuck on fences if you build a fence too close to a building, stuck in excavations (no ladder) which is worse if ALL your workers are stuck at the same place...
In any case, to easily fix some of these bugs, the dev team could implement a test to see if the peon travelled some distance since the "move" order, and if not then he is stuck and then just teleport him to the closest (moving) peon's location.
I really enjoyed playing the game! But the bugs, which have been here for long and could easily be fixed, are a pain in the foot, and the dev team should really fix these bugs before adding more features. Please don't repeat the mistakes of Left 4 Dead 2.
Great game overall anyway :)

Or at least, something like that. You get my point.
So, Stonehearth (gosh, that's one unfortunate title *cough*
*cough*) is a very promising *deep breath*
. Whew, that was long.
You start by choosing the background of your hearthlings, their place to settle and the difficulty. Then, you take the role of the taskmaster as you have to guide your people. Craft, build, assign jobs, harvest, defend against hunger, goblins, golems etc.
As nightfalls come and go, be advised that mobs will become slowly, but surely, more difficult to face.
The gameplay is all about choosing the best decision about your everyday actions and proper resource management (whether that's your hearthlings or your food). You have to direct your workers to crafting or collecting what you think you need mostly and prepare for the dangers that descend upon you every night.
You don't have to worry about that, since the game has a perfect pace to give you the time to think carefully about your choices and correct those that turned up to be a disaster.
One very unique aspect, which I enjoyed very much
, is the ability to
. True, you got the default building templates, but you can also choose the size, materials, style, decoration of each construction you plan to make and model it to your heart's desire. Kudos for that, it was an excellent idea from the developers and I don't think any other city building game has ever done that.
On the downside,
Be prepared for game-breaking bugs and it's a good idea to report them in order to help the devs improve the game as fast as possible.
The hearthlings' AI is a bit clumsy at times too, so don't be surprised if your people simply ignore the goblins stealing their precious resources or taking years to clear a specific side of the forest you ordered them to cut down. Hopefully, it will be improved in future patches and builds.
Overall, if you are into this genre, give it a shot when you can afford it and you won't regret it. *wink*

I get extremely motion sick from first person games but Dishonored is one of the few games of that type I've not only played to completion but also enjoyed every bit of.
What makes Dishonored (and hopefully Dishonored 2) so incredibly good is the woleveldesign and the flexible gameplay. When I first heard the word "Dunwall", I thought it's some boring, lifeless town with reused assets everywhere (like Kirkwall was from Dragon Age 2) - but was pleasantly surprised when I learned that it's everything but. The levels are memorable with some great design behind each one. I liked the 'Boyle Estate' and its surroundings the best.
In terms of flexible gameplay, I refer to the fact that not only can you choose your approach to nearly all missions, but that you have a wide selection of gadgets and playstyles to choose from as well. While it might not seem like it at first, a "purist" playthrough where you only use Corvo's trusty assassin's blade will feel entirely different than a playthrough where you use the crossbow and invest in the various spells available.
Memorable story, memorable characters, good narration, fun skills and spells, incredible level design, and an overall nice experience whether you are a completionist, purist or a filthy casual.
Highs and lows
+ Level design
+ One of the best assassin games on the market
+ Story and characters
+ Replayability
+ Much more
- Lows would include certain levels where the main objective was to go from point A to point B in a hazardous environment (the Flooded District level(s) had their charm but some of it took off from the "assassin experience"
- Some colour choices in graphics (I felt blue/grey (like Coldridge prison) overused, but that is an arbitrary opinion)
- DLC could have been a bit better (I liked the idea of playing as Daud and his mercenaries, but apart from Timsh and the main antagonist, there wasn't enough assassination to satisfy the craving~)

This game is a strange beast.
It's surprisingly addictive, but it's ultimately shallow : the strategy is pretty basic and it's mostly based on knowing what's coming next. This knowledge is acquired by dying & dying again.
I beat the game using a trick to backup & restore my save. Looking back on my run it feels very empty and meaningless without any special event nor excitement ; there's only the stress to be crushed by a horde of enemies coming unexpectedly without any warning... :-/
The game is ultra-repetitive, even with only 1 run of 12 levels ; it splits like this :
- Levels 1-3: learn the basics
- Levels 4-6: rolling easily, except for mistakes coming from the annoying interface
- Levels 7-11: running low on Dust, which means we have to use towers more & more to stop the big waves of monsters
- Level 12:
Luck (or its absence) matters way more than skill. I did & re-did many times some levels, doing more or less the same thing, only to win easily thanks to an efficient layout.
The Tower Defense part is dim in the 2nd part of the run, and totally negligible in the 1st part.
And the length of a full run (around 6-9hours) is just too long for starting all over again every time you die.
In a close concept, I'd highly recommend FTL which succeeds everywhere DotE fails (except it's not Coop ;-) ).
- Very unique set of rules & mix of concepts
- Very intriguing at 1st
- If you get into it, decent replayability with new modes offering slightly different rules
- Luck matters way more than skill
- Strategy is actually pretty basic
- Highly repetitive
- No special event
- Only 2 difficulty levels : "Too Easy" and "Easy" ; and "Easy" ain't easy, it's more like "Hard"... I guess the developers of this game must have a high esteem of the quality of their humor. They shouldn't.
- Pixel art is a total mess : it's nearly impossible to see what's going on when there's a ton of enemies crushing in the same room
No, the dungeon doesn't expand.
No, there's no noteworthy special event (the only one I can think of is the EMF that disables your towers for a couple of rounds ; that's not exactly super exciting).
No, they don't have psychoses (ie: it's not Darkest Dungeon ;-) ).
No, this doesn't have any influence on the gameplay (except maybe for the small "trust" bonus, but who cares about that?).
It's only monsters. (Again.)
Which are all pretty basic.
Might be another proof of the great sense of humor of the devs :
. The End.
Spent many offline hours as well. Highly recommened. Bumed into a bug here n there. Will play till the EMP hits.

If you like card games, this is a rewarding purchase.
As others have noted, it plays like a mish mash of other games. Poker, Go Fish - etc. Even so, it has its own style and play.
Your first couple of plays will be daunting. There is a short learning curve to conquer before you are winning any hands. But don't get discouraged - it is much easier than it appears.
Begin by memorizing the various plant types and winning hands. The game has a small Wiki of sorts to make this easy. Googling will also show you what cards match with what - seasons and flowers. There are some cards that are must haves - such as a cup can be slotted into several hands. The easy hands to win are hands with recognizable cards - the harder hands require memorizing banners.
It is possible to learn everything you need from the tutorial and the ingame wiki, but YouTube has some videos and there are plenty of informative sites out there.
Give it a shot.
If you have conquered poker and other favorites - this is a great game to add to your collection.

So, if you think you can play while multitasking... It won't work. There is no option to fix this within the game settings either.
Playing in either Quickplay or Collection mode, there isn't a significant difference besides collecting postcard images in Collection mode. So there really isn't much to go on. There isn't a change of difficulty either. So you're just playing a very linear game through and through.
When playing, you are stuck with mouseover hints and, if you accidentally click on a card where there are two options.... there are no take-backs. You HAVE to play that card. There is also no way to skip in-game animations either. So sometimes the game feels a bit stretched out than it should.
As others have said, it is a very basic hanafuda game and, for the price of $10, you may as well play it as a free flash game or get a free version for your mobile device. So even if you pay for the mobile versions, those at least give you a bang for your buck. To the very least, there are some of those that have a multiplayer option.

Sugar Cube: Bittersweet Factory is a friendly and colorful puzzle-platformer where the player plays a walking sugar cube navigating through various confectionary manufacturing plants. Like many puzzlers the theme is largely irrelevant as it resolves around an abstract concept anyway.
I only played this game for about 30 minutes before I essentially made up my mind so perhaps my review is inaccurate. I usually give a game a little longer before a review but I had some core issues with the game that I didn't see changing anytime soon.
Sugar Cube feels like a game that seemed like a good idea on paper but in practice just isn't fun. The central mechanic revolves around 'flipping' segments of the room to change the layout.  In theory this might sound interesting but my experience is that this quickly devolves into a tedious guessing game as there is often no visual cues where tiles need to be flipped so many puzzles you start out jumping around simply to locate where the necessary components are.
After the pieces are located the puzzles were not partciularly challenging or satisfying and if there was a challenge it was often because a pixel-perfect jump was required at some point. In my short 30 minutes of gameplay I played through the first world and half of the second and the challenge rating did not really increase. At the end of the first world a "boss" was featured but really he was simply a giant obstacle to avoid and was not any more challenging than any other level.
The game's artwork has very limited animations and animated characters in the game feature only a couple of frames and as a result the game feels largely still and lifeless.
This game does support USB controllers but all the ingame instructions refer to keyboard controls so you are left to guess which controller button does what or go to the options menu.
Score: 2/10

This game is one of the classics of Star Wars gaming, and one of the best early flight sims.  This is also, as that suggests, a very old game.  Although I have had extensive experience with this game when I was younger, I am going to try to make this a nostalgia-free review.
Also, for everyone having trouble with the camera, just press the 'view' button a few times (START on a 360 controller).
PROs
++Good flight handling.  I've seen plenty of more modern games that I wish had the same flight handling as the classic Rogue Squadron series.
++Fun game.  This game is just fun.
++Caters to fans.  The more you know of the SW EU (now "Legends") the more things, small and large, you'll appreciate in this game.
+Enhanced graphics (compared to the N64 version).  This game is about 200 MB or so, which is much larger than the old N64 cartridges could hold.  I presume that's mostly in better textures.
+Compatibility.  So far, I haven't experienced any problems other than a small default camera setting issue (as much complained about, as noted above).  It works much better than my attempts to emulate the game in the past.
CONs
--Graphics are old.  I noted that the graphics are superior to the N64 version, but that is not to say they are at all up to modern standards.  This is a game from 1998.  If you want nice graphics, this isn't for you.
--EU reliant.  If you don't know much about the EU, some of the later missions, especially, won't make much sense.
--Difficult.  If you want a challenge, this game is definitely that.  If you're a more casual gamer (like myself), I would recommend enjoying this game with infinite lives.
--No Alt-Tab.  This is a bit of a pain.

As a long time fan of this franchise, I can honestly say that THIS is the first step in the right direction that I've seen in a long time.  After the complete bombfest that was Unity and the Assassin's Creed Movie, this game is what we as a fan base needed.  Something different, yet fimiliar is the perfect recepie for a great revival of a franchise, and that's exactly what this is.  I do have a few negatives and I'll get to those in a few, but for now, here's what Assassin's Creed Syndicate got right.  By the way, I've played a LOT of hours on this game, so there's gonna be some spoilers...
-Jacob and Evie Frye are an excellent, refreshing combo that people will love for years to come.  Their brother-sister chemestry is on point, with the banter and smartass remarks feeding off eachother more and more as the game goes on.  Their bond is very believable and well-written, and honestly, I couldn't get enough of it.  Jacob would often jab with one liners to start and Evie would end up outsmarting him with a quip of her own.  Very comical and it definetly worked.
-London is beautiful, which at this point in the series isn't saying much, because EVERY world you play in in this series as of late has been remarkably and expertly crafted with character and it definetly has a life of it's own.  The lush blows in the wind, the bands play their tunes and it's really easy to just get lost in the big city and look around at everything and see how beautiful and well detailed everything is.  The designers definetly captured what it meant to be a citizen of London at this time in history, and I didn't hate any of it!
-The story, while predictable at times, was really well done too!  "Greeny," as I will forever know him, was a helpful and excellent 'mentor-ish' character, and a great companion.  People might say it's a little unorthodox that the twins crossed paths with the queen, but then again Ezio was buddy buddy with Leonardo DiVinci, so stfu.  All the Assassins run into extremely imprtant historical figures at some point in the game, deal with it.  Evie definetly had the better story of the two, in my opinion, because she was more interested in delving into the history of the Assassins, and recovering relics from the past and gaining a greater understanding for what it really meant to be an Assassin.  Jacob was more the shoot first ask questions later type.  Well, not literally, he definetly has a heart of gold, but he was definetly the more brash of the twins, which leads me to my next point...
-The skill system was a welcomed addition in my opinion and well integrated into the game.  You could choose to make your Rooks better or your own character first!  Really it was a nice addition to "play your own way," even though the additions weren't HUGE.  The thing I like the best about this though was the fact that Evie and Jacob are definetly different, so their skills reflect that!  Jacob is more the "beat the crap out of people" type, where Evie is more designed to be used for stealth, even if her invisibility is a tad over powered at certain times, but it's supposed to be, because it's one of the hardest things to unlock in the game.  And I loved how you could seemlessly switch between the two.  Definetly an excellent touch.
-2 unnessicary additions that were AMAZING
And now onto the negatives, and my dear Lord, there's a lot of them.  I'm gonna be honest, I love this series.  Hell, I'll go as far as saying I love this game, but it is definetly far from perfect.  And honestly, what game really is?  I just really love Assassin's Creed, and if being critical of it will someday somehow help future installments in the series, I'd say my two cents is worth it!  So here's my two cents...
-Crawford Starrick.  What a name.  He's definetly a menacing looking villian and that mustache is on point, but did we really hate him?  Yeah he was running an undergound empire and killing people but did we actually care?  I mean Greeny did and you definetly knew the Frye twins did, but did we as the players of the game actually hate him?  Honestly I didn't care for him a ton as the main bad guy.  I think it'd be better if Bella Thorne was the main bad guy, and she killed Starrick/left him for dead at the hands of the Assassins only to take over in his palce.  It would be very hard on Jacob, since she tricked him into helping her at one point.  That was a good plot twist!  But I can't help but think of that as a missed opprotunity.
-The overall lack of connection to other Assassin's Creed games was painful to me.  Yes, we did get to explore the home of Edward Kenway, where Haytham played as a child and even Evie was very excited by it in the game and so was I!  But there was hardly any mention of other Assassin history throughout the whole game!  I mean c'mon guys, there's literally hundreds of years worth of history and they go back even further if you want to talk about Minerva and Those Who Came Before.

I don't have too much to add that other reviews do not. I like the game. But, there is one real thing that bugs me.
You see, I like when a game provides difficulty through requiring the player improving his/her gameplay. Instead of leveling and providing a hard-locked difficulty (Craft/upgrade your gear to have a chance at killing these enemies in a fight), I prefer when each enemy offers a twist here and there that a player must understand and know how to exploit in order to defeat. There are a couple variations here, and good ones at that. But it really irks me that its spoiled by the need for levels.
In Assassins Creed III, there was the Jagers; the supposed "Badasses" of the game. You could not just attack them outright, you had to wait for them to offer you the opening.
That type of combat (which persisted up to Black Flag -- granted I never tried Unity) combined with the /much/ more fluent combat system presented here (more than one enemy tries to attack you at varying points in combat, it feels more like an actual fight over some kind of dance) would get my gums drooling.
BUT, that's just the one thing that really bothered me about this game. I can't really pick at anything else revolving around the core of the game (aside from the usual collector's hunt, where's muh multiplayer).
But if/when we see another assassin's creed, can you just -not- give me a tophat. Nothing actually wrong with it, but I hate that hat.

Pros:
Kholat's world is absolutely gorgeous, and the game does a fantastic job of setting up suspenseful situations with eerie soundscape as well as visuals. The graphics were awesome, and I experienced minimal framerate issues. The atmosphere is absolutely superb, and could be one of the best horror atmospheres out there. Rocks and trees started to look like people, and I found myself getting scared over things in the game that turned out to be nothing. At the same time, in the beginning of the game, it was difficult to tell the difference between "good" and "bad" NPCs, and that made for a terrifying and quick lesson to learn. I had a hard time playing this game alone, particularly because of the surround-sound setup that's integrated into the game. It was so real. The survival aspect to the game is interesting, although not as in-depth as I was hoping. Although it's recommended that you rest in camps and don't stay outside for too long (to avoid hypothermia, etc,) there are no repurcussions to staying outside for indefinite periods of time. On that note, I liked the idea of getting exhausted in deep snow while running, and it gave chases an urgent touch. Finding the notes to put together the story was awesome, and I only wish there were more notes to collect.
Cons:
The game itself is a little buggy, and there were several (more than six) times that I died in the game by falling through the ground, or by getting stuck on a rock and getting caught by an enemy. One part of the game requires that a door open in order for you to escape from being chased, (you can't open it, the game has to do it for you,) and the first couple times I tried it, the door wouldn't open. So, this was a tad off-putting.
The story felt a little railroad-y at times, and there were countless plot holes. I understand that, given the mystery of the events the game is based on, it's reasonable to include a fair bit of confusing "evidence" and multiple conclusions to the story. That being said, after finding ALL possible evidence in game to put the story together, the ending was not only unclear, but extremely anticlimatic and disappointing. I was expecting a huge plot twist to come out and make sense of everything, but instead, I was left feeling more confused.
Overall, Kholat is a gorgeous game, and worth a play if you like horror/suspense games, or the supernatural. Aliens? Ghosts? Government conspiracies? Psychological disorders? All are touched on, and it's mostly up to you to decide what's going on. Reading about the real-world events makes this game even scarier, and I'd recommend playing with headphones or surround sound. There are countless plot holes, and a handful of bugs in the game, but I feel like these are easy to get past, as long as you keep an open mind and focus on the story at hand. It's not a long game, (I played for almost 9 hours, and wasted tons of time,) but it is a spooky one. The concepts in the game definitely followed me outside the game, and for that alone, I have to recommend it.

As a fan of survival games i've been having my eye on The Long Dark for a long time, untill i finally purchased it on it's last sale in EA status. Having now played through the single player campaign, i decided to write a short review.
TLD is as beautiful and unforgiving as mother nature herself can be. The artstyle and sights are very nicely done and create a very distinct and memorable athmosphere. The gameplay is simple, yet complex; especially the survival mechanics, where you have to ballance several factors at once and constantly in order to survive (food, drink, warmth, energy, smell, light source etc.).
While some might say that the storyline of Wintermute might be a bit slow and boring through the first two parts, i found it kind of with David Lynch's Twin Peaks, where the story slowly progresses through random normal daily occurances in order to get all the pieces of a huge and terrible underlying secret.
I didn't expirience any bugs or slowdowns, probably becouse by the time i played it, they have been patched out.
Long story short: i reccommend The Long Dark to any survival game players who appreciate a thought-provoking story in an athmospheric enviroment with a distinct but beautiful artstyle.
P. S.: The in-game intro also introduced me to the duo First Aid Kit and their wonderful music, which was another awesome thing that came from buying the game :)

Hanafuda Koi Koi Japan is a card game which is easy to pick up, thanks to the tutorial and yaku (card set) checker, but challenging to master.
After a few games you do start to pick up which combinations score 1, 3, and 5 points or more.
For single player there are Training and Campaign modes of play. The postcard scenes earned in Campaign play are interesting. The game is expandable if you purchase the DLC, with more campaigns to unlock traditional woodblock images.
There is a very relaxing and pleasant background music track, which is customisable.
The core game started without multiplayer, but it has since been updated to allow games with Steam friends, Quick Play against other players and there is a lobby facility. Due to the low player population I use Quick Play and then play a single player campaign while I wait to be matched with a player. I think the flexible multiplayer system works very well.

Edit: Waifu displayed in the banner is available in the free DLC 'Enjoy pack', otherwise you only get silhouettes in wafuku
It's a pretty decent version of Koi-Koi, with nice graphics and great music (by decent, I mean most Yaku is integrated correctly). It takes a while to get used to the staccato animation (cards are animated when moving to your table, but not animated when they are placed on the board).
So far there are no rules customization, which I would like to see (in future updates perhaps?)
It's advertised as 'Optimized for Hanafuda Beginners', and it really is for beginners, the difficulty is not that hard. Veterans of Koi-Koi would be disappointed I guess. But it's great as a relaxing style Solitaire game :)
Also, you get achievements for assembling the different yaku!
I'd give it a solid 4/5, if more features like rule customization or customizable AI difficulty was present, I'd give 5/5~

Also known as UFO Enemy Unknown. The original (1994) was super buggy and nearly unplayable on newer systems, but thanks to these guys (the people working on the openxcom project) the game is now playable and with lots of bug fixes.
The game is pretty unbalanced and exploitable, here are a few tips:
-  Don't exit the craft in the first turn as the aliens, that have visual on you, will have full AP and will likely reaction fire.
-  Always have the maximum number of soldiers in the landing craft (while this might be obvious, I saw people that don't do this, usually the same kind of people that spend all the APs exploring instead of having some AP for reaction fire or retreat).
- Put the most expandable soldiers closer to the exit of the landing craft because the first ones out are the likeliest to get killed.
- Don't hurry, especially getting your troops out of the landing craft.
- Advance slowly, only extend yourself when you have an alien’s location and you can kill it because you don't want it to have a full turn while you are in sight. Expanding on this, try to kill all the aliens that you see in the same turn that you see them; that's why it's usually best to advance slowly (to have lots of APs) and have lots of soldiers (and implicitly firepower).
- You should use scouts (~rookies) that at the start of the turn will try to advance but also retreat at the end. This way you'll create a buffer and decrease the chance of enemies sneaking close enough to the rest of your (more valuable) soldiers.
- Exploit: After turn 20 the aliens are generally going to come and try to find you, useful for landed/crashed UFOs.
- A very good starting location is in west Lebanon so that you will have cover over Europe and a lot of the downed UFOs could be in North Africa where the desert maps are pretty smooth.
- The beginning (or better said the first half of the game) is going to be pretty brutal, use all the force that you can and don't shy away from explosives and leveling buildings even preemptively in some cases.
Pros: great feeling, nice combination of tactical game, researching stuff and base building while under pressure to survive.
Cons: exploitable, unbalanced, bad spotting/FOV mechanic, you see as much as the aliens only in full light which will lead to a lot of frustration.

At the time of this review (7-16-2016), I would say the game is already worth the purchase price. There are so many games that charge far more while delivering far less. And this game is only in the alpha stage.

If you are into city buidling games, farming,  creating your own army, job management, etc, this game does a very well job presenting the genre of city builders.  The art style has a very cartoonish feel, at the same time giving the game its own charm; style that cannont be replicated by any other city building games out on the market right now. There is a lot of flexibility on how you want to manage your new village/town/city/empire and however you want to play it. With the plethora amount of new villagers coming into your town, you will find that there are many jobs that you can assign each Hearlthing. Build your own army to fight off hordes of Goblins and other such monsters. Loot from your enemies after you slay them and use the resources to help further expand your empire. There are also a variety of landscapes and even races of humans you can choose from; even more hours to explore how you want to play. While the idea of all this sounds great on paper, Stonehearth manages to crumble all those dreams.
Yes you will have fun playing this game and yes you will enjoy the many hours playing this game. However, the one thing this game suffers greatly is the amount of bugs and gamebreaking bugs this game has. It gives Early Acess the perfect meaning of unfinished game, but somehow manages to make it even sound worse. The major bugs I have encounter mostly revolves around trying to build houses. More specifically customized buildings you try to build are very much broken and have been since the start of this game. Builders will continue to remove and build ladders to reach higher areas of the buidling, and be in an infinite loops doing this. Sometimes they will continue doing this until the building is destroyed or if you somehow make the AI build other buildings instead. Also you cannot destroy certain buildings, it doesn't even explain why it cannot be destroyed. It could also be because the way customizing your own building could be broken as hell.
One of the most essential mechanic of this game is broken and that's where I draw the line. A game that focus primarily on creating buildings is broken. Instead of the developers trying to fix this, they release more updates on combat and focusing so much into that. It is quite sad actually, made me not want to play this game for a while. I even contacted the developers about this bug, and they know it exists, they just dont want to do anything about it for now. Many other players also complain about this same exact bug. The only answer they gave me is to use console and to type in commands to instant build and instant destroy. Using a game's console to play a game, to even enjoy it is quite appalling to even hear, but that is the ONLY way to play this game without ripping your hair out of your head.
I've had a few problems with combat, but it mostly had to do with the Battle music playing in an infinite loop. Other than that the combat is fine and I have no problem with that. Farming, Smithing, Crafting, Etc. are all fine as well No problems there. StoneHearth is a great idea, I really really really really want to say this game is a Great game. I wish, but this game is not great, this game sucks, this game is garbage. this game needs hate rather than love to show the developers they need to change and fix their game. I always look at this game every week to see if there is an update, JUST MAYBE SOMEDAY THIS GAME WILL WORK PERFECT.
Don't buy this game until the bugs are fixed, don't even recommend or even mention this game to anyone. This game has the potential being the New way of playing city builders. The Next grounbreaking sim city game, it has that potential, THE DEVELOPERS NEED TO CAPITALIZE ON THIS GAME. I know this game has the potential to have a large following, just fix the game.

I would recommend this game. In fact, I told my roommate he should buy it!
Pros
- Adorable graphics
- Easy to pick up and play: Small learning curve to get started..
- So many options to be creative with building
- Lots of graphic and gameplay settings
- Replayability factor, you can focus more on militia or more on building cool buildings. You can build a farm village, or a castle fortress, or a deep mine cavern.
- New recent updates from the devs <3
- HUD is well organized and smooth and easy to use
- Two different map options (forest or desert). Would be awesome if there was more idealy, but the fact that I even got an option was awesome :)
- Villagers are so easy to get attatched to. They all look unique and have cute randomly generated names and random skills.
Cons
- Lots of bugs. But is to be expected, this is not 1.0
- Could be more furniture and block options for someone who loves to be build creatively (but again, this game is still getting updates)
- Building is way too clunky and difficult to figure out. You need to choose to build a whole house in order to build some paths which was confusing at first. It's a little difficult to alter your buildings, and maybe even impossible to alter them without demolishing after they've been built! (this may be my own error but I couldn't figure it out...)
- Torches turn on way too long after it's dark
- Wish there was more customaziable difficulty options (right now theres just the option of peaceful, normal, or hard...I want something between normal-hard)
- Hard to tell which items you have interactions queued for and for mining as well. The blocks you choose to mine are sometimes unreachable and the queue never goes away and theres no way to clear it (that I could figure out even after hours of play...)
- Hard to mine into deeper levels, your villagers often get stuck if you dont construct an elaborate staircase or remember to go back and add a ladder ;)
Overall this game is amazing. I'm discovering new things about it the longer I play and liking it even more as my small village grows! I am eagerly awaiting updates that are coming soon! :)

It's like a roguelike that turns into a tower defense.

Amplitude's best game by far is a fascinating mix of gameplay styles and genres, where you take your heroes through a randomized dungeon, opening doors, gaining levels, building and upgrading turrets, and finding equipment.  All the while, your crystal sits at the start of the level, and monsters will try to either kill your heroes or break that crystal.  (Don't let either happen!)  The monsters come out of the dark, but you can only light so many rooms.  Once you find the exit, you're not done...you have to assign a hero to carry that crystal to the exit.  The moment you pick it up, any room that's dark will just SPEW monsters at an alarming rate, so you have to make sure you're protected from them as you run the crystal out of there.
That's the basic flow of gameplay.  New heroes are unlocked by finding them in the dungeon, and the storyline is revealed through a scrapbook that's filled as you play (sometimes requiring specific combinations of heroes to be used).  Multiplayer for up to four players, or you can control everyone in single-player.  Definitely take it for a spin, especially if it's on sale (it'll be, like, $5).

A great traditional japanese card game. It's simple to learn, but the more you play it, the more you understand how to make the best decisions.
Basically you're trying to form suits (Yaku) that provide a variety of points. But you can only match cards into your suits if there's a corresponding card type on the field, if you can't match cards then you'll need to put down the card on the field, which you will be able to use next turn (Or your opponent might snatch it before it gets there.). So sometimes, if a opponent has almost a complete suit, and you know that your opponent might be waiting for a certain type to go onto the field, then you'll just avoid playing that 1 card so that your opponent might need to discard the card that he requires and you could take it for yourself.
It's a bit hard to understand but, if you play it just try to learn the Yaku and through experience you'll understand what type of yaku need to be matched with what cards. Each card type has a season/month related to it, and you can only match cards with the same seasons. If you play it, you'll understand it.

I will start by directing your attention to my 730 hours logged.  The game is crazy fun; TRS had lightning in a bottle, and they have screwed up in every conceivable fashion.
If a game is any good, hardcore competition will Evolve naturally.  The devs tried to bill the game like this from the very start, to the detriment of the majority playerbase.  The focus on competition at the expense of casual has lead to the community as we see it today; the remaining playerbase is elitist, salty, and generally all-around jerks.
Pros:
-The characters & story are genuninely engaging and fun.  Credit where credit is due, the universe of Evolve extremely entertaining.  The official forums has a writing section where the lead writer posts canon backstory & events.
-The customization options for a match are numerous and fun, but are virtually inaccessible (see Cons).
-Hunting, the thrill of the chase.  When both Monster & Hunters have the mindset of providing a good fight (as opposed to soley winning or stomping), Hunt is adrenaline-packed good time.
-Community challenge every 2 weeks awards a skin or set thereof.  I have like 50 in total now, and never spent a dime.
Cons:
-Complete lack of options for pub matches (non-Ranked).  You can't choose map or game mode, nevermind all of the really cool map effects and other fun options (extra critters for Monster, bonus Turrets for Hunters, adjust Strikes & Timer, etc.).  These things are exclusively available in private matches (solo or with friends).
-Ranked mode is the only way to consistently play Hunt.  Again, focus on competition at the expense of everyone else.
-Most Hunter skins are literally a single color change on the weapon.  A few Hunter skins are stand-out, and Monster ones range from 'decent' to 'lulz awesome'.
Summary:
The game is dead, and has been for quite some time now.  I'm just glad I got to enjoy the ride down.  At this point, nothing can save it short of the devs acknowledging their mistakes and directly all efforts to improving public gameplay.

An expansion to an almost 20 year old game was destined to be controversial, especially when we're talking about a beloved franchise such as Baldur's Gate.
Baldur's Gate: Siege of Dragonspear is Beamdog's first true attempt to write an original campaign in the Baldur's Gate series, with mixed results.
The writing has improved, if only slightly, from the developer's previous material in the Enhanced Editions (which weren't good I'll be honest, the monk was decent, though), it still falls short compared to the base games but that is to be expected. Still an upward trend one would hope. One great thing is the voice acting, that I'll give them. Major props for getting some of the originals back.
The gameplay is little different from the previous games and they do give you certain challenging encounters, though they made some strange changes to the interface which I don't like, but perhaps new players will find it to be better.
It does sadden me slightly that some characters are used as prompts in the play of identity politics and ideology pushing; it feels a little on the nose. Truth be told I would be more tolerable of it if it didn't come across as blatant virtue signaling, and trying to earn brownie points for being 'Oh so progressive'. But who am I to say which demographic the developers should target, I'm just giving you my impression of the game.
Anyway I did enjoy the game so it'll get a positive review from me, but be aware that it is a mixed bag, though more good than bad in my opinion.

It's at this point that I realise that I just don't like D&D, the philosophy behind all the characters is very thin and doesn't fit reality. I hated that two party members left me because they thought I was too evil... after killing a bounty hunter that attacked me first. I hated the bard that made fart jokes; the guy literally says ''PFFFT, hooh, that was a sharp one'' when you click on him. There's also the necromancer that says creppy things, but whines like a baby 50% of the time; what's up with that? It's wierd, juvenile and unappealing to the point of disgust. There is no way, absolutely no way, to think that the characters are interesting or developed.
But, I do appreciate the fact that there is close to no hand-holding. I really did. No pointer, no arrow, just you and the world.
