A great intro to the game of Koi-Koi.
The rules may seem daunting at first. The tutorial is alright, but because of the sheer amount of info (you're learning to play a new card game after all), much of it actually flies over your head even if you're paying attention. But when you start to play the interface lights up matching cards, which makes it easier especially for beginners.
After you get the hang of matching cards is when the real game begins. The AI is clever and is seriously trying to form the right cards, and will mercilessly beat you whenever possible.
Graphics are simple and clean, sound is alright. Music is traditional, which is perfect.
It has a sort of career mode called "Collection mode" where you challenge players from different regions to collect postcards.
All in all, great fun if you have the patience and determination to learn it.
- edit: The online multiplayer is a nice touch, but because of a lack of popularity there may not be a lot of players waiting in quick matching. Still you can play with friends, which is definitely better than what this game was before, as I was already happy with it prior to multiplayer being introduced.
The new UI makes it even easier to see possible matches, so you only need to worry about combinations.
One issue I had with the recent update though was that I was unable to update the game normally via Steam. Steam kept giving an error. So I had to delete local files first and reinstall. After that, no more problems. Still, it was a bit of a nuisance.

The only thing it doesn't do is provide you with a kimono-clad VR avatar.  But Oculus Rift is not out yet, so there's still time.
So, I will ask...  what is the fate of the world worth to you?  $1?  You never know when this might come in handy.

This is a really difficult game to rate. The gist of the game is: You navigate an area, finding notes/locations to tell a story. It's a mystery/walking simulator, with minimal scary elements dotted throughout the game. You're either going to like it, or hate it. I find it really hard to love, because it has one mechanic that was very annoying to me - you can only sprint for about 5 or so seconds, and if you exhaust your energy you become fatigued. The world fades, and you need to come to a complete halt to regain energy. If you just walk, you will be in this constant state of blurriness. So on far too many occasions, I was just sitting there for 5+ seconds waiting to move again. Poor design choice, in my opinion.
Overall, I enjoyed it despite the complaint about stamina/running.
+ Environment is crafted very well, and gives off a spooky/haunted vibe
+ Elements of mystery, intrigue and a couple jump scares add in to give what is basically just a walking simulator, a good pace
+ A pleasing game to look at.
+ Interesting story that is told by collecting notes (You will have to read at times)
- The stamina (or lack thereof) and regeneration of stamina is poorly implemented
- The being that follows you..or well...tries to deter you, doesn't really add much to the game
- Minor, but performance isn't the best. i5-4690k@4.4Ghz, Gtx1070 struggling to go above 40fps at 1440p? Meh.

Yikes. How the Should Have Been Mighty have fallen.
I've got 70ish hours into Evolve, but part of that is because I play with a buddy of mine. Together, we have a decent time of it. But, even a multiplayer game isn't allowed to stand on "well if you play with a full team of you friends you'll be fine," because not all of us have three other friends willing to drop 60 plus dollars for a game. So:
Evolve promised a lot, for a AAA title. Asymmetrical 4v1 combat? People versus monsters? Surprisingly risky for a big company, since so much could go wrong. And for the record, they did all that right. If you're on a competent team, it's thrilling to be chasing down the monster, trying to stop it before it reaches full power. The gunplay is fun, with none of the guns feeling similar (though plenty of them feeling underpowered- more on that later).
The monsters, in a word, are stunning. Visually unique, with fantastic powers that allow for a variety of strategies from player-to-player and even match-to-match, the monsters stand out as awesome.
The human characters, though, are a mish-mosh. Some are awesome, with crippling weapons and abilities that can shred monsters. Others.... are basically useless in all but the most specific situations. There are 4 distinct classes, and the Trapper class goes from "linchpin" to "dead weight" in a microsecond depending on the skill of the monster, the Trapper player, and even just the map. Balance amongst the human classes is something they need to work on, and haven't really fully addressed yet.
Part of the problem is that this is a multiplayer game, and the community has, by now, largely dried up. This is in part because of the disgusting amount of DLC they pushed; skins for monsters, new hunters and monsters, all sorts of rubbish that you all had to pay for /right off the bat/. Left a bad taste in a lot of people's mouths, and so people began to disappear quite quickly, leaving a gaming community that is polarized; on the one side, we have diehards who have hundreds of hours clocked in and can wipe teams in the blink of an eye. On the other hand, we have newcomers or casual players who picked it up on a sale and don't understand anything. They clash and both parties walk away with negative feelings.
Summary
Though starting off with a good concept, and well executed visually and in basic mechanics, Evolve is demonstrably less fun to play by yourself or with only a few other friends. In a close knit, team based game, this makes for a largely unpleasant gaming experience that leaves one baffled and frustrated at losses and often guilty after wins. The amount of DLC pushed by the devs quickly created a wasteland for players who balked at already dropping sixty dollars for a game, and then asked to pay even more to access what should have been starting content.

Right, so I gained 100% completion and I'll recommend it, but I'm gonna say this - the game is definitely not a masterpiece, but a fine game in all. What makes me say that? Well, after more than 2 years since release and some patches, let's get through the cons: Quality can be bloody frustrating at times - unstable engine (an average of 1 crash/10hrs of gameplay in a total of 70hrs). Frequent spikes which make the game freeze for more than 3 seconds, guaranteed due to engine issues rather than rig setup (I5 6th gen, GTX1060 3gb 192bit, 16GB DDR4). While trying to attain 100% completion, the client can go into an infinite loading screen when missions are loaded from the progress tracker menu. Other minor issues can be overridden.
It's ok to have collectibles, but Ubisoft decided again to overdo it. Mechanic can be idiotic at times. So, this is a pitty because the title could have been so much more.
The game itself can be enjoying at times especially if one liked the series/or similar parkour/stealth based games or if you happen to have a passion for London like I do.
Carriage driving is not very realistic, but not that bad after all.
PROS: Graphics are good; Having two characters to play with is welcome; The story is fine, good diversity with side missions for assosiactes and borough conquering system. Nice WWI bonus content. The tools available are more than one could ask for.
Anyway, you can give it a go, but be warned of engine quality and best to play it casually rather than focusing on full synch.

Ace of Words is one of these games I'm interested in for a potential educationnal value. So testing it was changing me from the F2P Lost Lands/Clover Tales or other hidden objects games (and Killing Floor 2 that keeps crashing on me since another update of theirs).
Do you know anagrams and Scrabble? Well, it's kinda a mix of them. You're given a list of letters and it's up to you to make the maximum words. The default mode isn't allowing you for 7 or 8 letters, so, go to the options and activate it, so that you will be able to make some achievements.
You can see the number of words available and they're revealed to you on the upper part of the screen. However, in order to access a new puzzle and keep your previous score, you need to reach the 100% bar. Also, you need to reach a certain level before unlocking the hint option.
But the best is that you change language. I could play in French, though I switched back to English. I'm maybe lacking words but at least, I'm not being frustrated. Let me explain: the game doesn't allow for words existing in French with accents. And trust me, there are a lot like that, that you can make but as the dictionnary included doesn't allow you to put them, you're frustrated.
It's the same for English. Where Letter Quest: Grim's Journey allows you a lot of words, Ace of Words is restricting. However, I'm surprise sometimes: some words are really weird and probably derives from scientific langages. Too bad, you don't have any little definition with it.
Anyway, Ace of Words is really a good game to exercise your vocabulary if you're not an English speaker for example. It's a real good moment to pass with it. Perhaps the price is high for that kind of game but yeah, if you can buy it during a sale or when it's bundled, go for it!

A quick premise: I absolutely prefer 3rd person view games, and I don't like FPS at all. I only played Half Life years ago, and catched up with Half Life 2 recently, mostly because they're not dumb shoot-em ups, and I did enjoy them. Still, they were still way too action oriented for how I like games, although fun. I find all those survival FPS horror games quite annoying, and walking simulators usually boring. Anyway, it's also a matter of aesthetics: I just find first person games unappealing, most of the times.
That said, I decided to give Dishonored a try considering the interesting trailer and envorinment, and what an experience I had! I absolutely recommend this whether you despise FPS or not, as good chances are that it will change your perspetives on the genre, as it did to me.
You play as Corvo Attano, the bodyguard of the empress who has just returned from a mission abroad. The city is suffering from a plague, caused by rats, which is decimating the population, and you have been sent to seek for help outside. Unfortunately, you're back with bad news. As soon as you get back to the city, you meet the empress' daughter, 10 year old Emily, and it's immediately apparent that there is a special bond between you two. Then, you deliver the bad news to the empress and hell breaks loose: an assassin gets there and, despite your efforts, the empress is killed and Emily abducted. As if it wasn't enough, you get blamed for both things and thrown in prison, and that's where the game really starts. 6 months later, where thanks to some help from outside you try and escape, in order to find out what happened and exact revenge.
That's the basic premise and it gets more and more interesting along the way. Gameplay wise, you can decide different ways of tackling the challenges ahead of you: you can try to be more stealthy, or you can kill everything you see. One doesn't prevent the other, as there are several ways to kill from the shadows, and you'll soon gain powers that help you greatly whatever way you follow. Anyway, the stealth aspects are where Dishonored truly excels: wherever you need to go, there always are multiple patsh you can follow, with different obstacles. Besides, believe it or not, you can actually finish the game without killing ANYONE, not even the bad guys, and that's something I found really novel and refreshing, not to mention a real challenge as it's often much easier to just go for the bloody way. What I found even more interesting is that how you choose to proceed will also impact both the people you interact with and the world around you, with bloody approaches obviously resulting in darker outcomes. I don't want to spoil it for you, so I recommend you experiment with both if you are a sucker for replayability.
I've read people complaining about the game's length and it being too short, something I can't relate to: it took me more than 20 hours to finish it, but I chose to explore a lot of the (amazing and immersive) environments and look for hidden secrets, which might explain why it took me longer. Nevertheless, I never felt as if the story was being rushed or things going too quickly: story wise, everything makes perfect sense and is perfect the way it was conceived and executed, and I personally don't feel there was any need to lengthen anything.
Long story short, I strongly recommend this game, and am now really looking forward to the already announced sequel. I haven't played the DLCs yet, but considering how much I enjoyed Dishonored I'll definitely play them too.

It seems a bit buggy on the multiplayer side of things but I can't comment on that as I never tried it.
From a singleplayer perspetive though this game is absolutly phenomenal! It seamlessly blends  Dungeon Crawler with roguelike elements, a bit tower defence and tactical elements akin to games like XCOM. This mix might seem bizarr on paper but it works so, so well!
You crash with a small party on a planet and your rescue pod digs deep into the earth. You find yourself inside the ruins of some sort of an underground facility and goal is to get out and escape. You do it by ascending from floor to floor. It's pretty much a game of limited resources. You need to juggle Power, Industry, Sience, Food, Level-Ups, Equipment, Storage, Health, Upgrades and the urge to explore vs minimizing risks by staying close together. All systems are interconnected in parts so you constantly have to weight your otions. And even though it is pauseable by hitting the space bar there is always a sense of urgency and hectic once you ascend further where resources become more sparse and the enemies increasingly difficult.
The game further pulls you in by discovering and saving new characters each run for you to then choose from on the subsequent ones. Those characters have some minor stories tying them together and hinting at something larger in the background, giving the game some form of narative depth.
To finish up this review - it's a decently hard game without any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG. But don't be fooled by the developers choice to label the difficulty choices "easy" and "too easy". ;)

In its simplest terms, this game can be thought of as a real-time strategy version of Minecraft with roleplaying elements. The comparison to Minecraft is regrettable, but with a creation toy based on blocks with monsters in is released, no matter what the actual pretext, it is now unavoidable.
Genuinely pleasant game, the aesthetics are fairly cutesie, but it does more to add to the game's charm, rather than deduct from it with unnecessary young-people appeal. The promotion system is sound, if a little inextensive. More jobs could easily be added, with only bolstering effects, war-type mages for the combat promotion path, for example, and several more crafting jobs could be though up with minimal effort. The modding capability is very high, for an Alpha game, but it should be noted that due to it's novelty and relatively small following, not many mods exist for the game, online.
On customisation, there isn't much in the way of characters, but as much can be expected when you can fairly easily amass a village of 14 people, and it can simply keep growing and growing. Though, that said, names of characters can be changed and jobs can be customised almost on a whim, if you have the tools to promote the Hearthling (or "person") to said job, most of which are very easy to create once you have a person who can make the tool in question (usually only a couple of units of fairly easy to obtain resources). Buildings can be designed to your liking and then saved as a sort of blueprint, to be placed as a prefab later, though, if design is not your thing, several prefab buildings exist when you first start the game.
On control, it is not possible to take direct control over your Hearthlings (with the exception of combat units), instead they perform tasks that are permitted to them by their job, and by restrictions you place upon them. This, while it saves time used in micromanagement, is fairly annoying in some aspects. Firstly, the Hearthlings seem to have no concept of importance, as tasks can not be set priorities, meaning workers will simply do whatever is closest to them, slowing down individual projects (buildings, deforestation, mining, etc.), and the mindset of "I can't control these people, they do as they please" is quite a jarring one to jump into when used to the industry standard real-time strategy games.
Bugs are encountered frequently enough to be noticeable, but never crash the game, instead, the software simply informs you of the bug (via an in-game window, from which the error code may be copied, if desired) and stops you from performing the action that caused the bug, carrying on in function as normal.
Difficulty could use some balancing, however. Even on a standard difficulty (of peaceful, standard and hard) , a fair amount of you Hearthlings are essentially required to be militaristic, (say up to 40%, depending on how cautious you are) due to the insane spike in difficulty past a certain point. Of course there are raids on your village regularly, which in and of themselves are of little concern, yet if a goblin village settles near you (or worse, a goblin war camp) you will be attacked 2-3 times a day in total, very commonly resulting in an overlap of attacks, the armoured goblins being able to put up quite a fight even by themselves, and they usually attack in bands of 2 or 3. If they were clever enough to focus their attacks on a single Hearthling, it would be simply unfair.
It is not yet implemented, but multiplayer is in the plan for completion.
Though, despite the gripes, it is a pleasing game to have in your library. As such, I would recommend Stonehearth.

In short:
- I really like the game! Nice Atmosphere and doesn't get boring even after hours because of the events.
- The often-mentioned errors in building can be solved!
- Huge recommendation to everyone who was a little disapointed from Banished (like i was)
I was looking for a game like this for long and was excited when i found Stonehearth.
Before, i tried Banished but after a short time, this game became boring because there wasnt much to discover and after setting up a basic economy you could leave the game to itself for hours with nothing happening.
LONG TERM FUN:
Hearthstone, instead, comes with a set of randomly occuring events (Like attacking goblins or vacant traders), as well as several different structures and/or mobs spawning on the map throughout the game. So there is always something to discover for you!
Your hearthlings can learn a profession, but in order to craft the advanced recipes, they need to learn and improve their skills. With new hearthlings coming to your town if you meet the conditions, you can progressively expand as you like.
BUILDING
Another cool feature is the building system. Although you need a moment to learn how to build a custom structure, it is a well made and well functioning mechanic. You can either build from a template or construct from scratch. And if you designed a cool new structure, you can save the blueprint and build it again and again!
An often mentioned deficit of the game is, that the hearthlings place every single block of a structure seperately - and sometimes get stuck.
If your hearthlings wont continue building, it is mostly because they cant reach a certain spot. There is some work to do on this procedure for the devs, i agree, but its no game-crashing bug!
If you use your brain a little you can relatively easyly determine, which block would be built next and then provide a path to it with ladders. Once the block is reachable, the work will continue.
For me, the only times this bug occured were, when i tried to build an underground strucure, or when i built too close to another building. Both time i presume, the space for the normally applied scaffolding was blocked and so the work couldn't be continued.
As i said, this can be helped by providing ladders yourself.
By the way, i think the scaffolding and "authentic" building is a big plus for the game. Not the usual "a worker beats the floor with a hammer while the building rises straight from the ground" - thing!
ACTIVITIES
So you can command your hearthlings to gather ressources or craft things in their profession. That is nice and all, but what i really like and searched for is that you have to defend your town, too!
Your hearthlings can become different kinds of soldiers as a profession (and level it up as well) and defend the others from incoming goblins, orcs and whatnot!
So on the one hand you have the Town-simulation and ressource management, on the other side you have a combat-simulation where you can show your tactical skills, too!
So i really hope this game gets developed further and i really look forward to new features!
A big thumb up for Hearthstone!!

Horror games usually stick to a few basic genres. First-person, adventure, and puzzle are all well-worn trails for spooky titles to travel down, but management is definitely an outlier. That’s right where you’ll find Daily Chthonicle though, a management game about sending reporters to dredge up and vanquish the dark forces afoot in your city. And it works, less as a horror game and more as a management title, by giving you a team to work with and mounting challenges to pit them against until either they or the horrors break. Just bear in mind that while you’re learning the ropes, it’ll probably be your team that falls first.
You’re the editor-in-chief of the titular Daily Chthonicle, hometown chronicle of the strange and spooky. Cultists, ghosts, and infernal machines are making life hell in your city, and the only way to stop them is with the mighty pen. Researching stories and publishing the truth is the goal, with every story you run earning you new funds and putting a dent in the eldritch forces that hold your fate in their ashen hands. You’ll need the right tools to defeat monsters and pass mundane and mystical barriers in search of the scoops, and if you don’t look out for your reporters well enough then madness and death can end your print run.
The interface for Daily Chthonicle boils all this down to the bare essentials. You have six reporters, and a city map of up to nine locations. Assigning a reporter to a location has them turn up new clues, contacts, investigations, and obstacles so long as they remain there. Everything you find gets published periodically and earns you money based on how much you uncovered, and once you turn up the entire story you can close the case in your files. Closing every open case wins you the game, and the only way to lose is to get all six of your reporters incapacitated at once.
Most of the gameplay here is in deciding what to do with what your reporters turn up. Clues and leads really don’t require any input from you, they’re just part of the stories and are assembled automatically in their cases. Sometimes you’ll come across a new lead and have the option to follow it, or continue in the track you’re on. The significance of this choice isn’t entirely clear to me but it seems like following can trigger more dramatic results, or nothing at all. Investigations and obstacles are the two big ones, both offering different tactical choices like equipping special items or taking risks like snapping pictures. The results of investigations hinge on how well your reporter is equipped, while obstacles can leave your people injured, insane, or incapacitated if they cannot overcome the challenge.
The money you make from running stories mostly goes into stocking up on weapons, forensic tools, bibles, whisky, and dogs to help get past obstacles. You can also mix and use potions from the lab at your office, providing potent bonuses at the cost of keeping a reporter off the streets to do the mixing. In the mid and late game you also get side funds to purchase upgrades and discounted equipment based on how much good your investigations have done the different parts of the city. On top of all this are your contacts and allies who can provide backup, special services, and perhaps other things I haven’t fully worked out yet.
There’s a great deal of strategy at play here, and on the lower difficulties you won’t need to worry about most of it. Keeping your reporters busy, saving up funds to splurge on equipment, and rotating people out when they get hurt or crazed is enough to close out all your cases. On Normal and above, however, the evil has ways of fighting back. Leaving certain threats unanswered for too long or failing key challenges can cause new ones to arise, potentially spiraling the situation out of control. You’ll have less margin for error and need to use all your resources intelligently to keep ahead of your eldrich antagonists, and the strategy is plenty fun to work out as you learn which descriptors call for which pieces of equipment.
What complaints I can level against Daily Chthonicle are mostly in the realm of polish. You can probably tell from the screenshots but it’s not a terribly attractive game, stuck with simple, overly-chunky graphics throughout. I don’t know if it’s an aesthetic choice or artistic limitations but it just doesn’t look good, and there’s very little sound design at all to even critique. The game feels very bare-bones because of this, sealing away the action of vanquishing undead mastodons behind static, blown-up scans of old pictures and poorly-formatted text. And speaking of mastodons, the randomized stories can have their moments but are mostly unimportant and unintelligible since the articles assemble themselves from the disparate pieces you find.
The core of Daily Chthonicle is extremely solid, building a compelling management sim that pits you against fantastic evils with only journalism (and a little magic) on your side. Were it more attractive or polished it would be an instant classic, but as it stands the aesthetic brands it with a pretty strong caveat. Assuming you aren’t put off by the poor graphics there’s plenty of random adventures and bizarre encounters to work through, with a decent learning curve that carries an equally decent sense of accomplishment. If you’re looking for a new take on old themes, Daily Chthonicle puts a load of strategy into eldrich horror and spices it up with creative flair.

Like the deranged, paranoid anti-heroes that inhabit Lovecraft's fictional universe,
makes a remarkably bad first impression but gradually makes sense if you can find the patience to stay with it. The visual presentation couldn't be much worse, the online help is poorly organized, and the tutorial fails at its task. Yet, after a few trial-and-error restarts, the mechanics and goals of DC became clearer and the interface much easier to manage. Basically, you function as editor of the eponymous newspaper, dispatching your
-inspired reporters to points of interest in a city where the sun never rises and citizens conspire to summon demons and sacrifice humans to dark gods.
Your reporters function less as journalists and more as paranormal police or ghost hunters. They don't just report the news - they make the news by challenging and defeating the zombies, liches, apparitions, and other evils. Much of the challenge is equipping your reporters properly, brewing buff-bestowing potions, and paying for medical help when reporters are injured in combat with supernatural forces.
Finally, I'm impressed with the algorithm that generates the random narratives. Most monsters that your reporters face are humans who've been corrupted by ritual magic. Inevitably, the corrupted individuals have named accomplices, friends, and victims. As your reporters investigate leads and defeat monsters, they also learn the identities of the plotters and their enablers, and all of this gets reported in a "Special Edition" of the Daily Chthonicle newspaper that wraps up each case.

Ace Of Words is a casual, anagram-esque game developed by Zerobit Games and published by Ocean Media LLC. With an easy interface, and an appealing look. The concept is just to try to spell as many words as possible with 6-8 letters available. From there you can spell up to 100 words and you have 120 seconds to get them all.
PROS
+ Easy Achievements
+ Steam Trading Cards
+ Steam Leaderboards
+ Colorful
+ Easy Concept
+ Fun
CONS
- Overpriced
- Not A Big Enough Dictionary
- The Highscore Resets Everytime You Restart Game
- Looks And Plays Like A Mobile Port

This game is not a big hit nor is it a miss. I have heard of some people having malware problems with this game but I have not experienced that. It is tons of fun, and has a solid concept that is executed fairly well. They just need to work on the dictionary aspect, its a small dictionary that is missing plenty of words and plurals. This game. Holy cow. What can I say about this game? It's hard to know where to start. I love stealth games but I think this is the first time I had one draw me in to this degree. It didn't take me long to get hooked. Of course I enjoyed the gameplay itself. Enough that I played it through in it's entirety twice. I really, really urge anyone playing for the first time to go for the High Chaos play first. It gives more impact to the Low Chaos play. And believe me, if you get as invested as I did, once you get the High Chaos end you're going to want that Low Chaos end. Can the Low Chaos play be frustrating? Absolutely. I put nearly 40 hours overall into this game, getting all three endings. (Yes. There's a third. It's considered worse than the High Chaos end. But you'll have to figure out how to get that yourself. No spoilers here. Though if you're paying attention it shouldn't be too hard to discern where the choice is that'll get you the third ending.) I feel like it has a strong story, good characters and manages to be fun despite being frustrating at times. I even managed to find Emily likable enough, when usually child characters are played up in a way that's somewhat annoying at the very least. I absolutely recommend this game. That said, if stealth games aren't your thing you probably won't enjoy everything this has to offer and might find certain aspects of the Low Chaos run very tedious or frustrating. I, personally, enjoyed this game immensely and look forward to it's sequel!

One of my all time favorites. It was one of my first ever games on a c.d. rom back in 1998-1999 (17th grade) and playing it now was just as fun, maybe even more,
Back than I had and awkward Microsoft Joystick, today I use the XBOX one controller.
Using the XBOX one controller the control is very confortalbe (after customizing it using the settings) and I had no problem what so ever to run the game. I had one crash during my 6 or so hours and that's it.
Important suggestion
This is for nVidia card owners, but I'm sure there's something similar for AMD cards as well
The game is from 1998. On modern screen the game is Jaggie as hell and even though you don't buy this game today for it's amazing graphincs, going into the nvidia control panel and changing the 3D settings specifically for this application, forcing Anti-Aliasin, Antistropic filterring and what not improved the visuals immensly. For example, in the mission select screen there are some kind of laser rays, before they basicaly looked like steps and after they looked almost completly smooth. And everything you do, no matter how 'expensive' it is in terms of GPU, it's on a 1998 game so no effect.
One very importnt issue for people planning on using the XBOX one controller on windows 10 (and maybe older windows versions). Tht triggers used to be buttons (with on/off state and that's it). now they are an axis (the value corresponds to how much the trigger is pressed). The problem is that older games that aren't aware of this keep receiving the 0 value of the tigger axis when trying to configure the controller in game. The result is that you can't configure the buttons the buttons.
I myself have the xBox one elite controller, and the software that comes with it allows me to set the middle point of the axis to a comfortable place (like the end of the axis), then when I configure the buttons I just press the triggers all the way and I can set the buttons - no problem. Did this with Rogue squadron and also Assassin's creed II. If you don't have the software this is harder to do, but I know there are some 3rd party configuration apps that allow to do just that. Another option is to use the XBOX 360 controller, but I don't like it as much. It's triggers however are plain buttons so no problem there.
One last comment.
I read some revires saying that this game is not configured well for the latest and greatest machines. Now I can't speak on behalf of anyone but me, but my rig is pretty strong (i7 6700k, 16GB DDR4, SSD, gtx 980 TI) and I had no problem at all. this is the very first AC game I have played and let me tell you, it's a hell of a blast. The graphics are overwhelmingly impressive, somewhat an upgrade from Unity, the free-running is more smooth and fluid, and the environment is definitely "living and breathing", as promised from the very first Assassin's Creed game. The story takes place in London, during the Industrial Revolution, with new allies like Alexander Graham Bell, etc.  Not sure if this is the first AC game wherein you can switch characters in-game but I have to say, this was a really good choice. Jacob and Evie have different expertise, Jacob being more confrontational, and Evie, of course, stealthier. The ability of leading a group of rebels, the Rooks, to aid you in fighting, transporting, and supplying is something unique that adds the opportunities that this game can offer. With the help of Aleck, you have access to a never-seen-before tool mechanism in AC, a rope launcher. It's like Spiderman, but in 1868. Your main weapon is cane-sword, which is a perfect marriage of aesthetics and deadliness Side activities like carriage racing, fight clubs, and gang wars creates a unique blend of replayability. 100% recommend this game. Pick this up on sale. Never full-price.

This game is amazing.
In other games I've always loved being the little guy in cat-and-mouse situations, from hunting tanks in Battlefield, to slaying dragons in Skyrim. Evolve makes an entire game out of that concept, even allowing you to play as the monster. And it's competitively balanced!
The hunters all have jetpacks and infinite ammo, and have to hunt the monster before it can eat enough to stage up. By stage 2, the monster is said to be on equal ground. By stage 3, it turns into a generator defense where the mosnter hast he advantage. At this point, a good amount of teamwork is needed by the hunters to win. Tricky in public games, but very satisfying when you can finally take out the monster.
And the game looks beautiful, being built on Cryengine. All of the plants and creatures in the game (some very hostile) fit seamlessly into the game world, making it easy to immerse yourself in.
And the DLC hunter releases are very high quality. They look stunning, are really fun to play, and have a surprising amount of lore brought with each release as well.
Most of people's complaints from release have basically been addressed. The only prominent issue right now is the size of the player base, making queue times for ranked extremely long. One can generally find a game pretty quickly in Quick Play, though.
I would highly recommend buying this. For you and your friends.

I have completed the game at super human difficulty short after initial release.
X-COM is the father of all turn based, tactical squad combat games and still today far deeper than modern games of the kind, although few.
Compared to the new release of X-COM which is the closest modern game available, UFO Defence is back on graphics, modern interface, tutorial and simplicity, but if you do not mind graphics and tutorial and like to venture deep into finding a complex game secrets in tactical squad combat and out of combat strategic decisions, UFO Defence is not a choice, it is your only choice.
X-COM in terms if time and what you see is the exact opposite of total war games, the 'map' which is the entire planet runs in real time or faster if you choose, and when you take any action like bases management or entering combat time pauses. In combat you play in turns, all other actions out of combat like base management are simply interface choices at paused global time.
Starting up, you have an underground base with some basic few equipment and personell. You job is to deal with alien threat on earth. To do that you need to intercept UFOs with you planes when you detect them so you crash them and then land and explore with your squad. Also you need to react to other alien activities already on ground like city attacks. At the end, you squad lands near the incident, kills alien opposition and accomplishes the goals. But kill the alien opposition is not exactly easy. The second part is about three main activities. Research on alien equipment, dead and alive aliens and theories will give you knowledge for better combat effectiveness, stronger bases and progress your investigation on aliens and to understand your enemy plan - the initial title was UFO Enemy uknown. The second is manufacturing, usually based on alien findings after researching. You can manufacture weapons, armor and gadgets for your combat squad, plane fighters and their weapons for stronger interceptions, better squad carrier crafts, base facilities and defences and other. The third thing is about your bases. You start with one but you can build 8 total.
The magic about X-COM is that you can do anything that later X-COM or X-COM like games restrict and present them as new revolutionary gameplay elements. But for X-COM veterans those were just restrictions. You can have a fully custom squad, from 1 man show to 32 total soldiers, replacing 4 with a mechanical small tank if you like, or two or as many tanks as you like, soldiers equipped with whatever gear from a large variaty of existing and later researched and manufactured options. You can complete a mission with dozens of real different tactics. You can expand your bases any way you like. You can build a 'research' base, or a 'factory' base or an 'interception' base or a 'military' base as i call them. Or just all your bases can be all-around.
As a matter of fact, any style you want to play is doable. And every choice has effect. A tank unit for example is definatetly stronger than a soldier at start but it does not gain any experience. Soldiers improve mostly after they kill aliens. On the other hand, if you have the transportation space you may get a tank with you to salvage the situation if all goes ill. Or just do not use tanks - i do not for example. They are not overpowered or anything, but i do not like them, i prefer soldiers.

This game is not for everyone, but it's one of the best puzzle games I've played in a long time; even long after I shut the game down, my brain keeps pondering ways to improve my solutions.
You are tasked with constructing automata ("reactors") and pipelines to take atoms and molecules, and break them apart and recombine them to form different molecules.  Building requires dragging and dropping visual components, a kind of "visual programming".  It's a little like "The Incredible Machine" in that regard; without the Rube-Goldberg-esque humour, but far more deep and challenging.
Any successful design will get you past a level, but if you're like me you'll continually revisit your solutions and try to improve them, by using fewer components, or making more efficient solutions.

Kholat is an Atmospheric Horror Walking Simulator game narrated by british actor, Sean Bean. Playing on my i5 4460, gtx 1060 at 1080p resolution on Ultra settings I was getting anywhere from 30fps in some areas of the game to 60 in most of it. If you're close to my specs (see Profile) I would recommend playing it on Medium, it doesn't look that much worse. Plays fine with a Mouse & keyboard but for my playthrough I used my xbox 360 gamepad.
The central story of the game revolves around the Dyatlov Pass incident, which according to wikipedia " is the mysterious deaths of nine ski hikers in the northern Ural Mountains on February 2, 1959. The experienced trekking group, who were all from the Ural Polytechnical Institute, had established a camp on the slopes of Kholat Syakhl when disaster struck. During the night something made them tear their way out of their tents from the inside and flee the campsite inadequately dressed in heavy snowfall and sub-zero temperatures." You play as a person who heads to the location of the incident to investigate what really happened.
Gameplay is pretty standard First Person Shooter controls minus the shooter part. You can walk, crouch  and sprint with limited stamina. There is no jump button so any path you choose to walk, well... just hope there are no obstructions. Learning how to navigate the old fashioned way is a must. You'll get no help from quest markers or a GPS. You'll need to know how to read map coordinates and a compass and also the terrain to keep track of your location on said map. As you go along and reach points of interest your character will add them to the map, so that really helps. Also there are campsites you can find that function as fast travels.
The overall objective is to go the last known locations of the 9 hikers and find clues that eventually piece together the story. As you trek from coordinate to coordinate you may also stumble upon extra journal entries or articles from past travelers of the mountain range that will help piece even more of the lore together. There are unknown entities that do wander the mountains so at times you will have a sense of danger, I don't want to spoil too much.
Personally, I think the strongest points of the game are the environment, which is freaking gorgeous yet still cold, desolate and lonely. The sound design is incredible, atmosphere enriching  and greatly adds to the desolation and lonliness. In fact I think it's the thing this game does best.
There really isn't much more I can say about the game. The world is well crafted and there is some semblance of a cohesive plot but just when the game really gets going, it ends. I played through it in 4 hours and although I missed some of the journals, I just do not think I can recommend this game. I would say get it if you really want to feel freaked out from being lost in a place with lots of scary noises, if that kind of thing scares you but otherwise, pass on it.

Dungeon of the Endless is a tower defense game with rogue-like elements.  You control a squad of up to four characters as you try and make your way out of a 12-floor dungeon filled with monsters.  Those familiar with Amplitude's other games will recognize the resources you'll need to survive: industry for building, science for research, food for leveling up your squad members, and dust for powering rooms.  To generate these resources, you build modules, open doors, and fend off waves of monsters when they decide to attack your "core" (a giant crystal).  The rogue-like elements include perma-death (although you may find your dead character again in a later floor), random dungeon layouts, and randomness when it comes to opening doors.  Once you learn the game's mechanics, the game can get easy.  However, it is fun to play with friends and the "unstable" cast of characters makes things interesting as you learn about the lore.  The soundtrack and pixel art look of the game are excellent and extremely memorable.
Solid gameplay, good replayability. The difficulty curve can be tough, but that's typical of rouge-likes.

Hanafuda, a traditional Japanese card, is well hard to describe.  It is like a combination of Go Fish, Old Maid, Bridge, Whist, Gin Rummy, Poker, Eucre, and Cribbage.  Instead of 13 cards in only 4 suits, there 4 cards per season or month with the added bonus of special higher point sets of 3 to 5 cards.  It is a bit confusing a first, I admit, but there is an in-game visual guide to the card hands.  Plus before beginning any card matches or tournment matches there is a very informative tutorial about how to play.  It also helps that your playing cards become highlighted along with the central "pot" cards to help find matches.  This card game is very challenging.

I wanted to like this one far more than I actually could manage.
With a little more polish, this game could be great. The setting is neat, with you running a newspaper that investigates supernatural events around town. Gods, how I wanted to love this one.
But the mechanics are more than a little bit clunky, and the instructions are kind of obtuse.
You're going to want to play through the tutorial as well as at least one game on easy, to make sure that you have a solid handle on how things play out.
The biggest issue, however, is the nonsensical plots that get spat out by procedural generation. It's not uncommon to see a case proceed like this:
"Bob, Tom, and Dave recently returned from abroad."
After further investigations, you'll eventually find a location with "zombie scientist"...who upon killing, you discover is Bob. Bob died of knife wounds.
You'll investigate awhile longer, and you'll find that Tom killed Bob for revenge, because Bob was blackmailing Dave, and Tom and Dave are friends. How Bob got turned into a zombie is never explained.
Literally any monster causes dead people to become zombies, for whatever reason, in almost every game I've played. Demonic maggots cause zombies, spiders cause zombies, people cause zombies, and even werewolves cause zombies.
The deeper you get into cases, the more nonsensical the procedural stuff becomes, just like most games that use procedural generation without limiting it or focusing it with sharper programming.
Reading recaps of the cases becomes almost headache-inducing, because of all the Mad Libs-style procedural stuff you encounter.
It's really a shame, because this game has so much potential to be an outstanding one.
I really would like to see what this group of developers can do with a bit more time and polish, because everything is there to make an outstanding game.
I'm giving it a thumbs-up recommendation, ON THE CAVEAT that you should buy this game on sale, and understand that it's flawed.
Your mileage may vary on this one, compared to mine.

Daily Chthonicle is a unique indie game where you play as the boss of a newspaper agency in an H.P. Lovecraft inspired world. You send your journalists out to not only find stories, but to make them.
You control everything from your office, where you are able to send your journalists out to fight and take photos of all kinds of mythical creatures or enemies reminiscent of the 1940s.
You have a laboratory where you are able to mix reagents to create potions, and to mix samples to create evidence to help you further along the cases you are investigating.
Overall this game takes place in a very interesting setting which could allow for an exciting storyline. Unfortunately, this game severely lacks a quality storyline of any kind. All of your story comes from randomized events that happen as you send your journalists out to explore, investigate, or follow persons to places or the places themselves. Due to how many journalists you can have out at once, your story usually comes in as small bits of about half a dozen different plotlines at once, making any interest hard to form, and stopping the story from having any real coherence unless you send out your journalists to one place and only one place at a time. (Which would make for a very boring experience considering you can only assign one journalist to an area at once.)
The gameplay, while unique, is severely lacking. Other than toying around aimlessly in the laboratory, you will find yourself staring at a map and clicking the clock over and over again to speed up time until you get a new event. Events are rather easy and are what make up the stories that get published in your paper, which you have no control of whatsoever and earn different amounts for with no noticeable pattern in the payday. There's nothing that lets you know what kinds of stories the people want and even if there were, there's no way to know what you're getting into or what stories you'll actually find. It's all random. There's no real in-depth management in this game. So if you're looking for a management-heavy title or newspaper boss simulator, this game, despite it's description, is none of that. It's actually just a random event simulator where you get to pick items and work with status effect in a trial and error fashion where you are essentially forced to play one specific way or else you lose.
The tutorial of this game is garbage. In this review I have already explained more to you about how to play the game and navigate the poorly designed UI than the the tutorial ever will. However, if you do make it through the tutorial then congratulations, they've already shown you everything there is to the game at least to some extent and you will never encounter anything new from that point onwards. You effectively beat the game already within 20 minutes.
The graphics are obviously very out of date. I personally don't mind them, but I know for many gamers this is a huge turnoff. If you want anything resembling a game that came out after the 90s in graphical fidelity, this game is not for you.
The sounds are decent. Never at any point did they help me get immersed, but then again they never really broke my immersion unless its one of those times where the music just start obnoxiously playing much louder for a few seconds upon receiving a new event.
Overall Daily Chthonicle was a rather disappointing game. Seeming to be a journalism-focused version of Zafehouse: Diaries, I was really excited to play this, only to learn that it is actually nothing like that at all. Unless you are a H.P. Lovecraft addict or a huge fan of minimalistic retro games, I could never recommend this to you. And as a side note, the fact that the official description for this game on it's steam page says you get to play as the "Boss and editor" of the paper is a lie. While you could be considered the boss because you get to order everyone around, you are certainly no editor. You never get to pick what stories get published, you never get to interact with the stories, you literally make no decisions related to your paper other than to read it or to tell a journalist to head into an available area to look for a story.
Daily Chthonicle earns a 2/10. Most gamers tolerant of the game's state will likely not get more than two hours of gameplay out of this game, making it's $4 price point ridiculous. That's $2 an hour for an indie title whereas plenty of indie titles will give you hundreds of hours of fun gameplay and almost always at a much lower rate per hour. I would not recommend this game. It is not worth your money.

The Daily Chthonicle is a fun little game. Much more fun than I expected it to be. Imagine a board game, Lovecraftian horror, mystery novels and Film Noir thrown into a witch's cauldron, along with the usual eye of newt and milk of a dragonfly, and shaken really well!
Gameplay:
The game feels and plays much like a board game. You control newspaper reporters who are in fact part of secret outfit that protects against supernatural threats.
Gameplay is complex, and involves moving your agents on several locations on the map, equiping them with items and dealing with encounters/adversaries, supernatural phenomena, events, obstacles, etc.
You also publish newspaper articles with your exploits and photographs that you may manage to take while solving cases. This is one of your sources of income that allows you to equip, train and care for your reporters.
There is a big in-game manual that I advise everyone to read, before starting the actual game. It is rather big and impossible to digest entirely in one go (you will visit it again many times, for sure) but even skimming through it, will give you at least an idea of what it is that you are supposed to do.
The tutorial mission also explains a lot of things as you play but you will find yourself clicking the "read more" item on the cards that takes you to the relevant sections of the in-game manual.
Fully describing gameplay here would essentially need to rewrite the in-game manual. Rest assured the game features several mechanics that will keep you engaged.
Graphics:
In the graphic department the game opts in for retro graphics with a film noir style (Did I mention one of your reporters is named Sam Spade? :D).
I believe the style fits the game nicely but art style is something objective. It may not work for everyone.
Music/Sound Design:
In this department the game is taking a very casual approach. Like soft piano music playing in the background, mixed with somekind of eerie ambience and very minimal sampled sound effects like the occasional sound you would hear in a newspaper office during the 40s.
Story:
There's really no consistent story. The game generates random cases that you have to solve. Each case is a short story involving the murder, the supernatural, cults etc.
Pros:
-Manages to blend several elements in a very nice way.
-Feels and plays like a complex board game.
-Randomly generated content keeps replayability high.
-Good in-game manual
Neutral:
-Retro style graphics are not everyone's cup of tea.
Cons:
I really could not find something I could consider a con.
Conclusion:
I have played many different games in the past 2 weeks and this one is the one I have enjoyed the most. Solid gameplay, intelligent and I love it's art style, the Lovecraftian and Film Noir references and basically everything about it!
Score:
Gameplay: 		9/10
Graphics: 		7/10
Music:    		        5/10
Concept/Story:	9/10

But if you have played the Dead Kings DLC of Unity and then compared it with Syndicate, then Syndicate looks much better. Also removing multiplayer and adding additional features in the game was a welcome change. The lead characters Jacob and Evie are diverse and their constant differences and arguments pretty much sums up for strong character development in this one. The game is very polished and the bugs are ironed out. The combat is well balanced, the open world is fun,the sandbox approach is way more polished and transportation is a lot improved(horse carriages, the most awesome AC2 set piece now implemented in the open world) and rope launcher is a time saver and it also doesn't restrict you to enjoy the old building climbing. Moreover the carriages are also not forced in each and every mission like most of the missions Batman Arkham Knight forces you to use the Bat-mobile and character customization is a lot improved and there is a better way to earn skill points than in Unity.And moreover the side quests are not boring.And the loading time is a bit less than Unity. The relationship between the two main protagonists, Jacob and Evie Frye, both twins, made for some delighting family banter and quips. The contrast between Jacob, who wants to liberate London from the Blighters, a Street gang, and Evie, who sticks to the tenants of the Creed, and who wants to find Pieces of Eden to stop the templars, was really nice. During story missions, however, you're usually locked into one character and will switch only when the game wants you to. I liked the customisation of your gang, the Rooks, allowing for backup on a fight. There's no more swords, and enemies now have a health bar on top of Thier heads. Only when this health bar is low enough can you kill them with a finisher, and these are delightfully brutal.The open world, it is ridiculously huge, Ubisoft wasn't joking when they said it was bigger than Unity's map by 30%. London is absolutely gorgeous.
Trains add a whole new magical element as far as I'm concerned, I adore anything to do with trains and think they're a brilliant addition.

The Short:
Great graphics here & there, útterly boring & frustratring gameplay. Grind, grind, grind to get level-ups needed to get at the heart of the game. It took me 13 hours of frustration and grinding to get at level 6 and get the story (simple as it is) rolling for a bit.
The Longer:
Point is, while the City is rendered in exquisite beauty in all its victorian splendor&squalor, it is álso crawling with clone baddies that are ESP-gifted, and are psionically linked to every other baddy in the vicinity. Meaning, when You attack one in a neighbourhood that isn't Yours, or one of them sees You, the game immediately spawns oodles of baddies, and cops with "super-batons" that kill in just a couple of blows. Which -in turn- leads to the standard tactics of : killing..get up to the roof, press "c" to go stealth, wait a bit, rinse & repeat ad infinitum. Gang strongholds can be cleared-out in the same manner. A fair bit of that carried-over into AC: digital world...ehh.. "Watch Dogs 2" grind, grind, grind. Stealth-kills fix that for a bit, but then the crazy of the ai comes bubbling-up: I tried to stash all bodies from stealth-kills out of sight. Well, I shouldn't have bothered. Stealth kill a baddie. Let the body laying around, and in most cases no-one sounds the alarm despite citizens making a ruckus.. weird.
All in all, the "open world" is a frustrating affair that can only be enjoyed from samey-samey-roofs. Get to street level to take-in "The Sights" the programmers have so lovingly crafted, and you're in for endless, boring assaults of cookie-cutter baddies.
What's álso seriously annoying is the utterly slów levelling. It feels like a purposely stunted levelling-system to make players spend áctual money on XP-Points. Sneaky, stinky CEO-Beancounter stuff.
On the rest of the game:
When a neighbourhood is (FINALLY) Yours, only thén do You get to admire the work the programmers & builders put into the game. But, by then, a lot of players will have put-down the conroller for good.
Is the game "hard"? No, not really. It's rather more like"artificially stunted" to make it seem "hard" but the base-mechanics are all standard AC-fare -apart from the Grapple-Hook, which is a nice addition to shorten trips around The City- with a somewhat wonky stealth-system.
On a more positive note: The clothes of Evie and Jacob, are a Steampunk dream. The rich brocades, something inocuous, like the movement of Evie's cape (loathed by many, oddly enough), the lace, the buttons even, it all defines "attention to detail" from people that love to design stuf.
Shame that it has to live in such a mediocre, grindy game. I cannot really recommend it, unless it's in a weekend-sale for $10.- or something.
Edit: You know when it fínally starts to get fun? With a trainer. While only using "infinite health", the game became far more enjoyable (for me, at least)

There are so many tower defense games out there. I decided to give this one a try. I appreciate the developers including this in a charity bundle that I purchased so I want to get that out there first. I made sure to try every game I recieved to help with indie devs.
This game was fun, and I could certainly spend lots of hours completeing every level to 3 stars. However, I feel that there are just so many TD games that there are certainly better and more enjoyable ones out there.
My main complaint is that they limit your earning potential. Like most games of this type, there is an object which increases the amount of an item needed to upgrade or build defense mechanisms. They purposefully limit the amount of these generators by only allowing them to be placed in certain areas. This ends up limiting you to only a few spots generating money and therefore allows the game to take advantage over you.
I am the type of TD player where I want to build overwhelming power over my foe and feel that this game just wants to put only enough in your level so you can squeak by with a 3 star win. After playing through the first island this became very clear.
Also, not that I expected it, the game does not support my ultrawide monitor. This is not taken into account in my recommendation. Just saying it for anyone who enjoys games in ultrawide. Overall, other reviewers mentions of this feeling like a mobile title ring true. The graphics are good, gameplay is good, but really feels like a title that was meant to make money from the collectors who would spend their day just playing through any TD game they can find just to have something different.

Good news is, I am willing to try it again and change my rating in the future. I will toss it in my "Maybe Later" game folder.

I didn't look into this game much, was this a port from a mobile game or not but it definitely feels like one. We got the diamonds that are used to upgrade towers, every other mobile game has diamonds that the player can buy to upgrade stuff. The graphics are straight from a mobile game. But those mechanics aside, i can live with them if the levels are fun and challenging. But sadly, they were not, except the few levels that had so overpowered enemies that i was forced to go and grind on the previous levels for more diamonds. This, to me was the biggest flaw of the game.
I tried surfing the web while my game was running in the background, but i couldn't since steam overlay paused the game right away. I then switched to windowed mode and tried doing some work with google's office apps, that didn't work either, game was again paused. So i was basically forced to sit there, watch the same levels over and over again. I usually play games on hard, but here i tried switching to easy, it didn't remove the OP enemies. I didn't find a way to avoid the grind.
Other than that, the interesting levels are few and far between Mainly those that limited your towers so you could build only 5-7 in a level, those were great and required a bit of planning! Most other levels feel like a copypaste from each other.  There's only the fixed paths for enemies: no change to build your own mazes, something that i think shuold be a staple in every tower defense game.
We have decent selection of towers, 3 basic ones that eventually evolve into different towers. It's a double-edged sword since it requires a good amount of silver to buy those "better towers" that have useful effects on them like breaking the enemies armor, or doing AoE damage but also encourages planning in advance. First the player has to upgrade the towers to level 3 before the upgrade to the better towers is possible, costing more silver. This lead me to the second biggest flaw of the game:
Gaining silver, the basic currency in this game has a bit randomness in it. Silver is gained by destroying junk on the levels or from factories bought with gold. Gold, then again is totally randomly dropped from enemies, i sometimes went 5-6 waves without any gold (the junk don't give much, just for the start) => no silver => couldn't buy or upgrade and towers then it was too late and i lost. Sometimes i had 2 factories up and running right on the second wave giving me too much silver.
No. There are a lot of better Tower Defenses, This game don't really offer much anything at all except frustration with grinding. Even as a fixed path-type of TD. it's extremely simple and relies sudden jumps on difficulty to provide challenge instead of clever level design.

Killing Floor- a game that is now nearly 7 years old- is a wonderful mix of skull cracking, limb tearing and blood bursting action. Whether you like to pick off ZEDs one by one with charpshooter, or go full pyromaniac and roast them as Firebug, Killing Floor offers a diverse playstyle to a range of audiences- in otherwords- there's something in it for everyone. While this game runs on Unreal Engine 2.5 the graphics and 'borderline' art style give the game a great look and feel- that is with the gore. Gore is a key part of this game and you can more or less paint a whole room red (with the blood of the dead!). You can even blow the head off a ZED and still have it running towards you, albiet much less faster.The charachter customizastion is good and you can purchase a while variety of skins for your daily ritual of mass ZED genocide. However- there are some weapons in the game tht pose an advantage over others and require DLC purchases giving the game (in the higher difficulties) a very slight pay to win feel. That being said these are only a few weapons and do not imact the game meta drasticly at all. There also seem to be some issues surrounding hitbox and hit detection, especially with ZEDs like Gorefasts and Crawlers. Another issue surrounding KF seems to be the very slow leveling systems- which outputs alot of people who will end up using SAM or 'perk leveling maps' to rank up while not really gaining any skills. There are also bugs when it comes to hosting a server- although much is not expected in this reigon from such an old game.
All in all KF is a very gory experiance which will get your heart pumping and palms sweating- but there are some issues that need to be solved which will be very unlikely due to Tripwire's discontiuation of updates for KF.
I would definitely buy this game if you're looking for a classic wave PvE survival.

I absolutely love this game... Atleast the concept of it but unfortunately in my opinion, it was executed horribly.
There is a TL:DR along with a criteria at the bottom of the review if you want to skip the bulk of this review.
When I first entered the game, I was given a beutiful town if no clear objective which was fine. Following the road and whatnot, feels llike it was a good way to start a game without telling you "Go this way please!" The graphics were stunning and the music was beautiful. But unfortunately this was the start to a slippery slope heading downhill.
When you enter act 1 you are introduced to the main items. A compass, Map and a Journal. Lets start with the Journal. The Journal was nice but uneccesary. It stores your notes (Notes are "important" so remember them) and some "Survival tips" My main problem with the journal is you will actually only use it once. And the information in there is useless.
The map and compass is a complete different story. Whilst it seemed like a nice concept at the beginning where you are in the center or entrance of the map and everything was easy to point as North, East etc. Towards the end, I had no clue where the hell I was. I was just guessing if I was going North or South because the map had zero indication other than these checkpoints. These checkpoints are the only hope of knowing where you are when you discover them before you get lost back into the maze of nothingness.
So what is the main object of this game? Well, that's to discover the mystery of what happened to a group of hikers who went missing and never got found. This is told by gettings Notes which advance the story. Whilst this was interesting and worked most of the time, at some times it didn't due to the simple fact that it doesn't pause the game whilst reading the notes... How is this a problem? Well the main threat in this game is a black husk from what I can tell without spoilers. It is mainly useless for the most part and wont chase you if you hold the shift button for longer than 5 seconds, but at the start when I was still kind of on edge, I ran to a note only to be killed as soon as the narrator started reading the note. My second problem with the notes is the fact that only some of them are voiced. My friend that I was playing with and I were sick and tired of these notes by the end. I usually read what was on the notes but by the end neither of us had the motivation to care what was happening. Expanding on these notes further would be how incredibly hard it is to find them at the closer end of the game... The main story notes are found via etchings in a rock that are completely missable with co-ordinates on them.
The main story itself is fantastic if you could be bothered to sit through all the clutter and the fact that you will be running across this map looking for notes and can be bothered to sit and piece together the pieces but I just can't recommend it as to the gameplay.
So what about the map? You may ask. Incredibly pretty but it's so boring and repetetive after a while... The best you're going to get as for variety from the snow is a small area which holds a forest and a cabin. You also have caves and a frozen lake area. The caves are great except for the simple fact that. Well. They aren't. They hold nothing new other than a slightly creepy atmosphere and another place to walk around the main threat in the game.
The mechanics of this game go as sprinting and crouching. Everything else it situational and/or are completely useless. Sprinting will only last for 8-10 seconds untill your screen goes blurry and you have to walk for 5 or so seconds. Whilst I still crouched at time I feel that was also completely useless. You had no reason to hide since you could just run around the main threat. The Flashlight as well was completely useless to me, even in caves although that may be my fault since I didn't change the brightness settings, but I still feel like I should have some trouble seeing through caves without one but I navigated fine.
Others problems consist of frame drops at random parts of the map. In this forest I went for 60 Frames to 5 Frames in a vital scene where I actually had to do something with this monster. Another problem both my friend and I faced were an invisible hole quite early in the game that put you 6 minutes or so back if you searched for extra notes. This happened to me but my friend managed to glitch back on track someone.
TL:DR
This game is more of an creepy atmospheric walking simulator which has it's fair share of problems. I highly recommend watching someone play some, like cryaotic or someone else play some before deciding. The story is absolutely fantastic but has problems and prepare to get lost in stupid locations due to the map. Whilst this game was up my sub-alley right next to rhythm games I just couldn't get myself to enjoy it at the end. Get it for the exploring factor if that's what you like but don't go into this game wanting a horror with tense jump scares and tight monster chases.
Story: 8 (But execution is around a 4) I absolutely loved this story and at one point actually studied it. I found it super interesting but unfortunately giving the player a confusing open world labrynth wasn't the way to do it. I just found that at the end of this game there was no reason to actually care.
World: 4 The world is stunning but quite large and hard to navigate. Whilst sometimes it's clear, others you will get lost and be running in circles with nothing interesting to actually do or see. It was creepy until the 100th times you walk past the same rock on tree.
Music/sounds 6 I give it a six purely for the music and the crunch on the snow. Other than that, there is no redeeming factor. The music in this game is absolutely fantastic but everything else is just unsatisfying. The monster sounds get repetetive and unjumpscary* after the second time. I actually think I got spooked twice and once was a door slamming and the other was confusion at a nicely done area.
Price? Not worth it at all at 20USD. Unfortunately and I hate saying this but this game isn't worth 20USD. I would said 10USD at the absolute best. I got by a dollar per hour scheme and whatnot and this definitely didn't entertain me for longer than 5 hours. (I say this because I watched cryaotic's playthrough. He somehow made the game interesting and all the boring bits I could listen to him kinda like a podcast whilst doing other things)
Overall 4/10
What I see is a game that could have been done really well, engaged the player and told the story the exact same way but it just turned out to be boring and repetitive toward the end with no real new feature being added. Get it whilst it's on sale if you really want it but prepare to either like it or dislike it. If you want want the most enjoyable experience out of this. Don't go into it with any hopes. Just ride it out and hope you like it.

Ace Of Words is a simplified scrabble game where you have to find words from a pre-determined randomized letters. There are a time limit in guessing the right word and a hint will be unlocked after you guessed a certain percent of all available words.
The graphics are simple and the UIs are not confusing. Plus, the game gives you a lot of different screen resolution to choose from.
The music is relaxing, although i admit that i snoozed a bit after playing it for a long time.
You will be given 6 or 8 letters (depends on your setting) and you'll have to find words from those letters. However, there are some missing words in the word database which will make it hard to find the available words, especially if you are aiming for 8 letters achievement. The hint only unlocks after you unlocked several percent of the available words, which makes it hard for people who's not really good at scrabble. You can skip the "level" to play with other set of letters after you unlocked certain percentage of words (or you can just quit the game and start a new one).
You'll have to be patient when you type. Sometimes, the keys won't register if you type it too fast (especially after animation). The hint is also quite messed up; if you press the hint button when you are still having some letters typed in, the hint will be invalid and you have to wait again to get your next hint.
The time limit is set in the middle bar, which can be quite confusing as there is no explanation about it. However, the time limit is quite long and it'll be refilled once you type a registered word so you won't really notice it unless you are patient enough to wait for it or afking.
There is a bug when the new set of letters didn't show up if you unlocked all of the available words beforehand. The game will automatically end and after that you'll be given a new set of letters which are working.
Pros:
- Help button
Cons:
- Help button can only be unlocked after you unlocked several words.
- Missing some words from the dictionary/database
