This game is still in early access at the time of me writing this review. What this means is that it is not finished yet, it currently only has an Arena mode. The main selling point of this game is that it uses the d20 combat system, which if you're not familiar with is a set of rules used with polyhedral dice and miniatures on a grid based map. It is most famously used in Dungeons and Dragons, which was the inspiration for this game.
Basically each character gets a turn where they can move, attack, or cast spells. Some spells heal, some do damage, and some have positive or negative effects such as increasing your strength or immobilizing you. As you level up your stats increase and you find more gear making your characters more powerful so that they can fight stronger bad guys to get more gear and level up etc. Right now that's all there is to it but the devs are working on an Adventure mode which will add a world to explore with hand crafted cities and randomly generated dungeons/quests.
The devs also plan to add more classes, more spells, and a DM mode of sorts. They also plan to support modding in the future but at this early stage in development the only mods people can add are for new portraits and icons to represent your characters. Development is slow but steady and the dev has stated that he will not abandon this project because it is his main passion. This game doesn't have super high-res 3D graphics or anything, it is just 2D art but is very well done.
I would mainly recommend this game to people who play Dungeons & Dragons and enjoy the tactical combat aspect of it. I've already got more enjoyment out of the Arena mode than I have out of many other fully finished games. The fact that the dev plans to add an Adventure Mode, more classes, races, spells, etc. is just a huge bonus. If you haven't played D&D but enjoy other strategy games such as Warhammer then you might like this, just don't expect amazing graphics and 3D animation or anything like that, this is a smaller indie project after all, not a AAA title.

Ancient planet is a basic tower defence game that does not feature particularly complex mechanics. I would rate it as a passable tower defence game, as long as you are aware of a few things:
- It can easily be finished under 12 hours (3 stars on all maps, along with 100% steam achievements; there is one more in-game only achievement that requires collecting 100500 silver if you really love farming).
- At some point, you will need to farm previous levels to get more upgrades as there is a significant increase in difficulty that cannot simply be overcome by using good strategy. This is probably one of the main criticisms of the game.
- A new easy mode, in which the enemies have -15% health, has been introduced. I did not use it, so it may lower the required farming. There are no penalties/rewards based on your selected mode, as far as I can tell.
- There is a survival mode which means that the game has replayability to some extent (you can also start new profiles), but I was not really interested in that.
- Hotkeys have been added to the game (see comments), it is nice to see the devs care about the game.
The mechanics are basic and mostly rely on the fact that there are two types of damages in the game, energy and piercing. All enemies are resistant to one of these two types, depending on their race. You always know what the next wave is going to be and need to plan accordingly.
Therefore, if you are looking for a basic tower defence game, this one may do the trick. Keep in mind that this game is rather short and requires some (rather mindless) farming. However, if you are looking for a more complex tower defence game, you may want to try something else.

The Long Dark is one of those Early Access gems that eventually get developed into a high quality survival game. The freezing Canadian Wilderness is an interesting location for a survival game. Survival is only possible when a careful balance between food, water, rest, and warmth is met.
There is an episodic story mode, and a simple survival mode. They have only released the first 2 episodes out of 5. The game runs smoothly, but it crashed 2 or 3 times in my 25 hour playthrough.
The visual style is a cartoon-like cell shading, something like the Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker.
I actually died 10 minutes into the tutorial on my first playthrough. I got bit by a wolf (my own fault, I was taunting him haha) and slowly bled to death before finding my first building. I learned I wouldn't survive if I kept dicking around. Surviving becomes difficult because every action you take requires time. Chopping wood to warm yourself up at a campfire will make you hungry and thirsty. Sprinting around looking for supplies makes you tired faster. It's a delicate balance.
I could say more, but I could also just say: This is a great game and if you have the chance, give it a try.

I'm new to The Long Dark. I happened upon the game whilst killing time on YouTube. A gamer was playing Interloper mode and before I knew it an hour had passed and I found myself wanting more. I watched a few uploads of the game and honestly thought I wouldn't stand a chance with the game but then Story Mode came along and I parted with my money straight away. I haven't regretted it.
You play MacKenzie. A pilot who is talked into taking a woman on a flight so she can complete a mystery mission. During the flight strange lights erupt across the sky and the plane is strangely effected. Instruments flash, sparks fly, the plane is going down!
You wake, there's wreckage all around. You feel a pain in your hand... what is it? You look at it.... your game play starts.
I love the art work and general feel of the game. In story mode it is quite forgiving and the artistry is a delight to look at as you stumble your way through an apparent maze of rugged territory. Items are found, animals are scary (and tasty!), and the story mode sends you on sub missions that slowly get you used to the controls. It subtle in it's teaching in parts and much more obvious in others. The pace is steady and you will get a good number of hours out of the game for your money.
As well as story mode there are challenges ranging in difficultly from 3 to 5 axes (although the three axe level challenge should probably be a 2 rating). These challenges will keep you busy, frustrated at the cold, and at times on the edge of your seat. Is that a wolf you heard?? Or was it your next meal!
I'm a big fan of the game and can't wait for the rest of the episodes on story mode to come out.

Shadowy conspiracies, supernatural voices, and fearsome blizzards. Mass murder, wandering spirits, and glimpses of a world beyond our own. These are Kholat's ingredients--ingredients that could have comprised an enthralling story, and one that Kholat itself doesn't tell. This exploration adventure squanders its foreboding icy atmosphere on a nonsensical tale that mixes age-old cliches like secret experiments and government cover-ups into narrative mud. Trudging through this mud proves exhausting; every story morsel is another bog to traverse, and the impenetrable ending is pure quicksand, sucking you and the hours you spent to reach it into a vortex of nothingness.
Story and atmosphere are all Kholat has, making its poor storytelling all the more egregious. The "based on a true story" setup is promising, at least: in 1959, nine hikers exploring the chilly Ural mountains died in bizarre circumstances, inspiring years of speculation, along with numerous novels, films, and television inquiries. Kholat has you retracing those real-life hikers' steps from a first-person view, taking its cues primarily from games like Dear Esther in which your primary way of interacting with the world is to wander through it and read the diary entries inexplicably littered throughout.
I say "inexplicably," though I presume there is a reasonable explanation for why these pages haven't become sodden by the falling snow or blown away by the howling winds of Dyatlov pass. Kholat's final moments have the air of a grand reveal; the cryptic narrator makes a resounding declaration, as if he is providing an answer to the game's mounting questions. This is to be the "a ha!" that ties it all together, but after two entire playthroughs, I'm not sure I can tell you what all the questions are, let alone make sense of the narrator’s answer. The clues are found in the pass itself, where metaphysical sights appear before you in eerie shrines and dark caves. They are also found in the diary entries left in the snow and tacked to trees, of course, which divulge confessions and weird science experiments in far more words than is necessary. In mystical stories like this, not everything requires easy explanation, but there's nothing to invest in when you can't make out a basic shape amidst the static.
You're left with snow, and lots of it. You cover a lot of uninterrupted space as you make your way around the pass, seeking the nine landmarks earmarked on your map. This map is Kholat's most promising aspect. The game does not feature a traditional interface; there are no waypoints leading you to your destinations, the map doesn't show you your current location, and you are given no standard quest objectives. Instead, you have a layout of the area, markers that show you the camps (that is, save points) and notes you have already found, and a sequence of geographic coordinates that indicate where you can find the vital landmarks. You journey forward based only on your reading of the map, and the occasional map coordinates that someone has scrawled across the rocks and walls throughout the region.
Navigation thus requires patience, thoughtfulness, and an appreciation for a measured pace. These aren't unreasonable things for a game to ask of you. However, Kholat doesn't progress at a pleasant adagio, but at an excruciating largo. The success of a slow pace rests on the impact of the moments that break it, yet such key moments are too rare, too broken, and too annoying to make exploration worthwhile. A few central revelations bring some percussion to the minimalist droning, including an event in which you flee danger amid a mass of glowing figures. The rest, however, prove problematic.
There are the ghostly silhouettes that roam a few of Kholat's areas, for instance, which kill you should you make contact with them. Sometimes, you collide with a spirit you couldn't have been expected to see; Kholat springs the entire mechanic on you without warning, and doesn't provide proper audiovisual cues to communicate when there is immediate peril. A couple of traps you couldn't have seen--or even suspected would exist--can have you falling onto wooden spikes and cursing at the 30 minutes you lost due to the infrequent save points. (You may also lose progress to the game's occasional hard crashes, an equally curse-worthy event.) Some ledges you are meant to drop down onto; other ledges of similar distance are off limits, and send you sliding into oblivion. "Gotcha" deaths are difficult to get away with in games, because they often feel unfair, but they can serve a purpose if used as a learning tool. In Kholat's case, there's nothing to learn from some of these deaths, because it isn't clear enough what you did wrong in the first place.
In many stories, blizzards and the frigid cold provide a specific kind of terror, and Kholat's moaning winds cry out tales of lost souls that the game ignores in favor of shapeless nonsense. Its ideas reveal the game Kholat wanted to be, but its aspirations soar far higher than the game it became. What good is a mystery if you don't care about what it might tell you?

My first suggestion to people is don't read reviews of people who only played a half hour of this game.
Ok. this game is not your usual, follow the path kind of game. You are required to figure out where you are on a map without a constant location indicator. Following a compass, using land marks and places that you have already located. Also there is some reading in the game to garner some extra tid bits of the story.
It is tricky to get a handle on the game in regards to what you are supposed to be doing. That is why I say don't read reviews less then four hours at least. This game is best played in a complete sit through or a couple of them. One for learning how it goes and one to finish the game and story.
Good suspense and a few jumpy bits makes the game what it is for sure. The combination of noise, music, action and lighting with some frustration in challenge make this game worthwhile.
Enjoy it in a dark room with a good speaker system or a good set of headphones. My wife watched along side while I played and was jumping and screaming at the good parts.
Cheers and good luck.

UPDATE: 13 JULY 2016: With the release of Alpha 17 and a great deal of improvement in the ability of the game to complete building works, I've reversed this from a Thumbs Down to a Thumbs Up. While there are still occasional times where buildings don't complete, it's much reduced and is likely to reduce even further with new Alphas.
This is what I like to call a "Fly By Wire" game. You don't directly control each citizen at all times. Rather you give them specific tasks to perform (mine this area, build this road, craft these items), and the game then determines how best the citizen(s) in question should perform that task.
In this respect, it's like many other Steam games available (Gnomoria and Timber And Stone would be two obvious and similar examples).
The issue with such games is that they will ultimately live or die by how accurately the game can interpret and how successfully it can follow the jobs you've ordered, and Stonehearth (currently!), like many other games in this "FBW" category has some major issues with that (both the development and main branches).
Too often, a building you've ordered constructed will not finish (particularly a more complicated custom designed one), or citizens will go inexplicably idle, roads won't build properly, or the build order won't terminate even after the road has completed (preventing further custom build orders). Many of these bugs are only minor inconveniences (often reloading the game can solve some of them and there are console commands that can occasionally deal with more serious player<->game disconnects), but sometimes, and unfortunately too often, they cannot be recovered from.
This can lead to buildings that just simply cannot be completed (or, more often, left with scaffolding still in place after completion), roads that cannot be used, or walls that cannot be removed (even with the console), and while each individual instance of this is nowhere near game breaking, the cumulative effect is to sap the fun from the game.
Too often the player is left fighting the game, and not the monsters within it.
It is for this reason mainly (though the CURRENT lack of multiplayer is another major miss) that I cannot yet recommend this game.
That said, this is definitely not a vapourware game, and I fully expect that with further development and bug squashing, I'll be able to re-write this review in 6 months or a year from now, and reverse my recommendation. The developers are active and responsive, the game is regularly updated (as always, too slow for some, but at a reasonable pace to me) and there are clear, and clearly communicated goals for the games development with steady progress being made towards those goals.
There is much to like about Stonehearth, and I fully expect it will one day be an excellent addition to the genre. It's many bugs are somewhat to be expected, since this game is still well inside Early Access, so my negative comments are not accusatory, but meant as constructive criticism, but for the time being, this is one to watch and follow, and only purchase if you're either (or both) looking to support the developer, and deal with it's many bugs.

Completed my beta testing sessions on this game. Patience ran out (nothing personal...full time worker here lol). Here is the list of current bugs and frustrations I have run across.
that make everything extremely difficult after around the 10th - 15th day. I just finished a session where, between game day 7 and 14, I was encountered by:
-12 wolves
-4 thieves
-a goblin raiding party
-4 zombies/skeletons (While I had 4 goblins raiding, thus citizens started dying left and right)
-2 varnus things
-a shiteload of those wood/stone gremlin things
This was on "Normal" mode, and in my opinion, this difficulty curve/cliff is a gamebreaker. It reduces the game from enjoyable cute fun, to frustration where I'm yelling at my screen "Give me a god damned CHANCE!" If the game is going to be enjoyable, I suggest deep, dynamic difficulty so players can modify the game to suit how they play. I'm a slow, meticulous gamer when it comes to games like these. I don't have time to ultra-micromanage everything, especially with very clunky unit management and controls. It's too difficult!
There are MANY bugs you'll encounter when trying to build anything larger than a small shack.
Everything else other than the above listed is going great. This game is one of my favourites ever, despite being incomplete, and I seriously hope the devs don't get lazy with it. That doesn't seem to be the case right now, because I'm constantly seeing bugfixes and updates. Support these guys! And one last request, when the game is released: Full mod support and API, so the community can grow the game, as well.
Keep up the good work; I want to see this game surpass Minecraft in playability some day. I mean, imagine that...Going first-person and playing this game like you would minecraft, but you also have a dynamic town that NPCs build. You can go from first-person, to town management mode (Current setup). Isn't that something everyone has always wanted? Keep that one in mind.
I'll return to testing at the Alpha 18 opt-in.

I am a big fan of puzzle games. I have spent many consecutive days playing similar games, such as Text/Word Twist.
This game as it stands now is buggy and there are many things the developers missed. Here are a few things I've notived:
1) As per usual, there are words missing that should be listed, but this is a frequent occurrence for games like these.
2) Once you complete a puzzle, the words you missed are never revealed.
3) The words are not listed alphabetically. It is nearly impossible to logic your way into completing the puzzle and to figure out which words you're missing.
4) I had to quit several times when I was unable to type any letters or click them to enter a new word.
5) There is no way to save your progress (as far as I can tell).
Unfortunately there are no good alternatives to this game on Steam, but if you're feeling an urge to play this, don't pay the $5 or play it for free online.

Absolute perfection.
The brothers Cuphead and Mugman gamble away their souls in the Devil's casino. The Devil offers them a chance to keep their souls if they can collect on some delinquent soul contracts. A basic premise,
Cuphead is a platforming game, with 6 stages and hella bosses to fight. The boss fights fall into two categories: air and land battles. I prefer the land battles, but every battle is uniquely crafted
. Each boss has ~4 attack patterns, and some battles have sections that are randomly chosen from a few patterns. The quality of each fight is incredibly consistent, and you'll feel a sense of accomplishment after every one.
The six regular stages were clearly added in as an after-thought, and aren't as fun as the boss fights. Still, they're solid stages. Their length against your 3 health makes them endurance tests.  I recommend completing them for the coins, but if they aren't your cup of tea, they're the one part of the game you can skip.
Cuphead is, of course, difficult, but if you're persistent, you'll naturally feel yourself get good over time. This is the first "hard" platformer I've tried, and I can't overstate how ridiculously satisfying it is to see how
everything looks in hindsight when you finally beat the game
It's perfect. It blows every other game out of the water. The visuals are stunning, absurdly authentic to the old cartoon vibe. The backgrounds are gorgeous, the bosses are gorgeous, everything is amazing. The music is equally great. Heavy-hitting jazz numbers accompany each fight; even better, the music is unique for each individual fight. The developers put their hearts into this game, and it shines through.
This is one of the best platformers of all time. If you don't enjoy platformers/boss fights, you won't enjoy this game. But, if you enjoy a good challenge and are persistent, buy it now.

owning the game since '14 i really loved it then for its ideas and the feeling of it.
it was "no zombies" survival and it looked very promising.
sure, it had some quirks and many design decisions were neither logic nor real life oriented then - but hey, it was EA ! they would work on that and it would broaden the experience and getting better and better.
so i thought.
and it did - for some time.
it got better, things got added and fixed and overall this made replaying interesting enough.
they added more regions and stuff to do, more crafting and difficulty levels.
some illogic things went away.
i praised the game as a good example for the EA concept.
and then it seems they stopped caring for the game mechanics at all.
reason, logic and any RL orientation went out of the window.
instead of carefully tuning the mechanics, bringing interesting and plausible mechanics into the game and getting rid of the still flawed and illogic things they went the easy way and made everything artificially restricted, unreal and hardcore at the same time.
from my PoV it looks the lazy path and not well thought out.
still, survival mode was ok as one could choose to play on easy to see all the regions and scenery - at least for one (last) time.
but now we have story mode - the long awaited story mode.
i did go through it - at least to give it a fair chance.
but it was not much fun and feels like i wasted my time.
where survival modes realism is artificially restricted story mode is even more so as most of the mechanics is disabled - "for stories sake" i guess.
no difficulty level - seems lazy won again.
and the narrative is not very interesting anyway.
the characters are one-dimensional and have little personality.
i did not expect AAA story quality but i dont even see the earnest effort.
my 2c:
IMO it would have been a better investment to let go story for a convincing RL survival game with convincing and logically profound game mechanics.
sure no simulation can cover all of RL survival aspects but at least you should have tried.

Ancient Planet is a surprisingly good tower defense game. I have played this game for several hours. Given that I paid only $1.25 during the Steam Summer Sale, I have gotten so much more than my money's worth.
It is easy to start and play but at the same time gets very challenging as you advance to later maps. It looks easy to figure out but sometimes executing on what you think is not the right strategy to get 3-stars in the map.
I don't get all these complaints about "grinding". What do people expect? Get a bunch of nuclear weapons from the beginning and breeze through the missions? This is a strategy game. You have to think and craft strategy to get through the map. A strategy game is not supposed to be just handed to you to win without thinking.
I like that I can reset earned experience points at any mission so that I am not locked into a particular offense/defense set of items. It is very flexible so that you are not trapped on a map forever.
The graphics are not super sophisticated but it works for the game. The humorous cartoons during the wait screens between missions works also.
Overall, if you like tower defense games, the game is a steal! I encourage the developer to make a follow-up. I really am enjoying this little masterpiece.

Dishonored might be one of the best stealth based games EVER made. Hyperbole aside, I'm not even kidding.
Dishonored places you in the very capable hands of the Empress of Dunwalls head bodyguard Corvo Attano. The game begins with everything very calm and rather jovial. The empress's daughter Emily even invites you to play hide and seek as a form of a tutorial. Soon after the Empress is attacked by assassins and Corvo easily fends the first few off, however one succeeds after restraining Corvo and quickly vanishes leaving Corvo lying next to the slain Empress. Thus, 'Dishonored' begins.
Near the beginning of the game you're greeted by someone known as the Outsider. He grants you the ability of magic to include teleportation, seeing through walls, among other things. For obvious reasons, he remains elusive throughout the game.
The freedom of movement is rather unique and something I've not really seen other places. The movement, the narrative and the setting (London-esk during the late 1800's ) Where technology and magic exist together though the latter remains known only to a select few; Comes together in a package that feels unique like no other games quite hit every spot right like this.
Additionally, the narrative goes along perfectly with the actual gameplay. Each target as well as each objective that your rag tag team of seemingly misfit people assign to you in an attempt to prove your innocence and regain order, can be dealt with lethally or non lethally (which leaves some room for ambiguity) This may seem like a trivial distinction in most games, you might assume that doing either will get the job done and your next task will be marked. However, this game keeps track of each kill, each time you where seen and a number of other things that all go into your overall chaos rating; which markedly changes the world. The way people react to you and what defenses may or may not be set up to dissuade you from completing your task.
I've played through twice now, DLC included (which is remarkable. Some of the best DLC I've played since Bioshock Burial at Sea and the Witcher 3 DLC. I am not even close to joking. And I wholeheartedly think you should play that as well should either having more missions interest you or seeing the story from another perspective interest you) I've taken the High Chaos and the Low chaos route; the game takes the best from Thief and adds more content and playability to make it a near perfect product.
You can be the stealthy rogue on a mission with a heart of gold or play the ruthless killer bent on revenge and the world will reflect that sentiment. I am in love.

Very good early access product with an outstanding potential to be something truly special. The Arena mode available at this point is tactical turn-based D&D style combat and it's freaking incredible. The mechanics of melee/ranged/magic is fantastic and the UI is clear, simple, and effective. It's got that "one more turn" feel as you want to play a couple of more arena fights to see what awesome new gear you can unlock and what new feats you can choose for your dual-wielding rogue on his next level up. The Adventure/Campaign mode will be released in the next couple of months and this could easily become an instant classic. This is a must have for anyone that enjoys turn-based combat or D&D.

This game is really amazing if you enjoy D&D style turn based tactical combat. The adventure mode isn't out yet, so no quests or towns or trading or exploring or anything. As of right now, you can make characters or use preset character builds, or even get some from the steam workshop if you don't want to spend time making your own. You put together a party of 6, and start fighting battles against NPC monsters, you get XP and loot after each battle, can buy randomly generated loot from the shop after each fight, craft new items, or upgrade current items, rinse and repeat battle after battle.
If you enjoy tactical turn based combat, getting loot, managing stats / feats / skills / spells for characters, you will really love this game, even in the current "arena mode" form, it has all the progression of an in depth RPG, just without the walking around and talking at the moment, just fight after fight. Great game, really looking forward to the adventure mode.

Too many bugs to play a file reliably. You build a pathway, some times it bugs out and can't be removed. You try and build under ground to reach the tunnels/dungeons, the camera can't turn the proper angle to create proper tunnels. Constant bug notifications pop up on your screen, some times crashing the file itself. Buildings still don't function properly. The soilders bug out in the middle of the fights if they try to haul. If your civilians all have 'mine' set on, they'll get stuck in a hole forever. Miners can't reach directly above their heads, causing them to get stuck forever if you don't click in a methodical order. If you don't do clean mining strips then you'll have messy blocks sticking/floating out and there's no way to fix it. Sometimes you civilians stop building, mining or doing a task with no reason.
The most annoying thing by far is that these games always fall for the same issue because the developers balance this game by being "arm chair scientists" rather than playing their game legitimately (without cheats/commands). This is a problem in every single game like this I've played, whether it's Banished or anything else I've unistalled. This problem amplfies the longer you have a file, and the more you develop a file. Your units need to eat, and sometimes while they're half way in to completing a task or walking to location. The result is an endless loop of them trying to complete/reach the location before ending up getting hungry and cancelling it to walk back to the designated 'eat spot'. This is a completely fatal issue, there's no way to combat this until the developers add in proper inventories so your peoples can hold some food in their bags. Assuming you manage to dodge the bug fest and end up creating a big town, the civs will get hungry just by travelling from one side of the town, let alone exploring tunnels or hunting mobs on the map.
Stoneheart is the only game from this genre that I enjoy and look foward to seeing developed. It's zelda-like elements and potential make it endlessly replayable once the content rolls in. However once the developers start ACTUALLY playing their game and realise their are some fatal bugs/issues like the 'Food Loop' they completely give up and open up the mod workshops *cough* Banished *cough*. So lets hope it doesn't go down like that. However, this game is pure Alpha, or even closer to Beta. Don't buy it.

I do recommend playing Baldur's Gate! Just not really the Enhanced Edition.
Albeit EE doesn't differ from the original much, it does in some significant ways. First of all, it allows running the game in high resolution. You can do it with the old BG too, but that requires a mod, and it's a nice thing to have it without doing anything. EE adds some magical weapons and other items to the game too. Not too many, which is very good, and they are balanced and fit in the game. Moreover, unlike vanilla BG, EE is not limited to Windows only, and can be run on other operating systems. A great thing is also the fact that BG EE has many languages to choose from (albeit no dubbings) so it might be a good way to practice one's language skills. Unfortunately these are the only positive things I can say about EE.
When EE was released it was full of bugs, even gamebreaking ones, but they were fixed by now. Most of them at least, because some things remain broken. For example I couldn't join Alora to my team, because her encounter was broken. Moreover, the quality of the writing when it comes to the new dialogues (and NPCs) is low, and it stands out from the rest of the game, definitely not in a positive way. Hence, it's better to play vanilla game without it. Moreover, for replayability there are many interesting modifications for Baldur's Gate, but they do not work with EE.
Play Baldur's Gate if you haven't already. To decide whether to choose BG:EE or BG you should consider quite a few things.
Why choose BG over BG:EE?
- no bugs
- quality of the game is the same all-through
- modifications
Why choose BG:EE over BG?
- multiple language versions (but no dubbings)
- multiple operating systems supported (albeit Wine runs BG just fine)

Do you like tabletop RPG? Do you enjoy Dungeons & Dragons? Would you like to play a 2D classic game with AD&D rules about fighting wizards, kobolds and wyverns? Then that's the game.
Protip: Beat BG:EE before playing BG2:EE

The Steam version is bug-ridden and doesn't run very well but the good news is that OpenXcom exists. It's a utility that uses the original game's data files (therefore you have to own a copy of the original game in order to play OpenXcom) but fixes all important bugs, improves the user interface, adds keyboard shortcuts, et cetera. It also enables modding, and there are a lot of major, active mod projects that either add lots of content, or rebalance the game entirely, or both. Notable mods include the Final Mod Pack (which adds a ton of content but is not known for being particularly balanced or coherent, since it aims to incorporate basically the entire modding community's work); Area 51 (which seems like a more coherent equivalent to the Final Mod Pack); Reaver's Faithful Megamod (my personal favorite to play with normally, which rebalances much of the existing game content and adds just enough new content to be exciting without overwhelming the original content); X-PirateZ (which I have yet to play, but apparently it's big. Like, really freaking big); The X-Com Files (Take a wild guess...); the list goes on. There is a prolific community for OpenXcom.
Technical suggestions aside, X-COM is (in my opinion) the greatest strategy game ever devised. It tasks you with defending the earth against an alien invasion, where you are the commander of a paramilitary organization funded by a shadowy council of nations. The nations have limited faith in your abilities, and you have a limited budget, but as you prove yourself defending countries against the invading aliens they will offer you more funding... unless the aliens infiltrate their government and cause them to withdraw all funding. Or just invade invade all of your bases and end the X-COM project directly. Manage soldiers and equipment, build new bases, shoot down UFOs, search the earth for alien bases, and if you are successful, take the fight to Mars and end the threat once and for all.
It's great.

Kholat fits the stereotype of poor walking simulators: an attempt at an engaging story that ultimately fails due to monotonous game play.  I view Kholat as an opportunity sorely missed.  This could have been a superb atmospheric horror adventure but instead everything is so spread out that the vast majority of your play time will be walking through an empty trail with nothing happening.  The graphics are great, the voice acting is great, the music is great, the environment is great... but the game play is terribly boring.
Kholat offers a unique environment with an engaging story, but the game ultimately fails to offer much enjoyment due to the constant need to backtrack through empty terrain and the Anomaly that will spawn in front of you, kill you, and force you to repeat up to 15 minutes of travel from your last save spot.  Also, there is no manual save, so there is no way around this annoying feature.
Here are some of the more notable pitfalls from this game:
This is the only game I've ever played where running actually seems to slow you down.  You almost immediately run out of stamina and then slow to a crawl to catch your breath.
The map is almost entirely useless.  The trails never actually seem to align with the points on the map, and several of the trails you can walk on aren't even marked.  I'd find a new note, which gives a new marker on the trail map, and every time I would think, "How the heck did I get all the way over here!?"
The Anomaly can spawn in front of you and kill you before you have time to react or escape.
You see coordinates written on rocks indicating where you can find something, yet there is no way to mark your map to record the coordinates.

An incredibly unique combination of roguelike, tower defense & 4X.
Try to lead your crew of survivors through a procedural dungeon, upgrading them & collecting new characters as you go. What makes it unique is the strategic layer added on top; you can place modules & turrets in any room powered by dust, which is a very limited resource. Every door you open is treated like ending a turn in a 4X; new resources are generated, research proceeds, & new waves of enemies randomly spawn in unpowered rooms. Your ultimate goal on each floor is to find the elevator to the next, & then have one of your characters carry your power crystal from the first room to that point. Endless waves of enemies will start spawning once the crystal is picked up, so you need to prepare the path so the crystal carrier has as safe a journey as possible.
The art & sound are beautiful, & it has the same amazing UI design & balance of depth & approachability that make Amplitude's other endless games such a joy to play. However, the biggest recommendation I can give is to say that there is nothing else quite like this game out there.

Greetings reader, I held off on writing this review because I wanted to fully complete the game twice. Once on high chaos, once on low.
Before I go anywhere with this review, I want you to know this is my favourite stealth oriented game and is brilliant from start to finish.
*SPOILERS ENSUE*
You play as Corvo Attano, a bodygard to the empress. This is my first point, you are roleplaying and the character you play is a complete badass. Corvo is gifted powers by the outsider, an unknown man who speaks to you in the darkness and tells you the futures of your targets. You can play as an evil assassin, or a good one.
I chose bad to start with, I killed everyone on sight and every alarm was rung. The way you play affects the end of the game, since I played badly, Samuel the boat driver ended up hating me, there were double as many weepers (walking corpses full of plague) and the lord regent ended up retreating to his safe room, which took an extra hour to get up to.
If you play nicely, Emily is seated on the throne, less weepers, smaller characters like Sokolov and Piero survive the mass killing at the Hound Pits by admiral havlock and you all live happily ever after.
Since I played through it twice I noticed significant differences between playthrough styles.
At the final level, overseer martin and lord pendleton are not fighting and you find overseer martin dead, but on high chaos you have to kill both of them, which in turn increases chaos.
GRAPHICS: Dull and dark, which is to say, brilliant. They captured the desired atmosphere perfectly. The dark, dank streets of Dunwall felt ominous and oppressive. This is exactly how you want to feel, as an assassin on the run, staying to the dark side of the street. I love it.
STORYLINE: Brilliantly enthralling. I was compelled to finish it the instant I woke up in Prison.
COMBAT: Now...people have said that the combat is limited, and to be honest, it is, to an extent.
You can use three different types of crossbow bolts to use on unsuspecting enemies, you have your trusty pistol and sword... and thats it, other than small things like grenades and springrazors, which you put on a wall and they cut guards into little chunks. If you are playing low chaos, you really only have your sleep bolts and the ability to knock people out, I still found it very fun to play LC, but some may find it monotonous and repetitive. I do honestly think its still got enough ways to allow you to have fun with the combat. But it did need a little more.
OVERALL: 9/10

This is a mild recommendation in the game's current state.
The good: Like all of the best card games, this is a fun, budget-priced time waster with a simple but clever mechanic. You scroll a 5x5 board of playing cards horizontally and vertically to try and make the best possible poker hands. You get an individual score for each row and column. There are two timed modes (Casual, Challenging) where you get a set number of boards to obtain a goal score with that goal getting higher with each level. There's an untimed mode that works the same way but without a time limit (helps you learn the tricks for achieving higher scores) and a "Mania" mode which is timed and auto-scores the board as larger point values are accrued. The game has global leaderboards for each mode,
The bad: Very barebones in regards to options. Not expecting FoV sliders or 4k textures or anything in a $3 card game but the current options menu is Windowed/Full-Screen and two audio sliders (to get rid of the monotonous music or the sound effects). All this would be fine but the game is currently limited to one resolution (1024x768?) and while you can put it in full-screen, it looked stretched and bad on my 16:9 monitor. This doesn't bother me much as this is the kind of game I'd like to be multi-tasking in the background with anyway but in this day and age, even a budget-priced game should have some degree of scalability.
All that said, I see the developer is active in the discussions and hope he/she will continue to work on it to iron out the current issues. I've already gotten my money's worth.

This is possibly one of the best games I've gotten from Steam. Nostalgia aside, this is possibly one of the best star wars fighter games made for PC, and yes, even better than EA's Star Wars Battlefront dogfights. See, the dogfights aren't as fun if there are no objectives, which is what EA doesn't seem to understand. Even Battlefront II's dogfights are better because you can choose to cripple the enemy capital ship, engage in 1-to-1 combat, or land in the other capital ship and wreak havoc. Anyway, back to my review.
PROS:
+Nostalgia value
+Dogfights with objectives
+cheatcodes for messing around in a Millenium Falcon, AT-ST, Naboo Starfighter, etc.
+Death Star trench and Battle for Hoth gameplay
+Racing minigame with T-16 Skyhoppers
+Decent difficulty, enough to make the dogfights not boring, and fun in most cases
+Amazing first person cockpit view (I tend to use this for all levels that don't require speeders. It's great to feel like you're in the actual cockpit.
+Very smooth, at what seems to be 60fps
CONS:
-Took a bit of research on my part to make the resolution match my screen in order to get the full screen, instead of 1/4 of the screen, to appear
-Defection from Corellia is the worst level ever. So many places where you can mess up, and you have to restart the whole thing if you mess up anywhere.
-1998 Graphics, although for 1998, these were excellent graphics
-Some of the audio is a little odd. For instance, when you beat Battle for Hoth, the General who commands you (Luke Skywalker) says that the Millenium Falcon made it out all right and warns you not to do anything stupid like flying off to Dagobah. HOW DID HE KNOW THAT LUKE WAS GOING TO DAGOBAH???!!!!
-Turning the ships around can sometimes be a pain in bulkier fighters
-No alt+tab support
-Happened once, so it might be a fluke, but I beat a level, and the game crashed. Before that, I had probably beaten about 7 levels, so it might have been some kind of pile-up error in the code. I beat more than 7 levels upon restarting the program and didn't have any crashing issues.
Verdict: 9/10
If you give me alt-tab support, I will switch this to a 10/10

This visual novel by Namaage and Sekai Project feature a male protagonist Yamada Ichirou who took up a teaching position at a secluded academy on an uninhabited island which consists of 4 female students Casserole, Mincer, Peeler and Oros zester, 2 male teachers Tsuji and Liang Hai and a female principal Matsuri. Upon witnessing the graduation of one of the students, Ichirou begins to question the validity of the practices in the academy.
I have mixed opinions on this visual novel. Having played through and reached all 3 possible endings in this visual novel, the game started out too slowly as a typical school life drama and only after episode 5 out of 9 possible episodes in this visual novel did it build more suspense and thriller and develop as a mystery visual novel and there are only 1-2 choices to make in the entire game which are near the ending and lead to a different ending each(The game storyline could do with a shortening of the school life drama section in the prologue and first 5 episodes if the mystery and thriller part could expand and develop more). Furthermore, although the game had nice anime artwork on the cover, CGs and character sprites, this is one of the few visual novels on Steam that did not have trading cards or achievements which would further reduce the appeal of this visual novel.
On the plus side, I would definitely say that the game in using music by Patirchev and Ara Hiroshi to produce a great opening and ending movie, theme song and BGM probably saved this visual novel from being just another forgettable visual novel I would uninstall after finishing this game. I managed to get the game on 60% discount in Steam store and I liked the soundtracks in this game enough to give this game a recommended review. It would also be nice if a soundtrack DLC were to be released for this game in future.
Overall, this game is recommended only for those who like a short mystery visual novel featuring a futuristic dystopian Japanese setting that is easy to reach all endings, nice anime artwork in the game or great BGM and soundtracks in the opening and ending movie(My favourite BGM is F.G as a soothing and inspiring soft music that is played only in the true ending and end credits). In which case, the game is recommended only when at good discount or bundle offer or when soundtrack DLC, Steam trading cards and/or achievements are added to the game in future.

I'd say overall this was pretty good. The main character was interesting (if kind of a terrible person) and I thought the story wrapped up quite well. The only real issue is that there are some typos in the translation, which seems rather odd. Also, there are certain parts of the translation where I had to wonder if that's actually what was said. I can't read Japanese, so I can't comment further on the accuracy of it. From what I can tell, there are three possible endings. Each of these splits off about 20 minutes to an hour from the end. The two bad endings are very, very abrupt while the true ending is a reasonable length. I also have to give it props for running flawlessly on Linux. The main downside to this is that the developer seems to have abandoned it, so I wouldn't expect a fix for the typos or any technical issues that could arise. Overall I'd give it a 7/10.

This isn’t your average happy VN, there’s mystery, violence and death. I enjoy those things, so I liked The Orchard of Stray Sheep. It’s a very short (mostly kinetic, with only a few choices, branching into 3 endings: 2 bad, 1 true ending plus epilogue) visual novel, and the truth about the girls surprised me a lot.
The art style is absolute lovely. It’s what caught my attention at first, then there’s the BGM which is also pretty good. The story was a bit rushed, but still managed to surprise me. I just wished that the developers would have explained more about the “Academy” and its system since it was interesting. The English translation is a bit weird, there’s some typos and grammar mistakes. It didn’t bothered me so much since English isn’t my native language, but it might bother other people.
I just have one problem with this game: its endings. This had a lot of potential, but I felt that the endings were so… blah? Even the true ending and epilogue. It would be interesting to see a spin off or a similar game tho.
5/10. Overall, I do recommend this VN on a good sale, and if you like short & weird stories like I do.

Before you start if you want to get straight to the point
of why I do not recommend this visual novel at all.
Developed by Namaage and published by Sekai Project onto steam. The Orchard of Stray Sheep is a short visual novel with a school theme on the surface set in a “academy” with 3 endings 2 being “Bad endings” and 1 being thee “True end”. On the surface The Orchard of Stray Sheep looks like your typical high school cliche visual novel, but it is not what you think it is, instead It has a darker side that you will discover as you read through the visual novel.
I will state this first before I start before reading The Orchard of Stray Sheep I have no knowledge of cherubim the garden of eden and dues ex machina. So I did my research on those to get a rough idea to of what The Orchard of Stray Sheep is referencing to. Next if you are wondering what is with the low score I gave it an explanation can be found below. It is separated from this area it’s because of its spoiler nature. Next do not get me wrong I really liked the theme and direction of the story is going but please read explanation of why I am not recommending this.
You will be met with a mystery at the very start wondering why are there metal rings above their heads which look like halos.
On a secluded island a small garden-like Academy stands alone a little Eden.. Ichirou Yamada which is the protaganist has been transferred there to work as a teacher. He is put in charge of Casserole, a beautiful, young girl who entered the school at the same time.
The days roll by at the Academy. Days that are boring but full of happiness a safe haven.
However, things are not what they seem at this “academy”…
Ichiro Yamada has finally found the peaceful days he’s always longed for, as well as that someone he wants to protect. He is still trying to overcome the loss and regret of his past amidst the warmth and tranquility of these days.
“Stray Sheep.”
All the while trapped by the words of the girl he lost so long ago.
Would I recommend The Orchard of Stray Sheep? As much as I hate to say this I would not recommend The Orchard of Stray Sheep. The reason is that the story is interesting for sure but the all 3 endings have literally no conclusion at all and after completing The Orchard of Stray Sheep the question “So what happened in the past or after the events?” will pop up in your head but then you will have no answer to it sadly as there are no sequel or prequel to  The Orchard of Stray Sheep.

This game is similar to Gnomoria, there are some important differences:
- graphic is much better (I like retro graphic, but Gnomoria was too much for me)
- game mechanics are simpler, or at least it is much easier to understand
- buildings!!!
I don't deeply know Gnomoria, so excuse me if this is not a correct list. In my opinion these were the three most annoying things in Gnomoria, so I was really happy when I found StoneHearth.
Pros:
- lovely graphic and atmosphere
- the settlement looks pretty cool with all the interesting buildings
- classes and abilities are interesting
Cons:
- still alpha, so lots of features are not finished (I hope underworld will be improved, ores will not be just a random drop), there are bugs, balancing issues. But development is active, there are releases every week, so I don't worry much about these.
- biggest issue for me are the buildings (this is in the same time the best feature of the game). So you first have to design the house (or use a template), and then your hearthlings will build it. First problem is that quite often they cannot build the house (this unfortunately happens with the templates as well). Second problem is that the game won't give you any warning or error message, the only thing you see is that the building is just paused. There are scaffoldings around the house, some walls are missing, but no one is doing nothing. I couldn't figure out what is wrong. The best thing I could do is that I built a few ladders here and there, maybe they were not able to reach some parts, but that didn't help. But the worst thing is that there is nothing you can do, you will have a half ready house with scaffoldings in the middle of your nice village. If you don't like that (I didn't) then the only option is to reload an old save where the building wasn't at all designed. That wasn't really a viable solution for me. There is a console command which erases a building, but it won't clean up the scaffolding, and also the base of the building will still be there (the hole in the ground). My feeling is that the devs were too optimistic about this type of building, I guess they think that there are problems, they can solve it easily for the next version, no need for error message or any tool which would help players work around a failed building. And then the next release comes, and there are still lots of buildings not correctly building. I think this is not a new issue, many recent releases had this. But I thrust them, I hope sooner or later they will be able to solve this, and players will be able to build a very nice village.

As an avid Assassin's Creed fan, AC Syndicate is a major disappointment. I had expected that the folks at Ubisoft to actually learn from their mistakes (Unity) and strive to make a better AC experience in through Syndicate. After giving this game so many chances to prove itself, ultimately it is still a major letdown by Ubisoft.
1) Controls are still very wonky and stiff
= Parkour are super-smooth and semi-realistic (if you would excuse all the extreme parkour of course), but the controls for the game was not improved. It is still wonky and stiff in execution, which leads to frustrating movements and maneuvers.
2) Uninspiring main characters
= Jacob and Evie Frye is still likeable, just not inspiring. Most of the dialogues are dull, with Evie sticks mostly to the plan and Jacob being sarcastic and relaxed in an almost lazy way. Interaction with other characters within the game are similarly dull and not exciting. Truly a missed opportunity especially when you have historical figures like Charles Darwin, Alexander Graham Bell and Karl Marx walking about.
3) Story is lackluster.
= The story lacks any form of inspiration or excitement. The story is too straightforward without any suspense or fear. It goes on sequence by sequence without anything memorable happening.
4) Limited Weapons:
= There are only three type of weapons in Syndicate: brass knuckles (which is awesome! Love fighting with these), cane sword and kukris (basically curved daggers). In comparison to Unity which had a lot more variety to offer, the limited structure of weapons in Syndicate is a letdown for sure, especially as a AC game.
5) Limited Outfits and Customizations:
= Apart from specialized skill tree for Jacob and Evie, there really is not a lot to offer when it comes to customizations. The outfits are very limited, and the corresponding color customization is quite boring (color does not pop). I expected more customizations for Syndicate.
6) Jacob and Evie can't walk normally with their hoods up.
= Jacob will wear a tophat and Evie will just leave her hood down in normal walking mode. As you trigger the stealth mode (entering the stealth mode), Jacob and Evie will pull up their hoods to accomodate their stealth movements. Although I love the fact that you can bring the hood up and down, at least give us a option to put the hood up while walking normally. I can't stand following Charles Darwin with my hood up while crouching. It looks off.
7) Buggy fighting system
= The fighting system in Syndicate is actually pretty smooth. Combat flows and executions, while limited, looks realistic and classy. However, some aspect of the fighting system is buggy. Sometimes a prompt does not appear when someone is about to shoot you, and the next thing you know, you're dead (from higher level enemies). Sometimes attacking an enemy deals no damage, and would get countered instead (almost immediately). I'm fine with a challenging fighting system, but when it bugs so much that it ruins the flow of the game, it is definitely frustrating.
There might be something that I missed in this. Sorry Ubisoft, but AC Syndicate is a major letdown for me. Come back better with an AC game in Feudal Japan, with samurais and ninjas. That, would be epic.

Dishonored is to me a puzzle, above all else. And it is a puzzle I will keep coming back to. The game encourages you to explore and exploit your environment, and it rewards patience and experimentation. This game has incredible replay value.
The game looks great, too. I've never seen an Unreal Engine game that has looked bad.
If you're looking for a brawler or a generic FPS, go look elsewhere. If you want a game that will challenge you and make you think, then step right up and prepare for a treat.

I like this game very much. It is basically a DnD arena game, which uses an older version of the Dungeons and Dragons type rules (5.0 maybe?).
That being said, the rule set is a bit frustrating. You have your traditional DnD classes (fighter, cleric, wizard, archer, etc.) and sub classes, such as fighters which are more like dwarven defenders.
Each character has various abilities, which are chosen by the game. The player does not customize their character, other than their name, race and equipment.
The equipment is fun. You find and can purchase both normal and magic items. These are traditional DnD things like platemail +1, +2, etc., longsword +1, cloak of resistance, gauntlests of ogre power, etc.
I found the rule set to be a bit frustrating. The game makers stuck true to the system, so it isn't their fault, but having a healer who can only heal every other round is frustrating.
As a seasoned DnD player, I was able to breeze through the challenges for quite a while. However, now that my party is pretty high level (8th) the boss challenges are next to impossible. My little 6-person party with mediochre equipment is facing around 20 8th level fighters, who are backed up by a mage or to, a healer and a couple of archers. I just keep getting slaughtered.
I know this is a beta version, but the increasing diffuculty needs to be toned down a bit, if the game is going to have serious replay value.
That being said, I have been looking for a game like this for years, having been hooked on the old school DnD type games, such as Pool of Radiance, Curse of the Azure Bonds, etc.
So if you have been looking for a game like that, look no further.
It looks like they are going to add an adventure expansion pretty soon. I am looking forward to it.

Grand Class Melee 2 is an eight round competitive battle arena. Each round you progress up your class tree. Your new class will have one default ability, and you can select any previous class abilities you have used as your second ability.
The classes are basically melee, archer, and magic (which can split into healing or damage paths). The skills are reasonably diverse and there are many combinations you can employ each round. Needless to say this can create balancing issues - however the GCM2 team has it reasonably under control. On top of this they have a player based balancing feedback system.
The combat starts out reasonably simple. All class have the same basic attacks, a slash, which has a wider parry radius, and a charge, which sends the character forward with a low parry radius. Magic classes get many options for different kinds of attacks. Melee have more passive options, some attack skills, and some passives that augment basic attacks. Ranged classes get a variety of circumstantial speed/damage boosts as well as a good selection of different arrows.
Scoring options can be tampered with which can help to make different playstyles better. (for example the last man standing may get 2 points, most damage inflicted 1, most damage received 1).
The maps are procedurally generated and the camera pans infinately. The camera panning is quite complicated - and after several tweaks from the development team it works exceedingly well.
There were many planned features in the development stage that have yet to be realised. These include a "way of the dark" class tree, of equal size to the current ("way of the light") path tree. Some of the planned skills were very interesting - including some necromancing elements. There was a parry shield planned, that prevented too many consecutive parries. And each class type (mage, melee and archer) had planned different charge attacks. Unfortunately none of these things have been realised as of yet - as far as I am awae they have been shelved to reconsider at a later date.
The price tag is a tad on the high side for current content - but this is generally speaking the case for early access games. This game is certainly conceptually sound, fun and original - and therefor worth the buy.

The baldurs gate series is one of the gems of the 90s but to truly appreciate the full story one should experience both games. The orignal Baldurs gate was at it's release n 1998 quite a big thing as it was the very first game to use the famous infinity engine. The game was so incredibly good for it's time not only because it used a remarkable new engine, but because it was the very first game to really give you a true dungeons and dragons experience in  a gaming enviorment.
The orignal game was extremly good and rare for it's time. The way you could chose different paths, be truly bad or good, having so many uniqe and different dialouge options and events was breathtaking back in 1998. Heck, the game gives you more freedom than most other rpgs released even to this day
I loved the game back in my early teens and now in my 20s i still love the game, because it was an incredibly important stepping stone. The way the sequel followed up on this beauty was incredibly impressive.
When I have talket to people who want to play the Baldurs Gate saga I always recommend starting with the origianl story since the games are heavily connected. And even though I feel that Baldurs Gate 2 is a superior game there's just something beautyfull about the game that started it all.
If your going to play it now and you come from games like divinity or pillars of eternity, you have to understand that the baldurs gate games are quite higher on the difficulty setting.
It also uses the old D&D THACo system which you really need to know because it's one of the most important stats in the game. the easiest way to put it is that the lower the number the better.
it can be a very hard game at times, but it's because of its difficulty compared to modern games, that killing a boss actually feels incredibly rewarding.

Quality horror game. Reminds me a bit of one of my favorites Miasmata.
Couple things about the game:
* Navigation is challenging, not overly so, but you'll find yourself in places you don't expect. Personally, I found this interesting since most areas loop and "try" to direct you correctly, but the gameplay is definitely non-linear.
* The things that can kill you are easy to evade in general, the game is not particurarly challenging in that regard, which IMO is correct for a horror game that is story driven.
* Plot is well rounded, the ending could be considered a bit speculative.
* The ambiance and "spookiness" of the environement is very well done. Little reliance on jump scares by establishing an overarching sense of dread.
* Quality of the voice acting is high.
IMO if you like games like Miasmata, Penumbra, Amnesia, SOMA you should like Kholat. So long as the navigation is not a turn off.
Gameplay time is around ~3-4 for completion. Full completion w/o a guide would probably take a while. Note that full completion (finding all notes) is possible due to hints ingame.

Time to write a review of this game, especially since the game hit its second anniversary, few days ago!
I spent many hours playing this game over the last two years. As many of the other "Endless"-games it is well produced and developed. It was already a fun game at release, but now it's way mature and polished.
This is one of many rogue-likes games here in steam, but it is the game in this genre which kept me coming back over and over again.
In this game it is your job to guide your crew, after your spaceship crashed on a planet, the way back to the surface. This will take quite some time, because between the surface and the starting point are 12 floors waiting full of monsters and other diffculties. Thankfully not behind every door is something deadly waiting for your team, but most of the time it does.
You have to manage your resources to equip your team, heal and level your crew and add new members to the party. There are spots in each room, which you can use to place modules to support your team.
The graphics are really nice if someone likes this kind of artstyle. I do, so nothing bad for me here, but I could imagine it could be not everyones kind of taste.
Playing this game in singleplayer-mode (guiding a full team) or with friends in multiplayer (each one playing a character) is a really interessting, exciting and fun experience.
tl;dr: Get this game and have fun!

This game is hard to decribe, but fantastic to play. Basically, it's a squad based stratégy game in which you don't decide what characters do, they act on their own when they are placed somewhere. It's a turn-based game, except that turns are counted by opening a door, which sometimes happen by itself in advanced stages of the game (enemies can open doors too !). It's a tower defense game, too, because you can build modules to help defend yourself. It's a dungeon crawler, also.
Whatever it is, it is awesome. It sucks you in for hours and hours, and then you wonder why the sun is rising already. Last game to hook me like that was Invisible, inc., so if you liked that one and do like tower defense / squad / dungeon crawler, you're gonna enjoy that one too.

Dungeon of the Endless is a treasure of a game. It's slow and methodical, and yet I always get tense as I go further in and try to escape the depths of the dungeon! There's so much customization in the game, you can build however you want to build and play however you want to play. It's a seamless blend of turn-based strategy, roguelike and tower defense and I haven't found anything quite like it since. It's so engrossing that you forget you have other obligations sometimes! Thus, for the Steam Awards 2016, I nominate this game for the "Just 5 More Minutes" award!

"Assassin's Creed Syndicate"
Publisher - Ubisoft
Developer - Ubisoft Quebec and other Ubisoft entities.
Instalment number (major releases) in the Assassins's Creed Series - 9th
Review by a very casual gamer :)
Even if I declare myself as a casual gamer, Assassins's creed series is something which is very close to my heart.
Right from the days of Altair/Desmond to Ezio/Desmond to various other protaganists of the series, it has left me in an awe and asking for more (I'm saying this keeping in mind the epic failure of Assassin's creed Unity!).
Jumping straight into the enviornment - London, right from a classic Victoria Era painting. The buildings, roads, pavements, clothes, horse-carriages, steam engines and every other freaking thing in the game has written London over it. I personally feel this is the best reproduction of the game after Ezio's Rome.
Into the gameplay, I will say it is a great improvement from its predecessor - "Unity"!
Bugs are almost extinct and the end result is a smooth and fluid sandbox game. Apart from the usual parkour mechanics of Assassin's creed, Syndicate introduces a new equpiment - Zipline. Yeah a freaking zipline!. This is a great shift from the evergreen climbing the buildings. You can also use it to zipline from one building to far away building, also hanging in the middle of the zipline to admire the view of the city (and also wait for your target to arrive below to air assassinate!)>
Story - You play two characters - Male and Female - Brother and Sister combo (Spoilers : No GoT action in the game [Thank God!]). Charracters are well written and the dailogues between reminds me of typical fights and coversation between siblings. The game also have few famous historical characters like Charles Dickens, Queen Elizebath, and many more for whom you have to complete missions to progress.
Overall this game is fantastic. A must play for every gamer irrespective of their alligances towards particular type of genre or series.

This game has a lot of good things going for it, and I think it'll get better.  The villagers and enemies are stylized in cute manner, and the little plot dialog that exists carries the cute theme as well - but that doesn't stop some battles between the two from being deadly serious.  Combat is simple once you figure out how to develop your battle team to survive with the difficulty curve (two tanking armored characters, backed by archers, with a cleric thrown in will get you by the majority of the battles).  I can easily see more event battles being added as this game progresses but it would be nice if enemy bases  spawned more often around the map - perhaps sending their own raiding parties.
However, the real bread and butter of this game is customizing your village exactly the way you want it.  This is the most complex part of game play and it takes a while to get the hang of.  Editing a blueprint is tricky and time consuming at first but I highly recommend saving one to greatly reduce time later.  If your Hearthlings stall during mid-construction, check your available recources needed, then try manually placing ladders in case they cannot reach the upper construction areas.  (I highly recommend a building blueprint that has doors and window frames, but no other furnishings or decorations which can be added later.)
What's really needed here is more terrain options like adding soil blocks for leveling surfaces and undo'ing building mistakes.  Far too often I found myself relying on back-up saves because nudging a building over 1 or 2 blocks or fixing an errant click while digging is not very forgiving at this point.
This game is good so far, and it's going to get better.  Highly recommended.

X-COM: UFO Defense is a fantastic game if you are the sort of person who likes turn-based combat mixed with basebuilding and management.
The gameplay consists of managing your base on a world map, where UFOs show up at regular intervals. After you've scrambled some jets and nailed those suckers, a "mission" becomes available. The mission consists simply of sending out your forces to the crashsite where you have to eliminate survivors in turn-based combat.
During the game your forces will become stronger and with the help of research, new and better equipment will be available for production. This will come in handy, seeing as the aliens also become stronger and more resillient as the game progress. I find that the difficulty curve is quite nice, up to a point when the most powerfull weapons become available, after that the game becomes a little trivial. Still, this does not happen untill late in the game, and that's more than a couple of hours of gameplay.
The turnbased combat I find very entertaining. There is a load of different aliens with different abilities, all of whom are dedicated to kill your elite soldier squad. Some will make you moan in annoyance, as they take control of your soldiers, and others scream in terror as they charge forward and impregnate your soldiers turning them into "zombies". Atleast that's what I did when I first played this game as a very young little boy.
The graphics and sound in the game is well, old, but many a great game survives purely on gameplay, and this is one of those games. The graphics are probably the games biggest weakness, but also one of it's charms I think. This is an old school game, for old school gamers, specificly for the type that likes turnbased combat with a mix of basebuilding. So take a trip down memory lane and give this little gem a chance - also make sure to get help on the boards on setting up the game...

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: First Person, Open World Survival Horror
The Good:
+ Amazing graphics with tons of different graphical options
+ Fantastic weather effects
+ The entire game is exploration. You start with no directions or any clues where to go. You have a map and a compass and that’s it. The game gives you a set of coordinates that you have to go to and pick up notes. However, there are also enemies you have to avoid. Avoiding enemies is easy enough and the majority of the game you probably won’t encounter too many but you still have to be careful. If you are the type of gamer that doesn’t like getting lost, you may want to avoid this game. If you love exploring and getting lost and looking at maps, this game is for you.
+ Haunting soundtrack
The Average:
I would have liked more variety within the environments. The majority of the game is a snowy forest, mountain areas and it starts feeling repetitive by the end of the game.
The story is told by finding notes and log entries, the story itself is pretty decent, however, I did find it cliché. The survival horror genre needs to think of some new story elements.
I would like to run more than 5 steps before I run out of stamina and have to wait to catch my breath.
The Bad:
-Nothing breaks immersion more than running into an ankle high rock and not being able to jump over it.
-The game is not that well optimized. No matter what specs you have or what graphical settings you choose, you will experience stuttering and frame drops.
Conclusion:
This is a slow-paced survival horror game focused primarily on exploration and not much else.  Strange as it sounds, I found this game to be more of a casual experience compared to many other survival horror games out there.

What Kholat really comes down to is holding down W, holding down Shift to run, using a map, collecting notes, avoiding traps, running away from a monster, and losing progress. Manual saving could have saved this experience for me, but trekking through the beautiful snow repeatedly at such a miserable pace hurts the game.
The environment can be quite beautiful, eerie, and haunting at times. The notes add to the atmosphere as you slowly unravel what's happening (the game is based on a real world mystery). The nice locales and vistas don't really do much to save the game from its uninteresting gameplay, but they are quite memorable, especially as you use them to navigate around the world.
There's nothing much required of you beyond finding major story notes that trigger an event and checking important locations off the map. There are no puzzles and hardly any interactions beyond pressing E to collect notes. Most of the gameplay was just holding down W and Shift after orienting yourself with your map. The stamina of the character is very low and to escape from the monster you need a nearly full bar of stamina. This cuts down on stamina usage because you definitely want some saved up since dying means going all the way back to the last checkpoint which can be really, really far away from where you were. There is a campfire fast travel system whenever you're at one, but that doesn't help soothe the sting of having to redo the walking. Keep in mind you die in one hit. I also one time had a save point where every time I loaded the monster was 15 feet away from me and I was in a dead end. That took some time. I think Kholat's strongest gameplay feature is the map and compass because I did derive some satisfaction aiming myself correctly and from saying, "Oh, I'm here now. Now let's see how I get over there."
I wish I could just save manually or had a bigger stamina bar, but instead, I'd rather just recommend SOMA over this title unless you're extremely patient or prefer the snowy setting. Reading up on the Dyatlov Pass Incident would be an okay way to spend your time too. Take note that I didn't finish the game, but collected most of the important notes. I became irritated with losing progress and having my time wasted.

Dungeon of the Endless is close to a tower defence game. I mean close as in theres a center point (your core) you have to defend and you can set up towers to defend your core and thats about all it has incommon with tower defence games. Instead of sitting back and just defending wave after wave you have to use your heroes to open doors which has a pseudo RNG chance of spawning waves of enemies. To advance further you need heroes, in other terms if you lose all your heroes you lose, if your core is killed you lose. I really enjoy this game but there are some infuriating mechanics and general hero balance just isn't on point. You will find out who the strong characters are very quickly when playing on the harder difficulty. But why are some heroes so bad? tankyness is about all it comes down to but ontop of that the people who are squishy typically do less than the tanky people unless they're some utlitity focus character or an operator in which case those are very strong in their own different ways, but squishy combat focused heroes? Trash and dead weight. The light mechanic is interesting but for the most part it will screw over your runs when you get unlucky and don't get dust(the currency that gives you light) from the RNG. Dust (light currency) is used to power up rooms, when rooms are powered you can set up turrets and modules that yields you more income on resources. But if you don't have the amount of dust to power rooms its dark and enemies can spawn inside these rooms unless you place a hero you own inside of them. Of all the balance designs they came up with they decided to make dust (the most game making or breaking resource) nearly 100% RNG with the only way to reliably light up rooms requires a massive amount of the resource "economy". Despite my dislike over some mechanics and the general balance of the game I still recommend this game but if you are looking for a tower defence like the ones you would find off of armor games this is next to nothing like those.
