I don't like puzzle games in general because they're either too easy, or are pure pixel hunt, or involve "guessing what the developer wants you to do." But this game is different. This game feels like real world design challenges. This game feels like a combination of programming, proving geometric statements and (just a little bit, despite of its name) chemistry.
This game's logic works like this: you have two loops running at the same time, each can carry out certain commands in their courses; your task is to time those commands so that they do the right thing at the right time, and in the end find a way to synchronize the two loops so that they can loop back to their oriignal starting point and the whole process resets. You have limited space to place your commands so you have to really think hard where you place them (like the steric hinderance effect in real world chemistry synthesis).
Overall, a really, really fun, thought-provoking game.

Unbeliavably fun! This game has amazing controls, fluid and responsive, they feel very natural and intuitive. It has a great double-jump mechanic that allows for some very precise movements and sometimes even ridiculous maneuvers, giving you a lot of flexibility in how you go through each stage. Also the killing animations are really bloody and fun, with some variation in how you can choose to deal with each enemy (from behind, from a distance, from up in the air or through dashing. All equally fun!)
The game emphasizes speed and you're urged to clear the stage as fast as you can, which makes the game challenging but exciting. There's something very satisfying about killing enemies while dashing, throwing shuriken before the sniper has time to shoot, and nailing a complicated jumping sequence one after the other. It really makes you feel like a ninja!
It also has a good amount of content with 7 worlds (around 5-7 stages each) and a simple story told in beautiful comicbook-like graphics. Another thing I appreciated is how in higher difficluties it's not just the enemies that become harder, but the stage itself changes subtly, so the game always feels fresh. Plus there's a TON of collectibles to explore and find.
All in all if you're a fan of platformers then this is definitely worth buying!

Over the last 15 years, I've logged at least 1,000 hours in this game. Initially, when I first played it back in 2001, I didn't know any strategies, secrets, tactics, hints, guides, or helpful advice existed. I just played and got my squads wrecked, over and over again. But, I kept playing. It was that good! Ten years later, I played it again, because I learned about the strategy guides which exist now. The game was even more exciting, because I could control the battles. Again I played in 2014, refreshing my experience and reliving the plight of X-Com. Anyway, down to the details.
The graphics, by today's standards, are cheesy, super-pixelated and difficult to interpret (at times). Even cheesier is the quality of music/sound effects. However, the sound is probably the single-most definitive characteristic in the game. The ominous sound effects severely impact the immersion in the battle. Without realizing it, I get sucked into the tension, because of the ominous pulsating background noise. Finally, the turn-based battlescape strategy style which beckons for perfection. Master strategists would struggle to survive some of those battles. One word: Sectopods.
TLDR: Sci-Fi themed, turn-based strategy (with a side of Real-time Spaceship chase scenarios), in-depth immersion.
P.S. - If you can't beat em, get a bigger Blaster Launcher.

I've been keeping an ear to the ground with this game since its intital release. At full price a mulitplayer only game with hardly a handful of hunters and even less for monsters seemed like a massive mistake by the production company. However the winter sale price of $13.59 the game is a bargain. For only a couple dollars more you can Season One pass and that's what I ended up buying since it's a great price for what you get.
Now that the price became reasonable I was worried about the lack of games being played due to all the hate generated from the games pricing. When I bought the game it was at a steady 400 gamers in the U.S. server. Currently it's be sitting well over 1000+ this winter sale. The game feels very much alive from my neck of the world.
So now it comes down to gameplay. Was it fun? How much replayability? Well this game is fantastic for a few reasons. For starters the monster/hunter unique gameplay is different and fun. The game does have its learning curve so don't expect to be good in your first preliminary ranked matches. The challenge can be rewarding and infuriating due to the current ranking system being subpar to most highly competitive games. But if you have a group of friends who are interested in this game, I think you will find a wonderful home in Evolve. This game was meant for the team play. All you lone wolf types don't fret, there's something really special for you too. Playing as the monster. You only get a few monsters from the base game but focusing on one of them at a time and learning its ability and the rest of the game mechanics will only make you a better monster player which the hunters depend on for a challenge.
So this game is a bargain at $13.59 winter sale. I would even say it's even a bargain at $20 just for the base game. Heck, even $35 would be just about right. You don't have to buy any of the DLC, it's mostly cosmetic anyway except for the Season One and Two for the different hunters. The very first hunters and monsters are the most used anyway. The additional ones are just to maker things different and more interesting but certain isn't a requirement to get the most out of the game.
I hope this has helped. Feel free to ask me any questions. I got about 24 hours of playtime in the game. It really feels like two different games.

I cannot find the proper words to adequately explain how disappointed I am in this game. I'm not sure I could present a unique enough opinion to paint you the proper picture. Plenty of other reviewers have talked about almost everything I've observed to be lackluster about Evolve. And I've only played for a grand total of EIGHT FREAKING HOURS, when I ordered the massive pre-order pack that claimed I would have immediate access to a whole bunch of extra DLC stuff.
I can't even get a full 24 hours of enjoyable play time. Heck, it was a painful learning curve for the FIRST hour, after the tutorial, and I'm a veteran gamer. THIS has been one of the most painful things I've ever played. And I played Maple Story. In fact? I think I played Maple Story longer than I've played this. And I gave that up in a week. It's just been unpleasant to play. And I'm supposed to trudge my way up the rankings to earn the extra content that I was promised I'd have immediate access to at launch? #$%& that noise.
Single-player makes the AI ruthless and OP even on it's supposedly 'dumbest' setting. The AI just plays too perfectly. Can't take them head-on. Can't actually ambush them. And forget 'stealth'. The AI seems to know what I'm doing and where I'm at way too precisely for it to be chance, and they're usually in my face inside of a minute even when I'm trying to 'sneak'. And when I'm playing the hunters? How exactly is an ordinary human being supposed to coordinate play between 4 different characters at the same time effectively? I try juggling between them, but as soon as I get one in position and start trying to actually play my role, the previously cycled characters AI wanders off to the other side of the map. It's like herding heavily armed cats. Not to mention the hunters weapons seem to get switched out for BB guns and slingshots when it's my turn with them, and appear to be completely ineffective even when the AI DOES decide it's going to coordinate our efforts. Whereas, when I'm the monster? It takes them roughly 2 minutes, give or take, to turn me into 5 tons of hideous swiss cheese.
And forget online play. It generally took 20 minutes waiting in que to get a party. I thought maybe that would give me something resembling a modestly more even playing field, against my fellow imperfect human beings, so I could maybe start slowly showing improvement. NOPE!
7 times I got matches where I started as the monster. And all 7 times my controls froze up after my first step forward. Just me. Leaving me completely helpless for the hunters to just come right up and take me out with literally no resistance at all. That's right. I would be mobile for one single step. Then nothing.
SEVEN. TIMES. Seven out of seven times. The extent of my attempts at online monster play.
The 7th time? The party must have been a bunch of other new players, because they found me and hesitated. They just stood there and watched me for a full minute before their medic ran up to me and jumped up and down in my face a couple times, then turned his back to me in what could only have been the person taking advantage of what they saw to be a screenshot opportunity, before they all came over and wiped me out once they realized I was completely unresponsive.
And playing in a hunting party? Forget it. When I could actually get a party together, it wouldn't actually stay together. Most times? The party would just fall apart. One person would leave, then the other two would leave, and then the MONSTER player would leave, leaving me alone. Trying to actually communicate with my party didn't help.... WHEN people responded at all. I'm not an elite so, by default, I wasn't worth playing with. Poof. Empty party. This player community has been very VERY uninviting. Other times? The party would disperse and bail the first time someone got floored by the monster.
As for skill balancing? I'm not sure it actually exists, and I'm not sure I'd recognize it in action if I saw it because I haven't had a decent enough play experience from which to judge my OWN abilities, let alone anyone elses. I just know that the AI kicks my butt way too fast and way too easily for it to say anything good about my skill in this game. It's just discouraging. I always felt very little incentive to try again, and less with each defeat. Even earning the incrimental pittance of XP or mastery at the bare minimum that would eventually guarantee me to SLOWLY rank up and unlock my supposedly immediately accessed extra contant wasn't encouraging enough to make me want to continue the uncomfortable slog through this deceptively disappointing game.
I don't know what this game is anymore. I have a loose idea of what it was SUPPOSED to be when I started following it after the initial announcement of it's development. I know what i was HOPING it would be as we grew closer and closer to launch, and I grew more and more excited about it's release.
And I knew I flat out blew a hundred bucks out of my ear on the big reserve edition, after discovering what a steaming pile of disappointment it turned out to be. Everything I've read about it from game journalists who weren't potentially paid off for good reviews, and from peers I've talked to about their own time in Evolve, has led me to one very intense and disheartening conclusion. A conclusion that I hope you, the reader, can take a lesson from. And that lesson is this:
I made a VERY expensive mistake buying Evolve. I got excited, I got my hopes up, and I got hyped. And it cost me.
It's a shame, though. Shear is fabulous and beautifully rendered. It's a delightfully alien world, with gorgeously foreboding environments and maps. It is a harsh, unforgiving, nightmarish world and it looks amazing. It's too bad that I've experienced enough reasons with the game to feel genuinely screwed over.
Make your own decisions, based off of your own experience from your own research. These are just MY opinions. Read MORE of the reviews for this game, from OTHER folks who have their own opinions and objective views as well. Decide for yourself. But I'm going to warn you, one more time.
Stay away from Evolve.

I don't believe I've ever reviewed a game on Steam, if so it's a rare occurance.  The Long Dark however deserves my utmost praise.
I've hardly touched the story, from what I can tell you probably shouldn't either, but boy is the sandbox good.  It's what I wanted in a survival game.  It's hard to put my experience in words, but in short it's possibly the most engaging experience I've ever had with any form of entertainment.  Every moment could be your last, and when you're dead that's it.  Game over, your character lived X number of days (or your session of 50 hours has come to an end)  Because of this you will try your best to ensure that doesn't happen.
I'll try to wrap this up in a couple of moments that I've experienced so far that had me feel the need to come write this review.
Mushrooms.  There is a type of mushroom that grows on tree stumps that you can make a tea out of that helps you recover from injuries faster and while fresh, keeps you warm for a period of time.  I hadn't created this tea for my first 20 hours of being in this world.  If I got injured I turned to pain killers, it's what made sense to me as someone who has lived in the civilized world.  So that's what I looked for.  I tried to hold onto the old world that was dying off.  I as a person would have tried to turn to a manmade remedy to a problem the game wants you to find a natural way to solve, because eventually you're going to have a hard time finding the man made solution to your issues.  The game doesn't just come up with a lore as a way to introduce you to the game mechanics, the way you experience those mechanics over time sell you that lore as fact throughout the game.
The second moment I had was with a wolf.  I'm no longer terrified of the creatures, I fear them yes, but out of respect. (Just because you get geared up as time goes on doesn't mean a wolf or pack won't take advantage of your mistakes) The wolves in TLD are rather inteligent in most cases.  They can see, smell, and hear you if you give them the chance.  I always tend to have a bit of meat on me as well as tools that clang together on my back so I tend to attract wolves from a distance.  Typically they go into a stalker mode where they follow you and wait for an oppurtunity to strike.  I try as much as possible to avoid a fight.  If I cant outwalk them, I'll put down some meat to keep them occupied while I get some distance between us.
So onto my story. A couple wolves had started following me on my treck to a forge to do some metal work.  I put some guts on the ground and one of the wolves took it and left.  The other one kep in pursuit.  I put down another string of guts in order to appease him.  It did not.  I kept moving and tried once more, he ignored those guts too and was getting ever closer.  I looked to where I was going and back to him following me.  I knew I was close to my cave where I cure deer hides so I lit a flare as a warnng that he should stay back.  Wolves typically fear fire and excessively loud noises.  This wolf didn't seem too scared of my flare.  I back into the cave and toss the flare at the entrance, drawing my gun.  "Don't do this.  Don't step over that flare."  I only have two bullets left in my rifle and they're not common, I find possibly one a week.  "Don't make me kill you. I don't need to kill you."  The wolf steps over the flare, I aim down my sights, he charges, I fire.  The wolf lets out a cry and falls to the ground inches from my feet.  I curse the wolf, "God damn it! Why did you make me kill you?!" I was literally angry in real life that this wolf had made me use a bullet that I felt didn't need to be used.  He could've walked away and lived a life chasing deer.  But instead he had to come at me and make me waste such a valuable item (For killing bears which are a significantly larger threat and harder to trick into leaving you alone).
Those two moments amongst many others have made this sandbox experience feel like a second life I get to visit from time to time.  It's great, go have some moments of your own in the world Hinterland has made.
Love this game ... well worth the money !!!

I have never played such a non-entity of a game before. Sure, there have been games that made me think certain developers should be legally withheld from making more games, but this, this makes me question the very core essence of a programs existence. It's not so much "how?" it was made, but "why?" it was made. As in, why do I have to install this? Why isn't this just part of Steam as a feature? Or more accurately, why isn't this a free flash game on the internet? Oh wait, it is. In various fashions.
What this game does isn't very unique. Typing and word learning games have been around maybe since they've had visual GUIs and an ability to input text in a computer (and earlier before that with things like Scrabble). Their biggest strides came in the 90's with Mavis Beacon, JumpStart Typing and even Mario himself.
Then people got bored with just mastering their WPMs, and thankfully SEGA fixed that with Typing of the Dead. As they realised there needs to be more of a goal to achieve, and thanks to TOTD, plenty of others have actually tried to be more edutainment rather than just stiff educational tools. They actually offer something, and if not some kind of engaging single player challenge, they have multiplayer, like Words with Friends.
Ace of Words on the other hand, has done nothing to further the cause of mastery of the english language. It's by no means a regression, but trying to think of what this game actually does well enough to be considered a game worth playing... well, there is none. You just... turn it on, play it for 90 seconds and then you're done. Maybe you try it once more, but climbing the leaderboard just isn't enough. There's no progression at all here. It doesn't even attempt to teach you new words.
This is one of the most forgettable games in my library, and what you see is what you get. I can't imagine that there are people clamoring for something so no frills, so lacking in personality, as there are so many more games that would be better to play that actually get you involved.
Better word games on Steam:
A pseudo RPG where you learn new words and relearn the definitions of old ones. Collect gems and buy better weapons to make your words hurt more. Really fun progression system.
What better way to test your WPMs than when the only way to survive is to go faster? Must go faster.
An oldie, but a goodie. Only problem is that they lack modern Steam support/features like the cloud or achievements. Still really quality titles.
This game just gives me an air of people that just didn't try hard enough. Like, just because it was a game about words, they only had to put in the minimal effort. They wanted to remain in their little box and tried to be as inoffensive as possible and be as uncreative as they could, and write it off as "Oh, it's just for some lame educational game! I don't REALLY have to try!". To me, a game being as inoffensive as possible is just as offensive as the worst games ever made. This game is as cynical as they come, and it doesn't even have to say a word.
There was a time when something like Ace of Words would have been useful. That time was the late 1980's. Thankfully, we have moved on, and so should you. To better games.

AC:Syn is an excellent addition to the AC family. Having just wrapped things up with IMO the blandest and least polished AC:Unity, AC:Syn was a huge about face.
Combat(5/5): A healty balance of difficult and fun(tougher than AC1,2 and BF and more polished that AC:U) You can tell that the issues from AC:U were fleshed out and polished. Less annoying off-screen attack's; ranged shot indicators were much better and combat felt....FUN, something I felt AC:U was very lacking.  Different weapons allowed freedom of combat style and the boxing ring was quite fun.
Parkuor(4/5): Moving around the city was a healthy balance of quick travel, carriages, ziplining and free-running.  All of these(based on how you played) felt they had their advantages and disadvanges and allowed you to change up your playstyle as you saw fit. Free running is still not perfected, but for a game that allowed you to basically grapple on almost any surface, some hang-ups were expected. Overall very good and only had a few times that were frustrating with magnetic hands.
Story(5/5): Prob one of the best stories I have played for an AC game. The mixing of twins was neat to play to stories, but felt niche rather than needed. It did help to show a bit of character development but wasn't earth shattering or show the same story from different perspectives, just like two seperate stories running parallel.  However interacting with historical figures, unlocking the city and the sheer civilain commentary was spot on and added extensively to the immersive gameplay.
Real world arc(meh): At this point I do prefer the almost cutscene version of the flash forwards as it was always a bit odd with AC2 how they tried to shoe horn it in.  It did finally have some interconnectivity and some clarity to the future story path, esp if you played the WW1 bit(and got to roll around with Churchy!).
Overall an excellent addition to the AC series that could sit equally with AC:BF and our love for Ezio aside, AC2.
Get it and play it, if AC:U turned you sour, try this one on, doubt you'll regret it.

I'm puzzled when I look at reviews that say "Mark Of The Ninja clone" or "Strider 2". These people have obviously never played the other titles or maybe they just idled the game for cards and took a guess based off the screenshots?
This game is a fast paced parkour platformer, it's actually closer to Rayman Origins than anything else. The game's all about how fast you can finish a level and how much of an item you can collect before finishing the level too.
Overall, I found it to be more fun than Mark Of The Ninja but less of an interesting story. It's easy to understand why people would compare this game Mark Of Ninja when they first (since both have that graphic novel vibe) see it but when you actually play it, it's a totally different story.

Its a solid game, although nothing special. Yes the game does play like a watered down version of Mark of the Ninja. The platforming mechanics are good, with double jump and dash working well. The wall jumping can be super finnicky, especially how pressing away when jumping off makes you actually jump less far away than not holding the dirction you're jumping (herp derp). The combat is ok, as sometimes you'll pull of the attack you want and other times you'll dash and it won't hurt someone, or your attack won't hurt them. The levels are pretty linear except sometimes theres a lack of direction and multiple different paths, some of which lead to secrets which you don't need. The checkpoints are generous but sometimes they can be misleading as there will be checkpoints that lead to dead ends. The levels and enemies get pretty repetitive, and there isn't much atmosphere or novelty to each level. Most of the time you are racing against a clock and so I just avoided enemies and jumped over them, which makes this more of a speedrun game than anything. The story has the most obvious unoriginal plot twist ever, and most of the time the characters just stand around asking riddles and questions, making random 1 liners about wisdom that don't actually make much sense when you think about them. That being said the platforming is pretty good, and when everything is clicking and you're jumping, dashing, and killing, the game hits it's stride. It's also super short, clocking in around 2 hours for me.
7/10.

I stumbled across Shadow Blade: Reload randomly before it was even out. Already looking quite cool, I noticed that Shadow Blade was on iOS, so I bought it. It had me so hooked, I instantly bought the Android version and simul-played it using Bluestacks. Later on, I completed both of them once again on newer hardware, and even the free version of the game called Shadow Blade Zero (Android). Bought this Steam release in early access and then bought it again on iOS and have 100% completed both. But why?
This game is kind of like the love child of Strider 2 and Shinobi 3D. It's fast paced, focuses on platforming and minimal effort put into actual combat (you are required to end enemies ASAP). All of it is done extremely well, from the well made level design to the careful enemy placement. Everything just clicks.
It also controls like a charm. Kuro is easy to handle, he can double jump, dash in air, use several different ways to attack, wall kicks when needed and puts many other ninja video game characters to shame.
The music is catchy, but nothing to write home about. Ever now and then I catch myself humming some of the better tracks, but it could be better.
The game is not perfect, every version of it (even the originals) has collision problems, stuff ending rather abruptly, enemies glitching up or spawning at incorrect places. Sometimes it can get frustrating. I don't care.
I don't care because I REALLY, REALLY loved this game. There's no perfect video game but as long as most of the game clicks together as in Shadow Blade: Reload, I will enjoy it. Can I recommend it? Hell yeah, it's easily one of the best ninja games out there and if you like those, or are into retro games, this will surely satisfy your needs.
It will last a while too. The game has three difficulty modes all with altered level designs and enemy placements, a challenge mode that offered some of the best thrills I've experienced in recent years (gaming-wise) and even a stage creation tool that also has the ability to upload it to the masses easily.
I get it, this isn't really a review and it certainly doesn't help that I'm raving over this game. But look at that trailer. If you think the game looks cool even just a little bit, you should probably buy it. I doubt it'll disappoint.
Still, I feel like this game was made for me. I have no other way to explain why I love it so much. It just clicks with me. Thanks for the awesome work, devs.

I wish I could give Kholat a glowing recommendation, but I can't. The story, visuals, voice acting, and map/compass navigation are actually quite good. But I was forced to reload the game, after becoming stuck, at least a dozen times. Why? Because the developers made the bone-headed decision to not include the ability to JUMP in a FIRST PERSON game.

I was also forced to suicide a number of times after walking near a cliff edge and not being able to return, due to a two or three inch tall ledge (or branch, or pile of snow, etc) that I couldn't navigate over. If you like conspiracy theories then you are probably familiar with the Dyatlov Pass incident. This is the story of 9 hikers who went missing in the Ural Mountains roughly 60 years ago. It is a mysterious story since all the trekkers were experts so one can only wonder why they disappeared and the cause of deaths was also strange for several people, for instance, one had her tongue missing, the other guy had a fractured skull and some bodies were irradiated.
In any case, if you purchase Kholat you can retrace the steps of these people in the mountains. The title refers to the very slope the students set up camp and where disaster, eventually, struck. The game was developed by a Polish developer company and, interestingly, the narrator throughout the game is Sean Bean (no, he does not die).
First of all, what you notice is how stunningly good the game looks. The snowflakes blown by the wind, the fire near every camp you find, the small pools you step into in the labyrinthine passages of caves and pretty much everything was done in a meticulous way thanks to the 4th iteration of the Unreal engine.
This is a walking simulator. As such, it can be completed in 4-5 hours and the emphasis is on the story immersion. You have no weapons just a compass and a map with you and in case you encounter enemies your best bet is to run away immediately. The game is divided up into 3 acts but the first and last are very linear and short; the core gameplay elements you'll encounter only in act 2.
I liked the game's atmosphere. You'd think all you see is snow and that you'll probably get bored after a while. Quite the contrary: as you walk down and enter the barely lit forest the atmosphere of the game becomes even more haunting. Up there on the slopes while you are carefully watching your steps you notice the skull-like shape of the mountains on the opposite side. Ever played Metro 2033? The howling sound you occasionally hear is similar to that of the Nosalises.
The downside of the game is the plot itself. While there are many reports, journal pages and articles scattered around getting them all is a chore and of course it is difficult to put together all pieces to find out what really happened to these people. And the ending does not help much. I'm not saying I do not like to reflect; but perhaps it's best to surf the internet to find out what ideas people came up with.

Kholat roots its horror in the feeling of being lost. Most video games out there conveniently provide you with a map that shows you where you are as if you were a walking GPS. Not this time.
In Kholat, you have a map and a compass. That's it. You will struggle to find clues about your location so you can determine what to do next. You will walk around with an eye on your compass and start doubting about whether or not you walked long enough before making that turn.
The Ural mountains are windy and hostile and the sun never comes up. Your perception of depth is diminished by the surnatural perpetual overcast twilight. You can still see where you are going without a flashlight, but the trees are dark and the shadows drive you crazy.
Storytelling is not really good. I had to read a lot about the story itself on the Internet to make sense of it all. Yes, Kholat is based on real events that occurred in Russia in 1959. The game is built around the same concept of "pages" lying around as in the original Slender Man game. After a while I stopped reading the pages because it was boring to listen to them. The voice acting was okay, I guess it's just because I don't like being drop-fed tiny pieces at a time. I think the pages could have been replaced with visions (or cutscenes) and been much more satisfactory.
There is also a monster lurking around and I appreciated the fact it wasn't necessarily always hunting us down. It appeared only surrounding areas of interest as a means of elevating our awareness. It did catch me a few times, but I think it was fine and wouldn't change it.
Overall, I liked this horror game and would recommend trying it as it was successful in creating a true psychological horror atmosphere where the player becomes afraid of his own imagination.

The first impression that SpaceChem imposes on it's audience is one of boredom. Complex gameplay mechanics, insufficient instructions and a non-illustrated storyline (which looked like it attained quite some inspiration from a generic fanfic) is enough to bore even the most patient gamer. But behind all that, you can leave your fast-paced FPSes behind and take SpaceChem with an open mind, it's actually a rather interesting game once you scrape the surface and get to the inner layers. To be fair, I still don't quite get some of the in-game mechanics, and I'm starting to struggle on the second planet, but that's the purpose of a puzzle game. If a puzzle game is simple, it's not a puzzle game; it's a test to check your sanity.
But anyways, this game may seem uninteresting and even dreadful at times, but it's honestly a well-thought out puzzle game that simply doesn't have enough shine on its surface to keep players on the game for more than 10 minutes. If you can dig past that dull surface and get into the heart of the game where the creative thinking comes alive, this game is certainly worth the time and effort.

Why haven't you played SpaceChem? Probably because you are intimidated by the trailer and think it's too complicated, or because you didn't know it exists. Well, this game does exist, and now you don't have an excuse anymore to not at least try the free demo.
SpaceChem is one of the best puzzle games I've ever played. It uses fake chemistry only as a backdrop for its puzzle mechanics. So don't worry, you don't need to know anything about chemistry in order to play this game. Your job is to design machines that transform a given input into a required output. For example, the game gives you single hydrogen atoms and demands hydrogen molecules (two hydrogen atoms bonded to each other). You can then use functions like grab, drop, input, output, bond, etc. to create a machine that automatically turns hydrogen atoms into hydrogen molecues. How you do this exactly is up to you. It can be very satisfying to watch your solution run, because it is YOUR OWN creation. You are not simply following a strict path the puzzle designer wanted you to take. And after each completed puzzle, a graph will show you how efficient your solution is compared to others, giving you extra incentive to make your solution work just a little bit faster or use less functions.
As you progress, more functions will be available like fusion or flip-flop switches, allowing you to create even more complex machines. Some levels let you link several machines together, so the output of one machine can be used as an input for another machine. The last couple of worlds are very challenging, but even if you give up there, you'll get your money's worth. And if the campaign isn't enough for you, there are still tons of user created puzzles to solve and challenges to master.
If you like puzzle games, or if you like programming, buy this game now! If you are uncertain, play the demo. It's pretty long and gives you a good look into the game. For some people the demo might even be enough.

Background: I do not have much background in Rogue-Like Adventures.
Replayability: By the very definition of a Rogue-Like game, It has immense replayability. There is a cast of unlockable characters and different game modes (Pods) available to challenge the player in unique ways. Each character brings its own set of abilities that are solo and Party based on timers or are Passive (100% uptime).
Combat Mechanics: Combat is automatic for the most part. You move into a room, your characters auto attack. The control you have as a player is the use of special abilities, healing, and movement from room to room.  Characters are assisted by room defenses the player can build.
Social Frustrations...: I normally put Mechanics here but so... man okay the characters you unlock between floors have conversations that give you a glimpse into their Lore. Sometimes though some characters do not get along and will literally kill each other between floors. It is a minor inconvenience on early floors but when it happens on the last floor its just frustrating. Not game breaking, just...Ugh!
Final Thoughts: DotE is a vibrant pixel based Rogue-Like Dungeon Crawler with some RPG elements and quick reaction gameplay make it a great and cheap addition to anyone's game list.

To me this game is a bit of a mix of Minecraft and Age of Empires.  There is some exploring, mining, crafting, and building.  There is some element of RTS when enemies appear.   And character leveling!  Yay!
As an alpha game for almost $25, I was holding off buying this for a while.  I'm pleased to say I'm really enjoying the game.  Although it is alpha, what you receive feels like a finished, well polished game, and it seems the devs are regularly adding to it  :)
I like that large areas of the map can be set for mining or resource gathering, and your workers will get to work while you go manage other parts of your town.  There is not a lot of exploring, each seed map has boundaries, put it's still worth looking around regularly because some enemies with nice loot will spawn, and if you don't go out and attack them, they eventually disappear.
Characters attributes are handled well, and adds gameplay depth as you assign jobs to create the most effecient and well defended town.  At this point, character leveling is a bit shallow, but from my understanding they recently added new jobs and classes, so hopefully this will continue to be developed.
As far as enemies, they start out pretty easy, attacking a bit randomly.  As you progress through the game, certain conditions must be met before harder enemies appear.
The game also has a building editor that is pretty easy to use.  I designed workshops for each of my working classes that are each a little different.  There are also a few default buildings if you're not into designing.
And an honorable mention for the game's composer.  The music in this game is top notch.
So far, the only thing I don't like is that in the building editor, there is no way to delete blocks directly.  So, for example, if you make a 2nd storey floor by clicking-and-dragging to make a 10x10 floor, then keep building, then realize you need a hole in the floor for the stairwell, you can't simply delete a few blocks from the floor.  You have to hit "undo", destroying all the building you did, until you get back to undo the floor.

Before Alpha 16 Stonehearth, while interesting, was a barebone system. Now it's a game, and with the new hard mode it's challenging exactly how you want it to be. With multiple military classes and new difficult enemies able to break through your doors you get yourself dragged into the turmoil of battles trying to keep your little sandbox settlement safe.
What games does Stonehearth resemble? Suddenly, Dungeon Keeper. There is no dungeon, yes. But the same "indirect control" and "build your town" principle is still here, and voxel retro graphics gives you the right nostalgic vibe.
Thanks to Stonehearth I have discovered Discourse - a free and open-source web 2.0 engine SH forums are built upon.
Thanks to Stonehearth I got myself deeply interested in voxel graphics. And finally installed Blender.
This game is built with love. But more than that, it is built with extreme mod-friendliness in mind, that, I won't fear to say, I've never seen before. Information is in an easy readable format. For every task, there is a free software available. If there is a downside, it's that skilled programmers are yet to turn their attention to the game.
For those who like looking at a pros/cons list (I'm one of those types), here's one.
+ Already playable and very enjoyable
+ Watch and influence development through Discourse forums, Twitch streams and Trello feature lists (with voting for feature priority)
+ Easily moddable (including translations, many are already available - check the forums)
+ Quite playable without any mods (unlike that dragon-slaying bestseller RPG)
+ Nice, if somewhat simple, 16-bit stylized voxel graphics
+ Create building templates, then share them (or not)
+ Nice music
+ Active development (unlike some other titles, Stonehearth is an example of an Early Access
)
+ Responsive dev team (weekly streams and short DT videos every tuesday about upcoming features or challenges)
+ Rabbits
- Bugs
Be ready for them. This is, after all, an alpha. While there is backward save compatibility now, I recommend starting a new game with every new major Alpha release. Some bugs have workarounds. Sift the forums. Stick to stable builds if you don't want to risk and make in-depth testing. Report bugs to the forums.
- Lacking pathing and priority
The cause of unfinished buildings in 80% cases is that hearthlings can't get to the next queued block with current scaffolding. Try building more ladders manually. It gets better with every major alpha, but still has issues. This system is currently having a major overhaul, expected to be rolled out around two alphas from now.
- The price is arguably a bit too high
I'd like to mention separately some things that are planned, but
:
- No water physics (latest alpha somewhat addresses that but the model is still very basic)
- No weather effects/seasons
- Some classes are missing (namely Magmasmith and Geomancer - yes, you will be able not only do digging, but raise mountains as well). Engineer is already there though.
- No multiplayer (it's late in the dev queue). I'm amazed how playable the game is
. Although latest videos showcase some very early cncepts of coop.
- Diversity of items is comparatively poor. Will be fixed, but the eyes of the devs' right now remain on gameplay (which is, in my opinion, totally justified). So no Cthulhu... yet. Can be somewhat fixed with mods (but still no Cthulhu).
- Building mode is still limited and lacking (gets better with every major Alpha, major overhaul expected)
- The number of biomes is currently limited to 2 (will be more). You can try fan-made ones.
- The number of playable races is currently limited to 2 (will be 3 or so)
You may think the review is full of flattery. Your right. Make your research, see for yourself. All and all, with no revolutionary things in the box, Stonehearth can still be your heartwarming casual pleasure. The source of modding frenzy. Or both.
The choice is yours.

What can I say?  The Baldur's Gate experience now 'enhanced' with added companions and quests, classes, weapons/weapon specialisations and too many other knick knacks to mention.
For some people this is a welcome thing, for purists though maybe not so much.
I first played Baldur's Gate a year or so after it's original release (1998) and was overwhelmed by the freedom of exploration and depth that was on offer.  Thats not to say the original was an overly complex game but it certainly requires an attention span to understand the second edition D&D rules and how the stats play with your character and companions you may acquire on the way.
This edition takes the original and augments it with some of the features I mentioned above but also changes some things which I feel are for the worse such as the cutscenes and some useless companions, but these are minor quibbles.  The combat is just as satisfying, the story just as good (yes I liked it, despite criticism from others) and Minsc's dialogue will never get old.
For purists I recommend NOT purchasing this.  Heading over to a certain site that specialises in games that are old and good to purchase the original and then installing the various mods that improve the base game and having a blast that way is the way to go.
For everyone else who wants the new and (arguably) improved Baldur's Gate experience then this is the purchase for you.
In short - the good:
*Compelling story
*Interesting companions
*Satisfying gameplay and dialogue
*Sense of wonder and exploration is still there
*Now playable across different operating systems
The bad:
*Some new additions lacking and not so fun
*New cutscenes aren’t so great
The ugly:
*NO CLOUD SAVE - WHY CAN’T YOU DO THIS.  This can be bypassed with dropbox but if you’re going to allow the saves to work across several devices and operating systems then this should really be there.  Beamdog have stated that save games for EE are compatible across OSX/Windows so it makes no sense not to enable it at least for steam users.

My favorite game ever.  The (pioneering) combination of tactical combat, with strategic base management, makes the game very non-linear.  I originally played this back before FAQs and Strategy Guides, so learning the research tree by trial and error was quite facinating.  The 2012 remake was a faithful remake, but this is the one that I will always come back to.  You as a player have to remember all the trivial aspects, such as remembering to save time for returning your soldiers to cover, crouching, and having time for overwatch.  Your soldiers have a high mortality rate, but (while alive) they have many individual statistics and personal growth.  It is easy to get familiar with a character, just to watch the character die in a later mission.

I've been playing X-COM since I was six years old, and watching my father play a few years younger.  I can't really just call it a game to me.  It's basically my life.
X-COM is not a game that has aged well, in terms of UI, aesthetics, and bugginess.  You are not about to love it for its polish, where the alien grenades look like jelly-filled doughnuts.  You are not about to love it for intuitive controls, it will feel like learning a new language without a dictionary.   However, this game has implanted a long-lasting and recently rekindled legacy in Western strategy games that rivals the influence of the 4X and the East's "Tactics" genres.
Even if you don't enjoy it, an extremely remote possibility, it is still worth trying out if only to solidify one's claim as a Strategy game enthusiast.

Ninjas, always hiding in the shadows, roofs, backroom, and other such shady places waiting for a chance to slit our throat then be gone in the darkness with no one none the wiser. Yeah Shadow Blade: Reload isn't one of those ninja games. As Kuro the black hooded ninja you carve a path of bloody rampage as you jump, slide, dash, and slash your way through a bunch of very short and pretty hard levels [but ultimately satisfying] in his quest to do stuff.
Yes that means no sneaking or whatsoever as you just run and avoid all the obstacles while raking up points for ratings and get to the end While playing through several themed world [that all share the same pool of enemy]. Anyways... review anyone?
You get those little *squick* noises as you stab and slice into the enemy, some beeping and shooting noises, and grunts for the SFX which isnt too bad really.
Music only  serves as ambient noises but it never gets in the way until it forces you to mute it and put on some other tunes. In fact it's pretty relaxing listening to it as you restart over and over again dying.
It's alright, nothing too fancy a little 3D here and there and at least the locale for the world changes for each of them. A shame the enemies don't even have a palette swap but hey I argue for gameplay purposes you want to be able to tell the enemy at a glance. Overall it's fine.
The game ran at 60 fps nearly all the time but there are dips here and there especially when part of the scenery contains an outdoor tile, those usually run my fps down by 20-25 down to 40. Testing with an Intel HD4000 yields playable framerate although dippings are far more noticeable with it.
Option menu is lacking to say the least, you get some audio options, SOME graphical options with some of them might help with your FPS if you're having issues such as resolution, AA, some other things. Overall it could be better but at least it does give you some leeway.
Controls, to preface I did not play the game at all the keyboard, sure you can rebind but god help me because this is a platformer game so you pretty much would want a controller for those precise controls, not that you can't play with a keyboard of course especially if you prefer it that way. At least the keys are rebindable. For controllers you might encounter a weird issue where the button on screen don't correspond to the buttons you actually need to press. But the controllers input are pretty solid other than the ledge grab being a bit too sticky at times.
Is pretty simplistic as far as platformer games go. There's no upgrade, no new weapon unlocks and all those other stuff. Instead immediately following the tutorial you get all the tools you need to pretty much finish the whole game with.
You have the dash, the jump, the double the jump, the sword, the shuriken and pretty much that is it. Kuro only has 1 life and if you get hit or anything you will have to restart back at the checkpoint with a point penalties.
Levels have you using all of these arsenals of yours to get from point A to point B without dying [too much] and along the way clicking buttons, stepping on pressure plates, dodging spikes in this improbable landscape architecture. Strewed throughout the levels in hard to reach places are kanji letters [that is Japanese letters for you folks] and orbs that gives a boost to your score. These serves no purpose besides grading you so if you prefer to just immediately run to the exit like what I did you are free to do that. Although the D can be a bit insulting. Replaying the level in higher difficulty not only changes enemy amount and placement but also adds more traps to the levels!
Enemies come in a few easily discernable form with some of them being immune to only a specific types of attack while others are pretty free kill. The homing enemy however can get a bit annoying since the homing capability they have on them last a while and they lock on hard to you. But once you do get to know all these fine gents you can easily counter them even when they come in packs of 2 and 3.
Levels come in 7 worlds with each world having between 5-7 levels each.
Overall that's how the game plays, get to the end of the level, kill enemies, collect points, and not die.
Conclusion? I like this game a bit. The story wraps up nicely while using pretty cool looking comic artstyles for the presentation and at least it's coherent and has an ending that ties everything up. The controls are tight and there's hardly any bugs for the times I played it and for $15 for a 2-3 hours worth of entertainment of slicing and dashing you decide whether its worth for you. Hey if you're a cheapo you can always get it on sale.

Ace of Words is pretty bad. It's a simple word jumble game, where players get a series of random letters and have to make words from them. The only impressive thing about this game is how it managed to screw this up, even with so simple and unoriginal a premise. Its dictionary is full of names, proper nouns, acronyms, and three-letter prefixes, but some words like "True," which are actually...well...WORDS are nowhere to be found. I could tolerate this but for the fact that you need to guess a ridiculous number of words in order to move on to the next puzzle and keep playing. Pair the time limit with a game that expects you to come up with fistfuls of fictional words and you have a recipe for frustration. For some reason this game has been in Early Access for months, so there's still time for these issues to be resolved. As things are now, however, this is a hard one to recommend.

Ace of Words is a decidedly average spelling game. There's very little to the game, simply unscrambling words with different letters on each level. It's only early access so possibly more stuff will be added (apparently multiplayer is planned), but for now the dictionary is really lackluster (bot and bots don't work). There was one instance where I had to type "tie" 3 times before it registered, It wasn't spelled wrong or anything, it just refused to accept it. The game seems to not register keys fast enough if you type too quickly and will just leave out letters that you pressed. All this kind of stuff makes or breaks a spelling game, and there are simply just better games out there if that's what you want. Play Letter Quest instead.

Definitely "Early Access". The dictionary is horrible and that in combination with the slooooooooooooooooooooooooooooow keystroke recognition makes this game next to unplayable right now. Oh, and as a bonus, the message bar which tells you if the word was accepted or not updates too slow. So you might be seeing "word not in dictionary" for that one misstype you made 17 words ago.
Also, the music is no peach. But that's not really an issue. ;)
At this point, I would not recommend this to anyone. However, this has the potential to turn into a nice, simple boredom killer. That is, unless they go and add a bunch of modes and options and extras and stuff like so often is the case. We'll see.

10/10 The Long Dark delivers expertly on the type of game it is trying to be. Both amazingly beautiful yet with a creeping horror to it. The dark nights can be especially terrifying. I have played The Long Dark for over 75 hours now and I start playing before coastal highway was even a thing. I am so happy to see what it has grown into today and after finishing the first chapter of the new long awaited story mode titled 'WIntermute' I just had to make sure people know about this game.
The cold, your biggest enemy and forever your provider of water as long as you have the wood to burn. The long dark is a very different kind of survival game compared to others out there as it pits you more against nature rather than fantasy elements such as zombies from DAYZ or cannibals in The Forest, I could go on. Instead it acts solely on what man is capable of and what one can realistically accomplish.
The game mechanics are polished so well that I beileve they are some of the best I have ever seen. No other survival game does mechanics such as cold, inventory encumberance, illness (especially afflictions) and shooting whether it be rifle, rock or arrow. The interface as well is very new user friendly being simplistic and easily identifiable. If I had to be honest though it looks like the developers are getting ready for a console port? News to me if thats actually happening.
I wish the developers all the best and anyone willing to jump into this immense game. I will definitely be looking to more of their games in the future.

OVERALL:
This is not a hack and slash game, but definitely a game which rewards exploring and planning, weighing risk vs reward opportunities, employment of some game theory, and resource management.
This is a definite buy if your looking for a survival game without zombies, or mindless shooting. You choose to play for 30 minutes or 4 hour settings without feeling that you are missing on parts of the game.
PROS:
1)The music is incredibility powerful, and appropriate which is a real rarity in games. The world is wonderfully rendered in from a limited palette. This is definitely a game where you take screenshots for the beauty of the landscape.
2)The mechanics of the game are fairly deep and provide a semi-realistic outcome to how the real world exists. For example: It is generally colder in the morning than in the evening.
3)Sandbox and challenge modes are where most of the players time will be spent. The sandbox mode really shines in immersing a player within the world of The Long Dark.
CON:
1) The storytelling is fairly average, while there is a tutorial feeling through episode 1 and episode 2, you can do some deviating by exploring or completing side quests.

I really wasn't impressed with this title. Do you remember all those old point & clicks which were so dumb you basically resorted to clicking around and mixing stuff randomly just to get forward because everything made little sense? If you do, this game is that in a 3D walking-simulator kind of game.
If you look at the store page, you would probably notice that the game is advertised as a humour piece. Well yeah, it kind of is, and while you can get out a chuckle or two out of it, it feels like the writers were told to make literally everything funny. Every flavour text, every line of dialogue is a weird attempt at trying to be funny. At the end of it all I was just rolling my eyes, because it was all just so dumb and not funny anymore. There is a thing called trying too much you know...
Graphically the game was... well, okay I guess? The textures seem kind of low rez, but the game is consistent about looking low-rez so there's that. What is bad however is the optimisation. The game stutters a lot, especially in the outdoor areas. There's also a very noticeable pop-in when you are transported between different areas. The game does use UE though, so it's not the engine itself... Or it shouldn't be at any rate.
There game can be a bit buggy sometimes too - I got stuck at least twice. Thankfully the game saves after each action, so you can restart without losing any progress. Still sucks, since the loading screens (thankfully they don't occur during gameplay, just when you first start the session) are fairly long for some reason.
Sound design? Just a bunch of ambient music. Nothing to write home about. Top Secret is a nice song though, I'll give them that.
Overall, there's just too many flaws to ignore, so I can't recommend this game. It's a decent saturday-night-procrastinating-while-also-wondering-about-my-life-choices-up-until-this-point kind of game, but really there are better titles to spend your time on.

As a Londoner playing this game, I was actually really dissapointed.
I went in with a pretty open mind. I know it got bad reviews and all, but I figured that they'd made the buildings to scale and I'd at least get to enjoy climbing some of my local sights. But actually climbing them when they're surrounded by seemingly random, fakey districts and buildings is really underwhelming. I wasn't nitpicking, it just felt pretty boring to climb St Pancras and have it in the middle of.. nothing. And then climb Big Ben and it's just plonked randomly in the middle of pretty much nothing.
Story wise, the game is outright cringe. I've never taken the AC games too seriously, but I actually think they tried to make this one a spoof and just got the tone wrong. The spoiler free storyline is that you play a pair of twins who randomly decide to leave Croydon 'because f*** Croydon' and go to London to start a gang. I genuinely thought it was a British humoured spoof storyline, that was going to be riddled with jokes and dry wit. But then everyone takes is super, super seriously like getting this gang to work is going to affect the fate of the world. And it actually does. The nitwit NPCs you round up in their lime green disgusting uniforms that you can spot sneaking around from the other side of town are legitimately meant to be your solution to saving the whole world.
And that's not even the most cringe bit. You legit 'bump into' Charles Dickens in the street and of course he rounds you up to help him write his book, as you would with every dangerous looking bloke who shoved you out of the way and had knives sticking out of every hole. It's the laziest thing I've ever seen writing wise.
The final piece of the puzzle in bad writing was the ridiculously diverse cast. I mean it's not bad to see a female character lead, it's not bad to see an Indian character playing central stage, it's not even bad to see various cripples and what not have their day. But all together at once and rammed randomly into the story, it's just a really shallow attempt to tick as many boxes as possible.
Gameplay wise, which is the main reason I play these games after the amazing experience of playing Black Flag, the main feature of swapping between the two main characters is utterly useless. You find yourself in a sneaky subtle situation, and think 'aha! I'll swap to the sneaky character now' but you can't swap mid mission. You find yourself in a football hooligan riot and think 'ok, time to play as the brash brawler character' but you can't swap right now. So Sneaky McGee ends up fighting a gang fight, and Brawler Bro ends up clunkily sneaking into somewhere in the dead of night. It just ruins the whole point of it and you feel like the game is a spoof of itself.
The clunky controls and bugs just stop you from ever feeling like an Assassin. You try to sneak round a corner and randomly charge over it. You try to hide behind something and you climb on top of it. You try to assassinate somebody you've somehow snuck up on with your wrist blade and you accidentally shoot someone several blocks away with your noisy pistol.
I hope this review helps you if you're on the fence. I got this game really really cheap on sale, and to be honest I'll keep it for when I want to muck about in a badly drawn London. But if that doesn't sound like your thing then skip this one.

So after playing the game for about four hours I wanted to give my two cents on the game thus far. Looking at my steam library over the years I have been gravitating towards the smaller development teams that focus on content and gameplay over the bigger titles. I believe Stonehearth has the potential to be one the great ones on my list. I've read a lot of reviews and I do tend to agree with some of the negative comments in that it is frustrating that your little town you were pouring into just got an error code and is going to wipe. BUT the fact that there is so much promise (and even content) in Alpha is very promising. The core of the game is very fun, minecraft style building on a larger scope (in that you control multiple people) with more diverse adversity in monsters. It can be simple for those that want the simple experience, and hard for those that want to play it with more strategy. There is something for a wide variety of players in here. Heck even for those that love games like the Sims where they just moderately intervene and enjoy watching the players live their virtual lives. There is a lot of talk about the price of the game and for potential buyers to just wait for a steam sale to pick up this title. While I agree that there may not be enough content (or enough duration of game play without a bug that stops the current game), the quality and fun of the gameplay is there, and please remember that the money does go to the developers that are creating a really unique and fun game. Do I think its necesarrily worth the pricetag in its current alpha stage? No not really. But from what I have played I am confident that it will be worth more that every single penny invested right now in the future.

You must manage village roles (like carpenter, mason, farmer, footsoldier) while still having workers to build buildings and harvest nodes. Traders will come by daily to trade or sell and there are (if playing on normal or hard) monster raids that can happen day or night. Villagers can even mine into the earth and hillsides, though I haven't played with this very much yet. Just remember to have a ladder on hand in case they dig too deep. If you don't have a ladder, you can always have your stuck villagers "mine" steps with the mining single square selection tool.
When villagers die, they drop all their goods and leave behind a tomb stone. It may sound odd, but I can't stress how much I appreciate this simple mechanic. It adds a small pinch of realism to the game, a reminder that a villager existed and it allows me to have a village graveyard.

Ever since I saw the first gameplay trailer of Cuphead at Microsoft’s E3 presentation, I’ve had a calm and restricted excitement with this game and at some times, skepticism . The game was to be a boss rush with a Contra shooting style with the run and gun sections added later on. The 1930’s rubber hose animation has always been aesthetically pleasing to the eye for me and throughout the development of the game, the hand-drawn animations have only gotten better and more amazing to look at. However, style over substance is a balancing act, that most new developers learn the hard way after their first game.
To my surprise, StudioMDHR has exceeded my expectations by delivering beautiful art, along with difficult but fair gameplay. Each boss is a creative new character that they adapt into multiple stages, making every boss feel like the final boss at the end of an epic 2D platformer. And with each boss being so unique and intense, it’s a nervous thrill to see the next stage of the fight or the “A KNOCKOUT!” text go across your screen signalling the boss’s defeat. The anticipation in waiting for a win is tense and exciting and the victory feels rewarding.
The game took me about 12 hours to complete with 284 deaths and throughout my playthrough, I couldn’t find anything that really upset me or that was faulty about the game. And any of the small design choices that I didn’t like would be too nitpicky to include. As far as I can tell, this is a game that you will love, or it just isn’t your style of game. If you’re a gamer that is looking for a different but familiar game that is done with near perfect execution, nothing is better for the price and quality. My game of the year.

Finished the game last night with one survivor. This game has a feel of Dungeon Keeper, an aura of Don't Starve, and a typical underground dungeon RPG romp but in bite size. It is short but sweet. The limited tactic to use would probably fall into having a character that is fast (can run and avoid enemies) and another that is strong (can deal and take big damage). Then just explore with the fast character, open doors, and run back to the room where your strong character is to help combat monsters. Usually that room is where the Crystal is or where the "choke" point is. That is the safest location wherein your heroes can make a stand as monsters passes through that passage way. In levels 10 and below, you will still be able to maximize resource gathering by totally exploring all rooms. But you will not have that chance in higher levels because you'll need to dash for the exit since the monsters will be too strong and too many to face. Focus on building and upgrading just two types of items that will augment your [1] Combat and [2] Defense capabilities. Rarely, you may also upgrade modules that increases Industry, Food, and (much infrequently) Science.  You will usually re-arrange the powered rooms once per level to fit your need to be protected in moving the Crystal to the elevator.
That is all there is to the game. It was fun while it lasted. Also, the Crystal Edition is not really very useful and so you don't need to buy that. I was not able to play components included therein  because I am already satisified finishing the game once. Just get the simple Pixel Edition.

A unique roguelike that skirts the boundaries between tower defense and RTS, with systems and energy management systems that all work together to create a challenging game set in the Endless universe that continues to get expanded with lore and crossover references that make the unvierse feel cohesive and connected even though the games take place eons apart from each other. A squad management systems allows you to recruit new party members as you go and level them up, forcing you to decide between new unlevelled prty members as you find them, and the team you've started the game with and invested points into. You need to carefully balance your team between members thta are good at combat, good at scouting, and good at taking care of the modules and towers you place down to help you when fights get overwhelming.
On top of this, the game sports excellent multiplayer at the expense of taking away the pause function - but with a second or third or fourth set of eyes, you shouldn't need to pause. Right? ... right? (no)
The music and dungeon ambience and aesthetic are fantastic as well, giving the right environment to crawling thorugh all of these old abandoned facilities and parts of the planet as you try to escape, and shutting down everthing but one sepcific route as you try to carry your Crystal through, FF: Crystal Chronicles style lightnig the way, gets incredibly intense and nailbiting. There's also unlockables available about all crew members and monsters to draw you into the world more and learn more about them.
And all of that is just on the basic default space-pod, which has no modifiers that change the way the game works on a basic level. There's more that change how every run works as you unlock them, and an Endless mode to see just how far you can go.

On top of that, the boss fights are not engaging at all, a lot of it is just waiting around for the boss to hit himself or destroy the wall to the next area - if you have this combat system, why not use it in boss fights where enemies can take more than one hit before going down??? In addition to this, you're going to get killed from off the screen a lot, from enemies with rifles, kamikaze bots, and especially homing rockets - honestly, homing rockets are alright in platformers but these last waaay too long. Following the vein of ranged enemies, Iron Fist, and the pink haired enemies have a ranged attack with next to no warning/indication of the direction they're going, why???
Overall, I enjoy the game, it's entertaining, but I often have to set it down because it feels like the enemies in conjunction with the level design is just so random and stacked against me.

At the point of writing I'm through the normal and hardcore modes and about halfway through master.
This game feels... incompetent, but generally well-intentioned. I get the feeling the developer wanted to make a really good platformer, but didn't really know how to go about doing that.
For one, let's look at the basic mechanics. You have a double jump because every game does now. You have a wall jump because every game does now. You have a dash because every game does now. Except these mechanics... don't quite work that well. The double jump is mostly fine save for instances where I ended up jumping the wrong direction (ghosting keyboard may be the cause of this though) but the wall jump is... a thing, it's really easy to detach from the wall instead of wall jumping, which is weird because the walls are also really sticky in this game to the point of annoyance. And then the dash, while fine in itself, doesn't let you perform any jumps after it, which is a massive limitation to the potential of platforming in this game and a baffling design decision.
The combat is really the biggest mechanic issue in this game. Aside from one type of enemy, the downward stab is an end-all in combat. In fact, it's so painful to try and use the combat system normally that I barely did unless absolutely necessary. The goal is always to one-shot enemies, trying to fight with multiple hits never works out well and usually gets you stuck in an enemy's annoyingly long parry animation, which will likely get you killed if any other enemy is in the room. The combat animations are also annoyingly long, though. Even the downward stab takes a bit longer than it really needs to, and the side-attacks are... well. Okay. Am I missing something or does it just randomly choose a different animation for every attack? There's one quick one where you barrel through an enemy, a slower one where you jump over them, an even slower one where you use some grappling thing to pull them towards you, and I feel like there was a fourth one but I'm not sure. But anyways. I can't tell why there's any difference in the animation length, especially because the longer ones will get you killed, often.
And then there's the enemy types. A few of them I really dislike; for one, HOMING MISSILES IN A PLATFORMER ARE ALWAYS BAD. Always. Without exception. This game is not the exception. They're actually especially bad here, the homing is way too strong, they stay around too long, and move too fast. Even worse when there are multiple at once, you're basically already dead at that point. And then, the kamikaze bots. You have one shot to shruiken them before they, most likely, kill you instead. And they move fast. And they attack you from far away. Sure, they're only prevalent in one of the worlds, but that world is probably the absolute worst because of them. The iron fist enemies are also annoying because the only way to kill them is side-attacks, and I had an instance where it refused to give me the tell-tale shine you need to perform a side-attack, causing me to basically become stuck in a level for a few minutes. Until...
...the glitches. Oy vey. Have you ever wanted to randomly phase through a wall simply by jumping against it? Because it's likely to happen. I also had an enemy push me down into the ground once, which is a -special- kind of awful. Aside from that, there are plenty of instances of my downstab outright not working, going right through the enemy, or getting me actually stuck in the ground and unable to move (thus dying to an enemy soon after). It's just impressive how much of this game fails to work on a functional level.
The level design is a mixed bag. Sometimes it works well, sometimes not so well. There are a lot of instances of offscreen enemies (usually the homing missile shooters) just killing you before you have time to react, and a lot of blind jumps or leaps of faith. There's also some confusing nonlinear levels where you have to go around an awkward maze of tunnels to collect everything. A few instances of awkwardly precise jumps, as well; this game isn't really based around precision and it never really feels like you have much in the controls department. There's a decent sense of flow to some levels, but many others lack that smoothness, and the experience in general leaves me feeling a bit dissatisfied. Even on the highest difficulty, the game is never that hard, and the difficulty levels do at least change up the level design somewhat, but rarely in a significant way, so it just feels like I'm playing the same levels again and again.
Oh, and, the bosses are all crap. Total garbage. First boss isn't really a boss, you just run a bit then have it blow up a wall. The second boss can be cheesed but is really obnoxious if you don't cheese him because he spams homing missiles. Third boss is a complete joke where the only challenge comes from trying to get him in the right position. Final boss is probably the worst, an RNG-fest where you're never given enough time to attack him effectively and he can just spam this shield attack that just drags out the fight.
The presentation of this game is fairly nice, though. There's a lot of detail in the backgrounds and each world feels unique even with the same black-rectangle style throughout, and the music's alright as well. Story's nothing special but the comic book style it's presented in is fairly nice.
Overall though this game just left me disappointed, it's not a horrible game and if a "meh" option existed it'd probably get that, but I can't really recommend this when there are better 2D platformers out there for the same price or less.

What can I say?  The Baldur's Gate experience now 'enhanced' with added companions and quests, classes, weapons/weapon specialisations and too many other knick knacks to mention.
For some people this is a welcome thing, for purists though maybe not so much.
I first played Baldur's Gate a year or so after it's original release (1998) and was overwhelmed by the freedom of exploration and depth that was on offer.  Thats not to say the original was an overly complex game but it certainly requires an attention span to understand the second edition D&D rules and how the stats play with your character and companions you may acquire on the way.
This edition takes the original and augments it with some of the features I mentioned above but also changes some things which I feel are for the worse such as the cutscenes and some useless companions, but these are minor quibbles.  The combat is just as satisfying, the story just as good (yes I liked it, despite criticism from others) and Minsc's dialogue will never get old.
For purists I recommend NOT purchasing this.  Heading over to a certain site that specialises in games that are old and good to purchase the original and then installing the various mods that improve the base game and having a blast that way is the way to go.
For everyone else who wants the new and (arguably) improved Baldur's Gate experience then this is the purchase for you.
In short - the good:
*Compelling story
*Interesting companions
*Satisfying gameplay and dialogue
*Sense of wonder and exploration is still there
*Now playable across different operating systems
The bad:
*Some new additions lacking and not so fun
*New cutscenes aren’t so great
The ugly:
*NO CLOUD SAVE - WHY CAN’T YOU DO THIS.  This can be bypassed with dropbox but if you’re going to allow the saves to work across several devices and operating systems then this should really be there.  Beamdog have stated that save games for EE are compatible across OSX/Windows so it makes no sense not to enable it at least for steam users.

I searched the internet for days, found multiple fixes (turn off antivir, start as admin, use compatibility with XP/Vista/Whatever, run windowed/fullscreen, increase/decrease framerate, countless number of workarounds), some of them seemed to be working, but all the problems were back in few minutes. The GUI is utterly basic with only a handful of options/menu choices, and as a fan of GameHouse games like Text Twist this is pretty disappointing. You can only play, restart, or quit, and there are no other modes besides timed play. Hint feature is unlocked after a certain percentage of words have been entered correctly and can be used an unlimited number of times to get enough words to unlock the next level.
Actually, the Hint feature is the best part about this game; the dictionary is so bad that you'll need it to move onto the next unnumbered level. Certain proper names and places like "Rosie" and "Paris" are in the dictionary, but basic words like "err" and "oes" aren't. I'm not sure why "Tesla" is in this but "Kant" isn't.
If it's in a cheap Steam key bundle, you might as well pick it up. It drops trading cards and has some easy achievements. But this is not worth $3.99.

I bought the game in June 2016 and have 200 hours. I still haven't set foot in half of the map regions. Mainly cause they still scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of me!  Fantastic difficulty settings and challenges to keep the sandbox mode engaging. It was a great game in Early Access and it's only gotten better with each new update. Smart devs mean it's the gift that just keeps on giving.  The updates don't just tweak but they also drop new content and new features to keep you coming back.
The Long Dark has a unique art direction that uses sound and dynamic weather graphics to establish a rich atmospheric experience. You really feel cold and hungry with a creeping desperation as the wind strengthens and the blowing snow makes it harder and harder to find your way home. Wolves make quiet footsteps and you'll start to hear wolf steps in the creaking trees as the wind blows. Wind even carries your scent to the wolves!
The minimalist UI enables the immersion yet still provides precise, intuitive information to facilitate a sophisticated game experience. The clothing system for instance is a constant battle between weight and the amount of temperature, wind chill, and waterproof protection that each article of clothing offers.  Item condition decay is slow taking several weeks before they take their toll. Some survival games consume items too fast and its a constant tree-pnching fest. In TLD you can gather fallen limbs after a wind storm but there's no totally unrealistic, mindless tree punching.
It's a proper survival game where your eventual death feels like a climactic ending: every death is a poetic story of the stupid mistake you made that got you killed. What's cool is that the bad luck and RNG usually aren't enough to kill you outright without the assistance of your own bad decisions to finish you off.
The Season 1 Wintermute story mode was really well-designed. The progression slowly reveals the game mechanics in a way that is engaging and accessable. It fulfills a tutorial function organically in the story telling. The limited map and gentle quest system were fantastic additions.  I hope a similar waypoint system that is based on finding notes is carried into sandbox so players can find the hidden cave connectors between regions intuitively without being tempted to Google wiki guides.
There was some undeserved internet drama from the small minority of haters. Hope gamers and devs alike ignore it and stay the course!
