LMA is cheaper than a trip to Starbucks and has taught me aparently games do not need too much in the way of story, graphics, advertising, and unique gameplay mechanics to be fun to play. In fact Low Magic Age does nothing (that I'm aware of) to change the tried and true DnD combat formula. As always it's a system that works well and makes the game engaging even absent any background story or polish. LMA one game mode is Arena and you run from skirmish to skirmish with a chosen band of the usual rpg suspects. You get solid tactical combat with a proven combat formula featuring progression and not much else is really necessary. There are bonuses and penalities for being in certain positions (flanking, behind cover, etc.) and the RNG is setup in a way that allows for tension without wrecking a good strategy.
Bottom line here is that Low Magic Age offers more than enough good times to justify forking over the $4 dollar US asking price and never look back. Updates seem to roll in almost weekly and there are more features yet to be added.

Syndicate is beautiful and better optimized than Unity. But other than that nothing else really works. Like controls. Any one function button does too many things. Example: hanging off the roof of a carriage. Drop down? Press E. Get in carriage? Press E. Hijack and drive? Press E. Right, then. But which one is going to happen exactly when I don't need it to happen? Or, chasing a dude with the intent of tackling him (also E). The police is chasing me. A gun is aimed at me, F pops up to evade bullet. I press F, but instead of the evasion F throws a knife in the back of the guy I was chasing and who was supposed to be caught alive. Or something as simple as climbing a telegraph pole in the WWI simulation. Not gonna happen. Thanks Ubi! All the testing hours really worked out for everyone. I mean... you.
Fight system? Yet another reinvention. 5th time? 6th time over course of nine games... But for the better this time. We have the "press E" for counter again. But it's more like a quick time event. Gold flashes above the head of bad guy prompts the counter. The higher level the player is, the more time they have to react. Not bad, I have to say. Kill streaks are back too, to make things easier when facing multiple attackers. At the beginning of the game, when the player might be lower level than most enemies it pays off to just carry a whole bunch of throwing knives and make a pin-cushion out of the really tough enemies. By the way, how come after an enemy was killed by a throwing knife I can't get the knife back when I loot their bodies? Doesn't make sense. Well, what does in an AC game, which feels like a never ending sequence of repetitive gameplay? After nine games we still can't have other activities beside tackling people (who by the way run as fast as a skilled assassin) and opening hundreds of chests?
The skill tree is a necessity if you are developing for Ubisoft (from Far Cry to AC, Splinter Cell or Watch Dogs). But in Syndicate it is a little out of place. Our two characters are already accomplished assassins, yet they have to "learn", how to double assassinate? Or air assassinate? Or throw a knife? Maybe. But to whistle? Really? It's almost as idiotic as the tattoo in Far Cry 3 to be able to choke and drag someone (haha, in Syndicate we also have to spend points on this very same skill!).
During the aformentioned World War I simulation, the back story is to eliminate the "sinister cult of spies". Spies who wear huge templar crosses on their shoulders. It must enhance their spying ability... you know, like showing your face and introducing yourself to every bad guy in the universe (Bond, James Bond). Someone must have been very high on something during the storyboarding phase, there is no other explanation for a script like this.
Other funny occasion: during a crowd event I save a guy's behind by assassinating two baddies. And what is his reaction? "Murderer!!!" Right.
The map is not that useful when it comes to inding collectibles. I could be standing right on top of music box (which contains a Secret of London), bombarding the environment with my X-rays and still nada. The item in question not popping up on the map. Never mind! As long as I have helix currency I can buy those missing locations online. And if not, I could still spend some more euros/dollars (on top of all the euros/dollars I spent to buy all the DLC-s, which together cost more than the original game!) to buy more helix from Ubi!
Social glitch? I'm sorry, what? Is that what you kids call a facebook user these days?
The wall eject is kind of like an erection over the age of 60. When you really need it, you just stand there hanging, and when it finally happens, it just leaves you in your own mess (falling to your death in AC, or tumbling onto a group of angry mobsters).
Syndicate is very boring. Exactly the same as Unity. Even the buildings are the same. The characters are utterly ridiculous. Evie and Jacob the "twins" who have nothing in common except for their height. Must have been two eggs and two fathers... Jacob is dumb and cocky, Evie is an arrogant smartie pants and they are equally annoying in their narrow minded way. Actually, you know what? The only characters who embodied good, righteousness and actually made sense in the AC series are Altair and Connor and perhaps Shay. They behaved like a true assassin should. Disciplined, focused, no charming and condescending bull****. And even though in all of the episodes Templars are made to be the bad guys, Rogue showed that the Assassins are equally bad. Then what's the point?
The story is nothing new either (as I wrote before, Jacob and Evie are already assassins, but we don't learn about their past, how they became assassins or who was their master). Templars are plotting to rule/better the world by mostly unethical methods (you know the end justifies the means), but here come the Assassins who kill them all while meeting some of the famous personalities of the period (who wear tremendous fake mutton chops and hulihees, not kidding, the worst facial hair in any game, ever). And of course the nutty professor type is present who invents stuff for them. Like the rope launcher/grappling hook. A ROPE LAUNCHER! Like Batman's. Except this one can't find a target a few yards away, but by turning a few degrees either side it suddenly finds one a hundred yard away! How stupid is that?
Not only the setting, the environment is similar to Unity, but the dynamic between the male and female lead character is the same too. Except for the love theme, the same bickering, same competitiveness and the different approach to missions is there in Syndicate. The lead females are in fact just males with a feminine look. I liked the strong females who didn't have to talk like boys and fight all the time, killing everyone to be charismatic or appealing. But it seems movie and game writers can only imagine a female lead in a single way.
There is no more online gameplay of any kind. In Unity it took me 200 hours to reach the Legend level, in Syndicate they tried to fill the gap with all the pointless collectibles and terrible minigames, like the carriage races (with rubberbanding, undefeatable opponents), escorts and highjacking, so as a completionist I will still spend about the same amount of time eventually. Boring and badly written stuff that completely lacks any entertainment value.
And the famous warning: assassins don't kill civilians. Right. How about not programming a dense population of aimlessly wandering pedestrians on the streets, so when I drive my carriage I don't have to run them over all the time?! Or that Templar Hunt mission where the target had to be killed by explosives. C'mon, Ubisoft! In the middle of a crowded park? Are you insane? And to make things worse, certain perks, which require skills are now have to be done not 1-2-3-5 times in order to get the achievement, but 25-50-75 times! Great. In a game, where succes (even 100 synchronization) largely depends on pure luck and the AI not bugging out.
I can only recommend this game to hardcore fans, who have steel nerves and like to do stuff to themselves with a cheese grater. You know... in a slightly amusing, but mostly painful way. As the great Ford Fairlane said it back in the day. Playing Syndicate feels exactly like that.

Stonehearth is a rather charming village builder. You start out with a handfull of "Hearthlings" to start out your village. By making buildings, gathering food, getting wealth, and keeping moral you can grow your population. I have been playing this on and off for the past year or so and have seen some great improvements from the devs and can't wait to see what is coming in the future. You kind of have to be in the right mood to play this game; sort of in a relaxed, animated fantasy sort of mood. But I suppose you kind of have to be in the right mood to play any game.
Today, I'm going to break the mold and start with cons:
-It's still in alpha. There are some bugs yet and I have found some in various parts of the game.
-There isn't much of an end game. (That I know of)
-the bugs that are fixed cometimes create new bugs.
Pros:
-The building aspect offers some cusomization with custom floor plan, building material, and a bit on roof design.
-Depending on which job you give your Hearthling, they will progress in levels and you can promote them to an advanced job or let them increase their level at the current job and be more productive.
-You have hard mode which offers a big challenge to your management with planning and managing.
-The devs are very active and take in feedback and bug reports and fix them within a few weeks.
-The devs also keep regular updates in blogs every other (or every) Tuesday about what's going on and near future plans.
-I enjoy the cartoony art style. The Hearthlings are cute and the monsters are kind of ugly but in a cartoon, funny kind of way.
-There is a job tree with various different jobs to give your villagers which is still in progress but improving with every alpha release.
Hope this helps.

A couple notes on playing the game;
Have at least 1-2 Farmers. Once you make one of them a cook, they help harvest, but you still need them to plow the fields.
Workers are VERY much so necessary. Although the carpenter, potter, mason and other occupations do help build/haul, you're going to want to keep the people with low-ranks down on the worker size (1, 1 and 2 for the body/mind/spirit; Keep them a worker)
Fighters and such need to be the most populace unit category (Archers, Knights and Footmen); At least have one of each with an herbalist. (For the three, high Body and Mind. Mostly so they don't run like cowards)
Herbalist and Cleric; Have one of each. One heals while the villagers sleep/get into beds, one heals just by walking around/in combat. (High spirit for these guys is necessary)
All "Worker-class" occupations need mind and spirit. All three are much so needed for the farmers than anything.
ALWAYS. ALWAYS remember there's a pause button that lets you keep playing. Helps you plan things.
Town watch; Love it, use it, learn it, remember to turn it off after everyone is done fighting.
Always go after goblin camps/"stray monsters" after the next invasion summon (Ents/Golems/Etc), that way your villagers aren't defenseless.

Baldurs Gate is tough and expect to die ALOT. The idea is that your character is just a kid in a quiet town known for their books. Your character is exactly that, a kid. When you start the game up your character is level 1, weak and brittle. You'll probably restart the game with a fresh character multiple times until you understand what class kits and good, and which are bad. You'll have to know what to do right off the bat and that's okay. The trial and error isn't monotonous, and can be completly avoided by looking up a walkthrough.
When I first started I just walked around with my dimpy little quarterstaff, doing the menial tasks that the game presents you with. These tasks are only menial because it sets the tone of how humble your characters start really is. On my playthrough where I beat the game, right off the fly I walked into Winthrop's taven bought a hammer on my dwarven defender walked around the town clockwise doing quests and getting stuff done. For the majority of the game I didn't know what was coming next but the first part I had done a million times. Because I restarted over and over and until I was happy with a character that was good and I knew I wanted to keep and import for baldurs gate 2. I was incredibly picky on my followers and only got the best.
None of that is neccesary.
You can play the game how you want to and not worry about whats good and whats bad, and that fine,
but it will be a lot harder.
I researched online on what was the absolute best until I eneded up with a party consisting of this:
Me
Imoen (Best thief in the game)
Khalid (Best tank)
Kivan ( Best archer)
Neera (Ok mage)
Branwen (Awesome Cleric)
By the time we reached level 4 (and leveling is very slow) we were tough customers.
You may start weak, but you become tough as nails. That's why in BG2, the game is even more fun.
Grinding out the early struggle is worth it because it just makes being strong twice as awesome.
TL;DR Version:
Fun game
You're very weak in the begining
You get really tough later on
slow leveling up
You will die a lot
You will probably restart the game a lot until you know what you are doing
BG2 is even more fun because you start at a high level and can wreck

I had this game on my wishlist for a long time. I'm happy to say that The Long Dark is definitely one of the most enjoyable survival themed sandbox games I've ever played.
The game offers a nice amount of challenges, there are many locations to explore and even a cool story mode. I like the fact that even when you choose a certain difficulty level, some areas in the game are more challenging than others due to the scarcity of the resources or the harshness of the weather.
The atmosphere is really gripping. You get that lonely feeling of being the last person alive on earth. Yet the sunrises are gorgeous. The graphics have a stylized, bulky look, but the game is not dull to look at. The color palette is beautiful and the changing weather conditions offer a nice amount of variety. I can't remember when I've last taken this many screenshots just because I enjoyed the scenery so much.
I guess my only nitpick is that it would be nicer to have a few more animal types in the game. After a hundred hours of gameplay wildlife encounters start to feel a tad repetitive.
I know there are walkthroughs that show the area maps and cache locations, but I haven't read them myself because I get more hours of gameplay when I prepare for those long hikes and search for the next grand location instead of just heading straight into the right direction. It's always really satisfying to come across something unexpected.

Once it dawned on my that this is a marathon and not a sprint, I realized how great this
simulator really is!
You will die quite easily by taking stupid risks and not being careful.  You will survive for weeks, and one slipup will land you dead.  I made mistakes like crawling through a window without cleaning up the glass, and dying from a deep wound on my hand that wouldn't heal quick enough, and I bled to death.
Scavenge, find a 2+ story safe house, start by coving the windows with sheets so the zombies don't see you, fortify it by barricading the windows and doors on the ground floor, and using sheets to make a rope to get in and out of the 2nd story window.  You will need a lot of planks, so dismantle doors and crates to get some.  Always carry bandages and disinfectant with you at all times.  Roam around stocking up on food and weapons...  You learn quickly what you need to do to survive, but don't be fooled, you will die, it's just a matter of how and when...
No matter how many times you replay, it's always a fun and interesting challenge!

This game is quite enjoyable. It’s fast, fun and often requires quick thinking. There are a ton of levels and a bunch of unique mechanics that can really be challenging at times. I particularly liked how upping the difficulty morphs the level – giving it harder paths, adding more traps, but it still has the same general layout. The controls feel responsive, the animations are nice and the music and sound effects are pretty cool too.
There’s even a degree of replayability, as you can always go back and try and beat your best scores on levels you’ve already completed, and if the devs end up adding leaderboards like they are planning to it will only add to that. Also, this is one of the few games that actually has a level editor. As it stands though, the editor is quite basic so could definitely do with a bit more stuff in it (I will update this bit if it changes upon the games release). Anyway, I’ve had a ton of fun with this and would definitely recommend it to anyone who’s into the Side-Scrolling Action-Platformer type genre.

The complexity of a Four-X game with the  brutality of an old Arcade game, plus Tower Defense. You wander through dungeons opening doors until you find the exit.
When a Hero dude/dudet opens a door, monsters spawn in dark rooms and go to "the Crystal" (which acts as a power source for lit rooms) with the intent of destroying it. You can place modules in lit rooms to defend them from monsters parading towards the crystal thing. Modules cost resources generated by opening doors; some Large modules increase the resources gained when opening doors. When you survive 12 floors, you win.
That's the beef of the game. The rest is details, but that's where the puzzle/experience of every game is too, even 4Xs. This game's beautifully modular design makes tiny DLCs feel revolutionary. It's awesome.
Not reccommended for Pixel-Art tourists; you'll be savagely eaten by the game's mechanics. If you're patient, you'll like it though.

I was given DotEndless from a friend with an extra key. Endless Legend was my first of the Endless games and this is my second.
Positive things first: The game's art, style and Amplitude's signature wit are all very much on point. I had many chuckles in my time playing this game and everything looked and ran smoothly. The game is also unforgivingly brutal, which for any fan of rogue-likes can come to appreciate. If you make a mistake you WILL regret it, but that makes victory all the sweeter. And there are also a decent number of unlockable characters for a good number of different takes on a run, as well as those required small victories one needs for a brutal rogue-like (you unlock characters by running into them in a run and advance 3 floors, you don't need to beat the dungeon).
All that being said I cannot recomend this game. Primarily because it teeters too far into more frustrating than actually fun in the rogue-like spectrum. I am infamously masochistic among my circle of friends and I still can't bring myself to WANT to play another run of this game after almost 24 hours of playtime. This is because DotEndless makes a classic mistake of roguelikes and does not doublecheck for actually impossible situations. And this isn't "it's so hard it may as well be impossible", I mean actually cannot progress within the game's constraints.
Aside from that, another negative factor to this game is something I have noticed with the Endless franchise. There is too much crammed into the game. As the trailer and tags states, there are TD, 2d, rogue-like, RPG, strategy, etc etc elements in the game. What they don't tell you is that in the bid to incorporate all those tags, the overall game suffers. The rogue-like elements conflict with the TD elements, the RPG elements conflict with the strategy elements, and so on.
The game's underlying premise and core mechanics are unique, and I WANT to like it. But I'm sorry to say numerous elements of this game need to be sacrificed for a better overall experience. DotEndless will draw you in for the first few hours and if you're stubbornly fond of brutal games like I am, you'll last maybe 20 hours before you start spamming restart for ideal starts or setting the game aside for another, better rogue-like such as:
Risk of Rain
Rogue Legacy
Crypt of the Necrodancer
----------------------

Good sound and music, but that's pretty much the only aspect I liked about Necromonads. A list of things I didn't like:
- Scanlines cannot be removed. The screen curvature
be removed, but only by darkening the overall image, which makes it look even worse.
- No d-pad support on dual-analogue gamepads. Also, the game does not have "Full controller support" as it claims. You can pause the game using the start button, but the only way to unpause it is using the keyboard.
- The game is locked at 60 FPS, which is fine, but there are frame-pacing issues that cause stutter when flying across the map. How much this bothers you will depend on how sensitive you are to stuttering (a fair amount, in my case).
All those problems could be overlooked, but Necromonad's biggest problem is that it is way, way too easy. Compared to
, this game is baby food. The enemies are never any threat to you, unless you accidentally collide with them. There's only one enemy that even fires bullets at your ship, but those bullets move so slowly you can literally fly circles around them.
There is no challenge whatsoever until at least level 15. And even after that, it becomes more tedious rather than difficult. You'll need to tap the fire button more and the stages will take longer to complete, but there is still no danger of actually losing.
I reached level 20 on my first playthrough (which took about 40 minutes). By that point I had gathered 7 extra lives (up from 3 at the start), received a perfect score (no captures or infections) in all but one stage, and was so bored I ended up killing myself 8 times.

With that out of the way, let's move on to the actual review. I just finished playing the game and well... it's a mixed bag. It has some good things, like the presentation, music, ambient sounds and Sean Bean.
It also has a few bad things. The map for instance. While the idea of reading the map using the environment, reference points and a compass to find your way is neat, it only ended up frustrating me as time went by. The save system is also rather annoying. The game only saves when you pick up a note or when you find a tent. So if you're all the way across the map and die, it's back to the last save point, whether it was at a tent or a random note you found somewhere.
Speaking of dying, you'll probably be doing a lot of that. The enemies in Kholat can be very frustrating. Once they spot you, they make a run for you and kill you instantly. Sometimes they even run straight towards you, even if you're hiding somewhere out of sight.
But... I still enjoyed this game, despite its flaws. It's a fun little horror game that had me on the edge of my seat and I commend the makers for their use of the ambient sounds and music to create an atmosphere of loneliness and fear.

Baldur's Gate: Cashgrab Edition (aka Copypaste Edition) is the 'improvement' of the original DnD classic. Including both the base game and the TotSC expansion pack, it also added some new super cool NPC-s and over 812963529 fixes blah blah blah...
Do yourself a favor, fellow RPG fan, and disregard Beamdog's self praises. This game offers NOTHING over the original game. 3 new companions - 2 completely unneeded and one hilaiously overpowered but just as unneeded, who the fk needs a monk in a lowlevel adventure, same for a wildmage when you have a specialist mage anyway - all with their own questlines which are so excit.... sorry fell asleep from the excitement. As for the 400 improvements/fixes/whatevers, I couldn't point out one, with the exception of adding higher resolution to the game (which you could achieve with a mod in 30 secs anyway).
Characters still bump into each other the turn back.
Characters still get stuck in each other/chairs/any imaginable obstacle that could be circumvented in 0.5 seconds.
Characters still pause momentarity EVERY GODDAMN TIME you issue a new order.
Characters still get lost and confused carrying out complex orders like: go down a hallway, go around a corner, go down the cliff and not just stand in the cliffside, etc. Pathfinding's as awful as ever.
Characters still rather just rush into battle with fists instead of switching to another batch of projectiles in their quiver...
Dice rolls are still hilaiously rigged (don't get me wrong, the game's fun and all but having my characters roll 2-1-1-3-6-2 without end while enemies roll 20-16-20-17-19 literally all game can be annoying, not to mention HP rolls).
And add to this list any other minor/major inconvenience the original had... Enhanced right? Nope. But at least there's a potion bag now, and some (totally irrelevant) BG2 spells.
IN SHORT: if you're an RPG enhusiast, but never played Baldur's Gate before, go for it. If you have hundreds of hours in other editions of BG like myself (originals on disks, GoG edition whatever) just pass, unless you want to play BG2 with a friend.
Because let's be honest here: why would anyone play BG1 for itself... It's just the ability point grab/xp farm for BG2, a game wastly superior in every aspect. And hopefully a game that has actually been enhanced, not like this.

After Minecraft, X-COM UFOD is my favorite game of all time. In fact it may be no coincidence that both games share common traits: they both have stellar gameplay and horrible graphics. Most game developers today seem to have forgotten a simple truth- Gameplay > Graphics. XCOM gives you command of an army of super-soldiers to fight off an alien invasion. Micro-managing is the key to victory and boy....there is plenty of that. You decide everything from where your bases will be / how large or small to how many bullets each soldier carries. The combat is turn-based and the enemy AI , while not as good as later games , can still be very sneaky.
What I enjoyed most is how your soldiers *slowly* ramp up in strength via reverse engineering of captured alien tech. There are times when ( if you havent been researching fast enough) you may encounter stronger aliens and still be useing simple guns! Defeating these stonger aliens with current weapons are the great story-making events of the XCOM game.
Oh did I mention the RPG elements too? Each soldier in your army has his/ her own stats. These stats can determine things like what weapon they would be best at, if they would make a great scout, a good medic, or if they should be sent packing.
Any fan of RPG + Turn-base + Sci Fi games simply cannot go wrong with this title.
Rivscore- 99 / 100
++NOTE++ Yes. That's right...99 out of 100. This game is almost perfect. If the Devs would pay for Scarlett Johanson to come to my next birthday party and blow...out my candles it would be 100 / 100.

I'm one of those old farts who rave about this game. As far as I'm concerned , it is the best strategy game every made. The AI isn't perfect. Aliens will do dumb things and get killed but they will also outflank and ambush you too. The graphics are pure 1980's. Nothing to write home about. The movement of your troops and the aliens is clunky.  The aliens don't look very scary on screen. But this is one of those games where you'll go "Oh, *&^% are you kidding me? How did that happen?" as an alien floater you can't even see sends a rocket into your Skyranger wiping out half your squad before you even move one of them out.  Or you've moved your favorite squaddie around a corner in a terror mission, only to see a Chrissalid about 10 feet away. You try to run, but a Chrissalid has 120 TU's to your measly 40 or so. You know you're toast when the aliens get their turn, even if you do a reaction shot, cause it takes more than one hit to usually kill a Chrissalid. But the Chrissalid doesn't kill you. He turns you in an alien zombie. Your own troops have to kill you. Isnt' that fun?
Playing Ironman in this game is masochistic.
This game isn't for the click-happy, over-adrenalined (is that even a word?) 21st century gamer. It's slow and methodical and takes  a while to learn to play properly. If you are willing to do some reading, there is a lot of information online for this game,  Strategy guides, tips and tricks and many other documents.  But if you're looking for a game that will challenge those little grey cells, this is it.
Not only do you control the tactical combat part ot the game, but you have ot determine what to research, when to do it, what kind of weapons your squad should use, which of your team you want to keep and nurture, and which you want to use as cannon fodder, as well as many other decisions.  The main game is all about micromanagement. And one wrong move. Waiting too long to research a tech or failing to shoot down a UFO coming to attack your base can mean the difference between winning and losing the Earth to the alien invasion. It's an awesome game and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes to use their head, wants a good challenge and likes strategy and micromanagement.
I highly advise playing this game a while before trying to tackle the sequel, Terror from the Deep. It's even harder than Xcom.
Oh, and try to refrain from throwing your PC out the window after you lose a whole squad on a terror misison.
An excellent game, no matter how old it gets it will always be one of the best.

This is a game before tutorials, before tooltips, and before the developers cared about what percentage of players could beat any given scenario. When it lists difficultly not by degrees of easy or hard, but by levels of experience, it means it. Beginners should start on beginner and graduate to experienced when the title fits. The game start doesn't have any sort of introduction, you're just thrown into the action without an explanation or briefing. You're not well supplied or well funded at the beginning either and you'll need to justify your budget each month, just like a real government agency. I started my first game, lost, and I started over during the first in game month. To help the next person in those shoes, here's a few bits of advice I picked up while learning to play: Rookies are cheap, buy more rookies before you worry about things like tanks; aliens can see in the dark while your soldiers cannot and the entire storyline including the game endpoint (as well as a few very useful research projects) come about after capturing an alien or two alive, so electro-flares and stun rods are not useless; and finally, if you ever see a hunched-over, black, bipedal crab-like alien, get the hell out of there.

Early Access Review: Project Zomboid
Me, during the zombie apocalypse:
"Oh, let me use this car to move all my valuables to a nice safe location"
*Miles from my cabin, spot zombies on the road, decide to kill with baseball bat to pretent vehicle damage*
*Finds some cigarettes and some good clothing on the bodies*
*accidentally tosses keys in the trunk with all my cargo*
*closes trunk*
...
*Tries to figure out what I did with the car key*
*realizes my tragic mistake*
*starts to rain, in the month of Febuary*
*Smashes passenger window to get access to the inside*
*Cant access trunk from interior*
*Soaked, in 30' weather, I freeze to death smacking on the trunk*
Amazingly dramatic for such a simple game, some of the most fun I've ever had.
The ismometric view is such a nice change from other early access zombie survival games.
There is alot this game does right. Survival and realism are unparred, and actually incredibly realistic for such a simple looking game. Fairly regular updates, which always seem to help.
Performance- without cars and base graphic settings a Radeon 5450 ran this at 45 frames per sec.
Yes.
In depth settings- you can select radio-stations on your car stereo, or select an AC setting for your vents. You can get injured in any possible way on basically any part of your body. Sprains, broken bones, scratches, gashes, bites, cuts with glass embedded, Infection in the wounds, different illnesses, you name it, you can die from it.
Overall, especially with the Winter Sale, this is a much needed game for those looking for something difficult and rewarding.

I spent WAY too long playing this one. It seems whenever I get into a large Western RPG something happens that keeps me from playing for a while. Fallout: New Vegas would crash on me, I spilled water on my laptop after KOTOR, and the school hit me harder than ever during Dragon Age. But I've beat it finally after all this time!
I played Dragon Age: Origins years ago in high school and I remembered liking well enough, but playing it now I enjoy it so much than ever before. I actually like it more than Knights of the Old Republic. My younger self would probably slap me right about now.
Dragon Age: Origins follows a pretty cookie-cutter fantasy storyline with a pretty cookie-cutter BioWare story format. You've got a ragtag team of about 9 or so people who gather together because a really big bad thing is about to destroy the country, and it's up to you a rare chosen warrior to fight off evil, all while exploring the country of Ferelden. This isn't a huge drawback on Dragon Age, but it is a very predictable set up with a predictable ending. The framework is old and familiar, but it's what's nestled inside that narrative framework that makes Dragon Age special.
Ferelden is a fantastic place to explore. The relationships each clan, faction, and even race share is wholly unique to this world. The lore is also so extensive and easy to explore in your handy-dandy Codex, which you'll be referring to often if you want to soak up every scrap of detail in this five-course meal of a game.
The characters are also very compelling too. I'd say Dragon Age has some of the best writers gunning for it, because I found myself so invested in this cast of characters. I don't think there was a single person I disliked in my group, which was a shame because not all of them worked in my party paradigms when I'd go out and explore. And the characters you speak to in the game vary all over the place, depending on their status and what the situation is around them, and because of that you're invested in whoever you're talking.
Along with that is choice in the narrative of Dragon Age. The world changes around you depending on what you choose, and there's no clear cut right or wrong in this game. All you have to go off of is whether your party members approve of it. I decided to defile the sacred ashes of Andraste because to me it was the greater decision of the two, and when I got back to camp I lost a party member. Forever. That's what kind of choices you'll be facing in this game, so play wisely. There's even an excellent choice towards the end of the game where you can negotiate and even recruit the final villain of the game. How cool is that!? BioWare took a lot of care in crafting this world and story and that's what makes Dragon Age so enthralling.
The gameplay is a standard BioWare fare. It's very similar to KOTOR, so if you liked that you'll feel right at home with Dragon Age. Some nice new touches include the ability to create splash damage with magic or explossive attacks, so there's another added layer of strategy to every fight you encounter. If there's anything I'd harp on gameplay-wise it's that a lot of enemies can get very same-y later in the game, and these random difficulty spikes that come out of nowhere and leave you unprepared. But other than that, Dragon Age is just as fun to play for the gameplay as well as the story.
The graphics have been outdated and there were a couple glitches I came across (but they are rare. I never had the game crash on me... except when I had the graphics set to their highest, oddly enough). But this game can look downright beautiful at some points. At others... it looks like a generic Western fantasy RPG, which isn't bad.
Now with the Ultimate Edition I also got to experience all the DLC Dragon Age has to offer (similarly to my replay of New Vegas), so I'll do mini-reviews of all the DLC below.
Awakening- A bit of a slow burner in the story department, but when it hits that climax you really start to consider the story from the Darkspawn's point of view. And I'd say the Darkspawn were the weakest part of the main game, since they were just evil for the sake of being evil. The new characters are nice and it adds new abilities and locations so I'd say take a look if it looks interesting to you.
The Stone Prisoner- This introduces the character Shale, who is one of my favorites out of the whole game. The quest to get him is alright, but he has been an invaluable asset to me throughout my main game experience and he is hilarious to talk to. I recommend you play this as soon as you can.
Warden's Keep- Eh. It's okay. Kind of forgettable. It adds a new dungeon with a somewhat compelling story and gives you a nice place to hide between quests, but I never used it after unlocking it. It's a nice detour from the story but nothing that gripping.
Return to Ostagar- I played this in the middle of my game and it added a surprising amount of sentimentality for the events at the beginning of the game and a little more sympathy of the shortly-lived King Cailan. That and the environment looks jaw-dropping. I recommend this one.
The Darkspawn Chronicles- I don't care for this one. It's got a neat squad building mechanic, but it's just the final battle at Denerim... only now you're the bad guys and you get to kill the good guys! Besides that novelty, there's nothing special to this DLC.
Leliana's Song- A pretty entertaining introduction to Leliana's character. If you play this, do so before you start the main game or maybe after you've met Leliana. The story itself is pretty decent and Leliana's banter with the other characters is pretty fun. It's some pretty decnet DLC.
The Golems of Amgarrak- Blech. I did not like this one that much. The story wasn't compelling and the DLC had so many of those obnoxious difficulty spikes that I started to get tired with this quest. I'd say play it if you're absolutely compelled to. It has no bearing on the story so don't feel bad if you choose to skip it.
Witch Hunt- Okay... so I'm back at the end of Awakening again for a forced conclusion with Morrigan. I mean, I don't mind it. And this is the official OFFICIAL ending to the Grey Warden's story but it feels so disingenuous. The characters are boring but the draw to find Morrigan one last time is well enough. If you want that ribbon tied, go for it.
Feastday Gifts and Pranks- Some nice gifts and pranks you can give to your party. It breaks the influence system on your party as well so if you don't want that ruined, don't touch this DLC at all.
All in all, this game is a treat. It kept me playing for about as long as I had with New Vegas and I'm sure if I come back I'll put in twice as many hours because there's just that much to explore. Dragon Age: Origins is one of the titans of the Western RPG world and it is a must if you're looking to get into a grand fantasy epic with compelling characters, a decent story, and some addicting gameplay. I'm gonna give Dragon Age: Origins an 8/10.

Kholat is a walking simulator with supernatural/horror elements thrown in. The environment is gorgeous and lends itself to some good screenshots, I used the game to bolster my wallpaper folder. Unfortunately, the game itself has a lot of problems that make it unenjoyable.
Firstly, you're given very little in the way of direction. This is fine in a more linear game, where you're bound to find your objective by moving forward, but the world in Kholat is fairly sizable and open. There is a map/compass system that isn't user friendly and there are coordinates strewn about the map, hidden on rocks and whatnot, that serve to tell you where you are.
Secondly, the way the monster is implemented is a huge problem to the game. SURPRISE there's a monster (anomoly) in the game. It's this weird gaseous thing that looks like it belongs in the Stalker series. The real issue with the monster is that there isn't a clear purpose for it, sometimes it's for jump scares, sometimes it's for tension, and sometimes it's just an annoyance.
I honestly don't know what I'm supposed to be doing. Am I supposed to find all the pieces of paper, ala Slender, or am I heading to some unknown destination? Too much is left unclear in this game.

I actually wrote this, hoping to try and get some sort of suggestion out.. The game itself.. Is pretty nice, however.. You've got to admit that it has loads of flaws in it.. And one of them starts to shine through best when you try and play in hard mode. Makes it (almost) impossible to get off to a good start in that game mode, and will really start to have you wondering exactly how stupid your hearthlings are...
Anyways.. the game needs some sort of way to prioritze things.. No.. I'm not meaning the little switches that say "This person should do farm, while this person builds." I'm meaning "Hey you stupid piece of meat, go pick up that herb. RIGHT NOW so that I can make an Herbalist or a potion." Without a way to give some sort of priority to what your hearthlings will gather.. Those who like to setup their villages to have a lot to do, won't usually have very much fun in hard mode.. If you try to plan too far ahead, the game will punish you greatly. As there doesn't seem to be a way to instruct your hearthlings to even drop all of their current queued projects.. And that is probably the most simple way to fix the issue.. It would suck to have to command your hearthlings to get back at it.. But It's better than having all of your starting hearthlings die, because you instructed them to build a house and they don't want to stop building that house to go get a herb until they're dead...
For crying out loud.. I told them to go gather some wild herbs, and had a farmer working on growing some herbs, and he ALMOST finished growing the herbs by the time my gatherers brought the herb into town... But to my surprise, they STILL WOULDN'T GATHER IT!
Either the AI need improved to recognize that a lack of items is bad, and make it so that getting items that are currently set at 0 is more important than carrying back the wood that you have 500 of or there needs to be a way to prioritize certain tasks.. Like by holding shift and telling them to gather this item.. They know that is more important to do than anything else.. Or even a way to over-ride it and say "This needs to be done first." Alternatively.. Like I said.. a way to tell your hearthlings to stop EVERYTHING. could work as well.
Maybe some of this is already in the game and I'm just not seeing it.. But before a hard mode can really be explored too much, little simple things like this really need to be fixed.. Even if there is a way to clear all commands.. A priority system would go leagues and bounds beyond it.. and make the game feel more professional as well.

I've been a Steam member for many years and this is my first review. 'Why' you ask? Well, because I'm a huge fan of this game and I really don't know why all of the hate for Evolve. This is what a team multiplayer experience should always be, very unique, very adictive and super fun all the way. Microtransactions you say??? Buy them only if you want, because none are needed to play and enjoy the game, even the core characters are awesome to play with, so you get an amazing game right out of the bat.
I know, the developers want to make as much money as they can. Those greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. It's a business. They want money. They wanted money from the moment they started making the game. That is why they made the game. Money is why every single game, song, movie, entertainment is made. They know that the game is good so they want to milk it and make as mouch money as they can. Can you blame them? We would all do the same if we had the chance. Well, I'd like to think that I wouldn't, but maybe you would...wink, wink... Anyway, grow up and get over it. Just don't buy what you don't want to buy. Nobody forces you to buy anything. I don't care for skin DLC, so I don't buy any, but the DLC characters are worth every single penny and I welcome every single one of them. In fact, I would pay for a third season if they make one, and I really wish they would. Each character is so unique and changes the gameplay in such a way, while maintaining a very good, not great, but really good balanced game, that makes all mindless Call of Duty and FPS games look dull and fail in comparison. Don't get me wrong, I love Call of Duty and many other FPSs, but I really wish more games were as unique as this one, that forces you to really play and think as a team in order to win, and still be as much fun. I seriously rate my experince and love for this game as high as those I had with Unreal Tournament, Quake, Doom, Half Life and Street Fighter back in the day, as well as many other past and present gems.
Most of the community playing is awesome. and we need more of you. It has a long and tough learning curve, so you have to be patient, but hang in there. All the time spent learning will pay off. After so many hours of my life in this game I'm still the worst monster ever and I am not that good at Assault, but I can seriously consider myself a great Trapper, a very good Medic and a decent Support, unless I use Sunny. I can be really good with her, and also with Jack and Val. I really love Jack, Sunny and Val, and they all provide such a different and unique gaming experience that playing as either one of them was totally worth the entry fee for both the game and the two season passes.
Now, keep in mind that the game is not perfect, the worst of it being the wait times between matches, and there might be some jerks that you meet once in a while, but these are things that you find in many other games. Also, most of the bugs are gone and the ones that are still present rarely come up, so they don't really take away from the experince. Try to play with people with mics, listen, communicate, take it seriously and stick together, so that you can learn from the veterans and experience the team tracking and combat tactics that make this game a total gem. I've met a lot of cool people playing and many have significantly enhanced my experience. I also play with friends on console where I have another 200+ hours played, which is where I've been for the last month, since we've had more time to play together; but there is nothing better than getting together a team of people that you met through the game, that share your love for it, and that know what they are doing, and are determined to win. Still, having a group of people, i.e. friends, in the mood for some mindless laughs is just as fun.
The point is Buy and Commit. Once you learn it, it will be incredibly hard to put down. Trust me. I'm about to travel for the rest of my vacation, and will be away from it for over a week, and I am already looking forward to my next Evolve gaming session...

I have not spent a lot of time on this game via my copy on Steam. I have played it an abnormally long time on my friends couch in co-op mode. When this game was originally announced and concept art floated around a bit on the web followed by rumors and insight about the music and the general process of development of this game I was convinced it was complete vaporware. Who in their right mind as a indie project spend so much time and effort on putting together a very niche product that could only be easily described as "Megaman inspired early American cartoon shooter". Cuphead is a labor of love clearly seen in the design and implementation of the entire package. Music, art style and boss design is top notch. Is the game as hard as YouTube videos and random message forums make it out to be? That is really up to interpretation and skill set with games that define the 80's and 90's for so many of us. I would not say the game is hard, but I can say that if a person has never played a side scrolling action shooter like Megaman or Contra then yes Cuphead will have a learning curve. The game throws a lot at you in that area, but it is never unfair or unreasonable.
Great music, animation and again level design make this a must purchase for anyone that likes unique games with polish. Playing this on my friends couch in both co-op and single player while watching each other get decimated and learning to overcome each battle has certainly reminded me of the games of my youth and I have nothing but praise for this development team that has recreated a situation in which I can feel again the way I did with games from that generation.

Time sink. I lose track of time playing Cuphead. Partially due to to its inherent  "Just one more time" gameplay.

This is the best zombie survival simulator to date.  Whether alone or in multiplayer, the game never fails to maintain the fear.  It is unforgiving, and one mistake can mean the end for a character's story.  The gameplay is slow pace but well thought-out.  The mechanics take some time to understand, and there is a steep learning curve; however, with that being said, it is well worth the time invested to develop an understanding of the game, for loads of survival content await.  There are also a ton of amazing mods on the workshop that really make this game pop.
It is important to understand that this is a simulator.  This is not similar l4d2, 7dtd, Nation Red, or ANY OTHER zombie game on steam.  This game is designed to test the player in the long run.  Will you make it through winter?  Will you survive your deep wound or illness?  Will you let your guard down at the wrong time?  Even a high leveled character can be downed to one mistake: you got bit?  Best enjoy yourself a bleach kock-tale to go out on your own  terms.  I can see how some people might be turned off by the idea of your character needing to spend 20 minutes ish real time to read a book for the xp boost, but that comes with the level of detail implemented with this game, and it just serves to add to the fear of death.  The last time I felt loss for a character as strong as I have felt for this game is Diablo 2.
Between the ever increasing number of zeds, the reality of what it means if the players is bitten, and the changes of season, the player is kept aware of the ever present danger.  Those that get comfortable are the first to die.  A backpack full of ammo wont save you against a horde of 1000+ strong, especially when your gunshot bring all the zeds to the yard.
As for the learning curve, be ready to play this game with the wiki up in the steam overlay, otherwise you will be turned off quickly.  Your best bet is to play with a group of friends to figure it out together, and if one knows the ropes, that's also nice.  The overall experience will simply be better with friends.
There are two cons to this game:
1. Hosting a server is not an easy thing, and the game is a ram hog in the long run.  I actually rent a server because of this, though, that should speak to the caliber of this game
2. It is never a good idea to be listening to music while playing this game.  That is how a zed sneaks up and bites you on the arm....*sigh* This happened to me.
The refund system will not really work for this game, and I say that because two hours is not nearly enough time to get a  taste of this game.  Vanilla, this game is a diamond in the rough, with a few mods and a private server with friends, this is one of the best games I have ever played.

In a nutshell, it's a machine to sell DLC.
From afar, Evolve seems like a good game.  Visually pretty appealing, the concept interesting and well crafted.  There just aren't a lot of asymmetrical games out that play well.  Evolve, for at least the first bit of time you play it, certainly does play well.  There's a lot of polish in it.  The problem is that it missed the mark on what would be necessary to keep it fun for a long time.  It feels like the entire game was just engineered to try and convince you DLC is what will keep it fun, rather than having unique or engaging experiences.
I think given that it's Turtle Rock, it's relevant to compare this game to Left 4 Dead.  In Left 4 Dead's versus mode, the survivors goal is escaping to safety.  It's getting from A to B alive.  Even without the special infected, they're inhibited by the environment and the common infected.  The player-controlled common infected have a goal of stopping and slowing them by any means.  In Evolve, more often than not the direct goal is for players on both sides to go after the other players.  Sure, the monster has alternative goals, but most of the time their primary goal is just simply running and hiding until they can get strong enough to fight the hunters.  The strategy is always the same.  The hunters are constantly chasing the monster, most often fighting their own lack of mobility rather than the actual environment.  The monster is always trying to get far enough away to eat and evolve.  Every match has its entire process boiled down to those elements and it gets old very quickly.
The issue isn't so much a lack of progression or even that the DLC exists, it's that the game just fundamentally loses its luster due to a complete lack of variety or dynamism.  Where you can go to an asymmetrical game like Left 4 Dead today and still have fun seeing people employ a host of different strategies in versus mode, you mostly just see people trying to exploit every single thing they can in Evolve just to break out of the repetitious bore that the gameplay offers.  Then when you throw on top of that how every bit of the game that could even begin to add variety is behind some kind of a paywall?  Well that really makes it a bad purchase.  DLC should not ever at any point be a hammer to smash fun into a game, it should be an addition that takes something good and spices it up.  People should like the game so much they're willing to pay to get more rather than pay more to get what they originally wanted.

I recommend this game on sale only.
There are a million and a half reviews about how this game is everything that's wrong with the game industry currently, and that's not an invalid assessment of the climate surrounding it's release. There isn't a huge amount of content in the base game, for all intents and purposes it's multiplayer only, and the DLC pricing is disgusting (as well as any of the quotes from the publisher you can dig up about the DLC). It's very unfortunate, because I find the concept and execution of the base game to be very fun, challenging, and engaging, and the graphics to be top-notch. I decided to write a review reflecting the game itself, and not the political outcry it caused, in order to counter some of the reviews on here.
The premise, for anyone who doesn't know, is that there's an ecological outbreak of massive, hulking monsters spreading across the galaxy and you are a rag-tag team of monster hunters tasked with clearing them out (or perhaps, a monster bent on total destruction). The game is Asymmetric Multiplayer, meaning there are 4 hunters versus 1 monster, and AI is available for either side. There are a few different types of objectives but the standard deathmatch is the most played, where the hunters try to find and kill the monster before it grows big enough to destroy the power relay.
For a casual gamer who likes or loves asymmetric multiplayer, you will enjoy this game. It has a neat take on the asymmetry while still being very accessible, which is a nasty feat. All the roles feel well balanced against each other and the developers have tweaked the game multiple times to ensure the meta favors neither side, nor any particular character. Whether it has staying power is a manner of taste in my opinion; I've found that despite the lack of content the premise is good enough to keep multiplayer interesting enough to continue playing.
For a power gamer, I'm worried about the higher-level meta. I don't play at a high level, but watching tournaments for Evolve was much more boring than other games. Basically only one monster, the Wraith, is tournament-viable, and because of the inherent "run and hide until you are strong enough" mechanic the game becomes a bit of a boring hide and seek. If the team can find the monster when it's level 1, they win. It's a bit of a tossup if they find him in level 2, but the monster probably wins 3 out of 4 times. Once the monster reaches level 3 the humans might as well just concede. Because of the amount of concentration and teamwork required at this high level of play, this sort of deterministic outcome does not affect anything below competition-level play.
I absolutely love asymmetric multiplayer games ever since Splinter Cell, so I bought this game on release for 60 dollars. It was not worth it then and it isn't worth it now, but for the 14 dollars the game is currently at, it is definitely worth it.
Now, about the DLC. I recommend that you do not buy the DLC, and you should note that getting the Digital Deluxe edition only gives you one set of hunters and monsters, not both, as Evolve had two "Season Pass" content sets. Yes, that's terrible and yes, even though I bought the game in the first place, I don't recommend purchasing the DLC because of that. The DLC packs, on sale, currently cost more than the game itself, which is ridiculous, and while I support any outfit that makes polished asymmetric multiplayer games I cannot condone the amount of greed shown by the publisher with the DLC packs. I hope one day they will come down to a reasonable price, but considering they are already 50% off that doesn't look like it's going to happen any time soon.
TL;DR like asymmetric multiplayer? get this on sale, it's a blast. Don't buy the DLC

Definitly not recommended for gameplay, business plan / customer treatment and technical reasons all together.
Gameplay: Evolve sounds great on paper. Asymetrical gameplay with various human hunters with different abilities such as tracking footprints / scent, locking down an area, cooperative hunting experience with close teamwork against a monster who has to run, hide, eat and grow as much as it can until the balance of power becomes favorable to it, and he prey becomes the hunter. Evolve offers that, and has great maps to support both the hunter crew and the monster, with having different monsters and hunters having different ways of movement: a monster may easily climb up a huge wall the hunters's jetpack cannot reach, or the hunters may cross a small cave the monster cannot run through. This all sounds great, right? On paper. In reality, the game is a ~10 minute running simulator, like as a hunter you literally do nothing else just run. There is a reason Evolve is widely known as "Running Simulator", and as like most memes / nicknames / jokes on games that are awful in a way, this too is perfectly fitting and true. As the monster, it's definitly more interesting, but there again: the game has to have 4 hunter players, and 1 monster player. It doesn't works if people don't want to be forced to play as either: trolls ruin games intentionally just so they can rush to the next hoping to get their preferred role, or matchmaking takes forever. I was hoping this wouldn't happen, but I expected it.
Business reasons: the game advertised itself with 4 hunters, 3 monsters +1 as a pre-order bonus, plus maps being free updates. While this on it's own is still true, the developers kept their real plans a secret until relase. On top of the "mandatory" season pass that could be pre-ordered before we've seen any gameplay pre-relase, the game got a SECOND season pass, ultimately having 66% of the content (hunters and monsters in both) locked behind a TWO season pass paywalls. And since Evolve is multiplayer only with drasticly different characters, it really limits you if you don't buy them both. Then just look at the DLC wall: all the weapon skins, monster skins in different brutally overpriced packages. Some may say "oh you don't have to buy them". That would be a valid point if the game on it's own would have such cosmetic things to unlock, but reality is _almost_ everything, I belive I can say roughly 90+% of the customization is locked behind paid DLC. The rest is "slightly different shade of red stripes for barely visible parts of the monster", versus the DLC's vastly outstanding changes. I feel like I'm arguing with somebody who likes them /lol. Well I'm not a cow, and last I checked my wallet wasn't either. I don't like to be milked, especially not when the business model turns out to be shady and change shortly after relase (=customers paid already, who cares).
Technical reasons: first of all the game had great betas, and got relased with tremendously worse performance and bugs that usually come from a poor console port and surprisingly wasn't present at the betas (such as having your hardware mouse on screen while having a crosshair too, and both move separately with different speeds). Then the game started to have unusually high matchmaking times, and while I cannot say for sure if these 3 main problems got fixed (they certainly were not 2 months after relase, if that says anything to you about what kind of support to expect), but it killed off the starting playerbase fast, on top of other reasons.
Overall: Evolve is a great concept poorly executed, helplessly poisoned with paid DLC avalanches (including gameplay and customization) without which you barely get ~30-40% of the game's content. Ignoring that, it may last a very few number of games that are really enjoyable (if the technical issues got fixed, beta was fun) but it becomes boring incredibly fast due to lack of gameplay variety and content, that is locked behind 2 season passes. Such a shame it ended up being like this, and the playerbase mostly left for the same reasons. If there is a wall of shame for gaming business models, cusomer treatment and information manipulation ("the news don't lie, they just don't tell everything") Evolve and Turtle Rock Studios should be the leading example on it. If you loved L4D, don't fool yourself - the people behind may be partially the same, but the idea, the leading philosophy and the execution quality of the endproduct is vastly different, for the worse.

No nostalgia here, my first playthrough was in 2015. While the DnD mechanics and interface take a bit getting used to; the game holds up very well. Deep character builds, interesting quests, even the graphics manage to hold up considering the games age. The combat takes some time getting used to but after getting a few levels some of the fights are really deep and entertaining. The black pits addon was really nice in letting you create your own party and really experiment with different builds, combinations, and participating in different fights.
My only complaint is that now I'm 10 hours into Baldurs Gate 2 and I see some problems with BG1. BG1 just feels like a setup for Baldurs Gate 2 and it lacks the deep character interaction that Baldurs Gate 2 has. In BG1 you meet many companions that seem like they could be interesting, but they are mute for the entire game. Luckily the Enhanced Edition characters have quests and dialogue that adds some flavor to the game. I found Dorn and Neera to be much more endearing than any of the vanilla NPCs.
The mainplot in BG1 feels a bit barebones and just serving as laying the groundwork for the sequel.  The game began to drag on a bit towards the end but that could be just my eagerness to start the second game. The late game dungeons like Durlags tower were not too enjoyable for me. Hundreds of traps everywhere with really obscure puzzles to solve. It seemed every lategame area was just traps everywhere with tougher mobs. I didn't find them too interesting. I actually enjoyed the earlier dungeons much more.
Overall though I can see how this game was a milestone for it's time and it still holds up today as an amazing RPG. Playing through the saga right now is a great experience in 2015 even with no nostalgia. While I am finding Baldurs Gate 2 to be far superior in every way, I think for a new player playing the first one and getting a feel for the game/the background story is a great idea. It was hard enough managing my level 3 mages as a BG noob, I couldn't imagine diving right into Baldurs Gate 2 and being bombarded with 20 spells to memorize.

The original X-COM game is quite simply one of the finest turn-based tactical games I've ever played. The game blends high-level global strategy with the small-scale tactical challenge of skirmish battles for a still-unmatched gaming experience.
The mechanics behind the tactical battles are incredibly detailed, and provide nearly unlimited flexibility and choice. For example, all terrain is destructible, your fighters have nearly unlimited choice of actions (they may even toss out-of-ammo friends additional magazines or even whole loaded weapons!) and each battle presents unique challenges. You command a small squad of approximately a dozen soldiers who gain experience, improve their abilities and accrue injuries over the course of the campaign. Missions are as diverse as clearing UFO crash sites and recovering alien artifacts, defending populated areas from alien terror attacks, raiding functional enemy vessels or ground bases and even defending your own base(s) of operations from a determined enemy attack! Each of these tactical battles is important to the global strategy component, so you don't want to lose a battle as it may have lasting consequences to the rest of the game, but by the same token sometimes you won't even be able to show up to a particular engagement as you are forced to pick your battles in order to win the war! For example, you may be more concerned with protecting a country that provides substantial income for you than one who is less monetarily crucial to you. Later in the campaign you can manage your greater resources to allow you to build additional bases, allowing coverage of more of the globe so that hopefully you won't have to make such compromises.
In addition to this you have the capacity to expand each base's facilities, increasing the number of fighters and transports at your disposal, or expanding your research or production capabilities. Research is an important aspect of the game, as you gather alien technology and reverse engineer working models for your soldiers to use in battle. As you progress up the alien tech tree new weapons and armour will be made available for you to produce, most of which outperforms your meager Earth technology. You might even start making ends meet, financially speaking, by selling some of the valuable alien tech you discover (or even create...) on the black market to the discerning, and wealthy, private collectors of the world!
The game's greatest failings (and they certainly do exist) are almost invariably caused by its clunky user interface and painstaking inability to remember previous choices. For example, performing actions with your fighters takes ages to complete - part of this is the price of such unparalleled flexibility, but part of it is just poor design. Worse than this though, you must equip each of your soldiers before every battle. The computer seems to randomly assign them the gear available, and then you need to sort through each and every one of them, removing gear, assigning it to another soldier, then giving them the correct equipment which the game gave to another soldier. It is tedious and would be an immense waste of time but for the fact that if you don't do it, no one will have the correct weapons at the start of the fight!
Bear in mind that those literally the only complaints I have against the game - it's otherwise poor graphical quality is forgiven on account of its venerable age, and its at-first opaque controls require a thorough read of the game manual to explain them (though this is available through steam). I would strongly recommend new players visit the X-COM wiki in order to familiarize yourself with the game, its controls and the mechanics before having a go, as its complexity can be daunting at first. However, once you get beyond that initial uncertainty the game yields endless rewards for anyone willing to play it through to completion!
Keep an eye on the still in-development 'Xenonauts' as it is described as the "spiritual successor" of this game. Xenonauts appears to be created with everything amazing about the original X-COM game while improving the graphics, user interface and overall making it more modern and appealing. I look forward to this game finishing development! (How they will avoid being sued with a game that is so obviously just a re-engineered version of X-COM is beyond me, but if they can pull it off you can be sure that I'll be all over it!) That is in contrast to the recently released X-COM: Enemy Unknown game, which stripped out all of the excellent features I've detailed above and left you with limited (and oftimes nonsensical) choices, extremely pretty graphics and little else. Despite its failings and age, I would recommend the original X-COM over the modern one every day of the week (and twice on Tuesdays).

Heres a fix for widescreens (cause my game got stretched and made it ugly) so you can play windowed mode, found it on the internet:
originally for apocalypse, but works the same..just look up the xcom ufo defense dir
The DOSBox file to tweak is dosbox.conf.
(Be sure to back up the dosbox.conf file before editing it.)
To run the game in a 1024×768 window, make the following edits.
fullscreen=false
fulldouble=false
fullresolution=original
windowresolution=1024×768
output=ddraw
If the game feels a little sluggish running under DOSBox, experiment with the cycles setting. Anywhere between 20000 or 30000 will do.
cycles=20000
I have my XCOM working at 1152x864 resolution, works perfectly in windowed mode. Make sure you overwrite the file by clicking on the original file when you save it (by viewing all files you will see the file, click on it overwrite and play).

This... could have been rubbish. A game where you're doing nothing but staving off hunger and fatigue until you eventually die? Where's the fun in that?
But surprisingly enough... it's brilliant. What seems to make the difference is the amazingly immersive nature of the environment. People might look at the screenshots and say "Huh? But it looks like a cartoon!" Somehow, that doesn't matter. It's almost the trick of giving you the outline and letting you fill in the blanks yourself with your imagination. The somewhat simplistic visuals allow the developers to put in a huge amount of detail in every location, making every part of the world feel unique. The world of the Long Dark feels real,,, and due to the almost complete absence of other people, it has a feeling of terrible isolation and loneliness about it that reminds me of the rather ancient PC game Midwinter. Also, the visuals really come in to their own when you have a good view, the environment is gorgeous.
A lot of this I have to say is due to the sound design. While there is plent of sound in the game... the source for nearly 90% of it is your character. The crunching of your boots on snow. The clanking of items in your over-full pack. Hell, just having a drink of water. All of it serves to remind you that it's just you against nature. There's no-one to talk to, no-one is coming to help, and you just have to keep going. Even sighting an animal is a significant event.
Balance has improved significantly since early access. When I first started playing, survival felt much more random than it is now. Encountering a wolf was a near-guaranteed death if you couldn't get indoors, and the ability to actually hunt for food was sorely limited if you weren't lucky in finding the right equipment. Now, however, the developers have added a multitude of different ways to hunt and survive, which makes the game more interesting. This makes the game slightly easier overalll... but really it's main purpose is to cut down on the number of "Gotcha!" deaths where the player simply couldn't have done anything to survive a bad bit of luck. Luck is still a factor, but it's much easier to recover from unfortunate events if you know what you're doing.
The story mode is interesting so far. I was somewhat concerned that the introduction of NPCs would ruin the experience, but it doesn't, and there's a definite mystery building here. It adds quests to be completed (that mainly involve using your survival skills) for those who need a bit more direction, but the rest of the mechanics work much the same.
All in all, a hearty recommendation. The Long Dark is a great game to get away from it all, to me. Play it on a dark night with the wind howlign outside for the full experience. If you enjoy watching Alone, you'll love this.

The Long Dark immerses players in a beautifully realized post apocalyptic world. I consider the survival mode one of my favorite games of all time. As someone who loves nature, hiking, and exploring, the survival mode is just awesome. I love the art, the sound, the music. I like that you can play how you want: hunting and killing, scavenging and living quietly, or just strolling around and taking in the breathtaking scenery. The game is very much worth a purchase just for the survival mode. I've put in 60+ hours in the survival mode and I still find it fun and relaxing.
The story mode is good, but not great. I like that it adds some goals/quests on top of the tried and true survival mechanics. In this way, the story mode is like a longer version of one of the various challenge modes available in the game (hunt a bear, gather X amount of resources, etc). This part of the story mode was pretty fun but not amazing. It didn't bring anything drastically new to the game that wasn't there before the story mode update. Where story mode lacks is, well, in the story. The cutscene animations, the dialogue, the characters, and the general story were just okay. Sometimes it was even borderline bad/eye-rolling, I'm sad to say. The story is just not of the same quality as the survival mode (which is incredibly high). All that said, I enjoyed my time in story mode and I look forward to playing future episodes.
I would think of the game this way: it's an incredible survival game with a bonus story mode that's just alright. I've really enjoyed my time with this game ('m pushing 100 hours as of this review!) and I do recommend you give it a try,

Hey there and welcome to this review of Dungeon of the Endless; likely the first roguelike of its kind, fusing together elements of tower defense with direct hero control with a healthy dose of resource management and dungeon crawling!
So, as stated, prominent features are direct hero control, resource management, dungeon crawling, and tower defense. So in order:
Direct Hero Control: You can have up to 4, and you right click to move, left click to select. Attacking or opertating (increasing efficiency of a structure at the cost of staying in the room for successive turns) is automatic, but requires you to be parked in the room you want to do it in. Most heroes have at least one active ability, which will display under their avatar at the top right of your screen. Click them anytime you feel they are best used. Various mechanics such as operating, the ability for your character to spawn block enemies in unlit rooms, and more make it so that you will often have to keep very active tabs on who is where, doing what, and when to change it. This can make the game much more friendly to those playing with friends, as you won't have to keep track of 4 heroes, their abilities, where they are, where they need to be, and constantly select different ones.
Resource Management: There are 4 main resources: Dust, industry, science, and food. Dust is for powering rooms, allowing you to make your path through the dungeon safe, or unsafe, at your choosing. Dust is the single most valuable resource going forward, as unpowered rooms can spawn enemies when you open new doors. It is also required to keep rooms with machines functional, so if you want to keep getting your resources from your generators every turn, they have to be powered. Industry is used as a resource with which you build things, so I would say it is of second highest importance because if you can't build new generators on each floor, you won't be able to get many resources at all. You either have it or you don't , pretty simple. Science is used for research, done in specific rooms if you discover them and spend the science to research from one of the available options, which can differ from naturally found research pods. Last comes food, an important but often dismissable resource that enables you to not only feed your character to heal them in an emergency, but to level them up. While doing both of these at times can be critically important, not having food isn't always the end of the world.
Dungeon Crawling: So every floor has a random amount of rooms, which can be powered or (mostly) unpowered, have heroes for hire, additional resources, shopkeepers, and various other surprises. As you explore more and more of a floor, you will require more dust to power important rooms while also trying to balance powering the most inconvenienent places for enemies to spawn in on you. Dust can come from newly explored rooms, machines, and killing enemies. There are also items and passive as well as active abilities that can increase your dust gain. There is an emergency generator machine that you can build to power a room and help with gaining dust, so research this technology asap if you find it. As you explore more of a dungeon, you will find yourself having to make decisions and sacrifices. Do you keep the sword for that awesome character you hope to find and unlock or the healing item for an emergency? Do you keep the piece of armor that protects you more, or lets you gain more dust? Can you afford to let that hero operate this machine, or will that place you in jeopardy? Essentialy, the dungeon crawling aspect of DotE is about quickly responding to new discoveries and how they may alter your priorities. If you can't tell, DotE is a very tactical experience.
Tower Defense: So yes, I'm sure you now have it firmly in your head that you can build generators to spawn resources every turn (door opened) but that doesn't cover the wealth of options. No, not just that emergency generator you need to find and research immediately, but also a shop for the shopkeeper to be relocated and operated, and various offensive and defensive pods that can be used as traps or buffs for your heroes that will be fighting in specific rooms. There are many otions here from direct attacks, slows, disables, health regen, offensive ability increasing pods, etc. You have to plan ahead and not place these wastefully, as you are not only limited in amount, but the landscape of the dungeon may change unfavorably as you open more doors, leading to a hole in your defenses you can't patch either due to lack of industry or lack of dust to power a room.
So. Can you utilize your resources and cunning to keep your heroes and structures safe as you uncover the whole floor? Do you make a mad dash for the end, knowing you no longer have the ability to sustain yourself? Or do you ultimately run out of options as you slowly die, trying to hold on for hope of a lucky find that will save you and let you get to the end and escape the dungeon?
Good luck!
