I am reeeeally disappointed. I've used the non-Steam version for 480+ hours. You should understand that you are not buying a click-and-export solution. The mobile export is not maintained. The instructions for basic setup are outdated and don't work, and you will wrestle with googling and trying different installs of underlying libraries; it took me the same amount of struggle to get the basic export working as when I did this with libgdx (which is free).
The Google and Facebook extensions/plugins are partly out of date and have outdated or no documentation. The current version of the Google-Admob extension simply does not support rewarded ads because it is out of date; these are the most recommended/least hated way of implementing ads. Support is fast for very small questions but nonresponsive (literally, doesn't respond) for significant issues. These are the things you're supposed to be paying $400 for.  If you end up manually wrestling with SDKs or buying an extension for these mobile features, you might as well be using a free engine/framework like Unity, Unreal, love2d, Godot, Phaser, libgdx, Monogame, whatever.  (And even there, if it's open source, there's a great chance someone's already done it for you.)
GMS2 itself is janky---the project database structure becomes corrupted, creates ghosts, and doesn't play well with teams using git. The IDE crashes when working with assets. Finally, you're not learning a real programming language. GML does not teach or lead to good programming knowledge, and, in fact, locks your hard work into a proprietary software with a company that I really don't think is going to last long in its current form. I am also uncomfortable supporting the corporate owner, Playtech, which is the world's largest gambling software company.
If you decide you want to make a desktop and a mobile game, and want to export to HTML5 (normal for game jams or demoing your game), then you're paying $100 + $400 + $150 = $650. If you want to get onto the Windows store or Xbox's "indie" channel, that's another $400 = $1,050.  If you ever want to go to consoles, that's an additional $800 annually, and the Nintendo Switch is not supported.
Bottom line:  use something else, probably Unity, or anyway one of the bajillion free 2D game engines out there, because you won't get what you paid for with this.
Updates 11/30/17:
* The developer has stated that rewarded ads are not a priority; there's no timeline for when they would become available without purchasing a third-party extension.
* The iOS export currently requires push notifications and cannot be disabled. (This is similar to an earlier bug, now fixed, where all Android apps required external storage access.)

I don't normally write reviews, but this compiler is really expensive and I guess that many developers want to know if this compiler works well, and so here are my first impressions. I have made and published Android apps with GM 1.
I only need to compile to Android (not iOS), and so I am a bit annoyed that I need to pay for iOS as well.
There are good instructions in the help menu and I suggest that you follow them!
Click on  Help  ->  Required SDKs
Provided that you follow the instructions to the letter, you should be able to compile to Android without any problems.
I really like how GameMaker handles all the Android Developer Requirements (which are about to change again (64 Bit, Security requirements, etc)). All I need to do is press the compile button (the good people at YoYo Games handle all the details and testing). This enables me to quickly and easily publish my apps on Google Play.
I normally complie to Android VM which is rock solid and identical to the desktop version. This means that I can develop and test my app as a windows app (quick and easy), and then compile to Android after all my testing is done.
The YYC option gives extra run-time speed (which I do not need), but it is worth noting that
(a) the compile time is longer
(b) your scripts need the exact number of arguments, otherwise your app will crash or the wrong script will be called! When I imported my GM1 app into GM2, my code changed from
myscript()  to script_execute(myscript,0,0,0,0,0)  and these extra agruments caused my app to choose the wrong script when I used YYC. Android VM worked perfectly.
I should mention that, apart from the above, the import from GM1 to GM2 worked without problems. I can just import and compile without changing anything.
Now for the good part:
It is now posible to create an object variable straight from the object editor AND then modify the variable's value directly in the room editor for each instance. Developing apps is now a pleasure! Low Magic Age is a great surprise; a real hidden gem. This game had a good but warm reception at launch, because it was only in available in chinese. At the end of February, more specifically on the 24th, the English version was released, with a great translation, by the way. At the moment, Low Magic Age has only one game mode: Arena. In it, you will fight several randomly generated battles on procedural scenarios. You have to win four battles, plus another one with with a greater difficulty (which serves as a kind of boss) to proceed. Fight, reach the next wave and repeat - that's it. As the game is still being balanced, you will face occasionally a situation where victory is not possible - with enemies knocking down your entire team in three hits, for example. Luckily, you can generate a new set of battles by paying a certain amount of the currency used in the game. This includes the possibility of choosing a specific difficulty level, which is cool to make a grind to collect money and equipment. Yes, random gear is won after a victory. In total, there are over 100 different monsters and over 100 different items.
The ability to hit or miss a hit, including critical hits, is entirely based on the d20 System. Thanks to the Open Gaming License (OGL) from Wizards of the Coast, a publisher specializing in tabletop RPGs and collectible card games, the developers of Low Magic Age were able to freely use this system, which came from the tabletop RPGs. To make everything clearer to the player, the battle log details the numbers that were taken and why they resulted in a hit or miss. Although this information is easy to consult, you must also take into account factors such as variables (more or less) caused by the equipment used, as well as the status of the characters.
While the Arena Mode can entertain you for many hours, keep in mind that the universe of the game will be greatly expanded. In future, devs will add a Sandbox mode, which is infinite and customizable, and Adventure mode, which will be an open world campaign, with procedurally generated dungeons and permanent death, as well as Tales of Maj'Eyal (ToME). And speaking of Tales of Maj'Eyal, the similarity in the graphics is no mere coincidence. The developers of Low Magic Age acquired a package of tilesets made by Raymond E. Gaustadnes (Shockbolt), the same one who created the arts for ToME. What for some may seem strange, to me it's great, because it reminds me of this roguelike that I like so much (but there are also one or another tileset not used in ToME).
Low Magic Age must remain in Early Access for at least six months, but this time may vary according to the demand. It's worth mentioning that the team that develops the game is always listening to suggestions, criticisms and answering questions in the forums. If you are interested in the game, I recommend getting it now, not only because the price will go up later, but also because it is quite fun, well done, and with a beautiful soundtrack.

So the game currently exists of numerous challenges in random small maps versus different enemies.

2) you get experience and level up

Combat was not what I played this game for, and not what got me hooked and kept me going through it. The characters and companions did. I actually had a hard time continuing the story through Awakening simply because my favorite characters were not present. From sarcastic and bitter Moragin, to sultry and bold Liara, to stoic and brisk Sten, the people you travel with in Dragon Age: Origins are nothing but colorful. Being the romantic schoolgirl that I was when I first started the game 5 years ago, I of course fell in love with the sexy and bold Alistair (I've read a lot of hate on poor Alistair, but I like to believe it comes mostly from salty single guys. Man, if you talked the way he does, I swear fewer of you would be single.) I felt a connection with all of them. Perhaps it was *because*it took me 5 years to complete the game after some Xbox malfunctions, several moves to and from contries, and the insufficient funds to buy the game on Steam until it was on sale, that the time in the interum made it feel like I knew them better. But I refuse to let 'Imposter Syndrom' get in the way of my opinion that it was a good story with good characters. My grandma always asks how I'm not bored now that I'm fully supported and no longer need to work. The answer is games like these. I tell her that its like reading a good book, or watching a good movie, but its made even better because *you* choose how it will end. Everyone has a different experience, and I think that is so perfect.
On to Awakening. I might edit this if I ever finish the game. I really *Really* wanted to love it as much as I loved Origins, but I just wasnt feeling it. The characters felt a bit dry and uninteresting. Anders felt like a cheap knock off of Alistair (He even has VERY similar facial features ?????), Nicholas seemed rather whiny, and Velaina was simply impossible to please. The 'favorite' that they brought back from Origins was probably the least favorite of mine, though thats only one girls opinion. All that, coupled with the very impersonal conversations where you talk to them, and it doesnt enter its own dialogue screen left me feeling unsatisfied as far as characters go.
Like I said about Origins, the combat was not really my style so there was nothing there to keep me interested. The added skill sets almost seemed exessive and unmanagable, making it so that some talents you simply didnt use because you were so used to your first 20 or so levels playing with what you had in Origins or because there simply wasnt room on your action bar.
I never made it through the game, it was that uninteresting to me after Origins. It felt a bit lazy. There was one point in the dialogue where you could hear a huge difference in the characters voice during a single line in a conversation, almost as if they used a different mic, or the voice actor had a sore throat one day and not the next. The lack of the aforementioned dialogue 'cutscenes', and the shortness of some of the side missions really felt mindless and not very engaging.
To sum it all up, Origins is for sure worth it. Awakening, I can live without. But we'll see. Maybe time between games is what I need to enjoy the differences in the two.

What can be said about this game that hasn't already been said? I originally played DA:O when it first came out, in physical copy. In essence, the game was sold as being a next gen equivolent of games like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale - a somewhat action oriented, classic style, pause and play, party based RPG, interwoven with a good bit of story telling and dialogue, with some elements of choice and consequence.
While it's not a perfect game, I think they suceeded for the most part. None of the Dragon Age games that followed it really capture that very well, as the franchise started to go downhill by watering down the depth of its RPG elements. If you are going to get a Dragon Age game, this is the one to get.
Characterization - One of the game's novel features is the whole "Origins" concept, which ends up giving characters multiple options for how the game begins depending on what type of character they play. This basically amounts to a handful of hours of variant gameplay per origin, and it also entails some potential consequences later in the game. This gives a certain element of replayability and variety of characterization choice.
Companions and important NPC's are given some serious effort into being memorable characters with fleshed out personalities that the player can potentially influence and unlock character developement for over the course of the game, as well as a good amount of party banter.
Story - The main storyline is a pretty typical save the world or fight the big baddie type of deal. Not necessarily the most creative or innovative, but they put a lot of effort into developing the lore of the game world and taken for it is they did a good job. There are factions that matter and have their beliefs and conflicts. There is also a little bit of simulationist moral choice that isn't always clear cut good and evil. It's definitely not nearly as morally ambiguous or otherwise dark as, say, the Witcher games can be though.
Graphics - The graphics and game engine could be seen in a way as one step or two in improvement from somewhat earlier titles like Neverwinter Nights 2. Not as impressive or detailed as some newer AAA games, but certainly better looking than any of the crowdfunded RPGs that have come out after.
Mechanics - The mechanics are in some ways simplified compared to a full on 3.0 or after D&D RPG (for example, there are only 3 base classes and about half a dozen basic skills shared across classes), though it uses some similar aspects to a D&D RPG in the stat system and some other areas. It also somewhat simulates more complex and varied character options through specializations and the ability to choose different skill trees.

This is a magnificent game that absolutely can't wait to chew your face off.
Right now, there are lots of mixed reviews being posted because of Story Mode, which launched at the beginning of the month I'm writing in. It seems to me that a lot of them - way too many of them - appear to be written by Long Dark veterans who are disgruntled about Wintermute's apparently simplistic mechanics and tasks & quests. For anyone coming into TLD from a background of having never walked a single mile along its bleak, snowy trails, take heart: a lot of these guys aren't reviewing it for you. You, at the beginning of your journey into this massive game, will probably find Story Mode exactly what you need right now. It holds your hand, it lets you edge into the wilderness with the game equivalent of a safety line attached, and it will teach you all the basics, so you can wander out into Survival Mode and...still die, terrifyingly quickly.
Part of the appeal of The Long Dark is how is lets you kill yourself with your own stupidity. If you're sloppy with your inventory management, if you risk something you would never think of risking in a real survival situation, and if you're attacked by wolves and discover you forgot to repair your sleeping bag so now it's ruined and ohgodohgod you're going to die, well, you're going to die.
Your biggest enemy isn't the harsh environment, or the wildlife. It's yourself. And wow, that's thrilling to see in a game.
(I'm a travel writer and avid hiker and bivvy-bagger, so seeing a game that really *gets* that feeling of empowering self-reliance - that's why this is my favourite game.)
It really feels like an achievement when you claw your way up to 50 days without dying, even on one of the lower skill levels (there are four, and the top one is an unrelenting nightmare).
Then you play it smarter, learn crafting and better strategies for caching equipment and preserving food, and you get your way up to 100 days.
Then you start playing the long game, finding the right base too keep going indefinitely, and 200 days get racked up somehow...
But your kit is slowly wearing out. You track back across the enormous interconnected regions, hunting for things you missed the first time round. A book of matches, a pair of socks....a whetstone feels like winning the lottery. The maps are vast, but you learn them, the way you learn anywhere in the world, with your feet and your mind's eye. The weather does its best to kill you, but you're too smart for it. You've mastered this game, you're invincible....
You see a bear, and feel sure you can take it down. For over 200 days you've been avoiding bears because they're too big, too scary, too risky, you've been admirably cautious - but think of 40kg of meat! You heft your rifle, aim and pull off a shot. A splatter of blood. You've winged it. It roars, runs around a rock, and rushes you from behind, way too quick to take a bead on it....
At 20% health with a ruined hat and gloves, you're no match for the blizzard that hits you half an hour later.
Story Mode will take your hand and lead you into the snow. Survival mode will leave you there, terrified and alone, in a world that coudn't care less if you live or die. Your choice, friend.
You've never played anything like The Long Dark.

Well, wow.  I've never posted a game review before, but seeing all these negative reviews makes me feel like I should add my input because I actually love this game.
I'll talk about the story mode first, as that seems to be the main issue people have.  Honestly, I'm not really sure what people expected with the story, but it's a SURVIVAL game.  Obviously most of the quests involve making sure you and the NPC's can survive (ie. gathering supplies, making sure you have working weapons, etc).  I personally think it's really well done, and after playing the sandbox for so long, it's nice to have some direction.  With every quest, you get more information about what's really happening and how everything ended up the way it is.  They updated many locations from the Survival Mode, so even though I'm quite familiar with most the maps, there are still new things for me to discover and explore during the Story.  Sure, it has some bugs.  I've never come across a game that was completely bug-free on release (or anytime tbh), and I don't see why people are so upset over it.  They are clearly working hard to remove all bugs as soon as possible.  As for the half cinematics/half unvoiced dialogue.. I don't have a problem with it.  For me it doesn't make the game any less playable or enjoyable.  Frankly, it's nice not having to wait for the NPC's to finish their sentence when I've already read it in the subtitles in half the time.  The wolves do seem slightly more aggressive as of late, but I personally haven't had any issues with it. If you make sure to get the Distress Pistol in one of the side missions, you'll likely not end up in a fight at all.  Or you know, just walk around them? That seems to work for me anyway.
The Survival Mode is a great freeform version of the game, which is both the extremely relaxing and extremely nerveracking.  There's nothing quite like the feeling of enjoying the serene wilderness one second to hearing a wolf and being in a fight for your life the next.  Permadeath makes every encounter so much more terrifying.  The challenges are a good way to discover the game, in my opinion.  They have the same Survival feel, just with a goal.  The Nomad Challenge for example, requires you to visit multiple locations in mutiple maps and is a good way to do some directed exploring.  I'm also the kind of person that likes to go for Steam Achievements, so that has given me plenty of goals in the game, in all three game modes.
Basically, it comes down to this: If you're looking for some fast-paced, action-filled game, this is not the game for you.  If you're looking for some magically perfect game and will get mad at the slightest bug, don't bother (and goodluck finding a game.)  This game is not about fighting (though you will end up in a few!) or winning or going on some exciting fantastical adventure.  This game is about surviving, realistically in a world that has so much to offer, and that's what I love about it.  So, if you're looking for an actual survival game, I 100% recommend this one.

Took me a while to realize how to heal and what ingredients to use and items to loot. It took ages before I found guns and ammo, then I quickly went back to using the good old spiked baseball bat. The noise of the shotgun in particular is like a vortex that will draw unwanted attention. If you use it you'd better keep running or get besieged until eventually you get out of breath after one too many close combat hits and you stumble and get bitten. Ciao bye bye within minutes. Your carefully organized house with sheets on all windows. Your little cemetary you had dug in the back and in which you had tirelessly massacred and buried there a good fifty of them. Your cupboard and the first aid kit and the handgun...oh God...just because you don't look behind you or you think that this little bathroom or shed will not have zombies in it, be sure that there will be one or two and that it'll get nasty quickly if you don't have a weapon equipped at all times. I'm 10 hours into a single game and my little dude Ben is having a rough couple weeks to say the least. He turned a food run into a Romero'esque supermarket siege that almost cost him his life. He has gotten his bedroom window smashed at night and almost got bitten but killed the zombie with a shotgun, attracting a dozen other biters into the house. He took his shotgun and a first aid kit and some food then bolted towards a secondary base, only to find it broken in with 3 biters ambushing him in the living room. Now he is in a small house further down the road and has massacred a hundred or so zombies so far to secure the surrounding homes. I'm pretty excited to see how this guy will end to be honest.

BIT.TRIP CORE is a pixel rhythm game loosely based off of Missile Command, in which the player must fire in one of four directions in time with music in order to "shoot" bits which are moving through the screen. It is the second game in the BIT.TRIP series, and sadly the only one of them which I wouldn't recommend. I would generally consider it to be among the more difficult BIT.TRIP games, and that is without getting into the imperfections there is with the timing in the PC release.
Like other BIT.TRIP games, as you string together a number of successful hits without a miss, the game will move to a "higher" mode which has more graphic effects, and as you miss enough without getting an appropriate number of successes, you will move to a "lower" mode, which has fewer. CORE starts the pattern of adding a new mode with each successive game, adding SUPER.
For people who really enjoy rhythm games, I'd recommend checking it out, but in another format - it's difficult to play in its current form, albeit not impossible. It's not a *bad* game, just a bit difficult to play.

This game is a rare case. It is an RPG that not only has characters and a story so well written and brought to life that the world totally immerses you within itself, but actually warrants multiple playthroughs.
The story is easily a 10/10, and the character development makes you care.That being said, the graphics havent perfectly withstood the test of time and the blood effects can get rather horrendous; but the game still looks beautiful, if a little murky at times.
The way the game handles character classes, romance and story progression, it is easily possible to go through two playthroughs for each class and still never have seen it all. The mage class is easily my favourite, and the magic system is stunningly in-depth. However, it is easy to fall into a pattern/combo of attacks and actions to get through combat and unless you are playing on higher difficulties this can make the combat boring and stale; the game does however do a decent job of scaling enemies as the game progresses.
The added content in the ultimate edition is an excellent bargain, however it is perfectly acceptable to wait for a sale to pick this up if the $30 price tag is a little much for you. It is certainly worth it.
All in all, this game has a few faults that come with the time it was developed, and these faults are never enough to really take away from the overall experience. I do however recommend playing on normal or higher as the combat is at it's best when you are outgunned and outnumbered, or at the very least at the same level as your opponents.
Ratings:
<Normal - 8/10 - story is great, combat is boring
>Normal - 10/10 - story is great, combat forces you to think and really helps reinforce the idea that you are fighting back against an unstoppable blight.

You know, I think it's about time I said something about Evolve. Evolve is by no means perfect; I think if you found this review then you probably have already seen a lot of conflict of views of the people who've also reviewed this game.
The design is flawed from a longevity standpoint; there's an undeniable thrill about the tracking and hunting of an elusive but powerful beast that one minute isn't a match for your team though a minute later could bite each of your heads off like those wax soda bottle candies. However, there's an undeniable lack of variety even throughout the growing assortment of gamemodes, maps, hunters, and monsters. The game is fun for a time, though after an extended period one notices the colors starting to run together. I feel though Evolve works best as a "pick up for a few rounds" kind of game; a game will rarely run over twenty minutes. I feel in this respect it is an excellent game for this purpose.
(TLDR: Game staying power/entertainment value is stronger when played now and then rather than continuously)
Next is the pricing. When Evolve first came out, no doubt you heard about the developers focusing not on the game but rather using the base game as a platform for future DLC. The DLC packages were also written in an subjectively confusing and unclear way. The base game around the time of release contained lesser amounts of free content for a greater price, though as time goes by and updates and price cuts take place I find the value of Evolve growing and growing. Take this present Christmas Steam sale for example; one can buy the base game and all meaningful character DLC for under $30, which is an excellent deal considering ordinarily the combined price of all of this content is far higher. A lot of the release DLC controversy stemmed from skins that do not affect character statistics and is thus easily passed over, plus the free addition of hunter alternate loadouts adds both free visual and gameplay variety to owners of the base game. Sadly, this likely push from 2K to sell Evolve's future multitude of DLC irreperably damaged the game's reputation to prospective buyers, though as time goes on the game becomes a greater and greater value.
(TLDR: Game DLC originally was expensive and confusing and turned people off, though over time the base game and meaningful DLC is becoming cheaper and free content such as maps, event skins, new modes etc are being added and making the game a better vaule than it was at release)
The last complaint I'd like to address are concerns over the game's balance; over time people would argue that monsters such as the Kraken and Wraith have gotten nerfed and hunters have gotten buffed, thus making it incredibly difficult for not just these but all monsters to win against a well coordinated team of hunters. I'm not going to say TR's balancing of both the individual characters and the hunter vs. monster dynamics have been always the wisest and best long-term solutions, though it shows interest in changing the game through player feedback and gathered statistics. I imagine much of the complaining of particular monsters being overpowered came from PUG players who had no way of organizing themselves to counter the monsters they fought, though competitive hunters would have a far easier time as they could work together more coherantly. I've never been a fan of competitive anything in games, but a lot of the changes over Evolve's lifespan have been the result in serving the interests of the numerous PUG players which you can take as you wish. There's still plenty of time for things to be balanced, and if you're truly concerned over this then I suggest watching some current Evolve videos and seeing if the playing field is to your liking.
(TLDR: Game's balance has shifted to make hunters stronger to suit PUG players who cannot work together as well as competitive players, but these changes are not set in stone... all changes somewhat subjective, see for yourself.)
Would I recommend Evolve? Absolutely. On sale, and with a grain of salt. I'm not going to be the person with almost 80 hours who screams about how the game is broken and unfun, because in my opinion the game's worth checking out if you're looking for a pretty good-looking, solidly-playing asymmetric skirmish every now and then. If you can get the base game and the character DLC for around $25, I absolutely think Evolve is worth it in good content.
(Total TLDR: Game has a rocky history and grainy present but could very well be worth your time for the right price and the right perspective. Don't not believe people when they tell you the things wrong with the game, but don't let them convince you to hate it before you try it.)

To start off, this game is good.  Lots of people say it's bad, and I can understand why.  I don't recommend this to everyone because some of the negatives are quite serious, but I still enjoy play regardless.
I haven't played it much, but I've managed to get what I think is a good snapshot of most of the gameplay.  The gameplay itself is nail-bitingly intense (or for me anyway) and every minor victory feels like you've won a war, but I'm not here to talk about that.  I'm here to talk about the stuff you're thinking about when purchasing this game.  Is the DLC too expensive? Is it unbalanced?  Are the queue times ridiculous?  Well to answer your questions: maybe, no and yes.  The "DLC's", which are actually just playable characters, monsters and their skins are generally quite cheap.  The bunch that come with the game more than satisfied me for quite a while, I had already played quite a bit before I opened the shop.  Now, my purchases were cheaper because of christmas sales, but I managed to clean up quite a few characters and skins with a bit of spare credit I had lying around on my Steam account.  So, if you're not used to Steam-credit transactions instead of in-game premium currency, as I know a lot of games use, it can be quite a change but when you look at what other games charge for premium items, it's not overly expensive.
Is the game unbalanced?  I don't think so.  Can some things be extorted?  Yes.  Can they be counter-extorted by skilled players?  Also yes.  Like a lot of games, it's not broken(mostly), you just haven't learnt how to overcome it.  Yet.
Are the queue times ridiculously long?  Yes.  No argument.  Don't even try to queue up for a PvP.  Find a Evolve-orientated forum like I did, and find a page where people post their Steam ID's with the intention to be friended.  It's a simple method to get PvP matches where they are otherwise difficult to come by.
Hope this helped.

Undeniably a "good" game.  The BETTER question would be "If evolve a good game for YOU".
Evolve is very difficult with a high skill ceiling, and a STEEP learning curve that revolves around a lot of mechanics that are simply "new" to general gamers. To play the game well you really need to have a firm grasp on the game as a whole- From mechanics, to techniques, to knowing each and every character and how they "work".  Changing one character in a match, be it monster or hunter- Changes the strategy completely for everyone involved. The same group of 4 specific hunters hunting 1 monster will change if theyre hunting a different monster.  Likewise as a monster, 1 hunter being different can change the entire mindset and tactics on how to defeat them.
The end result is a highly competitive game from start to finish.  And this is where evolve will or wont break down for you.  There is very, VERY little "Casual" gamer support.  Matches range from 5 to 25 minutes. A match can swing from a sure victory, to utter defeat with a single BAD mistake, on either teams part.
If that bothers you, no- Evolve is a *terrible* game for you. If that all sounds good to you, evolve may be a great game for you.  The community IS small online- But for the most part youll never have trouble finding a full and revolving match online.  The only trouble can be finding a match as monster in "ranked" mode- But this is because theres a disproportionate amount of monsters to hunter players.  You need 1 monster for ever 4 hunters in this mode- Theres simply more monsters than this ratio, so you end up waiting.  Even during free weekends when theres 5-10,000 people online at once, monsters can see long lines.
DLC- Its worth pointing out that yes, there are 2 "tiers" or "packages" of DLC characters you can buy, each package contains 1 character for each class (4 hunters, 1 monster).
BUT
To go with this DLC, it should be noted theyve ALSO given out, and will CONTINUE to give out free modes, free maps, free skins all the time, and FREE CHARACTERS.  Theyve started releasing what they call "Adaptation" characers- At first glance they look like simply "reskinned" pre-existing characters.  But in play these characters *completely* change the dynamics of the game, despite being similar at first glance.  The abilities they have are completely reworked, and basically 180 how to play that character.  Theyve got 4 of these characters out already (1 monster, and 3 hunters), with a 4th hunter and 2nd monster coming out just around the corner (January 2016).  They will continue to keep releasing these free characters, at a minimum until theyve gone through all the base characters.
Its also worth stating that no matter what DLC you do or dont have, it will never divide you from the community.  You will always be allowed to play with anyone and everyone, no matter what DLC they have, and are using.
Its got its ups, and its down. Due to its lack of casual support and highly competitive nature with a steep learning curve- Evolve is a VERY niche game and will NOT be a game for everyone.  If youre after a competitive game with a lot of unique and -very- dynamic mechanics, evolve is a great game.

Okay, so here's the thing: we all know that Evolve (and Turtle Rock by extension) ♥♥♥♥ed itself over on launch horrendously. They locked a lot of content that should have been in the game from the start behind paywalls on day 1 that should have been at the very least been passed out to players who prepurchased the game, if not just put in the ♥♥♥♥ing game for free. It is completely fair to leave the game for this reason, and to hold that massive and obvious mistake against Turtle Rock and never play this game or buy it ever.
BUT. AND A HUGE BUT. ( ay ;] )
The truth is that despite this insane PR suicide by Turtle Rock, the game is legitimately very fun and polished, and since returning to give it another shot I have enjoyed it quite a lot. After 2 full DLC packs of hunters and monsters, along with multiple map packs and game modes that were added free of charge (and even a couple hunter/monster variations), the game boasts a level of diversity that makes it very diverse and interesting from game to game. Also because map packs and game modes were put in for free, you can still play with just the base game and it works perfectly fine, no limits on matchmaking or anything like that.
If the CURRENT STATE of this game was the state of the game on launch, I garauntee that it would have exploded in popularity and would still be popular to this day, no question.
THAT BEING SAID, there is the obvious issue of the playerbase, which has dwindled significantly over time. Queues are difficult to find and full teams are rare at certain points during the day/night. There is a ranked mode that is pretty much superfluous because there's almost no chance you will ever get to utilize it properly with this few remaining players.
Now then, what does that mean for you, as someone reading this review? Incredibly addictive 'game'. This is one for the true lover of problem solving. It is NOT a casual puzzle game. The learning curve is steep, and it's very helpful to have some experience with electrical engineering or programming. The developers managed to pay some attention to detail when it comes to the chemistry (even though it's only superficially about chemistry) and it's nice to see things like real chemical structures and the right numbers of possible bonds etc.
When you find a solution to a difficult problem, it's a joy to watch it play out like clockwork. Despite the fact that you can fast-forward through the solution, once I have it worked out I usually run it at a leisurely pace and watch several cycles unfold. It's truly satisfying.
The game isn't perfect, and there are some annoyances, like the inability to save individual constructions while testing out a different way of solving a given problem. The interface is not perfect, and a better design of this may have made for smoother workflow. I also found the "research" levels to be the most enjoyable and would have preferred not to have the more 'gamey' production and defense levels.
Overall, this is pretty much as good as it gets for people that like difficult problem solving, and if it's up your alley, you will be able to overlook any shorcomings.

Okay so here goes. I am a State Level Emergency Manager, and I saw this game when I was recovering after a hospital stay. What they say they deliver not only is it a great game one of the only truly open ended games I have ever seen. It also follows pretty much what would happen theoretically during a wide scale Emergency Event.
The Vanilla game is good, drop some Mods onto it and the entire game gets a depth that I have not seen in other franchises. I have well over 2000 hours played on this game, but it needs to be said if you like a thought provoking game, where you will pay dearly for complaceny then this is the game for you. If you want a mindless game set in the zombie world then this is not the game for you.
I have to say this game will be one I play for years and with the mods and multi aspect of it it can be immersive as you want it. I played it with my kids (there is an option to lift the zombies out) and tought them some fundamental survival skills though a game normal survival concepts work and pay off.
I have also found the team at Indie Stone to be highly responsive to their gaming community and their pride in product shows. I recently showed this product to several state level emergency managers and they were impressed at the implications and concepts that could be taught, ala the Oregon Traill game in the early 90s.
I have not lived that long with any of my characters: top one year - however I understood how I died and in this game you learn from your mistakes, dont make them again and you live longer.
In closing thank you Indie Stone and thank you to all the Mod Developers and people that make this game so good and give it a depth that is almost never reached

First off, pros of Stonehearth; 10/10 on gameplay idea. City builder with a god-like building sturcture really adds an artistic touch to building a city. With the ability to create your own buildings, save them, and place them wherever you please is a tremendous step towards an in-depths open world strategy game. 7/10 UI system. A small menu at the bottom of your screen allows for an immersive feel without being bogged down by big buttons. Everything is organized into categories and sub categories making tasks easily finished. 7/10 skill play. As an alpha game, the skill needed to play is rather challenging, yet forgiving in the same path. Each day is a new possiblility to add to your town and comes with very specific requirements that are obtained quite quickly.
Cons of Stonehearth; 1/10 game engine. Although it is a block centered game, low fps and stuttering plague gameplay like zubats in a cave. This should be top priority of the developers trying to polish this game into a beta. It seems as if testers before the alpha release were only allowed an hour of gameplay and after playing almost 20 hours, I see game changing problems that weren't apparent in the first hour of play. 1/10 AI engine. At first, hearthlings (hereby called peons) stayed on task and provided a steady amount of work to increase the size of your town, but once you began to improve your town and build more expansively, meaning more than 3 buildings, the game starts to lose ability to keep peons working. For instance, buildings created by you and then used in game are only 3/4 built, granted this is early access and should be graded on such a scale I believe this is game ending to most players and should be kept as a priority in patching, certain professions are notorious for being "lazy" such as the trapper, footman, and farmer, and peons increasingly become absentminded about materials left on top of buildings, building primary buildings, and collecting "loot" from the monsters you kill. 4/10 Tech Tree. As in all games similar, there are simple tools, buildings, items, etc. that are the basic cornerstones to developing your city. In Stonehearth, peons are your main tech tree and must be leveled up in a previously job or skill before being allowed to become another. GREAT idea, yet poor in practice. Some jobs, such as trapper, are difficult to achieve in the beginning, while the level above trapper, aka shepperd, is available to set up at almost the start of the game. This area of the game needs an overhaul on how easy certain skills or jobs become available.
All in all, I would score this game in 3 categories: Finished game score, Growth of game score, and Developer skill score.
Finished game score: 3/10. This game is not finished by any means, and should be updated by the developers weekly if not biweekly.
Growth game score: 10/10. I find this game addicting with all its faults. $25 dollars to support something that, if kept up with by developers, will be in the  top ten games of the year when published is something I personally do not mind, however, if $25 is too steep, then wait till the beta. It will be worth it.
Developer Skill Score: 7/10. I see many customer developer conversations that end well and a very crowd pleasing mentality from the creaters and developers. What I do not see is a smooth game in 3 months which leads me to think that the development team is trying to please too MANY people at once instead of focusing their effort on a single problem. I guess that comes down to how a management team sees problems, but I feel in this particular game, a direct approach to a single problem would result in more improvements to the game in the long run.
In conclusion I would say I am pleased to own this game and wish with utmost energy that the development team, and the community of players who play keep at it in hopes of making it big. I would say WAIT TILL BETA if you are on the fence about alphas, but if you are willing to be a part of a test, then come spend your time and enjoy Stonehearth

I have played this game off and on for about 6 months and can honestly recommend the game. It is still in development, but the developers are extremely engaged and regularly release updates with bug fixes, new content, etc. The core of the game is solid and offers significant room for customization of the buildings within your town. At present, there are bugs, but this is expected. What is promising is that many of the bugs I have observed over the course of the past 6 months, have been taken care of. Do new bugs pop up when new content is released? Of course. However, they are typically resolved within a month, at most, of the new content's release.
The game itself is primarily a city builder with random raids of goblins, undead, etc thrown in to keep the game play interesting and varied. The combat system is a bit wonky at present, but has been steadily improving over time which is a good indication of future improvements to come.
Resource gathering has become rather staightforward and it is relatively easy to keep your villagers gathering what you want them to. It does require a bit of micromanagement as there is not a way to automate their gathering behavior at present (e.g. mine when copper is below 20 in storage, gather wood when inventory is below 15, etc). Once the resources are gathered, though, the tradesmen can be completely automated to maintain inventory levels of the items you wish to produce (e.g. set the Blacksmith to maintain 5 swords in inventory, etc)
In sum, despite the bugs that I have experienced and room for future improvement, I would highly recommend this game. It has vast potential, a very active development team that is engaged with the community, and is generally enjoyable to play.

This is one of my favorite games and I highly recommend it. I have over 200 hours in it and anticipate being able to enjoy it for a long time to come. That said, it is not for everyone, and even post-release and after a flury of patches, it has its charms and its flaws.
Pros:
- Atmosphere captures what it's like to be alone in the woods
- Beautiful world full of opportunities for discovery, exploration, and wonder
- Finding what you desperately need, high-end gear, or sometimes simply not dying is thrilling
- Ammo scarcity and sound-design makes firing a rifle or bow thrilling
- Game mechanics, particularly on higher-difficulty settings, create a constant pressure that pushes you to weigh risks and make tough, often fatal choices
- Dying is typically due to the above-mentioned choices
- 3 modes with which you can experience the game. My favorite is Survival, which is open-ended exploration of the interconnected maps, until you die
- Running into a bear, or worse hearing one and not being able to see it, is horrifying
Cons:
- Wolves, which, if not the cold, are your most likely cause of death, can be frustrating. They add a hunter/hunted aspect to the game, as well as a sense of fear, that keeps things lively. They also cut off routes to destinations, forcing you to choose a different path, risk a confrontation, or abandon your objective. Its a great feeling to so thoroughly best them that you can make a jacket out of their hides, but at other times they can seem overly pervassive. I have had them spawn near me while I was outside too, and have missed a shot I shouldn't have because they were too close, which feels unfair.
- Story mode came as a disappointment. I am not as disenchanted as some, but it limits the player's tool-kit to what the protagonist knows, which is a lot less than someone who has been playing survival mode in early-access. As a walking simulator, it's extremely linear to the point of actively blocking you from exploring areas that aren't relevant to the next puzzle.
In short, it's not much of a
, and much closer to an interactive story.
But it's zany and memorable. The corn and the teddy bear are well voiced and full of character (though the Teddy's incessant insults get a bit tired by the end of the game), and the ending was extremely satisfying, which is rare for any game.
When considering the price, note that this offers about 3-4 hours of entertainment, without a lot of replay value.

You mearly explore the full area you are allowed in at the time, pick up every item, and are told where to place each item.
There is quite a bit of decent world-building on display in side notes and collectable objects scattered around the environments, painting a picture of the buildings and several unseen actors. Unfortunately, it was mind-numbing for the middle 2 hours of my 3 hour playthrough, with a few interesting cutscenes along the way to provide a little bit of entertainment.
I will say, the final gameplay segment and ending had me grinning ear-to-ear. THAT enthusiastic style is what the whole game should have followed, in my opinion. So, it ended on a high note at least.

Okay, before I begin bashing, I will say: excellent sound and art direction. Before you're exposed to the actual core gameplay, you really are spooked and ready for what's coming up next. The soundscape alone was enough to make me jump a few times, initially. A very cinematic experience just from walking through the snow, and I did like the story exposition that you got through the scattered journals, even if that was a little hamfisted. Now...
The actual threats you deal with in the game really detracts from the atmosphere/subtlety of the game, and feels like a complete afterthought; when you do die, it's always completely unexpected and instant, and then you're spawned in some random place that you don't recognize, lost. I died enough times, and for such ridiculous reasons, that I just stopped caring/being immersed in the game at all. All of the carefully crafted atmospheric events and sound effects just stopped phasing me in any way.
Getting instagibbed by a monster you have no chance of ever outrunning, who can see you through rocks, trees, terrain, and other visual blocks even when crouching, is not fun. Neither is suddenly falling into a random trap and instantly dying. Also, lore-wise, why would there even be traps for you to get caught in? Do the demons in this game just spend all day digging spike pits for me to fall in, when they aren't walking around in circles guarding rocks? It's not like the hikers did it, so what's even the purpose? Very obviously just a tacked on obstacle to stretch the content out. I honestly think this game would've been a lot scarier to me if there weren't any actual, physical monsters, but just the THREAT of one. A few things that can kill a player in a game like this are good, but if it happens too often, or if it's too direct, you just get numb to it, and it annoys you, rather than scares you. I reached that point, and beyond.
I've also never been a big fan of the "realistic" map/compass system. It requires extremely good map design, landmarks, and visual cues to implement such a system so that all players can navigate it well, which almost no dev is willing to put the effort forward to do. It's usually falls flat on its face when used in games, and this one is no exception - you even get the impression that the developers were even aware of this, as there are many points on the map where you'll see glowing sets of coordinates to indicate where you currently are... Almost as if they realized after the fact that they had to implement some blaringly obvious clues like that, because their game world and mapping system is otherwise too confusing and counter-intuitive for normal play. The Russian compass, while "immersive", doesn't help.
Definitely one of the weaker and more frustrating horror games I've played.

It took me a long time to decide to buy EVOLVE. I was really turned off by all the DLC and all the negative reviews and all that normal stuff that seems to be bothering people. This game goes on sale a lot, if you don't want to pay full price, just wait and it will go on sale. and the DLC isn't too expensive and you don't even need it to have a good time really. I started the game with none then slowly got it all.
As for gameplay actually goes I think the game is made really well. Being a monster is really fun. Sometimes it's easy because the hunters are bad, and sometimes it's hard becuase the hunters are good. Maps are pretty balanced and so are the hunters. Sometimes you will be hunted by a team that is a really good comp and you will lose and feel like they were to powerful, but that's kinda one of the point as hunters, to build a good team to hunt with, so that's just the game working or you not being good.
As the hunters the game can be frustrating, because if one hunter isn't preforming their role correctly, it really messes up the team. But it is still really fun. As long as you put in a bit of time to learn the maps, the monsters, and the hunters. Once you figure out things like that, which you can do in a solo mode that is just like the online mode but is easier cause the bots aren't very smart in this game, being a good hunter isn't hard. If you have trouble finding good teams, you should probably friend people that you play with that do well, so you can party up. And honestly if you think your team isn't doing well, you should just get a headset and talk to them, as long as you aren't a jerk, people will usually work together, which is what this game is about.
this isn't a game that you are going to turn on, and start winning, unless you are pretty smart and already understand most of the game mechanics. Like other vets, I bought this game way back on Desura. Sadly, in 5+ years of development it's progress has been exceptionally minimal, even understanding some of the difficulties the team has faced.
The biggest problem, however, is that Cataclysm: DDA, which is free, just does everything better (albeit more in the roguelike vein than the semi real-time isometric vein).
Project Zomboid isn't really bad--it's just boring. There's no NPCs, very limited enemies (who are eminently manageable), no pressing survival curve/drive.
The skill system is not bad, in principle, but advancing in most skills seems only barely relevent to your survival (as opposed to C:DDA, where every new level opens up increasingly complex options).
Add to that a shockingly counterintuitive user interface (storage, so vital to a game of this genre, is an utter pain in the 'nads to manage) and I'd recommend you're better off waiting for this game to either finally rise from the dead... or be put down once and for all.

I have played this game off and on for about 6 months and can honestly recommend the game. It is still in development, but the developers are extremely engaged and regularly release updates with bug fixes, new content, etc. The core of the game is solid and offers significant room for customization of the buildings within your town. At present, there are bugs, but this is expected. What is promising is that many of the bugs I have observed over the course of the past 6 months, have been taken care of. Do new bugs pop up when new content is released? Of course. However, they are typically resolved within a month, at most, of the new content's release.
The game itself is primarily a city builder with random raids of goblins, undead, etc thrown in to keep the game play interesting and varied. The combat system is a bit wonky at present, but has been steadily improving over time which is a good indication of future improvements to come.
Resource gathering has become rather staightforward and it is relatively easy to keep your villagers gathering what you want them to. It does require a bit of micromanagement as there is not a way to automate their gathering behavior at present (e.g. mine when copper is below 20 in storage, gather wood when inventory is below 15, etc). Once the resources are gathered, though, the tradesmen can be completely automated to maintain inventory levels of the items you wish to produce (e.g. set the Blacksmith to maintain 5 swords in inventory, etc)
In sum, despite the bugs that I have experienced and room for future improvement, I would highly recommend this game. It has vast potential, a very active development team that is engaged with the community, and is generally enjoyable to play.

DoE is a fresh, innovative take on the rogue-like genre. Its door-opening mechanic drives the action of the game, and it is addictive. It plays a little like a really exciting and engaging board game, with your success relying on your strategy and planning a couple steps ahead and a little less on quick reflexes. Each opened door brings new challenges and rewards. The system of risk and reward results in numerous emergent stories to tell, especially when a baddie decides to bust down several extra doors, flooding you with enemies.
If you spend a little time playing (or reading) and learn the mechanics of the game, you'll be successful enough to face the challenges of the random-generated moments that can result in moments of the game reaally trying to kill you.
Additionally, it has a top-notch soundtrack and a fantastic art-style if you love pixel art like I do. The characters are vibrant and unlocking all the characters is difficult but satisfying. The cast of characters and the numerous "pods" which alter the game rules slightly (like, no health regen, but cheaper healing cost, etc.) will challenge you to adapt and learn different play styles and characters. The multiplayer option is really fun, as well.
In summary, its satisfying replayability and stylish flair offer endless fun ;)

One thing I certainly have to say for Dungeon of the Endless is that it's awfully hard to describe. You're basically in a ship trying to move a crystal from one floor to the next, killing enemies that spawn in unlit rooms which try to attack the crystal. The caveat being that you don't have enough power to light ALL the rooms.  Within that framework, you can make yourself better at killing enemies (leveling up or finding items) or research and drop some defenses and machines to help you do it. Playing the game typically comes down to thinking in advance about what could happen and taking chances. Should you build something that, over time, will help you research more defenses, even if you may not spend much more time in that particular level? Should you risk hanging out across the map maximizing food production, if your gun will mean the difference in whether your teammate is able to defend the crystal (or themselves).  These tense decisions keep the game engaging.

This game has a really unique feel to it.
Challenging, but mostly things that can be foreseen to a certain degree.
You do not control the combat directly.  Your character fights whatever is near them and you just tell them what room to go to.
Lit rooms do not spawn monsters.  Every time you open a door (you've ended your 'turn' by doing so) there's a chance that the dark rooms may spawn monsters.  If players occupy those rooms, they will not spawn there when the door is opened.  The monsters are basically trying to get to your spawn point -- this is one part tower defense.
After you've cleared a path you feel confident about and feel like you've gotten enough loot/XP from a level you have one person slowly carry the crystal to the exit.  Everyone has to be there when they hit it or you're dead as dead can be!
Very interesting game.  If you're looking for some weird challenging planned dungeon crawling, this is for you.  It will take a few runs to really understand what's going on and then it clicks.

Bit.Trip Core is the second entry in the Bit.Trip series, playing a bit more like a typical rhythm game in some aspects. The graphical and musical style from Beat is carried over from Core. In this game though, the graphics are not as crazy but still are trippy and weird, while the music is a lot more subdued. The story and cutscenes tend to revolve around Commander Video and 2 figures that look a lot like Commander Video.
The gameplay consists of controlling an object in the middle that can fire up, down, left, or right. The goal is to hit each block as it passes through a line. This felt a little bit like Guitar Hero in trying to match a block with a direction and firing the laser. Just like in Beat, blocks move on the screen and with different patterns or in huge groups. Bosses exist at the end of the level with 2 more Atari references, and included to the game are bombs to remove difficult blocks onscreen.
Core feels a bit flawed though. There are times when I was interested in the pattern of the blocks and the level designs, while other times I felt bored. Sometimes I would easily get the hang of a pattern and be in sync to the music, while other times I wouldn't and try to button mash my way out. The mellowed out design and more abstract gameplay in Core makes the game a bit harder to enjoy. As a whole, the game is roughly harder than Beat, although there are points where the game is easy and then it suddenly ramps up in difficulty. The time to beat Core is also roughly the same as to finish Beat as well.
Bit.Trip Core will be fine for players who played some of the other Bit.Trip games like Beat or Runner and want more Bit.Trip action. The game itself isn't perfect, but gives a different kind of game that isn't the most amazing, yet offers some interesting things to check out.
It's an interesting concept but it's way, way too hard.  You'd have to be an alien to be able to play it well.  Even harder than beat.

BIT.TRIP CORE is much easier than BIT.TRIP BEAT, but has many similarities as far as game styling.  I actually prefer this one for gameplay since the directional input is easier to manage than the tilt/mouse/joystick style of BEAT, though I think I like the music in BEAT better.  Overall, a good addition to the BIT.TRIP line and worth a play if you like the style.

Bit.Trip Core suffers from giving too little, too late. For the first two thirds of the game I was certain it was my least favorite of the Bit.Trip Saga that I'd yet to play, only to find the final third of the game (or in other words the third level) vastly improved on everything that came before. Even still, it's hard for me to even begin to recommend it, as by that point my experience was already soured and I was ready for it to be over.
As is the case with every Bit.Trip game, the gameplay of Core differs wildly from past games, placing you in the middle of the screen with the ability to shoot lasers in four directions. Blocks come out from the sides of the screen, and you need to time your shots to hit them as they cross over your line of fire. In theory and keeping with Bit.Trip tradition, these are supposed to line up with the beat of the audio track, but in practice there is very little rhythm at all to the patterns which makes it incredibly difficult to time shots with how short a window you are given. It's not until the last level that these designs finally come together and you can see what Gaijin Games was going for with a fantastic closer that feels really rewarding once you get in sync with the track, which makes it so disappointing that near everything that came before was just rubbish.
For a game you can finish in under and hour, it's hard to recommend Core when only a third of it is worth playing, and even then is likely to annoy those who don't posses a keen sense of rhythm. It's ideas are solid but its execution lacking, and on the whole I found little enjoyment to be had from what eventually showed itself to be an interesting concept. If only it had done so earlier.

BIT.TRIP CORE is a rhythm game and is the second entry to the BIT.TRIP franchise also being my favorite. Note that I have played the Wii (and 3DS) version of this game a lot more then I have on the PC so I have a lot more hours in the game then it shows.
The way CORE works is, you are playing at the + in middle of the screen. When a beat (square things) comes you have to take aim in one of the four directions and shoot the beats. The beats are in-time with the music and you will need to use the beat of the song to hit these accurately.
A staple to the BIT.TRIP franchise is the zones. The higher the zone, the higher your multiplier will be, thus more score. You zone up by hitting a certain amount of beats while not missing too many. Staying in higher zones results in more score, but it is really easy to fail out of it. The higher the zone, the better the music gets which is another thing to keep you motivated to keep doing better.
To fail a stage you will have to drop out of the Nether zone (the lowest zone) and there are no checkpoints. If you don't have experience then this game will be really hard at first. The difficulty curve is steep and the first level (Discovery) will be hard for first-timers. However once you get the hang of the game and mechanics, the next two levels will not be as hard.
Personally, once I pick up a good rhythm game I will spend too much time in it and this game is no exception. I find it very addictive to try to improve my score more and more.
Also, note that there are only the three 15 minute levels; Discovery, Exploration and Control. Playing through the game without failing will take just 45 minutes, but if you're motivated to get further improve your scores (like me), it shouldn't be a huge problem.
As a rhythm game, the game is partially dependent on the music, so is it good? Definitely, CORE probably has my favorite music of any of the BIT.TRIP games, though that is subject to opinion. Also as I said before, the higher zone you're in, the better the music gets. Exploration is my personal favorite. (*^▽^*)
As far as sound effects go, they're solid and they do the job well.
Between the three versions of the game (PC, Wii, 3DS) I feel that if you have the right controller (the Xbox 360's circular D-Pad design does not go well with CORE), PC is the best because of the increased resolution. Also, the challenges which flip the + 90 degrees are actually challenging on the PC cause you can't just flip the controller like you can on Wii. Don't bother with the 3DS version, it's basically broken as the music de-syncs after the first section of Exploration and Control.
BIT.TRIP CORE is up there in my all-time favorite rhythm games. The great music and addictive gameplay keep me coming back to spend even more time in it.
Despite the difficulty curve, this is a very solid game. If you are a fan of rhythm games, definitely consider picking CORE up, and check out the rest of the franchise for that matter.
Thanks for reading and I hope you'll like this game as much as I do if you decide to pick it up!

If Myst was a puzzle game for artists, and crossword puzzles are a puzzle game for linguists, SpaceChem is a puzzle game for programmers.

"Stupid idiot." - Vladdy

6/10. Anthropomorphic "sentient" corn. Reminds me a little bit of the Monkey Island games, but not as funny or complex.
I did enjoy my time with Maize, but the game feels... empty a lot.
The sticky note conversation between Bob and Ted are pretty entertaining... but predictable. (But not enough I got bored, just "well, there's a formula"). Vladdy's dialogue... he uses the words 'idiot' and 'stupid' more often than the word 'the.' The verbal abuse is sorta amusing sometimes but it gets old pretty quickly.
Which leads to what this game is like:
-wander aimlessly looking for highlighted items
-pick up item
-read description (might even tell you exactly where to use, although it only does this early on)
-figure out where item goes
-repeat
None of the puzzles are super difficult. When stuck, it usually means "wander around looking for an item you missed."
The real problem with this game, and why it's a "barely recommend" is because it's pretty empty. Whenever the corn shows up, it's amusing. And it's these bits that kept me playing through the game. But  the time between such encounters is longer than I would like, so at times it felt like I was playing a "run around and look for items" simulator more than a game. I didn't like the long stretches without other characters. Once Vladdy is there, it's a little less quiet, but his dialogue is... uninspired. He's worth a couple of chuckles, but after a while, there's a lot of missed opportunity there in his characterization.
If it wasn't for the sheer absurdity of the premise of this game, and the frequent sticky-notes with hints of backstory hidden around the facility, the game would be pretty boring. But I chuckled *just* often enough.
Children may enjoy this game. I did not.

Have to say I'm very disappointed in story mode. I've loved the sandbox mode although have played so much of it now that it's gotten tedious, challenge modes were great - So I was looking forward story mode to give me some direction and add in some new areas to explore.
Episode one is not AS bad as episode 2. The start of it is a little simplistic and linear but that's too be expected as it's teaching the mechanics, and to be honest was probably the best part of the story mode. Everything is looking kind of OK if not spectacular (wolves are annoyingly aggressive, but not really a threat... just enough to make you waste time and resources healing up and fixing clothing) until you get to the grey mother and it's all downhill from there, really. After the main dialogue is out of the way it switches to subtitles with no audio which just comes across as lazy and from there you get sent on fetch quest after fetch quest. There's no real incentive to explore as most of the essential items in the game (knife, hatchet, distress pistol etc.) are found in locations you go to for story mode, and not hard to find. Food, medical supplies and so on are abundant so no need to hoard those - really could do with a difficultly setting for story mode - and even if you do you won't be able to carry most of it when you leave the area for good. Doesn't take long to find decent enough clothes to last you through most weathers (or, that SHOULD last you - get to that in a minute).
So, you get through episode one, which is tedious and boring for the most part, and hope that it gets more exciting from there. It doesn't. For episode two you end in mystery lake which if you're an experienced player you'll know like the back of your hand with one or two minor changes - and as you'll already have most of what you need, and be bored out of your mind, exploring doesn't really feel worthwhile. Fetch quest to carter hydro and then you get sent on the mother of all pointless quests... To fix Jeremiah's rifle. Oh. My. Lord. This sodding mission involves travelling ALL the way across Frozen Muskeg, and then most of the way through Broken Railroad, just to click on a tool after a ridiculous cutscene where you trip over a body that you will have spotted a mile off in play mode. THEN after a brief spell of unconsciousness you're introduced to the aurora, which while very pretty seems mostly pointless - All it seems to do is make the wolves more angry and erratic, as if they weren't bad enough already, and make the flashlight you find when travelling to the hunting lodge nearby on yet another fetch quest work... But given the lantern works better and oil is abundant, you'll probably just use that anyway. After finding the obligatory rifle you then get to travel back to Mystery Lake. Oh the joys.
But it gets better! Then you have 4 fetch quests in a row, all collecting things you'll have already been collecting anyway (OK, you might not have fished yet or hunted deer, but that's because there's no shortage of food, rabbits are easy to kill, and you can't craft clothing yet, so why would you bother) in what I can only assume is some sort of belated tutorial. Great. And then there's the bear hunt and christ is it the biggest slog I've ever faced. You have to shoot this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 6 times in 6 different places and get mauled 5 of those times assuming you landed the shot each time (except the game glitched for me so I had to go back to each location after shooting it and shoot it again to get it to move on... luckily without a second mauling). You know those perfectly adequate clothes I mentioned earlier? Yeap, be prepared to spend hours repairing those and possibly lose some anyway, especially if you're a new player and don't realise the damage being done. Hope you stockpiled on shoes, because you won't have enough cured leather to fix them so you will lose them and have to wander around barefoot. If you're like me and have stockpiled skins and guts from all the fetch quests you've been doing you'll then be disappointed to realise that the plan of making better clothing is out, too. You'll also regret dumping the abundant medical supplies you found on the way in favour of being able to carry the 20 types of tools the game wants you to have as you'll be using a minimum of one bandage and one lot of antiseptic each time you're mauled. And you'll have to rest up for a while after each mauling, too, and then wait for the next bit of daylight, then wait for blizzards to pass, and before you know it it's taken you hours to kill one sodding bear. Oh, and if you happen to find you can't survive after a mauling because there's no way to prevent yourself bleeding out etc, well tough luck... The game saves after each mauling and it counts as a checkpoint, so you'll have to do the whole episode again. Didn't happen to me but I wasn't far off it at one point. In sandbox I love this "no second chance" brutally but I don't feel it is appropriate for story mode - Really needs the check points to be placed at points where you are guarenteed to be safe and healthy.
I'll admit I've not gone past this point yet but compared to the bear hunt I'm looking forward to the long journey trekking all the way to the radio tower. Probably worth noting there's been a couple of days or more between each time I've played it which is unusual for me.
Maybe if I hadn't been looking forward to story mode so much, maybe if there hadn't been so much hype and so many delays, maybe I wouldn't be so negative about it. But as it stands, I cannot recommend it for story mode... If survival is your thing and you can amuse yourself without a set goal, then it's worth picking up for the sandbox. Otherwise, right now, don't bother. Sorry, Hinterland, but you've messed up on this one. If I keep playing through story mode it'll only be in the vain hope that it will improve... But I'm not holding my breath for it. :/

The Long Dark is simply the best survival game I have played. The game has you take your time completing simple tasks, the most time consuming of which is simply exploring. Based strictly in reality, The Long Dark is harsh but captivating. Spending a few minutes thinking about how you might survive the night outdoors in a very isolated, resource-poor area might very well get you through another day. Accept the situation you are in, sort out how to survive, and appreciate the beauty of such a well-made game.
You will want to set aside 1-2 hours for each play session. Most time is spent walking (note: NOT running), looking for supplies and shelter. You will get frustrated when you discover a house with dozens of searchable fridges, drawers, and cabinets, 95% of which are completely empty, but this is a part of the charm.
Survival is not sexy. It is brutal.

This game is embarrassing to show people. There are so many flaws, technical, narrative, and otherwise.  It's a good thing Ubisoft is taking some time off to figure out what to do with this series, because this is the first main AC game I will have not finished, and would have divorced me from the franchise.  Unity was a technical mess, but I still managed to finish that.
This is a bad game with a terrible identity crisis; it is so obvious that it was touched by many teams comprising hundreds of people mostly strange to each other because there just isn't any polish to be found.  It's a plethora of systems and activites all competing to give the player something to do, in an open world context that is of such modern cliche that I can point singly to this title as the one that convinced me the concept is stale yet garish in its desperation to entertain you.
The controls have always been iffy in these games, but layers upon layers of iterations on contextual inputs and  finicky movement culminates into such a frustrating mess for Syndicate. They've solved the problem with the unpredictable parkour by just largely deprecating it with the grappling hook; the streets are so wide, and buildings so far apart, to accommodate the terrible horse & buggy "driving" system, that the grappling hook is necessary to gain any ground if you want to move or explore above street level.
This entry epitomises the series' fast and loose cash-in development cycles by being a buggy, discordant mess.  Frequent crashes, bugs, absurd AI behavior, disjointed narrative -- how they expect the player to invest in the activities being asked of them when it can barely bother to set precedence to do so is just incomprehensible.  I thought about just main-lining the story as I have in the past, but it is so heavily discouraged by flashing the proverbial "advertisement" for a new task / activity / chore every 10 feet you move, that trying to even make sense of -what- or -where- the next story mission is can be its own mini-game; especially given that, for example, you may have 3 different "Sequence 5" main story quests available at once. Which to pick?  It's like they purposely tried to disrupt cohesion around their narrative just out of fear that the player could possibly feel aimless at any given moment. Instead of guiding the player, they dissuade progress.
I also love how, instead of teaching me its systems, it would just inform in a tooltip that I have "51 new tutorial entries" to look at in the menu. Cool. I feel like I could go on, but I've given up on this game, and prattling on and on about a year+ old game's flaws at this point is just an excercise in self-flagulation.

+ Realistic multi-faceted survival gameplay that extends beyond just fighting zombies.
+ Very well fleshed out RPG-style system of traits and skills.
+ Impressively large, open game world with no transitions of any sort.
+ Engaging crafting and building system.
+ Easily customizable game settings can extend replay value.
- Solo play becomes very stagnant and boring once you gain an understanding of basic survival tactics.
- The traits and skills don't always feel terribly well balanced.
- By far the slowest development speed I've ever seen.
Project Zomboid is obviously targetting people who want a very realistic representation of a zombie survival scenario. In fact, even ignoring zombies, it's the closest I've ever seen to a realistic survival game. I would actually argue that it's much better to view Project Zomboid as a simulator instead of a traditional game, and in a lot of ways it won't engage you unless you invest yourself into making your own story.
So if the idea of playing a "zombie apocalypse"
with very realistic components appeals to you, Project Zomboid is probably the best you're going to find. Just keep in mind that it definitely favors realism over gameplay: some people will love that, some people will hate that.
Also, seriously, the development speed of this game is glacial. The developers have been great in the sense that they've consistently supported their product and continued speaking to the community unlike other games that get caught up in development hell in early access, but you should factor that in when you're buying this. This might still take years to get a full release.
