The first Baldur's gate is the best one. It is a nice worldly balance of good and evil, allowing for many different players of many different styles to play this game and be left satisfied with the end results. Having the ability to choose your path and your moral stance seems to do well in this game; since the world in itself tends to be as I said: balanced. The range of quests offer decent reward and the game's challenge is nice. The game plot wise is interesting and starts to develop and grow more as you play, which I must say is a great way for a game's plot to go.
While I am not particularly a big fan of the E2's THAC0 system, if you set up your character and companions with the right skills and are resourceful in using them, this game won't be a constant "miss, miss, miss, critical miss." If people don't like THAC0 or DND's sometimes unpredictable conclusions (in terms of fighting, etc); then you might not like it. The lore is somewhat gritty, but it gives you some room to fix things with nice endings; thus not being a complete waste of time for Good/Neutral characters.
The older game engine's pathfinding for your party as well as some other issues such as not being able to shift-click and see the "waypoints" for movement is actually a nuissance when a random member gets suck in your group while you are trying to move around an obstacle. Now correct me on this if I am wrong, but I was unable to find a way to maintain my party's formation, thus when I tell them to move it seems like they don't stick together, and whoever makes it first will likely be the first target from a enemy encounter. This can be very frusterating at times, especially when you want to assign who you want in the front of a column, etc and if they will walk "together" while holding the formation.
The game is old, but I would have expected that maybe the Enhanced Edition would have implemented some improvements in these areas. The sound effects are as old as the game, but they are not bad to begin with. The only issues I have with audio is that some magical spells are particularly too loud; such as the spider web trap or the thorn spells; they make lots of noise at a higher volume than you are used to. The inventory management is still the way it was  from the first release in 1998, where you can't have other members pick up gear if your current member is full. I was expecting maybe in the Enhanced Edition that the items on the ground could be sorted through the party's inventory, rather than me having to keep clicking different people and then having them pick up the items.
Overall rating:
6/10
Breakdown of Positives:
+ Good lore from an older game.
+ Enhanced Edition gameplay and interaction tweaks.
+ Additional characters introduced in the Enhanced Edition.
+ Game's atmosphere is well-balanced to cater to the choices of any moral alignment.
+ Starts at a nice pace and picks up mid-game.
+ Runs very good both on Windows and Linux from my experience.
Breakdown of Negatives:
- THAC0 is a flawed to-hit formula, was hoping maybe a change to the newer 3.5 forumla.
- Party pathfinding is around the same as the old games. Was hoping to see this improved.
- Inventory system was not improved really. I was looking for a easy auto-sort function for picking up loot.
- Some magical spells emit rather out of place sounds at higher volume, like thorns or spider-web.
- Party formations are nearly useless, since parties will NOT retain the formation upon movement, but rather break up whenever they run into something (including other members). This can be frusterating and end up with a confrontation with a broken unit coherency.
Conclusion: The game is fun and I definitely enjoyed the story and the openness of this classic, but some areas of the gameplay as mentioned make me question the significance of this "enhanced" edition..

So, I'm rewriting my review because many of the bugs I'd mentioned are either much diminshed or appear to be completely gone.  That's a good thing, and I commend Radient for their efforts.  Stonehearth is much more stable now.
Unfortunately, the game is nowhere near even a beta, and this thing was supposed to be a full release how many years ago?
And I'm sadly still not able to recommend the game.  It's cute, it's still being updated, and the devs seem at least marginally in touch with the fanbase.  This is promising.  There is still a long, long way to go for this game.  If you want to pay too much for too little right now, that's your business, but the current price point gives you a tiny town simulator with some mobs.  Building can be entirely too touchy, with custom houses not having an adequate undo function while designing and an unclear guideline on what constitutes enough space for your villagers (or rather, "hearthlings") and which decor will bring them joy.  Some character features still feel underdeveloped (no surprise for an alpha, but it's worth mentioning), and there are still a few issues with pathing, especially related to scaffolding.
What initially drew me to the kickstarter campaign was the promise of deep customization.  Given how finicky the building construction is, I don't see that happening anywhere but the far future, if at all.  I want this game to succeed, in no small part because I invested in it early.  Sadly, it seems it's just going to turn into a generic town builder given the current direction.

If You're looking for a somewhat modern interpretation of an Old School RPG, Dragon Age Origins is probably the best choice. It is a very well executed combination of Neverwinter Nights and Baldur's Gate in the sense that choices are very important and so is the depth of creating and building a character. minus the Dungeon's and Dragons ruleset of any kind making it extremely more accessible to newcomers. Gameplay is Real time with pause which allows for a tactical playstyle and strategizing. DA:O has 3 base classes (Warrior, Mage, and Thief) plus 4 specialization classes for each of the base classes allowing for many ways to play and making a character that suits your playstyle. Every class is enjoyable and has their strengths and weaknesses, you will need party members of each class as they synergize quite well in many situations. The setting is very inspired by D&D and Lord of the Rings which really drew me in but at the same time it feels very original and has a lot of depth in its history and worldbuilding. I'm not going to mention the story as I would like for you the reader to experience it yourself, I'll just tell you that I've never been a guy who has ever cared for story in a video game but this game hooked me hard back in the day (I first played it in 2012 on a ps3 before I discovered PC gaming so don't attack me lol). This is a game that I will personally remember for a very long time and I would greatly recommend it to any RPG fan as the choices feel very impactful and the gameplay is very engaging.

Endless Enjoyment
You look at the door and wonder what’s behind it. Salvation? Doom?
You’re not sure how long you’ve been roaming these halls now, working your way forward and upwards, through myriad savage encounters with sentient rocks, bugs, slimes, demons, and other cavernous creatures.
All you remember is that the escape pod of your prison ship crash-landed on this desolate planet a good time ago, straight into the lower levels of some kind of Endless underground facility, and your ragtag band of crew members and prisoners has been carrying the ship’s generator from elevator to elevator till now, powering up doors and automated defenses along the way.
Some friendly species, equally trapped as you and craving liberty or fortune above all else, offer their services for Dust, the mystical nano-elements that go for currency around these parts.
Amassing enough of this Dust substance attracts all kinds of nasty critters, but it also recharges the generator, and even provides the means to build food, industry and science stations, who in turn give you another slim fighting chance against said critters on every floor you pass by.
And chances are more slim than ever. You see your comrades in arms fall around you, and nothing can get them back up. But you keep pushing, using all of your skills and resources to survive the next onslaught, until you reach the next door. What will come next? Friend or foe? A powerful artefact, or the exit maybe?
And then what? If you reach the surface of the planet, how will you survive Auriga?
This is the Dungeon of the Endless.
This… is your past.

Alright, I really need to re-edit this. Before I start, I DO recommend this game, because you WILL have fun. A ton of fun. The game's great. Incredibly unique, fun, interactive, fun characters, fun concepts, etc etc. That being said, some elements of the game can be really, really frustrating if you're unlucky.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- RNG is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It really is. Just to put some perspective, I just did a Drill run aiming to unlock the next pod (requires beating 24 floors), and because of *1* single bad batch of RNG, I lost. No counterplay, nothing I could do, I just got a bad batch of enemies and was forced to lose after 2 hours of intensive playing. My characters had a great skill spread (Pyro / others for AOE work), were highly leveled, all of my modules were highly leveled and had a great mix of them, but nope, one unlucky batch of enemies and it was impossible to win. Keep in mind that I had absolutely NO difficulty WHATSOEVER with the first 20 floors. None. Just 1 bad RNG batch, forced to lose. Cool.
- Enemies are way too difficult to differentiate. After 30 hours I still struggle to tell which does what, and to my knowledge there's no way of knowing. There should be a monster encyclopedia that shows you and tells you their abilities. Speaking of which, explosive enemies feel hugely unbalanced. In a game where the spawns consist of a set few enemies per floor, if you get explosive enemies and some crappy RNG, you can get a huge wave of them and have them all explode at the same time trying to kill your modules, which actually just 1-shots your whole team and insta-kills any low HP characters you have. Almost no counterplay to this. You just bank mid-fight on killing them ASAP or at least negating as much damage as you can.
- The UI is messy. For around the first 20 hours I actually didn't delve in to turret upgrades because I struggled to actually differenciate what the turrets did and how effective they actually were. Hell, the creators of the game thought it was even appropriate to slap jokes and puns in to the actual descriptions of these turrets which made learning what they do even more annoying instead of just having a box that pops up with a joke if you hover your mouse over the icon.
- Items feel really, really lame. Anyone who plays the game can definitely agree with me on this. Some of the items are great and come with skill upgrades, and some of the items feel really good when you get them, but there are so many items that feel like filler items. They have almost identical stats to other items, but they'll just be strictly worse by "2 less attack" or something like that. It's not a matter of "It's a starter item, so it'll be worse" because the rarity of the items are the same. There's literally just one item that does the same thing as another, but better.
- The "Easy" and "Too Easy" terminology is really off-putting for new players. The game's really difficult, so clearly the devs were trying to be funny with those labels. In reality, easy is actually like hard, and too easy is like normal. There aren't any other difficulties. There are pods that you can choose from, and certain pods have effects that can make the game harder (which is like "Insane" difficulty in most games). New players are left wondering why the game is unbeatably difficult for them when they're only in "EASY'. I can only imagine a bunch of people gave up or refunded when seeing that "EASY' was way, way too hard for them. You're practically required to start off a bunch of runs in "Too Easy" to figure out the game for the first 10 hours.
- The game only has 1 song. Yup, 1 song (2, but the other is only briefly when you carry the crystal). It's basically a 15 second loop over, and over, and over, and over. Fortunately it's not an unpleasant.. "song", so this isn't all that annoying and you don't exactly notice in game. But really, they couldn't come up with some awesome 8-bit soundtrack? Would've been so good for this game if it felt more arcade styled.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall the game is fantastic, but there are some definitive issues that make it feel REALLY frustrating to play instead of a relaxing arcade-like experience. You get some good, clean runs, and you have a blast, but then you get 1 bad RNG experience and it completely puts you off from replaying. There's a lot here they should fix.

A great combination of rouge-like and tower defense with a cast of characters that have unique playstyles.  The player controls up to four heroes in an attempt to find the exit to each floor of the dungeon.  Opening a new door reveals a horde of monsters, treasure, or other events.  Action only occurs when a new door has opened; otherwise the player can strategically set up traps/modules and manage resources or inventory at their own pace (turn based).  This balance of crazy action and thoughtful, lonely atmosphere is great.
The game can be difficult, but I don't think it is ever unfair.  The one bad thing though is that the tutorial is severely lacking.  It is almost required to have a Steam guide alongside your first couple of playthroughs.  Once you have the basics under your belt, however, this becomes a deep and rewarding experience.
Other similar games I have enjoyed FWIW are FTL, Rogue Legacy, and various turn based strategy games.

Amplitude are most well known for their Endless Space and Endless Legend games, while Dungeon of the Endless seems to have gone a bit under the radar, which is a shame because it’s a brilliant genre mash-up that more people should play.
The Short:  A fun, tense and somewhat rogue-ish strategy/RPG hybrid that is enjoyable, surprisingly deep and defiantly very replayable.
The Long:
This game is brilliant in that it hits a sweet spot between having very simple systems at its core, but offers the player a lot of depth in how they approach the game.
Your heroes, who progress rpg style, havea limited number of resources to use (science, food, industry, dust) in order to get your energy crystal to the elevator in each level, building turrets, healing stations and such along the way.  Enemies spawn in waves, tower defence style, but you can control somewhat where they spawn – the only spawn in unpowered rooms.  However, you only have a limited amount of power in every level, and once you start the mad dash to the elevator with the crystal, the enemies keep spawning.  In order to succeed, you have to plan really well, using your modules, power and heroes to make sure the crystal gets to the elevator.  Oh, and there’s our old friend permadeth to mess with us too.  As you explore, every time you open a door can cause enemies to spawn, and it gets pretty tense as you never kno what you're going to find in each new room.
What it all boils down to is a really interesting strategy/rpg/tpwer defense game which forces you to make interesting choices as to how to use your ever smaller bag of resources in every level.  A run through to the final floor might take 3 or 4 hours, but this game has so much replay value in the procedural generation, different starting escape pods which effect the game a lot, and a wide variety of heroes to find and then get killed because you’re not concentrating on what’s going on.  No two runs will ever be the same...
And did I mention the wonderful pixel graphics?
My only beefs with the game are common beefs with all games that rely on RNG – it can be wildly inconsistent.  Sometimes its too easy, as you’ll find the elevator really quickly and have very little enemies to deal with.  Sometimes its unjustly punishing, with hardly any resources on a level and a ridiculous number of enemy spawns.  Or sometimes you’ll go levels without being able to find what you need – in one play through, I was on level 12 (I think there are 14 levels in each run) and I still hadn’t found any weapons for one character, despite each of the others having found plenty.  Although I was prepared for this through playing other RNG games like Darkest Dungeon and Crypt of the Necrodancer, it can be a cause of salt.  Nothing game breaking or spoiling though.
Overall, I really liked this game for its cool pixels, fun mash-up of genres, and most of all that it forces you to make difficult decisions with how you use your limited resources.  I really hope more people play this game and it gets some kind of sequel someday soonl there's nothing else quite like this out there (that i've played, anyway).

. This game is basically a turn based game. But at the same time, it is not. Because it is missing one thing that many turn-based games can't avoid: Waiting. In many cases, you will not have to wait alot. Because you can always do something. Research, buy and sell, upgrade, plan your upgrades, plan a new route and so on.
It forces you
and that is what I love the most about it. You will never have enough of everything and your enemies will constantly grow in numbers and in strength. So every turn is important. You will have to count in order to know when you will be able to research or build what. You will have to plan routes and prepare for hordes that might attack your vulnerable resources. You will have to understand the hero class you are playing and how your whole team would benefit the most of your actions. There is so much to plan and seeing it work out afterwards is extremely satisfiying. The moment you hope your route to the elevator is safe and you fight off hordes of monsters, never knowing if the teammate that carries the objective will make it is awesome. Thats another important point:
. If you don't make it, you were not prepared in most cases. But thats not the end of the story. If you die, you will still be present, can manage your resources and support your team and if they manage to find a new hero, they can hire it and give you control over him. So, this game shows you without any mystery, that you have to work as a team. You depend on each other. And if two people of the team die, the rest wont get far. If somebody simply opens the doors in a rush because of missing patience, the whole team will have to deal with the consequences and mostly, be punished. But, you will always know what you did wrong. So, now that I have said all that, I will mention the worst downside of this game: The multiplayer seems to be dead. Every now and then, I check if there is an open lobby, but all I see is emptiness. Don't get me wrong, you can basically play this game alone, but the real experience lies in the teamplay. So, if you would want to try this game, be sure to look for a group on steam or elsewhere, so that you have some people with you. It is alright in singleplayer, but the real game is in the multiplayer part.

BIT.TRIP CORE is a music/arcade action game where dots are flying around the screen, and you have to shoot them down by firing from the center of the screen. CORE is the second game in the BIT.TRIP saga, after BEAT. If this premise sounds similar to Bit.TRIP BEAT, well, the similarities don't end there. Like BEAT, doing well in CORE makes the music sound better and the graphics look better, but more distracting. Doing poorly makes the music worse and the graphics simpler, and when you're close to death, the game drops to black-and-white mode and removes all but the basic beat of the music, so nothing is left to distract you.
I think BIT.TRIP BEAT is wonderful because of the game's elegant game design. CORE is more of the same, but clunkier. To hit the dots, you have to hold a direction and fire, and the fact that you have to worry about two button presses per shot makes all the difference. It's hard enough keeping with the rhythm when the dots start hitting your line of fire on the off beat (which can be difficult even when there's enough warning, but is much harder when CORE starts throwing them in with no warning), but it's a lot more work also figuring out which direction to fire in when the game starts moving the dots around in an erratic pattern. I feel that the gameplay in CORE is a bit too unfair... you have to either have incredibly quick reflexes or simply memorize the tough parts to do well. Some of these same criticisms apply to BEAT as well, but the superior game design in BEAT makes up for some of those issues.
Ultimately, BIT.TRIP CORE is still a decent game, and if you liked BEAT, you'll probably like CORE well enough to tolerate its faults, because when you get right down to it, CORE is really just more of the same. Get BEAT before CORE, though. BEAT is much better.

Short: X-COM UFO Defense is simply a fantastic and immersive strategy game. It is very complex, but is still easy to learn and understand. The game gives the player lots of options and freedom in defeating the alien invasion. The variety of options also creates a large replay value.
Long: To begin, the Windows 7 version runs via DosBox. The default settings limit the cycle speed, meaning the game can have very low FPS counts sometimes. Manually changing the cycle limit will allow you to increase the FPS for smoother gameplay.
The controls via DosBox are all cursor-based, as far as I know. The keyboard is simply not used at all. Keyboard controls could be useful, so I will say this is a con.
The game itself has tons of options for players. There are some base management aspects, where you can build new facilities in the X-COM bases or build new bases altogether. This stuff is pretty simple (not really any micro managing) but allows for a large variety of different base configurations. Supplies and personel (soldiers, scientists, and engineers) can be bought/hired and sold/fired and can also be transferred between bases. Scientists research new technology from base labs which can allow your engineers to manufactor new weapons, vehicles, armor, or other useful things. Funding is a concern; your funding is automatically adjusted each month based on your performance in stopping the alien menace. You can also gain funds by selling supplies you find or produce.
The geo map view looks nice (for Dos) and is where you order your aircraft to shoot down UFOs or to land squads at landed UFOs/crashed UFOs/terror sites/alien bases. When you land at a site, you can customize the loadout of each soldier based on what equipment was in the landing craft. Tactical combat is solid but difficult; raw recruits and even semi-skilled soldiers are absolutely terrible shots. There is a variety of different weapons, grenades, and other equipment that your soldiers can use. There are several types of aliens that are mostly quite unique from each other. After neutralizing all aliens at a site, you also automatically collect their loot--the alien weaponry and supplies can be used by your soldiers or sold for profit.
By researching new technologies and interrogating captured aliens, the end-game content and final missions to beat the game are revealed. Overall, it is a very enjoyable experience and the variety of options means there is a great degree of replayability. I highly recommend the game.

Thanks to the developer and publisher of Maize, Finish Line Games, for creating a unique world for me to escape and explore.
Maize is one of the strangest games I have played in a while and I’m still on the fence on the overall experience. I think a lot of players will come to the same conclusion totally based on if they come in blind or have watched previews/ reviews. It gives a strong first impression but that opening feels misplaced from the mood and tone of the overall game and sets up mixed results in the end.
The story of Maize begins with you appearing in a cornfield of a farm that is actually being used as cover for a hidden government facility. You then make your way through the corn maze to your first puzzle and a note from your host. It’s very basic, linear gameplay of find items, place here to open door to proceed and that doesn’t change for the entire 5-6 hour play through. I found this totally disappointing as the puzzle component is very much hidden object level of difficulty. The objects you can interact with are all highlighted in the world and everything comes with a quirky written description such as picking up a rock that’s useless but you take it anyway and you give it a name.
As you proceed you will complete a mission to build a Russian talking Teddy bear companion, Vladdy,  who is the most miserable, negative character ever. Every sentence Vladdy speaks includes “stupid” or “idiot” and it gets annoying after a while. Also when walking, due to his mechanical frame, this machine sound is constantly in your ear. Vladdy is small so he is always moving and on a lot of occasions gets hung up on the environment. Vladdy isn’t bad but that’s all he is, a companion who complains and is used to go through air shafts or hack terminals. In some instances there are moments Vladdy is funny but it doesn’t outweigh the burdens he brings.  There of course are some other characters you will interact with and all of which are animated and voiced excellent.
Graphically Maize looks amazing from the outdoor lighting cutting though the tops of corn stalks to the excellant characters animations. There is a lot attention to little details whether it’s the names on cans in a cupboard to the rust on a wheel barrow the environmental artist and animators deserve high praise. However, the game runs like a potato (30-45 fps, 1080P max settings,Ultrawide) and it doesn’t help the graphic options are very limited. The worst part is no matter what option I turned down, it didn’t seem to change the frame rate. The game could have defiantly used some additional graphically options and maybe some more time for optimization.
It would not surprise me that the developers are Tim Burton fans because Maize, like Burton movies, is just weird. A majority of Burton films, in my experience, can be memorable for their writing, characters and story but not always positive for the enitre viewing. I want to like Maize but its simplistic gameplay, so-so story, annoying writing and terrible optimization makes it a disappointing experience and not the next Nightmare befor Christmas but {gulp} it feels like another Johnny Depp/ Tim Burton movie collaboration since 2005.

"Wander around aimlessly until you hit a story or a kill trigger" the game.
The game starts out with great narration and they build up suspense nicely in the intro cutscene. Then you stand at a trainstation and start walking with no indication of where to go. I played for 84 minutes and got stuck. It only seemed to save at tents and the last one must have been quite a bit ago so that really sucks. Minus the bugs (that happened in two different places but I managed to get out the first time), my first impressions were amazement at the graphics and atmosphere. Not for graphics sake alone, but for engrossment. I have to ask myself if I've ever been so immersed in a game before and it's hard to say I have. Having essentially zero UI and being in a first-person perspective along with the exceptional graphics (must be making use of tessellation I imagine) really pushes this over the immersion threshold for me. It really gives the word 'immersion' meaning which I've often had a hard time defining. If I was able to play this in VR (which I don't have) and not get sick, I imagine I would start to question reality. I definitely noticed myself getting lost in the game occasionally hearing sounds outside of my headphones and being sort of pulled out for those moments and I could imagine easily getting drawn in for hours at a time, which little concept of actual time.
The story is based on true events, but of course with their own explaination (so far) as to what happened to cause this group of nine Russian college students to all die and unexplained ways while camping in the snowy wilderness. I'm not sure what's true and made up (which is probably a compliment), but the journal entries are interesting enough and I'm interested to see more and where the story goes. It would have been nice to see a more grounded explaination of their deaths in this game, rather than the supernatural things I've seen thus far, but it's been done pretty well up to this point, even considering those.
The gameplay itself is actually rather boring, which should speak to how much the atmosphere and engagement. If you've heard the term 'walking-simulator' or the like before, this is a lot like that. There's no action or apparently any threat at all (except I take it this orange cloud thing chasing you would set you back) and you are sort of just walking around picking up pieces of the story (which is in a great, really high-res notebook, which is voice-acted for important parts and can be zoomed in on) as you occasionally run from an orange cloud/smoke thing. It would be great if there was more actual substance to the gameplay like in Penumbra: Overture which I've been reminded of, which has survival aspects. *Somewhat spoilery, but not really* There are parts where a sort of black ethereal monster walks towards you, but again I don't know if he's an actual threat, but him coming toward you with the music is definitely intimating. What I like about this game, compared to Layers of Fear, which I've been playing recently as well, is that there aren't jump scares. It's more of intimidation and immediate
of threat. I gasped at one point when I fell, not because I was startled, but because I felt like I was falling, being as consumed in the game (hard to call it that for good and bad reasons) as I was. That says a lot for me. As someone else said, it's not really a horror game (so far anyway) as much as something that feels tense like the movie The Grey (Liam Neison) where you don't feel abruptly startled, but rather intimidated by circumstance.
I really love this sort of realistic feeling of threat and would love to see it explored in more 'horror' games, maybe in a murder/mystery type game. Something where you're not being bombarded with pop-scares and magic tricks to scare you (though I like that about Layers of Fear), but rather real-world things to alarm you like a man coming at you with a knife.

Killing Floor is a cooperative first-person shooter video game developed and published by Tripwire Interactive. It was originally released as an Unreal Tournament 2004 mod in 2005. Retail release followed on May 14, 2009, for Microsoft Windows.
Killing Floor is a first person shooter, allowing each player to move through a 3D environment. Gameplay consists of two game types: Killing Floor and Objective Mode. In Killing Floor Mode, the player fights waves of zombie-like specimens, or ZEDs, with each wave becoming successively more difficult, until it concludes with a battle against a "boss" specimen, called the Patriarch. Objective Mode poses different challenges in addition to fighting against the zombie or zed specimens. Players earn in-game money for each kill, as well as for surviving to the end of a wave. In the time between each waves, players can visit a trader to buy and sell ammo, armor, and additional weapons, such as katanas, pipe bombs, flamethrowers, shotguns, and so forth; the Trader's location on the level varies at the end of each wave, discouraging players from camping in one location. Weapons may also be found randomly across the level. Players are encouraged to work together; they can trade items and drop money, healing is more effective on other players than on oneself, and the team can strategically weld doors shut to provide a temporary barrier from the oncoming horde while funneling the other creatures to specific areas.
Players select one of seven perks at the start of a match and between rounds. The perk, similar to the idea of a character class, provides bonuses towards certain weapon types, armor, movement, and other factors. Players can level up each perk to increase the benefits it offers. For example, the "Sharpshooter" perk, which provides accuracy benefits when using scoped rifles, can be raised in level by completing a number of headshots with specific weapons. The player does not need to play with that perk to raise its level. For example, the Field Medic perk requires the player to heal a number of points to level up, but this can also be done while playing any of the other perks.
As long as at least one member survives the wave, players that die during a wave will drop their current weapon and re-enter the game at the start of the next wave. If the entire squad is wiped out, they will have to restart the game from the first round.
Each game can be configured to alter the length and difficulty of the various waves. The number of creatures in the enemy waves are based on the number of players in the game, increasing in numbers if more players join the game in progress. All but the weakest enemies have some special attack that can inflict significant damage on a player. A feature called "zed time" awards particularly gory kills, such as headshots, with slow-motion, even in multiplayer mode.
Alex Quick, the lead level designer and texture artist, stated that "there are a whole bunch of ideas on the drawing board that we can add in after launch, including the 'Story' mode from the mod, for instance."[6] A software development kit (SDK) and level editor are included to aid in the creation of modifications and levels.

Bought this shortly after it was released in Early acceess and even in it's early stage it was clear to see that the sandbox mode was going to be awesome.
Since then the sandbox has been tweaked and tweaked too damn near perfect.
It's a lonely, cold, unforgiving wilderness where everything you do depends on your ability to scavenge, plan and learn.
You can spend days in one section of the map just hunting, foraging and setting up a camp in some abandoned shack/cabin/home/cave you might find.
You are not an overpowered high moutain rescue specialist or some kind of ultimate marksman commando, you're just a person, who is lost in a freezing wilderness.
Animals are equally hungry and desperate to survive which, makes perfect sense to me. However it should be noted that the wolves are usually the biggest point of contention here as they can be very aggressive. Given the environmental situations in the game it gfeels logical to me that a pack hunting animal in a wilderness were food is scarce would, tend to be aggressive towards other animals that could be potential prey.
So there are no zombies, but... there are still monsters.
The graphics are simple but beautiful and I feel like they really work, artistic but still immersive.
I still feel like it could be tweaked in some areas but after coming back to it after so long and seeing how much has been changed since the early, early release, it's night and day and it's a lot of fun to revisit the game since everything feels new. New features like mapping and multi-layering clothes for warmth. Just, a lot of cool additions and things that make sense.
Again, if you're hoping to get a great story out of it... meh. They've only finished the first episode but if this is what we should expect, I'm not excited for the rest. I'll reserve my opinion till they're done but man, it's been a long time coming and if this is their best... well.
BUT, that sandbox survival mode is one of my favorites so far.
If it goes on sale for $20 or less I'd say it's definitely worth picking up.
Else I'd wait till they are done with the story and the rest of the tweaks before thinking about paying full price.

The best puzzle game I've ever played? You betcha!
SpaceChem is joyous, it really truely is!
I love absolutely everything about this game, I love the music, I love the simplistic graphics, I love how smart it makes me feel when I figure it out, I love the critical thinking, I love the easter eggs, I love the user made content and I love the replayability of it.
This is a game that looks very intimidating and I think that may have hurt it, but trust me, it is very accomidating for beginners. First of all, you really don't need to know anything about chemistry, chemical elements is just the medium it used in order to keep the game flowing and to base the story line along something. I can't help but wonder if they had used shapes and colours like a pop cap game then maybe it would have looked a little less scarey. But even if you've never so much as glanced at a periodic table there is no real disadvantage. However, on the other hand, it really gives you this wonderful "mad scientist" feeling especially during the special stages where you may have to blow up a storage tank.
The difficulty is very high and even after playing for 20 hours I am still no where near finsished with it, I really do intend to finish it though one day and I can't wait to see it through and what insane challenges it will throw at me towards the end! The difficulty is high but it's never unfairly so. The game really does carefully ease you in and will give you smaller proof of concept experiments before throwing you into a big mission where you need to put everything you've learned together. This is where the replayability comes in, as you learn more you can go back to previous experiments and optimise them. You see, unlike a lot of puzzle games, there are many many many solutions to each puzzle, and you could spend months tweaking and speeding up previous solutions. At the end of each level it shows you how everyone else solved the puzzle so you can see how you did. There really is a strange sense though that often your particular solution is completely unique to everyone else!
The music, the music is absolutely fantastic! It really has all the feelings of the story rolled into it, theres a hint of paranoia, a touch of sadness, melancoly studying and reasearching music and a large section of triaumphant music as well. The music is on the standard of a movies orchestral score and its soundtrack is saved on my harddrive (thanks humble bundle!) and finds it's way into winamp often!
This game boasts a huge library of user made content too, I haven't dared to touch it yet because it looks feindishly difficult! This is something that will give it thousands of hours of replayability though.
I honestly cannot recommend this game enough! I have to give it a 10/10. This is the standard that all puzzle games should aspire to. I just hope I can win some day.

SpaceChem is goddamn brilliant. In the course of the game you use reactors to combine elements into molecules - that's pretty much the gist of it. However, it's done via timing mechanisms where you take in molecules and atoms and manipulate them via a series of steps - adding/removing bonds, fusing them, splitting them, teleporting them, the list just goes on. From an actual chemistry standpoint it doesn't make a hell of a lot of sense, but what's really intriguing is that this takes the essence of programming/circuit design and distills it into a fascinating game. Engineering students/programming students should CONSUME this game - it's a wonderful example of the sort of work we try to solve.
I got hopelessly addicted to this game for a good long while. It gets hard - REALLY hard. But the feeling of satisfaction upon finding a solution is just....so fantastic. Even more if you've got some friends who you can compete against trying to find more and more efficient solutions.
I cannot recommend this game enough. It's wonderful.

This game is one of the best i have ever played. Unfortunately i cannot play it any more, my mind spins with possible solutions for hours afterwards, keeping me from sleep.
It is at heart a programming game, but disguised into chemistry machine building.  In fact you are building a network of mutlithreaded realtime processors. The programming aspect makes this into a "sandbox" pussle; you must fulfill the objectives, but there are an infinite amount of ways to do so. Afterwards you get a comparison with others that have played the level, and get to se how well you did versus them. The interesting part of that comparison is that it rates you on both processsing time and design simplicity, and in general you cannot do well in both. This will either leave you with a feeling of that you chose the right optimization or (as in my case) trigger competitive insanity.
All in all: difficult and timeconsuming; requires concentration and effort. You might also learn something.

Flow puzzles were some of my favorite when I was younger, I don't know why.  I love the little games where you had a pipe of water coming out one side and you needed to channel it to the other side in the right amount of time, or via some complex complication where they shipped to many right bending pipes and not enough left bend pipes… they've always been fun to me.
This ends up being a little like that but taken to the extreme.  Labeled fake chemistry, you're tasked with assembling various molecules from their base elements including the number of bonds required to make the molecule.  The puzzlyness (new word!) is excellent.  Receiving two inputs on a reactor, you have you output your end goal.  Eventually, molecules are so complex that you'll need multiple sub combines in different reactors pumped into the other reactors in order to combine the final element.  There's 2 scales of assemble, one where goods are piped into and out of the reactors that to the combinations and then the actual assembly puzzles within the reactors themselves.  When you hit the go switch, the elements are pumped in at a fixed rate and everything must be processed and timed in order to get the right targets out the other end.
Hard to explain, fantastic to play.  Easily in my top five of puzzle games of all time.  Hard to find something bad to say about this game apart from it not having much replayability apart from making your designs more efficient. This is my first review, and I can barely imagine any other game for it. I started on Dragon Age, and its counterpert Mass Effect, when I was very young. It set rather high expectations for games, as Bioware does. I was utterly enthralled. The graphics were great at the time(and still arguably are), and the design really through me into the universe visually. The story is fantastic, filled with great content and direction and is dependant on your choices. You'll face complex dillemma, challenging combat(if you choose), grand story arcs both big and small, and map after map to explore and interact with. I've put hundreds upon hundreds of hours into this game alone between two platforms. That's right, this game's so good I bought it TWICE. The DLC are worth it to if they sound right for you, especially if they're on sale. There are certainly flaws, but I feel listing the pros and cons will be effective.
Pros:
-Fantastic story telling
-Amazing and engaging chracters to interact and build relationships with
-Large eviorments and world map
-Exploration
-Hidden unlockables
-Humor
-Hardcore feels
-Decisions matter
-Wide range of customization
-Amazing soundtrack
-Extremely replayable
-Vast universe and lore that is thought out and well crafted
-Surprises behind every turn
-Nice graphics
-Adaptable to the challenge(or lack thereof) you want
-Save the whole world... or maybe condemn it
Cons:
-Older graphics
-Controls can be considered clunky or clums
-Combat is... perhaps lackluster, not everything it could be
-Hardcore feels
-When you take a bad path you didn't want to, you better hope you focused on your stats and saved before major decisions
-Sometimes, no one wins and you'll have to live with that
-Generally speaking, you either like it or you don't, just to varying degrees
Notes:
-As with most Bioware games, be wary of how you balance your stats and skills. Depending on your playstyle, you need to focus more on some things than others. I would suggest consitution and charisma; consitution really helps boost your health points, and charisma and persuasion skills will give you plenty of story paths you'll want.
-Specializations are permenant, so choose wisely
-I found the game guide to be helpful. I usually do a playthrough of a RPG, then get a guide if I feel it will help with future playthroughs. Free online guides are always available, but official guides tend to be better organized in my opinion.
-You can carry your playthroughs over into the expansion, and from there to the sequel(which isn't amazing, but I still had some fun with it). That being said, you'll mainly have to use the Dragon Age Keep system to replicate a save into Inquisition.

The game  is finally shaping up to be the "Dwarf Fortress Lite" that I was hoping for. I backed Stonehearth three years ago on Kickstarter and can say that thus far I have no regrets. Is it taking longer than promised? You bet. Did I ever believe they'd get the game pumped out in the original timeline? Not really. I play Dwarf Fortress and, while a bigger development team, this type of game just takes a lot of time to piece together.
Pros:
+Nice, pleasant graphics.
+Job system is a nice way to elegantly handle workshop allowances and control workflows.
+Enemies can be challenging, even at normal mode.
+Building is fun and, after lots and lots of bug fixes, fairly functional.
+It's way more cute and light-hearted than similar games.
Cons:
-Surprise, it's an alpha. There are bugs galore.
-The job system is, for better or worse, restricting. Needing to upgrade your level 4 mason into a potter is not fun. It means you have to level up a new mason or make them dance back and forth. Sometimes this works okay and elegantly (eg. a cook will still help the farmers out when he has nothing to do. This is excellent, but I don't think it has been implemented elsewhere)
-The difficulty curve starts off smooth, but at a certain point (13-14 Hearthlings) goes absolutely off the charts. I wish I could say this was new to Alphas 15 and 16, but honestly it was like that way earlier too. Once again, understandable for an alpha though.
-Since it isn't fully finished, you may run out of stuff to do if you choose peaceful mode. I've checked out both modes and despite the difficulty spike, normal mode is just more fun. There's actual tension to the game with stuff to fight and defend against.
It's not finished, but what is there is an absolute blast. My final note is that the developers are super nice and responsive. I have been a lurker in their community, but I can say that they are immensely hard-working and transparent. In the day and age of sheisty Kickstarters/Early-Access they are saints.
If you like Dwarf Fortress and Banished, but want a more cute/light-hearted experience give Stonehearth a go.

While I love these type of sandbox/management games, this one seems to fall a little short. Originally, I bought this around the time I was playing Towns, and liked the idea that it was graphically superior to Towns and had a few more features in planning. Many features were still in development, but I don't mind supporting independent developers. Skip forward some months, and the problems inherent to this kind of development become self-evident. Even easy-concept games can be a nightmare when you start adding in features.
While the community is very strong and supportive, the developers communicate frequently and consistently, the game itself is fundamentally flawed. Gameplay is only tenable for about 12 hours, from there it's the same thing in a new setting. At the moment, many core features of the game are either uninteresting or broken. The engine itself is unsustainable or poorly written. AI still breaks itself after enough time has passed (or becomes so inept at tasks they become useless). Town areas are by default limited to 20 citizens, because the engine really can't handle much more than that. The map bogs down after about 10 in-game days with very little activity (2 gb ram and 16% of a decent quad-core processor on PAUSE).
If you're looking to purchase this game, wait. See if the developers iron out the bugs, but even then know that it's likely not going to be a game you're going to come back to or play for too long. It'll be something casual when you've got nothing else to do - download, install, play, get bored and repeat in a couple months.
Pros:
- Good looking UI and general landscape - blocky but tastefully done.
- Good conceptual design of core elements.
- Good balance between difficulty vs. reward - easy enough for new players, but can't immediately make everything.
- Consistent small updates, if a little slow for what the updates usually are.
- Consistent and constructive communication from developers and community.
- Implemented crash reporting that actually means something will get fixed eventually.
Cons:
- AI bogs very quickly.
- Processor hungry for package size.
- Gameplay can get repetitive (not talking about unimplemented features).
- Spend much time after initial rush just watching your citizens do things.
- Buggy as hell, but to be expected in Alpha.
- Gameplay is geared to non-expansion - there's no reason to really expand much beyond starting area. Just pick a good one and wall yourself in.
- Gameplay itself is very short. When you've done it once, it's the same thing on a different map.
tl;dr:
Wait a while if you're following this game. It's buggy and VERY casual. Devs are slow, but do communicate.

After you've hurtled through space and crash landed your ship on the surface of a strange planet, you will pick two survivors to make your journey to the escape pod with. Each character has different statistics, strengths, weaknesses and abilities.
There are a certain number of rooms per floor, and once you have discovered the escape route, you'll progress to the next floor. Sounds easy enough, right?
Wrong.
Apart from the room you start off in, you have a small number of resources (Dust) and you need to power the Crystal. Why? Monsters, obviously.
If you don't power the crystal, you can't light the rooms through the floor as you go. rooms that aren't lit will act as a spawn point for monsters, and then they'll come and destroy your crystalhead straight for your Crystal to destroy it.
Each time you open a new room you have a chance to obtain some dust allowing you to power other rooms. You might also get lucky and find self-powered rooms. These are great however you can't unpower the room and reclaim dust from it to use on another room. This makes your management of dust important, it also makes you think about which route you're going to take and forces you to plan ahead.
Once you've discovered the exit, you can retrieve the crystal from the starting room and make your way to the exit. On your way to the exit you will have to fight through waves of enemies which will constantly spawn in the unlit rooms until you leave the floor.
One thing to be aware of is that if your character dies then thats it, they stay dead, they don't just respawn on the next floor. All is not lost though as you can recruit other characters you come across to replace them. If you come across a character you haven't unlocked yet and recruit them you will unlock them but only if you keep them alive for 3 floors. This gives the game a lot of replay value if you're like me and wanted to unlock every character.
There is a certain degree of autonomy in Dungeon of the Endless. Turrets and characters will automatically attack any enemies in the same room as them, leaving you to just strategically place them along the monster's path. You don't have to sit and micro manage each of your party members or turrets.
The game also features research which allows you to get upgrades for your defences.
What i like about this game is that it makes you think, you can't just rush through each level unless you want to do so with major risk of death. The game makes great use of some beautiful pixel art and the variance between floors/ships is a nice touch. Funnily enough one of my favourite features is the games soundtrack which just fits in perfectly, each level brings its own sound. Even after putting 30+ hours into the game i still have fun with it whenever i jump back into it, for the money it's a gem of a game.

Well done fellas. A gorgeous blend of genres.
Pixel graphics are fascinating, the animation is minimal, iterative & very expressive, giving a feeling of swiftness during fights. Items are really low pixel sized, which I personally find too raw.
The ambient sound depending on which areas you fly over make up the atmosphere, full effect with the music which is a pure (litterally) gem !! Epic themes & hypnotizing melodies !..
Realtime gameplay is kept rather simple, for instance : 2 skills & 3 items (sometimes 2) per character, you cannot move a char in a specific location in a room...
There is a variety of each type of items (weponz, armorz, utilz) which can fill needs of team balance. Also for movements by ordering a char to move in another room, you can kite the enemy in some situations. There are a great deal of minor modules to make combos with and some useful major modules depending on your current progression in yo run :l
Unlocking all the chars is tricky. Then winning is very tricky. Learn gradually the balance of the game, what door could make too much waves appear on a low defended side, what of the 3 resources to focus on at what point of the game, what trade do and what items to keep or sell later... AND who's gonna level up ? :stress: Acquire awesome passives plz. Actives go from useful/spammable to game-changing. Too bad they're few of them, multiple chars will have actives in common... more unique endless sh*t plz
Some aspects can considered as unrefined, such as the ending, rather inconsistent but better than just a still image. As you'll do multiple (hopefully winning :stress: ) runs, it's not that of a flaw but I feel it needs more little drops of lore. All the chars & elements are these already, hence the universe appears really special. The charm did work on me and with multiples challenges hold my breath quite a long and exquisite time. (also " NooOOooOoOO **CK MY LOCKED CHAR Z DEAD NO NOT THIS F*C**N* MOB AGAIN YAARRGGH STARVIN' HELP HELP FFFUUUUUUUU- ").
Multiplayer also can be too long, even complicated/risky at 3 players (more? lolz) as there is no pause, management is really better done at 2 mates. A main cause is the unpractical UI (care for sharing/wiping zone in inv :p) and a lack of a global resources display (each player their own). Too bad but still with 1 friend by knowing the game well & nopause, game gives a particular thrill.
A bunch of play modes are more or less difficult to unlock, with an achiev goal for each. A bit of a shame those DLCs are pretty expensive for what they are. I've been occupied by XCOM for the past two weeks straight, and it's been a blast. XCOM: UFO Defense is simply one of the best games ever made.
The gameplay is deep, addictive and atmospheric, and does a surprising amount for a game from 1994. Your task as leader of the newly formed project for the defense of earth from aliens is to stop alien raids and abductions by shooting down their ships, ambushing their landing parties, and destroying their bases. Eventually you are tasked with taking the fight to the aliens and defeating them altogether. There are two modes of gameplay, the Geoscape and the Battlescape.
In the Geoscape (real time, variable time speeds), you build bases around the world, dispatch interceptors and dropships to deal with UFOs, do research, manufacture and purchase weapons and vehicles, and try to please all your sponsor nations so they don't reduce their funding. However, it quickly becomes apparent that both human technology and the funding from sponsor nations are both completely inadequate for the task. In order to survive and stop the aliens, you need to capture alien technology, research it, and produce your own copies, and then sell the excess loot for mounds of money.
The Battlescape on the other hand (turn based tactical, top down) allows you to control your squad of soldiers (who improve over time in surprisingly sophisticated ways) in attempts to stop the aliens. But don't think it will be easy. The Battlescape is an unforgiving world filled with aliens waiting to snipe at your men from distant cornfields and ambush you from around corners. The first several missions you play, it is likely that you will fail spectacularly. This is entirely intentional, and really contributes to the atmosphere of the game. You really feel like you are learning on the job, facing a totally unknown and technologically superior enemy who holds all the cards. A genuine feeling of satisfaction accompanies finally being able to defeat the aliens in a mission (albeit with heavy losses), or re-engineering your first bit of alien weapon tech. The lack of a tutorial actually helps the game in this way, as it is much deeper than it first appears, and it feels very authentic to learn the ropes of the game in this way.
The graphics and sound are marvelously retro, and might take some getting used to for some of the less open-minded gamers out there, but I assure you the reward is worth it. Overall, this is a game that you MUST play if you call yourself a PC gamer at all. It joins a myriad of other gems from the 90's that modern gamers are continually ignorant of, though they inform modern developers every single day. There is no better indication of the current stagnation of game development than playing a game like XCOM and seeing how incredible it is. This game with an extreme facelift would be strategy GOTY.

This game is just awesome! Super original, simple, but extremely hard.
It consists of a series of puzzles, where you must build a molecule with a pair of "workers", inside a reactor.
You must draw those workers' path, and place several activity points along those paths, like grab/drop what you're carrying, wait with other worker, rotate what you're carrying and create bond.
You make them pickup the atoms or molecule parts, and synchronize them so that they never let their atoms/molecules collide. Then, to form the molecules you usually have to make it so that one worker is stopped, and the other drops their cargo in the right place, and passes in a "bond" point.
From a programmer's point of view, this will basically consist of a series of semaphores and state-machines built using synchronization points.
This will all get nastier, when you must build a series of these reactors to build your final molecule...
I started trying this for a quick game, and when i noticed, two hours had passed. Very simple to understand and a lot of fun.
Beware, though. Don't try to optimize your reactors. You WILL spend the rest of your life doing so..

Here are some things that I found particularly enjoyable about
:
Connectivity to
- Right down to the equipment, combat tactics, roleplaying capabilities, and intriguing characters,
provides the sheer thrill of roleplaying that is offered by the tabletop renditions of the
games. The game utilizes a simultaneous real-time and turn-based approach to combat, which will be described under the Gameplay portion of this review. Included in this title are six playable core races, a multitude of classes that influence each character’s style of play, the ability to multiclass, and the capability to interact with party members, which further enhances (no pun intended) the roleplaying experience. Since it utilizes the same mechanics as those in the tabletop roleplaying system, concepts such as THACO scores, Initiative modifiers, and alignments make an appearance; to those that are not familiar with the concepts, they are very simple to grasp and there are online guides dedicate to both
and
that aide newer players in learning the roleplaying system.
Gameplay - As stated previously,
utilizes a combat system that is both turn-based and real-time in that actions rotate between characters within a confrontation as a sequence depending on each character’s Initiative score; basically, whoever’s quicker will end up going first in the rotation. The game also employs a simulated d20-or 20-sided die-roll to resolve the degree of success pertaining to given actions such as lockpicking and attack actions. Outside of combat, players can speak with other characters, both in and out of their own party, which may alter a given character’s alignment status. Some characters also have the ability to perform certain actions such as picking locks as a Rogue archetype (pressing V while out of combat), or casting passive
spells on non-player characters for specific gains. In all, the system is so intricate and open that you can practically do whatever you want, within the game’s limitations, of course. There is also a multiplayer component to
in which you can import characters you have created and play with friends throughout the game.
Truly Open World - At the beginning of Baldur’s Gate , you are given a background story, a sufficient reason to proceed through the main campaign’s questline, and the chance of receiving your first companion character. That’s it. From there, you are free to explore the massive map however you wish while obtaining side quests, battling formidable foes, and gaining companionship with other notable non-playable characters. There are also game modifications (mods) to expand the map and the game’s story. How much more ‘open’ can you get?
The Black Pits - If you are searching for a different pacing outside of the massive world within the main campaign, then the Black Pits game mode is for you. This story is primarily driven by combat, in which your created party of six must fend off waves of enemies who utilize various tactics and themes in order to liberate your team from the Black Pits fighting arena. As straightforward as this may seem, it is extremely fun in a tactical manner, and permits the player to enjoy the core combat mechanics of the game without having to worry about the text and speech components; of course, there are secretes to be found within the Black Pits proving grounds.
TL:DR - Like the person I would like to dedicate this review to, this game is an ‘original’ soul with intricate mechanics that will either make or break you. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open-world, roleplaying, or strategy titles, and would highly urge Baldur’s Gate to those who play tabletop roleplaying games, especially Dungeons & Dragons . Baldur's Gate is one hell of a game. Sarevok's reign of terror along the Sword Coast, the Iron Crisis, the progeny of a dead god wreaking havoc on the realm. It's a classic, make no doubt.
Though more of a fresh coat-of-paint than the remake we all wanted, Beamdog's Enhanced Edition is overall an improvement over the original game--especially now that the many bugs that plagued the game at launch have been ironed out. Of particular note are the additional party members and quest content, which are closer in quality to the quintessential sequel, Shadows of Amn, than the original.
Baldur's Gate is a masterpiece. I recommend--in the strongest possible language--that every gamer play both main titles at lease once. I must, in a heartbeat, recommend any gamer out there who hasn't already picked up Baldur's Gate to grab the Enhanced Edition immediately.
In a heartbeat.
But to gamers of the old school, my fellows and friends, I cannot say the same. Beamdog's Enhanced Edition of Baldur's Gate is nice, and in many respects superior to the original game, but the new content is far from game-changing, and there's simply too little there to justify a full play-through if you've already journeyed through the original game a half-dozen times. Unless you're a huge fan of the game, I guess. Like me. In which case: have at it!

I can definitely understand why so many people are upset at the slow patches, questionable balance, cash-only unlocks, low player base and original $60 price tag on this thing.
If you actually want to play the game competitively and don't die of old age before you find a good match, the skill cap is mostly based on map memorization (feed routes, good dome locations for either side, how to exploit what terrain...), how to combo effectively as the monster, and how to dodge effectively as the hunters.  It's mostly just technical and tedious.

As many of hours of fun as the game has provided me, I can't in good conscience recommend the game to anyone.
There's a crippling lack of content, first of all. A small number of hunters, monsters, and game modes. Of those game modes, only one is supported, Hunt, the rest of poorly designed and balanced filler. Even Hunt itself, even after a year of updates, is still an unbalanced mess.
The game is also plagued with game breaking bugs that they wait months to fix. Right now, the newest monster, has a bug that keeps him stuck poucing on a hunter. It's completely game breaking, yet they'll happily put out more paid content instead of fixing things they actually charge money for.
The game is completely multiplayer focused, yet doesn't have the player base to support adecuate ranked matchmaking and queue times.
Overall, the game doesn't have very good support, gives you little for it's price point, and can be daunting for newer players.
It's a sad tale, because the actual gameplay is fun. The idea is sound, it's the execution that's flawed. The game has given me tons of fun hours, but I see the game's future, and it's going nowhere, fast.
Edit: The newest update cleans up a significant portion of the game's flaws. In addition to having everything for free, the core game is now about combat, as opposed to running around aimlessly in the jungle looking for the monster. This means that even new players can see some action.
In the game's current beta state is is recieving patches every week, often with new content, and the game overall is improving even now. Occassionally they will make mishaps with this rapid pace, the last patch at this date created a few bad bugs, but hopefully it'll be cleared up quickly.
The game's boss battles are the centerpiece, and you'll get them more frequently thanks to the new tools they gave the hunter team. Since it's free, you lose nothing when giving it a try.
The game requires skill to be played accurately, so if you have the nerve to last awhile, it can be very rewarding to master dodging monster abilities.
All this being said, the game's population is dropping again, and they seem to make some changes that boggle the mind. New map variations are poorly done content that nobody in their right mind would have ever allowed to get into the game, and yet, there they are. They increase the cost of getting new characters without prior notice so players who are saving up are ♥♥♥♥ed. They release new characters in an unpolished state. All the while, the remaining 8 maps and the other game modes are MIA.
The core game I'd say has improved, it's better than before, but recently they need to evaluate where they are going.

A zombie game that takes charge of the 'realism' genre while also allowing you to build a base or explore the world of Knox County. Whats the best place to fortify? The Grocery store? The construction yard? The far away prison that's ransacked with zombonies? or maybe just your starter home.
The game always finds a new way to challenge you and make you think. Do you just want to throw up some ranshackle fences or move into a place that has them. Do you think you can live off of canned soup forever or will you hunt and grow your food?
Guns are pretty scarce, you can find some in residential and commercial places, but not much. You'll have to try and attempt a break-in at a police station or gunstore if you want to get some... If they haven't already been sacked.
While alone, it's definately not as fun, but its still a real challenge and it gives you some time to figure things out.
With other people it gets crazy and fun at the same time. Everyone will be able to divert skills and pick what is best to serve the group.
The sandbox options for the game pretty much turn it into whatever kind of apocalypse you want it to be. (Zombie wise of course) Do you want yours to behave like superhumans? Running everywhere, tipped off by the tiniest noise? Well its a quick way to die but fun to try. I prefer a normal or more scarce option with a classic romero kind of zombie. In the begining it may be easy. A couple zombies here and there, but over time the hordes stat forming. It turns from a game of kite and strike to "Okay if I lure them to the park, I can set them on fire and try to carve my way out with the shotgun." Tactics ensue.

MAIZE
PUBLISHER/DEVELOPER – Finish Line Games
GENRE – Walking Simulator/Puzzle, Indie, Adventure
THE BASICS:
You wake up in the middle of a corn maze with no apparent exit. Problem is, some of the corn is not only alive, but sentient, and capable of moving on their own, thank you very much. You can find all sorts of useful items such as vise grips, keytags, and of course, incredibly stale English muffins to help you on your way. The inventory system is blissfully simple: Items you no longer need disappear, and everything else is on a simple rotating list of items you can select from using the shoulder buttons on your controller (or whatever key you choose). Oh, and there's also a sarcastic, grumpy Russian Teddy Ruxpin lying about who accompanies you once you help him to get his gear together.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You'll piece together the story over time by collecting various files and documents about a grand, over-spendy experiment by a foolish, careless co-leader of a wealthy corporation. One of their major projects ended up creating the sentient corn in question. It's up to you to delve deeper into the mystery presented by going along and seeing what there is to see in their extensive underground complex, piecing together a picture of just how this all happened. E.g., the two scientists who head the corporation left sticky notes for one another all over the place; mostly about the absurd expenditures one of them is making (such as a solid gold toilet.
CONTROLS:
Keyboard or controller; note that controller support is limited, and does not yet work in menu screens.
GRAPHICS:
Well-done, if repetitive.  There's only so much you can do with the concept of a corn maze on a run down farm, or a suspiciously empty(??) office complex. Interactables in the environment are helpfully highlighted when you mouse-over them, helping to avoid the old “hunt the pixel” problems from days of yore.
SOUND:
Solid, with appropriately creepy ambient music and crisp sound effects.
OVERALL:
A bizarre, somewhat trippy take on the genre with a good sense of humor. Well worth checking out if that's your sort of game.

This game was one of the main games played during my childhood, a game which actually got me into the strategy genre and one which I have the most nostalgic memories of joy and rage.
For those of you who have played the most recent X-com remakes (Enemy Unknown and Bureau) this title is VASTLY different, and quite clearly from the screenshots shown above, a fairly dated title at that.  However the gameplay is solid, and those of you looking for a challenging strategic game will not be disappointed.
For some people this is what they will call a "wiki-game", there is no tutorial or instruction on how to play it.  As the newly integrated X-Com Commander, you are left to your own devices to decide how to deal with the alien menace, trying your best to keep your investors happy, your soldiers alive and the aliens dead.
Those of you who enjoy the aspect of figuring things out on your own with little to no hand-holding will really appreciate this concept.
What I will warn to all of the players who begin, is that with the learning curve aside, the game can be punishingly brutal at times, the aliens start off with better technology and a greater overall advantage over your own forces.  This game will take advantage of any mistake you make and will punish stupidity without mercy.
But for this reason alone, this has made this title the favourite strategy game for a grand audience who have been playing games since the amiga and commodore era, to this day the gameplay is still highly engaging.
If you do feel apprehensive about purchasing this title due to it's lack of tutorials or punishing combat, then I suggest you invest your time into one or two Let's Play series on your favourite video hosting websites.  You will no doubt find plenty to give you an idea of what's waiting for you in the cold of space.
But even now as I write this, the Steam Winter Sales have been trigged, with X-com getting a 50% discount at it's already low price of £2.99.  Which translates to about less than 5 bucks everywhere else.
I personally find that to be a bit of a steal, but then I have a lot of love for the game.  But if you ever wanted a cheap classical strategy title with challenging gameplay, then by all means, snatch this up.
And remember.
In space, nobody can hear you ragequit.

The atmosphere has it's moments but they are very few and far between and would be comparable to the much better (and entirely free)  "Passing Pine View Forrest".

The pacing is just awful and alternates between making a dash to escape falling rocks or the Orange Alien popping out of the ground and absolutly NOTHING happening for very long periods of time.
I will keep at it, and change my review accordingly but I really cannot recoment this game for the actual asking price.

HAHA oh this game.. Where to start ... alright so normally i try my best to log some hours into the game before just spending 10 mins inside it, being offended or disapointed and crying about it in a review like so many do.. but this game is something else.
Firstly im really glad i picked this up in a Humble Bundle package or otherwise id be gruffed because this game is literally nothing but confusion and unfortunately, the game has more Cons than Pros in my opinion.
First lets start off with its Pros.
its a beautiful game, absoluetely gorgeous, some of the best graphics I've seen, even the individual leaves on trees have their own physics. you can leave your own footsteps in the snow (which get used to the snow)
the environment is vast, interesting and changing from caves, tunnels, carverns , you name it. you can climb mountins and explore caves by the second Act in the game.
there are several bits and pieces of lore to be collected though i didn't start finding anythign until the second Act of the game, oddly by a rustling paper sound. the game does peice together a deep past and story of what (could have) happened during the actuall real life unsolved mystery of the Russian Dyatlov Pass incident. unfortuantely, finding this lore and collectables comes a price of huge frustration and risk of suddenly dying without any warning
now, for the Cons *cracks knuckles*
the map and compass are pretty much near useless. actuall mountain passes, trails and caverns may or do not always follow the map you are given, and there are no markers you can place on said map, or no indicators of where you are located at on the map itself. the map DOES however have cords scratched on the paper in the upper corner but there is no way to actually find those cords besides either pure luck, chance or pretty much hand crafting your OWN map in real life to flippin use. the compass, keeping with the local of Russia, has Russian letters on it so its even hard to figure out which end points north, unless maybe your already an outdoorsman and have a large experiance with compasses.
And yes, the environments are large and have the ability to be explored but your character does not climb or jump so you may find that journal paper five feet away from you but because there is a twig in front of your path that your disabled character appaerently can not step over, you can not grab it. this is not mentioning the mind numbingly large amount of hidden instant death traps and cheapshots littered across the environments that are nearly undetectable without either previous experianceing them or having a sixth sense.
To save the game, you have to find a campsite in a sort of Dark Souls-ish kind of way, but finding these sites is a headache, and it may take you ages  to even find one in the environment after you avoid the insta-death traps and enemies that kill you in 1 hit no matter what. IF you die, you lose all progress since the last save so perhaps you logged 2-3 hours and gathered several collectables since the last save but some Kretcher lookalike reject jumps out of a portal and ♥♥♥♥♥smacks you into next week? you just lost all of that progress you had.
Like i just said. there is NO self defense in the game, any enemy can jump out of some god forsaken portal  or cave and poke you with its fingernail..and you die instantly. i had some weird goblin thing jump from a fire-ish portal that appeared above me after i picked up a journal page and smacked me, causing me to die.
there is also NO interface..at all... i had to go into setting to turn on the dot you see in the center of your screen for interactions myself. ther is no health bar, stamina bar ..although your character obviously uses stamina, because if you sprint for too long he pants and has to stop running after a few seconds. there are no items you pick, and you have no inventory menu besides the Lore-based journal pages. and in fact, you dont even get those until the second Act of the game. there is also no hints or explinations of who your character actually is, they dont seem to speak and there is no intro for them. also seeing as how the game is in First-Person, you dont even know their gender, though im greatly assuming it is male.
the game has no tutorials, no pops ups saying "hey heres how you do this" no "quests" or objectives and no "hey idiot, go here" ... at the beginning of the game, you watch a rather nice summary of the basic idea of what the game revolves around on, then it drops you in this strange dead town thats in the middle of winter. you have ..literally ..nothing. no map, no compass, no directions. you will probably spend more time wandering around lost or trying to figure out what to do more than actually making any progress. the only way i progressed through the chapter was i found a strange "tunnel" made by a grove of trees shapped strangely and decided to investigate. Even the Voice Actor who is narrating bits and peices of (what im guessing is the antagonist) seems to have little to no idea what emotions to portray while reading the script.
---
Overall, the game has a wonderful concept and terrefic art style, but it seems vastly unfinished. id more assume that its  still in Alpha stage, or an Early Access demo . rather than a finished and released game.with a heavy state of confusion and lack of information to combat the said confusion, i think this is an empty plastic Easter egg. it looks nice but theres nothing to it.
