A fairly good horror experience. Picked this up in a humble bundle and I've been pleasantly surprised with it. Very atmospheric, good visuals and solid sound effects that really immerse you in the environment. The game does not go for easy jump scares, instead it builds atmosphere and tension slowly. The subtle and not so subtle noises will have your spinning ever which way to see what is making those terrifying sounds. Controls are slick too with good response times to mouse and keyboard commands.
The game is based on a real like incident that lends a great back story. If you don't know the legend the real life story the game is based on i suggest a little research on it it first. Again, this real life connection really helps you get sucked into the world and deepens your immersion.
A few negatives - Level design lets it down a little bit. A lot of the areas look very similar making it easy to get lost. As the story reveals itself through finding journals, getting lost messes with the game's pacing. There are a few very distinct areas that help you get your bearings but a lot of similar passes and paths can cause confusion.
The game Doesn't have any real replay value. There are no skill tress to experiment with, no alternate story or path choices you can take. Much as i enjoyed it, i don't feel compelled to give it another go.
Overall it is a thumbs up from me, i think this will please most fans of the horror genre. A flawed but pretty gem.

So this game is. A lot.
For a while I was putting off writing this, as for hte most part I played Fire Pro Wrestling the same way most others here did: As a simulator. I downloaded a bunch of real life guys, made a dumb little tournament, and then ran my own promtion. And for a while, it was fun; Kevin Owens and Rick Rude had a halatious matchup. But I realized that this way, I was simply playing a 20 buck fantasy booker, and I wanted to try playing it on my own. So I made a character and went through the tutorials, and here's what I learned.
The gamedoes not play like any other wrestling game I've tried; lockups are automatic and the natural state. While strikes are possible, I've never seen one done well. As such, pretty much everything is a lockup. Even things like chops and punches are done in lockups. It seems that the best way to win a lockup is just pure speed; press one of the buttons and a direction as fast as possible and you get it done. The general idea is to follow the flow of an All Japan style match; smaller moves like takeovers and headlocks leading into your big flashy moves near the end. While this works in theory, I've also done entire matches without using the small moves, going exclusively for big stuff. There isn't too much of a penalty for it anyway.
Character creation is the star of the show. While the main combat engine is fun, it's shocking just how well someone with a good sense of faces can turn even the admitatedly low definition characters adn sprites into something awesome. And the creator is "fun" in the sense that there are lots of parts to use and it's in theory easy to use them. It's a layer based sectional system; you work on one arm, then the other arm, and all of them are seperate parts rather than one cohesive body. Color seems to be an issue; I'd love a way to simply apply one base color and pattern across a body so I don't have to get the exact same color code eveyr time, but it's otherwise cool.
The real big problme is navigating all this. The menu looks and feels like a game from the PS2; the background image is just a static ring and the way they are navigated just looks ugly, especially in tournament setups. I've also been having trouble connecting to opponents online and getting rid of characters from the workshop; even after unsubscribing they are still there, taking up space and making the game load slower.
this game might be okay for some people... and i really liked the idea of the high amount of customization but... the mechanics are just too twitchy for my tastes.

If you like your puzzle games challenging, Spacechem is a towering acheivement.  Its gameplay and level design are elegant in a way that solutions feel like personal creations.  Its graphics and sound are clean and undistracting.  Its storyline's superfluous but entertaining nevertheless.  The basic game is quite long, and this length, along with the wonderful replay value in optimizing each level's stats makes the game a $/hr bargain.
As the creator has bemoaned in interviews, the name SpaceChem scares away potential players who believe that the game is chemistry based.  However, a chemistry background is about as useful as a degree in ornithology for Angry Birds.  What
help is programming experience,  since the atomic manipulation is a veneer for a deep sequential instruction "programming language."  In fact, this game would be a fun tool to indirectly introduce computer programming to kids.  Well, super smart kids, since the game is
.
Last, and for some, least, there's an unheralded "multiplayer" component in outdoing your Steam friends on each level.  Some of the most fun I've had with the game has been the playful trashtalking earned by one-upping my pal's best scores just to see him retaliate with an even better solution.  This back and forth improvment closely mimics the most satisfying part of the engineering process, and once again, is a testament to the fundamental elegance of the game's design.

Here’s a game I don’t like, but actually feel bad about not liking.
SpaceChem is a puzzle game in which you have to create chemical compounds inside reactors. To be more precise, your job is to create procedures that assemble those compounds - yes, assemble. It’s not so much a game about chemistry as it is about creating factory lines, or concurrent programs.
The concept behind the game is nothing short of brilliant, and I don’t think there’s a single game in the market remotely like it. I was taken by it in the first few hours. After that, however, the difficulty ramped up considerably, and I found myself taking way too long to figure out a single solution.
That’s my problem with the game, it’s just too complicated for its own good. You have to spend massive amounts of time on details trying to make the solution work, and forget about the story because of how much time goes by between scenes. It ends up feeling like a job, not a diversion.
Sometimes, I wish I could have gotten into it. I admire people who play this game well. In fact, I spent a lot of time at
trying out different solutions for levels, completely taken by how brilliant they were. But I saw no joy in trying to figure them out myself.
I guess SpaceChem can be compared to EVE Online in this regard. It’s a game that’s really fun to watch unfold, but only the most patient and dedicated can actually play. If you’re in that group, good, buy it, but if you’re like me, skip it. There’s not much for you here.

A must buy for stealth fans. Instead of giving you a linear map for each mission, dishonored gives you a small, open area full of enemies and innocent people alike. Not only that, but each map is the opposite of linear, offering many different paths and opportunities to missions. There are loads of side missions and you can play the game without killing anyone or being seen once, play the game killing everyone and everything sneakily, or play the game like bioshock, disregarding the sneaking altogether. All of this mixed with a somewhat good storyline, a good amount of abilities, great player progression, and buyable upgrades makes this not only one of the best stealth games I have ever played, but one of the most replayable.
There is a reason this game was made in 2012 and is still 20 dollars.
If you are still iffy about buying, the price drops substantially during sales, especially winter ones, sometimes to 5 dollars.

The Long Dark is one of my favorite games of all time. Survival games have a special place and my heart; they can offer some of the most immersive and intense situations in gaming and I love them. The Long Dark is a great survival game. It has one of the best sandbox modes I have ever seen, with deep and rich environments and in-depth survival mechanics. The inclusion of sandbox challenges gives a great distraction from the basic survival sandbox and are both fun and difficult, but not annoying. If you enjoy survival games because they are survival games, then you will love The Long Dark.
That being said, there is something I have to talk about. Many people are upset with how the game's story mode turned out. Many things that were promised have not been delivered on, and the loads of hype surrounding the story have not helped soften the reception. Still, the timer that hit us towards the start of the summer, the one that counted down to the story mode's *announcement* that the game would be released three months later, killed most of my enthusiasm. The story mode was out for a good few days before I dipped my toes into it, and even then I haven't finished the second episode.
But I don't want to talk about all the things that weren't delivered to us. I want to talk about the story as if I knew nothing about it and expected nothing from it. I want to look at it as objectively as I can muster (for now, at least).
So, let's just get on with it. The story itself, the one were crashed bushpilot Will Mackenzie is trying to find his... friend(?) Dr. Astrid, uh Wheeler (hell if I know what her last name is), is lackluster. First of all, Will is supposed to be trying to find his friend after they both crash in a zone of Canadian wilderness where some strange event made stuff go bad a decade ago. So, why is he taking his time to bother with an old blind lady, or a crazy, dying man? I think it had been close to ten days before I moved on from episode one. Do you know how much could happen to Astrid in TEN DAYS?
Let's focus on the blind lady for now, since I haven't really done much in the second episode. I won't go into spoilers more than the one where you meet an old blind lady named Grey Mother who *helps* you find your friend. Don't worry, this happens maybe a half hour into the game depending on your pace, so it's not really a spoiler.
Grey Mother is your stereotypical "blind oracle woman." She talks about how she "hears" the voices of your friend and others in the storm that happened a few days ago. This baits Will in (yes, she BAITS him. I'll get to that later). She promises to tell Will what happened to Astrid after she does some tasks for him. Will, with no better leads, agrees to help the lady. So, what does will do? Fetch quests. Loads of them.
Grey Mother sends you on one fetch quest after the next, each time giving absolutely useless "clues" about Astrid, dangling the hope of information about her in front of the player's nose before sending us off on another fetch quest. She is an evil old woman, taking advantage of a stranded man who is just looking for his friend; a friend who may be hurt or even thinks he's dead. To top it all off (spoiler coming, skip to the next paragraph to avoid), by the end of her quest lines, she doesn't even tell you anything useful. Seriously, we were no closer to finding Astrid.
Needless to say, I hate the character of Grey Mother. She is useless, mean (she constantly insults Will), and manipulative. When the story tried to get me to empathize with her about an emotional tragedy that she had in her past, I couldn't care less. I just wanted her to shut up and tell me where my friend was so I could advance the story.
So, overall, how is the story (at least, Episode 1)? I didn't like it. Not at all. As a writer myself (more dabbling, but still), I don't understand how the uninteresting dialogue made it past years of development. As a gamer, I don't understand how someone thought all these fetch quests were a good idea. Because they aren't. They're boring. They aren't FUN.
The story mode boils down to being uninteresting at best, to outright nonsensical and infuriating at worst. Honestly, I was a bit hyped for the story, but this is just ridiculous. No one likes fetch quests (okay, I'm sure SOMEONE does, but come on) and the story itself in slow and boring. I'll probably play Episode 2 just to say I did, but from what I've heard, it doesn't get better.
Okay, here's the part where I am really going to rant. Skip this paragraph if you want. We've waited years, YEARS, for what, fetch quests? Who thought hours of fetch quests would be fun? Who thought doing tedious and boring busy work of an old lady who makes it clear she doesn't like you would be fun? Because it isn't. It makes me mad. I always take the diplomatic route when I can, but I would have taken Grey Mother's gun and left her there if I could. It's total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. ♥♥♥♥ your fetch quests, Hinterland.
Okay. Sorry about that. Look, if you've made it this far, then I really do thank you. Buy this game and play the sandbox if that is what you are into, because you will enjoy that. But if you don't really like purely sandbox games, then don't get The Long Dark. Because while the story does direct your survival and give you goals to complete, they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ goals.
The Long Dark as a game, 9/10 great stuff.
The Long Dark as a story, 4.5/10 mediocre and flat.

Horrible, unbalanced, irredeemably broken, counter-intuitive game design that doesn't work. Yes it's "unique," but so is a bicycle with cubes instead of wheels. Does that mean it works as a game? No it does not, contrary to what the♥♥♥♥♥♥eating lowlifes at charlatan blogs like RPS might tell you.
I was initially drawn to this game because of its intriguing promise of a tower defense dungeon crawler. "How the heck would that work?" I asked myself. DoTE's answer was: "lol it doesn't, but thanks for the money." What we have here, ladies and gentlemen, is your classic Emperor's New Clothes situation. 90% positive reviews, naturally, because none of the brain surgeons writing reviews for this abomination wants to be the first to ask why the Emperor's strolling around in the nude. The RPS monkey ♥♥♥♥ers gave it a rave review based on ten minutes of cretinous button mashing at a trade show so it can't be bad! If your first instinct is to dismiss this as a cracked design due to its many fatal flaws immediately apparent to even the most casual connoisseur of game design, allow me to say you would be perfectly right in saying so.
What's wrong with it, you may ask? Where do I begin? It's a mix of real time and turn based which may strike you as totally counter-intuitive at first. Oh, and you can pause. So... why is there an RTS component again? Presumably the developers didn't have the imagination to create a turn-based TD game and instead forced RTS onto it because of the conventional wisdom that all TD MUST be in real time. Just like all shooters must be in first person, herp derp.
But I'm getting away from the point. This isn't necessarily a fatal flaw in the design, even if it is incredibly clumsy. The fatal flaw is introduced in the interaction between the game's janky real time combat and the permadeath system. As you might expect from a game advertising itself as a "roguelike dungeon crawl" this game has permadeath, which is fine. The problem is in how easily your characters (in whom you're compelled to sink huge amounts of resources. Did I not talk about that? There's no XP. Of course there isn't! Instead you have to spend the Food resource to level your characters. Because every game has to have that FIDS resource system crammed into its design.) die with ZERO warning. You can look away for a split second to build some towers or some♥♥♥♥♥♥and one of your characters will be dead when you focus on them again. Great game design. They aren't incapacitated or require reviving or anything, they are immediately DEAD when their hp goes down to 0, effectively ending your run. Contrast with the clever character permadeath system from something like Darkest Dungeon.
I could go on with other similarly horrid examples, but I'll spare you. Broken, non-functional, non-viable, vomit-inducing game that should've been aborted in the prototype stage, but instead astonishingly made it to release. I keep trying to find some good in it but come up empty handed at each attempt. And finally, the lazy hipster pixel graphics as the icing on this particular♥♥♥♥♥♥cake. Last time I give this studio any money, and I've already given them plenty.

A unique combination of roguelite, dungeon-crawler, and tower defense. Definitely worth a look. I love the graphics, and the music even more. If you own Endless Space and/or Endless Legend (Amplitude's other games), then it's worth it to buy the upgraded editions, as there's some unique content available by owning those other games. If you buy the upgraded editions of those games, you'll get added content for buying Dungeon of the Endless! None of it's essential, but some of it's fun.
I've played over 50 hours of the game and have unlocked all but 1 character, and only half of the pods (the 'ship' you start in--various pods alter the starting conditions and change the rules throughout the course of the game). There's plenty of content, and the formula works well enough to provide hours of gameplay. For some real fun and chaos, just add friends! You can't pause in multiplayer, and with 4 players, everyone controls their own character, making coordination vital and extremely fun, especially if you can get some voice chat going (which is easy now that steam's voice chat is pretty damn good these days.)
*One thing to be aware of: You do not directly control the actions of your characters, nor do you directly engage in combat! You click to open doors, interact with NPCs and objects, and move from room to room. The characters will automatically attack enemies based on certain priorities. You can activate your abilities on command, but that's it. When I bought it, I thought you controlled your characters like in Diablo or League of Legends or Dota, but that isn't the case and I was majorly turned off. But I quickly discovered that the more hands-off control lend itself very well to this game and quickly picked up on it and started having a blast!
9.5/10, would recommend. I subtracted .5 only because there are a couple minor annoyances regarding controls: I wish you could assign all your heroes' abilities each their own keybind. As it is, you have to select that hero and then press a key (or click an icon) to activate the ability. It's fine in singleplayer when you can pause it, but in MP when you're controller 2-3 heroes at once, it can be a pain in real-time.

This game is definitely a classic. If you know anything about The Forgotten Realms or Dungeons&Dragons in general, than you definitely need to get this. I am a Dungeon Master myself, and seeing rules and actions of a tabletop role-playing game is definitely exciting. Anyway, here is a full list pros and cons...
Pros-
Emersion, very emersive world with lots of lore. You don't need any prior D&D experience to really appreciate the vastness of the world. As a Dungeon Master, I have learned a lot about the Forgotten Realm lore from playing Baldur's Gate.
Dialogue, although this may seem like a small thing, it is something I thought I would point out. The dialogue is believable when it needs to be, but also very humorous in parts as well. Space Hamster Boo!
Combat, the combat is good and well balanced, each class actually serves a unique and power purpose. It is basically taking the combat straight from the tabletop RPG and putting it in the game.
Graphics, although the game itself is dated to some degree, graphically it is still good. The enviroment and atmosphere is nearly perfect, areas look believable, feel how they should feel. The characters and monsters fit the overall graphic theme, so overall the graphics just fit perfectly for this kind of game.
Cons-
Difficulty, this is more or less a problem, it really depends on what your starting class is. Early on you have to be careful as you have limited resources you can use. In later game the difficulty levels out fairly though.
Class Balancing, but didn't I say that the combat was balanced? Well, sadly Dungeons&Dragons has had a hard time trying to balance all of the classes to the "perfectly balanced" point. This is also true in the pen and paper/tabletop Dungeons&Dragons as well. This isn't really a problem in theory, but it does put more favor on certain class choices. Although early on the classes are all balanced, the late game is where the balancing can vary. Basically, I have noticed that Fighter/Mage duel class is completely overpowered in late game because of high defense plus defensive magic (actually did a solo run with a Fighter/Mage duel class). Anyway, moving on now...
Tricky Controls, at first the controls may seem a bit tricky, with little in the way of a tutorial (well, if you don't walk to where the "tutorial" is then you don't get anything really). Being able to control your characters is definitely tricky early on, with all of the combat and magic using and so on. You can always pause the combat and give commands, but this feels unnatural and slow.
Inefficient Interface, the menu layout is a bit confusing at first, but after a while you get the hang of it. Again, the menu layout and things aren't really explained in a tutorial or anything, so you are left to figure it out. Moving items around and things like that is also somewhat of a problem, having it open one characters inventory and moving it to another characters, so forth and so on...
Conclusion-
Definitely recommend this game, if you like classic Dungeons&Dragons tabletop gaming or things like it, then this game is a must. The game itself feels like you are playing a session of Dungeons&Dragons with your friends (just without your friends, and on your PC instead of on a table with pens and paper). If you are a Dungeon Master, then this is a must, even if you don't want it. The amount of D&D lore that this game prevides if massive. Anyway, hopefully this review has effected your view as to whether or not to get Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition.
May your adventures be many and always end in reward!
-Donoknight, Founder of the Tabletop RPG Gamers League

+
Character Creation:
This is one of my favorite parts of the game, creating your character.
In the original Baldurs Gate there already were tons of diffrent ways you could create your characters.
The Enchanced Edition however includes the Class Kits from Baldurs Gate 2 and with Multi-Classing and Dual Classing (which if im gonna try to explain the craziness of that this review would be twice as long) it makes for an insane ammount of replay value.
Gameplay:
I'v heard people say that this game is complicated  . .to which i say . . compared to modern versions like the Dragon Age games it kinda is, it can get really hard at times too but thats part of why i love Baldurs Gate and other D&D Games.
Its not the kind of game you can just rush through, you have to have some strategy, pay attention and sorta "learn" the game.
Music:
In general a Good soundtrack, don't have much to say here honestly, there's nothing really specal that sticks out.
Characters:
Apart from the character creation and having lots of diffrent dialogue options to choose from, there's a total of 29 party members to choose from in the game including 4 new ones added to the Enchanced version which is a nice addition.
You don't get to interact with them as much as you do in for example the Dragon Age and Mass Effect series and even though some of the Party members are more useful than others the ammount of people you can choose to have in your party alone makes for lots of replay value.
Story:
Bioware and Black Isle(Known as Obsidian Entertainment nowdays) have a talent for creating some great and intresting stories in video games and Baldurs Gate is no exception. It's one of the best things about this game in my opinion(dont wanna say much here because i dont wanna spoil anything)
Graphics:
May not look much compared to Modern games like the Dragon Age Series but(then again it is nearly 20 years old) back then i thought this game looked great dispite the awful resolution in the original version.
Thankfully the Enhanced Edition puts the BG2 engine into the game and makes the resolution extremely nice.

Baldur's Gate is one of those games that's almost indescribably important to gaming as a whole. One that's so influential and genre defining, that it still stands the test of time. Although not nearly as well as it's successor. This game shows it's age not just visually, but in design in some very annoying areas. Mostly the difficulty. This game is hard, like hazardous to your mental health hard. I nearly had a mental breakdown a couple times in this game. While the story is still (mostly) excellent the gameplay can get seriously tedious and irritating at times. This game carries over some of the  "hard for the sake of hard" retro difficulty that used to characterize games of this era.
You'll walk into a room and have your entire party neutralized by a confusion spell before you even realized what happened. You'll walk into a trap you had no reason to believe was there after hours of play without even seeing one at all. You'll constantly loose a party member in seconds. You'll die over and over again because of incredibly awful pathing issues. You'll cast a spell only to have your party member get hit by an arrow from across the screen and loose that spell from your pool. You'll walk into fights over and over and over again that can only be conquered from careful preparation and near perfect formation, that irritatingly can only be figured out after experiencing the fight once.
Dragon Age Origins had a problem with huge difficulty spikes, but this? This is completely absurd. There is far too many fights in this game that feel like horribly unbalanced crapshoots. One of the ways this game adds difficulty is to put most of the hardest fights in the game in tiny, cramped rooms and just fill them to the brim with mages. Trying to stop multiple mages at once from casting confusion spells that will wipe out half of your party if it gets off is irritating, and it's even worse in tiny rooms. The pathing issues are amplified to maddening levels here as your entire party bumps and slams into each other while mages are busy roasting your party in seconds. Baldur's Gate 2 added confusion protection spells which was a godsend. Here? You have to just take it, and it's incredibly annoying.
There is A LOT of stuff you are going to have to put up with to enjoy this game. Save often, and be prepared to load saves often. This game will kill you repeatedly with no warning, you have to be willing to deal with that to enjoy this game at all.
So with that out of the way let's talk about how this is one of the best RPG's I've ever played (It actually is.) When things go right in this game, my god is it satisfying. Buffing up your entire party with stat boosts and conquering enormous bosses with tactics that only you could come up with, feels... it's just amazing.
The RPG mechanics and gameplay are just near perfect here, building a proper character and party is easy and fun to do.  The loot is incredibly rewarding to equip and is numerous and interesting. Exploration is very rewarding here, make sure to check every inch of every area, (especially in the beginning.) The interface is one of the best I've ever seen, 17 years later and it's still a joy to use. It's one of those games that achieves a near perfect synthesis of RPG mechanics, story and exploration that provide an experience that's impossibly immersive.
After the 66 hours of infuriating and rewarding gameplay I can't help but say that I loved this game. I wanted to quit, multiple times during this playthrough. Especially in the middle section with the never ending Cloakwood Forest, but I stuck it out and really learned this game even when it killed me repeatedly with no warning. If you are willing to accept brutal and unforgiving challenge in reward for a wonderful story and immensely deep gameplay then this is the game for you. Not for the light of heart or the intellectually lazy, but absolutely worth the struggle if you can look past the retro difficulty.
One of my all time favourite, a little dated but still worth a play through.
Worth every penny and (slowly) keeps getting better with every update.

Just because this is the best simulation of a zombie apocalypse currently on Steam doesn't make it the most fun.  This is not a "fun" game. Left 4 Dead, Dead Rising, and Dying Light are fun. Telltales' The Walking Dead, This War of Mine, and Project Zomboid are not fun.
You play to survive. This involves not starving. To do this, you need to eat food. Ensure that you have food, the food is not rotted or rotting, it is preserved in some way, and the fact that you are eating it won't depress your player character to the point where they no longer have the will to fight anymore.
This doesn't mean it isn't a good game. Some of the most intense moments I've had in games stem from the zombies in Project Zomboids. If they see you, they will attempt to eat you. As a way to prevent this, you can put sheets on your windows. At one point, as I was putting the last sheet on the last window, a zombie saw me. They wanted to eat me, so they slowly waddled forward, and beat on a window. It broke. More heard. I proceeded to sit upstairs, holding a handgun that wasn't fully loaded, pointed at the locked door to my room. I could either try to fight my way past the crowd, that I heard slowly growing as more noise was made, or jump from a window, potentially injuring my leg and leaving me helpless. That was a suspenseful moment I don't find in many other games.
If you like games for the fear, dread, and opposite of a power fantasy, Project Zomboid is the game for you.

As a fan who originally bought this game on Desura about six years ago, it's important for potential buyers know that this is a game that will most likely be in early access for a while more. This is a game that has been constantly updated, slowly but surely, into the game that it currently is today. In the years since I bought it, they've added:
-Nutrional systems
-Medical systems
-A sort of nature taking over civilization mechanic (trees, weeds and grass grow over time)
-Seasons, with temperatures influencing your life
-Foraging, trapping and fishing
-Radio and television broadcasts for use in traps and communication
-Randomized safehouses and hand drawn maps
-Engineering
-Metalworking
-Multiplayer
As of this review, the developers are working on adding cars, with a related mechanical skill to tinker and repair any cars that you may find. This is much needed, as the map within the game is HUGE (google project zomboid map, its essentially a 1:1 scale of five small towns in Kentuky). In addition to all of this, the other two milestones that they are working on right now are an animation overhaul and the much anticipated NPC update.
Overall, this is a game that has been worked on by, I believe six people for almost a decade, and will most likely be so for a few more years. If you are the sort of person who would wait for a game to come out of early access before buying it, you're out of luck I'm afraid. However, the game itself is well developed as it stands right now, and is playable at this time. The only thing that you should know is that this game is HARD. It's a rogue game in every sense of the word; you can die from zombies, starvation, infection, hypothermia, and dehydration with relative ease if you're not careful. It's by far one of the best survival games out there, as it's takes every aspect of survival into account.

This game looked very promising, but I was, sadly, disappointed. I really wanted to like it.  From the screenshots it looked awesome, but it isn't nearly as pretty in game.  In fact, it gave me a bit of a headache after a while.
The puzzles are pretty brainless and incredibly linear.  Your path will be blocked until you have completed a task and an on screen tip will tell you exactly where you need to go next.  There is no map, but it's not difficult to navigate at all.  There is no freedom to do anything except the task that's been laid out for you already.  Exploring gives you some extra plot which is very predictable.
The story is silly and almost charming.  I actually found the text - both the tool tips that flash on the screen and the item descriptions - to be very enjoyable and humorous, but everything else fell completely flat.  Jokes are over done (you will hear "Stupid idiot" A LOT, and it isn't really funny the first time) and not very creative.  They come at you with plenty of time to anticipate them.  It's very tedious.
It's not a long game, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I was still asking myself "Is this game over yet?"  It crashed once near the end, but that was the only bug I recall encountering.  You can't do anything during the credits.  You can't skip them or speed them up.  You have to alt/tab and exit the game that way.  Unless you really enjoy the song (I did not), it's agonizing.
If your sense of humor goes along with the game, then I would say you can enjoy this in spite of how linear and simple the puzzles are.  Otherwise, I would not recommend this game.

Maize is... sigh... If there ever was a game to encapsulate the bad whimsical kind of horror themed comedies of the 80s, this game is exactly that. Nonsensical plot about mad scientists, soviet intelligent teddy bear spitting gibberish "russian" as a companion and words like "stupid", "imbecile", "idiot" and variations being about 70% of words in the script. Now, the whole concept could actually work, and that is exactly what is the saddest thing about the game is that it fails so miserably, mostly due to the fact that it recreates that vibe down to the "bad" part. Because it's bad. Not so bad it's good bad, but just bad as a comedy game.
And as an adventure game it seems to want to be it's even worse, since you just run back and forth and put items on other items and paths open and close in a very linear fashion so you never "solve" anything as much as you just "do stuff". What's also surprising is how ugly the game often looks, despite the use of UE4, some stunning models and good animations. You can be in a very pretty looking location to just turn the corner and find yourself in a terrible "my first UE SDK map" room that looks sickeningly bad. It's a game that could've been, but went very-very wrong and really isn't worth the time.

tl;dr version:
A fair price is...
- If you like turn based strategy, buy it for $7 or less.
- If you don't like this sort of thing, wait until it goes on sale for $3 or less.
More details version:
Pros:
- Lots of tactical decisions. Night/Day missions. Civilian defense missions. Combat tactics.
- Lots of weapons, species and lore to research.
- Loose win conditions. Ultimately you beat the aliens, but everything in between is your call so long as you don't lose.
- A lot of lore and hidden mechanics. Tactics exist and enemies have weaknesses, but you have to find them.
- Hugely rewarding experience.
Cons:
- This game does zero hand holding. There's no tutorial; you'll have to read the manual before you start.
- Can be very frustrating. I have had to uninstal this game out of irritation from time to time.
- Default steam settings on the Dos Box will take some tweaking so it runs well on your computer. Easy to correct though.
- Regardless of variety of missions, can become repetetive if you take a long time to figure out how to win the game.
- Did I already say it is very hard and frustrating?

This game literally demonstrated evolution. All the players who weren't good at monster switched over to hunter and got good there and vice versa. Then they both continued to get better respectively, and now there is a huge learning curve. Once you get past it it's pretty fun. Or if you feel like playing with bots you can. But since the game's basic shutdown, playing it is hard. If you've been with it since the first beta, not the stage 2 beta, then you still have all three of the basic characters. However playing it is a little difficult. Nine times out of ten you aren't logged in properly and have to restart the game multiple times. Other times you can't even find a proper game server. Worst of all when you do you're likely to lose your entire team and play a game against bots. With friends it's still a great game, aside from the bugs that will never get fixed thanks to 2k. But if you're trying to just play online then it won't work. It's currently gone to the final stage of evolution, Extinction.

*Stage 2 Review
So, all my progress if gone, skins are gone, Evacuation (the only worthwhile mode) is gone, and the general gameplay is changed so much as to be almost unrecognisable.
If you're a returning 'founder', don't come back. The game is worse for this, and we've ended up paying a ♥♥♥♥♥one of money for a downgraded game in the end.
For those who are of the second stage, best of luck to you. The game may well be worthwhile to you now that its free, not knowing that it was much better at one point. Give it a try, the asymmetric gameplay may well catch you. But for the love of all that is holy, be wary of giving the devs any kind of money. Chances are, it's not what you think it is and its overpriced to boot.
tl;dr Don't come back if you bought this the first time. Give it a try but beware of giving money to those coming in FTP.
*Stage 1 Review: for posterity.
Save yoruself the trouble. It's a decent $100 game, not the lower price core game you think you're buying.
The game itself is interesting, fun to play when there are people, and pleasantly tactical (with, in my opinion, Evacuation campaign being the most worthwhile and least repeditive part). It's pretty (of course), and you COULD potentially get plenty of hours out of this.
However, the pricing is terrible, being exploitative and manipulative. It is not 'pay-to-win', as the things you pay for are either cosmetic, or balanced with other parts of the game. However, the incessant amount of paying, and the amount you get for the price, is not worth it.
Basically, this game is worth it if all the DLC were free (or at least dramatically discounted for everything, including all season passes). This is likely not what the publishers want to do, and likely will never do.
For the sake of everyone in the game already, DO NOT PAY FULL PRICE FOR THIS GAME.

Here’s a game I don’t like, but actually feel bad about not liking.
SpaceChem is a puzzle game in which you have to create chemical compounds inside reactors. To be more precise, your job is to create procedures that assemble those compounds - yes, assemble. It’s not so much a game about chemistry as it is about creating factory lines, or concurrent programs.
The concept behind the game is nothing short of brilliant, and I don’t think there’s a single game in the market remotely like it. I was taken by it in the first few hours. After that, however, the difficulty ramped up considerably, and I found myself taking way too long to figure out a single solution.
That’s my problem with the game, it’s just too complicated for its own good. You have to spend massive amounts of time on details trying to make the solution work, and forget about the story because of how much time goes by between scenes. It ends up feeling like a job, not a diversion.
Sometimes, I wish I could have gotten into it. I admire people who play this game well. In fact, I spent a lot of time at
trying out different solutions for levels, completely taken by how brilliant they were. But I saw no joy in trying to figure them out myself.
I guess SpaceChem can be compared to EVE Online in this regard. It’s a game that’s really fun to watch unfold, but only the most patient and dedicated can actually play. If you’re in that group, good, buy it, but if you’re like me, skip it. There’s not much for you here.

The game starts simply, but the difficulty increases

This game is not for the feint of heart, the puzzles are
. But since the game operates within a well defined set of rules, you will find yourself thinking of solutions throughout the day. I found myself drawing sketches to solutions that I had brainstormed while at work. Then I'd eagerly wait until the day was over to get home, try out the idea, and refine any issues. Like I said, the game consumes your life. But when you find yourself stumped on a puzzle for hours, only to conjure a solution during the day, and implement it to great success, you will feel an immense amount of accomplishment.
Quite simply, this is one of the best puzzle games I have played. I wish there was more, I must have more. My only disclaimer is that if you don't like steeply difficult challenges, then you likely won't enjoy this game. I will say it once more, this game is

A fairly good horror experience. Picked this up in a humble bundle and I've been pleasantly surprised with it. Very atmospheric, good visuals and solid sound effects that really immerse you in the environment. The game does not go for easy jump scares, instead it builds atmosphere and tension slowly. A few negatives - Level design lets it down a little bit. A lot of the areas look very similar making it easy to get lost. Overall it is a thumbs up from me, i think this will please most fans of the horror genre. A flawed but pretty gem.

The game refreshingly throws you completely empty handed into its cold, dead world, with no indication where to go whatsoever. It left me pleasantly unsure what to expect and this produced a very authentic initial immersion. Once you recover your essential equipment (a compass, a map and a flashlight) and after you discover your first few key locations, the game keeps rolling on the same steady pattern until the end.
You spend the bulk of your time slowly exploring snowy grey landscapes to investigate a strange incident. The very convincing snow and effects convey a superb impression of extreme coldness and desolation. Realistic sounds of constantly blowing wind, creaking ice and footsteps in the snow are only surpassed by the spooky distant whistles and howls occasionally heard. The remarkable sound design also features brilliantly chilling music.
Overall the game looks great but is not without repetitiveness in between the few, more interesting and unique supernatural moments.
The very intriguing premise loses some of its appeal on first contact with the anomaly, mostly because it draws you to expect something more unconventional or inventive. The narrative leads to an appreciable journey into madness that nonetheless manages to stay intriguing throughout, albeit confusing.
Aside from the main event locations you must discover, the game is peppered with articles and journals hidden more or less uniformly through the world. Normally I rarely appreciate collectible hunts but Kholat handles these well. A very audible sound cue heard from a generous range informs you whenever you stand nearby a page, and once you hear it it is generally very easy to get to it. Discovering them is optional but adds greatly to the story's development. The notes are then marked on your map, which incidentally helps you reorient since it's so very easy to get lost.
It is notoriously difficult to use a map completely without UI guidance, especially for someone like me who gets easily disoriented. It is hard to keep track of where you've been since the map is also not explicitly detailed. Navigating around the environment is the game's sole challenge, so getting the hang of using the map and compass is imperative if you are to gain any enjoyment out of it. There are no puzzles to solve or situations that require thoughtful decisions.
The only thing to fear, aside from losing your way, are the various manifestations of the anomaly and the occasional trap. Death is instantaneous and wholly unnecessary to the plot. It presents the game's most annoying element as it only forces you to restart at the last checkpoint with absolutely no gained benefit. Your only way around is avoidance but you don't need to get smart.
Despite the harsh conditions, you never have to rest or get warm. This is not about survival. Your character does not even seem to be affected by the cold in any way. There may be an explanation for that in the game's ineffective ending but I will not spoil it, except to mention that it inspires ambiguous conclusions that are completely open to interpretation. It is only satisfying in the sense that it keeps you thinking about the story long after you've stopped playing but it offers no closure.
The game is short but it's really just about the right length for what it has to deliver. It offered approximately 5 hours for a normal run going at a casual pace. The only reason to go back would be to hunt the remaining story collectibles, which I am not inclined to do.
Get this only if you enjoy tense, long, slow walks in the snow, with a dash of unexplained paranormal activity.

KF1 is a fun game with straightforward purpose: Survive the waves of Specimens (failed clones) mobs, kill stuff to earn cash, buy better weapons and armor at the trader, defeat boss during final wave. Typically, you will want to buy items that align with your specialized role.
Roles specializations emphasizes the importance of team play. Difficulty scales with the number of people in your game, so you do want to play smarter as more players join. Generally, your safest team composition has a medic to heal, a commando to clear out weaker enemies, and a sharpshooter to pick off the most dangerous ones.
In terms of variety, there are many different maps. This keeps the game new and exciting because you need to move strategically around the map to get to the trader at the end of the wave. In my opinion, pacing and positioning are more difficult to master in this game than other apocalyptic shooters such as L4d. I think KF1 has aged well because of this quality is quite special.
In a world of extremely fast paced shooters, KF1 requires you to learn the balance between camping and always moving due to the barebones design of combat. For the uninitiated, the game feels “slow but fast" due to the mobs coming from all directions. It is easy to underestimate them and think that you won't be overwhelmed because they appear to move slowly. There is little to no explanation of the special weapons for different roles (medic grenades work differently than all others), different types Specimen (your character doesn't call out what they are like they do in L4d), etc.
Additionally, I prefer this older graphic style over the more colorful design of KF2. It preserves a grittier atmosphere. Combined with the metal soundtrack, harkens to the older era of video games that don’t hold your hand. This is apparent in the lack of explanations previously mentioned. You either get with the program, or you die!
My only criticism of the game is its barrier to understanding. In large part, the interface seems older and unintuitive. For example, the skill system for different roles can be very confusing without additional help from either your friends or from online guides. The UI design of the Trader window can also be confusing when you are trying to look at all of the options within the short time frame given (typically 30 - 60 sec). Lastly, it is a pain trying to figure out how to host a game with your friends. To this day, I’m not sure how you do it. One of our friends simply joins an existing empty server and sends the rest of us invites.

If you like building games with an RPG style for your citizens, this is quite fun. It's still in alpha state, but they working hard on it. I won't compair it with the most ambitious and genius builder game there is: Dwarf Fortress! If you do not know what that game is...you not really a building game fan...honestly you are an idiot if you do not know DF. But FF you are drifing offshore...
- The style is a bit like Minecraft...everything is made of square blocks. It has it's charm and it's done very nicely. I even got some ideas from this game build in Minecraft.
- The game has two kind of races and maps: Dessert and forrest. On the forrest map it's too easy, chop trees build wooden houses and mass produce wooden swords for trading. On a dessert map it's more difficult at start and you need clay to continue, build houses and so on.
- The RPG element is limited: If an citizen has no tool equipted it's a worker, that digs,chops and carries stuff around. If you equipt a tool it gains experience for that class. To a maximum of level 6. This is done very easily and imo far too fast to gain a long live expancy of this game. You gain a special skill once you reach this level. If you pick another profession for that citizen after level 6, it virtually must reach level 7. Leveling up opens up different kinds of classes and items it can make. For instance, a farmer needs to be level 2 to become a cook. And a level 4 cook can bake bread etc. Also some experienced classes have a change to make a nicer version of that item.
- Buildings are premade or you can design it yourself and even save them! This is great idea and very easy to use. Some bug here and there... If you want to change the colour of the walls, while the construction is already started, will leave the building unfinished. But I do not doubt they will get rid of that bug asap.
- Interface is easy to use, you can select for every citizen what he/she must do. (like dwarf therapist for DF) You can look at the map several ways, closed buildings, half open or x-ray. Which are very good and handy to place items or mine.
- To gain new citizens you need an amount of placed items and building and gold. And if you reach it on the start of a new day a new citizens will arrive. This is very cool and you will need to keep trading and building to gain new citizens. Also this amount will be raised once you reach it.
So in overal it's very fun to play, but it's way too easy! (especially if you expect a difficulty of DF) Also you can reroll your starting villagers till they all have six for the 3 stats they have. If you save just before sunrise. So when an new citizen arrives you can reload if you do not want that one. It's ahs some bugs but very good support and most bugs are gone within a week. Now that's something other developers can learn something about. Combat is funny to see but enemies are again way too easy...even giant skeletons are killed one on one by your 1 lvl soldier with a wooden sword... So I hope there will be more challence. Also I miss interaction between your citizens, they are just walking around, eating,sleeping but there is no communication between them...that's something they must implement asap! Cause now it's fun but boring after a while. Ohw yes I want a trader that drinks too much or goes to sleep while the traders are almost leaving! I want citizen that gossips about another citizen or even falls in love...if they put that into the game...wow!

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
-3/4 cup white sugar
-3 tablespoons cornstarch
-1/4 teaspoon salt
-1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
-4 cups fresh blueberries
-1 recipe pastry for a 9 inch double crust pie
-1 tablespoon butter
Directions:
-Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
-Mix sugar, cornstarch, salt, and cinnamon, and sprinkle over blueberries.
-Line pie dish with one pie crust. Pour berry mixture into the crust, and dot with butter. Cut remaining pastry into 1/2 - 3/4 inch wide strips, and make lattice top. Crimp and flute edges.
-Bake pie on lower shelf of oven for about 50 minutes, or until crust is golden brown.
Tip:
-Aluminum foil can be used to keep food moist, cook it evenly, and make clean-up easier.

Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 are some of my most nostalgic games and among my Top 10 Favorite games of all time, i could play the original version over and over again and never get tired of it, thus i bought the Enhanced Edition of BGEE1 which at first it seemed like a great remake of the original classic.
+
Character Creation:
This is one of my favorite parts of the game, creating your character.
In the original Baldurs Gate there already were tons of diffrent ways you could create your characters.
The Enchanced Edition however includes the Class Kits from Baldurs Gate 2 and with Multi-Classing and Dual Classing (which if im gonna try to explain the craziness of that this review would be twice as long) it makes for an insane ammount of replay value.
Gameplay:
I'v heard people say that this game is complicated  . .to which i say . . compared to modern versions like the Dragon Age games it kinda is, it can get really hard at times too but thats part of why i love Baldurs Gate and other D&D Games.
Its not the kind of game you can just rush through, you have to have some strategy, pay attention and sorta "learn" the game.
Music:
In general a Good soundtrack, don't have much to say here honestly, there's nothing really specal that sticks out.
Characters:

You don't get to interact with them as much as you do in for example the Dragon Age and Mass Effect series and even though some of the Party members are more useful than others the ammount of people you can choose to have in your party alone makes for lots of replay value.
Story:
Bioware and Black Isle(Known as Obsidian Entertainment nowdays) have a talent for creating some great and intresting stories in video games and Baldurs Gate is no exception. It's one of the best things about this game in my opinion(dont wanna say much here because i dont wanna spoil anything)
Graphics:
May not look much compared to Modern games like the Dragon Age Series but(then again it is nearly 20 years old) back then i thought this game looked great dispite the awful resolution in the original version.
Thankfully the Enhanced Edition puts the BG2 engine into the game and makes the resolution extremely nice.
-

Baldur's Gate is one of those games that's almost indescribably important to gaming as a whole. One that's so influential and genre defining, that it still stands the test of time. Although not nearly as well as it's successor. This game shows it's age not just visually, but in design in some very annoying areas. Mostly the difficulty. This game is hard, like hazardous to your mental health hard. I nearly had a mental breakdown a couple times in this game. While the story is still (mostly) excellent the gameplay can get seriously tedious and irritating at times. This game carries over some of the  "hard for the sake of hard" retro difficulty that used to characterize games of this era.
You'll walk into a room and have your entire party neutralized by a confusion spell before you even realized what happened. You'll walk into a trap you had no reason to believe was there after hours of play without even seeing one at all. You'll constantly loose a party member in seconds. You'll die over and over again because of incredibly awful pathing issues. You'll cast a spell only to have your party member get hit by an arrow from across the screen and loose that spell from your pool. You'll walk into fights over and over and over again that can only be conquered from careful preparation and near perfect formation, that irritatingly can only be figured out after experiencing the fight once.
Dragon Age Origins had a problem with huge difficulty spikes, but this? This is completely absurd. There is far too many fights in this game that feel like horribly unbalanced crapshoots. One of the ways this game adds difficulty is to put most of the hardest fights in the game in tiny, cramped rooms and just fill them to the brim with mages. Trying to stop multiple mages at once from casting confusion spells that will wipe out half of your party if it gets off is irritating, and it's even worse in tiny rooms. The pathing issues are amplified to maddening levels here as your entire party bumps and slams into each other while mages are busy roasting your party in seconds. Baldur's Gate 2 added confusion protection spells which was a godsend. Here? You have to just take it, and it's incredibly annoying.
There is A LOT of stuff you are going to have to put up with to enjoy this game. Save often, and be prepared to load saves often. This game will kill you repeatedly with no warning, you have to be willing to deal with that to enjoy this game at all.
So with that out of the way let's talk about how this is one of the best RPG's I've ever played (It actually is.) When things go right in this game, my god is it satisfying. Buffing up your entire party with stat boosts and conquering enormous bosses with tactics that only you could come up with, feels... it's just amazing.
The RPG mechanics and gameplay are just near perfect here, building a proper character and party is easy and fun to do.  The loot is incredibly rewarding to equip and is numerous and interesting. Exploration is very rewarding here, make sure to check every inch of every area, (especially in the beginning.) The interface is one of the best I've ever seen, 17 years later and it's still a joy to use. It's one of those games that achieves a near perfect synthesis of RPG mechanics, story and exploration that provide an experience that's impossibly immersive.
After the 66 hours of infuriating and rewarding gameplay I can't help but say that I loved this game. I wanted to quit, multiple times during this playthrough. Especially in the middle section with the never ending Cloakwood Forest, but I stuck it out and really learned this game even when it killed me repeatedly with no warning. If you are willing to accept brutal and unforgiving challenge in reward for a wonderful story and immensely deep gameplay then this is the game for you. Not for the light of heart or the intellectually lazy, but absolutely worth the struggle if you can look past the retro difficulty.
One of my all time favourite, a little dated but still worth a play through.

Baldur's Gate is often held up as the epitomy of Role-playing gaming, and a hallmark of excellent writing (there certainly is a great deal of text!) To a certain extent this is true, as Baldur's Gate has a reasonally well developed plot, a plethora of cut and dry standard fantasy characters and well constructed dialogue, that utilizes a quite advanced vocabulary by today's standards. Is it as great as the rose-tinted lenses of nostalgia make it out to be? The answer unfortunately is no, Baldur's Gate is advanced for its time but compared to some of the more modern RPG's is lacking in awareness of broader issues and ideologies. It's a simpler game from a simpler era, that layed the groundwork for the more advanced exploration achieved by later games.
As for Beamdog's Enhanced Edition, it adapts the graphics to run on modern resolutions however it still suffers from pixelation due to the nature of the original graphics themselves. The sound runs perfectly, and crystal clear with little to no distortion and the inclusion of the new content is welcome for those who want to experience the old mechanics, yet explore a slightly new adventure.

A few years ago, a mother and father decided they needed a break, so they wanted to head out for a night on the town. They called their most trusted babysitter. When the babysitter arrived, the two children were already fast asleep in bed. So the babysitter just got to sit around and make sure everything was okay with the children. Later that night, the babysitter got bored and went to watch TV, but she couldn't watch it downstairs because they did not have cable downstairs (the parents didn't want children watching too much garbage). So, she called them and asked them if she could watch cable in the parent's room. Of course, the parents said it was OK, but the babysitter had one final request… she asked if she could cover up the angel statue outside the bedroom window with a blanket or cloth, at the very least close the blinds, because it made her nervous. The phone line was silent for a moment, and the father who was talking to the babysitter at the time said, "..Take the children and get out of the house…we will call the police. We do not have an angel statue." The police found all three of the house occupants dead within ten minutes of the call. No statue was found.

TLDR: Ultimate Edition is totally worth it, one of the best RPGs and fantasies of all time. Game is slow at certain points, but worth a play. Bioware hallmarks are all there, but it's definitely different than 2 and Inquisition.
I should first point out that all my play time is either PS3 or a non-Steam copy of this game. That said, I've played this game extensively.
A quintessential RPG, the first in the Dragon Age series showcases classic Bioware: compelling characters, solid worldbuilding, and even moving romances, all paired with a truly well-written epic fantasy that's moving and tragic.  There are some moments where the game drags on, but there is so much content to enjoy 15 minutes feels like nothing compared to the scope of the story and worlds. The world is big, without the pitfalls of super-repetitive level design like 2, and large without being populated largely by fetch quests that don't impact the main story like Inquisition (if anything, side quests ARE more likely to have an impact than not).
A dedicated community of modders have added "fixes" that let you skip the most infamous grind, while others have worked to update graphics and even add new companions to play with!
If you're coming in blind: Dragon Age Origins offers a great introduction to the series. The choices you make actually DO matter and go places few RPGs will dare go in terms of outcomes. The Dragon Age series features a dark fantasy setting that's enjoyable, dramatic, and doesn't skimp on making you care for the majority of your characters, including your own player character.
If you've played Dragon Age 2 or Inqusition: The gameplay is different in this game. It's not as easy, and there's a lot more challenge as far as specializing your characters and combat goes, especially on higher difficulties. The romances/companion relationships are not as developed as later games in certain ways, and feature more of a gift-system but do retain the conversation approval system. In some ways the characters are more compelling than future games, though some are not as well-written. Though it's a departure from later games, if you can get over the dissonance of having a non-voiced protagonist and the different gameplay style, this is easily the best game of the three in a lot of ways.
Even the DLC is worth it: Leliana's Song offers a cool look at the backstory of a major side character, while Awakening is the size of a completely new game with a TON of new content. Witch Hunt, Return to Ostagar, and the other DLC are all also great fun to play, and put more modern DLC to shame in terms of bang for your buck.

Ingredients:
-3/4 cup white sugar
-3 tablespoons cornstarch
-1/4 teaspoon salt
-1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
-4 cups fresh blueberries
-1 recipe pastry for a 9 inch double crust pie
-1 tablespoon butter
Directions:
-Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
-Mix sugar, cornstarch, salt, and cinnamon, and sprinkle over blueberries.
-Line pie dish with one pie crust. Pour berry mixture into the crust, and dot with butter. Cut remaining pastry into 1/2 - 3/4 inch wide strips, and make lattice top. Crimp and flute edges.
-Bake pie on lower shelf of oven for about 50 minutes, or until crust is golden brown.
Tip:
-Aluminum foil can be used to keep food moist, cook it evenly, and make clean-up easier.

Fire Pro Wrestling World to put it succinctly is 'Better than the rest.'
The Fire Pro Wrestling series found its beginning back in 1989, the brainchild of Japanese programmer Masato Masuda who had already made waves in the video game industry programming the critical and commercial success 'Pro Wrestling' on the Nintendo Entertainment System. A much beloved title for oldschool gamers and wrestling fans alike.
When Fire Pro Wrestling made its debut on the market, no one would have any idea of the significance the series would have over an entire genre of games and yet remain completely niche and almost unknown to all but the most dedicated western audiences.
In truth, Fire Pro Wrestling is the father of modern wrestling games, innovating and refining many of the features we see in the games today.
To fully grasp the impact the Fire Pro Wrestling series has had over the wrestling game genre, we have to look at how two completely different cultures view Professional Wrestling in its entirety. While Pro Wrestling in the West has relied heavily on pageantry and characters to get over; Japanese wrestling is viewed as a legitimate sport, covered by the press and sports media. The ring drama does not unfold over a microphone or through awkward skits, but rather in-ring storytelling and match psychology.
This is where the fundamental difference between Western and Japanese developers have differed over the years in the wrestling game content they produce.
Western wrestling games have always relied heavily upon licenses and a particular brand to sell units. It never really mattered if the games were actually any good. Button mashing an opponents lifebar into oblivion while manipulating the cardboard cut out likeness of a real superstar has been the bread and butter staple of western wrestling games for decades. We loved it, and we continued to buy each installment of each licensed game, but ultimately were left with shallow gameplay and a complete lack of in-ring drama from developers who either didn't care or didn't understand pro wrestling, and some would argue, still don't.
Then along came the Fire Pro series. Through its early installments it began to build upon certain gameplay fundamentals. Unlicensed and unbranded, the series crammed the rosters with the likenesses of real wrestler and real promotions and focused solely on developing gameplay as the foundation the series would build upon through each installment.
Gameplay and customization is unequivocally the flame that has sustained the Fire Pro series from 1989 to 2017.
Giving players the tools not to beat a lifebar out of an opponent and slap on a guarunteed pinfall, but to actually tell their own stories with their own characters through their own preferred style of grappling.
The Fire Pro series was the first series to personalize its rosters with their own statistical parameters, utilize a customizable logic system and incorporate what we now consider basic features in a wrestling game such as stamina, fatigue and limb damage. Now Spike-Chunsoft have given the fans a new toybox to create in, and plan to throw in plenty of additional features as time progresses. With additional logo and ring editors entire promotions will rise and fall within the community and thousands of real and fictional wrestlers, grapplers and even MMA fighters will thrive and compete.
One of the staples of the Fire Pro series has been its minimalist presentation. The 2d graphics, simple introductions and focus on in ring action over amateur theatrics; while not necessarily appealing to the younger gamers of today, still remain colorful and beautifully hand animated. Many long time fans of the series also believe the 2d base allows for far more creative freedom in the editing process as well.
And creative freedom is what Fire Pro is all about. Molding your own unique vision, limited only by your imagination and not the lame narrative of some stooge writer. Fire Pro has a soul and is developed as a labor of love for fans, by fans, and is not just the annual mediocre churnout of a corporate brand.
The series isn't for everyone, but does boast an insanely hardcore following that even includes some of the wrestlers whose Fire Pro counterparts have appeared throughout the storied series. Some people are perfectly content with the offerings of the licensed brands; but those who love the Fire Pro series love it a lot and we owe a huge debt of gratitude to Tomoyuki Matsumoto, Tomozou Kantaku and all the developers at Spike-Chunsoft who have made this labor of love a reality at long last. With a PS4 console release on the way, it is safe to say many of us will be running across eachother on both platforms.
My Personal Fire Pro Wrestling history includes:
Fire Pro Wrestling G
Fire Pro Wrestlng D
Fire Pro Wrestling Z
Fire Pro Wrestling Returns (Japanese Edition)
Fire Pro Wrestling Returns (Agetec Edition)
Fire Pro Wrestling World (PC)
and eventually,
Fire Pro Wrestling World (PS4)

It is 2:30a.m here and I have finally finished the escape pod after 76 hours playtime. What a journey. I can honestly say Dungeon of Endless has captivated me like no game before it.
Amplitude have crafted a devilish game here that may turn you off initially but if you persevere or like a challenge it is just fantastic. I received DOE in a humble bundle and made a big mistake right off the bat. Do not complete the tutorial drunk! The dev plays to those people who are stubborn, like a challenge or are just straight up masochistic. You only have two choices of difficulty: Easy or very easy. I do like the idea of this game and I am sure that developers are definitely outdoors aficionados and know a thing or two about survivalism movement.
The game mechanics will keep you rapt for the first days. When in ordinary RPG-game you collect items to be stronger than other players and monsters, in this game you are looting things too survive. You are not getting stronger with the time and finding new stuff not always give you some tangible advantage, but collecting instincts are strong. Here, in this game, the last thing you want is to shoot a wolf. Ammo is the most expensive and hard to find substance in this world. Everything you have collected you want to save and make it last as the future is very obscure. However, at particular point the more your carry the more you are slowing down. Therefore, you need to decide what you want to take with you and what do you want to leave. In addition, you start to think that going elsewhere to get more brushwood is wiser than cutting branches loosing calories and blunting your axe. You become aware of all possible illnesses and ways to cure them (I wish somebody told me that you can heal frostbite), all the herbs and ways to get food in wilderness. This is mesmerizing and will keep you occupied for hours and hours.
But then goes the story mode. The boring, dull, shameful story mode. I do not know who has written the script and authored the quests but these people should learn that go-and-get tasks have never been popular. The plot has no twists and the storygoing is super slow. I wonder why Will pretends to be interested in Astrid? Authors forced the main protagonist to spend weeks wondering around doing meaningless stuff for TWO (I am not kidding) NPC. Remember Korean MMOs where you must gather 100 wolf pelts? Pretty the same. Does this make you to think that he cares about his ex-wife? To share his feelings? The story is a joke.
Dear developers, if you want to make story mode better please make it more alive. I may suggest playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl if you do not know what I mean. Please give us more tasks with different choices and outcome, more NPCs and plot twists. And do not forget to add voiceover. It is not so expensive.
Currently I do not recommend buying this game unless you are a fun of sandbox survival. Let us wait for the next three episodes.

I've had The Long Dark since early access, although I only played it every so often and never actually completed a challenge. In about 2 years I only racked up about 24 hours of gameplay. Then Storymode finally came out and in just a couple weeks I've played over 30 hours. Is storymode perfect? No. I've been fortunate not to have encountered any gamebreaking issues but games will never be perfect. I've spent a lot more for games with much larger budgets from bigger studios that have had more serious issues than what I've encountered in TLD.
The visuals of the game are quite gorgeous, especially when you witness that first aurora. The things that occur during that first aurora genuinely chilled me and really made me want to engage with the story and learn more about what happened here.
In terms of the quests, I do think the developers could have thought through their tutorials a little more. Kholat is an interesting mix of Cryostasis, Amnesia and Dear Esther, combining rather well the setting, the atmosphere and the exploration in a short and nerve wrecking horror experience.
The story doesn’t rise up to the expectations and it doesn’t do justice to the sad event that took place more than 50 years ago, but the game makes up for it through intense atmosphere supported by a surprisingly well executed tech part.
The Horror genre is nowhere near close to dying and with titles like Amnesia, Alien: Isolation, The Forest or Outlast being released in the last years it still has something to show for (and the indie developers are always coming with new ideas). Playing Kholat made me realize why I subconsciously avoid horror games. It is a preemptive fear for the things that I could feel while playing such games that prevents me from trying them out. Yet, fear is an emotion and as any emotion its intensity is subjective to each person. I can’t say how terrifying the atmosphere in this game is going to be for others, but speaking from my perspective, it made me want the feeling of fear again. Horror games, brace yourselves! I’m coming!
Pros:
+ Good graphics
+ Excellent sound design
+ Great music
+ Atmospheric and scary
+ Some intense scripted moments
Cons:
- The story is a gathering of clichés and the ending is messy
- Short
- The save system
- The character can barely sprint
- Getting constantly stuck in the game’s geometry

This is the game that XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Xenonauts was/are trying to remake. That right off the bat should tell you that there's something special about this game if people are trying to recreate it ~20 years after it came out. That there's something here that people just can't let go of.
Turns out it's the truth. The UI is extremely archaic, the graphics speak for themselves, and the game lacks many of those "modern improvements" like autosave and such. With that said, this game was vastly ahead of its time. And its still good despite its age. It's very similar to Enemy Unknown in many respects (aliens invade, shoot their UFO's down, stop terror attacks, eventually eliminate the alien leader, etc), but there's alot that didn't get to that game as well. Multiple bases, no class system, larger battles in general (the top level air transport allows you to bring something in the order of ~26 troops into a fight), assaults on your bases if you don't chase aliens away from them, and more. It's harder than EU, longer than EU (took me close to 50 hours to beat this opposed to 20-30 for EU), and in some ways is a larger game as well.
It's still a great game, though some might be turned off by how it looks. But if you can give it a shot, you can very well find a game that, even if it is one of the oldest games on Steam, is still an excellent mix of fun, challenge, and replayability.

Great survival game, probably the best survival game I've ever played. No monsters, zombies, dinos, or any of that sort of thing. Just nature and you. There are dangers from animals out there in the wild but the real danger is the climate, starvind or dehidrating.. Heck you can even become to tired to press on, and just pass out and die in the cold snow.
I've never been so on edge and hopefull for a break in any other survival game. It is a lot more intence before you learn the maps.. Because not knowing if you will run across a place of refuge or not is a big deal. If you know where everything is I can imagine that would take a lot of the thrill out of survival mode, however even then you still have to manage your food and water and cold.. Even knowing where things are, this can still be a challenge.
I would recomend not playing it on easy, I tried once after dieing from a wolf on day 2 of my first play through, I went right back to a harder difficulty. Easy mode is exactly that, easy mode, and it really ruins the game as it takes away any fear of animal because they all run from you no matter what. Those encounters and how to avoid them are a big part of the tension of the game. Later when you are better suited and you want to hunt such animals, if they are always running away at great distances I guess that could bring some difficulty back, but it's more fun being the hunter and the hunted for sure.
Very tranquil and yet nerve wracking with wolves at your heel.
