This was the wrestling game I've been waiting for. It accomplishes a rare trick- it's fast and easy to get started in, yet it's also a better wrestling sim than the WWE games have ever managed, somehow capturing the feel of a scripted sport in an open format. Matches go back and forth and have dramatic reversals which leave the crowd gasping, different wrestlers play differently thanks to variable AI, and you can feel tension building. It's honestly fun to just watch the AI go at it, and setting up your own federation and seeing who wins in dream matches is a joy.
Customization is, given the simplicity of the graphics, kind of entirely absurd. Playing with the various layers of attires can create some brilliant combinations, it's easy to import your own .wav entrance themes, and monkeying with movesets and AI can get you just about any concept you can envision.
Presentation wise it could still use a little finessing- the Mission Mode is really essential to learning how to play the game yourself, and there's a lot the game itself could explain instead of leaving to the manual. The graphics do occasionally show the odd bit of clipping (which is weird for 2-D) though nothing that obstructs gameplay. And to be sure there are a few things the game can't do yet- ladder matches, table matches, and huge 30-man royal rumbles and the like.
But overall, in terms of capturing the wrestling experience, this does better than anything I've ever seen. It's an easy recommend to any wrestling fan, and even if you're not, the fun of creating weird characters and making them fight in barbed wire deathmatches is hard to overstate. Just superb.

Fire Pro Wrestling is a game that until a few minutes before I played it I had never even heard about it.  I was told about the game and told that it was comparable to "WWF No Mercy" for the Nintendo 64.  While that is probably the best way to describe it to someone, it's so much more than that.
The game is just very smooth, the grappling feels totally worse than No Mercy until you get used to it and realize they made the small change for a reason.  The matches really feel like real wrestling matches, the game encourages it by allowing the build up moves to work more often in the beginning and you have to work you way up your finisher.  No more body slam over and over and spam taunt until your opponent gets up then fininsher, rinse repeat that you see so much in No Mercy.
The AI is really cool as well,  I've seen matches with characters based on wrestlers from WWE that were shockingly close to something you would actually see them do.
The shining moment in this game is the customization of the wrestlers, ring apron and arena as well as referees.  You can find almost anyone (or anything) in the workshop and some of the detail put into these wrestlers is insane.  The moment I downloaded Kenny Omega and realized someone actually went through the time to map out the "One Winged Angel" was insane.  I never thought I was see this in a wrestling game and if I did assumed it would be more new style wrestling game which I don't care for at all.
This game is fantastic and if you don't buy it very soon you're going to end up paying more for it because this baby is coming out of early access!  I think I paid like $20 and right now it's sitting at $13.39 which is a steal since the price is going up to $25 for realease I believe.  At any of these price points I think it's a good buy.

For my money, this is the greatest game ever made.  It certainly is my favorite by a mile. That said, it takes a certain type of person to get into this game. If you are not very creative or have a poor imagination, you may not like this game or even know what the hell to do with it. Every character is my own creation, even the referees; every ring mat and apron I designed myself; every theme song that plays, every move and grunt and groan and taunt a wrestler makes, I hand picked it myself. There is no story mode being force fed to you by the developers; it is a pure professional wrestling sandbox of endless possibilities. More than any other game, Fire Pro has let me create my own world, my own universe. When I fire up the game, I'm off to another dimension entirely.
I think the 430+ hours I've played in Early Access says it all. I adore this game. If you are an intelligent, patient, creative, and perhaps a bit odd and quirky individual with a penchant for pro wrestling, your search has ended. Look no further. This is your game.

Before buying this game, keep in mind that, unlike what you might think from the description, this is not a very complex rogue-like. While there are elements of tower defense, resource management, and levelled characters, there is little learning curve, meaningful decisions, or stat mongering in the game.
In short, it's much closer to a mobile game for PC than it is to NetHack. Which is absolutely fine, just something to keep in mind before purchasing.
POSITIVES:
- Immediately accessible from the first level
- Meaningful replayability via different starting conditions and Endless Mode
- Enjoyable world characterization
- Crisp assembly
- Fun
SOMEWHAT NEGATIVES:
- Fairly easy. I beat the hardest starting difficulty in three tries, and each scenario in one or two
- RPG elements are a little dull
- Individual levels often end anti-climatically
- Exploration lacks variety
- No voice acting
BOTTOME LINE:
This is a great little game that's perfect for killing idle hours. If the description intrigues you, it delivers. (But just don't expect a game of great depth.)
A sequal would be fantastic.
---
PLEASE NOTE BEFORE PLAYING:
This game comes with a free DLC that adds four Team Fortress characters to the game. This is pretty fun when you're used to the game, but it ruins the atmosphere to run across a Heavy or Pyro during your first couple playthroughs. I'd reccommend unchecking the DLC box on the game's page in your library before launching, and turning it on after a couple hours to see if you like it.

Kholat definitely uses the atmosphere to its advantage in order to send chills down your spine. It focuses on the Dylatov Pass incident and has an entire narrative around it, often presenting bits and pieces of the story through the use of letters, journal notes, and a cryptic narrator played by Sean Bean (who is just a voice so
die in this game).
The game itself is gorgeous. I know some may be averse to the similar looking areas and dense amounts of forest, but I thought it all looked very beautiful and there were zones that had distinct characteristics that helped to set it apart from others. Reading the terrain helped a lot, because, let me tell you, you will probably get lost in this game (I did!). It relies on using only a topographical map and a compass to guide you to points, so learning to read the land as best you can will save you from walking too far away from your destination. I liked the mechanic, but I admit to being frustrated with it sometimes, only because I'm bad with maps, but practice did help me. Due to this, the horror may be spread out a lot as you try to find your way around, which may break immersion for you.
Enemies are the form of shadowy and sometimes invisible monsters, who you may not notice until it's too late if you weren't paying attention to their footprints, which light up like the sun. They're not particularly fast, and if you're careful you can outrun them, but you probably will be trying to sneak by them most of the time. Getting caught means instant death, which can set you back very far away, and savepoints are scarce, taking the form of scattered fireplaces and campsites through the region (which you
have to navigate too. This can present a bit of challenge, especially if you're trying to naviagate to a specific place on your map. Nothing is worse than the dark forest, where you can barely see and enemies are EVERYWHERE. :C
The story itself is a standard "find out what happened" and centers only on that, so there is a bit of a disconnect between where you go/explore and what you learn. Due to this, a lot of this game can feel like aimless wandering, which can break immersion. Furthermore, the story culminates in a rather lackluster finale, even with the secrent end (obtained by 100% completion), and it doesn't answer questions set up by the narrative of the notes themselves. Don't expect a thrilling ending to solve all your questions.
Kholat does a good job being scary and relies heavily on atmosphere to accomplish this. It does its job well, but if you were following the story and mystery it can lead to something disappointing. I still recommend it for the scares, though, if you are decent at reading maps or want to get spooked solid in the cold.

I wanted to like this game, but found it too frustrating to get into. Save spots seem to be few and far-between, and I spent a lot of time re-playing the same areas of the game just because my progress wasn't saved as expected.
The monster, once revealed, is more annoying than scary. Since it's the only thing that can kill you, you spend much of your time just jogging around. Given the harsh winter environment, it would be interesting if you also had to battle the elements in addition to evading the forces of nature. Since this is not the case, the game is basically an enormous hiking simulator... but is also not as "open-world" as you are led to believe.
Getting lost in the woods at night in winter has never been easier.

Beautiful graphics, unique gameplay elements and amazing soundtrack didn't help me enjoy this tediously slow game. By the time I ran across enemies I was too bored to care. If you're the impatient type like me, the immersion isn't worth your it, which sucks because the atmosphere is top notch.

What you get: artistic graphics, foreshadowing storytelling, a unique walking simulator with some horror elements
What you don't: anything else
I can recommend this game only for adult (30+) players who care about atmosphere and story and need a daily refreshing break or a little time-off before sleep. If you like winter, snowing, darkness and solitude, KHOLAT is a must-have. Perfect choice for antisocial misanthrope orienteer introverts. Bizarre little puzzle game. I didn't know what I was buying when I bought it, but I enjoyed the product nonetheless. The beginning part was, I feel, the best. I enjoyed the atmosphere, which was quietly unnerving and I was unsure of what to expect. Not scary, but just gives a very uneasy feeling. Again, this could have been because I had no clue what I was buying, and I seemed to have missed that "comedy" tag.
Once the first "level" is complete, the groove of the game really sets in. The absolute highlight of this game is the humor, particularly the "written" humor. Everything you pick up, I encourage you to read the description of. There's a fair amount of items to collect and each of these has something funny written about it as well.
The only downside I would say is the follower you gain about a quarter of the way through the game. I found him incredibly annoying and he makes a noise everywhere he goes. He's also designed to teleport near you if you run too far away from him, so there's no real way of avoiding him.
Beyond that, I still say the game is enjoyable and pretty memorable. There's a quirky charm to it that's hard to find in other games. It's questionable if it's worth the $20 - it only took 3 hours to complete, and there were a couple instances where I was clueless on what aspect I was missing to progress forward, which ate into that time some.

A Spectacular FPS and dark game. Dishonored is a game about a Assassin gifted with supernatural and magical powers on a mission to clear his name. If you love Bioshock, you'll love this.
The Story:
You start off as Corvo, a bodyguard, returning to a city infested with the plague, you go there to meet the Empress and her daughter, when suddenly, a rogue gang of magical hunters attack you and the Empress, they end up killing the empress and kidnapping the daughter. When you hold the empress in your arms for her last dying breath, you are accused of her murder and are thrown in jail. The rest of the game is you trying to run from the enforcement while along the way achieving unique goals and objectives. Also you aquire special magical abilities from a person known as the outsider and you can wield supernatural forces to your bidding such as Teleporting instantaneously, Seeing in the dakr and seeing the enemies through walls, Bending time, Possession, Summoning a swarm of rats and using a whirlwind to attack.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is flawlessly amazing, everything is so smooth and the graphics are great. The Magical abilities are very fun and can be upgraded along with natural perks. The choices of how to go through the game is very fun as you can choose a variety of ways of completeing objectives such as using an ability, going in guns blazing and sneaking around. The weapons are very fun, especially the crossbow.
Overall:
This is a very fun and great game which is tons of fun for someone who wants something new or fresh.

The bottom line is this bundle of SimBin titles is at a price low enough, the games/sims considered a great starting point by most, and will provide a tremendous quantity and quality of driving fun while helping you to perfect some of the basic abilities you will need if you seek to delve further into Sim Racing. Updated Alpha 17
Stonehearth is a title i have many mixed opinions on. The development team behind it has been super friendly and open with the community about their progress. They've provided a steady stream of updates since they launched their series of alphas and their weekly dev blogs are a good way to see what they're working on.
That said their progress hasn't been particularly impressive, there are many bugs and glitches and essentially a time limit as the AI eventually becomes so bogged down that the game slows to a crawl. However as of their latest update they seem to have limited the population count to 20, at least in my play through they stopped coming at 20 (it could be a bug). The game still slows down considerably but at least they prevent the player from breaking their game with too many hearthlings.
The coolest part of the game, which lets you handcraft buildings was held back by bugs and glitches. However in their latest update they’ve begun to address this technical hurdle which is good to hear. Once this feature is fully implemented the game will probably open up into the more lego centric fun that I was hoping for.
As of the Alpha 17 this project has finally started to come together. The first of the AI storyteller “quest chains” seems to have been added which gives you a sense of progression and for the first time it felt like an actual game. The combat classes are fun to mess around with, and despite a few ai derps its handled well. It takes a lot of time and resources to create a fully armed fighting force and the effort pays off as your knights, warriors and archers mow down their opposition. I was able to play through this “campaign” without any game breaking bugs or UI glitches so they seem to have a handle on the worst offenders.
Maybe in another alpha or two the game will finally shape up into something I can wholeheartedly recommend. The feature I originally signed up for, the co op city building as well as multiplayer still seem nowhere in sight. The game still slows down towards the 20 hearthling population count, and it has a lot of work to do.

A great game with an amazing story, lore, and diversity. Although the story starts out slow, it greatly picks up the pace later on. Another thing, some of the dialog choices are pretty funny.
However, there are problems with this game.
1) It's a game that focuses on strategic combat. So some fights can be ridiculously hard. This might even be harder if you're someone who isn't familiar with knights of the old republic style of combat. It can also become tedious and tiresome.
2) Yes, the graphics are dated. If you're the type of person that can't play older style of rpg's, it might be hard to get into.
3) Because they put baldur's gate into the baldur's gate 2 engine, there are some nasty bugs which may have to do with the scripting. Examples being->everlasting battle music, certain quest items becoming unusable, and some bosses just despawning.
4) They didn't fix the pathfinding in this enhanced edition. So you have to baby sit your characters to make sure they go to the right place.
5) Most of the time you have a choice on what happens, but not in some instances. I won't make a spoiler, but some choices severely punish you. As in you're suppose to make a certain choice or you die.
If you can get over these flaws, you will find that Baldur's Gate Enhanced Edition is well worth a playthrough.

I've been looking at this game for a while now, something told me to stay away from it, but I gave in and grabbed it on a city builder binge. I'm sad that I did.
I like the defence/survival element of Stonehearth, where camps of enemies will spawn around the map and periodically attack your settlement, you can either attack them early and risk your guards, or just wait out the attacks for the XP. There are also loot boxes and such around the map to be discovered, usually guarded by some mini-boss creatures. That part they did right, it's fun.
For a game that's been in development for such a long time, I really wonder why there are so many bugs. I understand it's a early access game, but that's not really an excuse for the really terrible building mechanics. It's a city-builder game, if i was developing a city builder, the first thing i'd get sorted would be the building mechanics, at the moment they're extremely frustrating and unintuitive. You have no ability to change things once you've placed them, so if you want to extend your wall out by 2 squares, you need to undo everything you've done to get back there. This is really frustrating when building and planning complex structures.
I'd like to see defensive walls (properly) added, or at least the ability to create stand-alone walls outside of the custom structure editor, for a simple project like a perimeter wall the player shouldn't be forced to stuff around too much. I noticed also that it's very clumbsy at sticking to things. i tried to incorporate a pre-existing structure in my town into the wall, instead the custom structure editor decided that the sections of wall touching that building now belonged to it, and not my wall, so the only way to get rid of those walls was to destroy that building. Annoying to say the least.
Along with numerous bugs that caused my workers to get stuck on window ledges, placing objects is a real pain. I've been forced to build a cobblestone fence piece-by-piece because if i try to place more than one at a time, the workers freak out and wont complete the task.
At this point I can't reccommend the game, I feel like I was ripped off, to be honest.

It's very dated and repetitive. Neverwinter Nights provides a much more pleasant experience and superior story, without the illogical difficulty spokes and inability to dissuade attackers with persuasion skills. I recommend it for multiplayer (if it works for you.. there are many disconnects) and people who are die-hard fans of the series. I am currently doing a single playthrough with my best friend, and I'm enjoying bits and pieces of it, but we find ourselves taking breaks often. I am on the fence about this game, so I will put some + and - points.
+ Lots of classes to choose from!
Like a true d&d game, there are many classes to choose from. Fighter, Barbarian, Ranger, Paladin, Thief, Sorcerer, Wizard, Bard-- etc! Each of these classes has kits that modify certain abilities or restrictions, allowing for quite a bit of experimenting.
+ Large game with many areas to explore
You'll end up spending about two hours making your first character if you're googling for help at the same time. I actually enjoy the process of designing a new character so this is fine by me. After all that, you get a bit of story with not too much text, and you're off into the world. There are a lot of things to do, and the game does direct you to certain places, though very few places are restricted.
+ They let you be evil or good to people
I'm not into the whole being a jerk to people thing, but if you like that stuff then you'll at least appreciate all the murderous options given to you. As a bad boy/girl, you'll get into trouble with the nicer people in the world.
= Okayish story, not overwhelmingly so
I already know the plot, and it's kind of cool. Essentially you can explain the plot in two sentences but the game takes its time to introduce it to you. If you're attentive enough, you'll probably figure it all out before the great reveal.
= Multiplayer
Multiplayer is fun with a friend if it doesn't disconnect too much. There isn't much else to say about this, though. Some people might prefer to be alone because they'd have full control over all party members.
- The way stats work in this version of d&d
You don't get combat benefits from having 10-16 strength, but you do get it from having 17 or 18. Dexterity should always be 18 to get better armor (..which you'll need), constitution is a big deal, intelligence does absolutely nothing unless you're a wizard, wisdom is similar. They also force classes to have stats that they don't exactly benefit from! This version of d&d is just a bit too primitive in certain aspects, and I recommend Neverwinter Nights because all stats do something to benefit your character, and not having max stats is perfectly fine.
- Difficulty spikes, often killed instantly by attackers
The amount of times you get talked to by a mage and then get charmed/feared, after which you are killed because you lost control of your character .. is staggering. There aren't many ways to counter this, and I remember one quest that instantly kills your character during dialog with no warning or means to escape it. This means you'll end up saving and loading a lot, and possibly avoiding conversation just so you can get the first attack off on your enemy (ie: you fireball them before they can even see you). Sometimes the game becomes too easy as well.
- Not enough customization options
ENHANCED EDITION, it says. So let me play a redhead. It wouldn't have killed the developer to add some extra coloring options in the game, but at least they did improve things graphically a bit!
TL:DR: imbalanced difficulty, unfair deaths, save and load constantly, dated mechanics. Neverwinter Nights is better, but if you enjoyed Neverwinter Nights and want some more RP things, this might do if the price is cheap :) Heard that Baldur's Gate 2 is far better than this one, so working your way to it with the first game might not be a bad idea.

Kholat is an open-world walking simulator based on a true story: the Dyatlov Pass Incident, an unsolved mystery since 1959. It tells the story of the mysterious death of nine Russian hikers on Kholat Syakhl, a mountain in the northern Ural region of Russia.
You'll find a lot of information about what happened (according to the game) in the form of notes that are scattered around the huge map. Getting these notes and visiting the various camps on the map are also the only way to save your game. That often means you need to travel for various minutes back to the location you were killed. Yes, you can die in this walking simulator. In many parts of the game you'll be chased by a scary anomaly and although it isn't that hard to run away from it, it will get you once in a while. There's no fighting back.
Kholat has excellent graphics, great sound effects and an amazing soundtrack. The scary atmosphere of the game is very well done and that's one of the most important things of games in this genre. The game is built on Unreal Engine 4 and it's therefore a very demanding game system-wise. It surely could've been optimized better. Especially the lighting in some parts of the game will bring many pc's to it's knees, even on low settings.
Most interactive stories don't take that long to complete. 1.5 To 3 hours is no exception, but it will take you 4 to 6 hours to reach the end of Kholat. The end will leave you with a lot of questions.
Besides the performance issues and the way the game saves your progress, I've really enjoyed Kholat and can definitely recommend this game to fans of walking simulators.

Most of the jokes involve other characters calling the player stupid, calling each other stupid, or calling the situation around them stupid. Maybe the writers were trying to be a little self-aware and point out that game itself is stupid. But even in that case, I don't think it was funny.
I'm not exaggerating about the word stupid. I bet 20% of the dialog in this game is the word "stupid" or "idiot" or some other variation.
The gameplay is also incredibly shallow and surprisingly samey for a game that I finished in under 3 hours. Most of the gameplay involves picking up junk you see lying around the world and then using that junk on other junk. It gets to a point where you bear companion literally says "Why are you picking up so much garbage?"
Sometimes there is some light "puzzling" involved. This is usually along the lines of "combine this piece of tape with the fingerprint on the wall and then use the tape on the fingerprint scanner". On thing that stuck out to me was the amount of puzzle re-use that went on in some cases. For example, on that on three separate occasions I had to collect a bunch of random items to build a fake person to stand in front of a security camera so I could get through a door. It was amusing the first time, but by the third time it just stuck out as lazy writing.
In addition to the useful items you can pick up, there are 75 different "flavor" items to grab as you play through the game. A good number of these items just exist to try to make a joke. There's nothing inherently wrong with that but the jokes just don't land in many cases. For example, there's a rusty tire rim whose description reads "In a quiet moment, you will take this rusty wheel and roll it along the ground, wondering what it's purpose could be. Afterwards, you will forget you have it." You don't use the rim for anything, it exists purely for that description. Another example is a wooden pallet with the flavor text "You decided to pick this up because you liked the grain in the wood, and that it gives you splinters while holding it from every conceivable angle."
The game does have a good soundtrack include a catchy song written specifically for this game.
If any the quotes I referenced above made you laugh then you might just like the writing in this game and it might be worth a shot. Unfortunately, I can't say the same and I would not recommend this game.

Simply put, this is an absolutely wonderful game.
This is a retro-styled roguelike RPG RTS dungeon-exploring base-building mish mash hodgepodge of great art, well designed systems and utterly enthralling replayability. Your goal is to get your initial team of two heroes and lead them up to the 13th Floor and back to daylight so they can be rescued. How? By taking your ship's crystal over to the level exit of course !
But wait ... what's the catch? Well, this game works on a 'round' system while exploring - each time you open a door, you tick over to a new 'round' of the level which then adds more resources to your tally based on how many Industry / Science / Food modules you have built. Each resource is needed for a certain action - Industry for building modules, Science for researching, Food for leveling heroes up /recruiting new ones - but all three can be used at certain points to trade in for a shopkeeper's hero-boosting items or activate pods. Opening a door is integral to get more resources, collect items, find more heroes and scout the exit - but it also spawns monsters in unpowered rooms who make a beeline to your crystal. The only way to stop baddies spawning is to route power to the rooms using 'Dust' - but this resource can again mostly only be found by opening up more rooms.
This is what creates the balance of the game. Do you build up your modules on this floor, hoping that the exit isn't too close so you can maximise your resource gathering? Do you keep opening doors and beeline for the end, ramping up the likelihood of an unstoppable wave of enemies while potentially leading to a dead end? Do you split your team (and thus your power) between one path, or both? Do you prioritise Offensive mini-module research or Hero-supporting ones that boost defense? Who gets to lead the way? Is it worth leveling up your entire team, or just your Operator? Is it worth buying your main slugger a bigger gun or saving up for the unknown dangers of the next floor?
There is so much to consider, and yet in all probability you will still die after a brutal slog of bad luck. But it is worth it just to find someone (or something) new to add to your starting roster. Then there is nothing left to do but to go again !

I bought every single product made by Amplitude studio, and I must say one thing: I regret nothing.
Dungeon of the Endless is a unique blend of tower defense and rogue like, dungeon crawler rpg, which ask you to bring your heroes to safety while protecting your unique source of power, the crystal. You achieve this by opening door after door until you find the exit for that particular level, hoping that the next room won't hide any monster.
You can choose between a huge variety of character, each one with unique passive skills, active abilities and personality (yes, the guys from Amplitude managed somehow to wonderfully characterize every hero giving them a striking personality shown through descriptions and sentences screamed during battles), and those heroes can level up as you progress in your adventure.
This is DotE in just a few words, but you really have to play this gem to understand its value.
Quick positive and negative points:
+challenging resource management
+very well characterized heroes
+pixel art graphic
+deep and surprisingly wide lore that synergizes with the Endless franchise
+easy to learn mechanics
+funny and satisfying achievements
+very innovative gameplay (never seen anything like this)
+LOT of irony

SpaceChem is a puzzler that places the player in the role of a scientist or engineer that must configure molecule assemble line. The game challenges the player to come up with the most elegant solution (using the least amount of resources). Being an IT engineer, when I first watched the tutorial video, admittedly I thought in my head "oh great, this is going to be like my job" and while the gameplay does remind me a little bit like writing code, it was actually surprisingly fun.
The game's overall presentation is nice, somewhat simple but it's tastefully done. The music is good, although at times it made feel like I'm watching a movie from the 90s. The pacing of the game is well done; the player is sanely and graciously introduced to game elements.
The game's design allows for any number of solutions and after solving a problem the player is presented with a bell curve as to how they compared to "other engineers" (ie players). I really appreciated this aspect as it let me know that a more efficent and elegant solution is possible.
My only complaint with the game is that it actually did feel a bit like my job (but in a good way). The feeling of satisfation I got from completing a puzzle was similiar to the satisfaction I get when writing a piece of code I'm proud of at work. It's a good feeling but by the end of the day I'm usually more keen on relaxation instead of solving complex problems.
Overall this game is nicely designed and definitely worth consideration. This game engages the mind and respects the player with interesting and challenging puzzles. The world needs more games like this.
Score: 8.5/10

X-COM: UFO Defense is an often revered classic in strategy cirlces, more so now than ever before following Firaxis' re-interpretation of the series in their Enemy Unknown 2012 release.
Despite being nearly twenty years old, the 4X strategy aspects are as strong as ever. I appreciate how the interface and geoscape are presented to you with next to no hand-holding. The lack of any sort of tutorial or battle advice works effectively in immersing you in a reality where your enemy threats are truly alien and in every sense of the word too. Experimentation is key, with base building allowing for different types of manufacture and research that have plentiful bounties to offer. The X-COM unit itself can be treated as if a business of it's own which naturally has numerous benefits throughout the course of the game.
Yet the actual combat itself is where UFO Defence shows it's true colours, irrespective of how prepared you really are. It doesn't matter what armour you have, what guns you carry or even how experienced your soldiers are: the struggle always remains the same. Your units will miss painfully obvious shots, be felled by a single stray bullet or, most embarassingly of all, panic at the mere sight of a lone alien mook. It is because of the haphazard nature of X-Com's combat that it can feel slow and monotnous, especially as level structures repeat themselves and saves are reloaded numerous times in order to better chances against otherwise unbeatable enemies. Some people love X-COM's combat but I'm most certainly not one of them
Even so, UFO Defense was a major sign-post for the strategy genre because it took these crucial features in the combat and global contest and extended them into a larger experience. Not many games to this day match X-COM for it's scale and even fewer for it's initially brutal learning curve either. Most of you reading this have probably already made up your mind about the series and it's legacy either way, to those who haven't I would only recommend you try them simply to say you've done so. If nothing else, X-COM is capable of eating up weeks of spare-time when it engrosses the best of us and that genuinely is a good thing.

Keeping this short, I had high hopes for KHOLAT but sadly the game fails to deliver and stretches what little content it has way too far.
You're an explorer wandering the area where the Dylatov Pass Incident (Wiki it, it's a good read) happened, pretty soon you find yourself in the Siberian wilderness at night equiped with a flashlight, compass and a map. You wander around the bitterly cold landscape looking for notes and "anomalies." Sadly, the anomalies are just notes in areas that have some visual interest and change things up from the snowy covered trees and rocks. Around the anomalies are specters (black transparent humanoids) that patrol and try to get you, if they do you're dead. Sneaking by the specters or outrunning them isn't too fun, nor are the particularly scary. And really, most of the horror element stems from them so it doesn't quite work all too well.
Travel is a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ you're slow and your sprint is seriously limited. Honestly, it's probably the shortest sprint I've seen in any game I've played. Which ultimately, gets annoying. 90% of the game is just ice, snow, frost, trees, bushes and plants and you grow tired of it fast and just want to sprint your way through, but you can't because of the limited stamina of the main character. If you drain your stamina you're stuck for a couple seconds walking slower than the normal walking pace as your character regains his breath. It's a major annoyance.
The map will mark off any notes, anomalies and camps you find, but it doesn't say where the hell you are. I get it, maps don't do that, but this isn't a nitty gritty survival game and it REALLY doesn't need to have a map that doesn't pinpoint exactly where you are. It's terrible and leaves the map almost useless.
The last mistake the game makes is that death requires you to restart from the last camp or note you picked up. Yes, in a game where there's nothing to do in between locations of interest and where death can come easily if you die 10 minutes away from your last "checkpoint," enjoy making that massive trip again. After 6+ deaths I'm done and I don't think I'll continue with the rest of the game.
I'm a sucker for atmospheric "walking simulators" but this really ups the ante of annoyance which I just can't get behind. If you're looking for one, wait until a sale. Other than that give this a pass.

Kholat was a complete mystery to me, another game which completely fell under the radar, well, mine anyway until I noticed it advertised on here a few weeks ago.
A quick look at the synopsis and the positive Steam reviews persuaded me to buy it, as did my brief demo with an 'educational' version.
Suffice to say this is one of the most compelling and gripping horror survival/mystery games you will play for some time, although it is far from perfect.
Making exceptional use of the Unreal Engine 4, Kholat is based on supposed true events of a group of mountaineers who went missing in the location of the game's name, before a rescue crew went out in search of them and found only their remains, with massive questions over what happened, given the nature of exactly what was found.
That is the premise, and it makes for a good one - you are a mystery character who explores the locale, discovers journals and articles which give more information about what really happened here, all the while being pursued by an entity whose original is equally unclear.
The entity, I should add, is nowhere near as irritating as the Slender types who ended up saturating horror games - it's a chilling enemy but doesn't appear more than it should, and boo scares are more or less absent.
Meanwhile you explore the Russian wilderness, which, btw, is completely covered in snow and the weather effects of blizzards are some of the best you'll see - up there with The Witcher, trying to find more evidence and clues; your navigation is deliberately difficult - there is no waypoint ala Witcher or GTAV - only a barely understandable compass and a physical map which contains coordinates of interest and marks places you have already been - but it doesn't really help you find where you're going, and this helps add to the complete sense of isolation in this sad and disturbing part of the world - you feel truly alone, and lost, and extremely vulnerable. And it works very well.
Yes, in places it gets a little frustrating when you truly have no clue what to do next, but it's a rare game I've enjoyed without having the answers spoonfed.
In terms of the story, it's complex - there are answers, but they too aren't spoonfed - you have to decide for yourself what happened based on how you interpret the journals.
The ending itself is poor - pure and simple - it makes little sense and is a bit of a cop out, but the flesh was in all the stuff in between and there's where you can build the picture from.
On a technical level, Kholat makes beautiful use of UE4 - it's a stunning looking game for an Indie title, not unlike Ethan Carter, also UE3 and 4. It does struggle in places with poor optimisation (1080P occasionally stuttered on 980Ti SLI) but it's forgiveable.
You'll play worse games than this, just don't expect it all wrapped up in a nice bow for you.

Ok, Picture Gnomoria, but with better graphics, better UI, and Papa Johns Delivers.
Now you have your delicious or disgusting pizza, depending on where you live, and you can start your crafting and managing and building journey to keep your citizens alive. The crafting system is very simple and easy to learn, while still being of a good size for this early on in development. The raids on your town can be very simple and easy to fend off, to brutal cavity defiling, child sodomising, soul endingly devastating. So always make sure you have a Fighter or two ASAP. Focus on getting them better equipment over getting your next crafting milestone. Your people can live on without a Trapper for a few more weeks. They won't be living if a horde of goblins kill your Defenders and then your people because all they have for equipment is still padded armor and wooden sword and shield.
This game is very much still in progress but I like the progress thats being done. Most games in early access that say they are still in Alpha (Which this one tells you it is right at the start) have half the content, and 1,000 times more bugs and crashes. All this has that I've noticed so far is a couple of UI and AI bugs and logic loops, and a small tendancy for data leak. So restart your game every hour and a half or so and you will be fine. Also you have to turn on Auto Save, which was weird. Sometimes your Citizens will go to move an object you designated to be moved elsewhere and someone else will get to it sooner and that previous citizen will still go to where that object is. Though once they find out the object is there they move on to the next objective which is nice. Sometimes in Gnomoria (A finished and released game) Gnomes will do the exact same thing but instead get stuck in an AI Loop and you pretty much have to wait for them to get hungry or tired to reset themselves.
So far the majority of negative reviews about this game are about buildings not being able to get fully done. In my opinion since I have a fully functioning town with 12 buildings, 5 of which are custom design, roads, pastures, lengthy defensive works and what not, all of them 100% completed. That the complainers are idiots, and that they try to do multiple projects at one time, run out of materials and then complain that the game is broken. Much like that meme where a guy rides a bike then puts a stick in his own tire and complains about someone else doing it. Your citizens will do multiple projects at a time, and the game will tell you that you have enough resources for a building if the resources are still in your stockpile. That means that if you pause the game, and try to construct 3 houses, each time it will tell you that you have enough resources in your stockpile. If you are that tired and don't notice that logic issue, please go to sleep. Or stop being a moron.
A couple of suggestions that would be nice in my opinion.
-Make it to where when digging a mine tunnel, they auto construct ladders, since people will sometimes forget and well there goes 3-6 of your citizens.
-Possibly already in development but if there could be some sort of food preservation thing. Like an Ice box or something that will keep my fruits and veggies fresh longer would be nice.
- Lower the amount of food it takes to get a new Citizen at ALL levels. I am currently sitting at 15 Citizens and producing enough food for 80. Still can't get a new Citizen. I realize this may be due to the developers wanting to give people a possible Siege supply incase they take heavy losses to Food or Food production capability from a raid, but there is an option wether or not to accept a new Citizen. Let us take the risk.
-Developers. This tip more than all the others is the most important and I hope that if you read this review and take anything from it, that you take this one to the heart.

The personality system for the Heathlings is quite good but limited. It is a great start though and I am liking the direction they are moving in.

The Herbalist seems like a total waste of a class. It doesnt do anything at this point and the only reason to have one is to make a cleric. They need a major revamp of the herbalist because from what I played it is totally useless.
Overall the game seems to be coming along but it needs a LOT more content. I didnt get any stuck workers so it looks like they FINALLY got that problem resolved. Overall I am a lot more optimistic about what I played today then what I was playing last year but I still can't recommend it due to the low amount of content. Still no flowing water, weather, etc.

So, this game is really fun to play. I don't actually have very many complaints about the game but the couple I have are enough to push my review to negative.
For me, one of the main attractions in buying this game is the wide variety of mods that are available. There are a lot of great mods for this game that really appeal to me, it's just a damned shame that enabling and disabling them is one of the most annoying and tedious activities I've ever done.
First of all, it's not enough to just download the wrestlers you want from the workshop. First you download them, then once in game you have to manually move each individual wrestler out of the 'Retired' category into one of the other 'Team' categories. This gets very tiresome, very quickly.
Second, let's say you want to remove those wrestler mods. It is not enough to unsubscribe from the Steam workshop. in fact, that will do nothing at all. You will once again have to take the time to tediously delete each and every one individually all over again.
Third, as if this isn't enough. Let's say you want to download some ring textures from the workshop to create different rings. No problem, downloading those are a cinch. The problem though comes when you try to build the ring. While in the editor, the files you choose appear with the Steam ID# for them in the file name. This makes it so that the actual name of the file is completely cut off by the Steam ID# and you can't actually see anything you're selecting when you build your ring. For example; I downloaded a collection of WrestleMania rings. Each file, when selected in the ring editor, appears as 1182323812_ssr_WM and the rest is cut off from view.
I'd really like to recommend this game but until they sort out their workshop issues, I can't. Get it together, please.

I got this game in Early Access. Playing the survival sandbox was fun. The bear hunt, which most people know about by now, is an absolute ball ache, with no real purpose other than to annoy. Shooting a bear six times, getting mauled six times, and with a crappy keyboard disabling shortcut that means you have to sit there, six or more times, watching the same bear maul screen over and over instead of being able to quit and go back or just skip it and get on with it. And that underlines the most annoying thing about this game. Really bad game balance and mechanics. The wolves are now like super mutants, chasing you down from half way across the map and able to completely resist being stabbed multiple times, with running speed that would make the Flash look slow. The story mode though is the real killer for this game. I used to play this game for hours a day in sandbox, but after story mode I got so annoyed and aggravated by the crappy mechanics and pointless walking simulator that is the side quests (WALKING FOR 2 HOURS FOR ONE QUEST!). It seems much of the mechanics and plot is there to stretch out an otherwise short lived story mode. There about an hour or so of gameplay in story mode, and about 10hours of walking and taking stupidly long routes to avoid wolves, that respawn in minutes.
Stick to sandbox, even though they’ve gimped that with the new wolves aggressiveness too. All in all, 2 months ago, this was a great game. Now, avoid it. Save your £25, or spend on something else.

Great survival game, probably the best survival game I've ever played. No monsters, zombies, dinos, or any of that sort of thing. Just nature and you. There are dangers from animals out there in the wild but the real danger is the climate, starvind or dehidrating.. Heck you can even become to tired to press on, and just pass out and die in the cold snow.
I've never been so on edge and hopefull for a break in any other survival game. It is a lot more intence before you learn the maps.. Because not knowing if you will run across a place of refuge or not is a big deal. If you know where everything is I can imagine that would take a lot of the thrill out of survival mode, however even then you still have to manage your food and water and cold.. Even knowing where things are, this can still be a challenge.
I would recomend not playing it on easy, I tried once after dieing from a wolf on day 2 of my first play through, I went right back to a harder difficulty. Easy mode is exactly that, easy mode, and it really ruins the game as it takes away any fear of animal because they all run from you no matter what. Those encounters and how to avoid them are a big part of the tension of the game. Later when you are better suited and you want to hunt such animals, if they are always running away at great distances I guess that could bring some difficulty back, but it's more fun being the hunter and the hunted for sure.
Story mode, well... I half way dig it and half hate it. The restrictions are real... To much even. The interaction of the characters is awesome though. It would be great if they put the NPC's into a survival mode game.. Add that check box as part of the options "NPCs? Y/N" Give them perma death along with your own perma death per survival game.
Just a thought.
Anyway, buy it. It's awesome.

My favourite puzzle game. The puzzles get gradually harder and harder, but never seem too impossible. I've never had this much drive to force myself in to solving a puzzle and never felt as rewarded when I finally did. The best part is; the solution is most likely unique.
The game offers countless of ways to solve a puzzle and teaches the basic concepts behind programming while doing it. There is no right way to solve a puzzle, there are faster ways, simpler ways, more understandble ways and your way. If “Slender: The Arrival” made you scared of being alone in the woods at night with just a flashlight, this game might do the same for you about Russia’s Ural Mountains. It’s not about jump scares. It’s about the environment of the region, which changes as you progress in certain areas.
What makes this game difficult is not the slow-walking, semi-transparent monsters, or the orange smoke, or the primitive traps, or Sean Bean. It’s the fact that this game is a pre-GPS walking simulator. There’s no mini-map on the corner of your screen, with a dot or a triangle indicating where you are. All you have is a paper map that fills the entire screen and a compass, so it’s very easy to get lost. Fortunately, there are some places with coordinates handwritten on rock, so you can confirm where you are. Confirm or even find out you’re nowhere near where you expected to be!
Also, your character is physically limited. You can’t run for very long before losing your breath. Save the running for when you see the orange smoke or when your compass starts shaking.
The worst part is that you can’t jump nor climb. Given that you’re in a mountainous area, this can be very frustrating.
Basically, if you’re interested in the paranormal, if you like somewhat scary games, or if you’re looking for a unique experience, you should get this game. However, if you’re looking for something as scary or disturbing as “Amnesia” or “Outlast”, if you hate VERY long walks, or if you have no patience for the kind of exploration this game requires, you should stay away from it.
I suggest you only play this game in the winter. You’ll get a better feel of it that way.

I am a huge fan of Russian Science Fiction and Horror, usually in books and movies, but also in video games like Metro 2033 and the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series. So I felt it was my duty to play this game as well, and even if I'm not through yet, I can absolutely recommend it.
Let me state first: This is
an
! Your only weapon is
! This game bears Exploration game in its description for a reason, it's slow-paced, you're supposed to keep one eye on the compass, and one eye plus both ears on your enviroment - which is fairly beautiful but devastating - otherwise you're gonna overlook something important and/or die. If you're looking for a fast-paced action horror game you can finish as quickly as possible, shooting/beating down all enemies in your way (I've seen reviews comparing Kholat to Silent Hill and stuff...), then please look on, you won't have fun with this one. ;)
The controls are very close to reality. Imagine just for a second you're going on an expedition to the Ural with like -50°C at night - do you go there in shorts and t-shirt with flip-flops on your feet? Really? You're serious? xD Nah, you're not. I'm sure you don't...
So you're wearing heavy winter clothes, maybe even multiple layers, agree? And that's exactly what the controls feel like: You cannot move as quickly as you want to 'cause you're simply wrapped and packed in clothes to avoid hypothermia, there's fresh-fallen snow all over and maybe even ice underneath making it fairly hard to walk fast.
- Is there much to do in this game?
-- No, not really. It's mostly walking, observing your enviroment, sometimes running, finding (reading/hearing) records or hidden paths... And yeah, you might die a few times. That's pretty much all you can do (you might call it a walking simulator with a death feature xD) since it focusses on its story, and it is doing very well telling it in small bites. The biggest challenge is navigation with a compass and map, because that`s all you have beside your flashlight. Regardless of the map and compass you're probably going to get lost a few times. Even with fast travelling between the camp sites you're gonna walk alot, in fact most of the time! You can also try to sprint constantly,
- What about the story...
-- I'm not at it's end yet, but it definitly got me hooked after the first hour and I cannot resist playing, I must know how it ends, and how it began! You start hopping off a train in a small, quiet Russian village to find details about the Dyatlov pass incident. It's a beautiful place, so I definitly recommend taking a look around - you're not
in a hurry. Then you head to the forest. The next moment you find yourself in the middle of a snow storm close to the Dyatlov group's camp on Kholat... The storm is over, you start your investigation. Hard to describe without spoiling too much, so I'll keep it this short ;)
- ... and the atmosphere?
-- It's perfect. A perfect Russian psy-horror theme. If you allow to immerse yourself in the game, the snow and wind will make you freeze. The English voice actors have done an amazing job here, they bring the story to life (I'll check the Polish voices in the next run!). You can feel the desperation in this place, that something evil has happened, and someone or something is lurking in the dark, waiting for you to make only one false step. But most of all you feel lost in the middle of nowhere.
- Is this a Horror game after all?
-- In my opinion it is. Don't confuse Horror with Splatter, please! There are only very few jumpscares though. Therefore the "anomaly" poses a subtle and steady threat since you can easily overlook it, especially in shady places. And if it get's you, you die in an instant. So if you notice it, and it notices you: Run, run for your life and hope you don't get lost.
- Other reviews mentioned bad performance?
-- Yes, that's particularly true and unfortunatly I cannot deny it. The game is absolutely beautiful with fascinating graphics of realistic landscapes, but as the game progresses the framerate continues to drop on my machine. It started with 30 - 35FPS during the first one or two hours, then went down to 25 - 30 and by now it's around 20 - 25, sometimes (and only for a short moment, when turning around too quickly) dropping to 10 - 15. It's not as bad as it reads! To be fair: The game detected my machine could run it with ultra high graphics (AMD Phenom II X4 960T, nVidia Geforce GTX 660, 4x4GB RAM ganged @ CL 7-7-7-11) and I did not lower them since. If you're playing it on anything else but a low-end machine, then the performance issue should not bother you too much.
There's just one thing which is really annyoing me, and I feel like I must mention it, so maybe the devs read it, too: You can jump down slopes, twenty meters high, hopping from one snowy! rock to an iced! one to the next, and don't even stumble, but you're unable to climb a 50cm edge... C'mon, you must be kidding! Due to this the game doesn't feel as much open-worlded as it should ;) Whatsoever, I'm looking forward to the devs' next exploration horror project.
* see the Kholat Community Guides here on Steam for details ;)

One of the best RPGs using D&D rules in history. Even nowdays it outshines most of the titles of the same genre, for its memorable characters (Boo is still my hero) and the storyline, which is still one of the best around after 20 years. A masterpiece and personally one of my all time favorites, avoid it only if you hate the genre or games with an isometric worldview.
What's good:
-Tactical DnD combat, at higher difficulties it becomes prioritary to prepare for the toughest fights, besides choosing your companions wisely.
-Charismatic characters to choose from as your companions throughout the game, each one with its own personality and will. A practical example: you're the usual lawful good paladin, saving maidens right and left, feeding ophans and so on? Do not expect that chaotic evil semi-pedophile dwarven mercenary to stay long in your party.
-The game is full of side-quests, most of them rewarding and satisfying.
-Characters interact with one another (mostly with you of course).
-Romance system available for some characters, further developed in the sequel. You want to play something more like Dawson's Gate rather than Baldur's? Here you have it.
-Entertaining storyline and decision making power. You can kill almost everyone in this game, but beware to face the consequences (I myself messed the game up once.)
-Even without all of the side-quests, this game is pretty long. Without the expansion and all the side quests included in this enhanced edition, it will take you from 20 to 30 hours to beat the game, if you're not rushing it like mad.
What's bad/ possibly not enjoyable for others:
-If your a fan of 3D graphics this is not the game for you.
-A little dated audio packs in some cases, not a big deal considering the epic soundtrack but still...
-By contrast with what i wrote before, some may not appreciate the DnD dice based fighting system. If you're a fan of pure action oriented combat games you'll probably be disappointed in this one.
-Objectively dumb racial restrictions in some cases. Why in the world can't I be a monk if I'm an half-elf? Or an elven paladin? Nothing fun-breaking yet still unsettling.
To conclude, if you're a fan of traditional RPG or an open minded ACTION-RPG lover, this might be the game for you.
PS. Nevermind the hours of gameplay Steam shows, I've beaten this game thrice or more in a non-Steam version, besides the countless hours I spent on the original one.

Cuphead... what a game. Unfortunately, nothing in this life is perfect. Cuphead is no exception.
Let's start with what the game gets right. There's a LOT that this game gets right. First and foremost is the art style. Designed as an homage to the hand-drawn animation style of the 1930s and 1940s, Cuphead  really hits the high marks in regards to visual presentation. The developers even went so far as to include "vintage mode" as unlockables in the game, which are really just a muted color palette, black and white mode, and the mono sound type. Despite how mundane those sound, they actually add to the atmosphere of the game and feel like worthwhile rewards for the tasks they ask you to perform to unlock them. What makes the visuals all the more impressive though, is the fact that every single frame of animation and illustrations were HAND-DRAWN to maximize authenticity.
Secondly, related to atmosphere, is the game's soundtrack. There is a wide variety of genres incorporated into this game, ranging from jazz to ragtime, and even a samba rhythm. All of these are, naturally, musical genres that were in-style during the era that the game pays homage to. Many of them are so catchy that you can't help but tap your foot even as the level they play for kicks you all over the place again and again.
Third on the list is gameplay. I've never played a run-n-gun game before, so this was definitely a first for me. It also incorporated elements of the "bullet hell" genre. The combination of platforming and shooting made for an excellent experience. It's a great title to play if you're new to either of those types of games. The difficulty is selectable and more-or-less scales with the skill of the player, so there is very little cause for stress most of the time.
Now onto what this game could do with improving on. Most of these are gameplay related, so it makes as good a segue as anything else.
First up: the difficulty. TV Tropes lists this game under "Nintendo Hard" for a reason. It's very reminscent of classic difficult games like Contra and arcade shoot-em-ups like Galaga or 1943. Many modern gamers even compare it to the infamous Dark Souls series since that utilizes a similar style of difficulty in regards to player reaction and basis on skill rather than luck. As stated above, the difficulty mostly scales with the player's skill, so it becomes easier as they improve. For the most part, anyway. There are a few notable instances where the game felt more than a little unfair. To list:
1. All of the airplane bosses. I like the concept behind the airplane fights, and the bosses associated with them are good, but it seems like almost every fight that takes place in airplane sections is a slave to RNG. The biggest offenders in this regard are Cala Maria (Isle 3) and Djimmi the Great (Isle 2). During the first phase of both of these bosses, they have a selection of attacks that are decided at random, and when used in combination can result in situations where taking damage is unavoidable. In a game mostly filled with skill-oriented difficulty, cheap shots like that can cause a lot of frustration in a short amount of time.
2. Lack of consistent practicality with items. What I am referring to are the weapons, charms, and super arts. The weapons for the most part are fairly well balanced in terms of their in-battle applications and force the player to consider what the boss is going to do and which weapons would be best for countering it. There is minor issue in regards to the Roundabout weapon: it outclasses the Peashooter in all practical respects and thus makes the latter useless upon purchasing the former. There are very few situations that come to mind in which the Peashooter would be preferred due to its better initial range since the damage output and area coverage of Roundabout are much better.
Charms is where the game starts falling flat in usefulness. Probably the most useful are the Smoke Bomb, Coffee, Heart, and Twin Heart. Smoke Bomb changes the characters' dash/glide into a smoke vanish that provides invincibility frames (or i-frames for short) and is good for just about any situation outside of airplane levels. Coffee provides a constant generation of EX cards in order for players to execute more EXs and Super Arts, which is really useful in the airplane levels since shrinking provides a few i-frames upon activation. The two heart charms increase the health of the player characters while lowering their damage output as compensation. These charms are ideal for newer players as it gives them more chances to mess up on a level before dying and having to start over. For serious runs (such as A+/S-ranking), though, the damage penalty will have a negative impact on the time it takes to finish a level. The other charms are the Parry Sugar (P. Sugar in-game) and the Whetstone, which influence the parry mechanic. The P. Sugar gives a free parry if a player jumps into a parryable object, while the Whetstone turns the parry into an attack. The main issue with both of these is that the parry mechanic is only required for a small handful of the bosses in order to defeat them. There's also the matter of dodging an attack being preferable to running at it to try and reflect it, making the Smoke Bomb situationally better than either of the former charms.
Finally, we have the Super Arts. There are three of these in the game and they are unlocked by completing the Mausoleum levels. They each have their quirks, which will be explained:
Super Art 1: This is essentially a giant "laser" that covers a large amount of horizontal space in front of the player. The damage output is respectable, and the player has i-frames while the laser is firing. It's the middle-of-the-road Super Art that balances offense and defense. A solid choice for anybody.
Super Art 2: This one makes you completely invincible for ~6-7 seconds. Probably the most useful Super Art in the game since the player maintains control of their character for the entire duration and can utilize it either to get out of a tight spot or deal a massive amount of damage in a short amount of time without worrying about interruptions.
Super Art 3: This has the characters summon a manifestation of their soul to float around and rapidly punch anything that makes contact with it. It follows the character around and its movements are determined by how the player moves the controller (ex. You aim up, it moves up). While a good idea on paper, the actual ability is fairly lackluster. It is the only Super Art that has no i-frames whatsoever, so the player still has to focus on dodging incoming attacks while it is active. This can lead to situations where the player is forced to make the ghost fly off-screen in order to dodge an attack. If I have any suggestions, it would to be this: instead of granting true invincibility frames with this Super Art, make it so that if the player gets hit while performing it, it would lower the amount of time the Super Art has left instead of doing damage. This would make the ability worthwhile in many levels where there are bosses in the background that fill the screen with projectiles (like the last phase of Werner Werman or the Root Pack). As it stands, though, it just splits the player's focus even further.
3: Glitches and Bugs. All games have them, so this should come as no surprise. While most of the bugs in Cuphead are relatively minor and annoying, there are a few that stand out. Namely, there is a bug that causes the game to not respond to any player input after the end credits roll. This particular one can be annoying for players wanting to jump right back in after beating the last level as it forces them to restart the application.
Overall, Cuphead is a great experience that is as much of a thrill to watch as it is to play. It is definitely worth the money. 8/10. :)

Simply the best puzzle game I have ever played. A modern 'The Incredible Machine'. If you want to think, play this game.
Presentation: The Story is hilarious, if ultimately unimportant. The UI is clean and simple for the most part.
The gameplay is the heart of the game, in the puzzle solving. The puzzles curve well from easy in the beginning to mind-bending towards the end, not to mention the Research Net that's continually adding new puzzles. And beyond just solving them, the game challenges you to optimize your solutions in both speed and parts used, with online leader-boards for comparison.
The visuals are clean and simple, almost retro in how spartan they are. Nothing stands in the way of the 'puzzle' feel. Outside of the game board, it maintains a consistent, almost whimsical aesthetic. But don't come here looking for high quality 3D graphics, there simply aren't any.
The sound effects are largely very basic beeps and boops. The music is alright, but isn't particularly memorable, nor does it add greatly to the experience. I actually had muted mine early on, and forgot the game even had music.
In conclusion, this is everything a puzzle game needs to be, and little more. If you enjoy solving abstract puzzles, the game-play will carry this game, and you can completely overlook the points lost in other areas. There's a demo available, so there's no reason not to give it a try.

I've mainly played this game on the iPad, but I wanted to express my love for this title here as well.  It is a well crafted puzzle game that encourages creativity in its solutions.
In this game, there is a grid.  On this grid, you will place molecules, you will move molecules, and you will export specific, predetermined molecules.  The catch is, you have to do so by constructing a machine in advance, and then let it solve the problem for you.  Making such a machine is not easy, and it is rare that it will work as expected the first time.  The "machine" as I described it is composed of two tracks, with instructions along them.  A disc, which the game calls a WALDO, travels along each track, following the instructions as it comes across them.  The instructions include making an input molecule appear, making an output molecule disappear, grabbing/dropping a molecule, and bonding two molecules together.
There are many ways to beat each level.  Some are more efficient than others.  The great thing about this is that it encourages you to replay old levels to try to find the most optimized way of beating them.  You get to compare the efficiency of your solutions to the solutions of others.  This is probably the hardest puzzle game I've ever played (I still haven't beaten it, even on the iPad), but it is definitely the most satisfying.  There's a real joy when your contraption finally comes together and works as planned.  And the challenge is such that it ultimately feels fair.  There's always a "best" way to do it, but whatever you can come up with, so long as it gets the job done, is acceptable.
If you want a challenging, well made game that encourages creative solutions to puzzles, then look no further than this game.

A couple points to clear up possible misconceptions on gameplay.
- You have minimal control over your character.  You can move them to a room and use their "ultimate" abilities, but mostly they stand there and do what they do (attack, operate resource generators, etc.)
- Each "turn" starts when a door is opened, and causes monsters to spawn (possibly) in any unpowered or unoccupied rooms.  So opening two doors at once results in twice as many monsters (again possibly).
- Hoarding resources for the later levels is critical.  Dont just get enough food/science/industry to clear the floor, plan to take lots with you into the higher floors because stuff gets expensive.

It wouldn't be annoying if that characteristic was unique to them but its far from that way. Every other character is sarcastic clown type. Even the modern assassins joke at everything and don't take themselves seriously. The Templar's are often cruel for the sake of being cruel and they dress like nazis, its pandering as all hell and vast contrast to previous assassin creed titles.
Parkour: Is smoother now than ever! To bad you get a grappling hook early on and never have to really use it again. I think the grappling hook should have purchasable uses like the rest of equipment. You leave a wire behind when going from building to building so it would make sense to have limited uses at least when used in that manner It's a childish spamable
mechanic with no real give and take that overlaps the awesome parkour system.
"How do I get up there? Oh just use my batclaw."
Cons: Simple childish banter, story, characters and game mechanics(Unlimited use grappling hook). Pandering bad guys. To much HUD but most of it can be turned off.
Pros: GAME-PLAY really makes the game. Runs smooth, Very few bugs. Beautiful, London is Awesome, Fist fights, Much more interesting/fun stealth system. Parkour is super smooth.
I say a lot of bad things about this game here so why do I recommend? Because this game is amazing at what most people look for in a Assassins Creed title. Stealth game-play is amazing if not the best yet with gratifying assassinations, and super smooth Parkour, Beautiful open world environment with lots to do.

Just take a gander at my avatar. Then my name. Is there any question as to why I would be interested in such a game?
On top of that, I am quite a fan of horror games, and atmosphere is key to their success. So when an atmospheric horror game narrated by Sean Bean comes along, well, my knees go weak.
No, the entire thing wasn’t going to rhyme. What a senseless review that would be.
Alright, so step one, how is its atmosphere? It is very well done. I’ve had some of the biggest jumps I’ve had in a considerable amount of time playing this game, and that can directly be attributed to the atmosphere. It builds up a slow anticipation at nearly all times due to a wonderful use of sounds and environment, until, like a spring, the tension snaps and you jump. Now, would I call it scary? Not quite. Moreso chilling. Heh. Cause it's cold. But really, it doesn't make you feel like Amnesia, Outlast, or other such good games make you feel. Those games, I could only get a maximum of 30 minutes (and often much less) before I'd just have to stop and take a break.
The voice acting was good, not great. Well, except for Sean Bean. I didn’t feel as if the sense of dread or horror were adequately portrayed in some of the acting. They sounded almost calm when talking about fear and losing their minds.
The gameplay isn’t anything new. I never liked the term “walking simulator” but this is the type of game that will get that term. You find notes left behind and campfires (which you can fast travel between. Didn’t know that for the first half of the game. More walking. Yay!) that slowly uncover the story. So if you’re thinking “well, that’s nothing new,” you’re absolutely right! And if you ever played Amnesia a Machine for Pigs or SOMA, you’ll be delighted (not) to find that this game too flashes your flashlight when an enemy is near (and jiggles the compass). Why, oh why does this exist. Please stop implementing this awful feature into horror games. I cannot fathom why anyone thinks it’s a good idea. “Oh, you know sounds you’re hearing? They mean nothing. Nope, still nothing. Oh hey, now somethings there! Quick, run!” It definitely lessened the experience.
I didn’t want a huge paragraph, so here’s a new one. One last gameplay mechanic I wanted to mention, and that is the navigation. You have a map and a compass that you can use to navigate the world. Use them. Don’t wander aimlessly.
The story was alright. It was based on a real incident. Not too memorable. What was it about again? Ghosts?
Overall, I enjoyed the game. The other reviewers seem to have taken much longer, and I wonder why. Was it poor navigation? Did they replay it, and to what end? I don’t see any replay value with the game, unless it unknowingly unlocked a new mode. Or perhaps they wanted all of the achievements.
But yes, overall, good, not great. Stupid idiotic flashing light.
