Have you ever heard of the story behind a group of missing Russian students in the Northern Ural Mountains of Russia? Based on a true story, Kholat delves into the chilling story of those missing students. Filled with horror, the supernatural, and incredibly unnerving environments; Kholat takes you on a crazy journey that’ll leave you questioning why the hell you decided to play it at night time with only a lamp to light up your small room…
For those loyal GameReviewsAU fans out there, you’ll probably have learnt we like games that genuinely freak us out rather than ones that rely on jump-scares.
Kholat does a great job of being genuinely freaky by placing you in the middle of a relentless blizzard with only a map, compass and torch to help you get around. There are jump-scares, but because they’re so spaced out, you’re always left unprepared for what is waiting for you around the bend.
For gamers out there who don’t know the events that transpired in those freezing Ural Mountains, here’s a little excerpt taken from Wikipedia.
The incident involved a group of nine experienced ski hikers from the Ural Polytechnical Institute who had set up camp for the night on the slopes of Kholat Syakhl. Investigators later determined that the skiers had torn their tents from the inside out. They fled the campsite, probably to escape an imminent threat. Some of them were barefoot, under heavy snowfall. The bodies showed signs of struggle; Dyatlov had injuries to his right fist, as if he had been in a fist fight. One victim had a fractured skull and another was found with brain damage without any sign of distress to the skull. One of the skull fractures was so severe it was determined that he would not have been able to move. Additionally, one woman’s tongue was missing. Soviet authorities determined that an “unknown compelling force” had caused the deaths; access to the region was consequently blocked for hikers and adventurers for three years after the incident. –
Sounds pretty damn scary right? To this day, no one knows what happened up there. So here’s where the creative minds at IMGN.PRO join up to give us a truly spine-chilling experience in Kholat.
Armed with only a map, compass and torch you are tasked with exploring the massive area where the tragedy occurred and finding out what happened to the missing students. One of the best parts of Kholat is that the exploration is completely non-linear. You can go wherever you want at any point of the game. So long as you can read a map that is.
On your map are sets of co-ordinates. These indicate places of interest in the mountains such as camp sites. Other such places of interest can be found purely by chance or by finding extra co-ordinates that have been etched into the side of rocks. These co-ordinates can take you to notes that document diary entries by the students, reports of supernatural occurrences and the like.
Your compass is a bit pointless I found. As for one: I couldn’t work out which end of the needle was North or South, and two being that you can work out where you are with the map by itself.
In Kholat, there is no mini-map. There is no marker saying “You are here”. All you have is a map with highlighted paths drawn to show you which parts of the mountain are accessible. Only once you’ve found a place of interest will it appear on your map for reference.
You also have a survival guide that gives you some suggestions on how best to navigate the treacherous environment, as well as being a place to record previously found diary entries, reports, logs etc.
However, the survival guide can be a bit misleading. For example, the guide suggests, “Before setting off for a longer journey, rest in the camp“. Reading this made me think there must be some kind of stamina system which requires you to rest at a campsite before being able to set off again. That wasn’t the case though, as you can journey around the entire map without needing a single rest apart from regaining your breath after a sprint. Instead, what the campsites do is act as fast-travel points.
Sprinting is quite limited and, if you use sprint to it’s full extent, will leave you moving very slowly and not being able to see clearly. Therefore you really need to use sprint scarcely in case you get chased by anything.
What chases you? I still don’t know but they’re scary b*stards! They look like shadowy figures that walk around in the dark and leave behind glowing orange footprints. If you get too close, they’ll give chase and not stop until you’ve either outrun them, or they catch you and end your life. Sound effects alert you to when there’s one nearby, and also if it’s started chasing you, or disappeared because you outran it.
There’s no way to defeat them because you are completely unarmed except for a torch. “Maybe the torch can shine some light on what they are?” I hear you ask. Nope… Shine the torch on them and they’ll get slightly annoyed. Well not really slightly, more like p*ssed off to the extent that they chase and kill you.
Kholat is powered by Unreal Engine 4, giving us incredibly high quality graphics. For an environment that is completely covered by a blizzard you’d think there’s not much point to be so detailed, but IMGN.PRO have done an incredible job with giving us such an HD mountain to explore!
Sound-wise, the howling blizzard screaming all round you whilst in the mountains never becomes repetitive and keeps your ears pricked up for other sounds, such as rustling paper, which indicates a note is nearby.
Sean Bean even makes an appearance as the narrator of the story. Every now and then you’ll reach an area where Sean pipes in with his two cents worth of narration. It’s very comforting to hear a familiar voice when you’re up to your knees in snow at a place where a group of people went nuts. But his words aren’t very comforting…
Kholat is a true adventure game, placing you in a deserted mountain with only a map, compass and torch. I love that you don’t have a minimap because it forces you to use your noggin and work out where you are with only the few tools at your disposal.
Finishing Kholat one hundred percent will take around four to six hours depending on how generous you are with sprinting. There’s a good lot of achievements to unlock, so completionists may take an extra hour or so finding out how to unlock them.
I absolutely love the graphics, sound effects and narration by Sean Bean and had an absolute blast sh*tting myself by playing at midnight with little light source. I can’t wait to get back in and find the rest of the hair-raising reports to get a better idea of what transpired during the Dyatlov Pass Incident.

Kholat is an okay horror game. It isn't amazing, but it certainly isn't terrible. If you are a fan of horror games, this game is for you. There are some issues here and there... But it all works out.
PROS:
+Sean Bean narrates the game and his voice is perfect. There are other voice actors, and like Bean, they are wonderful. Whomever was the voice director really got their actors to... ACT!
+The story is pretty good. It is told through notes found and narrations by Bean. Walking in the snow can be linked to what is going on, but the game is meant to be interpreted.
+There is no "YOU ARE HERE" dot on the map. You must use the compass and pay attention to landmarks. This is great! It adds to the terror of being lost while something is hunting you down.
+The big bad monster will never jumpscare the player. There was one time where he respawned in front of me (and killed me) but, other than that one fluke, you'll notice him walking around, the flashlight flickering, or the compass spazzing out.
+Sprinting can only be done in bursts since the character will tire out. This is good since it adds to the terror if you're found by the monster.
+The level design is pretty good! I found myself enjoying the well designed snowy areas. But....
MIXED:
+/-...There's no jumping. I know this may sound strange since other games like this, such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, do not have jumping or removing the ability to jump would not change anything. The level design is far and wide and, as the game expects you, there are times where you have to walk down steep hills. The problem is that sometimes you can get stuck between two rocks, or there's a rock in the way of your path, both of which can be easily JUMPED over. The funny thing about this is that I really do think jumping was in the game at one point since there are some paths that are cut off by a high ledge. Even with jumping, it'd be impossible to get them. It doesn't kill the game, but it certainly hurts it because I'm supposed to be immersed in the game and the fastest way to pull me out of the experience is to put a small ledge that I could get over in real life by simply raising my leg higher to step over!
+/- The ambient sound is amazing, despite one detail: foot steps in the cave and water droplets. Throughout the game the sound is amazingly designed, until you reach the caves. Your footsteps still sound like you're in the stone and I could hear water droplets, but I could see multiple sources of them and they are all out of sync. Once I got out of the caves, the wonderful design came back, but it still ruins the overall experience.

While I got it as one of the additional games padding out a $12 HumbleBundle pack, I'm honestly disappointed they saw a single penny of my money. To sum it up in a single sentence:
is a prime example of how even the best premise in the world is nothing in the wrong hands. Early game spoilers abound, but you're honestly not going to be missing much of value.
Sold as a horror comedy about sentient corn, the hook sounds incredibly promising. Upon starting, however, the game gets off to an awful start by breaking the golden rule of suspense entirely: showing a glimpse of awful humanoid corn models disappearing into the distance, the game skips the whole "letting your imagination fill in the gaps" trope found in any medium that wants to keep you interested. Thankfully, this should hopefully set your expectations somewhat low from the get go.
From this point onwards, the game takes on the worst kind of walking simulator format, wherein the game might as well be a short film for the lack of interactivity that being a game brings. Any kinds of lore or plot are delivered entirely through post-it pickups and shreds of paper, which quickly becomes irritating when dozens are scattered in chunks across entire rooms. Anything usable or that can be picked up is given a white silhouette, basically making the game a point-and-click if the character only commented on about 5% of the given world. All items have descriptions that either flat out tell you what to use them on, or are totally irrelevant to anything. Topping this all off is puzzle logic that can only be solved with "try anything" -- the fuse box is noted to be missing a fuse, so I hope you don't spend your time looking for a fuse when the solution is to jam a rusty nail into it.
Should you keep giving the game more chances by pushing further onwards, things somehow manage to get worse. Upon actually meeting with a few sentient corn stalks, the dialogue is both cringy and painfully unfunny: hearing them argue about riddles without a shred of charisma makes it tortuous to sit through a three minute dialogue, though it's fitting since the area beyond is where the awful character writing really begins to shine.
Why does one of the characters have an elevator dispense pellets like a Skinner box with zero indication that using it is doing anything?
Why would two people form a scientific partnership when one is a mentally handicapped, insanely careless with money, and an outright slob when the other is the total opposite?
How would a man who thinks that removing a computer's RAM and hiding it away so it "doesn't get dusty" get to the position where he had access to insane amounts of money and authority?
Why does combining a computer and teddy with a robot arm make a tiny Russian character that follows you just to call you stupid?
To sum it up, what sounds like a good idea simply ends up as the petty humour that you'd expect from a confused, 13-year-old kid who desperately wants to be wacky yet lacks any solid ideas on comedy or humour or writing; you get corn stalks prattling on about "If a tree falls in the woods" like you would actually stop to listen to their flat dialogue that you know will end without a laugh. Use your money on something with actual entertainment value -- even "so bad it's good" is preferable to this dull farce.

Fire Pro Wrestling World is a game I was looking forward to ever since it was announced. When I first played it, I was not disappointed. The Fire Pro series has a long and storied history, but the fraction of American releases is only the tip of the iceberg so to speak. If you’re familiar with the series, you’ll probably know exactly what to expect. It picks up right where the last game left off. It adds a bunch of new features with more on the way. The added Steam Workshop feature is a godsend for downloading CAWs if you’re familiar with the pains of the older techniques for Fire Pro Returns. For those of you who’ve never played a Fire Pro game, it’s vastly different from your average 2k wrestling game. The most startling difference is the use of sprites for the wrestlers instead of 3d models, but this limitation turns out to be very helpful in the creation of convincing real life wrestlers. The controls are a bit hard to wrap your head around at first, but they get easier once you learn how to time your attacks. I recommend looking at a guide if you have trouble understanding the grapple system. The customization is where the game really shines. You can find pretty much any wrestler you could imagine on the Steam Workshop.  A vast amount of CAW parts allows for near endless amounts of potential creations. There are also a large variety of moves that can allow for various wrestlers’ move sets to be accurately represented. You can also name finishers, which is a feature I sorely miss from the WWE SvR series. The ability to tweak logic allows for wrestlers to play out nearly exactly like their real life counterparts. This makes the game a wonderful simulator for wrestling matches. The customization for rings also allows for a decent chunk of real life wrestling shows to be accurately represented. The only thing lacking customization as of right now are the title belts, which are the same models from over a decade ago. (Hopefully this gets changed during development as it’s still early access.) There are also a variety of different match types that allow for some really fun moments. From exploding barbwire deathmatches, to MMA cage fights, there is a lot of variety in the match types. You can have up to 8-man matches. (No 30-man royal rumble matches as of right now) The only match types you’ll really miss are WWE style matches like Hell in a Cell or ladder matches. This is due to the game being heavily Japanese Puroresu oriented. While the game has modes like tournaments and leagues, right now it is missing a proper GM style mode and career mode, both of which were in previous games. I have hopes that this will get added later as it’s still in early access. There’s also an online mode that is pretty fun, but I haven’t played much of it.
Here's a list of the pros and cons for me.
Pros:
Loads and loads of customization
Sprite based characters (Either a pro or con depending on your tastes)
Fun gameplay (Especially the deathmatches!)
Extremely accurate simulation
Lots of variety in match types (MMA, boxing, etc.)
Steam Workshop implementation is great
Closest thing we’ll ever get to a new NJPW/AJPW game
Cons:
Sprite based characters (Either a pro or con depending on your tastes)
Control scheme is a little difficult to learn (It’s easy once you get the hang of it though)
No WWE style special matches
No career or GM mode (At this point in early access)
Fire Pro Wrestling World is a game that I love, and I’d thoroughly recommend it if you like: old school wrestling games, simulating matches, Japanese Puroresu, and/or four-way exploding barbwire deathmatches between Duke Nukem, Kurt Cobain, Danny Devito, and Hatsune Miku.

Dungeon of the Endless provides a great level of replay value. If it’s not the different pods that increase replay value, it’ll be the number of characters to choose from. As of this review, there’s as many as 27 to choose from and each bring their own advantages & disadvantages. By default, you start with 2 & recruit more in the dungeon, but the maximum number is 4. Fun fact, if you set your team up correctly, they’ll share some unique dialog between floors and provide each other with a boost in stats & additional skills.
Speaking of pods, they are you game modes and as of this review, there’s 8 available to select, each providing their own variety of difficulty, disadvantages, perks & modifiers. Maybe the basic Escape Pod is good enough for you or you want the toughest challenge to date that is the Sanitary Pod, maybe you feel like going on a solo run in the Refreezerator Pod or you want to see how far you can go in the Drill Pod.
There are no higher difficulty option choices that unlocks as you play, as previously mentioned, the variety of pods provides that choice for you. Which makes the Too Easy & Easy option at the start of the game misleading, especially to first-time players.
Not useless, just misleading. Notable difference between the two difficulties includes less abundance of dust and resources, stronger monsters (obviously), frequent rooms where you can’t build any modules & overall luck.
Dungeon of the Endless also features multi-player function, which has it’s ups and downs. When looking at the ups, having multiple people manage their heroes can make it easier to plan your actions & assess the situation. But on the other hand, having multiple players, especially when playing with strangers, can also be confusing when one player is trying to figure out what the others are doing and your resources are split between the number of players.
In a nutshell, it adds more unnecessary time playing the game. Not to say that multi-player is completely unnecessary, a 2-player game with a friend is more than enough to have a good time as opposed to a maximum 4-player game. Less is More.
Since this review won’t acquire everyone’s intentions, all that’s left to be said is to buy the game & see for yourself if this game’s for you. Though really, what could go wrong? Open the Door!

*This review has been completely re-done to better reflect the reasons why I chose not to recommend this game.
Evolve is a game that saw awful DLC practices and lack of incentivizing PLAYABLE content make quick work of it's playerbase. Don't get me wrong, I supported this game for as long as I could and sunk as many hours as I wanted to into it. But now the time has come to say my piece about it in this review. What is Evolve like now? Is it worth it a second look? If you're new, should you buy it? I'll attempt to tackle these questions here. I hope you enjoy!
Welcome to Evolve, where you're invited to step into the boots of a well-trained Hunter tasked with saving colonies under siege on the planet Shear, or take control of the beastly Monster responsible for the attacks, on the run to survive against the invading Hunters. A lot of what Evolve has to offer is embedded in the idea of this 'Hunt', unfortunately, this is also the most is has to offer. This isn't to say the gameplay doesn't hold itself up, or that the quality of what you paid $60 for is unmatched. The problem arises when you're offered to PAY a lot more than you do to PLAY for. Evolve isn't pay-to-win, at least on the Monster side of things. For the Hunters, the characters you have to pay for are definitely welcome additions to the game and they don't do a whole lot more in terms of an advantage for you and your team to get an 'easy' win over using the vanilla characters. You still have the same learning curve to get through. The pay-to-win aspect comes in to a minor degree when one Hunter is just a little more proficient to use, which is based more entirely on your skill set and play style. Compare this to how a MOBA introduces new characters.
Evolve's main issue is not with the DLC, although it played a big part in where it finds itself today. What seems to hold this game back the most is the lack of incentivizing content, and I'll elaborate more on what I mean. Evolve gives you three ways to come back and play: Character Mastery, Public Level and Ranked Hunt. These three things are what you do to come back and try to complete the game for. Character Mastery basically means you need to complete three objectives per tier, of which there are also three; once you complete those, you gain access to the Elite skin. Your Public Level is like every other progression system you've seen before; earn experience points by playing the game to level up, whether that be in Solo mode or Multiplayer. Ranked Hunt wasn't added until seven months after release and came along side a huge title update that essentially changed the meta of the game and expanded a little more on the competitive side of things. In Ranked Hunt, you go through ten placement matches before you become ranked in one of three tiers: Bronze, Silver and Gold.
Outside of those three things, there are the modes that provide slight alterations to the normal Hunt mode with the exception of Defend and Arena. Arena being the more popular of the two because it's the deathmatch mode of Evolve. At Stage 2 with full armor and full health, the Monster is considered an even match against the Hunters. Put both sides in a never-ending Arena Dome until one side wins, that's how Arena works. Defend is a fun concept where the Hunters need to defend a fueling station that will allow a large ship to evacuate colonists off the planet.
CONCLUSION: Evolve is worth a second look, do more searching to see what other people have to say about it and get another perspective on it. I didn't lend too much in Evolve's favor in this review but that's because I want people to know that this game it's not what the tabloids and game journalists said it was. It wasn't perfect but it certainly wasn't a bad game, it just never got two feet off the ground and made bad first impressions on a lot of people because of the DLC practices by 2K games and lack of playable content at release. I will not place the blame entirely on Turtle Rock Studios, no one will ever conclusively know what happened in the meetings between 2K and TRS that made them market the game the way they did to us, so until we do know beyond a doubt, I will not be pointing fingers or making disingenuous assertions about the Studio. But with the playerbase dwindling below the 500's I cannot recommend it to anyone thinking about buying it on their own. Perhaps you can make friends and find a squad to play with but if your sole intention is to play Monster, good luck finding a match or making your purchase(s) worth while, because you'll be paying to get more, instead of playing the game as you bought it.

Very nice-looking game.
Unfortunately, this is the only positive moment I found here.
Every time I'm trying to play it, I find myself thinking "in SpaceChem it was better".
Hexagonal field is ok, it requires a significant mindshift, and it's interesting. But everything else...
SpaceChem was a puzzle – the requirement was to assemble complex molecules in very limited space.
Opus Magnum is totally casual – field is endless, so just put more manipulators and other stuff, if you need. Game doesn't make a challenge for you. Seeing other player's incredible super-minimalistic solutions is not a real motivation.
Instead, Opus Magnum introduces own, totally artifical restirctions.
First, shape of molecula matters now: proper bounds between proper atoms are not enough, now you must properly rotate them also. As result, often you have to rebuild your completely working solution because two atoms are connected under wrong angle.
Second – alchemical tools are very inconvenient. Join 3 atoms in a row – so primitive task, but here you'll have to build some crazy machinery around, because atoms can be joined either one by one, or 4 at once but under 120deg angle.
Both of these restrictions are not looking reasonable. They are annoying. Nobody even tries to explain why angles are so important in alchemy world, or why noone invented simple binding glyph for 3 atoms in a row. There is a difference between solving a puzzle and fighting a game inconvenience, and Opus Magnum doesn't understand it, unfortunately.
In SpaceChem you opened new advanced tools with a time (often accordingly to storyline), so it was a sense of progress in the game. You was interested to play further to find more content and much more interesting puzzles.
In Opus Magnum you immediately have access to everything you may ever need – except of a few very very special tools, available only in special levels (I saw 3 of them so far). No progress, nothing new – just again and again build the same overcomplicated machines for primitive tasks. Booooooring.
Finally, in SpaceChem there was a storyline – and gods, it was amazing. I won't even say about unique "boss fight" levels – just story itself. Pieces of exposition, describing locations, characters, situations, feelings and actions – it was like a real book, and I greedily solved puzzles one by one just to read next chapter.
And in Opus Magnum... well... we have that dialogs between levels. That soooooooooo interesting dialogs about love potion for old duke and about exiting of making an super-lightweight alhemist's rope. Dialogs, full of empty meaningless phrases, imitating a real communication. I can't say without swearing how boring and useless that dialogs are. 90% of phrases can be completely removed from the game and nothing will change. It's an epic fail.
As conclusion. I'll repeat myself: SpaceChem was a hard and interesting puzzle game; Opus Magnum is a nice-looking casual time-killer.
I see no reasons to spend money on Opus Magnum – better go play SpaceChem if you didn't.

Opus Magnum is a must-buy for any fan of programming puzzle games and Zachtronics games. If you have tried Zachtronics games like SpaceChem or TIS-100, but found them too difficult to enjoy, I still highly recommend buying this game. This game is so much more accessible than its predecessors and is actually easy to learn while still being very hard to master.
I have played many puzzle games and I could not beat SpaceChem or TIS-100. I was able to get a little over halfway through each game before hitting a wall and giving up. I have not hit a wall in Opus Magnum yet, and have already completed over half of the game. Best of all, I did not need to spend several hours figuring out how to play this game like I did with TIS-100 and Shenzhen I/O.
If you have never played a game in this genre before, then this game is the perfect place to start. The most beginner-friendly games in this genre are Opus Magnum, Prelogate, and Human Resource Machine. HRM is way too short and only the last few levels provide any real challenge, so I don't think it is worth the price. Prelogate is great and reminds me a lot of Zachtronic games. This game still takes the cake, however, as Prelogate is a bit bland and dull when compared to the beauty of Opus Magnum.
If you like puzzle games at all, then you need to buy this game.
If you like top-hats, hierarchy, people named Samuel, and mass death then I think you should check this out.

I recommend this game as another wonderful addition to the Zachtronics puzzler library, but I find myself liking classic Space Chem more than Opus Magnum.
As a SpaceChem veteran I'm a little disappointed by the length of the campaign; finished it in just under 10 hours. As with every zachtronics game there is still a bevy of additional content to tackle after the main campaign, and with user created content you're never really finished.
However the campaign is a lot easier to get through for newcomers to the genre, which I think is a good change compared to the rather difficult space-chem campaign.
I think there could have been more 'mini-challenges' to the campaign where you are limited in one specific way, causing players to brainstorm alternative strategies to do things, instead it seems the campaign is all about making bigger and bigger products, often with smaller and more basic reagents, leading to some painfully long programs, while not particularly complicated.
Management of these really long programs is quite a chore; made a little bit easier if you read the controls for selecting and copying. Sadly there seems no simple way to store a copy in a clipboard, it must be placed somewhere in the instruction set, which can get confusing.
Final Verdict; absolutely worth the value but you may end up liking SpaceChem more.

There was a time, when as a child, I purchased a RPG called Baldur's Gate. As I was absolutely overwhelmed by enjoyment and unknownness, all I wished for was to have a better understanding of the game mechanics to make the best out of my game.
Fast forward 20 years, and I find myself playing Dragon Age Origins, an spiritual successor to Bioware's masterpiece. Yes, the story is amazing. Yes, you will love, hate, laugh at and cry for the characters in your party. Yes, they have been voiced and the soundtrack is high-level. Yes, there are many build-ups for your characters (that now and thanks to guides and faqs I can understand and apply properly) and the combat systema (real time with a pause button) remains untouched. Yes the game is looong (~70hours) if you want to milk out all of its content.
All in all, no western-RPG fan should skip this title. While it's easy to feel overwhelmed at first, the game is so absorbing that you will be into it in no time. This game can look at Baldur's Gate and make it feel proud. Purchase it and you won't regret it.

Before I begin, let me say this:  I understand Stonehearth is in Early Access.  I don't expect everything to work flawlessly. That having been said, the game needs a lot of work.
I picked up Stonehearth based on a lot of Steam user reviews comparing it to Dwarf Fortress.  I like Dwarf Fortress, even though the game is notorious for its extremely obfuscated interface.  Stonehearth sacrifices a lot of DF's detailed simulation for a more accessible experience, which is fine with me.  However, as of March 2016, the current build is badly broken.
A few of the weird AI glitches I've seen include Hearthlings that join the settlement, but idle in one place permanently.  After accepting a new Hearthling (hereafter referred to as "plebs"), I watched her stand on a hill for a week, regardless of any orders I issued.  She was eventually eaten by wolves.  Footmen, Stonehearth's 'soldier' class, will charge after enemies they have no chance of defeating, regardless of their current orders.  When they're reduced to 1/4 health, they flee for a few moments, then turn back and resume fighting.  I've lost at least four Footmen because of this behavior.  Mobs also have a tendency to spawn in weird locations, like at the end of a long tunnel with only one entrance.  I got a notification informing me that one of my plebs was mauled to death by wolves, at the end of a mining tunnel with a closed door at the entrance.  Either something's up with the spawning algorithm, or all dogs don't go to heaven.
I'm saying they're ghost dogs.  Way of the samurai.
The building system is suprisingly robust.  The interface makes it easy to plot foundations, walls, upper floors, and roofs.  I actually designed some pretty handsome structures, and the process was fairly intuitive and straightforward.  However, once I actually placed my blueprint and ordered my plebs to build the structure, I ran into more AI issues.  On two separate occasions, my plebs stopped building before the structure was complete.  They'd build to around 3/4 completion, then idle, as though they had nothing to do.  Reloading the game did nothing.  Suspending all jobs, then re-assigning them did nothing.  I simply had a partially-finished shell of a building in the middle of my settlement.  I tried to remove it, but my plebs demolished about half of the building, then idled again.  My town looks like Detroit in 1996.  Shameful display.
Despite all the AI issues, I still like the game.  The art style is charming, and the UI makes it easy to place buildings and command your plebs.  Once they iron out the issues with plebs abandoning construction halfway through, I think it's going to be a joy to play.  The interface handles walls and roofs very gracefully, and building blueprints for structures is a breeze.  I remember placing roofs in "Towns," a similar town-building game, was a living nightmare.  Most importantly, while scanning the forums for solutions to my AI issues, I saw that the devs were very active, involved with, and respectful to their players.  That's a very good sign.
For the time being, I'm going to recommend this game.  I was excited enough about the premise that I didn't mind the $25 price tag, but if cost is an issue for you, I'd recommend holding off until they get a beta build up and running.  Bottom line:  despite some pretty rampant AI issues, the game shows a lot of promise.  As long as the devs stay active and listen to their player base, I think this is going to mature into a very enjoyable experience.
[UPDATE 3/13/16]  All of my footmen got thwomped by a one-two combo of ghost dogs and giant zombies, so I decided to start a new settlement in sandbox mode.  So far, I've experienced none of the AI glitches I saw in 'normal' mode.  It seems that something about combat, or placing my settlement on defense mode, breaks the AI.  I'm hoping the devs fix this, because I enjoyed the challenge of defending against sporadic attacks from invaders and thieves.  For the time being, however, I'd recommend you play in sandbox mode.

This is not a puzzle game. Puzzles have a single solution that you must ferret out. This game presents problems that need to be solved with creativity and ingenuity. It's basically a visual programming game. It's for those who want a mental challenge and it provides that in spades. After you finish each challenge you're given histograms (histograms! Why don't more games have these? They're so much better at providing performance data than useless leaderboards) of how efficient your solution was compared to other players in how fast it is, how many reactors it uses and how many commands it uses. It's wonderful. Long live the histogram.

Time to do some chemistry!
SpaceChem is a great puzzle-ish game with a gripping storyline. But it's not for the faint-hearted. The first few worlds are absolutely great, fun, and entertaining. After that, things get a lot more difficult. But not difficult in a bad way! It's the kind of challenge that you'll spend a while working on and then jubliantly celebrate your victory, fist-pumping, smiling, doing powerslides... whatever your "thing" is! My point being, this game is really quite rewarding, and you'll feel great when you finally crack whatever problem is troubling you (quite literally in the case of some molecules).
On top of all this, there's an absolutely amazing soundtrack, making this game a great experience for all.

It's like molecular programming.  This is one of the most thoughtful puzzle games I've ever played.  A relaxing soundtrack, streamlined interface and the ability to play windowed are just icing on the cake.  Compete with the community for space or speed efficiency with your builds.

You have various tools at your disposal to combine, split and fuse atoms and molecules.  The solutions vary greatly from task to task and the difficulty ramps up quickly.

==Forewarning: The developers of Dungeon of the Endless have been bought out by SEGA, this means that this game is likely going to see no more support, and no sequel. Keep this in mind when purchasing.==
An interesting mix of RTS and other genres, Dungeon of the Endless is a rewarding, but frustrating experience.
[Summary at bottom.]
You control 1~4 Survivors, from a small unlockable cast, and fight your way up 15 floors of randomly generated layouts. To complete this you can power individual rooms and build modules to harvest resources and fight the hordes of monsters, level up your Survivors to gain static benefits, and scavenge or purchase equipment and research. Each floor is started by your Crystal, which must be defended, and then escorted to the exit, which must be found.
The game is privy to an enormous amount of RNG; the only static things are the characters themselves, the 15 floors, and whatever modifiers you selected (through unlockable escape pods gained through various criteria) when you started this run. Everything else is steeped in uncertainty; from the monsters that will spawn on a given floor and from which unpowered rooms, to where and what kinds of rooms spawn and what lays within, to the presence of item chests and shopkeepers, as well as if and where Research Artifacts appear and what research is randomly avaliable, as well as floor layouts themselves (down to individual room sizes and module slots, and if theyre occupied) and finally the location of the exit of the floor, the goal of any given floor.
Learning to mitigate this RNG is critical to playing the game, moreso than any amount of game knowledge or unlockables can change; though at the end of the day you are completely at the game's mercy for the better part of any run; I've had more than a few runs end on the first floor or drag for floors on end without a single item. The game, in the vein of so many bad roguelikes and -lites, forgets the cardinal rule of random generation and gameplay: The ability to give the player mitigation. Players can only do so much in any given situation; and the game will punish you to a cruel extent if you aren't prepared in the specific way it demands from you.
The game itself is very fun, it has excellent sound design and though the pixelated artstyle isn't for everyone, it's good enough (I'm personally not a fan of the portraits, at all); and the cast and world of the Endless franchise is varied and interesting; some characters even have unique interactions if they survive together.
The gameplay is very hands-off, you only order the opening of doors, interaction of NPCs, and the destined room for a character; in addition to the building mechanic that compliments your Survivors. Combat especially is very non-player driven, there is no way to change the targets that a Survivor will prioritize, you only control their location, equipment, resource-based healing, and their 0~2 Active abilities, which have a lengthy cooldown and can only be used so many times per floor. For the most part, the player is left feeling very helpless as turns play out and choices are made, and hoping that everything just works out.
What makes this lack of control very important, is the degree at which the game punishes you for failure. There is little to no margin for mistakes in Dungeon of the Endless; if you do not immediately react to a situation and are not absolutely spot-on with healing and buildings, you will fail; and the effects of failure range from losing modules in combat, to the deaths of Survivors, to damage to your Crystal (which loses its distinct resource, used for powering rooms). Failure in Dungeon of the Endless comes fast and easily, and you have to be very familiar with the game to know what you can do about it, and any failure at all quickly snowballs into a lost run.
The game is mired in numerous small issues that gradually add up over the course of playing; things like being unable to pick the specific route of a moving survivor, the inability to use Active Abilities if you have more than one Survivor selected, survivors being unable to attack enemies moving between rooms, and the numerous issues in multiplayer (cannot pause, items often go to the wrong inventory, loading the game or changing control of a Survivor resets their 'floors survived' to unlock them, etc) are just a small, but noticable sample of frustrating details; that when added to the random nature of the game can turn a fun experience with friends into a shouting match in seconds.
SUMMARY
Dungeon of the Endless is a fun game, but it certainly isn't for everyone. The mix of genres and mechanics is interesting, but at the end of the day very unrefined and frustrating. The game is heavy on RNG, and doesn't give you many ways to deal with or mitigate it, and very little control in general; but 'most' games can be won. Expect to have a wiki open when new to the game.
If you're interested in the game; do your own research and really make sure it's the kind of game you can get into, otherwise you're going to be bitter about your purchase and everyone you were playing with.

So I picked up this version when it game out (I think on the same day or maybe a few after I finished it the first time) and played it again. The game is fun, challenging, and has a neat storyline. The graphics... it's a love hate situation; The digitally rendered backgrounds are all really amazing. They are beautiful and stunning to look at, especially after you have completely explored a place. The characters on the otherhand, they are so poorly rendered and animated that you can't even tell that they are actually 3D models and not crapily painted pieces. There are loads of places to go in the game, and a hell of a lot of quests in the game to complete (which is really nice that Beamdog added automatic journal noting so you can actually tell what's a quest and what's not). I'd reccommend this game to any rpg fan. I wouldn't reccommend this to everyone though, being that the AD&D ruleset is rather archaic hard to understand and comprehend for newbies.

*This review has been completely re-done to better reflect the reasons why I chose not to recommend this game.
Evolve is a game that saw awful DLC practices and lack of incentivizing PLAYABLE content make quick work of it's playerbase. Don't get me wrong, I supported this game for as long as I could and sunk as many hours as I wanted to into it. But now the time has come to say my piece about it in this review. What is Evolve like now? Is it worth it a second look? If you're new, should you buy it? I'll attempt to tackle these questions here. I hope you enjoy!
Welcome to Evolve, where you're invited to step into the boots of a well-trained Hunter tasked with saving colonies under siege on the planet Shear, or take control of the beastly Monster responsible for the attacks, on the run to survive against the invading Hunters. A lot of what Evolve has to offer is embedded in the idea of this 'Hunt', unfortunately, this is also the most is has to offer. This isn't to say the gameplay doesn't hold itself up, or that the quality of what you paid $60 for is unmatched. The problem arises when you're offered to PAY a lot more than you do to PLAY for. Evolve isn't pay-to-win, at least on the Monster side of things. For the Hunters, the characters you have to pay for are definitely welcome additions to the game and they don't do a whole lot more in terms of an advantage for you and your team to get an 'easy' win over using the vanilla characters. You still have the same learning curve to get through. The pay-to-win aspect comes in to a minor degree when one Hunter is just a little more proficient to use, which is based more entirely on your skill set and play style. Compare this to how a MOBA introduces new characters.
Evolve's main issue is not with the DLC, although it played a big part in where it finds itself today. What seems to hold this game back the most is the lack of incentivizing content, and I'll elaborate more on what I mean. Evolve gives you three ways to come back and play: Character Mastery, Public Level and Ranked Hunt. These three things are what you do to come back and try to complete the game for. Character Mastery basically means you need to complete three objectives per tier, of which there are also three; once you complete those, you gain access to the Elite skin. Your Public Level is like every other progression system you've seen before; earn experience points by playing the game to level up, whether that be in Solo mode or Multiplayer. Ranked Hunt wasn't added until seven months after release and came along side a huge title update that essentially changed the meta of the game and expanded a little more on the competitive side of things. In Ranked Hunt, you go through ten placement matches before you become ranked in one of three tiers: Bronze, Silver and Gold.
Outside of those three things, there are the modes that provide slight alterations to the normal Hunt mode with the exception of Defend and Arena. Arena being the more popular of the two because it's the deathmatch mode of Evolve. At Stage 2 with full armor and full health, the Monster is considered an even match against the Hunters. Put both sides in a never-ending Arena Dome until one side wins, that's how Arena works. Defend is a fun concept where the Hunters need to defend a fueling station that will allow a large ship to evacuate colonists off the planet.
CONCLUSION: Evolve is worth a second look, do more searching to see what other people have to say about it and get another perspective on it. I didn't lend too much in Evolve's favor in this review but that's because I want people to know that this game it's not what the tabloids and game journalists said it was. It wasn't perfect but it certainly wasn't a bad game, it just never got two feet off the ground and made bad first impressions on a lot of people because of the DLC practices by 2K games and lack of playable content at release. I will not place the blame entirely on Turtle Rock Studios, no one will ever conclusively know what happened in the meetings between 2K and TRS that made them market the game the way they did to us, so until we do know beyond a doubt, I will not be pointing fingers or making disingenuous assertions about the Studio. But with the playerbase dwindling below the 500's I cannot recommend it to anyone thinking about buying it on their own. Perhaps you can make friends and find a squad to play with but if your sole intention is to play Monster, good luck finding a match or making your purchase(s) worth while, because you'll be paying to get more, instead of playing the game as you bought it.

Opus Magnum, a puzzle game where your creativity is just as valuable as your ablitity to calculate.
TL;DR: Worth full asking price, Opus Magnum is an amazing title that inspires the engineer, artist and alchemist within us all. 9/10
Prior titles from Zachtronics, such as TIS-100 and Shenzen I/O, were a blast, but through the rigidity that is inherent in the environment of both titles (via the limitations of assembly programming/computer science principles), creativity is sacrificed and you must force yourself to see solutions that are appropriate within the context of the games logical limitation(s).
PROS:
+ This is where Opus Magnum really shines and easily becomes the most accessible title from Zachtronics. You aren't simply given a manual and then 'stuck' within certain low-level logic operations (transistors, logic gates, binary manipulation, registers, etc.) guiding your design decisions.
+ In Opus Magnum, you aren't looking for THEE solution, you are given the freedom to invent ANY solution that assembles the necessary output (product) from the originally provided reagents.
+ Opus Magnum is a beautiful visual representation of algorithms. Algorithm being defined as :  A finite set of unambiguous instructions that, given some set of initial conditions, can be performed in a prescribed sequence to achieve a certain goal and that has a recognizable set of end conditions.
+ The pool of 12 instructions that is utilized when 'programming' life into your various alchemy related mechanisms is elegant and effecient. Not having to actually write these instructions, but merely snap them into the timeline, births the freedom of creativity I was mentioning earlier.
CONS:
- WHY IS THERE NO 'BACK' (<--) BUTTON after automating the system? You have stop, step, and play, but when debugging, a simple back button would work wonders! Especially on longer solutions where your code (instructions) run for a considerable amount of time before reaching the appropriate section you wish to alter.
If you don't pause the cycling of your machine prior to this section of interest, you will have to run it again, from the beginning, and 'catch' the spot you want to edit.

A true headscratcher, from beginning to end, Opus Magnum is a contraption building puzzle like no other I'd seen before. It really made me think, and gave me a strong sense of satisfaction whenever I managed to solve a puzzle efficiently.
In the skin of a recently graduated alchemist from the world's most renowned alchemy college, you must now face the challenges of an alchemist's life outside the university, by assembling different alchemical compounds with your trusty transmutation engine.
What is a transmutation engine, you may ask? Well, it is sort of a meta-contraption of sorts, that gives you a series of parts that you may assemble into an useful machine that creates a desired output of molecules from a given input of atoms. At your disposal, there are several variations arms to grab and move atoms, gliphs to transmute atoms into different forms and join atoms into molecules, rails to move arms around and, of course, the atomic inputs and desirable output tray. The set of parts to use may seem rather small, but they allow for endless possibilities in each of the game's dozens of puzzles, especially considering that you may program the behavior of each individual arm separately through a set of simple instructions.
After you finish solving a puzzle, the game will evaluate the performance of your contraption on three criteria: cost, time taken and size. While it is not strictly necessary to optimize any of these three atributes in order to proceed, if you're like me, you'll keep trying to make the best possible machine before moving on. There is also a pretty interesting minigame called Sigmar's Garden, decidedly simpler than the transmutation engine, that serves as a welcome breather between regular puzzles, allowing you to relax and do something easier for a few minutes.
Other than the puzzles, which are obviously the meat of the game, Opus Magnum also presents a rather interesting story. As the head alchemist of one of the most affluent families in the city, you get to know more about each member's tribulations and problems as you set out to solve them with alchemy, and you befriend the sweet and funny Concordia Lem, that works at the house since she was very young.
To accompany the masterfully crafted puzzle mechanics and the nice storyline, there is an excellent soundtrack that manages to evoke a certain magical feeling without getting in the way of concentration, and satisfying sound effects that are triggered by the transmutation engine's many mechanisms.
The graphics don't disappoint either. From the simple, tiny graphics used in the transmutation engine's atoms and arms, to the character portraits and amazing backgrounds in the "hub screen", everything looks pretty, evoking feelings of a well organized, sumptuous steampunkish society.
This game is, in many different ways, a timesink. It will make you lose hours and hours of sleep trying to get your machines to be slightly better than your previous designs. However, unlike most timesink games out there, it didn't make me feel like I wasted my time when I finally let go of my five hour play sessions. Instead, I felt like it was all worthwhile, like the time I spent in it was more "invested" than "wasted", even though I'm fully aware this is just a game and won't make me rich or anything.

If you play this game long enough, it draws you in. At first it seemed that it would be just another walking simulator with little objective and nice scenery. However, in Act 2, the map actually has objectives to reach in the form of latitude/longitude spots, notes, and campsites. The challenge becomes reaching those spots. The map/compass (a Russian compass!) helps only a little as I struggled to guess where I was on it. The terrain is very unforgiving and made it impossible to walk in just one direction as I kept walking into rocks, water, trees, caves and high rising mountains that the character can't move through. The character has some limitations as well as he/she walks slowly, can’t sustain a run for very long and can’t jump. The character limitations sometimes broke the immersion as it was more frustrating than challenging (I mean -- really -- this character can’t jump over a fallen tree?!). If you fall, you die and have to start back at the last note or campsite.
The voice acting, music, sound effects and scenery is amazing and really did immerse me into the game. I can't emphasize this enough, they really did an excellent job on setting the mood. Sean Bean and his supporting cast is so convincing that I forgot that these were voice actors, the music is hauntingly beautiful and lonely, and the scenery with the accompanying sound effects really made me want to shiver in cold and bundle up in warm clothes.

So, KHOLAT...
You are dumped into this barren, snowy area with nothing but a map with coordinates scribbled on it for guidance. Track down the journal pages at each of the coordinates to advance through the story and track down other hidden pages along the way by finding coordinates scribbled about the place. The game would have taken longer to complete if I wanted to track down all the optional journal entries, but the ones I did find added so little to the game's story that it is not worth it to find them.
There is only one type of enemy which is easily avoided and not very threatening. Although there are some atmospheric parts with funky effects and times where you are being chased, most of the game is just trying to figure out where you are and navigating to the next set of coordinates, as the map does not show your current location.
Unfortunately even Sean Bean's excellent voice acting does not carry the weak plot, which makes no real sense at all.
This game is also incredibly short, as I beat it in 3 hours only. Overall I'm disappointed by this game but it was enjoyable enough in some parts. It is definitely not worth full price in my opinion, so try to buy it on a %50 or more sale if you are still interested in playing it.

Say hello to your brain again.

I eat Rogue like games for breakfast. I loaded this one up and died, died and died again. I was still on the first floor.
39 hours later I am one of 0.7% of people that has completed the Sanitary Pod ship. It can get quite addictive.
ABOUT THE GAME
Your spaceship crashes on a planet and you begin with two characters either chosen or randomised.
Your job is to escape and you do this by managing resources, shopping and building your party.
There is a tower defence element where you build modules that give you extra food, slow down monsters, poison them, heal your party and a hundred other things in between.
Doors. You won't ever look at them in the same way again. Every time you open a door in the dungeon ALL HELL CAN BREAK LOOSE.
CRY HAVOC. MANIC. The game can't respond quick enough to your commands and you ponder afterwards if ever a game needed a telepathic link this is it.
The Sanitary Pod is described as thus: Hard, cannot pause, stronger monsters, more unfavourable events, resources less common, healing much harder.
Ten fails later I can't believe anyone can do it. This time I am halfway through the levels and have a full party. I have concentrated heavily on industry to the detriment of science and food. My party are mostly fighters and none can fix my modules if they have been damaged by monsters. I sacrifice the worst fighter to recruit an engineer type.
The door bell rings and I discover hitting "Escape" does not pause the game. RING RING. CRAP. I run like a maniac to the door and run back. I lost the engineer. Later on in my mad rush to the elevator I forget to move all my party there and lose another character. Two characters left, two floors to go.
I have concentrated heavily on building generators as monsters only spawn in the dark. My party is underlevelled and won't be able to heal much if attacked. On the final floor my rag tag dying of food party need LUCK OF THE DEVIL. Will I ever find the exit before I am overwhelmed. Left or right, North or South.
Hallelujah brother! - I am one of the 0.7%.

Don't think you have seen it all once you complete a dungeon.

I've nominated PZ for 2017's "Labor of Love" award. The dedicated devs at Indie Stone certainly deserve it. I highly recommend PZ for anyone who enjoys challenging, zombie themed, survival games. It's the best of its kind right now, and absolutely has the most replay value.
There are several different cities to explore, and where exactly you choose to "settle" has a dramatic affect on your game experience and your odds of long term survival. Whether you make your way out to a cabin in the woods, a farm on the outskirts, fortify a house in the burbs, try to take an apartment or store front downtown, or build your own campsite or fortress, you'll encounter different benefits and problems with every option, and you will probably want different bases for summer and winter.
Character creation is pretty good, though there's room for improvement. There's an ever growing list of occupations and positive and negative traits so you have plenty of different character builds to play. And while there are both male and female character options, there are only two different skin tones, and the clothing is gendered.
As for gameplay options, there are various levels of difficulty, a sandbox option that lets you tweak all aspects of the game to make your own perfect post-apocalyptic world, different scenarios to test your skills, various multi-player options, loads of excellent mods in the workshop and different levels of beta testing to join.
Project Zomboid is worth every penny.

While it is a puzzle game, it is nothing like the popular puzzle games out now (e.g. bejeweled and its many clones). The game looks like it should appeal to Chemists, but the people that seem to enjoy and do well in this game are typically software/electrical engineers, computer scientists, mathematicians, and the like. The underlying link seems to be an understanding of programing logic to some extent. (I'm sure there are people that play and enjoy the game that haven't had a lick of programming experience, but I haven't seen many.) Indeed, the chemistry mechanic of the game is secondary and extremely questionable in terms of the reality of it.
While I really enjoy this game, there is a *sharp* learning curve. The tutorials can only teach you so much. This again reminds me of computer programing: you can know the basics, but that does not prepare you for the mental exercise of working out a complex challenge. That being said, there are few games that have given me the feeling of accomplishment and pride when I finally work out a solution.

A most brilliant game. It is called "Chem" but you will only learn a little about chemistry from this game. It is essentially a programming game that centers around building automatons (in the game called reactors). You need to design, test and debug sophisticated mechanisms that combine, decompose and move around particles.
It is a puzzle game with open solutions. Before I finished a level I always stopped and examined my plan, wondering if there was a simpler, more efficient and elegant design.

This game is OK, but it isn't worth the asking price for reasons that follow.
The interface is awful.  You're either locked into dragging and dropping MANY small components in tedious fashion or using arbitrary hotkeys strictly designed for right-handed players.  There are manifest ways the task could be presented, such as selecting a track and double-clicking icons to apply them, but Zachtronics took the easiest route to implement instead of the best.  There is textual dialog interspersed between the puzzles, and it's pretty awful.  The user is required to click many times to progress the dialog before being allowed to proceed through the cumbersome menu.  Because the process could be so dramatically streamlined without sacrificing absolutely anything in terms of presentation or gameplay, the effect feels like a great hindrance to the overall flow of the game and highlights just how vapid and childish the story dialog is.
The gameplay is OK, but it's not groundbreaking or revolutionary.  If you've played Infinifactory, Trainyard, or any of the similar games in the genre, you will pretty much understand what the game is, how it works, and what it is going to do to scale difficulty by the time you finish the tutorial.
Because of the very poor interface Opus Magnum presents, I rate it below Infinifactory and Trainyard.  The gameplay isn't superior to either of these titles and the price as of this writing is MUCH higher.  I find the game better than SpaceChem, by a very slight margin, but factoring in the asking price I would only recommend it for purchase over SpaceChem if the price is discounted to the same degree.  It simply isn't, in its current state, worth a price premium over the established titles.

This game offers an addicting balance between moments of pure aggravation and pure joy, where you spend an unordinate amount of time trying to figure out what the hell to do, followed by that crucial inspiration you needed to take the next step in the solution. The best part is that this is, to an extent, as difficult or as easy as you want to make it. The freedom to solve the puzzles in your own way is almost overwhelming at first, but it definitely helps in the more difficult levels, where you might want to just solve them before worrying about being efficient/cheap.
I had never played a Zachtronics game prior to this, but now I am a huge fan!

I'm a huge fan of all Zachtronics games, so this was an instant buy.
It didn't disappoint either, in many ways this is his best game yet. It's still the basic idea of having simple building blocks to produce a machine in the end, it's just more explicitly a machine this time around.
Having an inherently visual language like this makes the game much more approachable than previous games in the series. Optimizing for cycles just has more parts moving at the same time. Optimizing for size just uses a smaller area.

Because Zachtronics games usually require an IQ of over 200 to finish, I thought I had swore off buying any more puzzlers from them. Well, let me tell you that not only did
suck me back in, but it also managed to significantly lower the brain barrier required to participate and compete (and have fun).
There is no limit on the number of pieces you can use, or anything like that. Okay so now everyone can 'finish' the game. But that doesn't sound fun? Well, there are three unwritten goals with each puzzle. The goals are in the form of competitive leaderboards with your Steam friends; you want to aim to make your solution have 1) the smallest area, 2) the least number of cycles, and/or 3) the cheapest part-cost wise. Just finishing it is satisfying BUT the real goal is to make it elegant and competitive.

In retrospect I’m grateful for not having any previous knowledge about the game. Thus I will not spill any beans of importance, but merely convey why I think it’s surprisingly good.
Of late, the making of storytelling first person adventure mysteries has become a staple within the indie community. It’s a great way to tell an interesting and immersive tale, without having to be too technical and it suits even the smallest of teams. Many of them lacking direct interactions, rather using letters or clues left behind, to give you an image that people had been there before you. Almost none of them using cut-scenes or pre rendered animations. They seem to pay a too heavy homage to the “Myst” formula.
At first Maize seem to be like any other of those games. Then slowly: bit by bit the differences start to crawl to the surface. Not taking itself too seriously, with quirky humour and witty dialogue. The game gets more and more bizarre as the time goes by with an ending as grandiose and surprising as you would expect.
I won’t say anything more, I simply will not spoil the fun, now go and have a mystery.

Except for a rhythm mini-game at the end, it's entirely a first-person point and click adventure game. While the game does not struggle to explain or justify itself, the developers know (intend and acknowledge) that things are played a little fast and loose at times. But in a game with sentient corn and an animated Russian teddy bear, this hardly detracts from the experience. The graphics are of high quality and the voice acting is excellent.
The game is clever, but not overly so. Some of the jokes make invoke a smirk or a smile, but I wouldn't say you're likely to approach anything close to laughter. (Maybe I'm just too surly for this kind of game.)
I do have some nitpicks, however:
- There is a significant amount of backtracking, so be prepared to see a lot of the same scenery.
- All of the puzzles are fairly easy, with the exception of that sneaky tape bit.
- I would have liked Vladdy to have a more diverse vocabulary. You can only hear "This stupid thing is so stupid" so many times before it ceases to be amusing.
- For a game about sentient corn, there is surprisingly little sentient corn. The majority of the gameplay consists of you running around silently with the occasional crack from Vladdy. The corn makes brief appearances, except at the end, to push the plot forward at times when the plot really doesn't need any pushing.
I was also a little disappointed in the ending, though you really couldn't have expected it to end any other way.
Overall, I'd recommend this game as a fun little distraction for a couple of hours. It's a very well-polished little adventure, but set your expectations accordingly. This is not, nor was it intended to be, a game with high replay value or something that's going to really stick with you.

Okay, my original version of this review was terribad so I've decided to redo it to do this game justice. First and foremost, this is one of the best games ever made. It has been over 20 years since this game was originally released and it is still every bit as good now as it was back then. Not even Enemy Unknown (Expect a lot of comparisons by the way) can quite match up to how enthralling this game is.
So let's get some problems out of the way first; As much as I wish XCOM: Enemy Unknown would let you have more than a maximum of 6 soldiers in a mission at once, this game goes completely ♥♥♥♥ing overboard with it. At first it's not too bad, letting you initially field 14 soldiers a mission at once. It gives you a generous amount of troops without it being too unwieldy. However late game once you get the final transport you can field 26 soldiers a mission. This not only makes soldiers feel a little too expendable (Which can lead to some pretty hilarious things to happen when your higher ranking officers are in trouble) it also makes some battles incredibly laborious especially when you're unloading your troops from the transport. Then there is the user interface which will be completely baffling for new players. Seriously, it can take a while to actually get used to it. If you can get past it, though, then I guarantee you will fall in love with this game.
Okay now that that is out of the way; The actual strategic battles that take place are perfect. Fully destructable environments combined with every weapon being able to freely target any tile adds countless strategic value and can make or break any situation. Then there is the time units system. As great as the two move system in Enemy Unknown is, it doesn't exactly work as well as the time unit system in UFO Defense. Let me explain: Time units act as a kind of currency given to each unit on the field in order to perform any action be it moving, crouching, shooting, or looting. Oh yeah, that's another thing that's better about this game, you can loot dead enemies as well as fallen XCOM soldiers. This is a really good feature that allows you to have tiny victories by letting you take some alien artifacts or carcasses even when the aliens have almost completely annihilated your forces. Then there is also the game's night missions. Unlike in Enemy Unknown, depending on where the battlefield is taking place, night missions can be legitimately creepy and frustratingly difficult early game. It helps to build this really tense atmosphere that even in late game still retains a little bit of its magic, and it's only amplified if there's a chryssalid lurking around.
Okay now let's move on to the Geoscape... well there is a lot more micro management in this part than both the Battlescape and Enemy Uknown combined. I personally like it; it makes me feel more like I'm running a military base with all the little things that ultimately don't add much value to the overall game, but are pretty nice to have anyway. However I will always always ALWAYS prefer this Geoscape over Enemy Unknown's Geoscape. Why? Because this Geoscape actually let's you be proactive by letting you patrol your interceptors over areas that seem to have a lot of UFO activity instead of that god awful satelite mechanic in Enemy Unkown (which I will explain in more detail why it is bad in my review of Enemy Unknown once I finish the game.) The interceptor battles themselves don't have much more depth in this game, but they go by so fast it's not a glaring issue. Also, deploying your troops to deal with aliens doesn't run as much of a risk of losing a country's support as it does in Enemy Unknown, and as a result makes the aftermath of the council report much less annoying.

This game is unforgiving, because it requires you to solve harder and harder puzzles to unlock the next ones, and doesn't have any sort of 'hint system', nor a way of skipping puzzles.
This game is probably only for niche audiences, namely hardcore puzzle lovers or people who find programming so enjoyable, they'll even do it in their spare time.
This game's story is hard to digest, because it is only available in text form and progresses very slowly as you take more and more time to solve the increasingly difficult puzzles.
But honestly, I just freaking love it. From the fake chemistry of fusing atoms together in strange constellations that would not work in real life, to the story involving otherworldly beings threatening a far future version of an ever expanding human society. And of course, the hardcore puzzles, the programming and even the alchemy references, considering the predecessor to this game. These strengths are more than enough for me to forgive each and every flaw this game ever had.
"From the creator of The Codex of Alchemical Engineering" - 'nuff said

Buy? Likely, it's a periodic elemnts based puzzler. At first glance, it looks like something too daunting and requiring you to go back to grade school scient to understand whats going on, but the use of the periodic table is mostly for the theme amd a bit less scientific mechanics of what atom does what. You need to control the circles called "waldos" to grab and drop elements in a reactor to meet the ouput element requirement. This involves finding a way to path the waldos so they grab atoms, possibly bond them together, and put them in the proper output without having the items collide or break apart due to the instructions you give them. Realistically, it's still a bit complicated and I don't think I have the patience or smarts to finish it, but now that I dabbled with the tutorial and understand the mechanics a bit, I DEFINITELY see a solid puzzler for a gamer who wants to test their brain. I got a little joy and entertainment when I figured out how to use syncing of waldos to make the bonds act as needed. If you're in the mood for a good puzzler, look no further.

Now might be the best time for folks hesitant to try The Long Dark to give it a shot. The game received wide acclaim in Early Access for its brutal survival mechanics, but the complexity of balancing food, water, and heat in a wintery wasteland may have dissuaded some. However, the new "Wintermute" story mode offers a tutorial of sorts to gradually introduce gameplay elements, survival mechanics have been fine-tuned to allow more creativity in combating the cold, and the unique art style looks the best it has ever been.
My personal recommendation for The Long Dark is to anyone who enjoys games that are more about introspective thought and planning. There is nothing fancy in The Long Dark; it's just you against the elements. What it's really about is constantly making choices about your survival. Do I have enough wood to keep a fire going if a blizzard comes? Should I shoot this deer, or save my few bullets for the wolves? Is it worth it for me to scavenge a while longer, or should I head home before it gets dark...and cold? Such elements are pleasing, because when you survive--and the longer you survive--the more it feels like your own accomplishment.
The true beauty of The Long Dark is in its ability to throw you unexpected challenges. You never know when a wolf is in your path, and maybe you risk walking on thin ice to avoid it. You fall in; your clothes are wet, and you're suffering from hypothermia. Your energy is fading fast, and you need to warm up, but you don't carry heavy firewood with you--you'll have to find a tree limb to chop. You finally find some, your energy is drained, and your condition is rapidly deteriorating. You begin to light a fire, and are kicking yourself for deciding not to waste carry-weight on lighter fluid. You begin lighting a fire, and just as it is finally being nursed to life it gets blown out by the wind. You try again...and again..watching your matches dwindle away. Down to four matches. This time you finally get it...you survived! You put down a bedroll by the fire, warming yourself, confident that you have bested the elements. When you wake up, you find yourself in a blizzard with no visibility. You have lost your way, and can only hope to stumble upon a shelter with food, or you'll starve.
The above actually happened to me in a recent game.
Though The Long Dark also has its flaws. There are still bugs, and you may find yourself suffering from fall injuries without having fallen at all. The animation quality has a lot of visible flaws. More concerningly, the NPCs lack much depth or interest, and seem to withhold information purely for the plot convenience of the writers.
But make no mistake: if you can forigve the quirks of The Long Dark, you will be treated to a highly satisfying survival experience that is unlike any other I have played. The environment feels sufficiently threatening without gimmicks like zombies. You'll feel like your plan for surviving is important, and must be executed within a slim margin of error. And you'll feel very satisfied when you've conquered nature and are wearing clothing made from wolf pelts, and wielding the bow you crafted yourself.
