I don't take not recommending this game lightly, as I think this is one of the better survival games made in the last few years. It has a wonderful atmosphere and a unique artstyle that blends perfectly together to draw you into Long Dark's world. It doesn't focus on thousands of different resources and fuels that you have to micromanage. It doesn't have any generic base building mechanics. It feels dangerous, challenging, and rewarding much of the time. I got a solid 20 hours of fun out of the game. Unfortunately by that point it became apparent that the majority of time spent on this game is not spent playing it, but being taken out of the game while you wait for an hourglass to fill up.
I admire the fact that the developer's have stuck to their vision for this game, but too much of their vision has centered on building their world around bizarre and just plain not fun mechanics. I will only mention one, and it is one that prevents me from enjoying the game anymore - the timer/hourglass that you watch fill up for 80% of in game actions. Every time you take one of these actions, you lose control and watch as an hourglass fills up until the action is complete. Game time still passes at varying speed, depending on the action. Collecting more meat makes more in-game time pass, etc.
If you search a container, you wait and watch the hourglass. Skin a beast hide, watch the hourglass. Eat, watch the hourglass. Chop wood, watch the hourglass. Search a container, watch the hourglass. Sleep, watch the hourglass. Start a fire, watch the hourglass. Repair an item, watch the hourglass. This is not fun. There aren't even animations to go with the action, so you are quite stuck with nothing to do. Watching an hourglass fill up is not playing a game. Yet the majority of time you play The Long Dark you will be watching the hourglass.
Literally any other mechanic would have been preferable. Make a minigame for at least some of these actions! In most other survival games on steam, you can set something to craft while you go and do something else - like play the game. Why does the Long Dark not want the player to play it?
Bottom line, the majority of this game is about waiting for the hourglass, not playing it. And that is a damn shame, because there is a great game hidden behind that hourglass that's begging to be played.

Opus Magnum is the magnum opus of Zachntronics.
———
Joke aside, Opus Magnum is for those who enjoys puzzles or programming in general. It is the sort of game that you won’t fail in, but the global leaderboard will make you (likely anyway) go back to your finished contraption to make it faster, smaller and cheaper. It is self-motivating in a way that it doesn’t feel like it is a chore. The gif you can make within the game of your machine in action is very satisfying especially with the art.
A definite must buy!

Disclaimer:
I will be comparing this game to Spacechem for the context of this review as it is the only other Zacktronics game I have played and is the most similar to Opus Magnum. At the time of this review I am on the last puzzle of the third act which I assume is aproximately half way through the campaign mode.
Opus Magnum is a fantastic puzzle games made by the creators of Shenzen I/O, Spacechem, Infinifactory and TIS-100. To me, Opus Magnum it feels like the spiritual successor to Spacechem because of so many shared mechanics and puzzle styles. Fortunately, Opus Magnum seems like a more refined and polished experience compared to it's predecessor. First off the user interface has been significantly improved. Information is much more clearly displayed and player commands can all be easily edited unlike Spacechem where one mistake often meant rearranging half of your solution.
The majority of gameplay changes from Spacechem to Opus Magnum come from different methods of moving different puzzle peices. In Spacechem, atoms were moved along linear paths on a grid that snaked between eachother while bonding, rotating and unbonding before being deposited for collection. In Opus Magnum, diferent reagents are moved across a hex-based grid by mechanical arms, pistons and rails before being deposited for collection. Alongside these new methods of transportation, Opus Magnum throws away Spacechems concept of limited building area in favor of giving the player unlimited space to build in. While this change certainly makes it possible to make cool and crazy contraptions I also think it can make the puzzles in Opus Magnum significantly easier than puzzles in Spacechem. With nothing limiting the size or cost of your solution, you can simply make a super large and expensive machine that solves the puzzle instead of being limited by your availible space like in Spacechem. While limiting building area in Spacechem did make the puzzles harded it also made it so that if you couldnt find a way to fit all the manuvers you needed into the availible space you would be stuck on the level without any wasy to really progress withought finding the intended solution so I understand and appreciate that this change was made. Additionaly, this change makes the game much more accessible to players unfamiliar to Zacktronics games while still allowing veterans to create highly efficient and compact solutions.
Overall, Opus Magnum is probably the most accessible Zacktronics game to date due to its easy-to-learn mechanics, great visuals and excelent puzzle design.

have no idea where to start. I grew up loving wrestling, like all of us I'm sure. My cousin and I played a TON of WWF Royal Rumble and RAW on snes. We had a whiteboard we bought and laminated wrestlers that we moved around to make cards, and show champs etc. It was impressive considering I was like 7. Well some time passed, and in 1996 he graduated from high school and joined the Navy. We stayed in touch, and talked about wrestling a lot. He got stationed in Japan and started telling me about this game called Fire Pro Wrestling. So the legend was growing in my head, and as an idiot kid I wasn't too sure how to find things online yet. I used webcrawler and finally found Gamefaqs. Saw the SNES stuff, and begged my mom to buy it for me. Never happened.
1997 for my birthday, all I wanted was a Japanese Saturn and Six Man Scramble. Well this didn't happen either. So all this time I am still corresponding with my cousin. He's telling me all about 6MS in letters, and I am just beyond jealous. I get Warzone and Nitro, but the itch is there. Revenge, and World Tour are helping ease me out of the wanting Fire Pro so bad.
Fast forward to 1999. I read online, probably Gamefaqs, that a new Fire Pro is coming out for playstation. So I knew my cousin was coming home soon, so I just waited for him to talk to him about it. He comes home and I ask him how I get a jp playstation. He introduces me to modchips, and even shows me the action replay method that some people on his base use. So it's set, I am getting this game no matter what I have to do. I am 12 at this point, and living in the middle of nowhere deep south I score a job that summer on a farm. My mom gave my cousin money for the game when he goes back to Japan, and to just ship it to us whenever it comes out. So I know I have a few months before if shows up. I work my♥♥♥♥♥off all summer to get a Playstation, and I actually had enough saved up by end of July to get the dreamcast at launch. Somewhere end of June I buy my Playstation with Tekken 3, Silent Hill, an Action Replay, and Harvest Moon (and maybe NBA Live 98 for real cheap, can't remember.)
Anyway the game comes somewhere around mid to end July and I have no IDEA what I am doing. I get on gamefaqs, start printing stuff. Reading all of it through, start to kind of understand, but I am still confused. I made some edits, THEY WERE AWFUL, and mostly just played the game. I should go back to that game and try it again.
When D came out, I was older and wiser. Ready to tackle it from every angle. I was a lurker on FPC, never posted until R came out. Followed all the breakthroughs JB was making, and had 6 VMUs and knew what I was doing. I had a blast, introduced my best friend to the series with D. We had been wrestling buddies since 6th grade, and if you remember on the FPC person pack Adam and Lee as The Wacky Deli that's us. And we just went from there. He's the best KOC player I know. He's into the strong style, and I am more into the Dragon Gate lucharesu style. Good friendship, and we still play anytime we get together, which is super hard considering we live in different states.
This continued with Fire Pro R, and with World it is no different.  This is the game I always dreamed of when I was playing 20 years ago.  This is the series I love, but with a family and a full time job it makes playing a little harder.  I play when I can, and I still enjoy every minute of this game. Overall, this game is good. It's not great, but it's not awful either. I'm only giving it a thumbs up because there is no middle rating.
The setting of this game is decent. It's kind of a victorian steampunk-meets magic sort of setting. It's been done before, but Dishonored kind of handles it in a different way than say, Arcanum or something like that does it. There's also a rat plague going on and a mysterious figure named the Outsider who appears to be the source of all the world's magic. So there's definitely alot of interesting nuggets of lore in the game. The problem is that that's all there is, just nuggets. The game focuses mostly on the gameplay insread of the story and setting. I would have liked to see the world and lore be more developed, since the game does have a good foundation upon which to build. The developers claim it's completely immersive which feels like an exxageraton because the world is so poorly developed. I would say it's just, "meh".
Which brings me to the plot. Just like the setting, there's a GREAT foundation for a legendary story. Like I said, there's this crazy rat plague going on, a mysterious and mystical "outsider", etc. But what's such a buzzkill is that these things are SUPER important to the story, but we never really find out much about them. By the end of the game, we don't learn where the rat plague comes from or what's up with the outsider. There's just so many really cool plot threads that get totally shoved to the side and ignored, in favor of a generic assassination/betrayal plot. I really don't understand developers who focus on really mundane plots instead of the real interesting (and more important to the world) stuff. The ending feels like a wasted opportunity to do something really memorable and cool, but I'll probably just forget this one. The ending is really vague and generic, it doesn't feel as if what I have done had any importance. And as far as I can tell, it really doesn't matter what choices you made throughout the game like the developers claim. There's also a really cliche twist in the game which tries to copy Bioshock, but fails to have the same impact because they didn't make you care about the characters.
Which brings me to my next analysis, character progression. This is also heavily inspired by Bioshock as well. It's basically sword in your right hand and magic spell, ranged weapon, or special item in your left hand. Only, this system has even less complexity and customization than Bioshock. For one thing, there are very few spells in the game (about 4 I believe) and each only upgrades once. There are 4 passive improvements as well, each only upgrading once. This system is really shallow and a tad boring. Most of the time you can cruise through this game without much difficulty simply by spamming the teleport spell (which is utterly broken and OP). In fact, I'd say it's the most important ability in this game. Secondly, this game heavily favors combat over stealth. The vast majority of the abilities, upgrades, and items are clearly designed for combat. Grenades, pistols, lethal crossbow bolts, spike traps, spells that kill, sword upgrades, etc. The only two things useful to stealth oriented characters are sleep darts which are very limited, and the teleport spell. The possession spell is designed for stealth but is a bit clumsy to use for various reasons. So pretty much if you're playing a stealth character, upgrading is really boring because there's nothing that can help you.
The next point is gameplay. The gameplay is only mediocre. Stealth is rather boring because as I already mentioned, most of the upgrades and items in the game favor combat. Stealth gameplay basically consists of spamming teleport to move from cover to cover and using sleep darts if you get caught. It's super hard as well because you have a lot less options than in combat. The other flaw is that there is no non-lethal abilities for combat. A shock stick to replace your sword so you can merely knock guys out in combat would be nice. Gas grenades, spells that incapicate but don't kill, etc. The gameplay is divided into two binaries, stealth non-violent, and combat violent. You can use some stealth with a lethal playthrough but it is limited in effectiveness. But like I said, this game clearly favors the combat approach. Which is a shame because it sets up killing as evil and gives you a worse ending, and non-lethal which is good and gives you a happier ending. This is obviously a boring and kindergarten view of morality as well as choice and consequence.
So overall, this game doesn't live up to the claims the devs make. It does everything absolutely mediocre and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ With the game being so short, you would think they could put more effort into it. I can't recomend it for the full price, but it's not an awful way to spend a night if you've got five bucks.

The second screen is the Battlescape. This is where you take the fight to the aliens.
Gameplay here is turn based as you move your troops around the battlefield trying to kill aliens before they shoot your troops in the face with a plasma bolt.
You will shake your fists in anger as your rookie trooper fails to shoot a sectoid that is right in front of him. X-COM UFO Defense. To clear up some easy confusing this about the original X-COM, not X-COM Enemy Unknown that for some bizarre reason is marketed as UFO Defense in the USA.
UFO Defense was a bona fide classic even back when it was released. You play the role as the supreme commander of earth or some such and must build bases, train troops and research technology as you try to stem the tide of invading aliens. Most of the management aspects take place in a pseudo real-time interface where you look down on the Earth and pick where to build what, which soldiers to send where and so forth. Once you've shot down a UFO or simple found one that's already landed however the game switches down to a Turn-Based tactical map where you must find and eliminate every alien you see. Different elevations, as well as the ability to remove cover and peak into buildings by using explosives keep the game challenging.
As you progress through the game a bit of storyline unfolds as the aliens ramp up their invasion of earth and you are through a series of events lead towards the opportunity to stop it once and for all.
UFO Defense is a classic game that should be played by any fans of strategic/tactical games. It might not have held very well with age but it's still one of the best games in it's genre.

Every couple of months I remember that I have this game and reinstall it. I play it for an hour or so and enjoy going through floors, upgrading my heroes along the way and managing resources. Once I get to floor 7 or so, I quickly remember why it was uninstalled. With mounting dificulty and sprawling hallways, this rogue-like quickly becomes a game of chance. Opening the wrong door at the start of a level leaves your party with a useless, dangerous string of rooms that do nothing  but spawn hordes of enemies; the later levels leave too much to sheer chance rather than carefull play. Of course, other games of this style have similar problems, but the limited resources you can obtain and the limited player interaction makes it hard to blame defeat on the skill of the player.
The atmophere and art are excellent, but the game quickly becomes tiresome when you begin to see the dice being rolled against you.

This is one of the most complex games of Solitaire ever invented.
Play involves "drawing a card"- you "open a room", which may have a number of special properties, including suitability for installing resource generators, getting resources for free, etc.
This, in turn, involves drawing further "cards"- whether any monsters spawn from "cards" you have chosen not to "put into your deck" (using Dust to "power them up").
So managing your "deck" is essentially how you play this game; the "heroes", their levels and gear are mere mitigation used to hedge risk.
This sounds OK in theory, but in practice, this game is very poorly balanced, and due to severely penalizing modding (it's literally not allowed to set the difficulty upwards if you mod the game), it's never going to be properly balanced by modders and is therefore chock-full of newbie traps, poorly-designed difficulty curves and bad design decisions, like weapons that don't scale well with monsters, random item drops that don't scale, heroes that are basically just statistical trash, shops that frequently don't sell anything you actually want, regardless of cost, a "wit" system that's supposed to boost production but barely gives enough to be worthwhile with practically all of the heroes with the Operate skill (and items that can give it are worthless, since practically none of the non-Operator heroes have enough "wit" to matter), etc., etc., etc.
Worst feature?  You literally cannot get rid of party members if you want to trade up, short of suiciding them, with potentially disasterous consequences.  You meet a half-dozen other folks, but you cannot have them join you in any way.  It's a game design decision that makes me shake my head; the choice of whether to stretch one's Food to cover more people, but possibly get stretched too thin and die due to having a weak party, would have enriched the game.  But I suspect that the "4 is the limit" aspect was hard-coded into the UI long before "you'll recruit heroes you find randomly"- it feels like it, anyhow.
Basically, this is a messy experimental project where I think the developers lost track of the statistical meaning of their design decisions quite early in the process and, due to their absurd penalty on modding, it's unlikely to ever get polished and fixed by the player community, which is a real shame, because the central idea ("make the world's most complicated Solitaire and make it look like a RTS / Tower Defense game to get gamers to buy it") was very interesting indeed, and in theory, this should be a very good game.
But as it stands, this won't stay on my hard-drive for very long; once I figured out that certain combos of heroes work all right, and realized that runs are essentially pure RNG and involve very little actual skill, beyond managing the "cards" and doing statistical guesswork, and that more than half of the "upgrades" and "defenses" were basically worthless... well, I feel like this was a clever Idea that arrived half-baked, wasn't ever really addressed at a deep level by the developers and can't get fixed by modders, not that it would matter a lot at this late date.
It's too bad, really; this is a game where most of the problems are clearly fixable, but won't ever get fixed.

Now might be the best time for folks hesitant to try The Long Dark to give it a shot. The game received wide acclaim in Early Access for its brutal survival mechanics, but the complexity of balancing food, water, and heat in a wintery wasteland may have dissuaded some. However, the new "Wintermute" story mode offers a tutorial of sorts to gradually introduce gameplay elements, survival mechanics have been fine-tuned to allow more creativity in combating the cold, and the unique art style looks the best it has ever been.
My personal recommendation for The Long Dark is to anyone who enjoys games that are more about introspective thought and planning. There is nothing fancy in The Long Dark; it's just you against the elements. What it's really about is constantly making choices about your survival. Do I have enough wood to keep a fire going if a blizzard comes? Should I shoot this deer, or save my few bullets for the wolves? Is it worth it for me to scavenge a while longer, or should I head home before it gets dark...and cold? Such elements are pleasing, because when you survive--and the longer you survive--the more it feels like your own accomplishment.
The true beauty of The Long Dark is in its ability to throw you unexpected challenges. You never know when a wolf is in your path, and maybe you risk walking on thin ice to avoid it. You fall in; your clothes are wet, and you're suffering from hypothermia. Your energy is fading fast, and you need to warm up, but you don't carry heavy firewood with you--you'll have to find a tree limb to chop. You finally find some, your energy is drained, and your condition is rapidly deteriorating. You begin to light a fire, and are kicking yourself for deciding not to waste carry-weight on lighter fluid. You begin lighting a fire, and just as it is finally being nursed to life it gets blown out by the wind. You try again...and again..watching your matches dwindle away. Down to four matches. This time you finally get it...you survived! You put down a bedroll by the fire, warming yourself, confident that you have bested the elements. When you wake up, you find yourself in a blizzard with no visibility. You have lost your way, and can only hope to stumble upon a shelter with food, or you'll starve.
The above actually happened to me in a recent game.
Though The Long Dark also has its flaws. There are still bugs, and you may find yourself suffering from fall injuries without having fallen at all. The animation quality has a lot of visible flaws. More concerningly, the NPCs lack much depth or interest, and seem to withhold information purely for the plot convenience of the writers.
But make no mistake: if you can forigve the quirks of The Long Dark, you will be treated to a highly satisfying survival experience that is unlike any other I have played. The environment feels sufficiently threatening without gimmicks like zombies. You'll feel like your plan for surviving is important, and must be executed within a slim margin of error. And you'll feel very satisfied when you've conquered nature and are wearing clothing made from wolf pelts, and wielding the bow you crafted yourself.

I don't take not recommending this game lightly, as I think this is one of the better survival games made in the last few years. It has a wonderful atmosphere and a unique artstyle that blends perfectly together to draw you into Long Dark's world. It doesn't focus on thousands of different resources and fuels that you have to micromanage. It doesn't have any generic base building mechanics. It feels dangerous, challenging, and rewarding much of the time. I got a solid 20 hours of fun out of the game. Unfortunately by that point it became apparent that the majority of time spent on this game is not spent playing it, but being taken out of the game while you wait for an hourglass to fill up.
I admire the fact that the developer's have stuck to their vision for this game, but too much of their vision has centered on building their world around bizarre and just plain not fun mechanics. I will only mention one, and it is one that prevents me from enjoying the game anymore - the timer/hourglass that you watch fill up for 80% of in game actions. Every time you take one of these actions, you lose control and watch as an hourglass fills up until the action is complete. Game time still passes at varying speed, depending on the action. Collecting more meat makes more in-game time pass, etc.
If you search a container, you wait and watch the hourglass. Skin a beast hide, watch the hourglass. Eat, watch the hourglass. Chop wood, watch the hourglass. Search a container, watch the hourglass. Sleep, watch the hourglass. Start a fire, watch the hourglass. Repair an item, watch the hourglass. This is not fun. There aren't even animations to go with the action, so you are quite stuck with nothing to do. Watching an hourglass fill up is not playing a game. Yet the majority of time you play The Long Dark you will be watching the hourglass.
Literally any other mechanic would have been preferable. Make a minigame for at least some of these actions! In most other survival games on steam, you can set something to craft while you go and do something else - like play the game. Why does the Long Dark not want the player to play it?
Bottom line, the majority of this game is about waiting for the hourglass, not playing it. And that is a damn shame, because there is a great game hidden behind that hourglass that's begging to be played.

In the post-Christmas Steam Sale, I was down to choosing between two games. I bought Opus Magnum because I figured I don't want to sacrifice all my free time / career / awareness of the outside world to Factorio *just* yet.
I've had this game for less than a day, and I've already logged over 8 hours. Whoops. (Help)
I normally don't go for puzzle games. I can't even think of the last one I played. Strategy, sim are my thing. But this isn't just a puzzle game - it's something else entirely. Absolutely worth the price. You'll get lost in it.

Putting together a working solution is easy. Building an efficient machine that you are entirely happy with is hard. Opus Magnum allows you to choose the difficulty level that suits you. Use player histograms as benchmarks and incrementally optimize your creations until you convince yourself that you are the smartest person on the planet. Or don't. Nobody cares how ****ing smart you are anyway, and you can still finish the game.
Marvel at your own genius. Weep over your own ineptitude. Find equal beauty in both the simple and the complex. Go completely and utterly insane when things that should work don't. Experience braingasms when things that shouldn't work do.
Opus Magnum is one of the best games I've ever played.
